# Sonny V1 Implementation Changelog

Canonical progress/handoff record for Sonny v1 implementation. This file is the source of truth between chats — future implementation chats should read this before trusting memory or assumptions about current state. See `docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md` §21.0A (build sequence) and §24 (future-chat operating procedure, cross-agent review protocol) for the workflow this file supports.

Branch naming: a type prefix and a short kebab-case name, no per-agent prefix. **Five prefixes are in use — `feature/`, `fix/`, `docs/`, `chore/` and `refactor/`.** Counted two ways on 2026-08-30, at `7f67e53` and re-run at `806d00c` when the exclusion below was added, because the two populations are not the same population and the earlier reading of this line did not say which one it had. Over **`main`'s own first-parent merge commits** — 161 of them, every one parsing — the counts are **65 feature, 55 fix, 30 docs, 9 chore and 1 refactor**. **Those five sum to 160 against a denominator of 161, and the missing one is excluded rather than unmatched:** it is `hermes/implementation-plan`, PR #2. The arithmetic is closed by command rather than by hand, in both directions — `git log --first-parent --merges --format=%s main | cut -d/ -f2 | grep -cE '^(feature|fix|docs|chore|refactor)$'` → 160 against `… | wc -l` → 161, and the complement, `… | cut -d/ -f2 | grep -vE '^(feature|fix|docs|chore|refactor)$' | sort | uniq -c` → `1 hermes`, so the one that is not in the five is enumerated and not merely subtracted. **Why `hermes/` is not a sixth convention:** it is the oldest merge on the mainline (2026-07-03) and has been used exactly once in the 161 merges since (`… | grep -c 'hermes'` → 1). **It is not excluded for coming from a personal fork, and that reason would be wrong** — `sauranshbhardwaj/` is this repository's original namespace and carries 116 of the 161 merges (`git log --first-parent --merges --format=%s main | cut -d' ' -f6 | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c` → 116 `sauranshbhardwaj`, 45 `exploringthroughbuilding`), so the namespace separates nothing. The per-prefix histogram is `git log --first-parent --merges --format=%s main | cut -d/ -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`; the anchored form, which reads the whole merge-subject shape instead of trusting field position, is `git log --first-parent --merges --format=%s main | perl -ne 'print "$1\n" if m{^Merge pull request #\d+ from [^/]+/([^/]+)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`, and the two are byte-identical under `diff` over their `uniq -c` listings. Over **merged pull requests**, which is what this line used to count — 162 of them — the same five sum to 160 (`cut -d/ -f1 … | grep -cE …` → 160) and the **two** left over are enumerated the same way (`grep -vE …` → `1 hermes`, `1 revert-118-fix`): that same `hermes/`, and GitHub's own `revert-118-fix/...`, which is generated by the Revert button and chosen by nobody. Command: `gh pr list --state merged --limit 400 --json headRefName --jq '.[].headRefName' | cut -d/ -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`. The two disagree on exactly three branch names and nothing else — `docs/sha-citations-and-the-merge-decision` is on the mainline and not in the PR list, `fix/clarified-command-reaches-the-planner-whole` and its `revert-118-fix/...` are in the PR list and on no first-parent merge commit — which is stated as the diff the commands answer (`comm -23` / `comm -13` over the two sorted lists) rather than explained, because nothing here established *why*. Either population gives the same answer to the question this line is asked: five. Agent identity is tracked per-entry below, not in the branch name. This line named `feature/` alone until SONNY-290 counted the population on 2026-08-26, and said four — with per-prefix counts by then three, fifteen, fourteen and one behind — until SONNY-362 recounted it; `refactor/store-location-is-a-required-parameter` merged as PR #162 on 2026-08-29. `WORKFLOW.md` §2 said the same and is corrected with it.

## Workflow v2 (2026-08-02) — ticket-driven, single-agent

The process moved to `WORKFLOW.md` at the repo root: Claude-only (the Codex/Claude rotation is retired), work decomposed into Plane.so tickets grouped by branch, one CLI session owning one ticket start to finish, closing comments as cross-session context handoff, a fresh-session adversarial review before merge, and explicit parallel-session rules (disjoint tickets only, a worktree per *session* rather than per ticket, a concurrency cap, one live app instance, merge one branch at a time — this summary said "worktree per ticket" and "2–3 session cap" until SONNY-340 corrected both on 2026-08-29; `WORKFLOW.md` step 3 is the live text for each, and it carries the cap's new number, the constraint it now expresses, and the superseded reasoning). Commits/pushes to ticket branches are pre-authorized; merges remain user-only. Everything below this section that describes *process* (checkpoint cadence, cross-agent review, per-checkpoint approval-to-commit) is v1 history kept for the record; everything that describes *rigor* (wireframe fidelity, fix-in-branch, stop-and-report, evidence-not-assertion, hand-tracing during review) carried forward into WORKFLOW.md unchanged.

## Feature Branch Checkpoint Workflow (v1, retired 2026-08-02)

Each roadmap row below is one feature branch, but a feature branch should be implemented as a sequence of small, reviewable checkpoints on that same branch. A checkpoint should map to one migrated capability, subfeature, or similarly coherent leg of the branch.

Checkpoint workflow:

1. Plan the full branch scope before editing.
2. Implement one checkpoint on the feature branch.
3. Run the relevant tests for that checkpoint.
4. Report the diff and test results to the user.
5. Wait for the user's manual review/testing and explicit approval before committing or pushing that checkpoint.
6. Continue on the same feature branch for the next checkpoint.
7. When all checkpoints for the branch are complete, run the full required test pass, fill this changelog entry, append the next-chat kickoff prompt, and send the branch for cross-agent review before merge to `main`.

Do not batch an entire feature branch into one large unreviewed implementation. Do not create extra branches for every checkpoint unless this roadmap is explicitly updated. Never commit, push, merge, or open/modify a PR without explicit user approval.

Notes on sequencing decisions behind this table:

- Branches 1-2 are split (adapter contract alone, then risk/approval on top of it) so each proves one thing in isolation: "existing tools run through adapters without regression," then "risk/approval works on top of adapters."
- Branches 3-6 split the §4A.2-§4A.9 generalization pass into four smaller reviewable branches rather than one large one, per user decision on 2026-07-04.
- Branch 7 (local storage/Keychain hardening) is pulled out as its own branch, done before backend/auth work per §21.0A step 4.
- Branch 8 is scoped to the shared-state shell only (§4A.1) — the full Command Center UI (account/subscription/stats screens) is deferred to branch 13, once billing exists to gate it. A same-day post-completion review found branch 8's built pages fall short of the wireframes in content depth and information architecture (not token-matching, which is accurate), and a founder/designer conversation surfaced two features bigger than UI polish. Resolved in `feature/v1-strategy-replan`'s Phase 4 (2026-07-15): branch 8 is superseded, not reopened — see branches 9 and 10.
- **Branch 9 (`feature/command-center-depth-and-data-model`)** was inserted 2026-07-15 during `feature/v1-strategy-replan`'s Phase 4, replacing branch 8 as the "not started" continuation of that work. Scope: audit branch 8's built pages against `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` for the confirmed content-depth/information-architecture gaps (Insights needs an asymmetric bento grid it doesn't have; Workspaces needs an audit against the confirmed card fields — name, solo/team, task count, apps as an overlapping icon stack), plus task-to-workspace association.

  **Resolved 2026-07-15, during the UI/UX wireframe-fidelity design audit (implementation #3/Prompt B) that also produced this branch's proposed checkpoint sequence below:**

  - **Task-to-workspace association: narrow tagging, not a persistent active-workspace concept.** Only tasks explicitly dispatched via quick-workspace-dispatch, or an explicit "in workspace X" phrase, get tagged with the workspace they ran in — the broader option (a genuine persistent "active workspace" context with real session state and UI, giving every task row a tag) was considered and rejected. Reasoning: a persistent global active-workspace risks silently mis-tagging unrelated one-off tasks — a real correctness problem for a stats feature, where never being silently wrong matters more than full wireframe fidelity — and it introduces shared cross-surface state that could produce surprising behavior once branch 11's floating widget exists (a voice command from the widget silently inheriting whatever workspace was last active in the Command Center). Schema the new `CompletedTaskRecord` workspace field so this doesn't foreclose a persistent-active-workspace option later — don't hard-code narrow-tagging-only into the data model, just don't build the active-workspace UI/session-state now. Direct wireframe evidence for the *rejected* broader option, preserved for context since it's genuinely strong: the Home/Tasks screen (`9-MainAppHomeScreen.svg`) shows a "Personal" scope indicator near the top; the Workspaces screen (`13-MainAppWorkspaces.svg`) shows a green "Active" badge on one card with "Open" vs. "Switch" button semantics on the others — real signal for a Linear-style persistent-workspace-context interaction model, but `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` only ever confirmed the card *fields* (solo/team, task count, icon stack) as real Sonny intent, never this mode-switching mechanic itself, and the correctness/cross-surface risk above outweighs chasing it.
  - **First-run tier-2+ approval moment: polish the approval panel's own first-time framing, plus a light, non-forced version of curating one good example in the empty-state/onboarding — explicitly not a forced onboarding walkthrough.** Verified directly against the current code (`Sources/MacAgent/ContentView.swift:907-932` `ApprovalPanel`, `RiskApprovalCopy` in `Sources/MacAgentCore/RiskApproval.swift`): the approval panel today has zero first-time distinction — it renders identically on a user's 1st and 100th approval, five plain structured lines with no first-time explainer. That gap matters more than which specific task triggers the moment, since most real early tasks already resolve to tier 2 by default under the existing risk model (zip largest files, save routine, create workspace are all tier 2 per branch 2's entry above), so the natural-usage probability of hitting the moment early is already reasonable without engineering the triggering task. A forced onboarding demo step (§17.2) was rejected: onboarding is already dense (what Sonny does, why hosted AI, data handling, permissions, Power Mode, how to stop Sonny, English-only), and a scripted forced walkthrough risks reading as a demo rather than an organic first task — the exact thing this decision was told to avoid.
  - **Data Sent To AI Inspector (§6.13/§14.5): explicitly pulled out of this branch's scope, not given a checkpoint.** Verified directly by grepping `Sources/` for screenshot/OCR/redaction/context-capture patterns and reading `AIUsageRecord` in `Sources/MacAgentCore/TaskUsage.swift` in full: no context-bundle capture exists anywhere in the codebase today. `AIUsageRecord` (`kind`, `model`, `tokenSource`, `tokenCounts`, `audioDurationSeconds`) is pure token/usage metering for the billing meter — it does not capture or persist context sources used, screenshots sent, OCR text sent, files/excerpts sent, or redactions applied, which is what §6.13 actually requires. An earlier pass through this same audit incorrectly assumed the context-bundle capture already existed in the agent loop; it does not — corrected here before it could get treated as given. This feature needs its own real scoping/costing pass, the same rigor the first-run-moment decision above got, not a checkpoint added because it superficially looked unblocked; most of what it would depend on (§6.4/§12 screen capture, OCR, redaction) is itself unbuilt branch-14 (`feature/screen-intelligence`) territory. Revisit sequencing once branch 14 exists to build against.
  - **Routine detail view (System-B-inside-System-A liquid-glass panel, per `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md`'s Routines section) moved into this branch's scope, not branch 10's.** It has no dependency on branch 10's scheduling data model — it can show the routine's existing step list today and gain schedule fields once branch 10 lands later — and it's a pure wireframe-fidelity gap, squarely this branch's actual theme; branch 10 stays focused specifically on the scheduling architecture itself. See branch 11's note below, which now points here rather than claiming branch 11 builds this view.

  **Scope clarification (added 2026-07-16): this branch covers the full wireframe set except the floating widget (branch 11), but "full" excludes wireframe elements tied to interaction models already rejected above or out of v1's actual scope.** Specifically not built here, on purpose, not by omission: Workspaces' "Active" badge and Open-vs-Switch button branching, and Tasks' persistent "Personal" scope indicator — both are wireframe evidence for the persistent active-workspace concept the task-to-workspace-association resolution above explicitly rejected, so building them as shown would misrepresent that decision rather than complete it. Settings' full 4-row wireframe sidebar (Profile/Preferences/Notifications/Security & Access) and a literal Privacy & Permissions page — `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` is explicit that Settings' structure was left open for this phase to *propose*, not a fixed target to match, and CLAUDE.md treats that doc as authoritative over the wireframe where they conflict; only the two confirmed-missing items below are real wireframe gaps for this page. Workspaces' teammate avatar bubbles — implies a real invited-collaborator data model tied to the future Enterprise tier (branch 19), not v1's solo-user case.

  **Workspaces solo/team input mechanism, resolved 2026-07-16 (checkpoint 2):** a one-time post-creation control, not a persistent toggle on the card and not parsing from the creation command. Ruling out creation-command parsing: the planner is the only thing that ever sees raw command text, so any new signal it extracts is a schema change to `OpenAIPlanner.swift`'s prompt/schema/tests — real planner-regression risk this project already treats as high-blast-radius (see branch 1's golden tests on that exact surface), not worth taking for a field `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` itself calls secondary ("team" ties to the future Enterprise tier, explicitly "not v1's primary solo-user case"). Ruling out a hidden schema-only field with no visible control: founder-decisions.md requires the field/UI *pattern* to still exist on the card, which a fully hidden field would not satisfy. A one-time post-creation affordance — not a permanent always-visible toggle — is the middle path: it satisfies the visible-pattern requirement without giving a secondary, no-functional-payoff-yet field a permanent slot competing for attention with the fields that actually matter this v1 (name, task count, app-icon stack). Confirm the actual wireframe's solo/team treatment (static badge vs. any interactive affordance) before implementing, so this doesn't over-build past what the card actually shows.

  **Proposed checkpoint sequence for this branch** (design audit's proposal, not yet started — small reviewable checkpoints per the workflow at the top of this file): (1) Tasks status-grouped sections (Completed/Failed/Canceled, with counts, no schema change needed — `PriorTaskOutcomeStatus` already has the values) plus the status-dot icon shapes (wireframe uses 3 distinct shapes — ring/checkmark/gray-checkmark — current build uses one recolored circle; folded in here since it's the same rows, added 2026-07-16 after cross-checking the full audit findings against this checkpoint list found it had no slot); (2) Workspaces solo/team field (one-time post-creation control, not a persistent card toggle or creation-command parsing — resolved 2026-07-16, see above) + real overlapping app-icon stack (correction, verified 2026-07-16: no bundle→icon resolution exists anywhere in the codebase today — `MacAppService.swift` only has name→bundle-ID resolution via `MacAppCatalog.resolve`, no icon retrieval; this is net-new code layered on top of it, not existing code as originally assumed); (3) Insights asymmetric bento-grid restructure + section headers (layout only); (4) Settings "Display full names" toggle + "My Account" sidebar group header; (5) task-to-workspace association data model per the narrow-tagging resolution above; (6) Insights "Breakdown by Workspace" panel + Workspaces' real task count (replacing the current mislabeled saved-item count) using checkpoint 5's data; (7) routine detail view; (8) first-run moment (approval-panel first-time copy + light curated-example surfacing) per the resolution above.
- **Branch 10 (`feature/routine-scheduling`)** was split out as its own branch rather than folded into branch 9, specifically because it surfaces a real, unresolved tension with Sonny's own existing safety principles — not something found via competitive research, but via cross-referencing Sonny's own docs against each other. A scheduled routine runs unattended, but tier 2+ actions elsewhere in the product require a human present to approve, and Power Mode explicitly forbids unattended sessions.

  **Resolved 2026-07-15, during the same UI/UX wireframe-fidelity design audit (implementation #3/Prompt B):** an explicit per-routine "unattended trust" opt-in, with silent-skip-and-notify as a hard backstop for tier-3+ steps only — tier-3+ never becomes unattended-eligible regardless of the opt-in, no matter what the toggle says. Rejected: tier-gating at save time (block scheduling unless every step is tier 0/1) — too weak to ship as a real feature, since the routine-defining examples people actually want (save routine, create a workspace, the zip-files example) are tier 2 by default per branch 2's entry above; and queue-for-approval-via-notification (pause and notify at the first tier-2+ step, resume on tap) — functionally reduces to "notify me it's ready, I'll finish it myself," undercutting the actual point of scheduling given how common tier-2 steps are.

  **A finding surfaced during the same audit, confirmed directly against the code and load-bearing for why the per-routine opt-in is the right shape rather than a blanket auto-run policy:** running a saved routine is *itself* tier 2 by default, independent of its steps' tiers. `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter.defaultRiskTier` is `.tier2` (`Sources/MacAgentCore/RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter.swift:27`), and `assessRisk(plan:context:)` combines it with the nested plan's tier via `highestTier(metadata.defaultRiskTier, nested.defaultTier)` (line 44) — a floor, not a default that nested tier-0/1 steps can lower. So even a routine composed entirely of tier-0/1 steps still hits tier-2 gating today just from the act of running it. This means the real kickoff question was never only "what happens to tier-2+ *steps*" — it's whether a scheduled trigger gets an explicit, deliberately-designed exception to the outer routine-level tier-2 gate that a manual click keeps. That exception is exactly what the per-routine opt-in is: a routine owner explicitly consents, per-routine, to let that outer gate (and any tier-2 step gates) be bypassed unattended; tier-3+ is carved out as never-bypassable regardless of the toggle.

  **Implementation-level open item, not yet resolved, for whoever actually builds this:** the opt-in needs a new concept in `RiskApprovalPolicy`/`AgentRunner` (a per-routine override), not just UI — read both closely before committing to a specific mechanism, since this audit reasoned from this changelog's own description of the tier model, not a fresh implementation-level read of the current approval-gating code.

  **A related, smaller design question surfaced by the same audit, to resolve alongside the above:** the wireframe (`11-MainAppRoutines.svg`) has no manual "Run" button on any routine row at all — the implied interaction is toggle-to-enable, with the row itself opening the detail view (now branch 9's scope, see above) on click. The current build's "Run" button is an original addition, not wireframe-sourced, and now sits in the visual slot the wireframe reserves for schedule-time + toggle. Not wrong, but should be a deliberate placement call (keep as a quick-action alongside the toggle, or move into the detail view) once this branch's UI checkpoint is scoped, rather than left to persist by default.

  **Note:** the routine detail view (System-B-inside-System-A liquid-glass panel) previously associated with this branch has moved to branch 9 — see branch 9's note above. This branch's UI checkpoint is the cadence-grouped list only (section headers, schedule-time display, enabled/disabled toggle).

  **Proposed checkpoint sequence for this branch** (design audit's proposal, not yet started): (1) schedule data model — cadence, run time, enabled bool, plus the per-routine unattended-trust opt-in field — with migration for existing routines; (2) scheduler/execution-trigger component (does not exist at all today); (3) approval-policy resolution implementing the per-routine opt-in + tier-3+ backstop above; (4) cadence-grouped Routines UI (section headers, schedule display, toggle, plus the Run-button placement decision above).

## Entry Template (v2, 2026-08-02)

Copy this for each completed branch. Fill every field — "none" is a valid answer, a blank field is not. Product context, constraints, and non-negotiables already live permanently in the spec (§1-§26); do not restate them here, only reference section numbers. The one field marked **(required, no blanket claims)** — `Behavior preserved` — exists because a vague answer there is exactly how a later chat regresses something silently, and the two marked **(required, write "none" if true)** are there for the same reason. (This said "the two fields marked (required, no blanket claims)" until SONNY-290; exactly one field carries that marker.) Per-ticket history (what each ticket did, closing comments, blocked findings) lives on the Plane tickets, not here — this entry is the branch-level architectural record. The v1 template's `Implementing agent`/`Reviewing agent` fields and its kickoff-prompt block are retired: session handoff now happens through ticket descriptions and closing comments per `WORKFLOW.md`. **Every figure in the entry carries the SHA it was measured at, and that SHA is the head that merges** (`CLAUDE.md`, Claims and evidence): the entry is written before the PR opens, so when a fix round or a rebase moves the head afterwards, re-measure each figure at the new head or drop it — never carry one forward on the strength of the old head alone. The one thing that lets a figure cross a moved head is `WORKFLOW.md` step 5's tree-identity proof, covering every path that figure depends on: with the proof beside it the figure is a measurement *of* the new head rather than a stale one re-stamped at it. No proof, no carry. Once the entry has merged, `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` exits 0 for every SHA it cites; a SHA that fails that check is a timestamp on a branch, not a tree a reader can fetch.

**Where the entry goes, which the file itself does not make obvious.** New entries go **newest-first, directly under `## Entries`** — never at the end of the file. The order is **merge** order, read off `git log --first-parent --merges main`, not off the `Date:` line: same-day entries cannot be ordered by date, and a pull request that opens early and merges late lands later on the mainline than its number suggests (PR #87 and PR #57 are both that shape). **The file has two eras and the older one runs the other way, which reads as a defect and is not**: everything from PR #50 (`feature/vision-actions`) upward is newest-first, and everything from PR #3 through PR #49 (`feature/vision-foundations`) below it is oldest-first, the two runs meeting exactly at that boundary — so the last entry in the file is PR #49's and belongs there. Moving it would create a defect rather than fix one, which is why this paragraph exists (SONNY-225). **An entry appended at the file's end is the real mistake, and it is a quiet one**: nobody else writes there, so it raises no rebase conflict, and the clean merge is the tell. Five are recorded — PR #98's session and PR #130's review each caught their own and moved it in-branch; PR #93's and PR #106's were moved into merge order by PR #114 (2026-08-24) and PR #89's by SONNY-225 (2026-08-27), each by a later branch, because relocating another lane's record while its branch is open is not that branch's call.

Status: in progress | complete | blocked
Date: YYYY-MM-DD
Tickets: SONNY-<n>, SONNY-<n>, ... (with one-line outcomes)
Reviewed by: fresh session (per WORKFLOW.md step 7) — findings and their resolutions, or "none"

Spec sections covered: (list; flag any left partial and why)
Files changed: (actual list — not "see diff")
Tests: (exact command run, from CLAUDE.md) -> (pass/fail, counts) at <SHA — the head that merges; re-measured if the head moves after this is written>
Mutation plan: mutation/plans/<name>.txt (founder-triggered, not run on this branch)

Behavior added: (one bullet per new capability)
Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims): (one bullet per EXISTING flow this branch touched, confirming it still works — "everything else still works" is not acceptable, name them)

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true): (anything a future chat would get wrong if it only read the spec and not this entry)
Known limitations / deferred scope: (deferrals need the user's explicit decision and a named landing-spot ticket)
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): 

Next branch: feature/<name> (per roadmap above, or state the reordering and why)
``

Behavior added: a paid top-up row stays `granted` whatever settles after it; an `unconfirmed` row still takes the grant that resolves it; **a `declined` row takes a later grant** — the provider's `paid` beats its own earlier decline, and nothing else moves a closed row (the founders' decision of 2026-09-11, the fresh review's F1); **a caller whose settle wrote nothing answers from the row** — `200` with the pack when the row says granted, `402 topup.declined` when it says declined, `502 topup.unconfirmed` only when the row itself is unconfirmed — so the second of two attempts finalizing one order is never told the charge could not be confirmed while the row says the pack was granted (the fresh review's F2, fixed here by the founders' decision rather than deferred).
Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- A settle on a row nobody else touched is never refused: every settle a fresh attempt makes lands on a row that is `attempted`, and the resolution of an outstanding order lands on `attempted` or `unconfirmed` when no other attempt has closed it in between (the sequential half of `topup.db.test.ts`'s SONNY-435 block). **The first version of this line claimed more** — that no path in `attemptTopUp` settles a row the condition refuses — and the fresh review's F3 showed the resolving attempt in the ticket's own scenario is exactly such a path, and that the unit fake it cited took every settle and could not have checked it; the fake enforces the statement's rule now.
- `credit_topup_provider_order_idx` still refuses a second grant for one order (`charges one provider order once`, unchanged); two grants for one order leave one grant at the first settle's instant, and both callers hear granted.
- Every refusal a fresh attempt's own settle writes — `declined`, `unavailable`, `rejected`, `unconfirmed` — still reaches the route with the same code; only a settle that wrote nothing answers from the row.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A state machine's terminal states have to be terminal in the statement, not only in the prose.** 0019's comment splits `outcome` into resolvable and closed and calls the split "the whole recovery"; the settle statement did not know it, so the one writer of the column could move a row from any state to any state and the recovery held only while nothing arrived out of order. The condition is the schema's own table of states written into its one writer. The alternative — a `CHECK` or trigger refusing a transition off a closed outcome — was not taken because it would turn the late settle into a thrown error, and `chargeAndSettle`'s guard turns a thrown settle into `unconfirmed` for the *caller*; with the row now reported back, a refused settle is an answer read off the row rather than a stack trace, which a constraint could not give.

**"Closed in every direction" was one direction too many, and the review found it by running the direction nobody had** (the fresh review's F1; the founders' decision of 2026-09-11). Attempt A's finalize answers `declined` and A settles the row `declined`; attempt B, which had already read the row as outstanding, gets `charged` for the same order; B's `granted` settle matched nothing. The provider says money moved, the row says declined with no amount, the balance shows nothing topped up, and `billing-debts` reports nothing because `declined` is not debt — a charge nobody records, behind an answer B gave as a success. Before this branch the same interleaving ended granted. So a grant lands on a decline — the provider's `paid` beats its own earlier decline — and `granted` stays final; nothing else moves a closed row. Whether Polar produces that sequence has not been observed (a finalize retry after a `402`, or an authentication challenge the customer then completes), and on a money path the row has to say granted whenever the provider says paid.

**A settle that matched nothing was called "pessimistic", and it was the opposite** (F1 and F2). The first version said a refused settle costs one pessimistic answer — the late caller tells its client `unconfirmed` while the row says granted — and deferred fixing it to a comment on a closed ticket, which is the silent backlog `CLAUDE.md`'s fix-in-branch rule names. In the decline-then-grant direction the late answer was `granted` over a row that said declined; and even over a grant, §7.2 defines `topup.unconfirmed` as "money may have moved and nothing was granted for it", which was false of that row. The founders' decision: fix it here. `settle` reports whether it wrote and the row as it stands, and the caller answers from the row when its own write was refused; the store's contract changed, the one fake that implements it enforces the statement's rule, and the contract doc says what a late caller is told.

**A `WHERE` clause held by settles in sequence on one connection is not the ticket's interleaving** (F4). The four tests held the predicate and could not see what the late caller answers, nor whether the condition held under a real row lock. The second block composes `attemptTopUp` with the real store and a provider whose two finalize answers the test releases by hand, asserts the interleaving was built before releasing anything, and reads the caller's answer, the row, the topped-up credits and the debts report together; the same-moment case holds the grant's `UPDATE` open on a second connection and watches the late statement wait on its lock.

**A property about three states needs three tests, and a reviewer's surviving mutant is how the missing one was found.** The first round held `granted` and `declined` and called the condition "closed in every direction"; the review widened the set to include `provider_error` and the file stayed green. Unreachable today — a `provider_error` row carries no order id, so `readOutstandingTopUp` never hands one back — and still a hole in the property as stated, closed with the test and the mutant. The shape to remember: enumerate the states the sentence claims, and hold each one by name.

Known limitations / deferred scope: whether the provider can produce the decline-then-paid sequence for one order has not been observed against real Polar (nobody on this project has run an order against it, per `polar.ts`'s own comment); the code answers it correctly if it can. A grant onto a decline keeps the first settle's `charged_amount` only if the grant carries one, which every `charged` answer does or falls back to the configured price.

For the deletion routes a route's `SET` still governs its own statements in either direction; for these three the fix round makes the smaller of the remainder and the pool's bound govern, by construction rather than by the innermost `SET` — the previous draft of this bullet said "either direction" of these routes too, and that was the defect the fresh review's F1 measured, not a preserved behaviour.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A request-scoped budget, because the stores lease and the handler does not.** The deletion routes' wrapper takes the client the handler leased; these three handlers lease nothing — `EntitlementStore` and `CreditStore` lease internally by construction (SONNY-300's seam, which is why their transactions cannot be merged with anything), and `factsFor` is six statements on one lease. The choices were: a store built per request over one leased client (reshapes every store factory and every fixture that constructs one), a `WithConnection` decorator that starts the row's total at every lease (bounds the consent switch at two totals, thirty seconds wearing §12's fifteen — the "90-second bound wearing §12's number" the wrapper's own header warns against), or a budget the *request* carries that every lease reads. The third changes neither store and no fixture, and `AsyncLocalStorage` is what Node has for exactly this. Its cost is that the budget is invisible in a call signature: a reader of `postgresCreditStore(...)` in `app.ts` sees the bare factory and has to read the decorator to learn the lease is bounded, which is why the decorator's name says so and the comment at the wiring says when.

**Outside a declared budget the decorated lease does nothing, and that was decided rather than defaulted.** The first shape bounded every lease at the row's total when no request had declared one, which quietly *widened* the top-up route's reads and the gate's admit from the pool's ten seconds to fifteen — routes the ticket never named, loosened by a fix for routes it did. Nothing declared, nothing changed; M6 and two tests hold it.

**A budget's remainder is read where the wrapper anchors, or the wait between the two is free time** (PR #235's first review). `withDatabaseDeadline` anchors its deadline at entry; entry is after `withConnection` has waited for a pooled connection; a remainder computed before that wait handed the wrapper a budget the wait had already spent, and the reviewer's probe put numbers on it (1401 ms granted against a 1000 ms budget at a 400 ms wait, at `834a8c75`, a pre-rebase head). The general shape: when a budget crosses a boundary that can block, compute what is left on the far side of it. The pre-lease refusal stays because it is the cheap half — a spent budget should not take a connection to be told no — and the two readings are one line apart with the reason between them.

**Taking a wait out of the arithmetic is not bounding it, and the sentence that claimed both was wrong** (the fresh review's F3). Once the remainder was read after the wait, the wait's time was no longer added on top of the budget — and nothing ended the wait, so a 1000 ms budget was measured answering at 2996 ms behind a three-second holder and at 5003 ms as a `500` when the pool's own five-second connect timeout won. The wait is now raced against what is left of the budget, which is the one race PR #212's F1 does not forbid: that rule is about abandoning work that *holds* a connection, and what is raced here is the wait *for* one, before any work holds it; the callback the pool eventually runs checks whether its caller was already answered and, if so, returns the connection through the lease's own `finally` with nothing issued on it. The pool's own connect timeout inside a budget is the same wait ending for the same reason, so it is answered as the same `504` rather than the root handler's `500` — matched on `pg-pool`'s wording, because the error carries no code, with a real-pool test holding the wording to the library.

**A `SET statement_timeout` replaces the pool's bound; it does not cap it** (the fresh review's F1). The remainder handed to Postgres was the whole budget — fifteen seconds at a handler's first statement — on routes §12's own derivation gives ten, so an eleven-second statement completed inside the budget that was cancelled at ten outside it, and the contract's sentence that the pool bounds every statement these routes issue was false for one round. Each statement now takes the smaller of the remainder and the pool's bound, passed as a ceiling only by this lease so the deletion routes' recorded composition (where the innermost `SET` governs in either direction, on purpose) is untouched. Both directions are held against a real Postgres holding a lock, with the value Postgres was handed read back through the same bounded client rather than inferred from a timing.

**Restoring a hand-applied mutant with `git checkout -- <file>` restores from HEAD, and it took the uncommitted fix with the mutant.** `CLAUDE.md` says this of hand-rolled batteries in as many words, and the fix round did it anyway: M7 was applied over an uncommitted fix, measured, and restored — and the restore deleted the fix. What caught it was `scripts/mutate --check` refusing three mutants at the next commit, because their `from` blocks named the shape the fix has and the tree no longer had it; the fix was re-applied and the unpushed commit amended before anything was pushed. Commit first, then apply a mutant by hand, is the rule; the guard that fired is the reason to keep writing plans whose `from` blocks are the fixed code.

**A server-half mutation plan is new here, and the weekly battery cannot run it as it is.** `scripts/mutate-all` gives every plan one suite command — `MUTATE_TEST_CMD` for the whole run, else the flagged `swift test` — so this plan under the default reports six survivors nothing tested, and a run set to vitest reports every Swift plan the same way. The plan's header carries its exact command; SONNY-455 is the ticket for choosing the command per plan.

**A Postgres fake has to answer the admit hook's rate-limit counter, or every authenticated request is a `429`.** The first run of the route tests answered `limit.rate` on all three: `content.test.ts`'s fake passes an in-memory entitlement store, so its admit never touches the connection, while these tests deliberately build the real store over the fake and the real `admitRequest` increments `sonny.auth_rate_limit` first. One answered row, `count: 1`, and the fake is the gate's twin again.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the budget starts at the handler, so the gate's attribution read and admit before it are on the pool's bound alone, as the deletion routes' budget also is — a budget that started at request arrival is the "at the gate" shape the ticket names, and it is not taken here because it would put one more thing under a `504 provider.timeout` that the gate already answers differently. **The consent switch can answer `504` after its write has committed** (the fresh review's F2): its write and its re-read are two leases and so two transactions, the write autocommits on the first, and a budget that runs out in the re-read or in the wait for its connection answers `504` with the setting on; the Mac's one automatic retry ordinarily converges on the `200`, and a retry that also times out leaves the toggle showing off while the gateway holds consent until the next read. One lease in one transaction would roll the write back with the timeout and touches `CreditStore`'s seam (SONNY-300); recorded on SONNY-434 for the founders rather than taken. **A callback delivered by a connection created inside a budget can see that budget** (F8, recorded on SONNY-434 with the reviewer's D2 reading): every caller of the decorated stores today awaits a promise from a Fastify handler or hook, so "outside a declared deadline nothing changes" holds for today's call sites and not structurally. Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- LF files parse exactly as before (`robotsPolicyPrefersLongestMatchingRuleAndAllowTie`, unchanged and green); an empty line still ends a group; comments, the longest-match rule and the allow tie are untouched.
- The other four `components(separatedBy: .newlines)` sites in the tree were read and left: `CommandCenterView.singleLine`, `AgentActivityPresentation.truncatedCommand` and `ClarifiedCommand`'s fold all drop empty pieces, and `UntrustedContentBoundary.foldingLineBreaks` folds the CRLF gap deliberately (its own comment says so) — none treats an empty element as meaning, so none shares the defect.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**`components(separatedBy: .newlines)` is a split on characters, and CRLF is two of them; `Character.isNewline` is a split on line breaks, and CRLF is one.** The first is right wherever an empty piece is discarded or folded, which is every other site in this tree; it is wrong wherever an empty line carries meaning, which a robots.txt's group boundary does. The general rule for a parser of a line-oriented format from the wild: split on `Character.isNewline` (or on the format's own break rule), never on a character set.

**A fix tested only on the ending that was broken is a fix two wrong splits also pass** (the fresh review's F2). The old parser read a CR-only file correctly and so does the new one, and nothing said so: a split on `"\n"` alone, and a split on `"\n"` or `"\r\n"`, both pass the CRLF test, the mixed test and the empty-line test and both read a CR-only file as one line — the permissive direction this ticket exists to close, on the third ending RFC 9309 §2.2 names. The test now holds all three endings against the LF control, and R3 is the second of those splits, so the property "one element per line whatever the endings" is held rather than stated.

**A manual row whose expected result both builds produce records a pass on either** (the fresh review's F1). The page the row names answers 404 on its own, so the unfixed build fetched it and refused on the status while the fixed build refuses on the robots rule, and "refused, no note written" was true of both; only the sentence differs, and the row now quotes it — the same shape the research rows above it already use.

Known limitations / deferred scope: **the parser's own group rule departs from RFC 9309, and this branch pins it rather than fixes it.** An empty line closes a user-agent group here; the RFC ends a group only at the next user-agent line or the end of the file, so a robots.txt with a blank line inside one agent's block has its later rules dropped, in the permissive direction — the same failure shape as this ticket, on a different trigger. Pre-existing, kept exactly as it was so the CRLF change could be told apart from it, and pinned by `aGenuinelyEmptyLineStillClosesAGroupWhateverTheEndings` so a later fix moves it deliberately. Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A recovery door that only the banner names is a door a task failure hides.** SONNY-239 put the way out on the storage banner, which posts once and can be dismissed; the task failure the same condition produces sits on the surface the user is looking at, with a Retry that cannot help until the file is cleared. Every store loads before it writes, so any task touching a poisoned file lands there. The rule: when a condition has one recovery, every surface that reports the condition names it, from one constant.

**A wrapper that reports a failure by its words hides its type, and a type match cannot see through it** (PR #233's second review). `PlanItemJobError.everyItemUnavailable` carries the first dropped item's *message*, which is the right thing for it to carry — the job's caller wants a sentence — and it means the view model's `if case undecodableLocalData` matched the plain step and missed the job. The fix recognises the sentence as well as the type, from the type's own description rather than a second literal, and refuses to append the way out twice. The general shape: when a condition's recovery is attached by matching the error, enumerate every wrapper that re-throws by message, or match what survives the wrapping.

**A pressed control's catch is a door too, and there were nine of them behind one property** (PR #233's third review). Every one of them wraps a store that loads before it writes, so a Delete on the Memory page against a poisoned file — the very page the way out sends the user to — said the decrypt sentence with no door. The review found them by enumerating all 59 `localizedDescription` sites in `Sources/MacAgent/` (at `215cf190`, a pre-rebase head; the command is on the Tests line) and reading what each wraps, which is the enumerate-before-you-subtract rule applied to a fix: the first three rounds each fixed the door in front of them and claimed the property; the population is what the property is about.

**The block itself was not Sonny's**, and the ticket says so: the founders' snippets file would not decrypt (likeliest test 71's own `echo garbage` step run before its Delete half); the recovery is the Memory row's Delete, which test 71 passed on. The founders owe a rerun of test 19 after it.

**A population sweep that reads one call's shape misses the other channel and the string on the next line** (the fresh review's F1 and F2). Three rounds enumerated `setError(` sites; the doors that report through `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure`, and the one whose string sits on the line after `setError(`, were never in the population, and the review's awk over both calls and both layouts found twelve more, three of them pressed controls and nine of them a task's own bookkeeping. **The bookkeeping ones mattered more than they looked**: `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure` overwrites the notice, and `recordLocalStorageLoadFailure`'s republish guard — right, since a failure that posts every tick is a notification storm — then never puts the banner back, so after one successful task on a Mac with a broken task-history file the only notice left was the decrypt sentence with no door: test 19's symptom, on the notice channel, for a task that succeeded (the review's probe B, now a test). The founders' decision: the ticket's own title covers a task's bookkeeping, so all twelve sites take the helper here rather than on a ticket. The sweep is the entry's population now: `git show <head>:Sources/MacAgent/AgentViewModel.swift | awk` over `setError(` and `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure(` on the same line and the line after, which must answer the clipboard setting alone.

Known limitations / deferred scope: **the widget clips the way out off a prefixed message** (the fresh review's F6, recorded so the founders' pass does not read it as a regression): `WidgetFailurePanel` draws its message with `.lineLimit(2)` in a text column of about 362 pt with Retry, about 398 pt without; measured by the review with TextKit at SF Pro 13 (`WidgetType.caption`), the plain task failure of test 19 (107 characters) takes two lines at every width tried, so its way out shows, while a prefixed message such as "Could not stop watching …: A local data file exists but could not be decrypted or decoded. Open Memory in Command Center to clear it." takes three, and the third line — the way out — is cut on the widget. Command Center's failure text has no line limit and the widget panel carries the whole sentence in its hover help, so the door is reachable; changing the panel (the way out first, or no prefix on the widget) is a design call not taken here. The sweep's remaining site, the clipboard setting's save, writes without loading and cannot throw the decrypt error.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A model-authored refusal is a server-authored sentence with worse review.** `EntitlementCopy`, `SignInCopy` and `SonnyBackendCopy` each record why the app never displays the gateway's `message`: a sentence authored outside this repository and rendered as Sonny's own is a hole in the no-explanatory-copy rule that nobody here reviews. The planner's `unsupported` step description had been passed straight into `errorDescription` since the executor was written, and the model obliged by describing its own tooling. The reason still has a reader — the log — and the fix is the same shape the three copy types already use: a case maps to words this repository owns.

**The larger ask in the founders' note is SONNY-453**, not this branch: weather, calendar and reminders as capabilities, with the permission and provider decisions that are the founders'.

Known limitations / deferred scope: **the unified-log line is unguarded by the suite** (the fresh review's F5): no test reads the unified log, so its `privacy: .private` cannot be checked here and a mutant that drops the `notice` or makes it public survives; the act log is what the suite holds, through `aRefusedPlansReasonReachesTheActLog` and plan mutant U4. **The screen-control session's model also stopped receiving the reason** (F3): `AgentViewModel+VisionSession` returns `.failed(reason: error.localizedDescription)` when the planner refuses an instruction a session handed it, and `VisionSessionRunner` writes that into the vision model's history, so the model now reads "Sonny can't do that yet." where it read the planner's reason — recorded rather than restored, because only the model reads it and less planner text about the user's command now reaches the vision provider; the follow-up already on SONNY-447 covers both readers. The sentence is one sentence for every refused request; a refusal that names what Sonny cannot do ("Sonny can't read calendars yet.") would need a vocabulary of refusals this repository owns, which is a copy decision for the founders. **And a follow-up on a refused task now hands the planner the fixed sentence as the previous outcome, where it used to hand the planner's own reason** (PR #232's first review): `recordPriorTaskContext` records `error.localizedDescription`, so a correction such as "try again with Safari" arrives with "Sonny can't do that yet." rather than the cause. Recorded rather than changed. **The first draft of this sentence said a fix would conflict with the chain's next branch (SONNY-449), and PR #232's second review measured that claim false**: it built the hypothetical edit and ran `git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=9b48eebd <edit> cd829d83` — exit 0, no conflict, both changes present at every site — because SONNY-449's hunks change the `setError` lines several lines above the `summary:` lines (those two SHAs are the pre-rebase heads of this branch and SONNY-449's; the proof is about two hunks in one file, and the rebase changed neither hunk). The deferral stands on scope alone: a change to a branch whose review had closed, with a chain of branches behind it. Carrying the reason into the prior context is a small follow-up on SONNY-447, and the reviewer's merge proof is its evidence that it lands cleanly beside SONNY-449.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- Idle, the resume offer, and the too-old and update-available walls collapse after six seconds exactly as before; a notified outcome never collapses (SONNY-121) and a persistent failure is never cleared (`isCollapsible` and `shouldClearOutcomeOnDismiss` untouched); typing restarts the countdown.
- The zip's Reveal suggestion is still emitted at the same path; `RecentArtifactStore` still records the zip through the preview's writes and now also through the Open suggestion, the same path once.
- The draft, web-research and DOCX adapters' suggestions are untouched.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A result panel that draws its chip off one suggestion kind is only as complete as the adapters that emit it.** `WidgetResultPanel` reads `suggestions.first { $0.kind == .openFile }`; three adapters emitted `.openFile` and the zip emitted Reveal alone, so the one capability the founders' pass reached first had no chip while the checklist's confirmed chip row was about a draft. The rule is on the emitting side: a capability that produces one file emits Open for it, and Reveal beside it. The DOCX converter emits Reveal on a folder, which is not a file to open, and is left as is.

**A collapse timer that also clears is measured against reading, not idleness.** Six seconds is right for a widget nobody is using; a result is being read, and the same timer cleared it. Splitting the figure by state, on a type a test holds, is the least change; the alternatives (hover pauses the countdown; a result with a chip holds until the next command) are recorded on SONNY-446 for the founders.

**A delay read off the state is a delay for a panel that may not be on screen** (the fresh review's F2). `state` answers `.result` whenever `finalSummary` is set, whatever started the run, and `hasVisibleWidgetPanel` draws that result only for a widget-started run — so a Command Center run that finished inside its six seconds left the widget looking idle and holding for twenty. The delay takes `showsPanel` beside the state now; the twenty is for a result the user can see.

**A table tested only at the table is a table the view can stop reading** (the fresh review's F1). `WidgetAutoCollapseDelayTests` held the two figures and five of thirteen states, and nothing read `scheduleAutoDismissIfNeeded`, so the six-second literal could have come back into the view with the suite green — and a state moved into the no-clock group (the version wall, the update prompt, the resume offer) would have held the widget open forever with no test failing, which is exactly what SONNY-210 and SONNY-402 decided against. The view's timer is scanned from its own start, bounded by the scan's `#require`, and every state is pinned; the "cannot disagree" sentence is gone, because two hand-written exhaustive switches are held in agreement by tests, not by the compiler.

Known limitations / deferred scope: twenty seconds is the session's reading of "long enough to act on"; the founders may want another figure or one of the two alternatives. Two older shapes the review recorded and this round leaves: a summary rewritten while the state stays `.result` (`deleteLocalData`'s message) does not restart the countdown, and typing a follow-up over a held outcome and pausing for the full delay collapses the widget without losing the text.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- Hover still works while the panel is not key (`.activeAlways`, unchanged); the two arrival events still reach `onEnter` and `onExit` (`eachOverrideCallsOnlyItsOwnHandler`, unchanged).
- SONNY-179's lost first hover after a collapse under a stationary pointer stays fixed: the slot taken dismisses, dismissal clears the belt, and the next arrival shows (`anArrivalWhoseDepartureWasNeverDeliveredStillShowsTheHint`, unchanged and green, and the new slot-taken test).

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**An `NSViewRepresentable` overlay is a click sink unless it says otherwise.** `.overlay` puts a real `NSView` above the SwiftUI button, and `NSView.hitTest` claims every point in its bounds by default; tracking areas do not go through hit-testing, so hover kept working while every click died. The rule: an overlay that exists only to observe answers `nil` from `hitTest`. **The history this paragraph used to give was wrong twice** (the fresh review's F2): the overlay is not SONNY-177's — `git log -S "struct AlwaysActiveHoverTracker" --format='%h %ad %s' --date=short` → `d349f315 2026-07-23`, the commit that made the widget the sole command surface — and the founders did click the mic afterwards: the SONNY-283 row of the checklist, ticked and confirmed 2026-08-26, reads "the **mic button**, which used to be present and inert here; it should now record", against a `main` whose mic chain was the same one, with no `hitTest` override anywhere. The fresh review's in-process probe on this Mac (macOS 26.6.2) measured the mechanism as it stands: a plain overlay with the default `hitTest` claims the button's centre through its platform host, and this branch's tracker does not. So the click sink holds at this head, and **what changed between 2026-08-26, when a click recorded, and the founders' pass, when it did not, is unknown**; the two candidates, neither measured, are the move to macOS 26.6.2 on 2026-08-31 (`softwareupdate --history`) and the ui-ux-claude mic commits of 2026-09-09, `643848ab` and `01aa3be3`.

**A tracking area re-registered on a layout pass may be a synthetic arrival — a working hypothesis, and two records contradict it** (the fresh review's F1). The comment on the tracker said `.inVisibleRect` needed no re-registration; the code removed and re-added its area on every `updateTrackingAreas` anyway. The reading this branch shipped was that AppKit reports `mouseEntered` for an area added under a pointer already inside it, so the reminder's own expiry — the row leaving, the window shrinking, a layout pass — re-registered the area, re-arrived, re-showed and re-armed, every three seconds. Apple's documentation for `NSTrackingArea.Options.assumeInside` says the opposite of the arrival half: without that option, "the first event is generated when the cursor leaves the tracking area if the cursor is initially inside the area" — an exit when the pointer leaves, not an arrival. And the founders measured this very code on 2026-08-20 (macOS 26.5.2, build 25F84, the SONNY-179 row): the pointer moving slightly inside the mic for ten seconds while the row came and went, and the hint went once and did not come back, so the re-registering area produced no extra `mouseEntered` on that Mac, that build and that gesture. What differs between that measurement and the founders' pass that saw the blink is unmeasured: the same two candidates as above, the macOS 26.6.2 install of 2026-08-31 and the ui-ux-claude mic commits of 2026-09-09. Register once anyway — a re-registration that AppKit may or may not report is one moving part fewer — and the model's belt (an arrival after the expiry with no departure is not a new hover) holds whatever sends the extra arrival; it is what a test can hold, and manual row 2 is the measurement of the outcome. The SONNY-179 row carries a dated note pointing here, because its sentence "every mouse-entered now re-shows the hint" stopped being true after an expiry once the belt landed.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the SONNY-444 cause is a hypothesis with two records against it (above), and the SONNY-443 change since 2026-08-26 is unknown; both name the macOS 26.6.2 install and the 2026-09-09 mic commits as the unmeasured candidates, and the manual rows are the measurement. The hosted hit test asks AppKit's hit-testing, not a synthesised click: the fresh review's probe sent a mouse-down and mouse-up to the never-shown panel and the button's action ran zero times in every setup, with no overlay too, so row 1 is the click's measurement. No row covers keyboard or VoiceOver activation of the mic.

Mutation plan: mutation/plans/fix/the-gate-waits-for-the-check-it-started.txt (founder-triggered, not run on this branch) — seven mutants: the wait dropped, the moment ignored, every refusal treated as curable, the second answer discarded, the order swapped, the wait no longer ending on cancellation, the adapter's cancellation check dropped.

Behavior added: at the screen-control door, a refusal a refresh cures (no claim, an unreadable claim, another session's claim, a lapsed claim) waits once for the refresh `EntitlementService.evaluate` already started and reports the second answer; a stop pressed during that wait ends the run as "Canceled." at once (the fix round); the wait's bound when nobody stops it is the client's — 20 s for a gateway that accepts and hangs, about 100 s across three attempts for the retryable codes with a server-named `Retry-After` of up to 20 s each, plus one 20 s access-token refresh when one falls due (the fix round, F2).
Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- `EntitlementService.evaluate` still never waits: `claimConfirmation()` and `decision(for:)` answer at once, and the readiness row and the Account dialog read exactly what they read before.
- A signed-out Mac, a clock too far off, and a claim that says no are refused at the door at once, with no network round trip (`aRefusalNoRefreshCuresNeverWaits`); the allowance is still never asked for a refused claim (`anUnconfirmableClaimRefusesAtEveryMomentAndSaysWhichNo`, unchanged).
- A step boundary never waits on the network (`aStepBoundaryNeverWaitsForARefresh`); the allowance half of the gate, the top-up and both moments' exhaustion arithmetic are untouched.
- Every sentence is `EntitlementCopy`'s, unchanged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**An answer that never waits is right for a row and wrong for a door.** `EntitlementService` answers from the cache and starts a refresh on its way out, so nothing that reads it blocks on the network — right for the readiness row, the Account dialog and every free capability. The screen-control door is the one reader whose answer is the whole outcome, and for it "refused, refresh started" is a refusal the user meets while the cure is already on the wire; the same press a moment later is admitted, which reads as flakiness. The Account dialog had already met the same shape and reads twice (`refreshSubscription()`); the door now does the same, once, for the refusals a refresh cures, and only at `.sessionStart`. The rule: a never-waits cache is composed with a wait by the caller that needs one, never by the cache.

**The curable set is held by value over `CaseIterable`**, so a new refusal case fails a test until somebody says which side it is on — the same shape as `LocalStore`'s exhaustive switch.

**Recorded, not built**: the step boundary. A lapsed claim mid-session halts the session at the next boundary as before; waiting there would be a mid-session network stall, which the allowance branch of the same gate refuses to be. If the founders want a boundary that waits, it is a separate decision.

**A wait on an unstructured task's value has no cancellation point, and at a door the thing waiting is the run the user is trying to stop** (the fresh review's F1). `awaitPendingRefresh()` was `await refreshTask?.value` on a `Task<Void, Never>`; harmless in the Account dialog, where nothing on screen awaits it, and at the door it meant a stop did nothing until the refresh ended — the client's whole retry budget for a hung gateway — and then the run reported the refusal the cut-short wait produced, "Sonny couldn't check your screen-control allowance." with a Retry, for a user who had pressed stop. Two halves, both needed: the wait now ends on cancellation (`RefreshWait`, one continuation resumed by the refresh or by `withTaskCancellationHandler`'s `onCancel`, whichever first, the refresh itself never cancelled), and the adapter checks cancellation after the door and throws `CancellationError`, so the summary reads "Canceled." — the same check `requestVisionActionApproval` makes after its own await, for the same reason. The composed test holds the gateway's reply until the door has answered and asserts one request on the wire. A wait that ignored the stop does still answer, about 21 s in, once URLSession's idle timeout has failed the held request and the door has re-read and started a second refresh — so the regression is a second request, not a hang, and that is the assertion G6 fails; the claim-order expectation beside it cannot fail in this shape, since the reply is held until the door answers and the 60 s backstop outlasts the 20 s timeout (the delta pass: the first description here said "if the door answers at all the wait ended on the stop", which was the test as it stood at `564922c5`).

**Counts do not hold an order, and the order was the fix** (the fresh review's F3). The scripted confirmer counted asks and waits, and a gate that asked again *and then* waited satisfied every count — with the real service that re-read lands on the same empty store the first read did, which is test 55's refusal back. The swap passed the full suite. The confirmer records one ordered event list now and every test asserts it; a second test composes the real `EntitlementService` with the real gate and nothing cached, and the swap fails it every time (the gateway answers after 0.3 s, a margin the correct code does not need and the mutant cannot survive). This is `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample gotcha: the scripted second answer never passed through the refresh it was meant to follow.

**Sign-out does not clear the cached claim, and every record that said so was wrong** (the fresh review's F4). `SonnyAccountService.signOut` clears the tokens; `EntitlementService.discardLocally()` is called only when a claim belongs to another session (`git grep -n 'discardLocally()' -- Sources` → four lines at `a4b089f7` and at this head: a comment, the two calls in the foreign-claim branches, and the declaration — two call sites, neither of them sign-out). So a same-account sign-out and sign-in leaves the claim in the Keychain and the door answers from it — the first manual row passed on the pre-fix build too, and the second could not reach "no claim cached" the way it was written. The gate's comment, the checklist, the PR body and SONNY-442's Cause section named that mechanism; all four are corrected. What does produce a no-claim read while a refresh is in flight is a Mac with nothing cached, or a sign-in as a different account, whose first reader discards the old claim and starts the refresh. **Reaching the wait itself takes more** (the delta pass, F4): a sign-in and Command Center opening at launch both start the refresh, and a local gateway answers it in one round trip before anyone can type, so the door's first read finds a claim and a build without the fix admits the press too — two of the four new rows passed on either build. The rows that need the wait now pause the local gateway container before the command, one ending the wait by unpausing (the session starts) and one by removing the container (the refusal arrives with the refresh's failure); the different-account sign-in is not used to reach the wait, because against a local gateway it cannot. **What produced test 55's refusal on the founders' Mac is not established**: test 75 (sign out, sign in) sat between 54 and 55 in the pass, and if it signed back in as the same account it cannot have cleared the claim. The fix is right for the class the door now waits on; the founders' own case is recorded as unexplained on SONNY-442 rather than claimed.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the wait's bound when nobody stops it is the client's whole retry budget, not one request's timeout — 20 s for a gateway that accepts and hangs (`SonnyBackendTimeouts.auth`, a transport timeout not retried), about 100 s for `server.error`, `server.unavailable` and `provider.unavailable` (three attempts, a server-named `Retry-After` honoured up to 20 s each), plus one 20 s access-token refresh when one falls due; the door was given no bound of its own because a stop now ends the wait at once and the same budget is what the Account dialog accepts (the fresh review's F2, stated rather than shortened). Sign-out still leaves the cached claim in place, which is the existing design and not this branch's to change. The cause of test 55's refusal on the founders' Mac is not established (F4).

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A summary that counts is a summary that hides its subject, and the preview's details do not reach the result panel.** The paths were there all along, in `ActionPreview.details`, which the approval panel shows and the result panel does not; a tier-0 capability never shows an approval, so nothing the user saw ever named the item. The general shape: what a result *summary* says is the whole of what a user reads for an auto-run capability, and a summary written for a log ("Found N item(s)") reads as evasive on screen.

**The cap on a sentence is in the view, and a sentence written for "one line rather than a page" has to be measured against it** (the fresh review's F1). `WidgetResultPanel` shows three lines of SF Pro 13 in 436 pt; five names in the shape macOS gives screenshots ran to four, and the part that fell off was the count — the one thing a clipped panel must not lose. Cycle 2 had looked for a cap in the storage chain and found none; the cap was in the view. The sentence now opens with the total when there is more than one item, so no clipping reaches it, and adds names only while the whole stays within a character budget that `FinderSelectionSentenceFitsTheWidgetTests` measures with AppKit's own layout at the panel's real width — three Latin name shapes at two, five, seven and fifty items on three lines or fewer, with the pre-fix sentence measuring four as the control that the instrument can count past three. A character budget is a proxy for a width in points, and the entry says so below rather than claiming three lines for every script.

**What the whitelist hands back is not what the user selected** (the fresh review's F2). `validateInsideWhitelist` trims the path and follows symbolic links, correctly, for the check; the sentence took its names from that output, so a link named `Latest report.pdf` read as `q3-final-v7.pdf` and a name with a trailing space lost it — the defect the ticket was filed to remove, one layer down. `FinderSelectedItem` carries both, and the adapter names the selected half and acts on the whitelisted half; the test builds a real link and a real trailing-space file under a temporary root and drives the real resolver.

**The boundary is one past the limit, and a test that pins the limit and the limit plus two leaves it open** (the fresh review's F3). A mutant on the condition alone — naming the sixth item — passed five and seven; six is asserted now, and the condition alone is plan mutant F4.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the character budget holds three lines for the Latin name shapes measured, and wide glyphs (an all-capitals or CJK name) run over a character count sooner than a Latin one, so such a selection may still clip a name — never the count, which leads. A name containing ", " is ambiguous in the list (recorded on SONNY-441 after cycle 2, left as is); a name containing `:` reads with the colon, which Finder displays as `/`. The sentence's order is the order Finder's `selection` reports, which the branch does not show to be the on-screen order.
