Behavior added: `switch to <app>` and `focus <app>` bring a running app forward from the background, and a screen-control session started from the background brings its target forward before the first capture. **Two things this route does that the old call did not, both kept by the founders' decision of 2026-09-11** (the fresh review's F1 and F2): a running app with no window open gets one on a switch — Launch Services sends the app a reopen, which AppKit handles as a Dock click, so `switch to Safari` with every Safari window closed opens a new window, and a minimised window is restored; and an app that quit in the window between the running check and the open is started rather than brought forward, which Sonny now notices and reports in its own sentence, "<app> had quit, so Sonny opened it instead of switching to it.", rather than as "Switched to".
Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- An app that is not running when the switcher checks still fails by name (`No running app matched …`), through the same `noMatchingRunningApp`, and `RunningAppMatcher`'s resolution and the adapter's pin-once rule are untouched (`RunningAppAndRecentArtifactsTests`, `SwitchInWorkspaceRoutingTests` unchanged and green). "Switching launches nothing" is not a blanket claim any more: see Behavior added for the window in which it can, and what is said when it does.
- The vision runner's one activation, at iteration 1 when the target is not frontmost, still throws `targetAppNotRunning` when the app cannot be brought forward; the surrounding loop is untouched.
- `open <app>` and the workspace opener are untouched; they already took this route.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**`NSRunningApplication.activate(options:)` is a call that works only while Sonny is the active app, and Sonny is almost never the active app while a command runs.** Cooperative activation (macOS 14) lets a process activate another only when it is itself active or was yielded to; the widget is a non-activating panel by design, so a command typed there runs with the user's previous app still active and the call answers false. It passed every manual row that happened to run with Command Center in front — which is how the screen-control rows passed while the switch row failed — so a green manual row on this call was a fact about where the founder had clicked last. Launch Services (`NSWorkspace.openApplication(at:configuration:)` with `activates`) has no such rule and is the route `open <app>` always took; both activation sites in the tree now use it, through one helper, so the two cannot disagree again.

**A seam with a real-machine default is a fixture that reaches the machine by saying nothing.** The old class had a bare `init()` and read `NSWorkspace` itself; `VisionTestContext` constructed it in every vision test. The switcher's rewrite has no defaults, `forThisMac()` names the real wiring in words, and the vision fixture is inert. **The hazard is still open one level up, and this branch made it worse** (the fresh review's F3): `AgentActionExecutor.init` and `AgentViewModel.init` both default `runningAppSwitcher` to `forThisMac()`, and 28 test files construct one of them without naming the parameter (`git grep -lE 'AgentActionExecutor\(|AgentViewModel\($' -- Tests` against `git grep -l 'runningAppSwitcher:' -- Tests`, `comm -23`, at `9b98cee1`, minus the one file that names the type only in a string). None of those runs a switch step today, so nothing reaches the machine now; before this branch a stray switch in one of them was refused from the background, and after it the same stray switch would bring a real app forward. Removing the two defaults and handing those fixtures an inert switcher from `MacAgentTestSupport` is SONNY-460, filed by the founders' decision.

**"Switching launches nothing" was a check followed by an act, and the window between them is real** (the fresh review's F1). The running list refreshes only when the main run loop runs in a common mode, an app mid-quit stays listed until it exits, and the open is a separate hop; so an app that quit after the check passes it, and Launch Services, asked to open a bundle with no process behind it, starts one. The old process-bound call could not start anything, so this is a property the route traded away. The founders' decision: record it, and use what Launch Services returns — the completion hands back the app it activated, which either is one of the instances the running list held or is a fresh launch, and the switcher reports a launch as one in Sonny's own sentence rather than as "Switched to". The window itself stays open on this route; a process-bound activation through Accessibility would close it and would tie switching to that grant, which is recorded on SONNY-440 as the alternative not built. The synthesizer's activation does not tell the two apart: a session's frontmost re-check after settling compares only the frontmost bundle identifier, which a relaunched target passes, so that path continues with the relaunched app and reports nothing.

**A process identifier is not an app's identity, and the SDK header says so in as many words** (the delta review's N1; the second round). The fix round told a switch from a launch by comparing the pid Launch Services returned with the pid the switcher had resolved. `NSRunningApplication.h` on `processIdentifier` reads "Do not rely on this for comparing processes. Use `-isEqual:` instead", and "an application's pid may change if it is automatically terminated". Safari opts into automatic termination (`NSSupportsAutomaticTermination` is true in its `Info.plist`), and Safari with every window closed is exactly the row the founders kept — so that row could have read "Safari had quit, so Sonny opened it instead of switching to it." for an app that never quit and did come forward. Two more cases give a different pid without any launch: two instances started from one bundle (`open -n`), where Launch Services prefers to reuse a running instance without saying which; and running-application substitution, on by default, where the resolved copy quits inside the window and Launch Services activates another copy of the same app from a different path. So the comparison is the header's: the app Launch Services returns is `isEqual:` to any instance the running list held for that bundle identifier, read immediately before the open, or it is a launch. The comparison is a function of its own so a test holds it with real objects — a running app reached through two different `NSRunningApplication` objects is one app, an empty list or another app is a launch (the test process itself is no use for that: a bare test helper is not an app Launch Services knows, and its `current` answers pid -1) — and the seam's answer is now the outcome rather than a pid, which is also what removed the duplicated test the delta review found. Unmeasured, and recorded as such: whether an automatically terminated app stays in `runningApplications` — the header's "its pid may change" reads as the same object outliving the termination, which is a reading of the header and not a measurement; the founders' Safari row is the only measurement this will get.

**The alternative recorded, not built.** "switch to Safari" for a Safari that is not running still fails by name, by the tool's own description; offering to open it, or routing to `open_app`, is a design change for the founders (on SONNY-440).

Known limitations / deferred scope: **the fix's premise is unmeasured until the founders' first manual row passes** (the fresh review's F5): the evidence cited was row 21, `open Safari`, which launched an app that was not running, and bringing an already-running app forward from the background is a different operation that no session can measure. `RunningAppActivation.activate(bundleURL:amongHeld:)`, `forThisMac()` and the body of `SystemScreenActionSynthesizer.activateApp` are the AppKit edge and are not under test; the decision above them is. The two initializer defaults above the switcher are SONNY-460. How wide the check-then-act window is on a real Mac is not measured.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Behavior added (the founders' decision of 2026-09-11, recorded on SONNY-439): **clipboard history records on by default from the first launch.** What is recorded at launch is nothing: the pasteboard's contents at the moment Sonny opens are marked as already seen, and every copy made after that while the Settings toggle and the Memory recording policy are on is recorded. A switch going off and on — the Settings toggle, the Memory row's own switch, or the master switch — records nothing that was copied while it was off. A "Don't save this task" run's pause on clipboard history now holds through a Command Center refresh, a Memory delete and the master switch (each driven mid-run by a test, the master switch since the second round); the pause is a run's and never the setting's, so the setting on with nothing running stops nothing; it ends with the run, and the copy made during the pause is dropped rather than recorded late.
Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- The Settings toggle off stops the poll timer and on restarts it, through `applyClipboardHistoryNoticeChoice()` as before; it still writes `noticeDismissed: true`, so the file's shape is unchanged.
- The Memory page's master switch and the clipboard row's own switch still stop the timer rather than only the row (`theMasterSwitchStopsTheClipboardMonitorRatherThanJustTheRowItRenders`, whose two timer assertions the first fix round added — the delta review: this bullet called the test unchanged, and it was not).
- With no suppressed run in flight, the "Don't save this task" setting stops nothing: opening Command Center, or turning the Settings toggle or the master switch on, leaves clipboard history recording and the toggle reading on (`theDontSaveSettingWithNothingRunningDoesNotStopClipboardHistory`, three doors — the second round, after the delta review's F4).
- `ClipboardHistoryMonitor.poll()` still fails closed on an unreadable settings file and still skips concealed and transient pasteboard types.
- A suppressed run still pauses the monitor at its start and `finishRecordingPolicyIfSettled` still resynchronises before it restarts it; the settle test counts the start door's second resynchronise, and the pause now holds through the doors that used to undo it.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A consent flag outlived the only surface that could set it, and the toggle that replaced the surface reported the flag's default as the truth.** The gate was `noticeDismissed && isEnabled`; the notice went with the menu-bar popover; the toggle that replaced it shows `isEnabled` (default on) and writes both fields only when touched. So the product said on and did nothing until the first touch. The general shape: when a surface is replaced, every flag the old surface wrote has to be re-asked "who sets this now" — a flag with no writer that still gates is a switch that reads one way and acts the other. The founders' test sheet caught it only because one row (18) ran before the toggle was touched and another (73) after.

**The reading chosen, and the one not chosen.** Consent stays on the two switches that exist (Settings' toggle, Memory's recording policy) and recording follows them; the alternative was to make a fresh install's toggle read off until turned on, which would have contradicted the founders' own rows (18 expects capture out of the box; 73 turns it off then on). Recorded on SONNY-439.

**Recording from the first launch, and what "from launch" records** (the fresh review's F1; founder decision 2026-09-11). The first version of this branch started the poll at launch and the first tick saved whatever was already on the clipboard, before any surface had told the user clipboard history exists; the entry said "Behavior added: none" over it. The founders decided the default stays on and named what launch records: nothing that was there already. `ClipboardHistoryMonitor.lastChangeCount` starts `nil`, so the first poll of a process treated the current pasteboard as new; the start door now resynchronises before its first poll, and the fresh-install test stages a copy before the first start and asserts it is not recorded, then one after and asserts it is.

**A stop leaves the change count behind, so every restart's first poll recorded the off period** (the fresh review's F3). The suppressed run's resume had resynchronised for exactly this reason since SONNY-120, and the three switches' restarts had not: measured through all three doors, a copy made while a switch was off appeared the moment it went back on. The founders' decision was to build the resynchronise into every off-to-on path rather than ticket it, and one line at the one place a stopped monitor starts is that: the start door marks the pasteboard as seen before it polls, whatever brought it there. The tests drive each door and assert both halves — the off-period copy dropped, the next copy recorded — because "nothing was recorded" alone is equally true of a switch that never came back on.

**The start door asks the run's recording policy, because every other door reaches it mid-run** (the fresh review's F4) — **and it asks whether a run is in flight, because the policy alone is a setting the widget sets before anything is sent** (the delta review's F4; the second round). The first guard read `taskRecordingPolicy.suppressesTraces` and nothing else. The "Don't save this task" button renders only while no task is in flight and sets the policy then, and nothing watches the property; so with the setting on and nothing running, Command Center opening, the Settings toggle, the master switch, the Memory row's switch or a Memory delete each reached the start door, stopped monitoring and returned, and nothing restarted it — clearing the chip does not, and an ordinary run's end returns before its refresh because the policy is already `.record` — while the Settings toggle and the Memory row read on the whole time. The reviewer measured all three doors with a probe: monitoring off after the door, still off after the setting was cleared, still off after an ordinary run, toggle on. The guard now reads `taskRecordingPolicy.suppressesTraces && isTaskInFlight`, the widget's own in-flight predicate, so a parked question or approval counts as the run it is and a setting with no run behind it counts for nothing; the founders' decision as SONNY-439 records it is about a run, and the guard now says so. Gate on the state a decision names, not on the setting that usually accompanies it. A "Don't save this task" run stops monitoring when it starts, and Command Center's `.onAppear`, a Memory delete's refresh and the master switch all reach `startClipboardHistoryMonitoring` while that run is parked at its question; before this round each re-armed the poll and the next tick recorded what the user copied during the pause — on a fresh install, which this branch had newly exposed, and with the dismissed flag on file alike. One guard at the start door covers every caller, the way the Memory policy's guard beside it already did; `finishRecordingPolicyIfSettled` puts the policy back before it refreshes, so the resume is untouched. The test drives both doors on both files and asserts the timer stays unarmed, the policy stays, nothing is recorded, and the run's end resumes monitoring with the pause's copy dropped.

**A figure carried by argument was wrong, and the sentence beside it said every figure was re-measured** (the fresh review's F2). The C1 kill count was measured before the first fix round, which touched the killing test, and carried on the ground that the fix round did not touch the gate — but a mutant figure measures the tests as much as the gate, and at the merging tree C1 died on three assertions, not two. Every mutant figure in the Tests line is now measured at the head it names; a carry needs a tree-identity proof for `Tests` as well as `Sources`, and there was none.

**A "nothing was recorded" assertion cannot see a gate that a second gate downstream also enforces** (PR #226's second review). `poll()` re-reads the switch; so does the view model; a mutant that dropped the view model's read left the observable outcome unchanged and the test green, while the plan claimed that test as its killer. The measurement that catches this is not a battery — a survivor at least says so — but a reviewer asking which assertion reaches the mutated line. The rule: when a property is enforced twice, the test of the outer gate asserts the outer gate's own output (here, whether the timer is armed), not the shared outcome.

Known limitations / deferred scope: a copy made while clipboard history is off — a switch off, a suppressed run's pause, the second between a Memory delete and its restart — is never recorded, by the founders' decision; the timer assertions are what hold C1 and C3 now, since the resynchronise makes a wrongly armed start's first poll record nothing either way. Safe mode neither asks about clipboard recording nor pauses it, before or after this branch (the fresh review, recorded not filed).

### Branch: ui-ux-claude
Status: complete on the branch (PR #224, draft); not merged, by the founder's instruction that nothing on it reaches `main` without them
Date: 2026-09-08 (phase 1 in the morning; phases 2 to 6 the same day under the founder's free hand over the whole frontend, recorded phase by phase in `docs/ui-ux-claude-worklog.md`)
Tickets: none claimed (a founder-directed UI/UX pass run outside the ticket queue; SONNY-109 is the sitting it feeds, and the founder questions below belong on it)
Reviewed by: **adversarial review workflow over the merged tree at `3f615ef1`, six reviewers (one per surface plus a rules-and-tests reviewer) with every finding attacked by an independent skeptic before it counted: 27 findings, 26 confirmed, 1 refuted.** Two high: **F1**, the task detail sheet had moved from `TaskDetailPresentation.sheetHeight`'s measured height to a fixed 520, leaving the common receipt as blank canvas above its footer and that machinery dead in production while still tested; **F2**, the Ask Sonny action on ⌘N was an undocumented addition against the branch's own "entry points do not change" line. Twelve medium: the wider sheet's characters-per-line constant stale at 54; the workspace breakdown's fixed 120pt name column starving its bar in the bento's half-width cell at the window minimum; the scope-entry Remove demoted from red with no stated reason; an em dash in the Settings notifications placeholder; the widget's clarification Cancel with no Escape while every sibling had one; the mic's VoiceOver value reading two states where the glyph reads four; three composer chip clear buttons at a 10pt glyph's hit size; the routine detail's monthly clamping note removed without a record; step rows truncating with no tooltip; Sign out in the danger tone (found twice, by two reviewers). Twelve low: two spacing literals, a stale 189.6pt figure in a comment, an em dash in the screen-access subtitle (found twice), `WidgetType.icon` silently absorbing two 11pt glyphs, the theme picker's shorter accessibility label, "Save changes" collapsed into "Save schedule", the screen-access three-button row with no wrap at the narrower sheet, workspace cards' adaptive minimum needing a manual look at 900x620, the workspace-breakdown name truncating with no tooltip, and the removed relaunch-timing clauses. **The refuted one** claimed three hard-coded 32/28pt icon-tile frames exactly equalled unused metric tokens; the skeptic found the sizes are the brief's own numbers and no metric token holds them. **Resolution: every code finding fixed in `b2ec4e3b` except two left deliberately** — the chip clear buttons take the 18pt chip height as their target rather than 28 (the chip row is 18pt, so 28 would resize the composer), and the screen-access button row stays a plain `HStack` because its three buttons measure about 406pt in a 496pt row; **and every decision finding recorded** in `docs/sonny-ui-modernization-2026-09-08.md` (Ask Sonny as a flagged addition, tones by consequence, the founder-approved em dash kept, the removed scheduler sentences as a founder question).

**Phases 2 to 6, after the founder's answers (the diary is `docs/ui-ux-claude-worklog.md`; the decisions are 9 to 12 in `docs/sonny-ui-modernization-2026-09-08.md`).** Phase 2: every `SonnyTheme` token gained a light reading and `SonnyAppearanceModel` made Dark, Light and System real, the widget pinned dark. Phase 3: the account menu became Account, Settings (⌘,), Keyboard shortcuts (⌘/) and About Sonny, the Profile placeholder and the disabled Get help and Learn more rows went, the app menu gained Settings… through `CommandCenterCommands`, and Settings › Notifications (six per-kind switches honoured by a guard in the notification service) and Settings › Usage (plan, screen control, last top-up, the task's usage) replaced their placeholders. Phase 4: the menu-bar item shows Sonny's state through `StatusItemPresentation`. Phase 5: a ⌘K jump-to palette over pages, routines, workspaces and tasks, a sidebar that collapses on ⌘⌥S, Insights rows that open their task or workspace, the window's duplicate title hidden. Phase 6: a second adversarial review over phases 2 to 5 (six reviewers, skeptic-verified: 20 findings, 17 confirmed, 3 refuted, one verifier lost to a schema retry cap) and its fix round, `d2a8d78f`: the Usage page fetches what it shows, Insights rows are buttons only when they lead somewhere, a Window menu makes the shortcuts sheet's ⌘W true, and a dozen consistency items. Phase 7: `CollectionEmptyState` takes an optional action, and the Tasks, Routines and Workspaces empty states offer the page's own first action (`31ddef2f`). Phase 8: decision 13's claim that every remaining em dash sat in a test-pinned sentence was re-measured and found wrong for four, which took a period, a colon or a comma at `1c8540d8`; the branch's two value types went under a mutation battery by property, after a hand-trace of the plan added the two assertions the suites did not hold (`813a8089`). Phase 9: the menu-bar dropdown's first item is named as the sidebar names the same action, "Ask Sonny", and gains Settings…; the app menu gains About Sonny (through `CommandCenterCommands.aboutRequests`, the Settings door's twin) and the standard Hide Sonny, Hide Others and Show All (`9a1fa578`; the windows-menu installation moved out of the builder at `d525cf58` after the first full suite trapped on it, recorded under pitfalls below). Phase 10: a Help menu whose one item is the Keyboard shortcuts sheet on ⌘/, installed as `NSApp.helpMenu` so the system's search field covers every menu item, and `applicationShouldHandleReopen` showing Command Center when the app is opened again while it runs and the window is not on screen (`d9adc3fa`). Phase 11, the founders' first round after running the branch (2026-09-09; decisions 15 to 18): a countdown of the recording cap in the widget that stops the recording itself at 0:00 (`643848ab`), the Tasks page as a list beside a detail pane with a redesigned receipt, Run again, Edit and run and Follow up on every row and a new `editTaskAndRunAgain` door (`b9371e58`), secondary and destructive actions on workspace cards and memory rows moved into `SonnyOverflowMenu` (`ccfe63cc`, `a8471381`), and an information-density preference with a three-stop slider (`379808de`, run after the other three merged at `2a7fda0a`); then a third adversarial review (five reviewers, skeptic-verified: 21 findings, 20 confirmed, 1 refuted) and its fix round `01aa3be3`, plus one test the battery's design found missing (`edaa0cd3`). Phase 12, the founders' second round after running phase 11 (2026-09-09; decisions 19 to 23), four lanes in parallel from `ee88c3e4`: the Tasks pane only while a task is chosen, with a close control, and a page size for the list (`021df3d6`); the Insights bento's second row top-aligned and height-matched and the chart's hover count in a pill above the bar (`0e5dc010`); the memory row's menu last with View inside it and the workspace card's Open moved into its menu (`64baf46a`); Compact removed from density, the control a two-way segmented picker (`34f1512c`); then a fourth adversarial review (five reviewers, skeptic-verified) and its fix round `5ac01639`; and, after the founder ran it, the task receipt's layout reworked so the pane gets the width it needs (`46672792` and the review's fix round `0307de0d`). Phase 13, the founders' third round (2026-09-10; decisions 24 and 25), two lanes from `7d9aca1f`: the sidebar collapsed by default with its one toggle at the top, worded Open and Close sidebar; and the list column beside the receipt reworked, the workspace joining the row's second line and the toolbar dropping the search field to its own row when narrow; then a fifth adversarial review (three reviewers, skeptic-verified) and the review's fix round `300f33cf`. Phase 14, the founders' fourth round (2026-09-10; decisions 26 to 28), three lanes from `561e17fe`: two-line task rows on their own `twoLineRowHeight` and the Show picker with its margin; the hover fill given air on every row that lacked it; the window's default raised to 1280×840 under a new autosave name; and key-cap hints on the sidebar while ⌘ is held, through a local event monitor and a small model; then a sixth adversarial review (three reviewers, skeptic-verified) and the review's fix round `d7907310`. Phase 15, the founders' fifth round (2026-09-10; decision 29), one commit: with a task open the list is 60% of the panel and the receipt 40%, a share measured off the panel in place of the draggable split and its five width tokens; then a seventh adversarial review (two reviewers, skeptic-verified) and the review's fix round `0a6eab1e`.

Behavior added, phase 1: none by design. What a user can newly do is reach existing things faster: ⌘N raises the widget from Command Center (the same `widgetPresentationRequest` the menu-bar item and the hotkey raise), ⌘1–⌘5 switch pages, ⌘F focuses the task search and Escape clears it, Return and Escape answer every two-choice widget panel through the closures the buttons already called.
Behavior added, phases 2 to 6, all frontend and all under the founder's free hand: an interface-theme preference (Dark, Light, System) that sets the application's appearance; six notification preferences that gate the six notification kinds before they post; a Usage page that reads the subscription and the allowance and refreshes both on appear; ⌘, and Settings… in the app menu; ⌘/ and a Keyboard shortcuts sheet; About Sonny; a ⌘K palette that navigates through existing doors only (`select`, `requestTaskDetail`, and two new `CommandCenterCommands` requests the Routines and Workspaces pages consume); a collapsible sidebar on ⌘⌥S; a Window menu with Minimize and Close; a menu-bar glyph that follows `isRunning`, `approvalRequest` and `errorMessage`; Insights rows that open a task's receipt or a workspace's detail through those same doors. No task can be started or altered from any of these that could not be before. Phase 7's empty-state actions reach the same doors: Tasks' "Ask Sonny" raises `widgetPresentationRequest`, Routines' "New routine" and Workspaces' "Create workspace" call the pages' own toolbar actions. Phase 9's menu items reach the same doors again: the status menu's Ask Sonny and Settings… call `requestWidgetPresentation` and `openSettings`, About Sonny opens the sheet the account menu opens, and the Hide items are AppKit's own. Phase 10's Help item opens the sheet the account menu opens, from anywhere in the app, and reopening the app while it runs shows the one window it has when that window is not on screen; the widget's panel is not counted, and a visible window is left alone. Phase 11 adds behaviour by the founders' ask, each through an existing door where one existed: the widget stops a recording itself three seconds under the cap through the same `stopVoiceRecordingAndTranscribe` the mic's Stop and the hotkey release call; the Tasks page selects a task into its pane where it used to present a sheet, through the same `requestTaskDetail` request; Run again and Follow up on a row call `runTaskAgain` and `followUpOnTask`; Edit and run is the one new door, `editTaskAndRunAgain`, which fills the widget through `composeCommand` and carries the task's workspace, refused in flight and during a clarification; the moved menu items keep their actions, predicates and confirmations; and density changes sizes only. Phase 12 changes what is shown, not what a press does: the pane appears with a selection and goes with the close or Esc; the page size caps what the list draws and what the keyboard walks, remembered in plain `UserDefaults`, and a task requested from elsewhere is shown past the cap for that visit; View and Open reach the closures they always reached, from the menus; Compact reads as Default for anyone who had it. Phase 13 changes where things sit and what they say: a fresh install opens on the rail and a returning user keeps their choice; the one toggle keeps ⌘⌥S; the row's workspace name moves into its second line and its tooltip carries the full command; the toolbar's two-row form keeps ⌘F, the clear button and the focus binding. Phase 14 adds one behaviour, the ⌘-held hints: a local `NSEvent` monitor on the Command Center window, installed each time the window is shown and removed when it closes, returns every event untouched and feeds a model that shows the caps after a third of a second of ⌘ alone (Caps Lock, Fn and the keypad flag not counting as modifiers) and hides them on release, on another modifier, on any key, or when the window stops being key; nothing else changes what a press does. The window's autosave name change hands every Mac the new default once.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The design layer landed first, alone, and every page lane branched from it.** Rewriting `ContentView.swift` with every older token name kept as an alias meant the whole target built and the whole suite passed before a single page changed (3012 in 201 at `4d6cd26e`), so nine lanes could restyle nine disjoint regions in parallel and merge without a conflict. The aliases were deleted in one commit at the end, once `grep` answered zero call sites for each.

**A harness-created worktree can branch from the wrong head, and the tell is the SHA in `git worktree list`.** The first launch of the lane workflow used the tool's own worktree isolation, and its four worktrees came up at `6d7bf058` — `main`, not this branch — which would have had every lane restyling code without the token layer under it. It was caught within a minute by reading `git worktree list`, the run was stopped, and the lanes were relaunched creating their own worktrees with `git worktree add <path> -b <branch> ui-ux-claude`. A lane's first instruction now includes confirming its head's commit title before editing anything.

**A branch name cannot share a prefix with an existing branch's full name.** `ui-ux-claude/lane-tasks` is refused while `ui-ux-claude` exists (a ref cannot be both a file and a directory), so lane branches are `ui-ux-claude-lane-<key>`.

**A desktop-app worktree carries an absolute `core.hooksPath` in its own `config.worktree`**, which the repository's PreToolUse hook refuses before any `git commit` runs. `git config --worktree core.hooksPath .githooks`, run on its own line first, is the fix; it is in every lane's instructions and in the memory directory.

**Two lanes' first edit landed in the integrator's checkout rather than their worktree** (tasks and routine-detail), because the session's starting directory was the integrator's. Both caught it with `git status` there, restored the files with `git checkout --` before anything was committed, and redid the edits in place. The merge script refuses a dirty integrator tree, which is the second line behind that.

**Brief errors a lane should refuse, and did.** The routines brief asked for a trailing Run button on each row; the row has none by a recorded decision, and adding one would be a new task entry point. The lane skipped it and said so. The same brief called the streak badge a step count, the confusion `CLAUDE.md` already records a historical bug for; the lane kept the streak.

**Founder-verbatim strings and the branch's copy rules met seven times**, each resolved the same way: keep the founder's sentence, change only the notation, and flag it. The last four arrived through a wrong record: decision 13 had filed the scheduled-run notice, the vision pause summary, the partly-unreadable confirmation and the terminals-never detail as sentences a test pins by the dash, and none is — two are read by no test and two are pinned by fragments the dash sits outside. Each took a period, a colon or a comma with every word kept (`1c8540d8`), and the decision now carries the count and the command that produced it. The mic hint's chord is now key glyphs (the status line beside it draws glyphs, and two spellings of one shortcut on one surface is the inconsistency this branch removes); the unattended-trust label's em dash became a colon; "Delete Local Data" survives inside the confirmation dialog's button because the wipe sentence test pins that dialog by value.

**The review found a real regression inside a restyle, and it was the one place a lane replaced measured layout with a named size.** Every other sheet's height was a hand-picked literal and a shared size is an improvement on it; the task detail's was a function of its content with a tested estimate behind it, and giving it `.regular` threw that away. The rule that came out of it: a shared size replaces a literal, never a measurement. The `sonnyDialogFrame(width:height:)` variant exists for exactly that sheet.

**Two lanes' first edit landed in the integrator's checkout, and it happened a third time in phase 3** (the account-menu lane), caught the same way each time; the integrator's merge script refusing a dirty tree remains the backstop.

**A test that reads a subscription by the first occurrence of a publisher can be handed a different subscriber.** `StandingWatcherRunTests` finds the notification channels in `AppDelegate` by the first `viewModel.$errorMessage` and reads to its `.store`, expecting the `isUserWorkingInSonny` gate; the phase 4 status-item observer read the same publisher earlier in the file with no gate and the scan read it instead. It moved below the channels with a comment saying why (`6309bcd9`). The general form: a region anchored on a token that more than one site can hold is a claim about whichever site comes first.

**`hasUsageDetails` is not "tokens were reported".** It is true for any usage at all, audio included, so the Usage page's first tokens row would have shown a reported figure of zero for an estimated-only task; the lane that built it said so in its report and the integrator changed the discriminator to `reportedTotalTokens > 0`.

**A page that reads a model must fetch it, or say what it does not know.** The Usage page read `subscription` and `screenControlAllowance`, both populated only by the Account dialog's own `.task`, so a signed-in user who opened Settings first read "Signed out" (second review, F1). The fix is the same two refreshes on the page's own appearance.

**A builder that touches `NSApp` traps the test process the first time a test calls it, and the trap prints no count line and names no test.** `makeMainMenu()` set `NSApp.windowsMenu` on its way out, which was fine for its one caller, `applicationDidFinishLaunching`; the moment phase 9 made it internal and a `ProductShellTests` test called it to assert the wiring by selector, the full suite at `9a1fa578` ended with `AppDelegate.swift:590: Fatal error: Unexpectedly found nil while implicitly unwrapping an Optional value` and exit 1, with no count line, because `NSApp` is nil in a test process. It is the shape CLAUDE.md's `try #require` gotcha describes from the other side, a dead process rather than a red test, and `swift build` had passed minutes earlier, which builds no test target, so the only reader that could see it was the full suite. The builder now returns the menu and touches nothing global; the launcher installs it and looks the Window item up by title, and the test pins that title as wiring (`d525cf58`). The rule that survives: a function a test is about to call must not reach for `NSApp`, `NSApplication.shared` or any other launch-time global, and a builder is the wrong place for an install.

**Collapsing a native control's accessibility subtree throws away the control.** The density slider wrapped its `Slider` and the stop names under it in `.accessibilityElement(children: .ignore)` with a label and a value on the container, which reads well in a code review and leaves VoiceOver able to say "Density, Default" and unable to move it: `.ignore` discards the slider's own adjustable trait and its increment and decrement actions, and nothing on the container put them back. Three of the five phase 11 reviewers found it independently, and it was the round's one high finding. The label and the value sit on the `Slider` now and the row of names under it is hidden on its own; the rule that survives is that a native control keeps its own accessibility, and a label goes on the control, never on a container that swallows it.

**A view must not clear a selection on the strength of having asked for a delete.** The receipt's Delete task cleared `selectedTaskID` right after calling `deleteTask`, which returns nothing and has three refusal arms that leave the record in place and say why in the attention panel; the pane then dropped to "No task selected" over a row still in the list. The history refresh already clears a selection whose record is gone (`TasksSelectionPresentation.selectionAfterRefresh`, on `taskHistoryRecords`), so the view now does nothing itself and the one source of truth decides, pinned by `TasksPaneSourceScanTests`. Same family as the old sheet's `if viewModel.runTaskAgain(record) { dismiss() }`: a surface reacts to what the model did, not to what it asked.

**A "long enough" window in a test is a wall-clock bet, and a loaded machine collects.** Two phase 11 auto-stop tests armed a sixty-second window as "long enough that it could not fire on its own before this test's own manual stop does"; the insights lane's first full run, on a machine also building three other lanes, took 87 seconds inside that test, the window elapsed, the task fired, the recording stopped, and two assertions failed on a mutant-free tree. The same run passed alone in 0.14 seconds and passed clean on the re-run, which is exactly the shape CLAUDE.md's wall-clock gotcha describes and the shape that manufactures a mutation kill. The windows are a day long now; the rule the gotcha already states, that a window a test must not reach is bounded rather than eliminated and bounded far past any delay the machine can produce, applies to a `Task.sleep` deadline as much as to a `/bin/sleep`. **And the widened window found the second half of the same bet an hour later**: two of those tests observed cancellation by awaiting the cancelled task's value, which returns at once on the live code and, under the battery's mutant that drops the cancel, sleeps out the whole window, now a day, so the battery stalled on that mutant with nothing to report, a hang being the one result a battery cannot read. `cancel()` sets `isCancelled` synchronously; the tests read the flag and await nothing, and cancel their tasks again before they end (`559fa6b3`). A window a test must not reach has to be long, and a test must not have any path that waits for it.

**A window that opens at its minimum can be doing exactly what two silent defaults say.** The founders asked for a larger default window; the default had been 1180×780 since before this branch and the window had opened at 900×620 for everyone. Two things, neither an error: `NSHostingController` resizes its window to the SwiftUI root's computed size on layout, and a root that declares only a minimum computes the minimum, so the requested content size lasted until the first layout pass; and `NSWindowController.showWindow(_:)` clears a frame autosave name set on the window itself, so `setFrameAutosaveName` on the window had saved nothing since it was written and every launch was a first launch. `sizingOptions = []` with the content size re-applied after the content controller is set, and the autosave name on the window controller, are the fixes (`36f2e6ab`); the autosave name also changed so a Mac that had, against the odds, saved a frame gets the new default once. Nothing in the suite could see either: a window's size after layout is not a thing a source scan reads, and the founders' eyes were the instrument.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- The widget's three composer chip clear buttons have an 18pt target, the chip row's own height, not the 24pt floor the rest of the branch holds; growing them means growing the chip row, which `AgentActivityPresentation` sizes against. Left for the founders' widget look.
- The screen-access sheet's three-button row is a plain `HStack`; its buttons fit the narrower sheet with about 90pt to spare, and it would wrap only under a larger text size, which this app does not yet honour anywhere.
- The Inter, Golos and Instrument Serif font files are still bundled and registered; nothing draws with them. The founder chose to keep them on 2026-09-08.
- The widget stays dark under the Light and System appearances by design; a light widget is a System B decision the founders have not made.
- The palette's routine and workspace groups define "most recent" as the last five of the stores' arrays, since neither carries a timestamp; tasks use `startedAt`.
- One verifier in the second review hit its structured-output retry cap and its finding was dropped rather than counted; the finder's own list was read by hand and nothing in it was outside the seventeen confirmed.
- Task-row delete is still right-click only; the founders recorded that as their SONNY-109 call.
- The Insights bento is the first cut of a layout the founders asked for and have not seen; the tile spans are a design judgment.

Whether the sheet should offer it is the founders' (not added). (1) The receipt's "What Sonny planned" shows the plan summary only, because a founder decision of 2026-07-18 (row E, `TaskPlanDetailStore.swift`'s doc comment) says the stored steps are never rendered; the brief for the pane asked for the steps as a numbered list, so the founders decide whether that decision stands now that a task has a pane. (2) `TaskDetailPresentation`'s height section (`sheetHeight`, `resultTextHeight` and their constants) has no consumer since the sheet went and is kept, with its tests, until the founders say delete it. Everything the founders answered on 2026-09-08 and 2026-09-09 is closed and recorded in the decision record.

Behavior added:
- **One command the founders can run over every mutation plan in the repository**: `scripts/mutate-all`, which locates `scripts/mutate` beside itself, discovers every `*.txt` under `mutation/plans/` (recursively, a slash in a branch name being a folder, sorted bytewise), runs a stale-plan pre-check (`scripts/mutate <plan> --check`) before each one so a plan whose `from` block no longer matches the tree is named and skipped rather than aborting the run, runs the real battery for every plan that still applies, and prints one aggregate summary — every survivor and every unattributed mutant, each with its plan file and its target file — to both stdout and its own `summary.log` under `.build/mutate-all/`. Exit 0 only when every plan ran and every mutant was killed (an empty `mutation/plans/` also exits 0); exit 2 for a survivor or an unattributed mutant; exit 3 when nothing survived but a plan was skipped as stale; exit 1 when the run could not start, or had to stop, in which case it says which plans were never attempted rather than pretending it reached them.
- **A branch's mutation plan is now a committed artifact rather than a run**: `mutation/plans/<branch-name>.txt`, in the format `scripts/mutate --help` already documents, named in the branch's changelog entry. Nothing runs against it until a founder runs `scripts/mutate-all`.
- **`WORKFLOW.md`'s new `## Weekly battery` section** is the founder-side procedure: run on a clean `main`, read the exit code, file one ticket per survivor/unattributed mutant naming the mutant id, plan file, target file and run SHA, treat a skipped plan as a ticket for the branch that owns it to re-anchor rather than as a survivor, and record the run's SHA, summary line and summary path on SONNY-106 every time it runs.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **`scripts/mutate` itself is untouched, and this is measured rather than asserted** — `git diff --stat origin/main -- scripts/mutate scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures scripts/lib .claude/hooks` prints nothing. Every guard it documents (the dirty-tree refusal, the per-plan lock, the untrusted-failure declarations, the stop hook's live/abandoned battery handling) works exactly as it did before this branch; `scripts/mutate-all` only calls it, once per plan, sequentially, and holds no lock of its own.
- **`scripts/warnings` and the stop hook's mutual refusal against a live battery are unchanged**, because both read `scripts/lib/battery-state.sh`, which this branch does not touch, and `scripts/mutate-all` writes nothing to `.git/mutate.lock` — `scripts/mutate` itself still does, per plan, for the whole time that plan is running.
- **The scratch build directory (`.build/mutate-scratch`) is reused exactly as before** — it is `scripts/mutate`'s own fixed path for the checkout, not something this branch introduces or manages; `scripts/mutate-all`'s selftest proves the reuse happens across two plans in one run by reading the `build dir` line back out of both plans' own `scripts/mutate` reports and asserting they name the same path.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **`scripts/mutate-all` holds no lock and sources nothing from `scripts/lib/battery-state.sh`, by design.** The brief this branch was built from is explicit that this is a workflow and record change, not a tool change, so every refusal a session or another tool already relies on (`scripts/warnings` refusing beside a live battery, the stop hook skipping mid-mutant) has to keep working unchanged — which it does, because `scripts/mutate` still takes its own lock per plan, and nothing about running several plans back to back needs a second, coarser lock. Two `scripts/mutate-all` runs (or one and a manual `scripts/mutate` invocation) in the same checkout collide exactly where two manual invocations always did — at the second one's lock acquisition for whichever plan it reaches first.
- **Stale-plan detection runs `scripts/mutate <plan> --check` before every plan, rather than parsing the real run's pre-flight output.** `--check` matches every mutant and runs no tests, so a stale plan costs nothing beyond the match attempt, and it prints a message (`... were refused. Nothing was run and nothing was changed.`) this script matches by substring to distinguish "the tree moved" from every other reason `scripts/mutate` can refuse (a dirty tree, another battery's lock, a red baseline) — the latter bucket is treated as fatal for the whole run rather than as a reason to skip one plan, because those reasons describe the checkout, not the plan, and would repeat identically for whatever is left in the list.
- **`run_all_plans` ends every path with an explicit `exit N` rather than `return`, because it runs as the left side of a pipe** (`{ run_all_plans; } 2>&1 | tee -a "$SUMMARY_LOG"`), which bash forks into its own subshell — a plain shell-variable handoff back to the caller does not survive that fork, but the subshell's own process exit status does, and `PIPESTATUS`/`$?` read it correctly. Verified empirically before relying on it: bash 3.2 (`$BASH_VERSION` on this Mac, matching `scripts/mutate`'s own note about the toolchain) reports the *pipeline's* exit status via `$?` under `pipefail` correctly, but `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` read immediately after a `pipeline || true` fallback reads the fallback's own `0`, not the pipeline's real code — so the exit code is captured via `pipeline || rc=$?` (the same shape `scripts/mutate` itself uses for `run_suite ... || baseline_code=$?`), never via `PIPESTATUS` after a `|| true`.
- **The summary log path is computed once, before the pipe, and handed to the piped function only through global variables (`ROOT`, `SHA`, `LOGDIR`, `SUMMARY_LOG`)**, because the alternative — computing it inside the function that is itself the left side of the pipe — cannot tee its own header line to a file it has not yet decided the name of without either a second pass or scripts/mutate's own fifo-plus-trap machinery. Unlike `scripts/mutate`, nothing here mutates a tracked file, so there is no tree to restore on a signal and that heavier mechanism is not owed — a plain pipe is enough, and the only thing at risk on an interruption is an incomplete log, never a dirty tree.
- **The selftest commits every plan file it writes, unlike `scripts/mutate selftest`'s own plan fixtures**, which deliberately live outside its throwaway repository. The two tools disagree on purpose: `scripts/mutate` treats a plan as a transient, uncommitted argument, so keeping it outside the tree avoids the very dirty-tree refusal being tested; this branch's whole design instead makes a plan a *committed, tracked* artifact (`mutation/plans/<branch-name>.txt`), so a selftest plan has to be committed too, or every scenario would trip the dirty-tree guard before reaching the behaviour under test.
- **Proving the scratch-reuse claim needed a stand-in test command that *reads* as a SwiftPM invocation without actually being one.** `scripts/mutate`'s own `require_isolated_test_command` prints a fixed string, "not a SwiftPM invocation — it has no build directory to share", for any `MUTATE_TEST_CMD` that does not look like `swift test --scratch-path "$MUTATE_SCRATCH"` — and two stand-ins that both print that same fixed string would make "both plans' reports name the same build dir" true by construction, proving nothing. The selftest's fixtures carry a leading `# swift test --scratch-path "$MUTATE_SCRATCH"` comment line — inert at run time, but enough to satisfy that function's pattern match — so the reports carry the real, shared scratch path instead, and the assertion is a real comparison.
- **The "five levers" sentence in `WORKFLOW.md` step 3 (`A long lane is a coordination failure...`) named "step 5's scoped battery re-runs" as one of five; that lever is retired outright, not merely reworded, since there is no more battery re-run for a branch to scope.** Reworded to name the removal itself — "step 5's mutation batteries moving off the branch entirely" — as the lever, since eliminating a whole category of repeated work is a larger saving than scoping it ever was, and the sentence still needs to name five things. This is a judgment call this branch made rather than a reading handed down in the brief; flagged here rather than left silent.

- **The review's four high findings were all in the script's reading of `scripts/mutate`'s output, and each is now a shape the selftest drives** (`77001823`). (1) The killed count was taken from the first number of the counts line, which is the total selected, so a one-mutant survivor printed "1 killed, 1 survived"; the field is read by name now and a summary counts only when killed plus survived plus unattributed equals the total and the listed rows match — a wording change in `scripts/mutate` reads as unparsed rather than as a wrong number. (2) The per-mutant status line and the summary's section header share the `    UNATTRIBUTED — ` prefix, so reading the whole output listed an evidence line as a mutant row with no id and no file; only what follows `==> Summary at` is read. (3) An exit other than 0 or 2 — 130 from an interrupted run, whose trap prints no summary — was counted as RAN with zeros and could sit under a clean verdict; it is INCOMPLETE now, stops the run and names the plans not attempted, the one it was on included. (4) A plan is named after its branch and this repository's branch names carry a slash, so `mutation/plans/fix/some-name.txt` is where `fix/some-name`'s plan lands, and a non-recursive glob reported "0 plans" over a committed one; discovery is recursive and the convention says so wherever it is stated. The pattern across all four: the script's own selftest asserted the presence of a section and an exit code and never a count, an id or the absence of a spurious row, which is the shared-marker rule of CLAUDE.md's gotchas arriving in a shell script.

Known limitations / deferred scope: `mutation/plans/` starts empty because the founders handed this branch no plan files to seed it with — the first real plan lands with whatever branch is next to touch behaviour, per the format `scripts/mutate --help` documents.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none — every point in the brief this branch was built from was settled either in the brief itself or from reading `WORKFLOW.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `scripts/mutate --help` and its cited line ranges, and `scripts/lib/battery-state.sh`.

A cancelled statement raises `57014`, which nothing maps, so the route answers §7.2's case 6 — `500 server.error`, retryable — in §7.1's envelope. The point is that it answers at all.

- **Every existing database test passes unchanged**: `npm run test:db` moved from 1289 to 1292 and the three are this branch's own. That is the reach check that matters, since the bound reaches every statement the suite issues.
- **The migration runner and the seven operator commands are untouched**, because none of them leases from this pool — each opens its own `pg.Client` (`git grep -lE 'new pg\.Client\(' 39be942c -- server/src` → 7 files). A backfill that legitimately runs for minutes is not cut at ten seconds, which matters because SONNY-370 is about exactly those migrations, and `server/README.md`'s still-owed `lock_timeout` decision is about that other end of the same stall and is not discharged here.
- **The content-expiry sweeper keeps working, and it needed a change of its own to** — the sentence that stood here was wrong twice over and PR #223's F2 is that finding. It said the sweeper's statements are batched at 500 rows so none approaches the bound, and that a cancelled one is retried next tick. Two of the sweep's four groups are batched (`expireContentBatch` and `pruneExpiredResponses`, 500 rows each); `expireSnapshots` is one CTE over every expired snapshot, and `sweepClosedAccountContent` wipes a whole account through `deleteContentForAccount`'s fixed sequence with no `LIMIT` anywhere in it. And the retry could not converge, because nothing about a retry makes the statement smaller. The fix round's section at the end of this entry carries what was done.
- **No route file, no error mapping and no contract number changed.** `POST /v1/account/credits/top-up` stays SONNY-430's and is still unbounded.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

- **`pg`'s `query_timeout` is not a database timeout and would have re-introduced PR #212's F1 one layer lower.** It is a JavaScript timer: `node_modules/pg/lib/client.js` errors the query, sets `query.callback = () => {}` under the comment *"just do nothing if query completes"*, and outside pipeline mode leaves the socket alone. The statement keeps running on the backend, still holding its locks, on a connection that then goes back to the pool for the next lessee. That is precisely *a deadline around work holding a database connection that abandons rather than ends it* — the rule PR #212's fix round left behind. Only `statement_timeout` ends a running statement, because only the backend can.
- **The bound has to arrive in the startup packet, and a `SET` after connecting is a shape that reads as equivalent and is silently undone in production.** SONNY-428's `withDatabaseDeadline` sets and resets this same session setting per statement for the four content-deletion routes. `RESET` restores a parameter to its *reset value*, which a startup parameter supplies and a session `SET` does not. Measured on `postgres:17`, reading `setting`/`reset_val`/`source` from `pg_settings` around a route's `SET 15000` and its `RESET`: from the startup packet, `10000/10000/client` → `15000/10000/session` → `10000/10000/client`; from a `SET` after connecting, `10000/0/session` → `15000/0/session` → **`0/0/default`**, which is byte-for-byte what a connection that was never bounded reads. So under the wrong shape the first content deletion on a connection takes the bound off it for every later request that leases it, and nothing anywhere says so. **The control that makes those readings measurements rather than a probe agreeing with itself** is the third arm: a connection with no bound configured at all reads `0/0/default` from the start.
- **How the two compose: the innermost `SET` governs, in both directions, and `RESET` returns to the pool's bound rather than to none.** Measured with a 600 ms stand-in for the bound and `SELECT pg_sleep(5)` as the work: under the pool default alone the statement is cancelled at 614 ms; under a route's *larger* `SET 2000` at 2008 ms; under a route's *smaller* `SET 150` at 154 ms; after each `RESET`, at 602 ms again. The control — the same statement with no bound — **completes** in 1018 ms, which is what makes those five cancellations readings rather than a probe that cancels everything. The real case is the larger one, since `withDatabaseDeadline` computes its budget from §12's *total* (15 s) while this bound is that row's *upstream* (10 s): those four routes' first statement may run past ten seconds, which is not a breach but the stronger promise, because their bound is over the whole handler and this one is over one statement.
- **A per-statement bound cannot bound a sequence, and saying so is the difference between this ticket and the next.** Three of the four `/v1/account/*` routes do their work in several statements on one lease, so they can still sum past §12's total. That is **SONNY-434**, filed by this branch, and §12's sentence naming it is where a reader meets it. Deferring it was not a judgment call: both route files were on this ticket's never-touch list and one of them is SONNY-430's.
- **A `statement_timeout` in `DATABASE_URL` overrides this, because `pg` assigns the parsed connection string *over* the config it was given** (`connection-parameters.js`, `Object.assign({}, config, parse(config.connectionString))`), and `pg-connection-string` lifts an unknown query parameter straight onto the config: measured with its `parse()` against a local development URL carrying `statement_timeout=0` in the query, the parsed config comes back holding `statement_timeout: "0"`. **The URL is described rather than quoted, here and everywhere below in this entry**, because the shape of a connection string is exactly what `check-secrets.sh` is looking for and a doc line is not a thing to baseline. Nothing in this repository sets one (`git grep -nE 'statement_timeout|query_timeout' 39be942c -- server` exits 1 with no output; the control that the search can find a timeout that *is* set is `git grep -cE 'connectionTimeoutMillis|idleTimeoutMillis' 39be942c -- server/src/db/pool.ts` → 4). The test therefore reads the **effective** setting off a leased connection rather than trusting the option took, which is the same test that catches the override if a deployment ever adds one.
- **The blocked-route test fails in wording of its own rather than by hanging, and that is the difference between a kill and an `UNATTRIBUTED`.** Its natural failure mode under a mutant that removes the bound is an unbounded wait, which `itUnderHangBackstop` would report in wording `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures` declares — `CLAUDE.md`'s SONNY-259 case, a manufactured NON-kill on a run where the test failed for exactly the right reason. So it races the request against a thirty-second admission that sits *inside* the backstop's sixty, and the assertion names the winning branch. Proved rather than reasoned: with the bound deleted the three tests fail 3 of 3 and the third reports `the route was still waiting on the lock when this test gave up: no statement bound is in force on the pool`, which no declaration matches.

**The fix round after PR #223's review (2026-09-07).** Four findings, one of them a defect this branch introduced. Recorded here rather than only on the ticket because the second is a rule about where a bound belongs.

- **F1 — `npm run check:secrets` exited 1 at this branch's own head, and three records said 0.** The entry's `DATABASE_URL`-override bullet carried a connection string written out in full, with a short user-and-password pair in front of the host — the shape the scanner's name-free URL pattern is for, and one nothing allowlists. **It has now been written out three times and caught three times**, because each correction quoted the offending string in order to explain it: the fix itself, then this bullet, then the bullet below explaining this bullet. It is described in words everywhere in this entry now, which is the only form that stays fixed. Not a credential, and that is why it was worth a round: merging it puts one of step 5's five server commands red on `main` from a prose line, and the two cheap exits for the next lane are to stop trusting the scanner or to baseline a doc line — the second being what that file's own comments are written against. Rewritten to the local development connection string the scanner allowlists by name — the one whose user and password are both the word `postgres` — and then, after the coordinator's verification of this round caught the same shape in this very bullet, described rather than written at all; the baseline file was not touched (`git diff --name-only -- server/scripts/secret-scan-baseline.txt` prints nothing).
- **How a 0 was read where the tree answers 1, since that is the part worth keeping.** The reading was honest and the *stamp* was not: it was taken before the changelog entry existed, and then reported as a figure of the commit that introduced it. **The count in the record is the fingerprint that proves it.** `check-secrets.sh` scans `git ls-files`, so it counts what the index holds; the run reported `clean (636 tracked files scanned…)`, and `git ls-tree -r --name-only 39be942c | wc -l` → **636** against `de17ebfe` → **637**. So the tree it measured was the base's file set — the new test file still untracked, the entry not yet written — and the stamp named a commit with one more file in it and the DSN in that file. The scanner's own pattern is safe to quote because it does not match itself — `printf '%s\n' "$P" | grep -cE "$P"` answers **0** for `P='postgres(ql)?://[^:[:space:]]+:[^@[:space:]]+@'`, with a real connection string through the same pipe answering **1** as the control — so the population is `git grep -hoE "$P" <sha> -- docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md | grep -vcE "$ALLOW"`, with the allowlist **read out of the scanner rather than transcribed** — `ALLOW="$(sed -n "s/^ALLOW='\(.*\)'$/\1/p" server/scripts/check-secrets.sh)"` — which is both the only form that carries no connection string of its own and the only one that cannot go stale when the scanner moves, as it did under PR #218 in the middle of this branch; which answers **0** at `39be942c`, **1** at `de17ebfe` and `b3b59127`, and **2** at `6bc4fd7c` — that last pair being this bullet and the one above it. **The allowlist stage is the half a reader must not drop, and this entry shipped it dropped** (PR #223's delta review, R2): the figures were always the findings, but the command written beside them was `git grep -cE "$P" …` with no stage at all, which counts every matching *line* and answers **1 / 2 / 2 / 4** — so re-running the citation contradicted the number it was there to support. Dropping the stage is also the control, since it raises the answer by exactly the allowlisted lines, one at the base and two at `6bc4fd7c`. **It is a match stage rather than a line stage on purpose**: at `6bc4fd7c` one line carried an allowlisted and a non-allowlisted match together, so filtering whole lines would have hidden a real finding — which is the hole `check-secrets.sh`'s own comments record having been caught once before. **No tree-identity proof could have caught it either**, and that is the general lesson rather than this instance's: the proof this branch ran covers `server/`, and this command reads the whole repository, so the scope of a carry has to be the scope of the *command*, not of the change.
- **F2 — the bound reached the content sweep, whose statement is not batched and whose retry could not converge.** The reviewer measured four consecutive passes under a bound smaller than one closed account's delete: every pass threw `57014` having removed nothing, and because the account is chosen `ORDER BY a.deleted_at LIMIT 1` the one that cannot be deleted is permanently the oldest, so every account closed after it queued behind it for ever — while a control converged in two passes. The failure is silent by construction: the sweeper logs and keeps its timer, so against a cause that does not clear it is one line an hour and the product's own promise that a closed account's content goes is quietly not kept.
- **F2's fix, and why it is a budget rather than a batch.** §12's numbers bound *what a user is waiting for*; nothing waits on the sweep, which is a timer in the process holding nobody's connection open. Running it at a route's number is a category error, and undoing exactly that is the fix: `sweepOnce` sets `statement_timeout` to `SWEEP_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_MS` on the connection it leases and resets it in a `finally`. That number is `LONGEST_TOTAL_DEADLINE_MS` — §12's longest `total`, computed from `DEADLINE_MS` the way `entitlement/period.ts` already computes it — so no statement in this gateway outlives the longest thing the product ever waits for, and it is still a bound rather than none. **Batching was the reviewer's suggested cheapest fix and is the one this round could not make**: `deleteContentForAccount` is also the request path's own function, whose semantics this round does not change, and batching it splits the single `sonny.content_deletion` row it writes — a shape SONNY-436 owns. **The `RESET` is what makes the shared pool safe here**, and it is this branch's own measurement being used rather than restated: the pool's value arrives in the startup packet, so a `RESET` returns to it instead of to no bound.
- **F2's other half, which no budget could fix.** A budget does not help an account stuck for a reason that is not size — a lock held elsewhere, which `statement_timeout` counts. So a failed account is now named (`ClosedAccountSweepFailed` carries its id), deferred by the sweeper's own list, and excluded from the next pass's select; the list clears as soon as a pass finds nothing else to take, so a deferral cannot become an abandonment. That decision is the pure `deferralsAfter`, extracted for the reason the branch has already had to learn twice — the branch that matters is the one nothing observable would have caught.
- **The acceptance test, and the shape that had to be got right.** `sweep-budget.db.test.ts` rebuilds the reviewer's harness. **A whole-account `DELETE` is cheap however large the account is** — measured on this container at **1 ms for 400 rows of 4 KiB, 2 ms at 64 KiB and 8 ms at 256 KiB**, because Postgres marks tuples dead and leaves the TOAST to `VACUUM` — so making it exceed a bound by volume was not available. What makes it exceed one is what `statement_timeout` is there to count and what `server/README.md` names as this gateway's real case: **time queued behind another connection's lock**. **And eventual convergence turned out not to be the property**: the first version of the test released the lock as soon as the sweep queued behind it, and the mutant with the budget removed *passed* — cancelled at the pool's bound, then converging on a later pass once the lock had lifted. The discriminator is which of two things happens first, so the assertion names the winning branch: the pass must still be waiting when the lock is released.
- **F3 — §12 sent a reader to SONNY-434 for a route that ticket disclaims.** The sentence named four routes and attributed all of them to a ticket scoped to three. Split: the three `/v1/account/*` routes are SONNY-434's, and `DELETE /v1/tasks/{task_id}` is SONNY-428's, which wires the four content-deletion routes to this row's total.
- **F4 — the migration manual row could not produce the finding it named.** Every migration in the tree applies far inside ten seconds, so a founder would run the four steps, see them pass, and tick a row that had said nothing about whether the bound reaches the runner — the clean-zero family arriving in a checklist. Rewritten around a scratch migration whose `up` is `SELECT pg_sleep(12);`, which fails if the bound ever reaches the runner and passes if it does not.
- **The coordinator's verification of this round found F1 a third time, in the two sentences that explain F1, and the fix for that is above rather than here.** Both quoted the connection string in order to describe it, and the scanner matches a quotation exactly as it matches an original — so the round that documented the defect shipped it twice more, at lines 218 and 219 of `6bc4fd7c` and 224 and 225 of `5712eeee`. Nothing in this entry writes a connection string out any more. **The pattern is safe to quote and its own zero is controlled**: `printf '%s\n' "$P" | grep -cE "$P"` answers 0 for the scanner's pattern, a real connection string through the same pipe answers 1, and the same search over this entry answers **0** while over the whole changelog it answers **1** — the surviving hit being another branch's dated record, which is not this branch's to edit and which the scanner allowlists anyway.
- **And the file count went wrong the same way a second time, which is the more useful half.** This entry's round-1 line reported `clean (637 tracked files scanned…)` stamped at `6bc4fd7c`, and `git ls-tree -r --name-only 6bc4fd7c | wc -l` → **638**. The five commands had been run against the working tree *before* `git add` picked up `sweep-budget.db.test.ts` — which is precisely the mistake F1 documents, made again inside the round whose whole subject is that mistake, and caught by the same fingerprint. **The rule that follows is narrower than "stamp the SHA" and is what this branch actually needed**: a command that reads the index or the whole repository is run *after* the commit it will be stamped with, never before it, because for those commands the working tree and the commit are different objects and only one of them is what the stamp names.
- **The seven observations: three taken, four recorded and left.** **O1 taken** — a host that refuses the startup parameter leaves the gateway unbounded and fails green, which §12 now names, along with why this project's documented session pooler is not that shape. **O2 taken** — the hop is two conflict hunks in §12 rather than the one clause the PR body claimed; the body is corrected. **O3 taken** — the blocked-route test's precondition wait and its race shared one 30 s constant and are sequential, so the worst case was exactly `HANG_BACKSTOP_MS` and the file's claim to sit inside it was arithmetic it did not have; the precondition has its own 10 s budget now. **O4 left** — the precondition counts any backend blocked on any lock, which is safe under this suite's `fileParallelism: false` and a lane-derived container, and narrowing it needs a backend pid the test cannot cleanly get. **O5 left** — `statementTimeoutMillis: 0` is dropped by `pg`'s truthiness check and reads `0/0/default`, which coincides with Postgres's own meaning of 0. **O6 left** — a lock-blocked `/v1/auth/email/verify` burns the sign-in code and answers retryable, which is pre-existing and unchanged here. **O7 left** — the checklist heading has no blank line before it, which six of that file's other headings also do not.

Known limitations / deferred scope: SONNY-434 (the three account routes' total deadline, filed by this branch). `POST /v1/account/credits/top-up` remains SONNY-430's. `server/README.md`'s `lock_timeout` decision for the migration runner stays owed and is a different bound at the other end of the same stall.

Stage 1 reads **rendered** text and stage 2 read **raw markup**, so a phrase that renders contiguously need not be contiguous in the source: an inline `<a>` on the words "log in", or a `&nbsp;` between them, survives in the markup and defeats the substring match. That restores **8 of 8** in all three constructions, base against the shipped rule identical on **39 of 39**, and costs nothing on the innocent side: across **327** innocent pages **0** verdicts change and **0** become refused. **One direction of this is a widening rather than a restoration, and the record says so** (PR #222's delta review). It is still a coverage widening for `subjectPhrases`, and the warning above `wallSpeechPhrases` says a widening is its own decision, so it is named here rather than left inside "the fold rather than a second mechanism", which describes only the half that restores. **The population it can act on is thin, stated rather than rounded up** — only **3** of those 327 are below 200; the review's independent corpus found **0 of 245**; SONNY-245's own corpus statement is that every page under 200 in it is a wall.
