Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**SONNY-256's separator does not transfer to the login and paywall side, and that is the finding under every number here.** On the CAPTCHA side the *person of the verb* tells a wall from a reader: a wall says "verifying you are human", a reader asks "how do you prove you are human?". SONNY-245's three login and paywall wordings have no such difference available, because the reader is not paraphrasing the wall — they are **pasting** it. The commenter's string and the gate's string are the same string, so no rule that reads the phrase alone can separate them. Quotation marks were measured as a candidate signal and rejected: they sit beside the phrase on only **15 of the 56** innocent pages.

**The decision, stated on its own terms as the restored warning requires: this narrows SONNY-245's coverage, deliberately.** The warning above `wallSpeechPhrases` says widening or narrowing the list is a decision with its own false-refusal — and here false-*accept* — risk. What is given up is a login gate or paywall in the 200-to-2 000 band whose visible text carries one of the three and none of `wallSpeechPhrases`. **The page this costs is Google's account sign-in interstitial.** The first version of this sentence said zero such pages existed among the 68 real gates this lane fetched; that was a property of those 68, and PR #222's reviewer found the counterexample in one afternoon's fetching (F1). Re-measured here on all four of its hostnames: HTTP **200**, **843**-**853** visible characters, in the band, visible text opening `sign in to continue to gmail email or phone forgot email?`, carrying no `wallSpeechPhrases` entry — refused `login walls` before this change and served now. **Two of the four reach the detector at all**: `accounts.google.com/signin/...` and `drive.google.com/drive/...` answer `allows=true` through the shipped `RobotsTXTPolicy`, with the control (`Disallow: /private` against `/private/x`) answering false — and correctly rather than through SONNY-437's CRLF defect, since that host's `robots.txt` disallows six specific paths and then says `Allow: /`. **What is lost is the refusal, not the wall**: the extractor throws `noReadableContent` on all four, so nothing is summarised from a sign-in form and the user gets "nothing readable on the page" where they used to get "Sonny will not bypass login walls." It is one of the most-encountered login walls on the web, which is the fact the founders make the accept-or-veto call on, and the checklist row now names it. Measured on constructed gates, **11 of 14 real gate wordings placed in band-sized chrome lose the refusal** SONNY-245 gave them.

**No narrower wording recovers that shape, and the round measured it rather than assuming either way.** Under the inclusion rule, on a corpus sampled on the candidate wording itself, `sign in to continue to` matches **5** innocent in-band pages (4 distinct comments) — one of them a commenter quoting Google's own sentence, *"the google oauth flow which would say 'sign in to continue to <app>'"* — so it fails the rule exactly as the three did. `sign in to continue to your` reaches **0** innocent pages and **0** real gates, Google's sentence being "sign in to continue to *Gmail*". **Narrowing cannot escape quotation, because the quotation narrows with the wording.** The answer was no and nothing was added.

**The inclusion rule SONNY-256 wrote to stop an entry being added wrongly is what removes these three, and it needed no change to do it.** "A wording is in only if it matches zero innocent in-band pages across a corpus sampled on that wording itself" was written for additions. Applied to entries already present it is a removal rule, and the three fail it by **56 innocent in-band pages against 0 real walls** — `please log in` 44, `sign in to continue` 7, `subscribe to continue` 5. `verify you are human` was **not** re-measured under this round and stays exactly as it is; narrowing it is still its own decision.

**No narrowing was available, and the wordings that scored zero are the tell.** Fourteen candidate narrowings were measured beside the three. Every one that reaches a real-shaped gate wording also reaches innocent pages — `log in to continue` 15 innocent, `you must be logged in` 13, `members only` 52, `subscribe to continue reading` 4, `please log in to continue` 4. The only candidates scoring zero innocent pages — `please log in to access`, `sign in to your account to continue`, `become a member to continue reading`, `continue reading with a subscription`, `subscribe to read the full story` — are ones **no real gate in the corpus says and no commenter writes**, so each scored 0 innocent, 2 synthetic, **0 real**. Adding them would be fitting the list to pages this round invented, which is PR #210's F1 arriving from the other direction, so nothing was added.

**SONNY-256's second mitigation does not carry over, and is reported rather than borrowed.** That round could say `SwiftSoupReadableWebExtractor` threw `noReadableContent` on every newly-served page, so no note was written from any of them. Here **8 of 15** newly-served band-sized gate pages extract, because a page in this band has several hundred characters of body text on it by construction. A real gate of this shape would yield a **thin note** rather than nothing. The first draft of the type doc borrowed SONNY-256's sentence; it is measured and corrected rather than repeated.

**The claim SONNY-245 made about these three was true of its corpus and false of the world, and the mechanism is worth naming once more because it has now produced two defects on one file.** SONNY-245 reported that its four reader-addressed phrases fired on **zero** pages. They did — in a corpus of 48 popular home pages and gates, which contains no page whose subject is a wall. PR #210's F1 was the same shape one level down (a corpus sampled on the terms a change *removes* cannot falsify the terms it *adds*), and this is the same shape one level down again: **a corpus assembled to measure one property is silent about every other property measured on it, and its silence reads exactly like evidence.** The remedy both times is the sampling frame, not the rule: draw the population on the wording under test.

**The fix round, 2026-09-07 (PR #222, cycle 1), and the two absolutes it deleted.** Both findings above the bar were the same defect in the same direction: a corpus property written as a claim about the world, which is the failure this ticket exists to correct, arriving inside the correction. **F1** — "zero such pages exist among 68 real gates" — met Google's account sign-in interstitial, and the round then measured whether any narrower wall-speech wording recovers that shape under the inclusion rule, on a corpus sampled on the candidate itself: **no**, and the record says so above with the four innocent comments that settle it. **F2** — "below the contentless limit nothing at all is lost" — met the difference between rendered text and raw markup, and was fixed in the code rather than only in the prose, because the cheap fix restored every lost refusal at zero measured cost. **F3** is why F2 survived the suite: the test carrying that mitigation put every sample in an HTML comment, a shape the surviving route always sees, so its assertions were strong and pointed at a page the claim was not about — `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample gotcha in its milder form. `aGateBelowTheContentlessLimitIsRefusedHoweverItsSentenceIsWrittenInTheMarkup` is the version that holds it, over all three constructions, with a no-phrase control; and the assertion this branch had deleted — `Please&nbsp;log&nbsp;in now` refused as `login walls` — is restored beside an inline-anchor twin, because it was the one line in the suite that would have gone red on the gap. **F4**'s two Hacker News rows now say what a 403 means, since the site rate-limits uncached item pages, and a Google row was added that answers reliably and is where the founders' veto lands.

**Which of the review's seven residuals were taken.** Five were taken because each was a record that would mislead a later reader: the two-way concatenation in `aPageCarryingTwoPhrasesInMarkupIsNamedByTheEarlierListEntry`'s doc comment, now three-way; "425 real pages", now carrying the 159-fetched split the measuring comment already stated a paragraph later; "all on markup" for the base's below-200 refusals, which are on visible text; "verbatim" for four comments that are lowercased and two abridged; and "the whole page is one comment" for two pages that have replies. One was recorded at the code rather than changed — `publicWebPageLoaderRejectsLoginCaptchaAndPaywallPages` now says in its own doc comment that it passes by the markup route on a 46-character page and that its name reads wider than it proves, because a wider version would assert behaviour the product deliberately no longer has. **One was left, and it is the interesting one:** the reviewer could not reproduce **8 of 15** newly-served band gates extracting, getting **0 of 7** on its own nav-and-footer chrome and **0 of 4** on the real Google pages. That is two correct readings of different chrome rather than a disagreement about the rule — extraction depends on what filler a constructed page carries — so **8 of 15 is kept as the pessimistic reading** and the reviewer's figures are recorded beside it in the detector's own comment. Revising it down would be claiming the trade is cheaper than the worst measurement of it.

**A real fixture could not be added, and that is recorded rather than replaced by a synthetic one.** The natural fixture for this class is a real Hacker News comment permalink quoting a gate. `news.ycombinator.com` rate-limited this Mac to 403 after the corpus fetch and never recovered inside the lane, so 8 real permalinks were captured and none of them carries one of the three wordings exactly. `Tests/Fixtures/WebResearch/` is unchanged and its README still indexes six real pages: the README's own rule is that these are real pages saved verbatim, and inventing a seventh would break the property that makes the corpus worth having. The two new tests use **real comment text** — from the Algolia API, quoted verbatim — in this suite's existing synthetic-page helper, which is the same shape `wallSpeechReachesRealGateWordingsAndNotReadersTalkingAboutThem` already uses for its four controls.

**The measuring round's own population is 224 constructed pages plus 201 fetched ones, and the constructed half was validated by a control rather than assumed.** Each constructed page is a real comment's text placed in the committed `hackernews-paywall-comment.html` template. Rebuilding **that fixture's own comment** through the same path answers **327 visible characters**, which is that fixture's figure in the README — so the template is faithful — and a substituted control fires at 306 characters, so the harness is not answering a clean zero. The 8 real permalinks that did get through behave identically to their constructed neighbours, and **31 of 68** real Hacker News story pages carry one of the three in visible text, which is what says the content is real even where the page is built. What the constructed half cannot establish is how often such a page is asked for; the full limits are on SONNY-429's measuring-round comment.

- `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_2_ACCEPTED_UNTIL` — the overlap's end, read on every request. Past it the slot stops being accepted with no deploy.
- A numbered `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_<n>` this gateway does not read is a startup refusal naming the variable, rather than a silently ignored one.
- Migration 0022's `revoked_at` carries a `COMMENT ON COLUMN`, and its source comment says what the column means.

Behavior preserved (no blanket claims — each named):
- **A deployment with no rotation in flight is byte-for-byte the deployment it was.** `requireSupabaseJwtPolicy` returns a one-element list, `verifyAccessToken` computes one HMAC, and `loadConfig` refuses nothing new. `loads and starts with no rotation in flight, which is the ordinary shape` is the assertion.
- **Every forgery `token.test.ts` already refused is still refused** — the pin, `crit`, `typ`, the strict base64url decode, `iss`, `aud`, `sub`, the `session_id` shape check, `nbf` with no tolerance and `exp` with it. That file's original **57** tests are untouched and pass; `theSecondSecretGetsNoWeakerChecksThanTheFirst` re-asserts eleven of them against a token signed with the *overlap* secret. **This said 55, and the number came from counting the file rather than running it** (PR #218's R2): `npx vitest run test/token.test.ts` answers **64 passed (64)** at `7a7414f0`, and this branch adds seven plain `it(` lines and removes none (`git diff 061a2c36..7a7414f0 -- server/test/token.test.ts | grep -cE '^\+ *it\('` → 7, the `^-` form → 0), so the base ran 64 − 7 = 57. **One half of the finding's own derivation does not reproduce and the conclusion is unaffected**, recorded because a supporting claim nobody re-checks is how a right number acquires a wrong reason: it stated there is no `it.each` in the file, and there are two (`grep -nE '^ *it\.' server/test/token.test.ts` → `:80` and `:372` at `7a7414f0`, which is why 48 `it(` lines expand to 64 tests). Neither block is in the diff — the same `git diff` piped to `grep -cE 'it\.each'` → 0 — so their expansion is unchanged and the subtraction holds.
- **The check order is unchanged**: the signature is still decided before any claim is read, so a forgery is still never told which claim was wrong. `refuses the claim AFTER the signature` passes unchanged.
- **`requireSupabaseJwtPolicy`'s existing refusals** — both variables named when both are missing, the 32-character floor with the length reported and the value not, the issuer parsed and its value reported — all pass unchanged; the floor now runs through one function that both secrets use.
- **SONNY-237's denylist is untouched.** `server/src/auth/denylist.ts` and `gate.ts` are not in the diff; only 0022's comments moved, and `migration-round-trip.db.test.ts` walks the ledger green.
- **`auth/deps.ts` did not move**, which was predicted before the edit rather than discovered after: `AUTH_INTENT` is the three names meaning "this deployment serves sign-in", and an optional overlap slot is not one — a deployment mid-rotation and one that has never rotated must both be able to serve.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:

- **The direction is the mirror of a provider credential's, and a runbook written the other way is wrong.** A provider key is one this gateway *sends*, so `<PROVIDER>_API_KEY_2` is "another thing to try". This is one Supabase *signs* with and this gateway only *verifies*, so the list is "what to accept" and the overlap must straddle the moment Supabase's own value changes — which is not a deploy of this gateway at all. `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_2` therefore holds the **incoming** secret in the first deploy and the **retiring** one in the third. Written down because "the previous secret" is the natural name and is false half the time.
- **One overlap slot, not an unbounded list, and a numbered name outside `{none, _2}` is a startup refusal.** This is a deliberate departure from the description's letter, which said "the same shape as the provider credentials … stopping at the first gap". The two lists fail in opposite directions: `providerCredentials` stopping silently at a gap costs a credential to try, while a silently skipped *verifying* secret means every token signed with it is refused — the sign-out this ticket exists to prevent, reached through its own fix, with nothing in the logs. The count is two because the ticket's own security argument settles it: every extra accepted secret is another key that can mint a token for any user, and a rotation needs exactly one overlap slot.
- **The overlap's end is read per request, not at startup, and that is the whole difference between a number and a check.** The founders decided on 2026-08-30 that a retired secret gets a stated maximum overlap and left the number and whether anything checks it open, noting that "a number in a runbook that nothing checks is better than nothing and worse than a check". A deadline evaluated once at boot ends the overlap on the next restart — which on a gateway that does not restart is no ending at all — so `verifyAccessToken` skips a retired secret against the same `now` every other time-dependent check uses. The retired secret stops being able to mint a token for any user at the stated instant, with nobody remembering.
- **A deadline already past is deliberately not a startup failure, and this is the one place the design refuses to fail closed.** Every other invalid value here is a startup refusal, on this file's own stated reasoning that a gateway which boots and then refuses every request is indistinguishable from every user being signed out. A *past* deadline is the exception because refusing it would produce exactly that outcome — an outage caused by leftover bookkeeping — while allowing it costs nothing: a secret past its instant authorises nothing, because the verifier skips it. Fail-closed on the values somebody just typed, fail-open on the passage of time.
- **What the maximum does not prevent, stated rather than implied.** It bounds the *remaining* overlap at each startup, because this gateway cannot know when the rotation began. An operator redeploying every week with a fresh seven-day deadline extends the overlap indefinitely and nothing here sees it. What the bound does catch is the realistic mistake — a deadline typed months out, or with the wrong year — at the moment somebody typed it.
- **Seven days, and where the number comes from.** The overlap only has to outlive the longest-lived access token signed with the retiring secret: Supabase's default access-token lifetime is one hour and `auth/clock.ts` grants `EXPIRY_SKEW_TOLERANCE_SECONDS` past `exp` on top, so the functional requirement is hours. The rest is slack for three deploys done by people, possibly across a weekend.
- **The scanner's suffix is written out rather than generalised, and the reason is a measurement.** `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET(_2)?` rather than `_[0-9]+` or a trailing `.*`: the looser forms sweep in `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_2_ACCEPTED_UNTIL`, which is a date an operator must be able to write down, and they break the `ENTITLEMENT_SIGNING_KEY_ID` arm sitting three lines above — a name deliberately not a secret with an arm asserting it passes. Both directions are in the selftest.
- **The selftest's new arms were proved to fire rather than assumed to, and the first attempt at that proof found a hole in them.** Removing the suffix and running the selftest against the copy killed the two refusal arms, as intended. **Generalising it to `.*` killed nothing: 56 passed, 0 failed, exit 0** — a mutant this branch's own arms could not see, in the file whose whole subject is that the widening must not take the deadline with it. The cause is arithmetic rather than judgment. An *extended*-format instant carries colons, and colons are outside the value class, so its longest run is `2026-09-14T00` — thirteen characters, under the sixteen the pattern needs — and `.*` therefore reaches past the name and finds nothing to match. The **basic** ISO format has no separators: `20260914T000000Z` is exactly sixteen, so `.*` reports a date as a credential and `(_2)?` does not. One arm carrying that spelling is the whole difference between the shipped pattern and the over-general one, and it was added rather than the survivor being recorded — `WORKFLOW.md`'s fix-in-branch rule, and the reason a battery is run at all. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample rule: the arms were specific, non-vacuous and on the right line, and the fixture could not reach the property.
- **A test name that collides with three others makes a failure line unreadable.** The obvious name for the YAML-spelling arm was `its lowercase YAML spelling is refused`, which this file already uses three times for three different secrets; the control run above printed two failures under names indistinguishable from the passing ones. Renamed to name its own secret. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s shared-marker rule, arriving in a shell script's report rather than in a scan.
- **Migration 0022's `revoked_at` comment was made true rather than left as a below-the-bar residual.** It said "when this gateway was asked", which PR #215's fix round falsified by refreshing the column on conflict, and review-215 recorded the condition on this ticket: a source-comment edit does not move the migration's content hash while adding SQL does, and 0022 is applied to no environment. That condition still holds — `./scripts/deploy.sh staging` and `production` are stubs that exit 3, no host exists, and the first real remote deploy is owed on SONNY-126 — so both were done. The comment now records why "the most recent ask" is the only meaning available: the prune destroys an expired row, so a re-revoked session may have no first ask left to report.

**Round 1 of PR #218's review, taken in the branch.** Four findings above the bar and six accuracy records, none needing a founder decision, because each one makes the code match a promise it already carried. The three below change behaviour; F4 and the records change prose.

- **F1 — a zero-padded slot passed the guard written to catch it.** `refuseUnreadJwtSecretSlots` compared `Number(match[1])` to the slot number, and `Number("02") === 2`, so `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_02` and `_002` read as "the slot we read" while the Zod schema reads the literal name and nothing else. Set, unread, and unreported — the exact state the refusal's own message says it exists to prevent, reached through the guard for it, and reachable by zero-padding an index in a compose file. The comparison is textual now (`match[1] !== READ_JWT_SECRET_SLOT`, the constant being the string `"2"`), and the existing test's loop carries `_02`, `_002` and `_20`. **The scanner is the second surface and it went the other way: wider, not narrower.** `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET(_2)?` could not see `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET_02=<a real secret>` either, and nothing behind it would — the vendor-prefix list, the JWT shape, the PEM header and the Postgres URL all miss a Supabase project secret. The anchor is `_[0-9]+` now, **deliberately wider than the reader**, because the scanner's question is whether a credential is sitting in the repository and not whether this gateway reads the name. It still cannot reach the deadline beside the slot: after the digits the pattern wants `[=:]` and finds `_`, which is the whole difference from the `.*` the earlier round measured and rejected. Three new selftest arms, and the existing basic-format arm still separates `_[0-9]+` from `.*`.
- **F2 — a gateway holding a dead overlap slot said nothing, anywhere.** The founders' fail-open on a past deadline is untouched and this adds no refusal; what it removes is the silence. Nothing on the configuration path logged, `/v1/health` publishes status, version and environment, and the verifier's loop is the only reader of the list — so that deployment was indistinguishable from one holding no slot at all. `authWiringFrom` now writes one line naming the variable and the instant that passed, and never a value. **The direction that makes it worth a line is not the one the records emphasise**: every sentence about this deadline explains it as a bound on a *retired* secret, but the runbook's step 1 puts the **incoming** secret in the slot, and a past instant there is a typo that disables the secret the rotation is about to depend on. The message names both readings because the design cannot tell them apart. It goes to stderr, the channel `server.ts` already uses for a refused configuration, because this runs between `loadConfig` and `buildApp` and `app.log` is `buildApp`'s; the sink and the instant are parameters so a test drives both rather than a spy on the process.
- **F3 — the deadline parse accepted three spellings its own refusal message promised it refused.** `new Date(until)` with only a `NaN` check: `2026` is the first instant of that year, so a bare year in the past booted clean with the slot never accepted; `Sep 8 2026` parsed; and a **zone-less** spelling is read in the process's local zone, so one string means a different instant on a host west of UTC than east of it — moving the end of a second signing key's life by the host's offset, on the one variable whose entire job is to bound that. An ISO-8601 instant carrying an offset is now the whole of what is accepted, refused with the value because a date is not a secret. **A fourth spelling turned up while closing the three**, and it is the same shape: ECMAScript's ISO parser absorbs a day-of-month overflow, so `2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` is 2 March. The written digits are compared against the parsed fields to catch it — **and the first version of that check was wrong in a way that passed**: it built a `Date` from the written fields with `Date.UTC`, which normalises exactly as the parser does, so both sides rolled and the check reported agreement while `2026-02-30` sailed through. Found by re-running the measurement against `dist/` rather than by reading the code, which is the only reason it is not in the tree. `.env.example`, the README table, the runbook and the checklist all spell the accepted form now.
- **F4 — the runbook did not say that the deadline set at step 1 is a deadline for *doing* step 2.** Every sentence explains the variable as a bound on a retired secret; the table then puts the incoming secret in that slot at step 1, correctly, and nothing reconciled the two. A step-1 deadline that lapses before the dashboard rotation takes the gateway back to one secret, and every token minted after the rotation is refused until step 3 deploys — this ticket's own failure mode, produced by following its runbook. One sentence in the maximum block, and one in the manual-test row.

**Accuracy records, all six.** R1, a sentence carrying one command with two different stated answers, the second false — gone with the carry it justified, and its own paragraph records why that shape keeps arriving. R2, "original 55 tests" where the base ran 57; **half of that finding's derivation does not reproduce and is recorded beside the correction**, since it stated the file has no `it.each` and it has two. R3, `deploy.sh` naming `add_env`, which is defined nowhere — the function is `collect_passthrough` (`grep -c 'add_env' server/scripts/deploy.sh` → 0 after the fix). R4, a checklist row whose "set to anything" fires falsely on an empty value, which is deliberately not a refusal. R5, `config.test.ts`'s second assertion being a shallow copy of the first under a comment naming a property it did not check — the deadline's name is spelled out there now rather than relied on through the fixture, so removing it from `rotating` cannot quietly empty the line again. R6, three different `no-attribution` tallies across three records: **two of the three figures measure the object store and GitHub rather than the tree**, so no SHA can stamp them and each now carries the command and what it counted.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- Nothing mechanically notices an operator who extends the overlap by redeploying with a fresh deadline each week; the bound is on the remaining overlap, as recorded above.
- The three manual-test rows all wait on SONNY-192, because a rotation cannot be exercised without a deployed gateway and a real Supabase project. `deploy.sh local` forwards both names, which is as close as this can be taken today.
- **SONNY-401 is the same overlap one layer away and is deliberately not built here.** There this gateway signs entitlement claims and the Mac verifies, so index 0 is special and `/v1/meta` has to publish the set; here nothing is special about index 0 beyond being tried first. It stays in Backlog, untriaged.

Open questions: none.

Next branch: per the roadmap and the coordinator's routing.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

What it never traverses is the call path. DEADLINE_MS.topUp.total` was on no test's path and pointing it at the `auth` row's fifteen seconds also passed. **Writing the pitfall down did not stop the session repeating it**, which is worth more than either fix: the lesson was filed as a fact about one old test rather than as a question to ask of each new assertion — *does anything make the code take this path?*

That alone does not kill a use-site mutant, so the adapter also mints its deadlines through a `deadlineFactory` seam — `fetchImplementation`'s shape one field up, in the other direction: that seam lets a test assert what was *sent*, this one what was *spent*. The test sums the budgets a whole top-up asks for and compares against the row, so tripling at the use site is 72,000 against 24,000. The route's default is held by a test that drives the route with **no** override under fake timers and advances the route's own timer, asserting it is still waiting at the `auth` row's total and answers at its own.
- **The either/or in the ticket was answerable only as "both", and the arithmetic is what settles it.** A row derived from three attempts is 36 s upstream and wants a total near 42 s, which is longer than the Mac's 40 s client timeout and inverts §12's governing rule — and the client's number is on the app half, which this ticket could not touch. Folding the charge into the existing 10 s row is the other direction and is the money-unsafe one: three calls inside 10 s is about 3.3 s each, `TOPUP_CHARGE_TIMEOUT_MS`'s own derivation argues that even eight is not clearly above a healthy card authorisation, and every second cut converts a slow-but-working charge into an abort recorded `unconfirmed` — granting nothing for money that may have moved. So the third call had to go, and the row had to exist.
- **The wrapper covers `attemptTopUp` and not the two `position()` reads either side of it** (round 1's F4). Round 0's record listed the position read and the re-read among the seven things `total` covers; `routes/credits.ts` awaits one before the wrapper and one after, so the route's worst-case answer is 30 s plus two database round trips, and this gateway sets no statement timeout. In practice those are milliseconds. The enumeration is corrected rather than the wrapper moved — widening it to the whole handler is a behaviour change, and the honest statement is that the bound is on the charge rather than on the handler.
- **The deadline bounds the answer and never the work, and that is a money property rather than an implementation detail.** `withinTotalDeadline` races `attemptTopUp` and does **not** cancel the loser. Cancelling it is the one way this branch could have abandoned an accepted charge — killing the settle after the money moved — which is precisely PR #196's F1. Because the order id is written before anything can charge, the work runs on, settles its row, and the account's next attempt resolves it either way. A1 is the mutant for the opposite mistake, closing the row on a guess, and it dies.
- **The no-op `catch` on the raced promise is defensive, and the reason first recorded for it was false** (round 1's F5). Round 0 wrote that a rejection arriving after the timer decided the race would be unhandled and end the process. It would not: `Promise.race` subscribes to every promise it is handed, so the late rejection is already handled. The reviewer measured it on node v22.23.1 with the line removed — the process survived and an `unhandledRejection` listener saw nothing — against a control in the same harness where a genuinely unhandled rejection was observed and set a non-zero exit. The line stays because it makes the handling explicit where a reader asks the question; what does not stay is a durable record teaching a false fact about `Promise.race` in three places.
- **`504 provider.timeout` is the wrong answer on this route, and §12 already had precedent for saying so.** That code is marked retryable, and at the instant this deadline elapses a charge may be in flight — "try again" is how F1 bought a second pack. The section already records two auth routes that do not answer `504` on their deadline; this is the third, and the contract now says so rather than leaving a reader to infer the table's column applies uniformly.
- **Sharing a deadline is only safe because every exit from the read-back is non-terminal.** An exhausted budget arrives there as a rejected `fetch` and leaves as `unconfirmed`, which keeps the order id on the row. If that path could return `declined` the shared deadline would close orders on a guess — A3 is that mutant, and it dies.
- **The hop resolved §12 minimally, on the coordinator's instruction, because a third branch was queued behind this one.** PR #221 rewrote the same paragraph and PR #223 rewrites it again after this branch, so every line changed here beyond this branch's own is a line #223 has to resolve. PR #221's "Two routes … still deliberately not wired" count and its "three of the four `/v1/account/*` routes remain owed" sentence are left exactly as it wrote them: both stay true once this route is wired, so touching them would have been cost with no content. The round-0 wording that this branch itself had rewritten there — "Both remaining ones are owed and neither is claimed here" — was dropped at the hop for the same reason.
- **`AbortSignal.timeout` does not need its receiver, and the wrapper's stated reason was wrong** (the delta review's N1, taken in the hop). The comment said handing the bare reference around detaches it. On node v22.23.1 `const bare = AbortSignal.timeout; bare(40)` returns a real signal that aborts with a `TimeoutError`, and `bare.call(undefined, 40)` behaves the same — measured with `Map.prototype.get.call(undefined, "k")` as the control that the probe can see a genuine detachment. The arrow stays because it makes both arms of the `??` read as one kind of function; what it is not is a correctness fix. **This is the third record on this branch corrected for the same reason** — after F5's `Promise.race` claim and round 0's constant-pinning test — and all three are the same failure: a mechanism asserted from plausibility rather than measured.

A test that survives a change of direction keeps its assertion and loses its name, and nothing mechanical notices.

Behavior added:

- **All four content-deletion routes run under §12's total deadline**, and a statement that overruns it ends as `504 provider.timeout` with `retryable: true` — the same envelope the model routes send, through the same `sendUpstreamFailure`, rather than a fifth copy of it. §4.6 makes every one of these routes safe to repeat, so the retryable flag is honest.
- **`withDatabaseDeadline` in `model/routing.ts`**, the deadline for work that holds a database connection: the remaining budget is set on the connection before each statement, an exhausted budget is refused without a round trip, a cancelled statement (`57014`) is mapped to `ProviderTimedOut`, transaction control is exempt, and the session-level setting is cleared on the way out.
- **`CONTENT_DELETION_DEADLINE_MS` in `model/limits.ts`**, derived from `DEADLINE_MS.auth` rather than written as a second literal.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):

- **§4.6's three answers, on all three task-scoped routes.** A foreign `task_id` is still `404`, a task with nothing stored is still `200` with a count of zero, and every statement is still scoped by account whatever the ownership read said. The wrapper changes which client object the store functions receive and nothing about what they are asked.
- **`DELETE /v1/account/content`'s `before` bound and its counts.** The query parameter, its `400`, the `account_content` deletion reason and both response fields are untouched.
- **The bulk delete's `tasks_not_found` semantics.** Foreign ids are still skipped and counted rather than failing the batch.
- **The gate's population scan.** `gate.test.ts`'s protected-route list is unchanged in content; only SONNY-134's comment moved to sit above the case it describes, which was PR #207's hop leaving it above the bulk route.
- **Every other route's deadline.** `DEADLINE_MS` is not edited, so the five model rows and the `auth` row keep their literals and `model.test.ts`'s whole-table assertion is untouched — which also keeps this branch's lines clear of SONNY-430's.
- **The idempotency hook.** Not opened; the routes here are `DELETE` and take no claim.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

- **A deadline around work that holds a database connection is never a race that abandons — and the cooperative poll that replaced the race on `DELETE /v1/account` does not transfer here either.** PR #212's F1 rules out `withDeadlines` for all four routes, since every one does its work inside `deps.withConnection`. The obvious next move is the shape that route took, and it would have been decorative: that work is a *loop* of provider calls, so a signal read between calls is a real bound, while every path these four drive in `content/store.ts` — `taskOwnership`, `deleteContentForTask`, `deleteContentForTasks`, `clearScreenshotsForTask`, `deleteContentForAccount`, `deleteStoredResponsesForAccount` — is a fixed sequence of set-based statements with **no loop anywhere**, so the time is spent inside a statement and the gaps between them are where it is not. A poll between statements is a bound that cannot fire on the one failure mode this work has. The bound is Postgres's `statement_timeout` for that reason and not by preference: it is the only instrument that ends a *running* statement, and it ends it rather than abandoning it — the statement is cancelled server-side, the store's own `catch` rolls back, and the connection is healthy when it is released.
- **A per-statement timeout is not a handler deadline, and setting it once would have been §12's number wearing a bound six times its size.** Each of these handlers issues several statements, so the budget is a *deadline* — recomputed and re-set before every statement, with an exhausted one refused before a round trip. The cost is one extra round trip per statement, accepted because these are deletion routes rather than a hot path. **W5 is the mutant that makes this more than an assertion**: repeating `deadline.total` instead of the remainder is killed by two tests.
- **`remaining <= 0` is one character away from no deadline at all, and nothing held it until PR #221's review** (F1). `SET statement_timeout TO 0` is Postgres's spelling of *no timeout*, so under a loosened `< 0` a remainder of exactly zero — reachable whenever `Date.now()` at the guard equals `expiresAt` — would hand the backend a licence to run forever, answer the route's ordinary 200 with §12's promise silently off, and still emit the `RESET`, so none of the four route tests could see it. The reviewer's mutant **survived the whole suite** while six others in the same run died, which is what says the harness could report a kill. The shipped guard was already correct; what was missing was the test, and it is the ticket's own thesis that the bound is a bound. `refuses a remainder of exactly zero…` holds it now on a **frozen clock** — `Date.now` held at one instant with `{ total: 0 }`, deterministic rather than a tiny budget plus a sleep, which would be the wall-clock bet `CLAUDE.md` warns about and would race the mutant instead of catching it. It asserts **both** halves: the `ProviderTimedOut` rejection and an **empty** statement list, because the throw alone cannot separate a refusal from a `TO 0` that failed for some other reason. **W10** is that mutant in this branch's plan, and it comes back `KILLED by 1` — *refuses a remainder of exactly zero, the one value that would set no bound at all*, the test written for it and the only one that catches it.
- **Transaction control is exempt, and that exemption is this ticket's own defect reached through its own fix.** A `ROLLBACK` refused for want of budget leaves the connection in an aborted-transaction state, and `withConnection` hands it straight back to the pool, so the next request's first statement fails with `current transaction is aborted`. **W7** removes the exemption and dies, and PR #221's review added **W7b**, which narrows it to `BEGIN` alone so `COMMIT` and `ROLLBACK` become bounded again — the narrower half of the same property, since W7 deletes the guard outright. It is carried into this branch's own plan rather than quoted from the review, and measured here: `KILLED by 1`, *lets ROLLBACK through unbounded, so a cancelled transaction cannot poison the connection*, the same test that kills W7. **The refusal is the whole of the reason, and a second reason this entry gave is not real**: it also said Postgres might *cancel* a `ROLLBACK` under a one-millisecond remainder, which that review could not reproduce in **300** trials of `BEGIN; SET statement_timeout TO 1; <a statement that is cancelled>; ROLLBACK;` — 300 cancellations of the statement, which is the control, and **0** `current transaction is aborted`. Postgres disables the statement timer before the transaction-completion work, so those statements are not cancellable that way at all. The exemption stands; only the sentence was stronger than its evidence, and `routing.ts`'s own header carries the correction beside the code.
- **PR #208's F2 cannot arise on this file, and that is established by enumeration rather than by not finding it.** `idempotency/hook.ts`'s `preHandler` returns before it claims anything when `request.method !== "POST"`, and all four routes are `DELETE` — so no claim is taken, and none can be completed or released by a timeout. Recorded rather than left as an absence for the next reader to re-derive: if one of these ever became a `POST`, `provider.timeout` is already in that hook's `RELEASE_ON_CODES`, which is a second reason to answer with the shared envelope rather than mint a code.
- **The ticket's acceptance grep answers 2 on this file and both hits are prose, which is the count-is-about-text rule arriving inside an acceptance criterion.** `git grep -c withDeadlines -- server/src/routes/tasks.ts` → `server/src/routes/tasks.ts:2` at `7c94a76e`, and `git grep -n` shows both are comment lines in the header saying these routes deliberately do *not* use that wrapper — the code count is **0**. The criterion's intent is that every route the file registers carries a deadline, and the command that measures it is `git grep -c 'withDatabaseDeadline(' -- server/src/routes/tasks.ts` → **4**, equal to the routes registered (`grep -cE '^  app\.(get|post|delete|put|patch)\(' server/src/routes/tasks.ts` → **4**). **The `(` is the load-bearing anchor and the comment-line stage is not**: dropping the paren and changing nothing else answers **7** (the import line and the two prose lines), while adding a comment-line filter to the pattern as written leaves it at 4. Said that way round because a citation that greps a population its own file belongs to is where a decorative stage reads as a real one.
- **A test whose only failure signal is a hang cannot be counted a mutation kill, and the first version of these four route tests had exactly that shape.** The stalling fake modelled an unbounded statement as one that never returns, so an unwired route failed by reaching the backstop — whose every wording is declared untrusted in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`, correctly, which means the mutant would have come back `UNATTRIBUTED` on a run where the test failed for precisely the right reason (`CLAUDE.md`, SONNY-259). The fake now lets an unbounded statement run to completion, so the route answers its ordinary `200` and the assertion fails on a status. **W1–W4 are each killed by exactly their own route's test**, which is what that change bought.
- **The unit half and the database half each prove something the other cannot, and neither is worth much alone.** `content.test.ts`'s fake is a Postgres that *honours* `statement_timeout`, so the cancellation is caused by the budget the route itself set — a test that handed the route a ready-made `57014` would prove the mapper and stay green against a route that bounded nothing, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample gotcha. What no fake can say is that a real backend would cancel at all, so `content.db.test.ts` blocks a delete on a lock another connection holds and reads back `57014` from the real server, then asserts the connection is still usable. A lock rather than a sleep: nothing there waits on or races anything.

Known limitations / deferred scope:

- **The pool-wide statement timeout is still owed and is SONNY-427's.** What landed is narrower by design — four routes setting a budget for their own work — and the two compose rather than overlap: a pool-level default would sit underneath this and bound the routes that still have nothing, which §12 now names as the three `/v1/account/*` reads.
- **The bound is per statement, so a handler is held to §12's total between statements and at each one, not below it.** A single statement issued with the whole remaining budget can still use all of it, which is the correct reading of §12's row rather than a gap.
- **§12's total does not bound `COMMIT` time, so the worst case is the total *plus* the commit** (PR #221's review). Transaction control is exempt by design, and the measurement says Postgres would not have bounded it anyway: with `statement_timeout = 500`, a `COMMIT` whose deferred constraint trigger slept three seconds took **3058 ms** and committed. On a hosted Postgres with synchronous replication that tail is not always negligible. The exemption is still right — a bounded `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` is how a poisoned connection reaches the pool — and this is the limitation stated beside the per-statement one rather than a defect to fix here.
- **`DELETE /v1/account/content` is two units and a cancel between them costs the audit row, which is SONNY-436's** (PR #221's F2). `deleteStoredResponsesForAccount` is a bare `UPDATE` that commits on its own; `deleteContentForAccount` then opens its own transaction. A cancel in between leaves N response bodies deleted with no `sonny.content_deletion` row for them, and the retry the 504 invites finds nothing left to clear and records `stored_responses_deleted: 0`. **No user content is lost and nothing is left undeleted** — §4.6's repeat-safety holds and the `retryable: true` is honest — and nothing on the Mac decodes that field. What degrades is the record §10.3 makes load-bearing. **The shape is pre-existing and newly reachable**: the two units were never one transaction, and before this branch only a genuine error could land between them, where this adds a designed abort point. Making it atomic moves the stored-response clear inside the content transaction and changes the account-close path too, which is more than a fix round carries; filed rather than half-made.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the coordinator's wave order.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The per-period bound on automatic top-ups** (`claimTopUpAttempt`, `server/src/credit/topup.ts`) — untouched, and re-measured rather than assumed: 400 of 400 boundary races under load ended inside the bound.
- **The other 25 tests in `topup.db.test.ts`** — the sequential bound, the per-period `attempt_no` restart, 0019's granted-is-exactly-the-credited constraint, the settle path and the allowance read — all unchanged and all passing in the same 27.
- **The whole server suite**, 1289 with a database, one more than `main`'s 1288 and that one the test this branch adds.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Dispatching two database statements at once does not make them contend, and a test that assumes it does is testing the scheduler.** The arm read `Promise.allSettled([claim(a), claim(b)])` and asserted that exactly one won. `claimTopUpAttempt` numbers its row `coalesce(max(attempt_no), 0) + 1` over its own snapshot, so the two contend only while neither snapshot holds the other's row — and under three concurrent database suites the two Postgres backends sometimes serialise, the second numbering itself the *next* slot rather than the same one, both succeeding, and the assertion failing on a run where nothing is wrong. **The measurement, taken at `061a2c36` — `main`'s own head, worktree clean, before a line of this branch existed** (`git merge-base --is-ancestor 061a2c36 HEAD` exits 0, read with nothing between the command and `$?`), so no cross-head proof is owed for it at all. **One is worth recording as declined rather than silently dropped:** this lane's kickoff offered `git rev-parse 684dd3f6:server 061a2c36:server` as the baseline check, and it does print `e6d9a7a31aad8c6a773257ecc1a0526a62d059ad` twice at exit 0 — but `git merge-base --is-ancestor 684dd3f6 origin/main` exits **1**, and `684dd3f6` is one of the eight orphans the `fix/a-signed-out-token-stops-working-and-a-secret-can-rotate` entry lists by name — named by branch rather than by position, because this branch's rebase put PR #217's entry between the two, kept there deliberately as a comparison operand rather than a citation. It resolves on this Mac because every worktree shares one object store and nowhere else, so the check was true and not reproducible. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s ancestry rule arriving through an instruction that asked for the proof: **8 non-single outcomes in 3400 races** of the shipped statement driven from a scratchpad probe, and **3 in 3300 races** of the test's own assertions run inside vitest. **Every one of the eleven is the same shape** — `claimed=2 rows=2 attempt_nos=[1,2] distinct=2`, with the two `topup_id`s in the table equal to the two ids the two claims returned. So it is two rows rather than one row read twice, no slot was ever claimed twice, and the unique index was not violated because it was never reached. Unloaded, 20 of 20 gave exactly one claim, which reproduces PR #196's reviewer's 40 of 40 — the measurement the assertion was written on, correct then and about an idle machine.

**Not a money defect, and the zero that says so carries a control that fires.** The racing arm runs at `maxPerPeriod: 10`, where two winners take slots 1 and 2 and cost nobody anything, so it could not have shown an over-charge either way. Measured separately at the boundary — the period seeded to `maxPerPeriod - 1` and two claims contending for the *last* slot — **400 of 400** stayed inside the bound at `attempt_nos=[1,2,3]`, over-bound 0 and duplicate-slot 0. The same probe with `DROP INDEX sonny.credit_topup_attempt_idx` answers **99 of 100** over-bound at `rows=4 attempt_nos=[1,2,3,3]`: four charges in a period bounded at three. The probe can see a slot claimed twice; against the shipped schema it never does.

**The fix builds the contention instead of hoping for it, and nothing in it waits on a clock.** `twoClaimsForOneSlot` pins the contender's snapshot in a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction opened before the holder's row is committed. That is the same state READ COMMITTED concurrency produces — a statement numbering itself from a snapshot that does not contain a row already in the index — and it produces it every time: 300 of 300 for each caller under the same three-suite load, against 100 of 100 two-claim outcomes once the index is dropped, and 13 of 13 clean runs of the file itself at a one-minute load average of 49.9. **No poll and no lock-wait, deliberately.** The faithful alternative — hold the holder's transaction open, let the contender block on the index, and wait for `pg_locks` to publish that it is blocked — is a genuine signal and was rejected for what it does under a mutant: the mutant this test most needs to kill removes the index, the contender then never blocks, and the wait reaches `HangBackstop` instead of an assertion. `CLAUDE.md`'s SONNY-259 rule is that a test whose only failure signal is a backstop timeout can never be counted a kill, every one of that construct's wordings being declared. A construction that fails as an assertion is worth more than one that fails as a wait.

**A rolled-back contender is a probe that cannot fire, and this was measured in the wrong shape first.** The contender's transaction is committed rather than rolled back. Rolled back it leaves no row behind, so the index-dropped control reads back `rows=1 attempt_nos=[1]` — one correct row, under a schema with no unique index at all — and every assertion passes. It ran that way for one arm of the measurement and reported exactly that. This is `CLAUDE.md`'s clean-zero family reaching the *control* rather than the query: the control has to be shown able to produce the failing answer, and a cleanup step is enough to stop it.

**`undefined` means two different things, and the test that could not tell them apart passed under a tree where its own sentence was false.** `claimTopUpAttempt` answers `undefined` for the unique violation it caught and for a `HAVING` that refused to produce a row. **The first battery is what found it**: R3, the mutant that unpins the contender's snapshot, was `KILLED by 1 test(s)` — the open-period caller — and *not* by the boundary caller, whose whole sentence is that at the boundary the index rather than the numbering holds the bound. Unpinned, its contender numbers itself past the last slot, the bound refuses it, and `undefined` comes back looking identical. Postgres separates them: a unique violation leaves the transaction aborted so the next statement fails with `25P02`, while a `HAVING` refusal leaves it live. Both callers assert which refusal they got, and R3 is `KILLED by 2` at `a5235e6c`. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample rule — the assertion was specific, non-vacuous and on exactly the right line, and it could not reach the property.

**Mutation battery: 3 mutants, 3 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed, at `a5235e6c`**, baseline `PASSED 1289 passed (1289)`. One per property rather than one per changed file, and two of the three are in code this branch does not touch, because the property is the store's and the diff is a test: **R1** the per-period unique index is no longer unique (killed by both contention tests); **R2** the unique violation escapes as a fault instead of a full period (both); **R3** the contender's snapshot is no longer pinned (both). The whole plan was re-run after the second commit rather than scoped, because that commit edits the file all three killers live in — `WORKFLOW.md` step 5's second condition — and one verdict moved: R3, 1 → 2. **Across the rebase the three verdicts are carried, checked per mutant against step 5's four conditions rather than per round against the diff**: the merged range is PR #217 alone, `git diff --name-only 061a2c36 0aa5691f` naming `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/LocalStorageSecurityTests.swift` and this changelog, so no mutant's target file moved (0019's migration, `credit/topup.ts`, `topup.db.test.ts`), the killing tests' file did not move, no killer scans a population that range changed, and no killer drives a helper or fixture it changed. All four hold for all three.

**A fresh sighting of SONNY-381, recorded because a battery this small could have rested on it.** The first run's R1 came back `KILLED by 3 test(s)`, the third being `test/pool.db.test.ts > pooledConnections against a real Postgres > gives each caller a connection nobody else is using` — the flake SONNY-212's lane filed for manufacturing a kill on an unrelated mutant. R1 had two plausible killers of its own so nothing rested on it, and it did not fire in the re-run. Posted to SONNY-381 as a second observation.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the boundary test's `maxPerPeriod` is 3 rather than a production number, which is the same choice the file's other bound tests make — every allowance number in this system is an environment variable by design (`CREDIT_PLANS`, SONNY-212), so a test naming a real one would be asserting a deployment's configuration.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

- **The literal and the population assertion guard opposite directions, and keeping both is the decision the ticket left open.** SONNY-432 offered replacing `#expect(fileURLs.count == 13)` with a count against `LocalStore.allCases.count`, and said the literal's own recorded reasoning had to be argued against rather than preferred away. It is not replaced. The two fail on disjoint mutations, which the battery measured rather than the prose asserting: **W2** — the store built and written but dropped from the returned list — is caught by the literal, by both deletion counts *and* by the new set comparison, four recorded issues; **W3** — the fixture writing `pending-server-deletion.json`, fourteen files at fourteen URLs, fourteen deleted and none missing — is caught by the set comparison **alone**, one recorded issue, every other assertion in that test passing. A count against `LocalStore.allCases.count` would have passed W3 exactly as the literal did. And the literal covers what the set cannot: being population-relative, the comparison is satisfied by a fixture and an app narrowed *together*, which is the same blind spot `theEveryStoreWipeReachesExactlyTheClassifiedStores` records one screen up.
- **A set rather than a count, because a count says only that the sizes differ.** W3's failure prints both populations, so the message carries `pending-server-deletion.json` against `pending-server-deletions.json` and the reader is told which store, not merely that one is missing. That is the whole reason the assertion is a set, and W3 is the measurement that makes the claim more than a preference.
- **`CLAUDE.md` lists the behavioural fixture among the things a new store owes, "each enforced by a test that fails until it is done", and for this one item that was not true.** At `061a2c36` the helper constructed **13** stores (`git show 061a2c36:Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/LocalStorageSecurityTests.swift | sed -n '/^private func createAllLocalStoreFiles/,/^}/p' | grep -cE 'let [a-zA-Z]+ = [A-Z][A-Za-z]*Store\('`) against **14** `LocalStore` cases (`git show 061a2c36:Sources/MacAgentCore/LocalStoreClassification.swift | awk '/^public enum LocalStore: CaseIterable/,/^}/' | grep -cE '^    case '`), and the helper named the population **0** times (the same `sed` range, `grep -c 'LocalStore.allCases'`) — so nothing there could fail, and the suite was green. At `00895c50` those three answer **14**, **14** and **1** (that last with comment lines dropped, `grep -vE '^ *//'` before the count; without that stage it answers **3**, which is the control saying the stage rather than the pattern is what excludes this branch's own prose about it). **This branch audited none of the other five items on that list and claims nothing about them** — the enumerate-before-you-subtract rule cuts both ways, and "the only one of the six that was unenforced" is a claim nobody here measured.
- **The guard sits in the helper rather than in the calling test, at the point the population is produced.** There is one caller today (`git grep -c 'try createAllLocalStoreFiles' -- Tests` → `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/LocalStorageSecurityTests.swift:1` at `00895c50`), so the two placements are equivalent in effect right now and are not equivalent later: the property being asserted is the helper's own contract, and a second caller inherits it for free where a test-local assertion would not. A `#expect` inside a non-`@Test` helper is attributed to the running test, which is how all three verdicts name `localDataDeletionServiceRemovesAllStoreFilesAndToleratesMissingFiles()` and is the file's existing idiom.
- **The second assertion, that every returned URL exists on disk, is the half a list of URLs cannot carry — and it is the half SONNY-154 was actually about.** `LocalDataDeletionService`'s own list named `vision-sessions.json` correctly the whole time the fixture was failing to write it, so "the fixture returns the right names" would have been true and useless then. **W1** is the mutant for it: the store constructed and returned but never enqueued, caught by that assertion and by the deletion-result count, and by neither the literal nor the set comparison. It is why the helper's comments have said "created *and written to*" since SONNY-210 and why that sentence now has a test behind it.
- **The fixture writes at its own fixed instant, and the reason it is safe here is not the reason it was unsafe one line above.** `enqueue`'s `deletedAt` defaults to `Date()`; the fixture passes `.fixture` so the file's bytes do not depend on when the suite runs. `resumableTaskStore` directly above needs the opposite care for the opposite reason — its store drops records past an idle period on read, so a fixed instant in the past would make `save`'s own reload discard what it just wrote. `PendingServerDeletionStore` ages nothing out; `capped` trims only above `maxItems`, so the past instant is inert here. Two adjacent stores, two opposite hazards, and the store's own code is what decides which.

**Mutation battery: 10 mutants, 10 killed, stamped at `baaf0275` under the same proof** — one per property the ticket claims rather than one per changed file. D1 the gate never consults the denylist; D2 the sign-out records nothing; D3 the row is kept only to `exp`; D4 the prune drops every row rather than the expired ones; D5 a second sign-out shortens the window a longer-lived token had earned; D6 the sign-out route is not exempt; D7 a malformed `session_id` reads as an absent one; D8 the row is written only after the provider accepts; D9 the exemption is read for every route; and, added by the fix round, **D10** `revoked_at` is not refreshed on conflict. Killers by name are in SONNY-237's closing comment and its fix-round addendum.

**The first round left D4 alive, and the test that could not see it is the one whose name says it does.** `prunes a row whose token has expired, and only that row` plants one dead row, signs one live session out, and asserts what survived — which a prune widened to *every* row satisfies exactly, because the row it planted was the row meant to go. What separates the two is a **live row belonging to another session**: under the widened boundary, signing one user out un-revokes every other signed-out session in the system, which is this ticket's own defect arriving through its fix. The landing test signs two sessions of one user out in turn and asserts both rows present and both tokens still refused. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample rule — the assertion was specific, non-vacuous and on the right line, and the fixture could not reach the property.

**The whole plan was re-run rather than scoped to D4, and the re-run is what says why.** The round's edit is a test file, and `denylist.db.test.ts` is the killing test file of six of the nine — `WORKFLOW.md` step 5's second condition, which "what I just changed" does not see. Three verdicts moved: **D1 6 → 7, D2 8 → 9, D9 9 → 10**, the new test joining each. A scoped re-run would have touched none of them and left three stale numbers reading exactly as clean as the true ones.

Behavior added:
- **A sign-out stops the access token it was made with.** `POST /v1/auth/signout` records the token's `session_id` in `sonny.revoked_provider_session`, and every authenticated route then answers `401 auth.token_revoked` — §7.2's existing meaning, "clears the Keychain entry, opens sign-in". No wire code was added and none changed meaning.
- A row is kept until the token would have expired anyway and pruned by the next write (founder decision 2026-08-30), where "expired" is `exp` **plus** `EXPIRY_SKEW_TOLERANCE_SECONDS`.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The same user's other sessions are untouched.** The adapter asks Supabase for `?scope=local` precisely so signing out on one Mac does not sign out another, and a denylist keyed per session is what keeps the gateway agreeing with it.
- **`POST /v1/auth/signout` still answers `204` when the provider rejects the token, `502` when it cannot be reached and `504` when it times out**, and is still idempotent — the route is exempt from the consult, so the second call is not refused by the first call's own row.
- A token carrying no `session_id` is served exactly as before; the route logs that it could deny nothing.
- Every existing auth outcome is unchanged: `refresh`'s `401 auth.token_revoked` on a rotated-away token, `email/verify`'s three 400s, `email/start`'s uniform `200`, and `DELETE /v1/account`'s `204` and its cooperative drain deadline.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

- **A local verifier cannot un-issue a token and can still stop honouring one, and the difference is where the ticket's whole design sits.** SONNY-203's residual was written as a consequence of local verification, which reads as "nothing can be done short of asking the provider". Asking the provider is not the only way to learn a session is over: this gateway is *told*, by the sign-out request it serves. What the residual actually cost was a table.
- **The exemption for the sign-out route is a correctness requirement, and leaving it out is worse than the defect.** The row is written before the provider call, so without `DENYLIST_EXEMPT_ROUTES` a §9.3 retry of a sign-out the provider answered `502` to meets the record its own first attempt wrote, is refused `401` at the gate, and **the provider-side revocation becomes unreachable by anyone** — the local half succeeding closes the only path to the remote half. It is reachable on the first provider blip. D6 is the mutant, and two of its four killers are pre-existing `auth.db.test.ts` tests, which is the shape of the regression: the exemption is what kept them green.
- **The claim's absence is a real shape and the provider itself handles it, which is why refusing it would have been wrong and reading a *malformed* one as absent would also have been wrong.** GoTrue declares `session_id` `omitempty`; `internal/api/logout.go:52` logs `"user has an empty session_id claim"` and then falls through to `models.Logout(tx, u.ID)` — a **global** logout whatever scope was asked for. So absent is served and undenylistable, and present-but-not-a-uuid is a refusal, because treating it as absent would make the token silently undenylistable, which is the one property the mechanism provides. That is D7.
- **The provider fact the ticket said to verify was verified against published source rather than a project, and the method is `auth/supabase.ts`'s own.** No Supabase project exists to point at. Read 2026-09-06 at `supabase/auth` master `0907af9bd6be3c76f472c40a7dcc0dc34abeffaf`: `internal/tokens/service.go:88` declares `SessionId` inside `AccessTokenClaims`, `:726` sets it on every token that service mints, and `internal/api/token.go:311` reads it back with `uuid.FromString`, which is where the column type comes from. Dated rather than pinned, because it is somebody else's file — the same convention that file's 43-path count uses.
- **The same three lines were described wrongly twice, and the second time is the one worth reading.** The prune and the upsert touch one row in one statement. The first version carried an `AND session_id <> $1` to sidestep an interaction — `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` refusing a tuple the same command already modified — that does not arise; the condition changed no answer and was deleted, for the reason `token.ts` gives for deleting its unreachable `4n+1` guard. **The replacement then asserted the opposite mechanism, equally unmeasured, and it was false** (PR #215's F2): what happens is the `ON CONFLICT` arm running **on the tuple the prune matched**, not a fresh insert. Measured on Postgres 17.11 with the statement lifted out of `denylist.ts` rather than retyped and `revoked_at` as the discriminator, because `DO UPDATE` sets only the columns it names: no pre-existing row → stamped today; an expired row belonging to a **different** session → stamped today, which is the control saying the prune really does delete; an expired row belonging to **this** session → the planted timestamp. Both controls fire. **The outcome was right under either mechanism** — one row, the later expiry, no error — which is exactly why a wrong sentence survived a battery and a review round. The cost is the one the deleted guard was cited for, arriving in prose instead of in code: the sentence is what somebody reasons from when they next change the statement.
- **Eleven test files held a byte-identical fake of the gate's one database read, and the duplication was survivable until the gate grew a second one.** Each answered `accountForSupabaseUser` and threw on anything else, which is the right shape — an unexpected query fails loudly rather than returning a plausible row. Adding the consult turned all eleven into `unexpected query` at once. The fake is `test/support/connection.ts` now; the loudness is preserved and is why `where` is a required argument rather than a defaulted one.
- **One fixed `session_id` literal in the test token minter would have been a shared-state hazard rather than a detail.** Signing one user out records that id, so a single literal denies every *other* user's token in the same file. `support/tokens.ts` derives one id per Supabase user; and because the table references the account tree nowhere, a `TRUNCATE … CASCADE` on `sonny.account` does not reach it — the two suites that sign out truncate it by name, and without that line `auth.db.test.ts` failed with 401s and two sixty-second hangs naming nothing. The hangs are the shape to recognise: a test waiting on a deadline timer the gate had already refused the request before reaching.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **SONNY-238 is not started.** `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` is still a single value, `server/src/config.ts` and `server/scripts/check-secrets.sh` are untouched, and nothing here half-builds it. Its closing state is on SONNY-237's stop-and-report comment.
- **A token with no `session_id` claim keeps the old window** — its own `exp` plus thirty seconds. Nothing this gateway holds can key on it.
- **The row covers the tokens this gateway has been shown.** `session_id` survives a refresh, so `GREATEST` keeps the latest expiry across sign-outs; a client that signed out with a stale token while holding a fresher one would leave the fresher one working to its own `exp`. In practice the presented token is the newest, because refreshing is what produces a newer one.
- **The consult is a second statement on every authenticated request** whose token carries a session claim — one extra round trip on the connection attribution was going to lease anyway, a primary-key lookup on a table bounded by one token lifetime's sign-outs. Not measured under load; no host exists to measure on.
- **Nothing prunes when nobody signs out.** The prune rides on the write, so expired rows linger until the next sign-out. They change no answer — a token whose row is past `expires_at` is refused by `verifyAccessToken` first — and the table cannot grow without sign-outs to grow it.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

**The fix round after PR #215's review (2026-09-06).** Five findings, none of them a live product defect, and the
first is the one worth reading twice.

- **F1 — a set that could be widened to anything, and the asymmetry that made it visible.**
  `DENYLIST_EXEMPT_ROUTES` is the one door through which a token this gateway has been told to stop honouring is
  still served, and nothing in the suite said which routes it holds. The reviewer measured it rather than arguing
  it: a mutant adding `DELETE /v1/account/content` and `DELETE /v1/tasks` — which would let a signed-out token
  delete every task the account has ever stored — **survived all 1283 tests**, while the same widening applied to
  `PUBLIC_ROUTES`, the sibling set one screen up, was **killed by nine**. One set was pinned by value and the other
  was described only in prose, and the prose was this branch's own docstring saying "one route". **The second half
  of the finding is where the pin had to go**: every test that held the exemption's behaviour was database-gated,
  so the documented `npm test` — 445 skipped — said nothing about it at all. The pin is a value table in
  `denylist.test.ts`, which opens no socket, for the reason `theWipesOwnSentenceNamesEveryStoreItDeletes` is one in
  the Swift half: a containment check sees a missing entry and never an extra one, and an extra one is the whole
  risk. Re-run against it under the documented command, stamped at `baaf0275`, baseline `PASSED 843 passed | 445 skipped
  (1288)`: **W1 KILLED by 1** — *is exactly the sign-out route, and nothing else* — and the control **W2 KILLED by
  2**, `gate.test.ts`'s two population scans. W2's count is 2 here against the reviewer's 9 because the reviewer ran
  it with a database and the seven `content.db.test.ts` killers are skipped without one; the mutant and the coverage
  are the same, the suite is not.
- **F2 — the same three lines described wrongly twice, and the second description is the one that earned a round.**
  The replacement comment this branch shipped one round earlier asserted that the prune's `DELETE` is what the
  arbiter sees, so the upsert proceeds as a plain insert. It is the other way round: the `ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE`
  arm runs **on the tuple the prune matched**. Measured on Postgres 17.11 with the statement lifted out of
  `denylist.ts` rather than retyped, using `revoked_at` as the discriminator because `DO UPDATE` sets only the
  columns it names — no pre-existing row → stamped today; an expired row for a **different** session → stamped
  today, the control saying the prune really does delete; an expired row for **this** session → the planted
  timestamp. **Behaviour was right under either mechanism** — one row, the later expiry, no error — which is why a
  battery, a review and a coordinator's verification all passed over a false sentence. **And the test named as
  keeping it measured could not see it**: `re-revokes a session whose own row has already expired` asserted one row
  with a future `expires_at`, true either way. It reads `revoked_at` back now, which is the one assertion that
  separates the two, and `D10` is the mutant that proves it — removing the refresh, **KILLED by 1**, by that test
  alone. This is `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample rule for the second time on this branch, after D4 one round earlier.
- **`revoked_at` is refreshed on conflict, and the storage decided it rather than taste.** Migration 0022 calls the
  column the thing that makes a support question answerable at all, so it has to mean one thing on every path.
  "The first time this gateway was asked" cannot be that thing: the prune destroys the row, so a session re-revoked
  after some other user's sign-out pruned it has no first ask left, and the column would silently mean "the first
  ask, or a later one, depending on traffic nobody involved can see". "The most recent ask" is reachable on every
  path, and it keeps one row internally consistent — `expires_at` already describes the latest token the session was
  signed out with.
- **F3 — a fake whose promise to be loud had quietly stopped applying to the newest statement.**
  `signedInConnectionTo` answers the auth path's statements for eleven suites that are not about the gate, and its
  whole value is that a statement it has never heard of throws instead of returning an empty result set.
  `revokeProviderSession` opens with `WITH pruned AS (DELETE FROM sonny.revoked_provider_session …)`, so a dispatch
  keyed on the table name matched the **write** on the consult's branch. Nothing any suite asserted was wrong; the
  loudness was gone, for exactly the statement this branch added, and only a test of the fake itself could notice.
  The write has its own branch, tested first because its own text contains the consult's table name, and three arms
  drive the real statements through the fake with a control that throws. **What those arms cannot see is stated
  where they live**: both branches answer `{rows: []}`, so they would pass under the pre-fix dispatch too — what the
  separate branch buys is that the write is *declared*, so a later change to either answer can no longer silently
  apply to the other.
- **F4 — a count of 27 beside a command answering 28.** Writing this entry put the changelog into the population its
  own citation counts, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s ninth write-the-command defect reached through a `git diff` rather
  than a `git grep`. The enumerated list was right and complete at 27; the numeral and the command disagreed with
  each other. The command excludes the citing file now and the bare form is quoted beside it as the control.
- **F5 — an option with no caller**, deleted for the reason this branch had already given one commit earlier for
  deleting a condition that could not change an answer.
- **And this round shipped the defect the rule it was fixing exists to catch, which is recorded rather than
  quietly corrected.** The F4 sentence went into the tree carrying `<FIXSHA>` where the fix round's commit belongs,
  and was committed that way — SONNY-210's exact failure, a template left unfilled inside the very sentence
  demonstrating the rule. Filled in the docs commit above; it is written down because the count of times this has
  happened is the only thing that makes the next session check.

**Six things the review recorded below the bar and left, two of them corrected here anyway.** Corrected: the
