### Branch: feature/readiness-tells-the-whole-truth
Status: complete — SONNY-232 and SONNY-336 both done, in the coordinator's order smallest-first; one fix round after PR #216's cycle 1, three record corrections after its cycle 2, then the hop onto `main` at `4dcdd675`
Date: 2026-09-06 (fix round 2026-09-06; record corrections and hop 2026-09-07)
Tickets: **SONNY-232** (a scheduled run's recent-artifacts write failure reached no surface at all — no notice, no error, nothing) and **SONNY-336** (the Settings account row reported whether a session was held and said nothing whatever about entitlement, which SONNY-136 left deliberately unbuilt rather than approximate). One session, from `main` at `35519b50`, rebased onto `main` at `4dcdd675` two merges later (PRs #213 and #214) as the one hop `WORKFLOW.md` step 3 allows at merge time.
Reviewed by: **fresh-session review of PR #216 at `93a993ee`, one cycle — four findings, none a correctness defect.** Both tickets' behaviour held under every attack, including the reviewer's own five-mutant replay (5 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed at `93a993ee`), and every figure the branch reported was re-measured and matched. **F1** was a test-integrity claim that was wrong; **F2** a record claim that was wrong and pointed at an undocumented behaviour change; **F3** and **F4** were defects in the manual-test rows the founders work from. All four were taken in one fix round, written up at the end of this entry. Three residuals below the bar were recorded; **one** of them is closed here and the other two are left with their reasons. **Cycle 2 held all four and returned merge-ready**, verifying two of them by re-running the lane's own probes rather than reading its account of them — the guard's four readings and the immutable-file lever, both reproducing to the character — and measured that nothing the round changed reaches beyond the findings: `Sources/` moved by twelve lines, every one of them a `///`. It recorded four more notes below the bar, three of them in the round's own new text, and those three are corrected in the hop below rather than left.

Spec sections covered: §16.3 (a readiness row stays a presence check — `EntitlementService.claimConfirmation()` answers from a cached signed claim, does not block and cannot block on a request, which is what makes it admissible here at all); row 12's entitlement surface, and row 18's boundary (SONNY-23) left exactly where it was — this branch names no capability key.

**This branch gives the readiness page a new origin of network traffic, and the sentence above used to deny it** (PR #216's review, F2). It read *"a readiness row stays a presence check and asks nothing of the network"*. The second half of that was true and the first did not follow from it: `claimConfirmation()` runs `evaluate(capability: nil)`, and `evaluate` calls `startRefresh()` on **five** paths — `awk 'NR>=116 && NR<=201' Sources/MacAgentCore/EntitlementService.swift | grep -cE '^ *startRefresh\(\)'` → 5 at `93a993ee`, against a whole-file control of 9. Four are refusals; **the fifth is on the confirmed path**, at `EntitlementService.swift:165`, gated on `EntitlementJudgement.shouldRefresh`, which `EntitlementDecision.swift:110-114` defines as a third of the claim's life elapsed. `startRefresh()` is a real `refreshNow()` against the gateway, single-flighted and never awaited. So opening Settings → Permission Readiness — or any Command Center `onAppear`, the Refresh button, or `sessionDidChange` — now starts a request on a normally signed-in Mac more often than not, where `refreshPermissions()` started none before this branch. **The behaviour is right and was not the defect**: PR #152's F2 is why those refusals refresh at all, and the moment a user looks at the readiness page is a good moment to freshen a stale claim. Nothing blocks, nothing is awaited, and the row's answer is still the cached claim's, so the row is still a presence check and §16.3 still holds. What was wrong was the record — a negative established from one path, the return value, without enumerating what the call *does*, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s enumerate-before-you-subtract rule from the inside.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Entitlement has exactly one source on this Mac, and the readiness row's whole design is the consequence.** `EntitlementService.claimConfirmation()` is the narrowest door that service has: it answers whether this Mac holds a current, verifiable claim about its own session, and hands back no claim, no capability list and no plan. `decision(for:)` is the other door and it is the wrong one here, for a reason that is structural rather than stylistic — it takes an `EntitlementCapability`, no capability key exists anywhere under `Sources/`, and row 18 (SONNY-23) owns which capabilities gate what, so a row wired to it would have had to mint one and take row 18's decision inside row 12's ticket. That is the second notion of entitlement SONNY-136 stopped rather than build, and it would have arrived not as a wrong answer but as an invented question. `mainJoinsTheReadinessRowToTheOneEntitlementSource` pins `claimConfirmation()` and forbids `decision(for:` in the wiring, because both compile.

**A second published value rather than a fourth enum case, and the reason is that the two readings can disagree.** SONNY-336's own description flagged the choice and this is the answer: the session is read from `SonnyBackendClient`'s Keychain and the claim from the `EntitlementService` actor, at different moments. A single enum would have to pick one reading to believe and would have no way to say what the other one answered. Two values let the row report each honestly — and the disagreement is reachable rather than theoretical, so `planSentence(for:)` answers `.notSignedIn` by name instead of defaulting it, even though `claimConfirmation()` cannot produce that case on a branch the row only reaches when a session is held.

**One row for two readings, and the alternative is worse in a way that is easy to miss.** A second "Sonny plan" row would say "sign in" twice on a signed-out Mac, because `notSignedIn` is one of the refusals `claimConfirmation()` itself returns — two rows, one problem, two sentences. So the plan is consulted only once a session is held, and the row count stays pinned at eight by a test that already existed.

**`.ready` needs both halves known-good — an existing row's state changed, deliberately.** `ModelAccessReadiness.undetermined`'s own doc comment states the rule for the session half: a check that could not be completed is not a check that passed. Applying it to the plan half means a signed-in Mac whose claim cannot be confirmed no longer reads `Ready`, which is a real change to a row that shipped. It is the ticket's point: the row was reporting readiness while silent about half of what readiness means.

**What the plan half never does is push the row to `Needs action`, and that is the product call SONNY-336 asked for rather than a wiring one.** No capability is gated anywhere in this repository today, so an unconfirmed plan blocks nothing a user is trying to do, and a red row demanding action on something that is not stopping them is the one lie a readiness page must not tell — it is the exact failure the OpenAI row was deleted for, arriving from the other direction. `Check when used` is the literal truth: Sonny checks the plan at the moment something needs it. The day row 18 gates a capability, one line changes, and `aHeldSessionAloneIsNoLongerEnoughToReportReady` asserts the current rule in both directions so that change has to argue with a test rather than discover the decision.

**The row gets its own sentences and not `EntitlementCopy`'s, which is not a DRY violation but the avoidance of one.** `EntitlementCopy.message(for:)` finishes a *gate's* thought — "Sign in to Sonny to use this.", "This isn't part of your plan." — and a status row has no *this* to refer to. Sharing them would tie a settings row's wording to a refusal dialog's, so the next edit made for gate reasons would silently reword this page. What must not be duplicated is the *answer*, and it is not: three sentences for seven refusals, grouped by what a user can actually do — connect once, fix the clock, or nothing at all — with the grouping asserted as a count so that inventing four more sentences meaning "nothing you can do" fails.

**A `nil` seam that maps to `.undetermined` is why the wiring needs a scan, and the direction of the default is the whole argument.** `entitlementConfirmation` is Optional, and `refreshPlanReadiness()` answers `.undetermined` when it is unset — which is honest, because a build nobody wired has not asked anybody anything, and `.undetermined` is never reported ready, so saying nothing cannot acquire a green row by omission. The cost of that honesty is that **deleting the `main.swift` wiring line compiles and leaves a green suite**, with the row reporting "Sonny checks your plan when it needs it." forever on a Mac whose plan is fine. That is PR #153's F3 in its own words, arriving at the half this branch added, so it gets F3's own instrument: a brace-matched scan of the closure's body rather than a token search, which an empty closure beside a stray mention would satisfy. Mapping `nil` to a *refusal* instead was considered and is the opposite error — it would tell a user Sonny could not check their plan when nothing had tried to.

**A test that hands the mapping a decision never exercises the call that produces one.** Every cheap test here injects an `EntitlementDecision` directly, which leaves `claimConfirmation()` — its store read, its signature check, its clock defence — upstream of every sample, and `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample gotcha is exactly that shape: assertions that are specific, non-vacuous, correct, and about nothing. So one test drives a real `EntitlementService` with a real signed claim, offline, in **both** directions in one run — one claim inside its life and one thirty days past it, same signer, same store, same service — because asserting only the expired direction would pass just as warmly against a service that refuses everything. A second does the forged-key direction with the matched-key control beside it.

**The scheduled bookkeeping gap was an enumeration's blind spot, not an oversight at the call site, and the shape recurs.** `AgentRunner` sets `lastRecentArtifactFailure`; the enumeration that gave the scheduled path's other bookkeeping writes a channel (SONNY-208's rounds) looked at the *view model's* own writes and never saw it. Two of the three `runner.execute` call sites read it and the third did not, and the comment SONNY-209 left at that site said so in plain words for two branches. `CLAUDE.md`'s enumerate-before-you-subtract rule is about the same asymmetry from the other end: the evidence against a negative lives wherever the enumeration did not look, and here the enumeration's boundary was a *type*, not a path.

**A test that proves a bookkeeping write failed needs a run that actually writes something.** `RecentArtifactStore.recordGeneratedArtifacts` records only paths that exist as regular files, so a scheduled routine doing arithmetic never asks the store to write and the store can never throw — a fixture of that shape passes this branch's test with the fix reverted, which is the whole failure mode being tested for. The routine writes a real Markdown draft (`createLocalDraft`, tier 2, so the scheduled path's fixed `.approved(.tier2)` ceiling covers it, and its one escalation to tier 3 fires only when the output already exists, which is why the path is a name inside a directory the test just made), and the whitelist is rooted at that directory so the write cannot reach the real `~/Desktop`. Reverting the fix and re-running fails at the `localStorageNotice` requirement with `nil` — the defect in its own words.

**Two enforced enumerations fired during this branch and both were doing their job.** `ProductShellTests`' stored-property classifier named `planReadiness` and `entitlementConfirmation` as unclassified; `UnprivilegedGateTests`' directory-locking census went 15 → 16 because the new scheduled test locks a directory. Neither is a defect and both are recorded here because a session meeting them for the first time should know they are the guard rather than the problem.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **A delete door is a door onto the server only if it holds the key, and this one never did.** The three controls SONNY-404 routed each remove something filed under §5.1's `task_id`. An unfinished-task record holds no such key: `ResumableTask` stores ten fields and none is a backend id (`awk '/^    private enum CodingKeys/{f=1;next} f&&/^    \}/{exit} f&&/^ +case /{c++} END{print c+0}' Sources/MacAgentCore/ResumableTaskStore.swift` → **10** at `0040d465`; the same command with the block terminator dropped answers **20**, the control showing the terminator is what bounds it), and `git grep -cE 'currentTaskID|backendTaskID|task_id' 0040d465 -- Sources/MacAgentCore/ResumableTaskStore.swift` exits **1** with no output while the same pattern over `Sources/MacAgent/AgentViewModel.swift` answers **16 at `35519b50`** — the control that makes the zero a measurement rather than a pattern that could not match. **The control is stamped at the base rather than at the code head, and that is the correction PR #214's F1 asked for.** It read 16 beside `f682a560`, where the same command answers **18**: the two extra matches are this branch's own new doc comment in the file being used as the control, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s ninth write-the-command defect — a citation greping a population its own file belongs to, inflated silently, and re-running it reproduces the inflation exactly. Of the two repairs the review offered, the base is the one that stays true: `35519b50` is an ancestor of every later head, so nothing this branch or the hop writes can move it, and PR #213's comment edits land in this very file. The zero it controls is unaffected either way and is read at the head of the day, `0040d465` now. **The hop proved the choice rather than merely vindicating it**: `35519b50` is still an ancestor after the rebase (`git merge-base --is-ancestor 35519b50 HEAD` exits 0) while `f682a560` is not (exit 1), so an 18 stamped at that code head would now be a figure beside a commit `main` does not contain.
- **And it could not hold one id even if it wanted to.** `beginNewTaskIdentity()` mints `currentTaskID` afresh on **every continuation of one of these records** — `continueResumableTask` dispatches through `performStart` with `preserveUsageForNextStart` unset — while `beginResumableTask` writes `id: continuing?.id ?? UUID().uuidString` so the record keeps *its own* id across those continuations. (It is not *every dispatch*, which is what this bullet said until PR #214's R1: `performStart` skips the re-mint when that flag is set, and the one site setting it is the voice transcription's completion, never a continuation of an unfinished record.) One record therefore spans as many wire ids as the task had attempts, and anything closing this gap later needs a persisted **list** rather than a field — which is why SONNY-433 says so rather than leaving the shape to be re-derived.
- **The two run shapes rule out queueing for two different reasons, and only one of them is about the door.** A run that **failed** wrote a history row under its wire id and pointed it at the record through `CompletedTaskRecord.resumableTaskID`; this press leaves that row standing, so the server's copy stays reachable through *Delete task* and *Memory › Task history › Delete*, and queueing here would delete the server's copy of a task the user can still open on the Tasks page — the opposite of `PendingServerDeletion.scope`'s own rule that the queue carries what the delete reached on the Mac. A run that was **interrupted** never wrote a row and never will (`ResumableTask.id`'s doc comment says exactly that), so nothing on this Mac names its content and the press has nothing to send. The second shape is a real gap; it is SONNY-433's rather than this door's, because it is there whether or not anyone presses Delete.
- **The defect was a confirmation describing a different control's effect, and no completeness check could see it.** Two controls act on one unfinished task. The widget's × keeps the record — the founders' decision of 2026-08-25, taken so that no control in the widget can lose work irreversibly — and Memory's per-entry Delete is the one that loses it. That Delete's confirmation read *"Sonny stops offering to carry on with this task"*, the ×'s promise word for word, and `everyDestructiveConfirmationAndEmptyStateHasRealWords` passed on it for as long as it stood, asserting only that it was non-empty. That is `theWipesOwnSentenceNamesEveryStoreItDeletes`' lesson arriving somewhere else: a check that asks whether words are present sees a missing one and never a wrong one. The new sentence is pinned by value.
- **The fix says nothing about servers, deliberately.** The standing rule against explanatory copy in the product is the one PR #207's own R5 was swept under, and "the servers keep their copy" in front of a press would be exactly that. What the user is told is what the press does to their work.
- **A "queues nothing" test proves nothing unless the fixture can reach the thing being refused, and this branch shipped that mistake for one commit.** The first version of `theUnfinishedTasksPerEntryDeleteReachesTheServerNotAtAll` wrote a task-history row and an unfinished record with nothing joining them. The only route by which that press could name server content is the reverse join, so M3 — walk the join back, queue a whole-task obligation — would have found nothing to queue and the test would have passed over it: refusing nothing while reading exactly like a test that refuses the thing the ticket is about. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample gotcha, reached from the other side — there the sample skips the mechanism, here the mechanism has no sample to find. The fixture carries the link now and M3 is what proves it.
- **A fixture timestamp that is fine for one store is dropped by the one beside it.** `writeTaskRecord` dates its rows from a fixed instant, which task history keeps forever; `ResumableTaskStore.loadAll` drops a record nobody came back to, so the same instant wrote an unfinished task the view model then never published. The symptom is `resumableTasks` coming back empty, which reads as a publishing bug rather than as the store doing its job. The resumable helper dates from `Date()` and says why.

Known limitations / deferred scope: **SONNY-433**, filed from this branch and untriaged. An *interrupted* run leaves retained content on the gateway under a `task_id` nothing on this Mac records — before the press and after it — so no per-task control can name it and only the whole wipe's account-wide obligation reaches it, otherwise it ages out on the content clock. Not deferred work of this ticket's: this door is neither the cause nor a possible fix, which is the third bullet above.

Open questions: none.

### The fix round, 2026-09-06 — PR #214's two findings and two residuals

**F2 — the guard passed the faithful implementation, and two of the reviewer's mutants proved it.** The entry's own best
pitfall, above, is that a "queues nothing" test proves nothing unless the fixture can reach the thing being refused. That
was half the lesson. The fixture carried the join; nothing kept it there, and it was written in a shape this Mac never
produces.

- **Nothing pinned the link.** No assertion in `theUnfinishedTasksPerEntryDeleteReachesTheServerNotAtAll` mentioned
  `resumableTaskID`, so deleting the argument changed no assertion — the reviewer's **M7**, which SURVIVED at `b342e0af`.
  The recurrence the pitfall warns about had a comment standing against it and nothing else.
- **The linked row was `.completed`, and production never links one.** `writeTaskRecord` hardcoded that status, while the
  row's `resumableTaskID: activeResumableTask?.id` is read *after* `settleResumableTask` has cleared that handle for
  `.completed`, `.canceled`, `.prepared` and `.dryRun` — so only a failed run carries a link. The reviewer's **M8**, which
  is M3's reverse-join queue with `&& $0.outcomeStatus == .failed` and nothing else changed, therefore found nothing to
  queue and SURVIVED, while M3 — the same queue written loosely — was killed. **A guard that refuses the sloppy
  implementation and passes the faithful one is not a guard.**

The fix is what the review proposed: `writeTaskRecord` takes an `outcomeStatus:` parameter defaulting to `.completed` so no
existing call site moves, this test passes `.failed`, and the join *and* the outcome are asserted before the press. **Both
mutants now die by the same test M3 does**, proved with `--only M3,M7,M8` at `f66d40be`: 3 killed, 0 survived, 0
unattributed, each reported `KILLED by 1 test(s)` naming
`theUnfinishedTasksPerEntryDeleteReachesTheServerNotAtAll()`. **That head is orphaned by the hop** and the reading is kept
as the record of when the fix was proved; the verdict that describes the merged tree is the eight-mutant run at
`0040d465` above, where M7 and M8 are killed by that same test.

**This is the same failure this branch already caught once, arriving through the door it had just closed.** The first round
found the unlinked fixture by writing M3 and reasoning about what M3 could reach; it did not go on to ask whether the link
it added was the link production writes, or whether anything would notice if that link went. `CLAUDE.md`'s held-sample
gotcha says a sample entering downstream of the mechanism tests nothing; this is a third direction on it — the sample
reaches the mechanism, in a form the mechanism never emits.

**F1 — a control figure stamped at a head it was never measured at, and this branch's own prose is what moved it.** The
correction is in the first architectural bullet above. It is `CLAUDE.md`'s ninth write-the-command defect, whose most
dangerous property is that re-running the command reproduces the inflated number exactly — so that rule's own remedy
confirms the defect instead of catching it. Repaired by stamping the control at the base rather than at a code head:
`35519b50` is an ancestor of every later head, so nothing this branch or its hop can write will move it, and the hop meets
PR #213's comment edits in that very file. **It landed exactly that way**: PR #213's merge did edit comments in
`AgentViewModel.swift`, and `35519b50` survived the rebase as an ancestor while every branch head this entry had stamped
did not.

**R1 — the wire id is not re-minted at *every* dispatch.** `performStart` skips the mint when `preserveUsageForNextStart`
is set, and the one site setting it true is the voice transcription's completion, for a spoken command and a spoken
clarification answer alike. Neither is a continuation of an unfinished record: `continueResumableTask` dispatches with the
flag unset, so the claim the argument actually needs — every continuation of one of these records mints a new wire id — is
true, and it is what all three sites say now (this entry, `deleteResumableTask`'s doc comment, and the test's).
**The sweep afterwards searched for the OLD wording and needed an emphasis-tolerant pattern to find it**, because the
corrections themselves quote the retired claim as `*every* dispatch`: a plain `git grep 'at every dispatch'` over
`Sources Tests docs CLAUDE.md` matches none of them, which is the markdown-emphasis trap `CLAUDE.md`'s quantified-claim
rule names, met while obeying the rule that produced it.

**R2 — SONNY-433's title is narrower than its body**, which already says "the attempts that left no history row" and so
covers the earlier attempts of a task later continued and failed. Recorded as a dated note on that ticket rather than a
title edit, so its filed identity does not move under anyone who has already read it.

**What this round did not change is any behaviour.** The confirmation's words, `deleteResumableTask`, `declineResumeOffer`
and every store are untouched in effect; the diff is one test-fixture parameter, two test assertions, three doc comments
and this entry.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

- **A default that equals the contract's number is indistinguishable from wiring, and a battery is the only thing that says so.** This is W9 in general form. Two spellings of one value make the code that reads the real one deletable with no observable effect, which no test can see and no review reliably catches — the diff looks like belt and braces. The fix is always the same: delete one spelling and let the type system ask for the other.
- **Only the timeout could be shared, and that is what makes `sendUpstreamFailure` the right call here rather than a fourth copy.** `model/routing.ts` maps all three upstream failures for a model route, and this file cannot use it that way: every one of these routes maps a *rejection* differently — three 400s on `email/verify`, `401 auth.token_revoked` on `refresh`, swallowed on `signout`, a uniform `200` on `email/start`. So one arm is routed through the shared mapper and the rest stay local. PR #208's own lesson was to route through the thing that already decides; the corollary is that it has to be deciding the same question.
- **`routes/auth.ts` imports `ProviderTimedOut` from `model/upstream.ts` while its `ProviderRejected` and `ProviderUnavailable` come from `auth/provider.ts` — two pairs of classes, same two names.** `sendUpstreamFailure` deliberately does not recognise the auth seam's pair and rethrows anything it does not know, so passing it one would reach the root handler as a `500`; it is called only inside an `instanceof ProviderTimedOut` guard for that reason. The module's *name* is now narrower than its role — an auth route importing from `model/` — and moving it is **SONNY-316**'s, which already owns deleting `routes/model.ts`' duplicate copies of both helpers.
- **An abort through the route's signal reads as `502 provider.unavailable`, not `504`, and that is the auth seam's mapping rather than a slip.** `auth/supabase.ts` turns an aborted `fetch` into this seam's `ProviderUnavailable`, which is older than this branch and is what `supabase-provider.test.ts` already pins for its own timeout. The `504` comes only from `withDeadlines`' total-deadline race. Both are retryable under §9.3, on different schedules; the upstream bound fires first for a stalled socket, so the everyday answer for an unreachable provider is unchanged.
- **`vi.useFakeTimers()` cannot be used in this repository's database suites, and the failure is a hang with no output rather than a red test.** Measured on this branch: a version of the three `auth.db.test.ts` deadline tests using `toFake: ["setTimeout", "clearTimeout"]` ran past five minutes printing nothing and had to be killed, twice. `support/backstop.ts` and `pg` are both holding `setTimeout`, and `vi.useRealTimers()` discards whatever they scheduled inside the fake window. The interval is therefore asserted in `authdeadlines.test.ts`, which opens no socket, and the database-backed tests assert the two things a fake cannot forge instead: that the provider was handed an `AbortSignal` at all, which exists only if the wrapper is in front of the call, and what the route answers.
- **`AbortSignal.timeout` is a platform timer that vitest's fake timers do not intercept**, so the duration a signal was built with is not observable from the signal — measured by writing that test and watching `signal.aborted` stay `false` after advancing past the bound. It is why W9's answer is a required parameter rather than a test.
- **§12's row names more routes than this ticket wires, and each exclusion is a different reason.** `GET /v1/health` and `GET /v1/meta` await nothing at all, so a deadline around either is a timer that cannot fire. `DELETE /v1/tasks/{task_id}` is `routes/tasks.ts`, on this lane's never-touch list while PR #207 holds it. **Three** of the four `/v1/account/*` routes wait on the database, and `db/pool.ts` sets a connection timeout and no statement timeout — so bounding those is a change to how every authenticated route reaches Postgres (SONNY-427). **The fourth, `POST /v1/account/credits/top-up`, is not database-bound at all**: it charges at the payment provider with up to three sequential twelve-second calls, so its upstream work can run several times past this row, and bounding it is a wrapper at a call site rather than a pool-wide change. It is **SONNY-430**. All four are in §12 with their reasons rather than left as an absence a later reader reads as an oversight.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **SONNY-237 and SONNY-238 are not started**, and are the remaining two of the lane's three. Nothing in this branch anticipates them: no migration was added, `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` is still a single value, and `server/src/auth/token.ts` and `server/src/config.ts` are untouched. The one thing they inherit is the seam's new optional `signal`, which neither needs.

So the one-line auto-merge in `routes/auth.ts` changed nothing of this branch's, and no resolution diff is owed.
- **What `main` brought into the same file.** PR #207 changed eleven files under `server/`, and the one both sides touched is `routes/auth.ts`: `deleteContentForAccount(client, accountId, storedResponses)` gained a fourth argument, `"account"`, about sixty lines below this branch's deadline block, inside the account close's wipe. Both changes are present at the new head, and `git diff 8fdc68c6 c46cc72a -- server/src/routes/auth.ts` is exactly that one line — the whole of what the rebase added to this file.
- **The changelog was the only real conflict, three times over** — once per docs commit, each side having written at the top of `## Entries`. Every entry is kept and this branch's sits above PR #207's, because only the newest entry may be unmerged and this branch has not merged. `scripts/changelog-order` exits 0 with **184 entries**, read with nothing between the command and `$?`.
- **`CLAUDE.md`'s rebase gotcha was the thing to watch and it did not bite**, which is worth recording with the reason rather than as luck: the conflicted-file list is not the population a merge can break, and `deleteContentForAccount` changing arity is exactly the shape that rule describes — a type's signature moving on one side while the other side adds a caller. This branch added no caller of it, `npm run typecheck` exits 0, and the whole database suite runs against the schema `main` brought.
- **The whole plan was re-run rather than carried, and four of the twelve were re-run past what was owed.** W1, W2, W3, W4, W6 and X1 target `routes/auth.ts`, which moved. X2 and X5 target `revocation.ts`, which the range leaves alone, but their killer drives the account-close handler through `buildApp` into `content/store.ts` and `idempotency/store.ts`, both of which the range changed — step 5's third and fourth conditions, the ones no file-level check sees. **W2 was not on the list the review and the routing gave and is re-run anyway**: its target file is `routes/auth.ts` like the other five, and the rule is per mutant against the four conditions rather than per list. W8, W9, X3 and X4 were licensed to carry with an argument, and were measured instead, because their killers reach `buildApp` too and a carry that has to be argued is worth less than a number.
- **The database suite ran against the schema that now carries migrations 0020 and 0021**, the second of which — *a wipe leaves the account open* — is about the account-close and wipe interaction this branch's handler owns. 1261 passed, exit 0.
- **One failure appeared on the first full database run and did not reproduce**, recorded rather than dropped: `topup.db.test.ts`'s *lets exactly one of two racing claims win the same slot* failed with `claimed` length 2 against an expected 1. That file is touched by neither this branch (`git diff --name-only 8fecd5e8 c46cc72a -- server/test/topup.db.test.ts` prints nothing) nor the merged range (`git diff --name-only d14eba65 8fecd5e8 -- server/test/topup.db.test.ts` prints nothing); it passed **3 of 3** run alone and the full suite passed on re-run. It is a race under whole-suite concurrency in somebody else's file, filed as **SONNY-431** rather than absorbed here.

**The pre-rebase SHAs are orphaned, and they are recorded rather than repointed.** `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` exits **1** for every head this entry cited before the rebase: `cd1000fa`, `aaa6ae3d`, `61587806`, `d3540e46`, `4d8c1371`, `8fdc68c6`, and `d72dc159`. Each still resolves on this Mac, because every worktree shares one object store, and each names a real tree — which is exactly why they are listed: a stamp that resolves and fails the ancestry check reads as checkable while describing a tree outside this branch. **They are not translated onto their replacements**, because a rebase replays onto a moved base and the figures beside them were never true of the new tree; every figure in this entry was re-measured at `c46cc72a` instead. (That is the opposite of the 2026-08-24 and 2026-09-03 history rewrites, where each pair held an identical tree and repointing was right — `WORKFLOW.md` §8.) The two SHAs this entry cites that are *not* orphaned are `d14eba65` and `8fecd5e8`, both on `main`.

**The fix round after PR #212's review (2026-09-06), which changed how one route's deadline is applied at all.** Five findings, one of them a defect this branch introduced. Recorded here rather than only on the ticket because the first is a rule that outlives this route.

- **F1 — a deadline around work that holds a database connection is never a race that abandons.** That is the rule; the instance is that `DELETE /v1/account` wrapped `drainOwedRevocations` in `withDeadlines`, which is a `Promise.race`. When the deadline won it rejected and **abandoned** the drain — harmless for the four routes whose work is one HTTP call, and a correctness defect here, because the drain holds the pooled client the handler leased. The route answered `204`, `withConnection`'s `finally` released that connection, and the drain kept writing on it: **`pg` does not refuse a query on a released client**, and `pg-pool` hands the same client object to the next `connect()`, so those statements land inside whatever transaction the next request has open. Nothing logs it, because the race has already subscribed to the work and swallows the later rejection. Worse in one respect than the corruption: the abandoned drain's mark-done statement stamps rows revoked, so the route's own log line saying the rows stay owed was false, and so was this entry's. The route now builds an `AbortController` on the same `total`, hands the drain the signal, and **awaits** the drain's termination; the drain reads the signal at the top of its loop and stops between iterations, before it claims a row. The bound is cooperative and is documented as cooperative: a single hung statement is bounded by nothing here, which is SONNY-427's, and the word "deadline" must not be left to imply otherwise.
- **F1's test, and why the mechanism the review assumed is not the one that reproduces it.** The review's probe used a fake `withConnection`, which does not queue; a real `pg.Client` **serialises** the statements issued on it. So a drain blocked on a *row lock* also blocks every statement the route issues after it — the wipe queues behind the drain's `UPDATE` — and the route cannot outrun it or release ahead of it even with the race in place. Stalling the **provider** is what leaves the connection idle, which is the window the race actually opened, and it is what the landing test does. Both of its assertions kill the restored race: the route has not answered when the deadline fires, and no statement is issued *or settles* after the release.
- **F2 — the adapter half had no test, and W9 was not a substitute for one.** Two mutants the reviewer wrote survived the whole suite: dropping the real adapter's `AbortSignal.any` composition, and wiring `deps.ts` to `90_000` instead of §12's number. Every test in the repository that observed a signal observed a *fake provider's parameter*; nothing observed the one real adapter composing one, and `AbortSignal.timeout` does not report the duration it was built with, so the wired value was unreachable by any behavioural route. The composition is now driven by aborting a caller's controller and reading the signal the adapter put on its `fetch`, in both directions; the wired number is asserted against `DEADLINE_MS.auth.upstream` **and** against `10_000`, so neither the wiring nor the pair can drift alone. The adapter's `timeoutMs` is readable for that, and is asserted beside a real abort at a twenty-millisecond bound so the field cannot become a third spelling of the number — W9's own lesson applied one level out.
- **F3 — the fix that killed W7 was unheld and wrong about its own mechanism, so it is gone.** It rethrew a `ProviderTimedOut` from the drain's `catch`, reasoning that the wrapper's race raised it there. The race rejects the *outer* promise and injects nothing into the work, and the one real adapter maps every abort — the route's signal included — to `ProviderUnavailable`, so the line was unreachable outside a test fake. The loop's own read of the signal replaces it, which is reachable and is what the deadline actually does. **The property needs two identities to be observable at all**: with one, ending the drain and filing one failure and continuing produce the same `204`, the same `deleted_at` and the same owed count, which is why the landing test could not see the mutant. The new test closes a two-identity account, stalls the provider on the first, and asserts one provider call rather than two, one identity still owed, and **no lease left held** — the drain stops before it claims.
- **F4 — an exception the lane had enumerated and every later record dropped.** §12, `model/limits.ts`, this entry, the PR body and the closing comment all said the four `/v1/account/*` routes wait on the database rather than on a provider. `POST /v1/account/credits/top-up` charges at the payment provider, spending its charge timeout up to three times in sequence, so its upstream work can run several times past a row of 10 s and 15 s — and bounding it is a wrapper at a call site, not the pool-wide change the sentence implied. The lane's own opening comment on SONNY-425 carried the exception verbatim; the five durable records did not. **This is `CLAUDE.md`'s enumerate-before-you-subtract rule failing at its last step rather than its first**, which is the harder half to notice: the enumeration was done, and then the summary of it lost a quarter of the set. **SONNY-430** owns the route now, filed so the gap has a name rather than an absence.
- **F5 — a file listed as changed that was byte-identical to the base.** `authdeps.test.ts` appeared in the closing comment's files list and in this entry's, and `git rev-parse d14eba65:server/test/authdeps.test.ts 61587806:server/test/authdeps.test.ts` printed one hash twice. The list was written from what the change *needed* rather than from the diff, and the diff carried thirteen paths against a report naming fourteen. **A count of paths is not a comparison of two lists**, and the coordinator's verification — which counted — could not have caught it.
- **A seventh thing this round did to itself, recorded because the repository already names it.** The first attempt at these edits sliced this entry with a file-wide `index("Behavior added:")`, which the **Entry Template** above also contains — so the slice inverted and duplicated forty lines of preamble, `## Entries` heading included. `scripts/changelog-order` caught it in one run, by the arm that has nothing to do with ordering. It is the same shared-anchor defect `CLAUDE.md` records for this very tool. The edits were redone against the entry's own heading range, sliced out first.

**The scoped verification round after PR #212's cycle 2 (2026-09-06), which found the fix's own test could not hold it.** Four findings held. F1's *code* held three ways — the reviewer's cycle-1 probe no longer completes against this tree, a discriminator probe reports no statement after release, and the branch's own test passes unskipped — and its *test* did not.

- **The test failed only when both halves of the fix were gone, so a mutant removing one half survived it.** It resumed the stalled provider one microtask after the deadline callback, before the route could have finished its wipe; under a race that abandons the drain the mark-done was therefore issued and settled *before* the connection was released, both post-release lists stayed empty, and `settled` was still false on the line meant to catch it. The reviewer restored the race in the route alone, left `revocation.ts`'s check in place, and reproduced F1 underneath a passing suite: `answered WHILE the drain was still running: true`, one `UPDATE sonny.identity_provider_user pu` after the release.
- **What it waits on now.** Whichever comes first: the lease coming back to the pool, or the connection going quiet. Under the race the release is *caused* by the abandonment, so it arrives in single-digit milliseconds and the assertion — which names the winning branch rather than checking a status — fails. Under the fix the release cannot come at all while the drain is stalled, so the quiet fallback is the only reachable branch. **A bounded number of turns was the wrong fallback and is what let the race through**; quiet is defined as no statement issued and none settled for a window, which is progress rather than clock, so load widens the window instead of closing it early.
- **The release had to become a count rather than a promise**, which is a small thing that failed loudly and would have failed quietly the other way round: this app leases and releases twice while signing the account in, so a promise resolved on the first release had already fired before the request under test began, and every waiter returned `released` on the clean tree.
- **A verdict this branch reported did not survive being re-measured, and that is worth more than the correction.** The fix round reported `X1 KILLED by 2` at `d3540e46`; the reviewer reported the byte-identical mutant `SURVIVED` at `4d8c1371`, and `git rev-parse d3540e46:server 4d8c1371:server` prints one hash twice, so it is the same tree. Both readings are honest and the reviewer's is the right one about what that test *guaranteed*: under the race the route answers early, so whether `provider.revokedUsers` had been pushed by the time the assertions ran depended on scheduling. **That is a manufactured kill in this repository's own sense** — a test that bets on a window reads as evidence when it wins the bet — and it is the reason a battery verdict is only as good as the determinism of the test producing it. Both tests are deterministic now: the F1 assertion is on a signal the abandonment causes, and the F3 assertions run only after a resume that the same signal gates.
- **A hang-shaped mutant against these two tests was silent by construction, and is not any more.** Every wording the server hang backstop emits is declared in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`, correctly — a sixty-second wall clock over work another process owns is a statement about the machine whatever the margin — so a mutant whose only effect is to make one of them hang came back `UNATTRIBUTED` on a run where the test failed for exactly the right reason. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s SONNY-259 case, and the remedy is the caller's: both tests now record a second issue in wording no declaration matches. **The gate is progress rather than tick rate, and the departure from the Swift half is measured rather than preferred** — the declaration file records that an observation floor was tried on this suite and rejected, because the event loop ticks at 167-178 per second against a nominal 200 at load averages up to 194 while the work gets ten times slower, so a floor below the healthy population would call a loaded run a deadlock. A connection that has issued and settled nothing is stopped rather than slow, which is the distinction `.stuck` draws, read off the resource this suite actually waits on. **The cascade above it is closed**: the gate runs only after the resume, because a wait whose own precondition never arrived would reach the quiet threshold at a perfectly healthy cadence every time.
- **Measured at `d72dc159`.** `X1` alone against that one test — `scripts/mutate … --only X1`, suite filtered to it, baseline `PASSED 1 passed | 46 skipped (47)` so the test demonstrably ran — **KILLED by 1**, *does not release the connection while the drain is still running on it*. Over the flagged subset, `X1` **KILLED by 2**, `X2` **KILLED by 1**, and the new **`X5`** — the drain parks forever once the deadline fires, so the route never answers — **KILLED by 2**, with the declared backstop's own failure listed beneath them under *Also red, and NOT counted above*, which is the whole demonstration: the kill comes from the undeclared wording and the declared line is correctly not counted.
- **Two residuals the review recorded and left, and one of them is this entry's.** The addendum's control for F4 was offered as exiting 1 with no output and in fact answers two legitimate matches — the corrected sentence and the paragraph recording the error — so the correction is real and the line proving it was not. It is the write-the-command rule's own failure mode, the parenthesis getting less checking than the number, and it is corrected in this round's records with the anchored form and a positive control. The other is the reviewer's qualification that once a row lock lifts, the drain and the wipe interleave and whether anything lands post-release is then a race between two query streams — real, and not a property a test can assert.

### Branch: feature/every-delete-reaches-the-server
Status: in progress
Date: 2026-09-05
Tickets: SONNY-404 — the other three delete buttons reach the server too: the whole local-data wipe says which promise it is, the Memory Task-history row queues every row's server deletion as one bulk call, and "Delete what Sonny did on screen" gets a route that takes exactly that task's screenshots.
Reviewed by: pending (per WORKFLOW.md step 7).

**The three decisions this branch carries were the founder's, taken 2026-09-05 and recorded on
SONNY-404, and none of them is reopenable here.** They also *reverse* the decision recorded on that
ticket the day before, and the ticket's comments are append-only, so a reader meeting the 2026-09-04
comment first will read the opposite of what shipped. The later comment is the live one:

1. **Settings › Data › "Delete Sonny local data" is a promise about this Mac, not about the
   account.** The control is named local data, account-wide deletion is a different promise that
   `DELETE /v1/account` already keeps, and a privacy wipe must not depend on a network call. So the
   queued server deletions the wipe abandons are **intended behaviour** rather than a residual, and
   the words say which promise it is. The alternative — the wipe also deleting every server copy,
   with new words, its own confirmation and a rule for a wipe performed signed out — was declined.
   (The 2026-09-04 comment had taken exactly that alternative.)
2. **"Delete what Sonny did on screen" gets a narrower server route.** Screenshots are the most
   sensitive content the gateway holds and snapshot copies of them carry no expiry today. The
   alternative — the button stays local and its words stop implying server reach — was declined.
3. **Memory › Task history › Delete queues every row's server deletion, as one bulk call rather than
   one call per row.** Follows from the 2026-08-16 rule that delete means deleted everywhere.

**Why decision 3 could not be "enqueue one entry per row", which is the shape SONNY-333 left
behind.** `PendingServerDeletionStore.maxItems` is 200 and `TaskHistoryStore.defaultMaxItems` is
10,000, so one entry per row would hand 9,800 obligations to the cap's silent eviction — from the
single press that asks for the most. The queue entry therefore names a *list* of task ids, and "one
bulk call" and "one queue entry" are the same decision seen from the two ends. That changed the
store's on-disk shape, which in this store is dangerous in a way it is not in the other thirteen: a
decode failure here is *healed* by quarantining the file (PR #194's F1), so a reader that could not
parse the old shape would have thrown every outstanding obligation away and reported nothing — the
exact failure this whole feature exists to prevent, arriving through the door built to prevent it.
`PendingServerDeletion` therefore has a hand-written `init(from:)` that reads the legacy `taskID`
key, and `loadKeyed` re-derives every dictionary key from the value it decoded rather than trusting
the key on disk.

**The two scopes do not subsume one another, deliberately.** A task can owe both a screenshots-only
delete and a whole-task delete — delete the screen record offline, then delete the task — and both
are delivered. Neither order is a hazard: whichever lands second finds its content already gone and
answers a success with a count of zero, which is §4.6's own rule that a delete already true is not
an error. Collapsing them would mean deciding which ask wins, and there is no reading under which
the narrower one should cancel the wider.

**A partial-ownership bulk answer keeps the whole obligation rather than narrowing it.** §4.6
reserves `404` for a task belonging to a different account, which SONNY-333 reads as "not
deliverable by *this session*, never not deliverable"; the batch says the same thing with
`tasks_not_found`, and any non-zero value keeps the entry. Narrowing the entry to the refused ids
would need a fourth store door that rewrites an entry mid-pass, and what it would buy is a smaller
request on a Mac that is already re-sending ids the gateway deletes a second time for free. The cost
is one bulk request per launch until the other account signs in — exactly the cost SONNY-333
accepted for the single-task case.

**A body on a `DELETE` is a constraint on the host, and it is written into the contract rather than
left here.** An intermediary that strips a `DELETE` request body turns every bulk delete into a
`400` no client can avoid, so §4.6.1 names it beside §6.1's payload size and §12's wall-clock as
something SONNY-125 has to prove of a candidate host. The alternative, `POST /v1/tasks/delete`,
would have obliged §9.1's `Idempotency-Key` on an operation §9.3 already calls naturally idempotent.

**The screenshot delete is an UPDATE to NULL and not a DELETE of a row**, because a row of
`sonny.retained_content` holds the screenshot beside the request text and the served response. That
is also why the record needed a migration of its own: `sonny.content_deletion`'s `reason` CHECK
admitted four values and none of them was this one, and `content_rows`/`snapshot_rows` count rows
*removed* — reusing them would have changed what those columns mean for every reader that predates
this route.

Spec sections covered: contract §4.1 (two rows), §4.6.1 and §4.6.2 (new), §4.7, §9.3, §12. No spec
section is left partial.

- `server/src/db/migrations/0020_a_screenshot_can_be_deleted_without_the_task.sql` (new — the

- ~~Both surfaces describing the whole wipe say it deletes "from this Mac", and the confirmation

- ~~**The whole wipe still takes the queue file** with every other store, and still sends nothing.~~

  deleted screen record is still indistinguishable from one that aged out.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **A store whose decode failure heals is a store whose on-disk shape cannot change carelessly.**
  Every other local store propagates a decode failure, so a shape change there fails loudly; this one
  quarantines and starts fresh, so the same change would be silent data loss wearing the mask of a
  feature working as designed. The legacy decoder and its test exist for that reason and not for
  tidiness.
- **The two new client calls live on `SonnyBackendClient` while SONNY-333's lives on
  `SonnyTaskDeletionService`, and the asymmetry is deliberate rather than drift.** The kickoff's file
  boundary put them there, and there is a reason that reads as one: the single delete's body is
  never decoded, while the bulk delete's answer decides whether an obligation is finished — a call
  whose caller must read its body is a call with a decoder.
- **`SonnyTaskDeletionService.swift` was edited although the kickoff note's file list did not name
  it.** The delivery pass is where an obligation becomes a request, so the note's own requirement —
  two new calls — cannot land without it. Recorded here rather than assumed, per WORKFLOW.md step 5.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The bulk route's `tasks_not_found` is a count and not a list**, so a mixed-ownership obligation
  is retried whole. Stated above with what it costs.
- **The bulk obligation is capped at 10,000 ids by the route** — the Mac's own history cap, so no
  press this product can make exceeds it. A future history cap above 10,000 moves both numbers in
  one change.
- **Nothing surfaces what the queue owes**, unchanged from SONNY-333, and still on SONNY-109's list
  along with the cap's silent eviction.

Open questions: none.

**Fix round, 2026-09-05: the first of the three decisions above was reversed back, and the wipe now
reaches the account.** Both founders restored the decision of **2026-09-04** — "Delete Sonny local
data" is a promise about the **account** — and recorded that the 2026-09-05 answer this entry was
first written against was a coordinator's error: the settled question had been re-asked as an
enumerated option without the standing decision being named. The second and third answers stand
untouched, and no line of the screenshots route or the bulk route moved in this round.

**What the press does now**, in the order the steps have to run in:

1. **Drains the queue**, before the file holding it is removed — the founder's own condition on this
   decision, in those words.
2. **Deletes everything the gateway retains for the account** — `DELETE /v1/account/content`,
   contract **§4.6.3**, a new route, additive under §8.1 and with a row of its own in §4.1 and §9.3.
   Live content, every training-snapshot copy, and the response bodies §9.2 keeps for twenty-four
   hours. **The account stays open**: closing it is `DELETE /v1/account`, a different promise with no
   control in the app today.
3. **Deletes every local file, the queue among them**, so no task id survives the press whatever
   happened above it.
4. **Only if step 2 failed, writes one obligation back** — `.everythingUnderTheAccount`, the queue's
   third scope, which **names no task**. That is what makes it safe to be the one thing a privacy
   wipe leaves on disk, and what makes it *sufficient* is that it is strictly wider than every
   obligation step 3 just discarded: an account-wide delete reaches everything each per-task
   obligation named.
5. **Says once and plainly what happened**, including what is still on the servers and what will
   happen to it. `LocalDataDeletionCopy.outcome` owns both sentences.

**Why a new route rather than a `scope` on the bulk one**, which the coordinator's note offered as
the shape to weigh first. Extending `DELETE /v1/tasks` would have made `task_ids` optional, and on a
delete route an absent or empty body would then be one typo away from meaning *everything* — the most
expensive possible misreading, and one a 400 currently prevents. A separate path is also
unambiguously additive under §8.1's first bullet, gets its own §4.1 row and its own line in the
deny-by-default gate scan, and reads correctly beside `DELETE /v1/account`: the two paths differ by
exactly the thing that differs in the promise.

**Why the record needed migration `0021`.** `sonny.content_deletion.reason` already carries `account`
for a *closed* account's wipe. Filing this act under that value would be the closest wrong answer
available — `sonny.account.deleted_at` distinguishes them only until the user does close the account,
at which point every earlier content wipe reads as a close. So `account_content` is its own reason,
and `deleteContentForAccount` takes the reason as a required parameter rather than a defaulted one,
on this repository's own recorded ground that a defaulted parameter is a decision nobody reads.

**The press waits on the network now, and that is the decision reversing rather than an oversight.**
The superseded reading argued a privacy wipe must not depend on a network call; the standing decision
requires it to, because it is promising something only the network can deliver. What it must not do
is fail silently, which is what step 5 exists for. `deleteLocalData()` is therefore an asynchronous
entry point with a chained handle, and eleven existing tests across four suites had to await it —
they were asserting on a press that had not finished.

**The one obligation this press really does abandon, stated rather than left to be found:** an entry
the drain kept on a `404`, which §4.6 reserves for a task belonging to a *different* account signed
into the same Mac. The account-wide delete cannot reach it, and the queue file cannot keep it,
because keeping it would mean leaving behind a file that names a task. It is the cost of the rule
that whatever survives the wipe names nothing the user did.

**Second fix round, 2026-09-05: an obligation belongs to the account that pressed it.** PR #207's
fresh review found five things above the bar and seven residuals. F1 is the one that mattered and it
was a cross-account data-loss path, reachable with no unusual action: the obligation the wipe left
behind named **no account and no time**, nothing cleared the queue on a session change, and the
launch sweep delivered with whatever token was current — so a wipe pressed offline by one user,
followed by a second signing in on the same Mac, deleted the **second** user's everything, silently;
and the same obligation, delivered days later, reached content the first user created after the
press. The per-task obligations were never exposed to this, and the reason is the point: §4.6's
`404` refuses a task id the gateway knows under another account, which is a bound the account-wide
scope has no id to carry. Three parts, each pinned by a test that fails on the tree as it was and by
a mutant:

- **Every queued obligation carries the account it was pressed under**, and is delivered only under a
  session for that account. The Supabase user id, which is an *account* identifier and says nothing
  about what the user did. A per-task entry with no account — a file written before the field — is
  delivered as before, because §4.6's `404` is exactly the protection SONNY-333 designed for it.
  Reading it synchronously needed a seam: `SonnyBackendClient` is an `actor`, and the enqueue runs
  before the local deletes, so `SonnyTaskDeletionService` takes an `accountIdentity` closure the app
  wires to the token store. SONNY-333 looked at this same wall and dropped the stamp for it.
- **The account-wide obligation carries the instant of the press**, and `DELETE /v1/account/content`
  gained an optional `?before=` that bounds what it deletes — additive under §8.1's "may add an
  optional request field", with its own line in **§4.6.3** and §4.1. Each table is bounded on its own
  notion of when the content happened: `occurred_at`, `source_occurred_at`, `claimed_at`. An
  unparseable value is a `400` rather than a fall-through to "no bound".
- **A session change discards what the outgoing account owed, with the reason recorded.** Delivering
  first is impossible after the fact — signing out clears the tokens — so the discard is the honest
  half of that pair, wired at `main.swift`'s `sessionDidChange`. **Signing *out* keeps them**: the
  account that owns them may sign back in, and the per-entry gate holds them safe until it does.
- **A wipe pressed with nobody signed in records nothing at all**, and says so: an obligation that
  cannot name whose content it is about is precisely the one that deletes the next account. The
  outcome sentence has three states now rather than two, and the third tells the user to sign in.

**F2: the obligation is written on both paths.** `deleteAllLocalData` collects failures and throws
only *after* deleting everything it could, and the queue is one of the files it deletes — so a wipe
that failed on any single file landed in the `catch` with the queue already gone and step 4 never
reached. The server held everything, the Mac owed nothing, and the sentence named only a local file:
the state the founder's condition forbids, through the failure branch. The review named
`aPartialWipeKeepsTheMemoryPagesSentenceForTheFileStillOnDisk` as the test already driving that
throw, and it now reads both halves of the message and what the queue holds afterwards.

**F3: the wipe holds a claim across the whole sequence.** The `!isRunning` guard was read on the
press while the body then awaited a drain and a server call — the client's whole multi-attempt budget
on a 20-second route — before touching a file, and a *scheduled routine* sets `isRunning` from a
timer with nobody watching. `isDeletingLocalData` is set synchronously at the press and read by
`start()`, which is the door every caller passes through and where `isRunning` is set.

**F4 and F5 are records, corrected in place.** The checklist section's preamble told the founder the
superseded decision directly above the corrected row that asks them to confirm the opposite, and its
row count was stale; the two Behavior bullets above stated the superseded wipe as shipped and are now
struck through inside their own corrections, so a sweep for the old wording finds it labelled as
history rather than finding nothing. R1 through R6 are swept in the same round — **R5 among them**:
the confirmation's middle sentence was how-it-works copy before a press, and what happens when the
servers cannot be reached is said *afterwards*, by the outcome sentence, in the state it happened in.
**R7 is not this branch's** and is filed as SONNY-426.

**Fourth round, 2026-09-05: the claim is held per chain, and the cutoff reads the server's clock.**
Review-207's cycle 3 found F1, F2, F4 and F5 held and R1 to R6 swept, and **F3 held for one press and
not for two** — a defect above the bar in production code left by the fix round itself, which is what
the founders' 2026-08-21 directive reserves one extra cycle for. This round is scoped to it and to
the reviewer's G1; G2 and G3 are recorded below rather than fixed.

**F3's second half.** `isDeletingLocalData` was set by every press and cleared by every completion,
so a second press chained behind the first had the *first* wipe's completion drop the claim while the
second was still draining, still calling the gateway and still about to delete every store — the
exact window the claim exists to close, re-opened by pressing twice. And Settings' Delete was
`.disabled(viewModel.isRunning)` alone, so it stayed pressable for the whole of it, because
`isRunning` is false during a wipe. Three changes:

- **The claim is owned by the chain, not by a task.** `localDataWipesInFlight` goes up before the
  press returns and down as each wipe ends, and `isDeletingLocalData` is derived from it and from
  nothing else — so only the last wipe can release it.
- **The control is disabled while the claim is held**, which is what makes a second press unreachable
  through the product.
- **A model-level refusal was considered and rejected**, and the reasoning is at the code: returning
  early from a second press would drop a press the user made, and it would make the property
  untestable in the bargain — with no second wipe there is no chain, so nothing could tell a claim
  released by the last wipe from one released by the first, which is the defect itself.

**G1: the cutoff is the gateway's clock, not this Mac's.** `?before=` is compared against
`occurred_at` on the gateway's own rows, so a skewed Mac bounds the deletion at the wrong instant —
running behind, the immediate wipe under-deletes while reporting the servers' copy gone; running
ahead, the queued obligation's cutoff sits in the future, which is the over-deletion the parameter
was added to prevent. `SonnyBackendClient.serverNow()` exists for exactly this (§3.5's offset) and is
what `EntitlementService` and `SonnyAccountService` already read; it is `public` now and reached
through `SonnyTaskDeletionService.instantToBoundAPressAt()`. **It is the Mac's clock plus a
correction, so it is never unavailable**: with no observation yet the offset is zero and the value is
`Date()`, which is what the press used before. **The wire truncates it toward the past by up to a
second** — §2.1's format carries no fractional seconds, so a bound of `…00.750` goes out as `…00Z` —
and that error is always in the under-deleting direction, which is the safe one for a bound whose job
is to stop a delayed delete reaching too far.

They are timestamps on a branch, and the figures beside them are true of that branch at that moment and of nothing else. The base-side SHAs this entry cites — `17533148`, `6cc9e189`, `d0b3a7a9` — and the new base `460bb029` all pass the same check with exit 0.

Two earlier batteries are superseded and named so the record reads in order: 5/5 at `7157785e`, with R1's killers lost to a trapping dictionary comparison, and 5/5 at `55061f7d` after that was fixed and the plan re-run in full.

Behavior added:
- **A short page whose *subject* is a wall is served.** The ticket's own example — `simonwillison.net/2006/Dec/19/botbouncer/`, HTTP 200, 1 110 visible characters, one sentence mentioning a CAPTCHA service — was refused as a CAPTCHA gate and is now read normally, as are Hacker News comment pages discussing paywalls and every other page in that class.
- **A short page carrying Google's required reCAPTCHA attribution is served**, with no carve-out naming the notice. Any page with a reCAPTCHA-protected contact form, signup or comment box carries that 93-character string by licence; under the old rule every such page under 2 000 visible characters was refused. It stopped mattering because `captcha` stopped being visible-text evidence, which is a cheaper answer than a vendor allowlist that would need extending for the next badge.
- **Wall coverage widens where it was measurably thin**, by adding `verifying you are human` beside SONNY-245's unchanged `verify you are human` — so Cloudflare's "Verifying you are human" now matches, a wall `interstitialVisibleTextLimit`'s own doc comment named as a miss. Two further wall wordings join it on the same evidence: `confirm you are human`/`confirm you are a human` (ScienceDirect's own sentence) and `proves you are human`/`proves you are a human` (Bluehost's page and Cloudflare's legacy interstitial). **The first version of this branch widened differently and wrongly — `you are human`, `you are a human`, `are you a robot` — and the pitfall below is what that cost.**

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **Stage 2, markup evidence, loses no coverage — but it is not untouched in behaviour, and this bullet said it was** (PR #210 review, F3). It still searches the whole page, still requires under 200 visible characters, and the list it searches is a literal superset of SONNY-245's seven phrases, because all seven are in it verbatim. What *did* move is the **order**: `phrases` is `wallSpeechPhrases + subjectPhrases`, so `captcha` is no longer first, and `firstPhrase` returns the first entry that matches. On a page whose markup carries two phrases the refusal is still raised and the noun it names can differ — a contentless page carrying both a reCAPTCHA script and `Please log in` was `CAPTCHAs / captcha` under SONNY-245 and is `login walls / please log in` now. Fail-closed is intact in every case; `Finding.phrase` and the noun the user is shown are what changed. `aPageCarryingTwoPhrasesInMarkupIsNamedByTheEarlierListEntry` pins it in both directions, and it is the test this bullet used to contradict — the Zillow PerimeterX fixture, which the next sentence cited as the check, carries no wall-speech phrase and cannot exercise the ordering at all. Zillow is still refused on markup at 0 visible characters with the same reason, phrase and evidence.
- **Both limits keep their values.** `interstitialVisibleTextLimit` is 2 000 and `contentlessVisibleTextLimit` is 200; the edge tests that pin them at 1 999/2 000 and 199/200 are unchanged and pass.
- **Genuine walls that speak are still refused.** The ScienceDirect gate fixture is still refused on visible text at 523 characters — on `confirm you are a human` now rather than on `captcha`, which is the split working rather than a weakening. (This named `you are a human`, a wording the fix round deleted; `theScienceDirectGateIsRefusedOnWhatItSaysToTheReader` asserts the live one.)
- **Both encyclopedia articles are still served**, and the old rule still refuses all four original fixtures, so the two rules still disagree in exactly the places SONNY-245 made them disagree.
- **`PublicWebPageLoader`'s ordering is untouched**: a 4xx is still refused on the status before the detector runs, and a 200 block page still surfaces the wall's name.
- Locale-independent folding, the whitespace collapse, the `<script>`/`<style>` removal and the inline-icon guard are all unchanged and still pinned.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The ratio the ticket proposed was measured and rejected, and it is worse than the rule it would have replaced.** SONNY-256's hypothesis was that a wall's message is essentially the whole page while an article's mention is a small fraction of it. Scored over the 45-page stage-1 population, the strictest threshold that keeps both genuine walls refused leaves **19 of 41** innocent pages still refused for the sentence-share ratio and **21 of 41** for the block-share ratio, against **12 of 41** for a re-tuned absolute length. The premise is false of the wall we have: ScienceDirect's gate spends 14.0% of its visible text on the matching sentence — most of the rest is footer — while a Hacker News comment page whose whole body is one comment about a paywall spends 63.6%, and one spends 86.3%. **A ratio fires hardest on exactly the pages this ticket exists to stop refusing.** The full table, the corpus and the commands are in SONNY-256's measuring-round comment.

**No length separates them either, which is why the fix is not a re-tuned threshold.** The wall at 523 visible characters sits above twelve innocent pages at 291 to 472. Length was being asked to stand in for a distinction it cannot express.

**What separates the population is which phrase fired, and it is not subtle.** Every one of the 43 false refusals fired on `captcha`, `paywall` or `subscription required` — nouns that name the subject, and a page is allowed to have a subject. The other four phrases, all of them instructions addressed to the reader, fired on **zero** pages in the corpus. So the list splits by what a phrase *is* rather than the page being corroborated by how big it is.

**Link count separates the corpus perfectly and was deliberately not shipped.** Every innocent page in the population has at least 25 links and both walls have 8 and 1, a clean gap. It was rejected because it is a threshold fitted to two positive examples, which is precisely the "second wrong threshold" the ticket warns is worse than a known one — and because a wall drawn inside a site's full navigation would defeat it on the first encounter.

**Nothing was added to the phrase list speculatively.** `to continue reading` was tested and rejected: it matches an innocent Hacker News comment. Five further paywall wordings (`already a subscriber`, `subscribe to read`, `sign in to read`, `log in to continue`, `to read this article`) matched nothing on either side and were left out rather than added on the strength of no evidence.

**A trapped test costs a mutant its evidence, and this branch produced a textbook instance.** The first battery reported R1 — a subject noun put back into `wallSpeechPhrases` — as `KILLED — the run failed but named no test` in 38 seconds. The cause was in the test: `eachPhraseKeepsItsOwnRefusalNoun` compared through `Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues:)`, which traps on a duplicate key, so the mutant killed the process and took the whole run's evidence with it (`Fatal error: Duplicate values for key: 'captcha'` at the end of a log that named none of the tests which had caught it). The mutant was genuinely caught and nothing in the report could say by what. Both lists are compared as ordered arrays now — which also pins the concatenation order, worth asserting on its own account since `firstPhrase` returns the first match and the order therefore decides which noun a refusal names. The battery was then re-run in full rather than scoped, because the fix edited the file every one of the five killers lives in.

**A corpus sampled on what a change removes cannot falsify what it adds, and the first version of this branch shipped exactly that** (PR #210 review, F1). The split moved three subject nouns out of visible-text evidence, and the corpus's comment pages had been sampled on those same three nouns — so the population could measure the split perfectly and was blind, by construction, to the three wall-speech wordings the branch added beside it. Re-measured over 224 pages including 70 Hacker News item pages drawn on the added wordings themselves, `you are human` matches **17** innocent in-band pages, `you are a human` **18** and `are you a robot` **6**: a comment about turning down a company ("if you are human you will do from time to time") refused as a CAPTCHA gate, and a complaint *about* robot walls refused as one — the failure this ticket exists to end, arriving through its own fix. **The generalisable form: when a change both removes and adds terms, the sampling frame has to be drawn on the added terms, or the measurement can only confirm the half that was already safe.** The remedy shipped is an inclusion rule stated at the code above the list and checkable against it — a wording is in only if it matches zero innocent in-band pages across a corpus sampled on that wording — with SONNY-245's deleted warning that widening the list is its own decision restored above it, now carrying this as its worked example.

**A proposed remedy is a hypothesis too, and this one did not survive the same test.** PR #210's review measured a narrower verb-keeping list and reported it serving all 20 of its counterexamples. Scored over this round's wider population it refuses **16** innocent pages — `prove you are human` (6), `verify you are human` (5), `verify you are a human` (3), `prove you are a human` (2) — the identical trap one level down, because that sample was drawn on the three bare wordings and so could not falsify the verb forms it proposed. What the data separates is the **person**, not the verb: a wall says what the challenge does ("completing the CAPTCHA **proves** you are human", "**verifying** you are human", "please **confirm** you are a human") while a reader discussing walls uses the infinitive ("how do you **prove** you are human?"). The shipped list is a third one and refuses **5** innocent pages, against 40 for the list under review and 63 for SONNY-245's rule — all 5 on SONNY-245's own unchanged `verify you are human`, kept with its cost because removing it narrows SONNY-245's coverage, which the restored warning says is a decision to be made on its own terms.

**Selection bias was designed against rather than asserted away.** The Hacker News half of the corpus is every third hit across the Algolia result set for three phrase searches, not the top hits; the Simon Willison half is every post on his own `captchas` and `paywalls` tag pages; the contact-form half is candidate-and-filter, because every search engine tried refuses this machine, and the filter is whether the fetched page actually carries the notice. Two of the pages became fixtures, from two different templates, so the fix cannot read as a property of one blog's markup.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The error this chooses, stated at the code as well as here, and it is wider than "a bare noun"** (PR #210 review, F2). The class is *any* wall in the 200-to-2 000 band whose visible text carries a subject noun and none of `wallSpeechPhrases`. Measured over 14 real gate wordings placed in ordinary nav and footer chrome, **5 lose the refusal SONNY-245 gave them**: "Please complete the CAPTCHA below to continue", "Access denied. Please solve the CAPTCHA below to continue to this page", "Access denied. Please solve the CAPTCHA to prove you're not a bot", "Subscription required. This content is available to subscribers only", and "This article is behind our paywall. Members can read it in full". **Three of the five are full instructions to the reader about this page's access** — `wallSpeechPhrases`' own definition of wall speech — so they are served because they use the noun, not because they are bare nouns. A sixth, "Checking your browser before accessing this website", is served by SONNY-245 too and is not a loss from this branch. **Two mitigations, both measured rather than reasoned:** below 200 visible characters all **14 of 14** are still refused (8 on visible text, 6 on markup), and `SwiftSoupReadableWebExtractor` throws `noReadableContent` on **all five** newly-served pages, so **no note is written from any of them** — the user gets a different error, not a summarised wall.
- **The wall side is small, and half of it is synthetic.** Three real walls — ScienceDirect's gate, caught on `confirm you are a human`; Bluehost's security step, on `proves you are human`; Zillow's, on markup — beside 14 constructed gate wordings placed in ordinary chrome. A synthetic page establishes what a wording does to the rule and never how often that wording occurs, so the corpus can falsify a candidate list and cannot rank two that both survive. A wall that speaks, answers 200, and uses none of the ten listed wordings is served. (This bullet named `you are human` and `you are a human` as the two catching both walls; the fix round deleted both, and it also grew the wall side past the two pages this sentence described.)
- The corpus is one machine, one network and one afternoon. ResearchGate's status was already known to be unstable across networks (PR #108's review), and several sites that answered 403 here would reach the detector from elsewhere.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the coordinator's queue.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:

The kickoff note on SONNY-372 groups SONNY-397 under *Claims and evidence* and sends SONNY-410's bytes-versus-characters note to the gotchas; each ticket's own text says the opposite — SONNY-397 asks to sit "beside the shared-marker scan entry it is a sibling of", which is in the gotchas, and SONNY-410's comment says the bytes note "belongs with the write-the-command rule", which is in *Claims and evidence*. Both were placed as their own tickets ask. The net effect is the same two sections; only which rule goes where differs, and either is a one-line move if the coordinator disagrees.
