The founders superseded that on 2026-09-04 (SONNY-106): Tavily ships v1 and the move is revisited after release, so that weight no longer waits on a pre-release migration. The screen-control half stands in substance, and one parenthesis inside it had gone stale the other way and is corrected too: "screen control records no usage at all today" was measured on 2026-08-16 against `main` at `9cfa090` and stopped being true when row 12's metering landed — the gateway meters `screen.analyze` and row 13's credit accounting reads exactly those rows (`server/src/credit/store.ts`'s `PAID_ROUTE`). What is still missing is not the recording but a deployed gateway to record against, which SONNY-192 owes, so the number is still unmeasured and still not guessed.

**The sweep, run against the OLD wording rather than the new — and two things it cannot see.** Population `docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md`, pattern `Pro and Max|Max tier|Pro/Max|Trial state if offered|Power Mode is paid-only|350 credits|2,500 credits`: `grep -cE` answers **8** matching lines, of which **0** are unmarked — the same pattern through `grep -nE ... docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | grep -vcE '~~|[Ss]uperseded|Cancelled'` answers **0**. **The count of matches does not fall and was never going to**: a struck line still contains the words it struck, which is exactly what §23's own paid sweep records about itself. So what is checkable is that every match carries a supersession marker, not that the matches went away — and **the marker filter is proved capable of a non-zero answer** by a control on wording that really is live, the same filter over `Billing portal\.` answering **2**.

**The first thing the sweep cannot see is a block.** Repo-wide over tracked files the same pattern matches **18** lines and **4** carry no marker on the line itself: three are sub-bullets of the Open Decisions section's branch-13 ladder, whose supersession sits on the block's head line rather than on the bullets, and the fourth is a line of this entry. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s "a grep of this kind finds lines, not blocks" arriving inside the sweep written to close this class. The ladder is not a live claim and it is outside this lane's changelog boundary, so it is recorded here rather than edited.

**The second is this entry itself, and it moves the number in both directions.** Writing the retirements down puts the retired wording into the population being swept: **five** of the 18 lines are this entry's own prose. One shows as unmarked and is the fourth above; the other four pass the marker filter, three because the sentence carries the word "superseded" and **one because it quotes the filter pattern itself**, which makes it match two of that filter's three alternatives. So a repo-wide reading of this sweep counts its own report, in both directions, and only the spec-scoped reading above measures what the ticket asked about. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s ninth write-the-command defect — a citation matching a population its own file belongs to — reached from the side where it is visible: the extra matches are enumerated here rather than silently inflating a number.

**Two figures in the roadmap's row-13 cell were wrong and are corrected in place rather than replaced quietly.** SONNY-211's pull request was **#178**, not #179 — `git log --first-parent --merges --format='%h %s' main | grep -E 'pull request #(178|179) '` shows #178 as `feature/the-subscription-reaches-the-entitlement` and #179 as `fix/a-control-is-named-for-where-it-goes`, which is SONNY-338 and has nothing to do with billing. **Where the figures above were measured, and what the rebase did to that.** This branch was rebased once, at merge time, onto `2e58e189` (PR #203's merge, docs only), and **every figure in this entry is re-measured at `01b802d0`, the rebased head, rather than translated across the hop**. The two counts over `Sources` and `server/src` in the retired trial bullet are stamped at `2e58e189` and hold at every head on this branch, because it changes no code — `git rev-parse 2e58e189:Sources 01b802d0:Sources` prints `65a08090297b3486537cfbe1404ed3fb10d85b76` twice and the same pair on `server` prints `4be60f85801e889597168ebac1bd9c1457632cde` twice, against a control on this very file, where the two hashes differ. **The rebase also proved the two documents this branch must not have moved a second time did not move**: `git rev-parse 6eba92d0:docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md 01b802d0:docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md` prints `5cee942db6193fae01a2a787e199cde292a9f69a` twice, and the same pair on `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` prints `44816e700ef1e617d547f3f3036fc3197ddd5428` twice — so the conflict resolution touched the changelog and nothing else. **The two pre-rebase heads this entry used to stamp are orphaned and are recorded as such rather than repointed**: `09573faf` and `6eba92d0` each still resolve and each exits 1 under `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD`, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s stamp that goes bad without going missing; a rebase replays onto a moved base, so its figures are re-measured and never renamed. **This paragraph's own commit sits on top of the tree it records**, changes only this file, and adds no line that either sweep matches, so it moves none of the figures above: re-run there, `scripts/changelog-order` still exits 0 over 176 entries, the spec-scoped sweep still answers 8 and 0 against a live-wording control of 2, the repo-wide reading is still 18 and 4, and the branch-entry count is still 9 anchored against 14 unanchored.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **A row's records ticket reads the row's closing comments, not the planning comment that spawned it.** Three of this row's founder decisions were made after planning closed, under implementation pressure, and exist only on the tickets that hit the questions.
- **A passage that still holds is not superseded by a decision that agreed with it.** Striking §16.4's no-trial bullet would have been the tidy-looking move and would have destroyed a live resolution; it is annotated as confirmed instead. - **A supersession sweep's count does not fall, because the struck text stays.** What is checkable is that every match carries a marker, and that the marker filter is capable of a non-zero answer. A sweep that reports a dropping count over struck-through prose is measuring something other than what it claims.
- **A line-anchored sweep marks lines, and a supersession can be attached to a block.** Three unmarked lines repo-wide are sub-bullets under a head line that carries their supersession. Whoever automates a sweep of this kind will re-find that.
- **A status cell goes stale in the ordinary course and nothing comes back to it.** Row 13's cell has now been corrected four times — "Not started" (2026-08-26), "the billing half is not started" (2026-09-03), and this ticket's two figures plus its opening. Tickets: SONNY-422 — read what Sonny actually writes into the macOS Keychain, record whether Migration Assistant is expected to carry each item, and add the manual rows on two Macs that turn that expectation into evidence. Filed on the founder's decision of 2026-09-05 on SONNY-253 (option C): no in-product backup and restore ships in v1, so Migration Assistant is the migration path and this is what proves it rather than assumes it.
Reviewed by: coordinator-verified against the real diff, per `WORKFLOW.md` step 7's right-sizing — a records-and-docs diff, no fresh-session reviewer launched.

Spec sections covered: none — this is a reading of existing code and a manual-test contract, and it adds no product behavior.

Files changed: `docs/sonny-manual-test-checklist.md` (one new section, four unchecked rows), `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` (this entry).

Tests: none owed and none run, and the reason is the rule rather than a judgment. The diff touches only `docs/`, so it reaches neither half of the repository — `WORKFLOW.md` step 7's docs/comments exemption covers the Swift suite and `scripts/warnings`, and nothing under `server/` changed either. `scripts/changelog-order` **exit 0, 175 entries, both eras** at `88fa238` — the one check this diff genuinely owes, being a diff that touches the changelog. Its baseline on `main` at `6cc9e189` was exit 0 with 174 entries, so this entry is the only one added.

Behavior added: none.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims): none to name — no code, test, script or configuration file changed, so no existing flow was touched. Stated as an enumeration rather than a blanket, per `CLAUDE.md`: `git diff --name-only 6cc9e189 HEAD` names two files and both are under `docs/`.

**What the reading actually found, since the whole ticket rests on it.** Sonny writes **three** items into the Keychain, not the two the ticket's description names, and every one of them goes through a single function. `KeychainSecretStore.baseQuery` (`Sources/MacAgentCore/KeychainSecretStore.swift:73`) builds every query from exactly three keys — `kSecClass: kSecClassGenericPassword`, `kSecAttrService`, `kSecAttrAccount` — and `save` adds `kSecValueData` and nothing else before calling `SecItemAdd` at `:54`. So the add dictionary has four keys, and the three tenants differ only in their service and account strings:

| item | service | account | declared at |
|---|---|---|---|
| the device key (32 random bytes; every encrypted store depends on it) | `com.sonny.local-storage` | `local-data-encryption-key-v1` | `LocalStorageEncryption.swift:39-40`, saved at `:73` |
| the signed-in session (access and refresh tokens, one JSON blob) | `com.sonny.account` | `backend-session-v1` | `SonnyAccountTokenStore.swift:108-109`, saved at `:137` |
| the cached entitlement claim | `com.sonny.account` | `entitlement-v1` | `EntitlementStore.swift:71-72`, saved at `:101` |

**The third one is why the ticket's "the device key and the session token" is worth reconciling out loud rather than silently.** The description names two items and then, in the same requirement, names `EntitlementStore` as a file to read — and that file writes its own account on the session's service. The entitlement is a third item by every measure that matters here: its own account name, its own write, its own arrival or non-arrival on the new Mac. It is reported as one.

**No protection attribute is set anywhere, and that zero is the load-bearing fact.** `git grep -nE 'kSecAttrAccessible|kSecAttrSynchronizable|kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain|kSecAttrAccessControl|kSecAttrAccessGroup' -- Sources | grep -vE ':[0-9]+: *(///|//|\*)'` exits 1 with no output at `6cc9e189`. **A clean zero is the one answer that looks like good news**, so it was controlled twice, per `CLAUDE.md`: dropping the comment stage answers 2 (both lines of `EntitlementStore.swift`'s own doc comment, at `:62-63`), and keeping the comment stage while searching for `kSecAttrService|kSecAttrAccount` answers 2 (`KeychainSecretStore.swift:76-77`). Both controls fire, so the pattern and the stage both work and the zero is a measurement. The app is also not sandboxed and declares no keychain access group — `Packaging/MacAgent.entitlements` says so in its own words at `:59-66`, and repository-wide `git grep -n 'keychain-access-group\|app-sandbox\|data-protection' 6cc9e189` → 1, that comment line alone. **Read at a commit rather than over the working tree, deliberately**: the same command without the SHA answers 2 here, and the second hit is this very paragraph quoting the pattern. That is the self-matching citation `CLAUDE.md` records as the ninth defect of the write-the-command rule — the dangerous direction, because the count is plausible and re-running the command reproduces the inflated number exactly — met while writing this entry rather than merely described in it.

**The prediction, and the line between what the code proves and what it does not.** What the code proves is the negative: nothing pins these items to one machine, and nothing asks for iCloud sync. What follows from that is platform behavior rather than a fact this repository can demonstrate — `SecItemAdd` without `kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain` writes to the file-based login keychain, `kSecAttrSynchronizable` defaults to false, and Migration Assistant carries `~/Library/Keychains/` along with the home folder that holds `~/Library/Application Support/Sonny/`. So all three items are **expected to arrive**, the stores are expected to decrypt, and the user is expected to still be signed in. That reading is not this session's alone: SONNY-128's adversarial security review reached the same one independently on 2026-08-26 and filed it as SONNY-304, whose own words are that the item "is not marked ThisDeviceOnly in any form, and the login keychain is carried by Time Machine backups and by Migration Assistant". **Two readings agreeing is still not a run**, which is exactly why the ticket's second half exists: no agent can drive Migration Assistant or a second Mac, so the four rows are where this stops being a prediction.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **The already-decided fix for SONNY-304 would break the migration path this ticket exists to establish, and the premise it was decided on has since been removed.** This is the finding, and it is a founder's to resolve rather than a lane's. SONNY-304 carries a founder decision of 2026-08-30: set `kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly` **on both tenants**, the device key included, so the item "never travels in a Keychain sync or an encrypted backup". Its stated reasoning leans on SONNY-254 — "SONNY-254's backup and restore is the deliberate, password-wrapped exception to device-binding" — and SONNY-254 was taken out of wave 6 and re-scoped six days later by the SONNY-253 decision of 2026-09-05 that filed *this* ticket, on the ground that the password it needed does not exist. So the exception the 2026-08-30 decision routed migration through is gone, and if SONNY-304 is implemented as written, the device key stops travelling and **every encrypted store on the new Mac becomes unreadable, with no second copy of the key anywhere**. The two decisions are individually sound and jointly incoherent; nothing in either ticket points at the other, and a session implementing SONNY-304 from its own contract would meet none of this. **Not fixed here** — the ticket's never-touch list is `Sources/`, `Tests/`, `server/`, `scripts/`, and the instruction on finding an attribute that stops migration is to stop and report. Nothing in the tree stops it today; what was found is a decision that would, and it is recorded on both tickets.
- **"Thirteen stores" is one behind the tree, and it is written that way in more than one place.** `LocalStore` has **fourteen** cases at `6cc9e189` (`sed -n '/^public enum LocalStore:/,/^}/p' Sources/MacAgentCore/LocalStoreClassification.swift | grep -cE '^ {4}case '` → 14), the fourteenth being `pendingServerDeletions`, and it is on the shared encrypted pattern like the rest (`PendingServerDeletionStore.swift:69` — "On the shared `LocalStorageEncryption` pattern exactly"). SONNY-422's own description says thirteen and so does `CLAUDE.md`'s local-store gotcha, whose own text anticipates a "fourteenth". This changes nothing about the reading — all fourteen depend on the same one key, which is the point — but the count is the kind that goes stale while reading as current, exactly as that gotcha says, so the checklist rows deliberately name the stores they check rather than counting them.
- **A refused Keychain read presents to the user as "could not be decrypted or decoded", which names the wrong cause.** Traced rather than assumed: `LocalStorageEncryption.decode` catches `LocalStorageEncryptionError` and rethrows it, and wraps everything else as `.undecodableLocalData` (`LocalStorageEncryption.swift:233-237`). A `KeychainSecretStoreError.unexpectedStatus` — which is what a denied or cancelled keychain prompt produces — is not a `LocalStorageEncryptionError`, so it takes the second branch and the user is told a file "could not be decrypted or decoded" when the file is fine and the key was simply not handed over. Worth knowing at the manual pass, because it means that banner on the new Mac has two possible causes and they are not distinguishable from the banner alone. Recorded rather than fixed: the wording is correct for the case it was written for, and changing it is code this ticket may not touch.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The prediction is a prediction until the rows are run.** Nothing here was executed against a second Mac, and no agent in this repository can execute it — `CLAUDE.md`'s rule that all manual and visual verification is the founders' applies with full force to a whole-machine migration.
- **One thing the code cannot answer at all: whether macOS prompts for the login password on the new Mac.** A file-based keychain item carries an access-control list naming the application that created it, and `Packaging/signing-identity` is a local development certificate — `Sonny Local Dev`, created per machine by `scripts/create-signing-identity.sh`, whose private key never leaves the login keychain it was made in. Whether the migrated app satisfies that list depends on which binary the founders run on the new Mac and how it was signed, which is not a property of this tree. The first checklist row therefore asks the founders to record a prompt if one appears and treats it as information rather than as a failure.
- No ticket is filed for the SONNY-304 conflict above. It is a contradiction between two recorded founder decisions, not schedulable work, so it is recorded as a comment on SONNY-304 — where the next session to implement it will read it — and on SONNY-422, and reported to the founder. Filing a ticket would presume the resolution.

Open questions: one, and it is the founders'. SONNY-304's `ThisDeviceOnly` decision and SONNY-253's Migration-Assistant decision cannot both be implemented as written. Either SONNY-304 is re-decided for the device key (keeping it migratable while the session token still hardens), or the migration path needs something other than Migration Assistant, which is the option-B iCloud-Keychain route that waits on the Apple Developer enrolment.

Next branch: per the roadmap.

### Branch: feature/sonny-renames-one-file-and-asks-first
Status: complete
Date: 2026-09-04
Tickets: SONNY-385 — Sonny renames a file or folder, asking first; "rename all of these" is refused with a clarification rather than guessed at.
Reviewed by: pending (per WORKFLOW.md step 7).

**The decision this branch carries was the founder's and not the plumbing** (2026-09-03, recorded on SONNY-385 and not reopenable here). Batch rename takes **no rule in v1** — option D of the four the ticket priced. A pattern (`2024-{name}`) needs a mini-syntax the planner emits and the user reads inside an approval; a sequence makes *ordering* a second decision with no obviously right answer, whose mis-ordering is invisible until somebody looks; a substitution misses every item without the substring, producing partial batches. A wrong bulk rename cannot be undone through the product and a question is cheap, and that asymmetry decides it. **Substitution is the named first candidate** if the question turns out to annoy people in real use; a sequence is not to be built until somebody asks for one.

**The refusal is a *question*, and that is the whole of the feature rather than a nicety.** "Rename all of these" reaching the user as red text would refuse the request and give them nothing to do with the refusal. So `AgentOperation.jobTemplateRefusal` stopped being a `String?` and became `JobTemplateRefusal`, which carries how its words reach the user: `.refused` for `start_watching`, where there is nothing to answer and the next move is to ask for the watcher on its own, and `.asks` for `rename`, where there is exactly one thing to answer. `PlanItemJobResolver` throws the matching error and `AgentActionExecutor.prepare` converts that one error — and only that one — into a clarification, through the same `clarificationPlan` a missing routine or workspace already went through. So the widget's panel, its answer field and the re-entry that sends the answer back through `start()` are reached by exactly the path a planner-authored `clarify` step reaches; nothing new was built for it.

**Why the type changed rather than a second property being added.** The property's own comment already said the classification and the words the user reads are one decision in one place — and the second entry is what showed the string was carrying two decisions rather than one. A `.refused` rename would still refuse batch renaming, and would refuse it by telling the user the run failed instead of asking them for the names: the founders' decision reversed with the membership test still green. `theOnlyOperationsAJobMayNotRepeatAreTheStandingCapAndTheOneThatNeedsAnAnswer` asserts the whole value rather than its message, which is what makes that reversal fail.

**`jobTemplateRefusal` now has two bars, and the second one arrived with the second entry.** The first is `start_watching`'s: each copy consumes a share of something capped and standing that outlives the run. The second is rename's: the operation takes a value that is **different for every item and cannot be derived from the item**, so repeating the template repeats that one value. That bar does not reach the ordinary job operations — every one of those takes the item itself as its input, which is exactly what the expansion supplies. Rename is the first operation to want a *second* per-item value, and `PlanItemField` has no way to carry one.

**The item-field trap SONNY-235 recorded is the thing this branch tested first, and the honest answer to it is not the convenient one.** A `[rename]` job declares an `itemField`; rename has two fields an item could plausibly go into, and `PlanItemField` can only carry `inputPath`. So the item lands on the path and every copy keeps the template's single `newName` — forty steps renaming forty files to one name, the first succeeding and thirty-nine colliding with it. The tempting shortcut was to answer `[]` from `itemFieldsRead` for rename and let the field check produce the refusal. That is a table lying about one operation to achieve an unrelated effect, and `theItemFieldTableMatchesWhatTheAdaptersActuallyRead` would have caught it, because the adapter really does read `inputPath`. The table answers what the adapter reads; `jobTemplateRefusal` is the door.

**Renaming is destructive on every run, which is the difference from every other write in this package.** `create_local_draft`, `create_zip` and the web-research writer escalate only when their output path is already taken, because there the ordinary case replaces nothing. A rename has no such case: the name a file is filed under is something the user chose, and renaming replaces it every time. So `RenameCapabilityAdapter.assessRisk` raises an **unconditional** `.destructive` escalation and the consequence rule (2026-08-13) does the rest. `theRenameEscalationIsDestructiveAndAsksEvenWhenNothingWouldBeOverwritten` lives in `ConsequenceRuleTests` beside the other construction sites rather than in the rename suite, so that file's claim to classify *every* site stays true, and its control is a folder holding nothing but the file being renamed — where a collision-keyed escalation would have produced `.autoRun` and no prompt at all.

**The collision fails, and it fails on Sonny's terms rather than Foundation's.** `FileManager.moveItem` happens to refuse an occupied destination on macOS today, so the check could be omitted and the observable behaviour would look the same — which is exactly why it is there. What the call gives back is `NSFileWriteFileExistsError`, naming neither the file in the way nor the item being renamed, and the behaviour would be a property of Foundation: an overwrite flag, a different filesystem, or a call swapped for `replaceItemAt` would silently turn the refusal into the destruction of a file the user never named. The refusal is also raised at `prepare`, so nobody is asked to approve a rename that cannot happen.

**A case-only rename is not a collision, and on this Mac it looks exactly like one.** APFS is case-insensitive by default, so `readme.md` "exists" at `README.md` and the naive check refuses a rename people genuinely ask for, over a file that is the item itself. Measured at this branch's head before the code was written, on a temporary directory: `fileExists` at the case-changed path answers `true`, `fileResourceIdentifier` answers **equal** for the two URLs, and `moveItem` then performs the case change successfully. The exemption requires **both** halves — same path modulo case *and* same file identity — and neither alone is right: on a case-*sensitive* volume `README.md` beside `readme.md` really is a second file, and **a hard link** reports the same identity as the file it is linked to while being a second name the user can see in Finder. Everything else falls through to the refusal, which is the fail-closed direction.

**That sentence named a *symbolic* link until PR #200's F3, and it was false rather than loose** — recorded here rather than quietly edited, because it is the kind of wrong reason that survives a review by sounding right. A symbolic link reports a **different** identity from its target, so it never reaches the exemption's second half at all: the identity check already refuses it, and the case half is doing nothing about it. What the case half actually stops is a **hard link**, which does report equal identity, and that reason appeared nowhere in the code, the tests or this entry. Re-measured independently on this Mac, Darwin 25.6.0, rather than transcribed from the review: symlink identity **differs** from its target's, hard-link identity is **equal**, hard-linked paths are not equal modulo case, and `moveItem` throws `NSCocoaErrorDomain 516` onto either. **Bounded honestly:** dropping the half destroys nothing — `moveItem` refuses a hard-linked destination anyway, so the cost is Foundation's wording instead of Sonny's, which is exactly the property `refuseCollision` exists to guarantee. The guard is kept and is held by a test now (`aRenameOntoAHardLinkOfTheSameFileIsStillRefused`), and the mutant that drops the case half dies.

**The defect that case actually found was in the destination, not in the check** — and it was found by writing the test, not by a battery. `PathWhitelist.validateOutputFile` returns a **canonical** URL, and canonical is the wrong thing to move to: `fileExists` finds `readme.md` at `README.md`, so `resolvingSymlinksInPath` rewrites the requested spelling to the one already on disk, and renaming `readme.md` to `README.md` came back as a path identical to its own source — reported to the user as "readme.md is already called that", for a rename that changes the name. The door is still called, for its *refusal*: it re-checks containment and that the parent is a real directory, and the discard of its return value is deliberate rather than an oversight. Composing the destination by hand is safe for the same reason the discard is: the folder is canonical because the source is, and the new name holds no separator and is neither `.` nor `..`, so the result is a direct child of a validated directory. `R10` is the mutant that puts the old line back.

**A rename is not a move, and the refusal of a path-shaped name is the operation's definition rather than a validation nicety.** `~/Documents/a.pdf` renamed to `../Desktop/a.pdf` lands somewhere the user was never shown, squarely inside the whitelist and therefore past every containment check — which is why `validateInsideWhitelist` cannot be what stops it: it is answering a different question and would say yes. Sonny has no move operation; one arriving through the rename field would be a capability nobody decided to build. `outputPath` was the field this could have reused and deliberately does not, for the same reason: it holds a destination *path* everywhere else in the plan language.

**What a new operation had to answer, and the six that a test named for us.** The compiler named four exhaustive switches — `ResumeRepeatSafety`, `AgentActionExecutor.workflow(for:)`, `PlanScopedResources`, and `PlanItemJob`'s two — and the suite named six more populations: the capability registry's operation cover, the egress classification, the workspace-scope table and its `allCases.count`, the resume-repeat sets in both directions, the job's item-field table and refusal population, and the planner boundary's schema shape and golden. Two more came from adding a *field* rather than an operation: `AutomationStoresTests`' resolver-only strip classifier and `SpokenPathTests`' path-field table, each of which fails on any new `AgentStep` property whatever it is called. **`newName` is planner-writable and is not a path**: a spoken folder phrase expanded into it would turn a name the user said into a rename Sonny then refuses.

**A rename is `.safeToRepeat`, and the reasoning is the collision rule rather than a judgement about how bad a second one would be.** Repeating a rename that already finished is refused with the **collision** message, naming the renamed file as the thing already there; repeating one where the user has since put a new file at the old path is refused the same way. Neither destroys anything and neither reaches anyone but the user, which is that classification's bar. **This said "finds no source and fails" until PR #200's F7, and that named the wrong gate**: a resume re-prepares before it runs, `prepare` previews with `requiresExistingSource: false`, so the missing source is skipped and `refuseCollision` answers first on the file now sitting at the destination. The not-found answer is `execute`'s and a resumed run never reaches it. The classification is untouched — what was imprecise is which door speaks, and the message a user actually reads after resuming an interrupted rename that had already landed is the collision refusal. It is also never a *silent* repeat, which is what the property is actually about: every rename carries the unconditional escalation, so a resumed one asks exactly as a first one does.

**A rename is not on `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations`, and that is a decision.** A routine naming a specific file and a specific new name is a routine a user can legitimately author and run by hand, where it asks like anything else. A *scheduled* run cannot perform one: the unattended path grants a `standingGrant` consent whose ceiling is tier 2, and a rename's escalation targets tier 3, so the ceiling refuses it — the same way it refuses every other member of the destructive family. Adding it to the list would have been a second mechanism for something the ceiling already does.

**The workspace boundary is told about both paths, and the second is derived.** A rename reads one file and writes another, and the written one is a path no field of the step holds — it is `inputPath`'s own parent with `newName` in it. Reporting only the source would answer a boundary about the file being read and say nothing about the file being created, which is the direction that silently blesses. The derivation lives once, on the adapter, and the classifier calls it; a second copy is a second answer waiting to disagree. `WorkspaceScopeTests`' probe gained a `newName` for the same reason it carries `workspaceFileLocations`: left nil, the row would collapse to the source alone and pass while saying nothing about the derivation.

Behavior added:
- **Sonny renames one file or folder**, given a path and a name, keeping it in the folder it is in.
- **It asks first, every time**, under the consequence rule.
- **A rename onto a name already in use fails**, with a message naming the file already there, and nothing is replaced.
- **A rename that only changes letter case works**, rather than being refused as a collision with itself.
- **A new name that is a path is refused**, so a rename cannot become a move.
- **"Rename all of these" comes back as a question with an answer field**, and no file is touched.
- **The planner has the word**: a tool description, a schema enum entry, and the `newName` property.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **A job over many items** (SONNY-235) — the resolver's two template checks run in the same order, the watcher refusal still arrives as a failure through `forbiddenStepOperation`, and only the new error converts to a question. `ItemJobTests` and `StandingWatcherCreationTests` both still pass.
- **The clarification path** (`clarify` steps, and `prepare`'s missing-routine/workspace conversion) — the two synthetic-clarification returns were factored into one helper that builds the same three parts; the two returns that hand back the planner's *own* clarify plan were deliberately left alone, because they return a different plan.
- **The consequence rule's existing construction sites** — the replace-on-save trio and the output-collision trio still assess `.destructive` at tier 3 with `.explicitApproval`, and the advisory sites still auto-run.
- **The routine store's resolver-only strip** — `newName` is planner-writable and joins the strip's *planner-writable* half, so nothing new is cleared.
- **Spoken folder phrases** — `inputPath` and `outputPath` still normalise, and `newName` deliberately does not.
- **The Anthropic prune** — `prunedSchema` still rewrites every type union in the real schema as an `anyOf` and leaves none, at the new count, and `cerebras.test.ts` reads the same regenerated fixture and asserts no count.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **`PathWhitelist.validateOutputFile` answers a containment question, and its return value is canonical.** Using it as a *destination* silently collapses a case-only rename onto its own source. Call it for its refusal; compose the path you are going to write.
- **A refusal that has an answer wants a different door from one that does not**, and encoding that as a second string property would have let the two drift. The delivery belongs in the same value as the words.
- **Answering `[]` from a classification table to achieve an effect elsewhere is the shape a source-scan backstop exists to catch.** `itemFieldsRead` answers what the adapter reads and nothing else.
- **A count pinned in a test is pinned wherever grep says it is.** The serialized union count lives in three places — two tests and one stale doc comment — and only a `grep -rn` over both halves finds them all.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Batch rename takes no rule**, by founder decision. Substitution is the named first candidate; a sequence is not to be built until somebody asks. Neither has a ticket, deliberately — the decision is that they wait for real use.
- **A rename does not consume a previous unit's artifact.** "Convert this and rename the result" needs a rename with a blank `inputPath`, which `ChainedArtifactCarry` would have to be taught; a rename names its own path today, and one with none is refused with its own sentence. Not filed, because nothing has asked for it.
- **SONNY-416** — the stale union count in `server/src/model/anthropic.ts`, filed and untriaged.

Open questions: none.

Next branch: per the roadmap.

The `410` half needs no call site: it sits inside `SonnyBackendClient.send`, the one place every route's refusal passes through.
- **A typed too-old state driven by `version.unsupported`, carrying the `upgrade_url` the `410` body now holds.** `SonnyBackendAPIError` decodes §7.1's conditional field; `ClientVersionState.tooOld(link:)` carries it, already validated.
- **§8.4's two headers read on every response**, successes and failures alike, because the gateway sets them in `onRequest` precisely so they reach a reply no route handler produced.
- **Copy for both states, in `SignInCopy`'s pattern**, owned by `ClientVersionCopy` and read by four callers — `SignInCopy`, `SonnyBackendCopy`, the widget and Command Center. `version.unsupported` stopped being unmapped: `SignInFailure.updateRequired` is a named case now.
- **An Update Sonny button that opens the link in the default browser when it parses as `http` or `https`, and otherwise the message with no button** (founder decision, 2026-09-04, recorded on SONNY-402). The warning carries a **Not now** beside it; the wall does not.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The widget's existing precedence, all eleven states.** Nothing was reordered: the two new branches were inserted, one above `.failure` and one below `.resumeOffer`, and `ClientVersionSurfaceTests` drives a real view model through `.clarification`, `.failure`, `.result` and `.idle` to show each still wins where it used to.
- **`CommandCenterAttentionPanel`'s three states on all five pages.** `MemoryCommandCenterTests.everyCommandCenterPageRendersTheSharedAttentionAndStorageSurfaces` still walks `CommandCenterDestination.allCases`; the panel is the same panel with two more self-gating branches.
- **`SignInFailure`'s other eleven cases and every sentence they map to.** `SignInCopyTests` asserts all of them literally and its population is `allCases`, so the new case joined every existing test rather than sitting beside them.
- **The retry ladder.** `version.unsupported` was already non-retryable with `maximumAttempts` of 1; nothing about `isRetryable`, `attemptCeiling` or the `Retry-After` bound moved, and `aCodesAttemptCeilingAgreesWithWhetherItMayBeRetriedAtAll` still runs over every code the contract names.
- **The token refresh and the `401` path.** The new branch in `send` sits below the refresh branch and above the revoked-token branch, and touches neither; the ten-concurrent-401 single-flight test is unchanged.
- **The composer.** `composerState` answers `.ready` in both new states and is unchanged — a build behind the wall still runs every free local capability (§16.3), so the field a user types into must stay usable.
- **The local-data wipe.** Four new stored properties, all classified `outsideTheWipe` with their reasons, and `clearInMemoryLocalDataState` is untouched.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **"On any `410`" recurses unless something stops it, and the thing that stops it has to be a parameter rather than a path check.** §8.3 requires the gate to refuse `/v1/meta` too — "on every endpoint, including `/v1/meta` itself answering honestly" — so a walled-off build gets a `410` on the very request the previous `410` started. `send` carries `allowingMetaRefresh`, false only for the meta fetch, and V2 in the battery is that parameter inverted.
- **The state machine's hard part is what *clears* it, not what sets it.** Three rules, and the middle one is the one a reader would get wrong: a served `2xx` with no deprecation header clears everything including the wall, because it is proof from the deciding party that this build is above both bounds; a deprecation header can never lower a wall, since the gate cannot produce that pairing but a proxy in front of it can produce nearly anything; and a *failing* response carrying no header changes nothing at all, because a `500` or a load balancer's `503` says nothing about which builds a deployment serves. Reading that silence as "current" would clear a warning on a bad gateway day.
- **The wall goes above `.failure` and below every parked continuation, and the second half is the one that needs arguing.** Above, because the failure panel offers Retry and this is the one refusal §9.3 defines as permanent. Below the four screen-control questions, the live session's HUD and an unanswered clarification, because §16.3's free local capabilities keep working through the wall — a local run really can park an approval while every backend call is refused, and a widget that declined to draw one would hang it. The warning goes last of all, below the resume offer: it is not about a task at all, and the band lasts until the user updates, so anywhere higher would hold every other panel off screen for weeks.
- **The warning had to become dismissible, and the wall had to not be.** Same root: a state that persists for weeks cannot occupy an attention surface unconditionally. Dismissal is one boolean, cleared whenever the state changes, so a dismissal answers the state it was pressed on and the next thing the deployment says is heard.
- **`SafeURL.validateWebURL` is the wrong validator here and reusing it would have broken the manual pass.** It also refuses loopback, RFC1918 and `.local` hosts, correctly, because its subject is a URL Sonny itself would fetch. This one goes to the user's browser at the user's press, and the deployment a founder points a manual test at is a locally configured gateway whose `UPGRADE_URL` is very often exactly such a host. `ClientUpgradeLink.openable` is `http`/`https` plus a host, which is the founder's rule and nothing more.
- **The check runs where the value enters, not at the press.** `ClientVersionState`'s link is a `URL?` that has already been through `ClientUpgradeLink`, so a `file:` or `javascript:` string never becomes a `URL` anywhere in the app and no surface has to remember a scheme rule. The button's absence follows from the same `nil`.
- **A stored `@Sendable` closure was not available for the notification and `AsyncStream` was.** `SonnyBackendClient` is an actor and every surface that wants this is `@MainActor`; under this package's language mode a stored `@Sendable` closure capturing one of those does not compile. The stream yields the state it already holds as its first element, so a surface that starts observing after the launch fetch is late rather than wrong.
- **One owner for the words, because the two panels cannot be one view.** System B may not leave the widget and System A may not enter it, so `ClientVersionCopy.prompt(for:)` is what has a single home — the same shape `ScreenControlSessionPresentation` holds for the session line, and for the same reason. `bothSurfacesReadTheVersionPromptFromOneOwnerAndNeitherHandWritesIt` counts each literal at zero in both files, with the owner's call counted at exactly two per file so a third reader arrives at the test.
- **The mirroring is checked by position rather than by presence.** `bothSurfacesOrderTheSharedAttentionStatesTheSameWay` reads both `state` properties, finds the five shared conditions in each, and asserts the offsets are sorted — so a branch moved on one surface and not the other fails there rather than at a founder's manual pass. Each token is also counted at exactly one per chain, because a second branch reading the same condition would otherwise hide behind the first one's position (`CLAUDE.md`'s shared-anchor rule).
- **What clears a wall is decided by the status code, and the first version of this decided it by the header — which made §8.4's own rollback unreachable** (PR #202's review, F1, fixed in branch). The rule as shipped refused to lower the wall on *any* response carrying `Sonny-Deprecation: true`, so the served-`2xx` rule beneath it was never reached. That reads harmless until you notice which configuration it describes: the ladder's prescribed way back from a minimum armed too aggressively is to lower it to at or below the shipped build and leave `recommended_client` above it — the warning band, where **every** response is served *and* carries the header, so no header-free `2xx` exists for the other rule to fire on. A running client stayed walled off, and the wall has no dismiss control, so quitting the app was the only way out. The reviewer measured it against a real gateway in exactly that configuration and reproduced it in the app half with a control that fires. **The threat model the guard stated did not survive its own third rule**: it argued that a proxy must not be able to lower the wall with a header, while the same code already let that proxy lower it *completely* with a bare `2xx` — the stricter handling applied to the response carrying **more** information. What actually bounds a proxy is the status code, so that is what the rule turns on now, and forging a served answer is forging the gateway's own. **The four cases are pinned as one table rather than four tests**, because the property is the pair and four separate tests each pass against a rule that has the other direction wrong — which is how this survived a battery of eighteen: three of the four were covered and the fourth was the one the ladder needs.
- **A manual row is only a row if the setup it names can produce what it asks the founder to watch for, and the one written to prove F1 could not** (PR #202's cycle-3 verification, corrected in branch). The row asked for a running app to come out of the wall after an operator rollback, without relaunching. On `./scripts/deploy.sh local` with no Supabase credentials that cannot happen: a running app leaves the wall only on a *served* response, the app builds exactly four unauthenticated requests — `/v1/auth/email/start`, `/v1/auth/email/verify`, `/v1/auth/refresh` and `/v1/meta` — that gateway `404`s the first three because the auth routes are not mounted, and `/v1/meta` is called only at launch and on a `410`, neither of which follows a rollback. Everything else is bearer and comes back `401`, a failing response the fixed rule correctly refuses to lower the wall on — so the founder would have seen the wall still up, which was the **first item in the row's own list of what would be a finding**, and a `401 auth.unauthenticated` would have signed them out on the way. **The row is withdrawn rather than repaired**, and the reason is the transferable half: a row that cannot produce its own expected outcome does not merely fail to test the fix, it reports correct code as broken, which is worse than no row at all. **No code changed for it, and that is the decision rather than the easy way out**: on a real deployment this recovers by itself, because every served response clears the wall and the token refresh is one — `performRefresh` goes through the same `send`/`perform` path as everything else, so a walled app whose access token is expiring gets a served `200` and comes out before the user does anything. The gap is the rig's, not the product's, so what would be bought by a third `refreshMetaDocument` trigger is a manual row rather than a behaviour, and §8.3 names two triggers on purpose.
- **An assertion satisfied by a neighbouring branch reads exactly like one that holds the branch it sits under** (PR #202's review, F2, fixed in branch). `#expect(viewModel.hasVisibleWidgetPanel)` sat in the test that puts the wall above an ordinary failure — which sets `errorMessage` first, so the predicate was already true from the failure branch two terms below the wall's, and deleting the wall's term left all 2888 tests green. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s shared-anchor class in assertion form, and the cost is not hypothetical: this predicate *is* `FloatingWidgetView.showsPanel`, so with the term gone the state still resolves to `.tooOld` and the panel that draws it is never on screen — the widget renders nothing at all for the wall while every backend call fails, which is SONNY-299's shape verbatim on the one state whose whole purpose is to be readable when nothing else works. The remedy is the same one that rule always asks for: assert the term with nothing else set that could satisfy it, in both directions, and rule the other branches out by name rather than by assumption. The warning's mirror gets the same arm, and the misleading assertion keeps its place with a comment saying which test actually pins the term.
- **A mutant on a recursion guard hangs rather than reddens, and this branch paid for that twice.** The first battery's V2 flipped `allowingMetaRefresh` to `true` in `performMetaFetch`; `refreshMetaDocument` then awaited its own `Task` from inside it, which does not error — it suspends forever. Measured at **0.0% CPU for over three minutes** before the run was killed. The second battery's V4 stopped the deprecation header being read, and `theStreamCarriesEachChangeOnceAndRepeatsNothing` sat on a bare `await iterator.next()` for a change that would never come: an `AsyncStream` that stops yielding does not end. **Both were real defects rather than bad mutants** — the first a permanent hang one edit away in production code, the second a test whose failure signal was a hang, which `CLAUDE.md` records as unmeasurable by construction. Both are fixed in branch: a boolean replaces the `Task` handle, and both stream reads are collected by a task under `HangBackstop.waitOrAbandon` with the real assertion after the wait. **What is left over, stated rather than implied:** the recursion property itself still cannot be measured by a battery, because two guards now stand behind it and removing either one alone changes no behaviour while removing both produces a hang. `aRefusalTriggersExactlyOneMetaCallAndTheMetaCallsOwnRefusalTriggersNone` asserts two requests and no more, and `twoCallersAtOnceMakeOneRequest` is the arm of the second guard a mutant can reach — V2 in the final plan, killed by 2 tests.
- **A mutant that does not compile reports `KILLED` and carries no evidence, which is the harness working and not a result.** V7's first form put `let host = url.host ?? ""` in a `guard`'s binding list, which is a type error, and the report said so in as many words — *"this says the mutant does not build, not that it is covered"*. It was rewritten as a tautology that compiles (`url.host != nil || url.host == nil`) and re-run alone at that head, where a real test killed it; the compiling form is what the plan carries now, and it is killed by 1 test inside the run the figures above report. The transferable half: read the verdict *and* its qualifier, because a build failure and a real kill print the same first word.
- **The changelog's first heading had to be corrected before this entry could sit above it.** `### Branch: chore/attribution-rewrite` names a branch that landed by force-push and never as a pull request; `scripts/changelog-order` resolves a heading against a merge subject and exempts only the *first* entry from that arm, so any entry prepended above it turns the tool red. Found by SONNY-403 on 2026-09-04, and every wave-5 lane carries the identical three-edit correction inside its own changelog commit so the hunks merge clean at every hop. Ratified as a bounded exception to the own-heading-range rule by the coordinator's comment of 2026-09-04 on this ticket: that file, those three edits, nothing else outside this entry.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Nothing armed anywhere, which is SONNY-204's decision and not a gap here.** `MINIMUM_SUPPORTED_CLIENT` and `RECOMMENDED_CLIENT` both default to `0.0.0`, so no deployment refuses or warns anybody, and both manual rows configure a local gateway by hand. Arming a real one is a founder's call and §8.4 makes raising the minimum past a version that had no deprecation period a breach of the contract.
- **The kept `/v1/meta` document is used for one thing.** It answers the upgrade link when a `410` body carries none. Its version bounds are decoded and deliberately not compared: which band this build is in is the gateway's answer, and re-deriving it here would be a second implementation of §8's arithmetic — build metadata dropped, one to three components, prerelease suffixes — that can disagree with the one that actually decides.
- **`entitlement_keys` is not decoded.** §5.3's key set is `EntitlementKeys`' subject and a second reader would be a second answer to which key verifies a claim. Publishing a rotation overlap is SONNY-401.
- **The no-button path is not manually reachable.** A gateway refuses to start with a non-http `UPGRADE_URL`, and refuses to start with an armed minimum and no `UPGRADE_URL` at all, so a correctly configured deployment always supplies a link. It is held by tests on both sides instead, and the manual section says so rather than leaving a row nobody can run.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the wave the coordinator sets; nothing here blocks or is blocked by another lane.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **What places a name on `deploy.sh`'s credential array is `billing/deps.ts`'s own requirement list, not a judgment about secrecy.** `PASSTHROUGH` prints an absent name; `PASSTHROUGH_SETTINGS` is silent; neither refuses anything, and the refusal a half-configured billing container makes is `billingDepsFrom`'s `ConfigError` and exit 78. So the trigger and the four names it makes required go on the credential array — the same required-when-a-feature-is-on shape `ENTITLEMENT_SIGNING_KEY`, `SPEND_CAP_UNITS` and `CREDIT_PLANS` already have there — and the two that are optional and defaulted go on the settings array. `BILLING_PROVIDER` in particular cannot go on the silent one: its absence is the failure the ticket was filed for, and silent absence is a container answering 404 to the provider's delivery.
- **`UPGRADE_URL`'s note is the closest argument the other way and it does not reach.** It keeps a no-default name off the credential array because listing it as missing on every run is noise. Its trigger is itself a defaulted setting sitting beside it, so that cluster is coherent where it is, and no key is behind it. Two of billing's five are keys.
- **A source scan over `deploy.sh` would have been satisfied by the comments explaining the change.** Both arrays sit under screens of prose naming every variable they discuss, so a regex for `BILLING_WEBHOOK_SECRET` inside the `PASSTHROUGH=(…)` region passes with the entry deleted — `CLAUDE.md`'s citation-matches-its-own-text defect, reached by writing the documentation the ticket asked for. The test sources the real script instead, with an unrecognised target so the `case` falls through to `usage` before `docker` is named, and an `EXIT` trap calls the script's own `collect_passthrough`. Bash's parser knows what a comment is; no regex here has to.
- **The self-heal's `period_start` filter stays, and the boundary case gets its own record.** The tempting fix — look back one period — is wrong because of what `finalizeTopUpOrder` does rather than what it is called: it does not only ask, it charges a draft that was never charged. Across a boundary that has two outcomes and both are bad. An order already paid settles as `granted` onto a row whose `period_start` is the old period, and `readToppedUpCredits` sums only the current period's rows, so the user gets nothing for money already gone. An order still in draft is charged **now**, for credits landing on a period that has ended. Turning "may have been charged" into "certainly charged, certainly worthless" is not a direction to move a money path in.
- **Granting into the current period instead is a different design, not a wider filter.** 0019 says a top-up is spent against the period it was bought in, and `attempt_no` and the unique index that makes the per-period bound exact are per period. Moving a row's period would break both, which is why this was not the cheaper half of the same choice.
- **The report's labels model what the self-heal actually scopes by, and say what they cannot check** (PR #201's F3). `readOutstandingTopUp` filters on account, provider, period and outcome, and `attemptTopUp` refuses on withdrawn consent before it ever reads the order — so a predicate answering only the period question, documented as answering "is this row past the reach of the self-healing path", printed `resolvable` over a current-period row bought at a provider this deployment no longer runs. `reachOfSelfHeal` now answers four ways, `main` passes `BILLING_PROVIDER` (the same variable `billingDepsFrom` turns into `deps.provider.name`), the report names the half it could not check when that variable is absent rather than quietly guessing, and the `resolvable` paragraph names the three conditions the report does not model — consent first, because turning auto-top-up off is the likeliest reaction to a surprise charge and is exactly the account whose `unconfirmed` row is outstanding. **The label is the whole value this report adds over `SELECT *`**, which is why a mis-label is worth a round even though the row was reported and the exit code was already 1.
- **A money report defaults to reporting, not to hiding** (PR #201's F4). Both vocabularies were closed `IN` lists with nothing tying them to the migrations' `CHECK`s, so an outcome a later migration adds fell silently on the not-debt side: measured by the reviewer, an eighth `billing_event` outcome as the only row in the table produced `no unresolved billing debt` and exit 0 — the clean-zero family, on the one report whose whole purpose is that somebody is told. Both queries now exclude the states **known** not to be debt and report everything else, an unrecognised outcome is labelled `UNKNOWN` and carries the non-zero exit, and the two non-debt sets are exported constants that carry the reason each state is not debt. The cost is a harmless future outcome showing up until somebody classifies it, which is a person being asked a question rather than a report keeping quiet.
- **A manual row that is a ticket's substitute acceptance criterion must not be able to report that ticket's own failure on a fixed tree** (PR #201's F1). SONNY-405's proof row read a 404 on `POST /v1/billing/webhook` as "the names did not travel", and `registerBillingRoutes` is gated on `billing && billingStore` while `billingStore` exists only with `auth` — so a container given all five billing names and no Supabase names answers 404 with the passthrough working perfectly. Measured on the built gateway: 404 with the five alone, **401** with the identical five plus the auth prerequisites. The row now reads the container's environment with `docker inspect`, which is the property its own title claims and needs no Supabase, and a second row states the gating so a 404 met anywhere here is not misread.
- **The report is separated from `main` so the exit code is a value.** The one thing this command promises is that it exits non-zero while debt exists, and a `process.exitCode` set inside `main` is unreachable from the suite — so `reportBillingDebts` returns the code and `main` is three lines. The mutant that returns 0 with debt outstanding is killed by that.
- **One correction carried by every wave-5 lane, ratified as a bounded exception to editing only inside one's own heading range.** The changelog's first entry named `chore/attribution-rewrite`, a branch that landed by force-push and never as a pull request; `scripts/changelog-order` resolves a heading against a merge subject and exempts only the *first* entry from that arm, so any entry prepended above it turned the tool red. The heading now names `docs/what-the-comment-filter-could-not-see`, the branch that merged as PR #197 and edited that entry without adding a heading of its own, its `Status` reads `complete`, and the entry carries a paragraph saying why. Found by SONNY-403 on 2026-09-04; the record of the landing itself stays in `WORKFLOW.md` §8.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **`npm run billing-debts` resolves nothing, deliberately.** An `unmatched` delivery needs a human to work out which account that customer is; a `conflict` needs somebody to decide which of two subscriptions is real; a top-up order can only be resolved by an act that charges. None of the three is a decision a gateway can take, so the command reports and exits non-zero and a person acts.
- **Nothing runs it.** There is no schedule and no alerting, for the reason `revocations` has none: no host exists yet (`deploy.sh staging|production` exit 3). Wiring it into whatever check runs on the first real deployment is that deployment's work, on SONNY-126.
- **The founders' three billing rows still need real provider credentials and are still theirs to run.** What this branch adds is the two rows that prove the passthrough without a Polar account, so the three can be reached at all.
- **`BILLING_API_BASE_URL` and `BILLING_GRACE_DAYS` are not among SONNY-405's five and are forwarded anyway.** The ticket's own argument reaches them: the SONNY-216 checklist row that sets the first cannot be run against `deploy.sh local` while it is unforwarded, and the second is `CONTENT_RETENTION_DAYS`' shape exactly — a default the founders may move and could not.

The fixture keeps `Calendar.current`, and **the property that makes that right is the time zone rather than the calendar identifier** — the first version of this entry said an explicit Gregorian *would stop agreeing with the code under test*, and that is false (PR #198's review, F2, settled by a mutant rather than by argument: an explicit Gregorian at the machine's zone **survived**, the same explicit Gregorian pinned to UTC was **killed**). `RoutineScheduler` does default to `calendar: Calendar = .current` and `checkScheduledRoutines` passes no calendar, but its arithmetic is `calendar.date(byAdding: .day, value:)` and `calendar.date(bySettingHour:)`, neither of which is identifier-sensitive for a solar day and an hour of it. Re-derived here by replicating those two calls against the 3-hour daily catch-up window, on a machine in `America/New_York`: shipped (`.current`/`.current`) resolves the occurrence at `2026-08-31T13:00:00Z`, age 3600s, **due**; an explicit Gregorian at the machine's zone gives the same instant and the same verdict; a *non-Gregorian scheduler* against that fixture is also due; and only pinning the fixture to **UTC** moves the occurrence to `2026-08-30T13:00:00Z`, age 75600s, **missed**. So what a fixture must not do is pin a zone — which is exactly what four sibling routine fixtures do, filed as its own ticket.

A mutant collapsing the offset — `tenAM()` returning `nineAM()` — **survived the whole suite**: at `now == occurrence` the age is 0, `RoutineScheduler.swift:59` compares `<= catchUpWindow` and `mostRecentDaily`'s `candidate <= now` is satisfied at equality, so every window admits it. The honest reading is that the offset places `now` inside the catch-up window and nothing pins the offset itself — a coverage observation about the fixture rather than a property of it. **The battery's figures are carried across one docs-only commit under `WORKFLOW.md` step 5's tree-identity proof**, not re-stamped: `git rev-parse ${old}:Sources ${new}:Sources` prints `e2ac097d` twice and `${old}:Tests ${new}:Tests` prints `baa92e80` twice for `old=bc0ded75 new=b81356df`, with `${old}:docs ${new}:docs` printing two different hashes as the control that the check can see movement; `git diff --stat` over that range is the changelog alone.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **`Calendar.date(from:)` does not refuse components its calendar has no room for — it rolls them over, silently and a long way.** The first version of the changed fixture's doc comment asserted that a lunar `Calendar.current` would return `nil` for a 31st, which is the intuition the `?? Date()` fallback was presumably written against. It is false, and it was caught by measuring rather than by review: over all **27** identifiers Foundation ships (this entry first said eleven — PR #198's review, F3; the population is the compiler's, since a `switch` over `Calendar.Identifier` naming 16 cases with no `default` does not build and the error names the other 11), every one resolves `year: 2026, month: 8, day: 31, hour: 9` and none answers `nil` — `.islamic`, `.islamicUmmAlQura` and `.islamicCivil` all land on **2587-11-23**, `.hebrew` on **1735-04-25**, `.chinese` on **4009-10-02**. The fallback was unreachable rather than merely unlikely. This matters beyond one fixture: a test that pins an instant through `DateComponents` and a non-Gregorian calendar is not pinning the instant it reads as pinning, and nothing anywhere goes red.
- **The sweep that defines this ticket's population answers a proxy question, and its blind spot is larger than the population.** It finds files holding a *quoted* ISO literal beside a bare `Date()`. A fixed instant written as `Date(timeIntervalSince1970:)` or `DateComponents(year:)` is invisible to it. Measured at `2856840` over `Tests/*.swift`: 28 files hold a quoted ISO literal, 75 hold a fixed instant in any of those three spellings, 25 hold a bare `Date()`, and the intersection of *any* fixed-instant spelling with a clock read is **16 files** — of which this ticket's sweep names 6. The remaining 10 are recorded on a discovery ticket rather than read here.
- **A sibling fixture had half the shape this one lacked, and the grep that found it was the one looking for the old wording.** `MemoryCommandCenterTests.MemoryFixture.nineAM` (`:3688`) uses an explicit Gregorian calendar in a fixed zone and `?? Date(timeIntervalSince1970: 1_700_000_000)` as its fallback. **Only the fallback is the better half**: the first version of this entry called the whole shape better while the bullet above it called the same shape broken, which is the self-contradiction PR #198's review caught under F2. A fixed sentinel beats a clock read; a *pinned zone* is the thing that breaks off this machine's zone, so that half is a defect rather than a model. This bullet also said the sibling *carries the same doc sentence*, which does not check out textually and is recorded as a residual rather than restated as a claim. It surfaced only because `CLAUDE.md`'s rule to grep the OLD wording after correcting a doc comment was followed — a grep for the new wording would have found nothing and the duplicate would have stayed unknown.
- **A verification grep counted this entry's own prose, and the figure was re-stamped at a head instead of re-measured — `CLAUDE.md`'s ninth write-the-command defect, in its inflating direction** (PR #198's review, F1). The records for the ratified heading rename cited an anchor-uniqueness count of 1 for the old heading string, true at the commit before this entry landed. Then the `Known limitations` bullet above quoted that same string while explaining the exception, so the file held two occurrences and the figure was stamped at a head where it did not hold. Nothing invited a check: the command is real and re-running it reproduces the wrong number, because the prose joined the population it measures. **The general remedy is the one CLAUDE.md already gives** — a citation greping a population its own file belongs to needs a stage excluding the discussion, plus a control that fires — and the specific one is that a count is re-measured at the head it is stamped at, never carried onto it. The three checks beside it (the two heading-anchored greps and `scripts/changelog-order`) were unaffected, so the conclusion held while the figure did not.
- **A fixture that mirrors a contract's whole body is not a fixture with unused fields.** Three separate decoders in `Sources/` — `SonnyTokenResponse`, `WireBillingPortal`, `WireEntitlementResponse` — each declare fewer fields than the gateway sends, and each carries a doc comment saying which field is deliberately not read and why (decoding a field no caller consumes invites a later reader to cache on it). Every calendar literal in this ticket's population that looked like a bound is one of those undeclared keys. The rule for the next sweep: before classifying a literal in an HTTP-body fixture, read the decoder's declared properties, not the fixture.

### Branch: docs/what-the-comment-filter-could-not-see
Status: complete
Date: 2026-09-03
Tickets: SONNY-407 — remove every Claude attribution from the commit history, repoint what the rewrite orphans, and record the map. The prevention half is SONNY-406, merged as PR #195 before this ran.
Reviewed by: fresh session, per `WORKFLOW.md` step 7 — pending at the time this entry was written.

**Why this heading names PR #197's branch rather than the branch the work was done on.** The rewrite landed as the force-pushed tip 356ad4d from chore/attribution-rewrite, which was never a pull request, and its correction clause merged as PR #197 from docs/what-the-comment-filter-could-not-see, which edited this entry and added no heading of its own. scripts/changelog-order resolves a heading only against a merge subject and exempts only the first entry, so the original heading passed exactly as long as this entry sat first and turned the tool red for every wave-5 lane that wrote an entry above it (found by SONNY-403, 2026-09-04). The heading was renamed so the tool's model holds; the record of the landing itself is WORKFLOW.md §8.

**The record of the rewrite itself is `WORKFLOW.md` §8, beside the 2026-08-24 one**, because that section is what stops a future reader treating an orphaned stamp as a broken citation. This entry carries what a *branch* entry carries: what was decided, what was measured, and what would be got wrong by reading only the section.

Spec sections covered: none — this is repository history and records.

Files changed: `WORKFLOW.md` (§8 gains the 2026-09-03 subsection), `docs/sonny-attribution-rewrite-map-2026-09-03.tsv` (new, 1567 pairs), `scripts/rewrite-attribution`, `scripts/verify-attribution-rewrite`, `scripts/repoint-citations` (new), plus **79 files whose citations were repointed** — the changelog, `WORKFLOW.md`, the API contract, `CLAUDE.md`, eight other docs, and real code: `Sources/MacAgentCore/RiskApproval.swift`, sixteen other Swift sources, fourteen test files, `scripts/mutate`, `scripts/warnings`, `.claude/hooks/verify-tests-before-stop.sh`, `server/scripts/deploy.sh`, two SQL migrations.

Tests: **both halves were run, and the sentence that first stood here said they were not owed.** It read "every one of those 79 files changed only inside a comment or a prose line", and that was wrong by five lines. **Four repointed tokens sat inside Swift string literals** — the labels of a fixture table in `UntrustedContentBoundaryScalarMatchingTests.swift`, of the form `("UntrustedContentBoundary.escape at <sha>", """` — and a string literal in `Tests/` is not a comment, so the flagged suite was owed; a fifth was a prose line under `server/`. **The suite was re-run at the candidate rather than argued**: exit 0, 2842 tests in 193 suites, 7 known issues, zero failed-after lines. `npm test` 780 passed / 391 skipped — **byte-identical to the neighbouring lane's post-rebase figure**, which is the strongest line in the check because it is a comparison rather than an absolute — and `npm run typecheck` exit 0. The labels do turn out to be message-argument copy, consumed only as `#expect(…, "\(label): …")` while the assertions run on `calls` derived from `snippet`; that reading is why the claim felt safe, and reading is what got it wrong. **The defect in the claim was asserting a negative without enumerating** — CLAUDE.md's enumerate-before-you-subtract rule, and the evidence against it lived exactly where the filter did not look, since a filter for comment lines cannot see a SHA inside quotes. The honest form of what was known was "no executable expression I inspected changed"; what was written was stronger and unearned. `scripts/verify-attribution-rewrite` exit 0, **15 assertions, 2 of them controls that fire**. `scripts/no-attribution history` answers **0 of 1643** on the pushed history against **10 of 1642** on the old tip, which is the control that makes that zero a measurement. `scripts/changelog-order` exit 0. `scripts/verify-attribution-rewrite` exit 0, **15 assertions, 2 of them controls that fire**. `scripts/no-attribution history` and `tree` both exit 0 after the rewrite. `scripts/changelog-order` exit 0.

Behavior added: none. Ten commit messages lose an attribution; 1567 commits get new SHAs; no tree anywhere changes.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **Every tree in the range**, by construction and then by proof: the rewriter reuses the original tree object, and the verifier compares all 1567 pairs and the two heads.
- **Every signature's presence or absence, per commit.** Not "all signed" — signing was switched on partway through this repository's life, and a blanket flag would have put the founder's key on hundreds of attestations nobody made.
- **Author and committer identity and both dates**, across all 1567.
- **The 75 commits below the range**, untouched, with the 11 signatures among them intact.
- **Every figure beside a repointed citation.** Each pair holds a byte-identical tree, so under `CLAUDE.md`'s rule this is a rename and not a re-measurement.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:
- **The obvious tool silently widens the blast radius, and it does it below the range where nobody is looking.** `git filter-repo` strips signatures from commits whose messages it does not change. Run here it rewrote a 2026-06-25 commit purely to remove its signature, and the cascade took the rewrite from the authorised count to 85 commits more than anyone had approved. A tool that quietly does more than asked, in the direction that looks like success, is the clean-zero family `CLAUDE.md` records — this time in a history rewrite rather than in a grep.
- **`.git` is a FILE in a worktree, and the first run of the rewriter died on that after rebuilding all 1567 commits.** The objects survived; the map — the entire deliverable — did not, because it was being written to `<repo>/.git/…`. `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` is the answer. Worth recording because every session in this repository works in a worktree, and any tool that composes a path from `<repo>/.git` will hit it.
- **Re-signing is restoration, not invention, and the distinction is what made it acceptable.** A signature covers the commit's own content, so changing a message invalidates it under any tool. The choice was between leaving hundreds of commits unsigned — a real degradation nobody asked for — and re-signing with the key that signed the originals. Preserving each commit's original state changes least, and it is the founder's key and his machine.
- **Sequencing was the load-bearing part and it is easy to get backwards.** SONNY-406's guard merged first, on the pre-rewrite `main`, because the branch carrying it was rooted at a commit this rewrite destroys. A record of a rewrite left unmerged on a branch the rewrite orphans is precisely the failure §8 exists to stop.

- **A comment filter is the wrong instrument for "did this change any code", twice over, and both misses were found by someone else.** The first is the four string literals above. The second is subtler and would have been a red suite rather than a wrong sentence: two of the repointed files are **SQL migrations**, changed only inside `--` comments, and this repository hashes migration content. That hash turns out to be unaffected **by construction rather than by luck** — `migrationContentHash` digests `executableSql(up)` and `executableSql(down)`, and `executableSql` strips `--` comments, which the pure test pins directly at `executableSql("-- why this exists\nSELECT 1;")` being `"SELECT 1;"`. **The edge that would have inverted that was checked rather than assumed**: `executableSql` deliberately *preserves* comments inside dollar-quoted bodies, so a repointed comment inside a `$$ … $$` block would have moved the hash. Counted rather than eyeballed — the repointed line in `0014` is line 180 with zero `$$` occurrences before it, though the file contains six later on, and `0017` contains no `$$` at all. Both outside, so stripping applies. Worth stating in this form because "the migration hash test passed" is true and says nothing about why, and because the db half of that test was among the 391 skipped, so the green was silent about it — what exercised the stripping was the pure test.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **PR bodies are not history and were fixed separately.** PR #192's body carried the same footer and session URL; the coordinating session removed both on the founder's instruction, verified by reading the body back from GitHub. Nothing in a repository can reach that surface, which is why `scripts/no-attribution prs` exists.
- **Every SHA this rewrite replaced resolves nowhere afterwards.** That is the convention below §8's map, not a defect: a branch SHA records when a measurement was taken. The map is committed so a reader meeting an old one can find its replacement.
- `gh api` and F9 remain open on SONNY-410 from SONNY-406's review; neither is this branch's.
