The orphaned six appear below and in this branch's code comments **only inside dated records of what a round found at the time**, which are events rather than live figures. Every live figure is at `93726f7`.

Spec sections covered: row 13's third long-running shape, the four the founder chose on 2026-08-22. Shapes 1 and 2 are SONNY-210's; shape 4 is SONNY-236's, running in parallel.

**The decision that carries the ticket: "for each of these" is a plan-level declaration, resolved and expanded into ordinary steps before anything else sees the plan.** `AgentPlan.itemJob` names where the items come from — a folder's own contents, or the Finder selection — and `AgentActionExecutor.prepare` resolves that once, pins the concrete list into the plan, and replaces the template steps with one copy per item, each stamped with `AgentStep.itemIndex`. Everything downstream receives an ordinary plan: preview, `assessRisk`, the approval gate, `chainSegments`, unit dispatch, and SONNY-210's `completedStepIDs`. **No capability adapter changed**, and none can be made to change by adding a new kind of job.

**The two alternatives the ticket names were rejected against the mechanism that has to carry the feature, not on taste.** *A new step operation* (`for_each` with a nested plan) fails on resume granularity: the executor's finest "this is done" boundary is a **unit**, one adapter call, and a `for_each` step is one unit however many items it walks — so `completedStepIDs` could say nothing about item 17 of 40, and the whole point of the ticket would need a second progress mechanism threaded into one privileged adapter that could run arbitrary work, which is `execute` under another name. *A property of an existing step* (`AgentStep.items`) fails on the cost the ticket warns about: the item has to land in a *field*, and which field depends on the operation, so either every adapter learns to loop and substitute or the executor keeps a per-operation substitution table — adapter knowledge stored somewhere else. It also cannot express a unit of more than one step, and `[scan_docx, convert]` is one adapter call across two.

**One approval covering a whole job is a consequence of that shape rather than a change to the rule** (founder decision, 2026-08-31: a job asks once, with visible progress and a stop control). The expanded plan is one plan, so `RiskApprovalPolicy` assesses it once and asks once, exactly as for every other plan. Neither the risk engine nor the consequence rule was touched. `aJobOfManyItemsIsAssessedOnceAndAtTheSameTierAsOne` pins that five items assess at the same tier with the same escalations as one.

**The preview finding, and why it changed the shape rather than adding a branch.** The branch first shipped with execution failures isolated per item and preview failures not, on the stated ground that no preview path reaches an individual item. That ground was wrong, and it was reproduced against this branch before anything was changed: `DocxConversionCapabilityAdapter.preview` scans the folder it was handed and refuses one with nothing to convert, `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter.preview` enumerates it and refuses an empty one, and `prepare` previews every unit before anything is approved — so a three-folder job in which one folder held no Word document died at `prepare` with a message about that one folder, no approval prompt and the other two untouched.

**Isolating preview alone would have moved the death one stage later, and isolating assessment as well would have opened a hole.** Assessment reaches the item too — `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter.assessRisk` validates the folder it is about to read — so preview-only isolation leaves the same job dying at the approval gate instead. And isolating assessment is not the symmetric fix: an item whose assessment threw would still be in the plan, so if the world moved between the prompt and the run it could execute under an approval it was never part of. That is why an item that cannot be previewed is **dropped from the plan** at `prepare` and recorded on `PlanItemJob.unavailableItems`: with its steps gone, preview, assessment and execution are all about exactly the items that will be attempted. A job in which no item can be prepared is refused with the first item's own message rather than asking approval to do nothing.

**Two side-effects of that shape, stated as costs because a reader meeting either cold will think it is a defect.**

- **Previews are recomputed over the trimmed plan rather than filtered from the first pass.** `claimed` and the carried artifact accumulate across units, so a set produced by a walk that visited a unit no longer in the plan is subtly not the trimmed plan's. The second pass is paid **only when something was dropped**; a job in which every item previews cleanly pays exactly one pass, as before.
- **A plan carrying an `itemJob` always takes the chain walk, even at one item.** `chainSegments` otherwise refuses a single segment and the plan falls through to one `executeCapability` call, which knows nothing about items — so a job trimmed to its last item would report that adapter's own sentence ("Ran Shortcut Summarise.") instead of "Worked through 1 of 3 files", and would lose skip-and-continue and the per-item carry reset with it. One item is reachable in ordinary use: a job whose other items could not be previewed, and a resumed job with one left. `segmentPlan(from:steps:)` deliberately copies no `itemJob`, which is what stops that classification recursing on itself.

**What happens when one item fails: skip and continue, and a cancellation is never a failed item.** Stopping is what an ordinary chain does and stays what it does — every plan that is not a job reaches the same rethrow unchanged. For a job it is the wrong answer: the user approved forty items in one press, and abandoning thirty-seven because the third was locked leaves them a job to restart and re-approve. Retrying was rejected as a second policy (how many times, how long between) over work that may already have had half its effect. **The cancellation half is the one that makes the stop control usable**: swallowing a cancellation the way an item failure is swallowed would turn Cancel into a button that grinds through the remaining thirty-seven items and reports them as failures. `SonnyBackendError.isCancellation` is the predicate, and the loop asks `Task.checkCancellation()` at each item boundary so a stop lands with the items after it untouched and resumable.

**What counts as one item being done, and where it is recorded.** An item is done when **every** step of it is done, which is the only definition that survives a unit boundary being coarser than a step. That is derived — `completedStepIDs` read through `AgentStep.itemIndex`, by `ItemJobProgress` — and is deliberately not stored: SONNY-210's record already owns it. What is stored is the one thing nothing can derive, `ResumableTask.itemJobFailures`, because a failed item and an item that never ran look identical by that route. A resume starts that list empty, since a failed item's steps are still in `remainingPlan()` and Continue re-attempts them.

**`PlanItemJob.maxItems` is 50, and the number came from a measurement rather than a round figure.** A job that cannot be checkpointed cannot remember its place, so the cap sits where the expanded plan still fits `ResumableTaskStore.maxEncodedPlanBytes`: a fifty-item two-step job over 120-character iCloud paths encodes to **34962 bytes** against a 65536-byte budget, and the same shape at a hundred items encodes to **69717** — over it. `aJobOfTheLargestPermittedSizeStillFitsTheResumableStoresPlanBudget` is the test that set it. What no item count can bound is a template's own size, so the residual degrades rather than lying: the store refuses an oversized plan on its own terms, the caller reports a write failure, the run continues, and what is lost is the offer rather than the work.

**The schema record, which is a fact about this gateway rather than about this feature.** The obvious spelling for an optional object — `"type": ["object", "null"]` — **is not sendable**, and nothing a reader will be looking at says so. `prunedSchema` in `server/src/model/anthropic.ts` rewrites a type union into an `anyOf` and leaves every sibling keyword on the parent, so a nullable object comes out as a bare `{"type": "object"}` branch carrying no `additionalProperties` — which `server/test/anthropic.test.ts` refuses, correctly, because the structured-output subset requires it on object nodes.

**Teaching the prune to carry `properties`, `required` and `additionalProperties` into that branch was considered and declined, and declining the general case is the decision.** Three reasons, in order. The naive fix is wrong rather than incomplete: `additionalProperties: false` on a branch that carries no `properties` forbids the very object it describes, so the keywords have to *move*, not be copied. Moving them is a redesign of `withoutTypeUnions` for a shape nothing else on the wire sends — that function's own comment declines exactly this kind of speculative machinery, and its one documented residual (a node carrying both a `type` array and its own `anyOf`) is left unhandled on the same ground. And it is a change to how **every** schema this gateway serves is pruned, made by a lane whose ticket is about the client. So the nesting stayed and the nullability moved inside it: `itemJob` is a plain object whose fields are nullable, "not a job" is a null `source`, and `PlanItemJobDecodingSignal.notAJob` is what turns that back into `nil` in `AgentPlan.init(from:)` — caught by that one signal and nothing wider, so a job declared with a source and no `itemField` is still refused rather than silently becoming an ordinary plan that runs the template once. A future reader who needs a nullable object starts at `AgentPlanSchema.itemJobSchema`, which carries this record beside the code.

**The item goes into every step of the template except a *trailing* one that takes the previous unit's output, and both halves of that rule were paid for.** `ChainedArtifactCarry.consumesPreviousArtifact` marks a step whose input is whatever the unit before it produced; such a step's input is not the item, and writing the item there does not merely mis-fill a field — the predicate reads *blank* path fields, so an item written into one makes it false and the step stops working. "Convert the documents in each of these folders and open the result" refused a folder outright until the exception existed. **And the exception stops at the template's first step**, which the next battery's baseline is what caught: a consuming step *leading* the template has no previous unit inside its own item, so that is the one place the item really is its input, and exempting it too broke every "reveal each of these" job — each step arrived with no path and every item failed. Filling in only blank fields cannot express either half, because the consuming step's field is blank in the template too and that blankness is exactly what marks it.

**Two population scans caught new fields, and one of them is worth naming.** `AgentStep.itemIndex` had to join the routine store's resolver-only strip — a step index into a job's item list has no meaning inside a routine, whose steps have no plan and therefore no item list — and `AgentViewModel`'s four new stored properties had to be classified against the local-data wipe. Neither was found by reading; both were red tests naming the field, which is what those scans are for. While extending the wipe's row-13 block, its comment was corrected from "two in-memory slots" to three: it had been clearing three since SONNY-282.

**What ships is the mechanism, and neither of the two examples in this entry's own `Tickets:` line can be run** (PR #185; founder decision 2026-08-31). Sonny has no summarise capability and no rename capability, so "summarise each of these forty PDFs" and "rename all of these" have no per-item verb to call. What a job can do today is whatever an existing capability does to one file or one folder: run a named Apple Shortcut on each item, convert the Word documents in each of a set of folders, reveal each item in Finder. The gap is invisible from the code — every part of the machinery is present and tested — and visible only from those two sentences, which is exactly why a reader of this entry would otherwise conclude the feature is complete and never look for the follow-up. **SONNY-384** records the gap, **SONNY-385** is renaming and is in v1, and **SONNY-386** is summarising and is to be sized. The founders decided on 2026-08-31 that the mechanism ships as it is with those two filed rather than waiting for either.

A battery that measures nothing is not a battery that measured zero.

**What the batteries actually bought, because three of this branch's real defects came out of them and one came out of writing a test for a survivor.** The first run, 14 mutants at `369cbc3`, returned 11 killed and 3 survived.

- **R3** — the rest of a failed item is attempted instead of skipped — survived because every failure test used a one-step template, where an item has no second unit to skip. Held now by a two-workflow template.
- **R14** — a job draws one row per item again — survived because the choice lived inside two SwiftUI view bodies and nothing here tests one. The decision moved out into `ItemJobProgressPresentation.RunRows`, a value a test holds by equality; what stays untested is the drawing rather than the choice.
- **R4** — the carried artifact leaks across an item boundary — survived, and still does, in both walks. See below.

**Writing R4's test found the `consumesPreviousArtifact` defect above, which no mutant in the plan could have found**, because it is a hole in what a job can express rather than a guard that was missing. **And the fix for it was too broad by one case, which the *next* battery's baseline caught** — the suite went red before any mutant was applied, on the view-model test driving a reveal-each-of-these job. Neither of those is a mutation result; both are things a mutation run produced.

**R4 is a recorded survivor rather than a gap to close, and the mechanism is why.** Deleting the cross-item reset leaves the whole suite green because the carry re-seeds from a unit's last *suggestion* fifteen lines below it, and every folder-shaped capability returns one naming the folder it worked in — so an item's own conversion unit replaces the carry with its own folder before that item's opening step runs. For the reset to be live, an item's first unit would have to produce **no write and no suggestion** and then be followed, inside the same item, by a step that consumes an artifact; no combination of today's capabilities does that, because the ones that suggest nothing also give a consuming step nothing to consume, so the item fails at the consumer and its later units are skipped. The line is kept — the invariant is right, it costs nothing, and a capability that succeeds while producing neither would make it live *silently*, as the wrong file opened under a run reporting success. `executeChain` says all of that at the line, and the test that looked like its guard now says in its own doc comment that it is not one: it pins the outcome a user would notice and does not claim the reset.

**Three process pitfalls, recorded because each cost a run.** A battery refuses to start on a dirty tree and also **aborts if the tree becomes dirty mid-run** — editing two `docs/` files during one stopped it after R1, correctly, and it restored the mutant. A **filtered** suite is not enough before a battery: this branch ran `--filter "ItemJobTests|ItemJobPresentationTests"` after a source change and could not see the `ProductShellTests` failure that the battery's baseline then refused on, so the full suite goes *before* the battery rather than after. **The fix round for PR #185's review, and what its own battery found.** Five findings, one blocking, all taken; the round's figures are below and its battery is a second one of 10 mutants at `d6cda07` -> **9 killed, 1 survived, 0 unattributed**.

- **F1, blocking.** `remainingPlan()` rebuilt the plan from three fields and let `itemJob` default to `nil`, so a resumed job kept every step's `itemIndex` and stopped being a job — an unpreviewable item killed the whole resumed run at `prepare` again, skip-and-continue was gone, neither surface showed progress, the widget drew one row per remaining item in the approval prompt, and a second interruption wrote a record that had forgotten it was ever a job. **The obvious one-line fix is wrong**, which is why the count is scoped with the carry: `ItemJobProgress` and the job summary both measure the items *this plan is responsible for*, or a resume of the last two of forty reports "Worked through all 40 files". The earlier attempt's `unavailableItems` are cleared on the way, for the same reason its failures are. And the resume's carried artifact is withheld when it would cross an item boundary, because Continue bakes it onto the remainder's leading step before `executeChain` runs and no in-loop reset can take a value back out of a plan.
- **What hid it longest was a comment.** `initializeStepStatuses` said in so many words that a remainder reports "0 of 40 done" and climbs — a behaviour the code could not produce. That is the third time on this wave that a false claim in a comment kept a defect invisible, and it is why the two contradictory comments in F4(a) were worth fixing rather than leaving.
- **F2, the class rather than its two instances.** Nothing checked that the declared `itemField` was a field the template's steps read, so a `[invoke_shortcut]` template declaring `.inputPath` ran the Shortcut once per item with **no input at all**, recorded zero failures and reported "Worked through all 3 files" — a job that touched none of its items and called itself a complete success. `AgentOperation.itemFieldsRead` is one exhaustive table in the plan language, read only to refuse a declaration and to decide where the item is written, with a source scan against the owning adapters as its backstop. The item is written only into a step that reads the field, which also closes the narrower half — a leading consuming step handed a field it does not read kept both path fields blank and stayed a live consumer of an artifact from outside its own item. **And the refusal asks `writesTheItem` rather than `itemFieldsRead`**, because `[create_local_draft, open_generated_artifact]` has a step that reads the field and it is exactly the one the expansion skips; a mutant reading the looser question survived the first round's battery until that case got its own test back.
- **F2's table was checked from the other end, and the check matters more than the table.** The classification is only worth having if it agrees with the adapters, so cycle 3 measured the population from the adapters' side: `inputPath` is named in 14 files under `Sources/MacAgentCore/`, of which 4 are capability adapters, and `shortcutInput` in 7 files of which 1 is — and those five adapters own **exactly** the seven operations the table classifies as reading something. **The backstop is a real guard rather than a decorative one**, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s standing requirement for a source scan: a cycle-3 mutant mis-classifying `invokeShortcut` was killed with `theItemFieldTableMatchesWhatTheAdaptersActuallyRead` among its killers. What that scan still cannot do is fail when an adapter's *file* cannot be read — it treats an unreadable file as "no adapter, so it claims nothing" — which is the clean-zero family arriving inside a backstop, and is recorded on the ticket rather than fixed here.
- **F3's two guards.** The symlink filter is held by a test now. The per-item whitelist validation is **kept as a recorded survivor**, R4's treatment: three guards reach every escape before it — the link filter, and `FinderSelectionResolver.whitelistedSelection` for the Finder source — and its comment used to claim it "catches anything else `validateInsideWhitelist` knows about that a parent check cannot see", which nothing demonstrates. They cover for each other, which is exactly the arrangement in which deleting one later opens a hole with a green suite.
- **F5.** A manual row that quits mid-job, presses Continue and reads both the progress line and the final summary. Eight rows existed and not one resumed a job, which is why nobody caught F1 by hand.

**The fix round's battery was re-run in full rather than scoped, and that was the only correct action** — checked per mutant against WORKFLOW.md's four carry conditions rather than against what the round happened to edit. Between `08db3aa` and `d6cda07` the round moved two files: `Sources/MacAgentCore/PlanItemJobResolver.swift`, which five of the ten mutants target, and `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/ItemJobTests.swift`, which holds **every one** of the nine distinct killing tests the first run named and the `makeExecutor` fixture all of them drive. So condition 2 fails for all ten and condition 4 with it; nothing was carriable, and the entry's two stamped batteries are two full runs rather than one run and one carry.

**This is worth stating because it is the shape SONNY-391 was filed for**, from the branch running beside this one, which hit it twice in one branch: *scoping a battery by what a round changed is not scoping it by whose evidence moved*, and the two diverge precisely when a round edits a file other mutants target. The substitution reads exactly like obeying the rule. The defence here was not vigilance — it was asking the four conditions per mutant and finding the answer was "none", which is cheaper to check than to reason about.

And **waiting on `pgrep -f "scripts/mutate"` never returns on a founder's Mac**: the pattern is machine-wide and matched four other lanes' batteries running beside this one — wait on this lane's own log instead.

**Every figure above is measured at the head that merges.** The Swift suite, `scripts/warnings`, the server's five commands and the battery are all stamped at a head this branch's docs commits sit on top of, and the carry is proved rather than assumed (WORKFLOW.md step 5): a docs commit touches `docs/` alone, and `git rev-parse ${BASE}:Sources ${NEW}:Sources` prints one hash twice, as do `:Tests`, `:Package.swift` and `:server`. All four mutation carry conditions hold for the same reason — no target file moved, no killing test's file moved, no scanned population moved, no fixture moved. **The braces are not decoration**: `$BASE:Sources` is a zsh substitute-modifier and mangles the path silently, which `git rev-parse` answers for with a commit SHA and no complaint at all.

**One figure is deliberately outside that proof, and saying otherwise was this entry's own defect** (PR #185, F4(b)). `scripts/changelog-order`'s entry count depends on `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` — the very file a docs commit changes — so it cannot be carried across one and is measured at the merging head directly. The blanket sentence that used to cover it was the shape `CLAUDE.md`'s carry rule warns about: the proof was real, and it was about the wrong tree.

### Branch: feature/a-watcher-waits-for-something-to-change
Status: **partial by design — the scope narrowed mid-branch with the founder's agreement, and the remainder is SONNY-382.** SONNY-236 covers the mechanism: a watcher exists, is checked, decides what changed, is capped, and tells the user. It carries no way for a *user* to create or stop one; that is SONNY-382 ("A user can start and stop a standing watcher"), which takes the creation path, the Routines listing with its Stop control, and the founder manual rows for both halves. The split was proposed at this lane's first checkpoint and agreed rather than discovered at the end.
Date: 2026-08-31
Tickets: **SONNY-236** — long-running work, shape 4 of the four the founder named: a standing watcher that waits for something to change.

**Two founder decisions of 2026-08-31 shaped this branch more than the ticket did**, and both are recorded on SONNY-236 as comments.

- **A watcher notifies and does nothing else.** It may not open, write, send, file, delete or run anything. Acting on a pre-approval given when the watcher was created — "when the invoice arrives, file it" — is the better product and was *declined for v1 rather than rejected*, because the consequence rule cannot express "approved earlier, for later" and this ticket's own constraints forbid changing that rule to fit. **So there is deliberately no route to acting in the tree, switched off or otherwise** — no operation, no plan, no executor reference, and the notification category carries an empty action array for that reason rather than for a design one.
- **A watcher is free and capped.** It draws nothing from the paid allowance, so "screen-control runs left" stays the single number a user tracks. The ticket's own sentence requiring watcher checks to be metered is **superseded by that decision and marked superseded rather than deleted**. What replaces metering is the cap, and designing it was this lane's.

**Why a watcher can be free, which is the load-bearing half of that second decision.** A check is `PublicWebPageLoader.load` — a direct `URLSession` fetch of a public page, a `robots.txt` check, a refusal to follow a redirect onto a host whose robots were never consulted, and local readability extraction. No gateway request, no model call, no search provider. The cost of a check is the user's own bandwidth, so `checkInterval` is set against the watched site's politeness budget rather than against a bill.

**The cap, and its five numbers.** Release-time inputs like everything else in row 13, in one value (`StandingWatcherLimits`) so setting them from measured use is one edit: **5** watchers at once, a check every **15 minutes**, a **7-day** lifetime, **4** unstable readings before a page is called unwatchable, **8** consecutive failures before it is called unreachable. A watcher is **one-shot** — it stops on the first confirmed change — so the stopping condition is part of the cap rather than a convenience, which is what the founder's comment asked for. The four endings Sonny decides (changed, expired, unwatchable, unreachable) all notify; **expiry notifies too**, because a watcher that dies quietly leaves the user believing Sonny is still watching, which is the forgotten background process the cap exists to prevent.

**The trigger: its own checker, on the existing pulse — decided explicitly, as the ticket asked.** `checkStandingWatchers()` rides `startRoutineScheduling`'s 30-second timer and wake observer, because those are already the app's "something might be due" heartbeat. It is **not** a branch inside `checkScheduledRoutines`, and the reason is that method's own guard: a scheduled routine *starts a task*, so it must refuse while one is in flight, and it sets `isRunning` while it runs. Folding watchers in would make every watcher blind for the length of every routine and every typed command, for nothing — a watcher starts no task. So the guards here are narrower and the omission of `!isRunning` is the decision rather than an oversight; what is guarded is re-entrancy, because a fetch can outlast the pulse. `aWatcherIsCheckedWhileATaskIsRunningEvenThoughARoutineWouldNotBe` asserts both halves, with `checkScheduledRoutines` in the same state as the control.

**What "changed" means: normalized readable text, confirmed twice.** The digest collapses whitespace runs and **keeps case** — a status recapitalised from "Pending" to "PENDING" is a real edit on the pages people watch, and this is the one place in the feature where hiding a difference is the expensive direction. SHA-256 rather than the text, so the record stays a fixed small size and `resumable-tasks.json` never accumulates the readable text of every page the user has watched.

The ad-slot problem the ticket names is answered by **not notifying on the first difference**. A reading unequal to the baseline becomes a *candidate*; only a second consecutive reading equal to that candidate promotes it. **The cost is stated rather than hidden: notification is one `checkInterval` later than the change.**

**This is a filter with a known failure rate, not the absolute this entry first claimed** (PR #184 review, F4). It defeats content that never repeats consecutively — a clock, a nonce, a shuffle over many items. It does *not* defeat a rotation over a small pool: `k` variants supply two consecutive equal readings with probability about `1/k` per check while a candidate is held, over up to `maxLifetime / checkInterval` checks, so a false "changed" is likely rather than remote for small `k`. `maxUnstableReadings` is the only thing racing it and is the weaker mechanism, because any reading equal to the baseline resets it and a rotation whose pool includes the baseline's variant supplies that regularly. And a page **alternating** between the baseline and one other reading reaches neither ending — never `.changed`, since the two never land consecutively, never `.unwatchable`, since every return to the baseline resets the count — so it runs to `maxLifetime` and then says "It did not change", which is the sentence `.unwatchable` exists to avoid. Whether to strengthen the mechanism, and whether `.expired`'s sentence may assert "It did not change" when a candidate was ever recorded, are founder calls recorded on SONNY-236.

**The store: one file, two collections, and `ResumableTask` untouched.** `resumable-tasks.json` stays the thirteenth local store — SONNY-210 built it, SONNY-235 extends the task record, this adds a sibling collection, and none of the three adds a fourteenth. The file's root becomes a container, and a file written as a bare array still decodes: the legacy shape is recognised **by shape** (`decoder.unkeyedContainer()` succeeds only on a top-level array) rather than by catching a keyed decode's failure, because try-and-fall-back would make a corrupt watcher read as a legacy file and then fail with a message about the wrong format entirely. Nothing forces a rewrite on load; the container is produced by the next write that happens for its own reasons.

**A watcher is a sibling of `ResumableTask`, not a field on it**, and that reverses what that type's own doc comment anticipated on 2026-08-22 — written before the notify-only decision, when a watcher was still expected to act. Under notify-only a watcher has no plan, no steps and nothing to resume, so folding it in would produce records for which `isResumable` is false, `mayBeOfferedForResume` is meaningless and the Memory row's "unfinished task" count is wrong, leaving roughly fifteen readers each needing a filter nobody can see is missing.

**The cap refuses rather than evicts, and only on an insert.** Every other cap in these stores drops the oldest record, which is right for something nobody asked for; a watcher is the opposite, because the user said the sentence that created it. An **update** is how a check records its own result, so a cap that refused one would freeze every watcher's state the moment the fifth was created — and the save that then failed is the one carrying the reading that would have fired.

**The delete: a row labelled *Unfinished tasks* stopped deleting watchers** (founder decision, decision A of 2026-08-31). Command Center's Memory row deleted through `LocalDataDeletionService.deleteStoreFilesOnly()`, which unlinks the file — correct while the file held one kind of thing, and a **mislabelled delete** the moment it held two: the press destroyed the user's watchers with nothing failing and nothing on screen saying so, which is what `CLAUDE.md`'s account of PR #110's F2 calls silent in every direction.

- `LocalStoreRowDeletionScope` routes a store to the right door and is exhaustive, so a fourteenth store must answer the same question; `deleteSharedFileRowContents` lists the twelve whole-file stores rather than sweeping them into a `default`, so the classification and the door have to change together.
- **The unreadable branch deliberately stays file-level.** A collection-scoped delete rewrites the file, which means decoding one whose decode has already failed. It is `deleteStoreFilesOnly()`'s own readable/unreadable asymmetry reaching one door further. **"Nothing is lost" was this entry's claim and it is true only of the bytes** (PR #184 review, F5): quarantine keeps the file, but it moves it out of the path the checker reads, so every watcher in it stops permanently and **none of the four endings fires** — a fifth, quiet ending, contradicting the rule stated in three places that a watcher which stops says so. It is not `.cancelled` either; the user pressed a control about unfinished tasks. Recorded on SONNY-236 as a founder call.
- **The row's own sentence needed no change and that was verified rather than assumed.** "This deletes every unfinished task Sonny is keeping…" stays true and complete once the delete is scoped, which is the point of scoping it instead of relabelling the row.
- **The press stopped reporting a file count for that row.** A collection-scoped delete removes no file, so the sentence every other row gets read `Deleted unfinished tasks — 0 files.` on a press that worked. It now reads `Deleted unfinished tasks.` — no count, and not the sibling "starts over" phrasing, which would render "Unfinished tasks starts over."

**The wipe's sentence names watchers, and the mechanism that got it there is the part worth reading.** Settings' whole wipe still deletes the file, so it still takes watchers — and the sentence a user reads immediately before an irreversible press is built from `LocalStore.allCases`, which watchers add no case to. A second collection inside an existing store's file is how something arrives in the wipe without arriving in the sentence.

- `deletionCopyName` became `deletionCopyNames: [String]` and the sentence `flatMap`s it: **a store is a file, and a file can hold more than one kind of thing.** The alternative kept the old shape and produced "…, common output locations, and unfinished tasks and standing watchers" — two conjunctions deep at the end of the one sentence in the product that most needs to be read.
- The thirteenth store derives its two phrases from `ResumableTaskFileCollection` rather than spelling them, so a third collection reaches the sentence by existing.
- **`theWipesOwnSentenceNamesEveryCollectionInEveryStore` binds that declaration to reality by counting `ResumableTaskFile`'s stored properties against the enum's cases.** The `Mirror` count is the load-bearing half and the exhaustive switch is not: a switch guarantees every *case* has a phrase and says nothing about a stored property that never became a case, which is the direction a new collection actually arrives from. Proved by adding a third stored collection and watching it fail with both counts named, then reverting.

**The notification.** Its own `SONNY_WATCHER` category with an empty action array, and here the emptiness is a founder decision rather than a UI preference: a watcher may not act, so the `error` category's Retry would have put a route to acting on screen without anybody choosing to — and that button runs `retryLastCommand()`, which re-dispatches the user's own last submitted command, a task with no relationship to the watched page. Same shape SONNY-113 and SONNY-187 each found one channel earlier. Bookkeeping writes go to `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure` and never to `errorMessage`, which outranks a result in the widget and would blank the outcome of a task that had succeeded.

**The fetch seam, and why it has no default.** `StandingWatcherObserving` is injected into `AgentViewModel` undefaulted — SONNY-240's argument applied to a network call rather than a write, because this is driven by a timer rather than by anything the user pressed, and "a test that predates the parameter cannot know to pass it" does not care what the parameter is for. `LiveStandingWatcherObserver` is named only in `atItsRealStoreLocations()`. `UnreachableStandingWatcherObserver` **throws rather than returning empty text**: empty text is a *reading* — it digests to a real value, differs from any baseline, and would drive the promotion path with fabricated content, so a fixture that accidentally ticked a watcher would exercise the change machinery and pass.

**PR #184's review, and what its three rounds found.** Cycle 1 raised six findings, four blocking; cycle 3 raised two more, both blocking and both introduced by the fix round. They are recorded here together because the pattern across them is worth more than any one.

- **F1 — a watcher that fired while the user was in Sonny told nobody and then deleted itself.** The channel was gated on `!isUserWorkingInSonny` like the four older ones, and unlike all of them nothing renders `watcherNotice` — so the gate was not deduplication, it was deletion, in what is arguably the feature's most common case. The gate is gone; the comment that argued it was safe "because the notice is visible in Command Center" was false about this tree.
- **F2 — Settings' whole wipe was undone by a check in flight**, because `deleteLocalData` guards on `!isRunning` and a watcher check deliberately does not set it. The wipe now abandons the check *and* the check refuses to write when its generation has moved; a cancelled `Task` still runs its continuation and the observer need not be cancellable, so neither half works alone.
- **F3 — one page that never answers stopped every watcher, indefinitely.** The single re-entrancy slot was cleared only by the body finishing and nothing bounded the fetch, so no failure was ever recorded and `maxConsecutiveFailures` was unreachable through that door. A check past `checkTimeout` is abandoned on the next pulse and counted as a failed reading, decided on the injected clock rather than by racing a timer.
- **N1 — a watcher whose delete keeps failing re-notified on every pulse.** Measured by the reviewer at **11 notices across 11 pulses** with the store directory read-only: `finishStandingWatcher` publishes then deletes, a persistent throw leaves the record, and the expired branch re-decides `.stopped` on the *pulse* rather than the check interval. Nothing downstream coalesces — no `removeDuplicates()`, a fresh `UUID()` per request — and **F1's fix had just removed the gate that was damping it**. `notifiedWatcherIDs` is the only-when-it-is-new guard, the same one PR #110's F1 established here for the identical shape.
- **N2 — the retry cadence of a hanging page is `checkTimeout + checkInterval`, not `checkTimeout`.** Measured at fetches on **t=0 and t=960** with the shipped numbers; 90 seconds in the founders' shortened build. The abandonment stamps `lastCheckedAt` and due-ness is measured from it. The manual row said otherwise, and the composition test's own doc comment promised a cadence assertion its body never made — F6's class, reintroduced by F6's fix.

**The pattern, which is the thing to carry off this branch: three of the eight findings were a comment asserting something the code did not guarantee.** F1's comment claimed a surface that did not exist. N1's claimed the repeat was bounded — true of a transient failure, false of a persistent one. N2's claimed a third assertion the test body never made. None of the three is a code defect on its own and all three hid one, because a reader who checks the comment stops there. A green suite cannot see any of them; two were found by a reviewer reading the claim against the code, and one by a mutation battery.

**Verification, and it is all re-measured at the post-rebase head rather than translated.** The branch was cut from `988df89` and **rebased once, onto `60298ca`** (PRs #181, #182 and #183) as the last thing before merge. That range moved 40 files including nine under `Sources/`, so every figure this entry carried from before it was true of a smaller tree and none is carried across: the suite alone went from 2614 in 176 suites to **2652 in 179**, a 38-test difference the merged range brought.

- Flagged suite at `9ea53bc`: **2652 tests in 179 suites passed**, `SUITE-EXIT=0`, **0** real issues, 7 known issues, 7 pre-existing skips.
- `scripts/warnings` at `9ea53bc`: **0 warnings**, tree clean.
- `scripts/changelog-order`: `EXIT=0`, 156 entries, both eras.
- Mutation battery at `9ea53bc`: **21 mutants, 21 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed**, `EXIT=0`.
- No Postgres: nothing under `server/` is touched (`git diff --name-only 988df89 HEAD | grep -c '^server/'` → 0, exit 1, against a control of 117 over `main~40..main`).

**The rebase's own hazard was checked rather than assumed** (`CLAUDE.md`'s rule that a conflicted-file list is not the population a rebase can break). The merged range added `entitlementNoSubscription` to `SonnyBackendErrorCode`; **five** test files reference that type at this head and four did at `988df89`, the fifth being `BillingPortalSurfaceTests.swift`, which the range itself added. This branch touches exactly one of them, `VisionSessionRunTests.swift`, at two property accesses on a single case rather than a `switch`, and `SonnyBackendErrorCode.allCases` appears nowhere in `Sources` or `Tests` — so nothing enumerates the type and a new case cannot break a test at compile time. Real in shape, empty in fact; the suite is what settles it either way, because a compile-time answer says nothing about a behavioural disagreement.

**Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered**

- **A defect this branch shipped for one commit, which its own full suite caught: two clocks in one decision.** `checkStandingWatchers(now:)` decided due-ness on the injected clock and then called `observeStandingWatcher`, whose own `now` defaulted to `Date()` — so `lastCheckedAt` was stamped from the real clock while due-ness was computed on the caller's. Milliseconds apart under a filtered run and seconds apart under a loaded parallel suite, and the symptom is a check that should have been due reading as **not** due: one silently skipped check, surfacing as a wrong *count* (`consecutiveFailures → 6` where 7 was expected) rather than as anything that names its cause. In shipping terms a watcher would have checked less often than its own cap says under any real load, with nothing anywhere reporting it. **The clock now travels into the fetch**, which also means `lastCheckedAt` records when the check *began* rather than when the page answered — the more honest of the two, because the interval means "how often Sonny asks" and a slow page should not buy itself a longer gap.
- **It was found only by the full suite, and the filtered run that missed it was this lane's own.** A `--filter StandingWatcherRunTests` run was green and was reported as green; the full run at the same head was red with three distinct defects. That is step 5's "run the whole flagged suite once before you push" doing exactly the work it is there for, and it is recorded here rather than smoothed over.
- **A test-support helper can trip a source scan by pointing at the *opposite* of what the scan is about.** `UnreachableLocalStores.fileURL("task-history.json")` matches `onlyTheShippedConstantsTestsNameAStoresRealLocation`'s `.fileURL(` needle exactly, at a call site whose whole purpose is to name a path nothing can find. The permitted list was **not** widened — that would license the real thing in that file forever — and the five missing store vendors were added to `UnreachableLocalStores` instead, so the dotted spelling stays in the one file the needle does not reach.
- **A `Task` handle assigned after its own body is a silent, permanent stall, and the safety here is isolation rather than luck.** `standingWatcherCheck = Task { … }` is safe because the method is main-actor isolated and nothing suspends before the assignment, so the body cannot start first and clear a handle that has not been set. Written down at the code because if it were ever wrong the symptom is a handle left non-nil, which stops every future check with nothing reporting it.
- **Not put in `CLAUDE.md`, by founder decision.** The defaulted-clock-beside-an-injected-one shape is one instance and is a branch record; a second occurrence would be a ticket.
- **A mutation battery was scoped by "what this round changed" twice, one round apart, and that is not the rule** (SONNY-391). Step 5 scopes a re-run to the mutants whose *evidence* moved, which is four conditions. The first instance: 16 killed at `b9a1418` was reported as carrying to `a9cbe90`, where the file holding **W5**'s and **W12**'s killing tests had moved — condition 2, unchecked. PR #184's cycle-3 reviewer re-ran those two and they held. The second, one round later and in the same direction: F4's fix edited `StandingWatcherEvaluator.swift`, which **six** mutants target — W5, W7, W8, W9, W19, W21 — and only the two this round had just written were re-run, leaving four carrying verdicts measured before their target file moved. Condition 1, unchecked, in the round that recorded the first instance.
- **Both stamps in that history are non-ancestral now and are kept as history rather than repaired.** `git merge-base --is-ancestor b9a1418 HEAD` and the same on `a9cbe90` each exit 1 after the rebase; they are timestamps on a branch, and the live figure is the 21-mutant run in the verification paragraph above.
- **The second instance surfaced only because `scripts/mutate` refused, and the refusal was luck.** F4's stamp landed *inside* W5's `from` block, so the mutant matched 0 lines and the harness aborted the whole run — a mutant that does not apply would otherwise run an unmutated suite and report a clean pass. **One line outside that block and W5 applies cleanly and reports a kill against a file it was never re-measured on**, with nothing anywhere disagreeing. The guard is against a stale `from` block; nothing guards the scope, and the two coincided.
- **Why the wrong scope is the one a session reaches for**, which is SONNY-391's point rather than carelessness: "what this round changed" is visible from inside the round, the four conditions are not, and it fails in the reassuring direction — a smaller re-run that reports the same clean result. The rule was already written down. What was missing is that a plausible substitute for it exists and looks identical from where the session stands. **A carry that has been argued is worth less than a number that has been measured**, which is why the final battery here is all 21 rather than a scoped subset.
- **F4's "cheap half" was not cheap, and the reason is worth the sentence.** The founders' decision was that `.expired` may not assert "It did not change" when a difference was *ever* seen. Every existing record of a difference on `StandingWatcher` is reset by a reading equal to the baseline — `candidateDigest` and `unstableReadings` both — so a sentence conditioned on either is right about half the time on exactly the alternating page the finding is about, depending on which of the two states the last check happened to see. That is worse than being consistently wrong. So it costs a persisted field, `firstDifferenceAt`, set once and never cleared, with a `decodeIfPresent` path for records written before it. The cheaper spelling that needs no field is to have `.expired` never assert the stronger sentence at all, which loses it for genuinely unchanged pages; that trade is recorded on SONNY-236 rather than taken here.
- **The instability-counter change F4 also raises is deferred to SONNY-390**, with the cost it has to answer: counting a reading against the *previous* reading rather than the baseline makes the alternating page reach `.unwatchable` in four checks and say so honestly, and makes a page that genuinely wobbles once a fortnight accumulate toward unwatchable over its life instead of being forgiven.
### Branch: feature/the-subscription-is-managed-where-it-was-bought
Status: complete
Date: 2026-08-31
Tickets: SONNY-216 — a link from Command Center's Account section to the payment provider's hosted billing portal, and the current subscription state read from the entitlement. No custom billing UI: the provider's portal does that job, which is a founder decision rather than an implementation shortcut.
Reviewed by: fresh session (per WORKFLOW.md step 7) — one deep adversarial pass on PR #183, at `ba9ecd0`, with its own 6-mutant battery (2 killed, 4 survived). **Fourteen findings; the founder capped the round and thirteen were taken**, the fourteenth (a `hasLiveSubscription` pre-check on the portal route) proposed as its own ticket because it reads the store the ratified boundary was drawn around.

**F1 and F3 were the round, and they are one defect seen from two sides.** `currentSubscription()` is the **only** writer of the entitlement store — `decision(for:)` has no caller anywhere in `Sources/` — so on any Mac that had not previously opened Account the cache was empty by construction, the first read started a detached refresh and returned `nil`, and **nothing re-read when that refresh landed**: the row stayed absent until the dialog was closed and reopened, which is the branch's own headline manual item. It was invisible because of F3: every fixture passed `SonnyEntitlementKeys.shipped`, which is empty, so **nothing in the repository ever produced a non-`nil` subscription** and a mutant returning `nil` from `currentSubscription()` passed all 2579 tests. The ticket's Verification line asks for "a test that the state renders from the entitlement" and there was none. `refreshSubscription()` now reads, and — only when the first read is empty — waits once on the refresh it started and reads again; a suite-level signer mints claims that actually verify, and the tests that produce a real snapshot are what hold F1 and F2 as well.

**F2** was PR #152's F2 reintroduced through the new door: the foreign-claim case answered `nil` without discarding or refreshing, and `shouldRefresh` was then evaluated against the *foreign* claim — so a second person signing in on a Mac holding a fresh claim would have seen no subscription row for up to eight hours, with nothing in the product able to shorten it. `currentSubscription()` now discards and refreshes exactly as `decision(for:)` does.

**F4** — the portal press was routed through `SignInFailure`, whose own doc comment carries PR #133's F9 warning that reusing it outside sign-in makes a wrong sentence the moment another route does. It did, on the two errors most likely to arrive: `provider.rejected` — whose definition is that a retry fails identically, and which is the rotation outage `server/README.md` describes — rendered "Try again in a moment", and `entitlement.no_subscription`, which had no name in `SonnyBackendErrorCode` at all, rendered "Sonny couldn't finish signing you in." to a signed-in user. `BillingPortalFailure`/`BillingPortalCopy` are the portal's own vocabulary, the wire code is named, and **the server half's retryable/not-retryable taxonomy now survives to the last step**, which was the point of building it.

**F6** — the eight-second budget's stated justification was false and was stated in four places (`polar.ts`, this entry, a ticket comment, and a server test's own name). It argued from the Mac retrying a typed `504`; `hostedBillingPortalURL()` passes `isRetrySafe: false` and `SonnyBackendClient.send` gates every retry on that flag first, so this route is retried **zero** times. The number stays at eight seconds and its reasons are now the true ones — the user meets the gateway's typed, logged `504` rather than the Mac's generic transport failure, and an unbounded call in a handler is how a route stops answering. The cross-half relation is pinned by a test on each side, following `ModelRouteNumbersTests`' precedent; a mutant raising it to 30 000 had survived the whole suite.

**F5's other direction** was the one nobody had examined: a 404 is also what a wrong origin or a dropped path prefix answers, so mapping every 404 to `noCustomer` meant that under a misconfiguration **every paying subscriber** would be told "This account holds no subscription to manage" — verbatim the outcome the 422 reasoning calls a support incident that reads like data loss, and one the client's second defence cannot catch, because those users hold claims and their row renders. A 404 now has to carry a JSON-object body to read as a missing customer, and a second manual row reaches the direction the first one structurally could not.

The rest, each in one line: **F7** the URL guard was asserted only against `file:` and a mutant weakening it to `scheme != "file"` survived, so it is now `SafeURL.validateWebURL` — the repository's existing gate, which also blocks loopback and RFC1918 — plus the https narrowing, with both negative cases tested; **F8** the unparseable-expiry guard was held by nothing and removing it turns a 200 into a 500, since `new Date("nonsense").toISOString()` throws; **F9** the new service method's doc comment had swallowed `signOut()`'s, leaving the ordering argument for sign-out attached to the wrong symbol; **F10** `429` was classified not-retryable, which this gateway's two older provider adapters had already decided the other way, in words (`src/auth/supabase.ts:521-525`); **F11** the rotation runbook could not tell "deployed" from "working", so a typo'd token deploys cleanly and the operator then revokes the only working one — a verify step now sits between 2 and 3; **F12** `BILLING_API_BASE_URL` was validated for parseability only, and it decides where a bearer credential is sent, so it must now be https with no path; **F13** `subscription` was not cleared on sign-out, so the next user's signed-in view rendered the previous user's plan line for one async read; **F14** the surface-width property is conventional rather than structural and both records said otherwise.

**The gateway makes its first outbound call to a payment provider, and holds its first provider API credential. That reverses a property SONNY-211 established deliberately, and a reader should meet it as a decision.** SONNY-211's closing record states that its hosted checkout "needs no provider API credential and makes no outbound request" — both halves of that stop being true on this branch, for one route.

**The reason is identity — and this branch reached it through two wrong arguments before the right one, both recorded, because the third rests on much less than the first two claimed.**

**The first was possession**: that a portal edits payment methods, so holding a portal URL is worse than holding a checkout URL. Wrong — the provider authenticates the human with a one-time emailed code before showing anything, so possession of the static URL is not enough.

**The second was the relay address**, and it was the vivid one: that a Sign in with Apple user's provider record carries `abc123@privaterelay.appleid.com`, so they could type nothing that would be recognised. **Also wrong, and retired here** (founder correction, PR #183). Sonny sends **no email address to the provider at all** — `checkoutUrlFor` sends only `customer_external_id` — so the address on a provider customer record is whatever the *buyer typed at checkout*, which may well be one they can reproduce.

**What survives is weaker, checkable, and still decisive.** Sonny's identity key is `(provider, subject)` and "is never the email address" (`docs/sonny-identity-linking-rule.md:14`), and this gateway passes no address to checkout — so **Sonny does not hold, and cannot show, the address a customer's provider record is keyed on.** A billing portal whose only key is an address the product deliberately does not know is one a user can be locked out of with no recovery Sonny can offer: not because the address is unreachable, but because nobody can tell them which one it is. A credential is a cost the founders manage by rotating it; that one is a cost the user pays.

**The lookup needs no new state, which is what kept the change inside its ratified boundary.** `checkoutUrlFor` already sends the account id as `customer_external_id` (`server/src/billing/polar.ts:81`, with the reasoning at `:73-80`), so the Polar customer carries it as `external_id` and `external_customer_id` on the session request resolves it back. Nothing on the portal path reads `sonny.entitlement`; no column and no migration moved.

**The never-touch exception, asked for and ratified before any edit.** `server/src/billing/*` and `routes/billing.ts` are this ticket's never-touch list, and nothing in the repository produced a portal URL — `grep -rn -il "portal" server/src server/test Sources Tests docs/sonny-backend-api-contract.md` answered **2** at `988df89`, both Wikipedia web-research fixtures under `Tests/Fixtures/WebResearch/`. (Control, because a clean zero is the answer that looks like good news: the same search for `checkout` over `server/src` answers 5 files.) The founder ratified five files — `config.ts`, `billing/provider.ts`, `billing/polar.ts`, `routes/billing.ts`, one contract §4.1 row — with the discharge condition that nothing else on the list moves. **The never-touch half held exactly**: `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD -- server/src/billing/store.ts server/src/db/migrations server/src/billing/webhook-signature.ts` prints **nothing**. **The diff is thirteen files rather than five, and the eight extra follow from the four scope items the same instruction set**: `.env.example` and both `check-secrets` scripts are where a credential is registered, `README.md` is where the rotation story was asked for, `deps.ts` wires the configuration, and three are tests. Stating it as "matches the ratified list exactly" would have been the wrong claim; the claim that holds is about what must not be touched.

**The four things the session shape owed, each taken as scope rather than as polish.**

- **The credential.** `BILLING_PROVIDER_ACCESS_TOKEN` joins `check:secrets`' name-anchored list as the **third** name on it whose leak is a write, with both directions in the selftest — the token refused, the API origin beside it not, so the list does not train anyone to baseline the scanner. **Its rotation is in `server/README.md` and is deliberately not the three-deploy overlap** the model credentials use: Polar kills a revoked token the instant an operator presses the button, so an overlap this gateway controls cannot exist. It is three steps ordered **create before revoke**. The section states what doing steps 1 and 3 together looks like, and that is the part worth reading — `POST /v1/billing/portal` answers `502 provider.rejected` and logs at `error` while subscriptions, webhooks and entitlements all keep working, so the outage is invisible to anyone not exercising the portal. A credential that cannot be rotated without downtime is one nobody rotates.
- **The timeout.** **Eight seconds**, chosen against the Mac's own budget rather than against a guess at Polar's latency, because what the number decides is *which* timeout the user meets. The Mac spends `SonnyBackendTimeouts.auth` = 20 s on an account call (`Sources/MacAgentCore/SonnyBackendClient.swift:28`); a typed `504 provider.timeout` from this gateway is retried once and the Mac's own transport timeout is not, which that file's comment at `:33-39` spells out. So this budget must be comfortably the smaller. An unbounded outbound call inside a request handler is how a route stops answering at all.
- **The account the provider has no customer for.** A new `409 entitlement.no_subscription`, the mirror of `entitlement.already_subscribed`, and documented as the **ordinary case rather than an error** — it is what a signed-in user who never subscribed looks like, which is most accounts. **The client half is the half that matters**: the Account section renders no subscription line and no Manage control for such an account, because a control that only fails when pressed is a broken control.
- **The reversal is stated where a reader meets it** — the commit message, `.env.example`, `config.ts`, `polar.ts`, the contract's dated change row and this entry — each naming SONNY-211's own sentence.

**`PortalLink`'s cases are named for what the caller must do, not for what went wrong upstream**, so the route maps each onto one status with nothing to decide: `noCustomer` to the new 409, and `timedOut`, `unavailable` and `rejected` onto §7.2's existing `provider.timeout`, `provider.unavailable` and `provider.rejected` with their retryable flags unchanged.

**One judgement made without evidence, in the safe direction, and routed to a manual row.** A **422** is mapped to `rejected` rather than to `noCustomer`. 404 is Polar's documented not-found and covers the common case; 422 is the other plausible answer for an unknown external id, and **nobody on this project has run this request against real Polar**. The asymmetry is what decides it: an unknown id answered 422 today reports a loud fault to a user with nothing to manage, which is harmless, while the opposite mistake tells a **paying subscriber** they have no subscription — a support incident that reads like data loss. `treats a 422 as a refusal rather than as a missing customer, which is the safe direction` carries the reasoning in its own name, and the manual row names which response to provoke, what the app does under each mapping, and that a 422 observed in the wild flips it.

**The Swift half: `EntitlementService` gains a second public reader, and it is deliberately not a claim accessor.** `decision(for:)` is a narrow surface on purpose — a caller names one capability and gets one answer, and cannot enumerate what the account has. Handing out the `EntitlementClaim` would widen that in the direction that matters: a caller holding the claim reads `capabilities` directly and decides entitlement for itself, without `judge`, without the session check and without `effectiveNow`'s clock defence, none of which is enforceable on a value that has left the actor. So `currentSubscription()` returns a purpose-built `SubscriptionSnapshot` — a plan key and one of two states — which **carries no capability list, so that it cannot become a second answer to the permission question**. It is local and instant exactly as `decision(for:)` is: it reads the cache, verifies against a held public key, makes no network call, and a stale claim starts the same background refresh.

**A reader meeting `currentSubscription()` cold will wonder why it is not simply a claim accessor, and that question deserves its answer in one sentence: a claim accessor is a second answer to a question one function owns.**

**The property is conventional, not structural, and this entry said the opposite until PR #183's F14.** Through *this* door it is structural — `SubscriptionSnapshot` has exactly two stored properties and `grep -c capabilities Sources/MacAgentCore/SubscriptionReading.swift` answers **2**, a doc comment and the single expression that reduces the list to a boolean. But the sentence that framed it — that handing out the claim would let a caller read `capabilities` and decide entitlement for itself, without `judge`, without the session check and without `effectiveNow`'s clock defence — describes something the same actor already permits: `EntitlementService.refreshNow()` is `public`, `@discardableResult`, and returns the `EntitlementClaim` itself, one method below the door this entry said was deliberately not opened. `EntitlementStoring.load()`, `StoredEntitlement`, `EntitlementVerifier.verify` and `EntitlementClaim.capabilities` are all public too, so a second route composes from three public symbols — and this is the branch that first puts an `EntitlementService` in the app target at all, so that composition became reachable from app code here. **The design decision is right and unchanged; the word was wrong.** Making it structural means `refreshNow()` returning `Void` — its only caller, `startRefresh`, already discards the value — which is a public-API change to the entitlement integration and is proposed as its own ticket rather than taken here.

**What the state line may say was a founder decision, and the consequence is recorded as a fact rather than as a limitation.** The signed claim carries `plan` and `capabilities` and no status — `server/src/entitlement/claim.ts:174-176` returns exactly those on every path. Adding one was declined: it changes the claim's shape, a §4.1/§5.3 contract change under §8.2's breaking-change rule, on work that merged the same day, and not a trade worth making for a status word inside a ticket scoped to a portal link. So the line says what the claim can prove. **During the grace window a customer whose payment has failed still holds capabilities, by §16.4's deliberate design that billing never cuts a user off mid-task — so this line reads `Active` while their card has been declined, and their only notice is the provider's own dunning email.** §16.4 exists to stop a surprise wall and that is a quiet route to one. Filed as **SONNY-380**, together with the unreviewed 14-day `BILLING_GRACE_DAYS` default it compounds with; **nothing here builds for it**.
**Appended 2026-09-05 (SONNY-380), and the sentence above stays verbatim as the dated record it is.** *"Nothing here builds for it"* was true when it was written and is no longer: SONNY-380 shipped on `feature/a-past-due-customer-is-told`, and this line no longer reads `Active` for a customer whose card has been declined. **The three decisions were the founders', 2026-09-05**: the customer is told in the app; the word comes from a separate unsigned read (`GET /v1/billing/payment-state`) rather than from a field on the claim, so the §8.2 cost this paragraph declines was declined again and not paid; and `BILLING_GRACE_DAYS` was **reviewed and kept at fourteen days**, because the in-app line removes the silence that made the length dangerous. The paragraph's reasoning is therefore still live in full — what changed is not the claim's shape but what sits beside it. **This annotation exists because the successor branch's own entry claimed it had been made and it had not** (PR #206's F1): a reader who followed that sentence here would have found a live *nothing here builds for it* about work that had shipped, and been told by the record they were reading that it was corrected.

**The one place the Mac depends on a literal whose meaning is set on the other side of the wire.** `SubscriptionReading.absentPlan` is `"none"`, which `server/src/entitlement/store.ts:133` mints in `unprovisioned` and whose own comment says it "is not a tier name. It is the absence of a plan record. SONNY-212 owns the real keys." That sentence is what distinguishes a never-subscribed account from a revoked one, and without it the former reads as `.ended` and is offered a Manage control that leads nowhere. It is named in one visible place rather than left as a bare string in a view, and `theAbsenceOfAPlanIsNotASubscription` is what fails if SONNY-212 renames it.

**The plan key is shown to the user opaque, capitalised and otherwise untouched.** `EntitlementClaim` states that this repository never enumerates plan keys and SONNY-212 owns what the plans are, so a translation table here would be taking that ticket's decision inside this one.

**No explanatory copy, and it is asserted rather than left to review.** `theLineNamesThePlanAndTheStateAndExplainsNeither` pins the rendered line by exact equality, so a mutant appending a sentence about what "Ended" means fails. "Manage subscription" is named for where it goes rather than for what lives there; listing payment method, invoices and cancel would be the product explaining itself, and the portal's own page says all of it anyway.

**The conflict exposure this ticket was flagged for is largely not there, which is worth recording because the wave was planned around the opposite.** The Account surface is `SignInDialogView.signedInStep` in `Sources/MacAgent/SignInView.swift`, not `CommandCenterView.swift` — that file holds only the account *menu* and presents the dialog. SONNY-214 and SONNY-215 both touch `CommandCenterView.swift` and neither has reason to open `SignInView.swift`.

**`EntitlementService` was constructed nowhere in the shipping app before this branch** — only in tests, which `grep -rn "EntitlementService(" Sources` (exit 1, no output) established. So this branch also wires it: `SonnyAccountModel` builds one from the same client it already holds, with `entitlementStore` and `entitlementKeys` as **required parameters with no defaults**, for SONNY-240's reason applied to the Keychain — a default store would reach the one Keychain every packaged build on this Mac shares, and a fixture inheriting it would read and delete the founder's real entitlement. `atItsRealKeychainLocation()` is the one named place that asks for the real pair. **The shipped key set is empty in every release build**, which is `SonnyEntitlementKeys`' own recorded state rather than a gap introduced here, so no claim verifies and the subscription row renders for nobody until a gateway exists to have signed one; `aMacThatCanProveNothingShowsNoSubscription` asserts exactly that.

**A number and the command beside it disagreed, and it was caught before it was quoted rather than by a reviewer.** The hand-back comment on SONNY-216 said "13 tests" citing `git diff origin/main...HEAD -- server/test/billing.test.ts | grep -cE '^\+  it\('`, which answers **14**. Both numbers are real and they count different things: one of the fourteen added `it(` lines is the *rename* of an existing population guard, so it is 13 new tests and 14 added lines. That is the shape this rule is hardest against — a figure whose command is right there and still does not match it — and the parenthesis is what made it checkable in seconds.

**Rebased once, at merge time, onto `1dbbbb3` (PR #182's merge, SONNY-212), by founder instruction.** Ten commits replayed with **one conflict**, in this entry's own file — the usual both-branches-added-an-entry shape, resolved by keeping both with this branch's above SONNY-212's. **`server/src/config.ts` did not conflict**, which the review had predicted it would: both branches add to the same three regions and git merged them textually. That is the case `CLAUDE.md` warns is merge-clean-but-possibly-incoherent, so it was checked rather than assumed — `CREDIT_PLANS`/`creditPlans` answer **4** each and `BILLING_PROVIDER_ACCESS_TOKEN`/`billingProviderAccessToken`/`BILLING_API_BASE_URL`/`billingApiBaseUrl` **2** each, `testConfig` carries all three new fields, and `gate.test.ts` carries both populations (`billing/portal` → 2, `account/credits` → 2). `git diff origin/main...HEAD --numstat` over the seven auto-merged files shows **zero deletions** on six of them and three on `gate.test.ts`, each of which is this branch's own replaced line rather than anything of #182's.

They are timestamps on a branch, not trees a reader should fetch.

App half: `swift build` **0**; the flagged suite **2602 tests in 177 suites passed** exit 0; `scripts/warnings` **0 warnings** exit 0, its report stamped `40ddc2f (clean)`; `scripts/changelog-order` **0** over **155** entries across both eras.

**This branch's own tests are 29** — 9 in `SubscriptionReadingTests` and 20 in `BillingPortalSurfaceTests` (`git grep -c "@Test func" HEAD -- Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/SubscriptionReadingTests.swift Tests/MacAgentTests/BillingPortalSurfaceTests.swift`), plus **19** added to `server/test/billing.test.ts` — `git show HEAD:server/test/billing.test.ts | grep -cE '^\s+it\('` answers **54** against **35** for the same file on `origin/main`. (Written as 20 first, from the wrong pair of commands; the difference is the point of writing the command beside the number, and this is the third figure on this branch the rule has caught.) The suite total moved 2564 → 2602 across the branch **and** the rebase together, so it is no longer this branch's arithmetic alone: `main` gained tests of its own in the merged range, and the 29 above is the figure that is this branch's.

**Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered.**

- **A static hosted-portal link is unusable for any product that does not key on the email address, and the reason is invisible until you ask who cannot reach it.** The security framing — a portal edits payment methods, so its URL is more sensitive — is the wrong lens and was the one this branch reached for first; the provider authenticates the human before showing anything, so possession is not the issue. The identity mismatch is, and it produces a silent, unrecoverable lockout for exactly the users a privacy-preserving sign-in creates.
- **A result type whose cases are named for the caller's next action collapses a mapping layer.** `PortalLink`'s five cases each have one status, one `retryable` and one log level, so the route's switch has nothing to decide. Naming them for the upstream condition instead — `notFound`, `serverError`, `badRequest` — would have put that decision at every call site.
- **A guard added in a fix round is exactly as likely to ship untested as any other guard, and three times on this branch it did.** R3, U6 and V3 are one shape across three rounds: written carefully, believed covered, held by nothing. It concentrates in fix rounds because the guard arrives as the answer to a finding — the reasoning is written, the reviewer has agreed, and the thing that usually forces a test, not knowing whether the code works, is missing. The habit that catches it is running a mutant at the guard you just wrote, in the same sitting, before the round is reported.
- **A test can assert the right answer and still not hold the property its name claims.** `theFirstReadNeverWaitsOnTheNetwork` seeds a fresh claim, so no refresh is ever started and the guard it appears to cover is never exercised; it asserts the answer, not the absence of a wait. The replacement separates the two cases by *plan* rather than by timing, so it needs no wall-clock assertion — which is also what keeps it out of the family `CLAUDE.md` warns about, where a test that races a threshold manufactures kills.
- **"KILLED by the compiler" is not a kill.** Two of this round's app-half mutants broke switch exhaustiveness, so the suite never ran and the report said so in as many words. A mutant that does not build measures nothing about coverage; it has to be rewritten into one the compiler accepts before its verdict means anything.
- **A boundary test that does not sit on the boundary reads exactly like one that does.** `R3` survived because 503 and 501 are on the same side of `>= 500`; the assertion looked like a boundary test, was named like one, and located nothing. The cheap general form: when a branch is `>= N`, assert `N` itself and `N - 1`, not a value comfortably past it.
- **The provider's own not-found status is a guess until someone runs it, and the two ways to be wrong are not symmetric.** Writing the mapping in the direction whose failure is harmless, naming the reasoning in the test, and routing the question to a manual row is cheaper than either guessing silently or blocking the branch on a live account.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The spend cap (SONNY-135) is untouched.** `unitsForMeteredCall` still returns one unit per metered call, `admitRequest` still reserves and settles the same way, and nothing in `src/entitlement/store.ts` or `src/entitlement/hook.ts` changed. `entitlement.test.ts` and `entitlement.db.test.ts` pass unchanged.
