One session, one branch, cut from `main` at `65a7fc9` (PR #168's merge), not rebased. **Every figure below is measured at `f139755`**, this branch's implementation head after the rebase onto `4c5f2bc` (PR #172's merge), over a clean tree; the docs commit above it changes only this file. Each carries the command that produced it.

**The rebase orphaned every SHA this entry previously stamped**, which is `CLAUDE.md`'s rebase gotcha arriving on schedule: `1687bf3`, `55e681d`, `d127837`, `60a8b82` and `066d44f` all still resolve — `git cat-file -t` prints `commit` for each — and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` exits **1** for all five, so every one is a timestamp on a branch that no longer exists rather than a tree anyone can fetch. Every figure was therefore **re-measured** at `f139755` rather than re-stamped, and the round-by-round history below now names rounds instead of citing heads that resolve and mean nothing. `65a7fc9`, the base this branch was cut from, is the one that survives.

**The hazard, and why it is reachable rather than theoretical.** `sonny_meta.schema_migration` held an id and an `applied_at`, and nothing hashed the file. So "0014 applied" was true and said nothing about *which* 0014: two deployments could report identical ids and hold different schemas, and `npm run migrate status` answered with ids, so it called them identical. Development, beta and v1 are three deployments receiving the same image at different times (`docs/sonny-row-12-host-decision.md` §12.2), so an edit landing between two of their deploys puts them permanently out of step on the one thing that defines the database. Every migration now carries a sha256 over both halves' executable SQL, written inside the same transaction as the SQL it describes; `up` and `down` refuse before touching anything when an applied migration's file no longer produces what was recorded; `status` never refuses and reports `applied` / `pending` / `CHANGED` / `unverified` per migration instead.

**The comment decision is the whole design, and the alternative was not merely stricter — it was self-deleting.** A whole-file hash makes PR #167's comment-only edit to an already-applied `0014` a hard failure on every environment that had already run it, and that edit was deliberate and correct: it records that `0015` changed what one of `0014`'s columns may imply. This repository writes long explanatory comments into its migrations on purpose — `0014`'s header is about fifty lines of argument, `0009`'s explains the defect it exists to fix. A guard that turns annotating an applied migration into an outage is one that gets removed the first week it fires, and it takes the annotation practice with it. So the hash is over what Postgres would run: comments and layout stripped, behaviour still caught.

**Where the line is drawn is on what reaches the database, not on what looks like prose.** A `--` inside `'…'`, `"…"` or `$…$` is not a comment and is kept. That is not caution, it is correctness twice over: eight of the sixteen shipped migrations define plpgsql functions inside `$$ … $$` (`git grep -lE 'CREATE (OR REPLACE )?FUNCTION' -- server/src/db/migrations | wc -l` → 8 at `f139755`) and several of those bodies carry `--` lines of their own — `0003`'s explains at its lines 30-31 why the trigger fires only on the transition into closed. Postgres stores those bytes verbatim in `pg_proc.prosrc`, which is why `migrate.db.test.ts`'s own schema fingerprint hashes `md5(p.prosrc)` and already treats a function body's text as schema. Editing one changes the database, so it changes the hash. And a lexer that read those as comments would not merely mis-hash the file — it would truncate the literal it was hashing, so two genuinely different `INSERT`s would agree. **This is why the normalizer is a small state machine and not a regex.** It also nests block comments the way Postgres does and C does not (a depth-blind stripper stops at the first `*/`, leaving everything after it in the hash as executable SQL) and does not read a bind parameter as a dollar quote (`$1` would otherwise open a literal that never closes, swallowing the rest of the file). Neither construct appears in the migrations today — `grep -nE "\bE'" server/src/db/migrations/*.sql` and `grep -nF '/*' server/src/db/migrations/*.sql` both answer nothing at `f139755` — which is exactly why the tests carry them: the first migration that uses one arrives long after anyone remembers this decision.

**An absent hash is carried as unknown, and the alternative was a lie about when the measurement was taken.** The column is nullable, and an existing database gets it from an `ALTER … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` beside the ledger's `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`, which does nothing to a table that already exists. Backfilling those rows from today's files would write the current text's hash against a row recording an apply that happened long before, and the guard would then report a match on a comparison it never made — the shape this repository keeps recording, a check that reports success about a question nobody asked. So `null` is compared against nothing and reported as `unverified`, with `status` saying in as many words that those migrations are **not** known to match. A row leaves that state only by being rolled back and re-applied. **There is deliberately no `adopt` command** to stamp a hash onto an existing row on an operator's say-so: an adopted hash and an observed one would be indistinguishable in the ledger, which puts the guard back where it started. In practice the unknown path is nearly unreachable today — no deployment exists, `./scripts/deploy.sh staging|production` still exit 3 — and it exists because a founder's local Postgres outlives this change.

**The refusal is a finding, not a fault, and that changed its shape.** Left as a bare `Error` it arrived from the CLI as a Node crash dump: the source line echoed above the message, four stack frames below it, and the one paragraph an operator has to act on buried in the middle — observed on this branch before it was fixed. `MigrationDriftError` is caught by `main`, which prints the message alone and sets the exit code; everything else the runner throws still gets its trace, because a migration that failed mid-statement is a fault and the frames are the point. **The exit code is `65` (`EX_DATAERR`) from all three commands**, so a caller can act on it without knowing which one it ran — not `78`, which this runner already uses for a missing `DATABASE_URL`, and not `2`, which means the command line was wrong. `status` returning 0 while printing `CHANGED` would have been the clean zero this repo's Claims-and-evidence section is about, so it does not.

**PR #169's review round, and F1 is the finding that matters, because it arrived through the argument this branch had already made.** `migration-hash.ts`'s own header says the normaliser is a lexer rather than a regex because a stripper that read a `--` inside a literal as a comment would truncate the text it was hashing, so two different `INSERT`s would agree. F1 is that failure, reached through a literal form the lexer did not know: Postgres **escape strings**, `E'…'`, honour backslash escapes, so `\'` ended the literal early, everything after it was lexed as code, and a `--` in there was stripped. Verified rather than argued — on **PostgreSQL 17.11**, `INSERT INTO t VALUES (E'a\' -- one');` and `… -- two');` are both accepted and store two distinct rows (`count(*)` 2, `count(DISTINCT v)` 2, values `a' -- one` and `a' -- two`), and running both versions of the normaliser over that pair shows the pre-fix one collapsing them to the same truncated `INSERT INTO t VALUES (E'a\'` with **equal hashes**, against distinct hashes after the fix. **Reachability today is zero, and that is not what made it blocking**: this entry stated that no migration uses the form and that its absence was precisely why the tests carried the case — and no such test existed. An argument that rests on a test is a defect when the test is not there.

**The remedy is the enumeration rather than the one form named.** The header now lists every string form §4.1.2 of the Postgres manual defines, with what the lexer does about each: `'…'` and `"…"` plain, with `''`/`""` doubling; `E'…'`/`e'…'` its own branch, the prefix honoured only at a token start because Postgres's scanner is flex and longest-match wins, so `code_e'x'` is an identifier followed by an ordinary string; `U&'…'` and `U&"…"` deliberately **no** branch, because their backslash introduces a *unicode* escape and cannot escape a quote (`SELECT U&'\0441 -- inside'` returns `с -- inside` on 17.11, so the `--` is content either way); `B'…'` and `X'…'` plain quote rules behind a prefix letter; `$tag$…$tag$` its own branch. The single assumption, `standard_conforming_strings = on`, is written down rather than guessed and was read off the server the suite runs against (`SHOW standard_conforming_strings` → `on`).

**F2 — the refusal was right and the sentence under it was false.** It ended "Comments and layout are not hashed, so this is a change to the executable SQL", which is wrong for the edit most likely to produce a surprising refusal: a line of prose inside a `$$ … $$` body *is* hashed, correctly, because Postgres stores it in `pg_proc.prosrc`. Reproduced through the real CLI with one reworded comment line in `0003` as the entire diff — `up` exits 65, and the message now names what actually moved. A refusal is read exactly once, under pressure, by somebody whose deploy has stopped, so every clause has to be true in every case that reaches it.

**The locking regression, re-measured here rather than carried from the review.** The ledger's `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` takes `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` to evaluate its own `IF NOT EXISTS`, so run unconditionally it queued behind any open ledger writer on every run after the first and then released having changed nothing. Behind one writer holding a ten-second transaction, read-only `status` took **8.17 s** unconditional, **0.15 s** with an `information_schema` check in front, and **0.13 s** on the pre-SONNY-364 ledger SQL; with no holder at all the three are **0.15 / 0.13 / 0.12 s**, which is what says the 8.17 s is the lock and not the work. The `IF NOT EXISTS` stays on the `ALTER` for the two-runners-at-once race, and the mechanism is pinned by a test that no `ALTER` is issued rather than by a timing assertion. **The first attempt at that measurement was false and is worth recording**: two of the three runners were crashing on an unresolvable `pg` import and reporting 0.14 s, which read exactly like a passing comparison. A sanity check that each runner actually prints 16 migrations is what caught it — the clean-zero rule met in the shape of a clean *number*.

**The review's surviving mutant, and the second one my own battery then found.** `dollarTagAt`'s character classes were unpinned: the bind-parameter test cannot reach `TAG_START`, because widened to `[A-Za-z0-9_]` the sequence `$1 ` is still not a tag — the space defeats the closing `$` either way — so it takes a `$` immediately after the digits to tell them apart. Three tests pin the rule now (`$fn1$`, `$my_fn$`, and `$1$` which may not be one); `TAG_REST` narrowed to `[A-Za-z_]` is the one that costs real coverage, since `$fn1$` then stops being recognised at all and every comment in that function body silently leaves the hash. **Then the round-2 battery found L3 surviving** — dropping the doubled-quote branch inside the escape-string scanner — and the reason is worth keeping: every byte is copied verbatim either way, so reading `''` as "close, then reopen" merely re-partitions `E'it''s -- fine'` into two literals whose bytes concatenate to the same text. Nothing lands outside a literal, nothing is stripped differently, and the obvious assertion passes on the mutant. Diverging the partitions takes **both** quote forms in one literal: `E'a''b\'c'`, which 17.11 reads as `a'b'c`, is one literal read correctly and three pieces plus a never-closing literal read without the branch — and that last piece swallows the following comment instead of stripping it.

**A second defect the battery found was in the test file rather than the runner**, and it is the kind only a battery produces: a mutation run aborts tests mid-flight by design, and this file's `reset()` did not drop the function its F2 arm creates. A killed mutant left it behind, and the *next* battery's baseline failed with `function "sonny_hash_probe_fn" already exists` — which reads as a defect in the branch and was leftover state. `reset()` and `afterAll` now remove everything the file can create.

**Exit 65 is covered rather than justified, and the number the review gave was close.** `main` carried the whole dispatch and every exit code `server/README.md`'s command table promises, reachable from no test: **63 lines, 55 of them neither comment nor blank** before the split (`awk '/^async function main\(\): Promise<void> \{/,/^\}$/' server/src/db/migrate.ts | grep -vcE '^[[:space:]]*(//|\*|/\*)|^[[:space:]]*$'`). `runCommand` is now split out with the output sink and the migrations directory injected, so the dispatch — **50 code lines by the same command** — is exercised from the suite, and the same command over `main` answers **18** at `f139755`: argv, the `DATABASE_URL` check and the connection. `status`'s stderr summary also names the changed migrations now, so it stands alone the way `up`'s and `down`'s refusal does; an operator who had redirected stdout was previously told only that "1 migration" had changed.

**Cycle 2 turned the last written assumption into a check, and the argument for it is the one that generalises.** `standard_conforming_strings = on` was recorded in the header as a note: the default since 9.1, unchanged anywhere under `server/`. **`DATABASE_URL` alone falsifies it**, with no file this repository controls changed — `?options=-c%20standard_conforming_strings%3Doff` turns it off for the session. And with it off, F1 comes back through the branch the lexer treats as **safe**: a backslash escapes inside a plain `'…'` too, so two `INSERT`s storing different rows collapse onto one hash. Measured on 17.11 under `SET standard_conforming_strings = off`: `INSERT INTO u VALUES ('a\' -- one');` and `… -- two');` are both accepted, `count(*)` 2 and `count(DISTINCT v)` 2, values `a' -- one` and `a' -- two` — and this lexer returns one hash for the pair. `applied()` now runs one `SHOW` before it takes any lock (the function ran three queries; it runs four) and refuses the connection outright with `EX_CONFIG` **78** rather than 65, because nothing is wrong with the ledger or the files and the fix is in the connection string, which the message names. Verified end to end through that exact `?options=` URL. **The reasoning is the part worth keeping**: a written assumption is a likelihood argument, and this design refuses likelihood arguments everywhere else it matters. The lexer is deliberately *not* taught the off behaviour — it cannot know which setting produced a file and guessing would break the default — so the collision is asserted as a test documenting why the guard exists, which fails the moment anyone teaches the lexer without removing the guard.

**A test's name claimed what its assertion cannot deliver, and the twin next to it was the tell.** `keeps a doubled quote inside a string literal rather than ending the literal there` passes on a lexer with **no** doubled-quote handling at all. The plain branch's `''` handling is an **equivalent mutant** — 462 divergences in 400k fuzzed inputs, **100%** containing an `E'`, against **zero** divergences in 12,093,234 exhaustive strings for the plain twin — and the reason is provable rather than statistical: both readings consume quotes in pairs from the same index onto contiguous slices, and every byte is copied verbatim, so the emitted text is identical either way. Round 2 had documented exactly this for the escape branch (L3) and had not checked the twin. The test is renamed to what it holds, the equivalence is recorded with its proof instead of as a survivor, and the header says plainly that only the escape-string twin is observable. The handling stays because it is correct; it simply cannot be pinned.

**Two enumeration entries were wrong, both harmless, both corrected — because the enumeration is now the guarantee.** A doubled quote does **not** double inside a bit-string: `SELECT B'01''01'` and `SELECT X'1F''F'` are both `syntax error at or near "'01'"` on 17.11, so "plain quote rules behind a prefix letter" was not quite true; this lexer is more permissive there, which is unreachable on text Postgres accepts and therefore cannot put two *valid* migrations on one hash. And `'a'` newline `'b'` is **quote continuation** — one constant returning `ab` with `length` 2, with a comment able to carry the newline — where the header called them "two literals to the scanner", which was simply wrong. This lexer emits two literals with the whitespace collapsed, and `SELECT 'a' 'b'` on one line is itself a syntax error, so no two *valid* texts can differ only by that newline's presence. Both are now pinned by tests as well as described.

**A wrong answer that looks populated is a different shape from a clean zero, and this branch produced three of them in one cycle.** `CLAUDE.md`'s false-zero family — the broken `&&` chain, the `\b` git-grep, the `bytea` `LIKE` — is entirely about a *search that comes back empty*: the tell is the emptiness, and the remedy is to make the search find something. **The sibling is harder and has no entry there yet: a query that asks the wrong question and answers with a perfectly plausible number.** Nothing about it looks empty, so there is nothing to notice.

Three instances, all on this branch, all in cycle 1-2:

- **The locking measurement.** Two of the three runners were crashing on an unresolvable `pg` import and reporting **0.14 s** — a number in exactly the right range, sitting in a table beside a real one, reading as "no regression". Caught by a check that each runner actually prints 16 status lines first.
- **The killer-delta re-derivation.** The report glob resolved to the `--check` runs, which carry no summary, so the comparison printed `unchanged` for **all thirteen** carried mutants. Thirteen plausible answers, and the true answer was that ten had moved. Caught by a control line printing how many killer rows the grep had found at all: `0 0`.
- **"Twelve of the thirteen."** Written from reading the list rather than counting it; the answer is ten. No tool was wrong here — the query was a human one, and it still returned a populated, plausible number.

The reviewer's own cycle-2 fuzz was the fourth: an exhaustive search reported **0** divergences for *both* doubled-quote branches at depth 6, and the control failing — not the zero — is what revealed the space had never been searched. That one is the classic shape; the three above are the sibling.

**The rule this branch would add:** a control has to produce a *known value*, not merely run. For a search, make it find something. For a **number**, run the instrument against an input whose answer you already know — a runner that must print 16 lines, a grep that must match some rows, a list whose length you counted by a second method. A control that only proves the command executed cannot tell a right answer from a plausible one, and a plausible one is what all three of these were.

**And a surviving mutant found the guard's fail-open direction.** Narrowing the precondition from `!== "on"` to `=== "off"` passed the entire suite, because every test that reached it set the setting to exactly `off`. The two readings differ only on an answer that is *neither* — an empty result, or a value from something between this runner and Postgres that is not the two-valued GUC it expects — and on those the narrowed form falls through and hashes anyway. Fail-open on a precondition is the one direction this guard must never take; an empty result, an empty string and an unexpected value are each pinned now, with `on` still let through so the arm is not a guard that refuses everything.

**The rebase onto `4c5f2bc` owed real work, and it is the two-branches-jointly-incoherent shape exactly** (`CLAUDE.md`'s rebase gotcha). PR #172 gave every `.db.test.ts` a hang-backstop declarator, wrapped hooks and a schema rebuild, with two guard files enforcing it; this branch's `migration-content-hash.db.test.ts` was written before any of that existed and tripped every count — **18** bare `it(`, **2** raw vitest hooks, no route to the shared helper. Neither branch was wrong and nothing conflicted textually: the file merged clean and failed four guard assertions.

The backstop half is not negotiable and carries no exemption, so all 18 declarations and both hooks took the wrapped forms. **The schema half resolved better than the exemption planned for it, and the planned entry would have failed.** `NEEDS_NO_SCHEMA`'s own earned-check refuses any member matching `sonny(_meta)?\.`, and this file names `sonny_meta.` twelve times — so the exemption argued for on this PR could not have been taken, and the guard would have said so. What the file actually needs is `dropSchema` rather than `rebuildSchema`: the door `migrate.db.test.ts` already uses, which the helper guard accepts, and which needs no exemption at all. The reason is the same one in different words — this file's subject is the ledger's own lifecycle, and `rebuildSchema` would apply all sixteen migrations and record a hash for every one before each test, which is the state in which every question this file asks has already been answered.

**Both files needed adding to `MAY_REACH_THE_MIGRATION_RUNNER`, which had not come up until the population was counted.** Fourteen files imported the runner on the pre-#172 tree; the list holds four. The other ten each called `up(client)` as setup — the call #172's shared rebuild replaces — so after it, only genuine tests-of-the-runner still import it, and both of this branch's files are left doing so and unlisted for the dull reason that they postdate the list. That is the list's existing category applied to two files that did not exist when it was written, not a new argument. One edit each rather than two: the guard compares its scan against the Set itself, so the value-pin updates with the membership.

**The `0000_probe` prefix stays, and the measurement changed which reason it stays for.** Its stated reason was the neighbour's — `migrate.db.test.ts` finds "the newest migration" with `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`, and a probe row sorting after the real ones would have become that. SONNY-366 ends that: every database file starts from its own schema, nothing here reaches a neighbour's run, and this file's only `ORDER BY` is **inside a doc comment describing the neighbour's query**, so it has zero executable dependency on sort order. It is load-bearing for something it never claimed instead: `reset()` and the teardown remove exactly this file's rows with `DELETE … WHERE id LIKE '0000_probe%'`, and that pattern is what makes "exactly this file's" true. It needs to be *distinctive*, not low-sorting. The old reason is recorded rather than deleted, because a precaution removed when its neighbour changed is what somebody re-adds later without knowing why it went.

Spec sections covered: none directly — this is runner correctness under `docs/sonny-row-12-host-decision.md` §12.2's staged hosts.
Files changed: `server/src/db/migration-hash.ts` (new), `server/src/db/migrate.ts`, `server/test/migration-content-hash.test.ts` (new), `server/test/migration-content-hash.db.test.ts` (new), `server/README.md`.
Tests: `npm test` → **600 passed | 321 skipped (921)**, exit 0; `DATABASE_URL=… npm run test:db` → **921 passed (921)**, exit 0, no file skipped; `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run check:secrets` (**542 tracked files, 12 patterns**) and `./scripts/check-secrets-selftest.sh` (**46 passed, 0 failed**) each exit 0 — all at `f139755`, each exit code read with nothing between the command and `$?`. The `test:db` run used this lane's own container per `CLAUDE.md`'s derived recipe (`sonny-gw-db-lane-3`, Docker-assigned host port).

**Mutation battery, round 1: 14 mutants, 14 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed** (pre-rebase) (`scripts/mutate`, `MUTATE_TEST_CMD` scoped to the four migration-runner test files, baseline `PASSED 63 passed (63)`). The plan mutates **the property** — that a changed applied migration is refused — rather than one mutant per changed file: the drift check dropped from `up` (R1) and from `down` (R2), the refusal downgraded to a report (R3), a mismatch not counted as drift (R4), the hash not recorded on apply (R5, which is the original defect restored), an absent hash compared instead of carried as unknown (R6), the ledger's `ALTER` dropped so an existing database never gains the column (R7), the rollback half left out of the hash (R8), comments not stripped at all (R9 — the whole-file hash this design refused), a dollar-quoted body lexed as ordinary code (R10), a `--` inside a string literal read as a comment (R11), block comments not nested (R12), whitespace not collapsed (R13), and a bind parameter read as a dollar quote (R14). **Round 2 re-ran the lexer and ledger mutants only — 11 mutants, 11 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed** (pre-rebase) — scoped that way because F1 and the tag-class survivor are both lexer changes and R1-R6 and R8's evidence did not move: `refuseOnDrift`, `driftedMigrations` and the ledger insert are untouched by the round. R7 was re-run as L7/L8 because the ledger's `ALTER` moved. Its arms are escape strings lexed as ordinary strings (L1), the backslash carrying no escape (L2), the doubled quote no longer holding the literal open (L3 — the survivor above, now killed), the `E` prefix honoured mid-identifier (L4), the two tag character classes (L5, L6), the `ALTER` back on the lock path (L7) and never running at all (L8), the false refusal sentence restored (L9), `status` reporting a changed migration and exiting 0 (L10), and a CLI drift refusal exiting 0 (L11).

**Mutation battery, cycle 2: 27 mutants, 26 killed and S2 surviving; S2 fixed and the four precondition/exit-code mutants re-run, 4 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed** (both pre-rebase) (baseline `PASSED 86 passed (86)`). It was one battery doing two jobs. The new arms are the precondition accepted (S1), only a literal `off` refused (S2 — the survivor above), a CLI refusal exiting 0 (L11) and an unsafe-connection refusal exiting 65 rather than 78 (L12).

**The second job was restating round 1's killer lists at this head, and it is the reason this entry re-measures rather than carries.** A killer list recorded against round 1's head is a lower bound presented as a measurement, because every test added since can only add killers — recorded as **SONNY-369**. Re-run at cycle 2's head, **ten of the thirteen** carried mutants had gained killers: R9 **10 → 17**, R13 **9 → 15**, R10 **3 → 8**, R5 **5 → 9**, R4 **7 → 10**, R1 **3 → 6**, R3 **3 → 6**, R11 **4 → 6**, R2 **2 → 3**, R14 **1 → 2**, with R6 (5), R8 (2) and R12 (1) unchanged. (Written as "twelve of the thirteen" first, from reading the list rather than counting it — the two reports are `.build/mutate/1687bf3-20260830T142055-446/report.log` and `.build/mutate/60a8b82-20260830T172152-32638/report.log`, kept on disk under heads the rebase has since replaced, and the diff between them is the count. Cycle 1's review noted the same reviewer measured R4 at +2 against an earlier head than this one; the deltas here are against round 1's.) Every one is still killed, so the carry was sound — but a reader chasing "killed by test X" against the old list was being handed a number that had stopped being true. R7 is absent on purpose: the ledger `ALTER` it mutated has moved, and L7/L8 replace it.

Behavior added:
- A content hash over both halves' executable SQL, recorded in `sonny_meta.schema_migration.content_hash` inside the transaction that applies the migration.
- `up` and `down` refuse, before applying or rolling back anything, when any applied migration's file no longer matches what was recorded.
- `status` reports four states and exits 65 when any migration reads `CHANGED`; it never throws, because it is the diagnostic reached for once one of the other two has.
- `MigrationDriftError`, so the CLI can print the finding without a stack trace.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- `loadMigrations`'s rollback-or-refuse rule, its filename ordering, its non-SQL skipping and its up/down split are untouched; `migrate.load.test.ts`'s 7 tests pass unchanged.
- `migrate.db.test.ts`'s whole suite passes unchanged — apply, idempotent re-run, rollback with a schema fingerprint comparison, re-apply, the empty-ledger case, the half-failing migration leaving neither schema nor ledger row, 0007's plus-tag fold, 0010's index, and the ledger living in `sonny_meta`. Its "newest applied migration" queries still find a real migration: this branch's own probe rows are `0000_`-prefixed by construction and removed in `afterAll`, so they can never be `ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1`.
- `up(client, someOtherDir)` against a database holding the real migrations still works — three existing tests apply throwaway migrations that way, and the drift check compares only the intersection of ledger rows and files present.
- Every other `*.db.test.ts` file (auth, authgate, authlimits, content, entitlement, idempotency, linking, metering, pool, races, supersession) calls `up(client)` in its own setup and is green.
- The per-migration transaction, the one-migration-per-`down` rule and the `pathToFileURL` CLI guard are unchanged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **A guard that forbids annotating an applied migration would end a practice this repo relies on**, which is why comments are stripped. Anyone tightening this to a whole-file hash should read `src/db/migration-hash.ts`'s header first: the cost is not strictness, it is that the guard becomes the thing that gets deleted.
- **A comment inside `$$ … $$` is stored in the database**, so it is hashed. That falls out of writing a correct lexer rather than being a special case, and a "simplification" that strips comments everywhere silently loosens the guard over eight migrations' function bodies.
- **The selftest arm caught its own fixture first.** The db suite's `reset()` queried `sonny_meta.schema_migration` before `up` had created it, so the first assertion threw and seven downstream tests cascaded into states the run never reached — the ledger is bootstrapped in `beforeAll` with `up` over an empty directory now. Worth recording because the cascade read as eight failures of the guard and was one failure of the fixture.
- **An assertion keyed on a refusal's wording breaks when the wording is corrected.** Two db assertions matched `/no longer match the file/` and went red when the message was fixed from "match" to "matches" — behaviour unchanged. They key on `MigrationDriftError` now, plus the migration id, which is the part an operator actually needs.
- **`status`'s classification was extracted out of `main` so it could be tested at all.** `main` is only reachable by spawning a built `dist/db/migrate.js`, which a suite running from source cannot do without depending on a prior `npm run build`. `migrationStates` returns the four states as data; the one line left untestable is the `process.exitCode` assignment, which is why the count comes back rather than a boolean.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **An applied migration whose file has been *deleted* is still not reported.** Nothing is left to hash, so nothing is compared, and `status` iterates files rather than ledger rows so the row is invisible entirely. Same family of hazard, deliberately out of this ticket's scope rather than half-built; recorded on SONNY-364's closing comment.
- **The hash says nothing about the schema itself.** It compares a file against what an environment recorded when it applied that file. A hand-run `ALTER TABLE` against production is invisible here, and always was.
- **The CLI's remaining uncovered surface is `main`'s 18 lines** — argv, the `DATABASE_URL` check and its exit 78, and the connection. Every exit code the README promises is asserted from the suite through `runCommand`; `main` is still exercised only by hand, against a throwaway database on this branch.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the roadmap and whatever is claimed next in Plane.
### Branch: fix/a-server-test-measures-what-it-claims
Status: complete — SONNY-366, SONNY-357 and SONNY-354; written 2026-08-30 before the PR opened
Date: 2026-08-30
Tickets: **SONNY-366** (eight `.db.test.ts` files run against whatever schema the last invocation left, because `up()` is a no-op), **SONNY-357** (`migrate.db.test.ts`'s timeout does not cancel its `down()` loop, so one slow test corrupts the tests after it) and **SONNY-354** (the server suite inherits vitest's 5000 ms default, so machine load fails a different set each run — and a battery reads that as a kill). One session, one branch, cut from `main` at `65a7fc9` (PR #168's merge), not rebased. **Every figure below is measured at `97b9f59`**, this branch's implementation commit, over a clean tree; the docs commit above it changes only this file and one `reason` line in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`. `65a7fc9` figures are readings of the base for comparison, taken with that revision's own copy of the file rather than translated.

**They are one problem in three parts, and the part that made them one branch turned out not to exist.** SONNY-366's own comment sized the schema rebuild at taking the first file "from about 18 s to about 57 s", warned that eight more of them would push the suite into SONNY-354's timeouts, and concluded the two tickets pull in opposite directions. Measured instead of inherited, a rebuild costs about **130 ms**: five consecutive drop-and-apply cycles over this repository's 16 migrations against an idle local Postgres in Docker read `drop 63/32/28/25/26 ms, up 110/96/106/86/115 ms`, against a no-op `up()` of 17 ms (a throwaway `node --experimental-strip-types` probe calling the two statements and then `up`, deleted after). Ten of those is a little over a second. The whole suite went from **22.32s at `65a7fc9` to 24.12s at `97b9f59`** with 14 more tests in it (`npx vitest run --reporter=default` with `DATABASE_URL` set, both). So there was nothing to sequence around, and the fix is the plain one — every file rebuilds, no memoisation, no once-per-process fixture, no shared-schema cleverness. The 57 s figure is described on the ticket as uncontrolled and does not reproduce: `auth.db.test.ts`, the file that already rebuilt, runs alone in 4.52 s at `65a7fc9`.

**SONNY-366 — the population is seven files, not eight, and the difference is the grep-is-evidence-about-text rule again.** The ticket's eight comes from `for f in test/*.db.test.ts; do grep -q "DROP SCHEMA" "$f" || echo "$f"; done | wc -l` → 8 at `65a7fc9`, which counts `pool.db.test.ts` — a file that leases connections, runs `SELECT 1` and names no table, so it needs no schema and gets none. The files that actually called `up(client)` as setup, **and had no `DROP SCHEMA` above it**, were seven with eight call sites between them — two of those in one file's two suites. The two conditions have to be read together and the counting command answers only the second: `grep -c "await up(client)" test/*.db.test.ts` at `65a7fc9` answers for all twelve files (auth 1, authgate 1, authlimits 1, content 1, entitlement 1, idempotency 2, linking 1, metering 1, migrate 6, races 1, supersession 1, pool 0), and the seven are what is left after removing the four that already rebuilt and the one that needs no schema. This parenthesis presented that subset as the command's own output until the rebase, when re-running the commands rather than only re-reading the stamps caught it — the same shape as PR #162's F6, a figure taken with one command and cited beside another. All seven now call `rebuildSchema` from `test/support/schema.ts`, and so do the three that carried their own `DROP SCHEMA` pair, which is ten files reaching one helper; `migrate.db.test.ts` calls `dropSchema` alone, because its first test asserts what `up()` applies and that needs an empty database to be a question at all.

**What changed in verification behaviour, measured in both directions rather than reported as "no reds appeared".** A full run at `97b9f59` is green — **838 passed (838) across 36 files, exit 0** — and so was the run before the change, so nothing in this container was passing on leftover state, which proves nothing on its own: the container was created that morning. The mechanism was demonstrated instead, by planting the exact divergence the ticket describes (the `sonny` schema dropped, the ledger left holding every migration, so `up()` has nothing pending) and running each of the seven files alone under both revisions. Under `65a7fc9`'s copies: **176 tests failed, 7 of 7 files exit 1**. At `97b9f59`, same poison before each: **176 passed, 7 of 7 exit 0**. `auth.db.test.ts` is not in that seven because PR #167 had already fixed it, and its position is why the residual exposure was still large: it runs first, so it healed the schema for everything after it *in a full-suite run* — leaving single-file runs, which is what `--filter` iteration and a scoped battery are, exposed.

**The guard is two files because a scan and a behaviour are two different claims.** `test/schema.test.ts` reads the tree: every `.db.test.ts` file reaches the helper except `pool.db.test.ts`, whose exemption is re-derived (it must name no `sonny.`/`sonny_meta.` identifier) rather than believed; nothing under `test/` reaches `src/db/migrate.js` except the four files whose subject is migrations; and the population is refused at zero **on its own terms** rather than by comparison, because every other arm is satisfied by a scan that enumerated nothing. `test/schema.db.test.ts` is the other half — it plants the divergence, calls `up()` against it and watches it apply nothing while the missing table stays missing, then calls `rebuildSchema` and watches it come back. Both were proved by breaking them: pointing one file's setup back at `up(client)` fails three arms naming that file, and pointing the scan at a directory with no database tests fails three arms — including, exactly as designed, the one that exists to refuse a zero, while the arm that hunts offenders passed on the empty population.

**SONNY-357 — the fix is a barrier, and the ticket's other option is rejected with a reason rather than left open.** `test/support/settling.ts`'s `track` runs a test body and remembers it; `settle` aborts it and does not resolve until it has actually stopped, and `migrate.db.test.ts` calls it from an `afterEach`, which is the one hook vitest runs *and awaits* after a timed-out test. Both rollback loops now check `signal.throwIfAborted()` each iteration. The ticket also asks whether those tests should hold their own connection: no, and the reason is that it fixes the smaller half. A `pg.Client` serialises its own queue, so a neighbour's danger is landing inside the abandoned transaction — which a private connection does fix — and the schema changing underneath it, which a private connection does not fix at all, because both connections address the same database.

**Demonstrated against a real client, in both arms.** A throwaway probe file (deleted) declares a test with a 300 ms deadline whose tracked body loops eight `SELECT pg_sleep(0.2)` steps, followed by three ordinary tests that each time their own `SELECT 1`. With the barrier: the loop stops at **2 of 8** steps and the three followers wait **6, 1 and 5 ms**. With only `await inFlight.settle()` removed and nothing else changed: the loop keeps advancing under them — **2, then 3, then 4** steps done as each follower runs — and those followers wait **108, 214 and 204 ms**, queued behind an abandoned test's work on the client they share. That is the corruption route the ticket describes, reproduced and closed. `test/settling.test.ts` is the permanent coverage, and it asserts on a recorded event sequence rather than on elapsed time — a test of a fix for a lost race must not be able to lose one. Four mutants against `support/settling.ts` prove it is not decorative: dropping `settle`'s `await stopped` kills 1 test, dropping its `abort` kills 2, un-swallowing the tracked rejection kills 4, and re-wrapping the body's error kills 3.

**SONNY-354 — the declarations route stays open, as the ticket's own correction says, and the migration is the whole database population rather than a list.** All **303** tests in the **13** `.db.test.ts` files are declared through `itUnderHangBackstop`, and since cycle 2 all **42** hook call sites go through the matching hook wrappers (`grep -hcE '^ *itUnderHangBackstop[(]' server/test/*.db.test.ts | paste -sd+ - | bc` → 303, the same with `it[(]` → 0, `(beforeAll|beforeEach|afterAll|afterEach)UnderHangBackstop[(]` → 42 and the six raw hook names → 0, all at `9df5d27`); the non-database files keep vitest's default. The line is the file suffix and there are no exceptions, including four synchronous tests in those files that touch no database — an exemption list is the thing that rots, and one `async` keyword each is cheaper than maintaining one. **The line is drawn from measurement.** A database test waits on work in another process whose cost this one does not control, and the thinnest margin in that population is `migrate.db.test.ts`'s rollback chain at 2483 ms of the 5000 ms default, a factor of two; every non-database file runs in-process at under 300 ms for the whole file, so its slowest single test has something like a 500x margin against a worst measured load-induced slowdown of 10x (`support/backstop.ts` carries that measurement). Five hand-written deadlines are folded in: four `{ timeout: 60_000 }` option objects and one trailing `60_000`, all of which set vitest's ceiling and left its message generic. `backstop.test.ts` gains two arms — a bare `it(` in a `.db.test.ts` file fails the suite, named with its count, and the population is refused at zero on its own terms — both proved by breaking them.

**The review round (PR #172), and its blocking finding is the third instance in a week of one mistake.** `backstop.test.ts`'s new arm counted `/^\s*it\(/` and required zero — which is *one spelling* of a surface with many. `test(` is vitest's own alias for the same `TestAPI`, and `it.each(`, `it.skip(`, `it.skipIf(cond)(` and the rest walked straight past it; the reviewer added a `.db.test.ts` declaring tests that way, watched both new guards pass with it present, and got `Test timed out in 5000ms.` out of a hanging `test(` — the undeclared repository-wide message the whole construct exists to replace. **The population is now derived from vitest's own types rather than listed.** `@vitest/runner` declares exactly two names — `declare const test: TestAPI` and `declare const it: TestAPI` — and everything else is a chain hanging off one of them: `concurrent|sequential|only|skip|todo|fails` plus `each` and `for` as properties, `skipIf` and `runIf` as chained *calls*, and `extend`, which returns a whole new API **under a name of the caller's choosing** and which no call-shape pattern can ever follow. So the arm that actually closes it is the **import**: `globals` is off — asserted as its own arm, because that is what makes the import exhaustive — so a declarator must be imported before it can be called, and every `import … from "vitest"` clause is parsed for the name it binds, by *imported* name so an alias is caught, with a namespace import refused outright because it brings the surface in under one name no specifier list can see. **Ten evasions were each written into a real `.db.test.ts` file**: `test(`, `it.each(`, `it.skip(`, the `.only/.todo/.fails/.concurrent` group, `it.skipIf(cond)(`, ``it.each`table` ``, `import { it as t }`, `import * as v`, `test.extend` bound to a new name, and bare `it(` — **all ten exit 1**, and the correct `itUnderHangBackstop` shape exits 0.

**F5 is the same defect one file over and is fixed the same way.** `schema.test.ts` matched a *mention* of the helper, which an unused import satisfies — and an unused import is exactly what a half-finished new file has. It parses the helper's import clause now and requires a call to one of the local names it binds, so an alias must be called under its alias and a namespace import through its namespace.

**Both parsers carried a bug that a negative control found by not firing.** A lazy `[\s\S]*?` import clause starts matching at the file's *first* `import` keyword and runs to the module in question, so it hands back every import above it glued together, and the greedy brace extraction then reads names out of the wrong statement — which is why "helper imported, call deleted" still passed: `pg` and vitest's own bindings had been swept into the name list. `[^;]` keeps a clause inside its own statement. Both sample tables now carry the shape that catches it, in both directions. The lesson is the one the finding is about: **the negative control is the test of the guard, and a control that does not fire is a finding, not a formality.**

And its drain uses `setImmediate` rather than three `Promise.resolve()` hops — Node exhausts the microtask queue before a macrotask, so one turn flushes any finite promise chain, where three hops flush three, which is fewer than the barrier's own `.then().finally()` chain needs; a shallow drain let two more single-slot mutants survive. **Seven mutants now, all killed** (exit 1 each, restored 8 passed): settle waiting for nothing (4 tests), settle not aborting (4), the rejection un-swallowed (3), the body's error rewrapped (3), only the first body tracked (1), only the latest body tracked — the defect as shipped (1), and only the latest controller kept (2). The two single-slot mutants are each killed by exactly the ordering that exists for it.

The headroom was never the complaint; an inherited number was. `testTimeout` is written down at the 5000 ms it already had, so a future change to it is a decision rather than a default that moved, and `backstop.test.ts` asserts both against the constant so config and construct cannot drift.

The **query-slowdown** half did not: mean query time did not move under `pgbench` plus 40 spinners (**40.8 ms → 39.0 ms**), because Docker Desktop holds its own vCPUs on that machine and the load never reached Postgres. So the **2527 ms** figure, and the "ten times its unloaded cost" it is quoted for, rest on one machine's measurement. The rejection does not depend on them. `support/backstop.ts` says so beside the number, which is where a session re-deriving from it will be standing.

**Cycle 2 of the review (PR #172): four findings, none blocking, all in code this branch wrote.** F1 is the one that matters most, because it was this branch's own subject inside the arm added to close it. `vitestConfig.test?.globals ?? false` cannot distinguish *globals is off* from *there is no `test` block at all* — and the second is reachable, because `defineConfig` accepts a function form. Against `defineConfig(() => ({ … globals: true }))` the globals arm **passes**; what fails is the neighbouring `hookTimeout` arm, saying `expected undefined to be 90000`. So the tree was protected by a coincidence in a different arm rather than by the one whose name says it, while the arm *did* work in the direction it was written — which is exactly what makes a vacuous arm hard to see. It reads through a `configuredTest()` that refuses anything but a plain object with a plain `test` block and reports **which of the two** it found, and a new arm named for reading the config asserts the block is present and non-empty before anything reads a field out of it. Measured three ways at `9df5d27`: `globals: true` in the object form fails the globals arm **alone**; the function form, with and without globals, fails the reading arm, the globals arm and the deadline arm **together**. That is SONNY-224 through the hook path, and the path is one SONNY-366 widened by putting a ~230 ms schema rebuild into every `beforeAll` where seven files had a 4 ms no-op `up()`. The argument was already made for the test population and had to reach the same conclusion here: `support/backstop.ts` gains `beforeAllUnderHangBackstop` and its three siblings, each running the hook body under `underHangBackstop` with vitest's ceiling above it, and all **42** hook call sites across the twelve database files go through them. **Proved rather than argued**: with `HANG_BACKSTOP_MS` dropped to one second and a `beforeAll` hung, the run carries `waited 1.0s for: a beforeAll hook` and the declared fragment, and `Hook timed out in` appears **nowhere** in it. The guard grew to match and is derived the same way as the declarator half — vitest exports six hooks, and all six are refused in a database file: the four with wrappers, plus `aroundAll` and `aroundEach`, which have none and are refused **fail-closed**, so the first file that wants one adds a wrapper rather than quietly reopening the hole. `onTestFailed` and `onTestFinished` sit beside them in the same export list and are deliberately not included: they register a callback inside a running test rather than a hook with a deadline of its own.

**F3 — there was a fourth ordering, and it makes `settle()`'s loop load-bearing.** `while` → `if` survived all eight tests, because every one of them has both bodies tracked *before* `settle` takes its snapshot of what is outstanding. The reviewer's probe does not: body two is started **by** body one, after that snapshot, so a single pass resolves without ever having seen it. Taken, and — per SONNY-360, which this repository learned the hard way — not taken on trust: the arm was confirmed to have actually executed (`✓ … waits for a body that a tracked body starts after settle is already waiting`, `9 passed (9)`, nothing skipped) and then confirmed to fail on the mutant here, `1 failed | 8 passed (9)`, killed by that arm and no other. Nine mutants against the barrier now, eight killed and one equivalent: the reviewer's second observation, that deleting the trailing `live.clear()` survives, is **settled rather than chased** — every entry in `live` is removed by its own body's `.finally()` and the loop cannot exit until each of those has run, so the line clears nothing. It stays as the statement that `live` is empty on return, with a comment saying it is a confirmed equivalent mutant.

**F2 — three of nineteen evasions escaped, and the reviewer's characterisation is the useful part.** The import arm and the call arm cover for each other *except where a parser miss coincides with an alias*, so what got through was module plumbing and two regexes rather than a spelling anyone missed. Two are parser work and are closed: an import clause is now bounded by "contains no second `import` keyword" rather than by a semicolon — a semicolon can sit inside a **comment** in the clause, which ended the match early, and that edge was fail-safe in `schema.test.ts` and fail-**open** in `backstop.test.ts`, which is why it was found on that side — with comments stripped from the clause afterwards, safely, since an import clause holds no string literal a `/*` could hide in; and the imported name has its quotes stripped, because ES2022's `import { "it" as t }` binds the same declarator. The third was a decision rather than a regex, and the decision is **extend, not record**: no module under `test/` that is not itself a test file may reach a declarator, with `support/backstop.ts` the single exemption, because without `globals` a declarator reaches a database file either through that file's own vitest import or through a module it imports, and the only modules under `test/` that are not test files are helpers. All three now fail the guard, each by the arm written for it, and the correct shape still passes. **The residual is stated in the arm rather than left to be found**: a database file importing from a *non-database* `*.test.ts` file, which legitimately declares tests of its own. What it buys is one deadline for this suite to reason about instead of two; what it costs is 91 s in a wedged file against 10, and about 20 minutes worst case against about 2, and that worst case only arrives when the database is already broken, in which state the run is not a measurement of anything. `vitest.config.ts` carries that reasoning now, including which of the two numbers to change if the trade stops looking right — this one, not the constant, which is the tests' bound and derived from their own load measurements.

**Rebased onto `0706b9a` before merge, and the figures above are restamped rather than restated.** The branch's three stamped commits were replaced — `1d45b22`→`97b9f59`, `3ac15b8`→`9558605`, `b430cd4`→`9df5d27` — and a rebase moves the base, so a figure only survives if the tree it was measured on did not. Behavior added:
- Every `.db.test.ts` file rebuilds the `sonny` and `sonny_meta` schemas from the migration text in the working tree before its first test, through one shared helper.

The 303 skipped is exactly the database population the new `backstop.test.ts` arm counts, which is the two figures agreeing from opposite directions.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **A schema rebuild is cheap and the ticket's cost figure was not measured.** 130 ms, not 39 s. Anyone tempted to memoise this per process should re-measure first — and note that a per-process cache would have to know when `migrate.db.test.ts` had left the schema rolled back, which is the implicit ordering coupling the ticket exists to remove.
- **`up()` being a no-op is invisible to every test that depends on it.** The defect produces no error, no warning and no slow run; it produces a green file measuring a schema nobody asked for. The only way to see it is to make the ledger and the schema disagree on purpose, which is what `schema.db.test.ts` now does on every run.
- **A first-running file that rebuilds hides the defect for everything after it in a full-suite run, and hides nothing at all in a single-file run.** That is why the poison experiment above is per file: run the whole suite poisoned under `65a7fc9` and `auth.db.test.ts` heals the database before the other eleven files start, so the suite is green and the defect is exactly as present as it was.
- **vitest's timeout does not cancel anything, and no widening of it ever will.** SONNY-354 and SONNY-357 look like one ticket and are not: raising a deadline changes how often it is crossed and nothing about what happens afterwards. The barrier is in `afterEach` because that is the only hook vitest both runs and awaits after a timed-out test; a `finally` inside the test body does not run, because the body was never resumed.
- **A private connection for the migration-chain tests was considered and rejected**, with the reason in `support/settling.ts`'s header: it fixes transaction bleed and not the schema race, and the barrier fixes both.
- **The declaration that makes a hang backstop safe is also what makes a genuine hang uncountable, and widening it widens that.** Two tests' worth of that trade was already accepted; this branch makes it 302. The direction is the safe one — `UNATTRIBUTED` exits 2 and is reported — but it is a real reduction in what a battery can attribute, and it is the reason a bare-timeout declaration is still refused: that would excuse a hang *everywhere*, including in the 536 tests that keep vitest's default.
- **A test that only counts `it(` in a scan cannot see a local wrapper.** The new arm in `backstop.test.ts` counts bare `it(` and requires zero; a file that defined its own `itSettling` alias would satisfy it while hiding every test behind a name the scan does not know. `migrate.db.test.ts` therefore calls `inFlight.track` explicitly inside each of its nine bodies rather than through a local helper — verbose on purpose, and the same lesson PR #156's F2 paid for on the aliased-import evasion.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- The barrier waits for the step in flight rather than interrupting it, so a Postgres that has stopped answering a single-statement rollback reaches the `afterEach`'s own deadline. That is a broken database rather than a slow test, and it fails loudly, naming the file, instead of quietly downstream. Cancelling a query genuinely mid-flight needs `pg_cancel_backend` from a second connection and is not built.
- Only `migrate.db.test.ts` uses the barrier. The other twelve database files have no multi-step loop that outlives a test the way its rollback chain does, and wiring `track` into 293 more bodies for a hazard none of them has would be cost without a property. A file that grows such a loop should adopt it; nothing mechanical enforces that, and a scan for "a loop that issues queries" is not a check this repository could keep honest.
- `test/settling.test.ts` proves the barrier against promises rather than against a real `pg.Client`. The real-client demonstration in this entry is a throwaway probe, deliberately not committed: pinning it permanently would mean asserting on elapsed milliseconds, which is the wall-clock bet `CLAUDE.md` forbids and the exact mistake these three tickets are about.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

The three pre-rebase names — `260ca25`, `69db340`, `58aa08d` — are each non-ancestral now and none is cited below. **Nothing is carried from the pre-review round** — the review's findings 4 and 5 changed `EntitlementService.swift`, so every figure was re-taken rather than translated, and the one that used to name its own head no longer does. Each figure carries the command that produced it.

Reviewed by: fresh session (per WORKFLOW.md step 7) — nothing blocking; six findings, all taken. **Finding 4** was a real coverage gap and is fixed with a test (below). **Findings 2 and 3** were false statements in this entry and in the code comments, both corrected below. **Finding 5** was an unreachable branch and its doc sentence, both removed. **Finding 6** was a test protected by an accident, now protected by name. **Finding 1** is a hole in `WORKFLOW.md` step 5 rather than in this branch and is filed as **SONNY-369**; its re-measurement is done and is what the figures below are.

Files changed: `Sources/MacAgentCore/SonnyBackendClient.swift`, `Sources/MacAgentCore/EntitlementService.swift`, `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/EntitlementServiceTests.swift`, `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md`. **`server/` is untouched and that was a scope fence rather than a judgement made while implementing** — three other lanes owned it this wave — and the fix needed none of it: `git diff --stat main...HEAD -- server` prints nothing at `a5ef9b3`. Nothing on the gateway would have helped anyway; the whole failure is a client that believes a number without bound, and a gateway cannot fix that by sending a better number.

Tests: `env CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH="$PWD/.build/clang-module-cache" swift test --disable-sandbox -Xswiftc -F -Xswiftc /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/Frameworks -Xlinker -rpath -Xlinker /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/Frameworks -Xlinker -rpath -Xlinker /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/usr/lib` → **passed, 2501 tests in 173 suites, exit 0** at `a5ef9b3` (exit read with nothing between the command and `$?`). **The delta is arithmetic rather than a borrowed figure**: this branch adds **5** tests and **0** suites (`git diff main...HEAD -- Tests | grep -c '^+    @Test'` → 5, the same with `'^+@Suite'` → 0), all five into the existing `EntitlementServiceTests`, and changes no other test's existence — so the base is 2496 in 173. `scripts/warnings` → **0 warnings, exit 0**, measured at `260ca25 (clean)` off the script's own header rather than inferred from HEAD.

Behavior added:
- **A reported server instant is held to the pace real time can account for.** `SonnyBackendClient.corroboratedInstant` caps a `Date` header at the previous observation carried forward by `ContinuousClock` plus `maximumUncorroboratedForwardJump` (300 s). Server time advances at exactly the rate of real time, and `ContinuousClock` measures real time in a way nothing on this Mac can set, so that projection is the ceiling a legitimate advance sits under.
- **A high-water mark past the end of the window of the claim it is being stored beside is reset to that claim's own signed `issuedAt`**, and the client's in-memory observation and this process's anchor go with it. `EntitlementService.markKeptOrReset` is the whole of it.
- **`adopt`'s replay guard yields to a live claim once the stored one is dead.** Same condition, and it is what turned a wrong mark from an outage into a state the next refresh repairs.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **A clock rolled back offline still cannot re-enter a lapsed window** — `aClockRolledBackOfflineCannotReEnterALapsedWindow`, unchanged and green.
- **An older claim replayed at this Mac still does not replace the current one** — `anOlderClaimReplayedAtThisMacDoesNotReplaceTheCurrentOne`, unchanged and green, and now joined by `aStoredClaimTheMarkHasNotYetKilledStillOutranksAnOlderOne`, which puts the mark **exactly at** `honouredUntil` so the new condition's boundary is pinned at the notch `judge` still answers `.entitled` at.
- **The high-water mark still only ever moves forward** — `theHighWaterMarkOnlyEverMovesForward`, unchanged and green. It was worth checking rather than assuming: an earlier draft of this fix clamped the mark against the arriving claim's `issuedAt` unconditionally, which fails that test outright and would have killed the replay guard for every claim more than five minutes old. That draft was abandoned for exactly that reason.
- **A server saying more time has passed is still believed over this Mac's own clock** — `aServerSayingMoreTimeHasPassedIsBelievedOverThisMacsOwnClock`, unchanged and green, and it is the test that decided one of the two open questions below.
- **The stale-mark, relaunch and offline-answer paths** — `aStaleMarkIsOverruledByOneFreshObservation`, `theMarkSurvivesARelaunchSoTheRollbackIsStillRefused`, `aGatedCapabilityIsAnsweredOfflineFromTheCachedClaim` — all unchanged and green.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:

- **The failure, traced before anything was designed, because the headline understates it.** Two values are poisoned, not one. `recordServerClock` had a guard against an instant going *down* and none against how fast it may go *up*, so one header wrote a year into `lastServerObservation`; `effectiveNow` derives its trustworthy instant from that and `persistMark` writes it into `StoredEntitlement.observedServerTime`. That is the mark, and a high-water mark only ever rises. But the **claim** is poisoned with it — a gateway a year ahead signs `issued_at` a year ahead — and `adopt`'s replay guard (`current.issuedAt > claim.issuedAt`) then *preferred the future-dated claim over every real one the gateway signed afterwards, forever*. So the state is self-consistent and invisible while the gateway is wrong, and becomes permanent the moment it is put right. Fixing only the mark leaves a Mac answering `.clockUnusable` instead of `.lapsed`; fixing only the claim leaves the mark killing whatever replaces it. Both had to move.
- **The direction chosen, and the one refused.** The obvious fix is to bound the mark by the *local* clock, and it is wrong in a way that is easy to miss because the mark is a floor and a ceiling on its advance looks harmless. Traced: a Mac whose clock is permanently set back never lets the mark rise past `localNow`, so after one relaunch the mark is a year behind, `serverNow()` is rolled back with it, and a lapsed claim reads live indefinitely — which is precisely the attack the mark exists to stop, handed over by the fix for a different problem. The clock used here is **monotonic elapsed time**, which is neither the local clock nor the gateway's: it is the only reading in the system that no party can set. That costs the accuracy of an absolute reference, and the cost is real — see the residual below.
- **A rate bound cannot detect a constant offset, so a bound alone can never be the whole fix.** It needs an anchor, and the first observation of a process has none; a gateway consistently wrong passes every rate check trivially. That is why the repair exists, and it is worth stating flatly because the ticket's own proposal was the bound alone.
- **The repair's cost, which is a security/availability trade and is made here deliberately rather than deferred.** A response the Mac's own owner can author can now lower the mark: serve a captured, correctly signed claim old enough that the mark sits past its window, and the mark resets to that claim's issue time. That needs TLS to the gateway broken from inside the Mac — the same person who can read and write the Keychain the mark and the refresh token both live in, which is the bound `adopt`'s doc comment already recorded and which this does not widen. **It is not the case the mark exists to stop**, which is somebody moving their Mac's clock in System Settings: that moves `serverNow()`, which is excluded from the mark, and it cannot on its own make a claim old enough for the repair to fire. Weighed against the alternative — a paying user's Mac permanently refusing every gated capability after an honest ops mistake, unfixable by reinstalling, signing out or signing back in, because the Keychain item survives all three — this is the right way round.
- **Capping rather than refusing is the half that keeps the bound from being a different bug.** A gateway that steps its own clock forward is ahead, not wrong. Refusing such an observation freezes this client's idea of server time behind it *permanently*, because every later response is ahead of the same frozen projection; capping absorbs 300 s per response, so a real correction is taken up within two. **"And a year never is" stood here and was false** (review, finding 2): the cap is spent per *response*, not per second, and it compounds — a year is 31_536_000 / 300 = **105,120 responses** and the amount that actually matters, enough to reach the end of a claim's own window, is 345_900 / 300 = **1,153**. Those numbers are what make capping safe rather than an absolute refusal, and a client that made 1,153 requests against a gateway stuck a year ahead would get there; what stops that being permanent is the repair, not the bound. The true mechanism was already stated three paragraphs on, which is how a false sentence survived beside its own correction.
- **§3.5's offset is deliberately left unbounded, and this was written both ways before the tests decided it.** Capping it too removes a transient: `EntitlementService` judges at the *later* of `serverNow()` and the mark, so one header a year out refuses every gated capability until the next response arrives, and a bad host in a healthy fleet does that intermittently. But the refusal is bounded and cures itself — the refusal is what starts the refresh, and `recordServerClock` runs on every response including a failing one — while capping the offset makes `serverNow()` stop meaning "the server's clock as last reported", which is the frame token expiry is reasoned in and which `aServerSayingMoreTimeHasPassedIsBelievedOverThisMacsOwnClock` holds by name. That test failed against the capped version, which is how the question was settled rather than argued.
- **"The offset is never written down" was false, and the true reason the conclusion survives is a different one** (review, finding 3). It reaches the Keychain: `refreshedSnapshot` writes `receivedAt: serverNow()`, `WireTokenResponse.tokens(emailAddress:receivedAt:)` turns that into `accessTokenExpiresAt`, and the token store persists it — so a header a year out is written down as a session that expires a year late. What makes *that* non-permanent is that **a token has a second party and the mark does not**: the gateway refuses a token this client believes is live as `401 auth.token_expired`, and §3.3's reactive refresh rewrites the record from a fresh, correct `Date`. Nothing on the network ever disagrees with the mark, which is precisely why the mark needed a bound and a repair and the offset needs neither. The distinction is the reason, and it was not stated.
- **A second, real consequence of one bad header, found by a fixture and worth writing down:** the proactive token refresh reasons in server time too, so a header a year out also makes the access token look a year expired and the client renews the session before it will send anything. Two of the new tests carry a long `expiresIn` for that reason, stated at each.
- **The two layers overlap, and the shape of the overlap changed under this branch's own last commit — which is finding 1 and is worth reading twice, because it is a hole in the rule rather than in the work.** At `347a359` only `aGatewayClockSteppedForwardIsCaughtUpRatherThanRefusedForever` isolated the bound: under R1, with the forward bound removed entirely, `oneWrongDateHeaderCannotRunTheObservationPastWhatRealTimeAllows` still passed, because the repair caught the poisoned mark at the very next `adopt`. Then `9a980d7` tightened that test's assertion from `<=` to `==` for an unrelated reason — the race below — and **that made it bound-isolating**. Re-measured at `a5ef9b3`, R1 and R2 are each killed by **two** tests, the second being the one this entry had recorded as surviving them. **The carry proof could not have seen it.** It hashed the mutants' *killers* and the mutated `Sources` tree, both unchanged; the test whose kill status moved was one the proof had no reason to look at, because every carry condition in `WORKFLOW.md` step 5 is about killers a mutant already has and none can see a test that *became* one. The direction was favourable — a figure that understated coverage — which is luck rather than a property of the method. Filed as **SONNY-369** against step 5; nothing is owed from this branch beyond the re-measurement, which is what the battery figure below is.
- **A test that passed under `--filter` and failed under the whole suite, which is the pitfall to carry forward.** The bound is spent *per response*, so an exact assertion about the mark is an assertion about how many responses have happened — and `decision(for:)` starts a detached refresh, which is a response the test did not write. Under the filter it had not landed when the store was read; under the suite's load it had, and the mark read 660 against a bound of 360. The fix is not a wider bound: the mark is read at the one point where the count is fixed, `awaitPendingRefresh()` settles the refresh the refusal starts, and the last assertion is stated as the property because by then the count includes a response the test did not write. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s rule about never sleeping-then-asserting on something another task is racing you to — here the racing task is one the code under test starts on its own.

Verification:
- **Mutation battery: 8 mutants, 8 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed**, measured at `a5ef9b3` — the head that merges, nothing carried (`scripts/mutate .build/sonny344/plan.txt`, report kept at `.build/mutate/260ca25-20260830T161553-37817/report.log` (the directory keeps the name the run wrote it under, which is the pre-rebase stamp)). One mutant per decision that carries the property, rather than one per changed file: the bound removed (R1), the bound refusing instead of capping (R2), the replay guard never yielding (R3), the mark kept rather than reset (R4), the observation left in place (R5), the anchor left in place (R6), the reset boundary loosened by a year (R7), and the reset boundary loosened by one notch (R8, added by the review's finding 4). The suite command was scoped to `--filter "Entitlement|SonnyBackendClient"`, which can only ever *under*-count kills, and every mutant was killed inside it anyway. `git merge-base --is-ancestor a5ef9b3 HEAD` exits 0.
- **The review ran a battery of its own and two of its mutants are recorded here rather than only in the round.** Its P5 — `>` loosened to `>=` in `markKeptOrReset` — **survived**, and it is not equivalent: `judge` answers `.entitled` at exactly `honouredUntil`, so a mark on that instant belongs to a live claim and resetting there rolls the mark back by the claim's whole 96-hour window, which is the one direction it must never move in. The identical boundary one function away was already pinned by name, which makes its absence here a gap rather than a judgement. It is R8 above and `theBoundaryOfTheResetIsTheLastHonouredInstant` is what kills it. Its P8 also survived and **is** equivalent — `highWater` could never be `nil`, so the branch handling that case was unreachable and the doc sentence describing what a `nil` mark would mean was a claim about a state that cannot occur. Both are gone; `highWater` is a plain `max` now.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The residual the monotonic clock cannot close, stated as the honest bound rather than a gap.** A rate bound needs an anchor, and a persisted mark carries no monotonic reading across a relaunch — the app may genuinely have been closed for a year — so the first observation of a process is taken as reported. That residual is what the repair covers, and the repair only fires when the gateway hands this Mac a claim, so a Mac that is poisoned and then never online again stays poisoned. Closing it needs a time source that survives a reboot and is not the user's, which this Mac does not have.
- **A gateway whose clock is *behind* is not addressed here and is a different failure.** It signs claims that are already expired by real time, so the mark refuses them — fail-closed, self-curing the moment the gateway is fixed, and never written down. Named so the next reader does not mistake its absence for an oversight.
- **No manual test is owed.** Nothing here has a surface; every path is exercised by the suite, and the one user-visible sentence (`EntitlementCopy`'s `.lapsed`) is unchanged.

One session, one branch, cut from `main` at `65a7fc9` (PR #168's merge), not rebased. **Every figure below is measured at `a0cf3c5`**, this branch's last implementation commit; the docs commit carrying this entry sits on top of it and changes only this file. Four files change (`git diff --name-only 65a7fc9 a0cf3c5 | wc -l` → 4): the stop hook, a new selftest beside it, `WORKFLOW.md`, and `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md`. Nothing under `Sources/`, `Tests/`, `server/` or `scripts/` is touched — four other lanes were live in those.

**SONNY-361 — the check now fires, and the half that decides that is the committed one.** `scripts/changelog-order` passed on `main` and ran only when somebody thought to run it. `WORKFLOW.md` step 7 named it as owed verification, which is the standing `scripts/warnings` has and is a different thing from a check that fires. The `.claude/` stop hook now runs it whenever **this branch** has touched the changelog — uncommitted in the working tree, **or committed since the merge-base with `main`** — before it considers the Swift suite. The obvious implementation is the working-tree reading alone, and it would have fired essentially never on the branches that matter: step 7 has the entry written *and committed* before the PR opens, so on the last turn of the branch whose entry is at issue the tree is clean. That is not an edge of the trigger, it is the common case, and the selftest holds it as its own arm.

**A finding is held rather than thrown**, in a variable every exit from the hook emits, because the Swift fast path (`git status --porcelain -- '*.swift'` empty → `exit 0`) is the path a docs-only branch takes every single time — and a docs-only branch is exactly the branch that writes an entry. Held, not thrown, also means the suite still runs on the same turn instead of being displaced by the block.

**It respects the battery state rather than working around it.** A live battery still skips everything and the message now names both checks instead of the suite alone; an abandoned mutant still blocks ahead of everything. Skipping the changelog check during a live battery is a decision and is written into the hook: the check compiles nothing and would be safe to run, but the answer this hook gives during a battery is that it has said nothing about the branch at all, one check running would make that answer false, and a battery cannot start over a dirty tree anyway — so an entry being written mid-battery is not a state this can be in.

**Every way it can fail to produce an answer says so, on three channels.** A missing or non-executable script, an `exit 1` refusal to measure, and the live-battery skip each go to the session on stderr, to the user as a `systemMessage`, and to `.git/battery-skips.log` through the existing `battery_journal` — the only one of the three that outlives the terminal. `exit 1` blocks nothing, because "cannot measure" is neither a pass nor a finding.

**The guard is shown flagging what it names.** `.claude/hooks/verify-tests-before-stop-selftest.sh` builds a throwaway git repository per case — a real `main` of merge commits in GitHub's subject form, real copies of `scripts/changelog-order` and `scripts/lib/battery-state.sh`, and the real hook — and drives the hook through its real command line and its real stdin payload: **18 arms, 0 failures, exit 0** (`.claude/hooks/verify-tests-before-stop-selftest.sh`, `a0cf3c5`). `scripts/changelog-order selftest` is **12 cases, 0 failures, exit 0** at the same head, and the tool over this repository's own changelog is **140 entries, exit 0** (this entry makes it 141).

**A passing selftest proves nothing until its arms are shown to fail, so seven mutants were run against it** in a scratch copy of the three files, never in the tree: the committed half of the trigger deleted, the finding held but never emitted, the live message reverted to naming the suite alone, the skip notice silenced, the first-entry exemption defeated, the journal call removed, and the `systemMessage` removed. **Six were killed and one was not.** The mutant that survived was the silenced skip notice, because every assertion matched stdout and stderr as one string and the `systemMessage` still carried the same words — a hook that stopped telling the session anything, passing. The assertions are channel-aware now (`both` / `err` / `out`) with the journal asserted separately, and all seven are killed at `a0cf3c5`; the control run over the unmutated file is 18 arms, 0 failures.

The first wording of the two-check message dropped that phrase. Checked rather than assumed, and proved in both directions at `7f67e53`: with the phrase, `scripts/mutate selftest` is **332 `PASS` lines, exit 0** (`grep -c '    PASS  '`); with the wording that dropped it, **331 and exit 1**, on `FAIL  and says the suite was not run — output did not contain [test suite was NOT run]`.
