### Branch: fix/one-lane-does-not-own-a-shared-path
Status: complete — SONNY-355 and SONNY-356 Done; written 2026-08-29 before the PR opened
Date: 2026-08-29
Tickets: **SONNY-355** (the documented test-database container name and port are fixed, so two server lanes collide on one database) and **SONNY-356** (a battery's report goes to a caller-chosen path, so two lanes redirecting to the same file lose a run's whole evidence). A container name and a host port are machine-wide; `/tmp/mutate.log` is machine-wide; neither was written by anyone who was wrong at the time, and both stopped being right when the wave model arrived. **Every figure below is measured at `85bfd88`**, this branch's implementation commit, over a clean tree; the docs commit above it changes only this file. The sweep that found it was the union of the container name and the port rather than the command — `git grep -l 'sonny-gw-db' 711c92f | wc -l` → **7** and `git grep -l '55433' 711c92f | wc -l` → **9**, union **9 files**, of which four are outside the command grep: `WORKFLOW.md`, `server/package.json` (the `test:db` fallback), `server/test/support/database.ts` (the fallback constant), and `Sources/MacAgent/Resources/Fonts/InstrumentSerif-Regular.ttf`, where those five bytes occur inside a font. A wider engine costs you a false positive to read past; a narrower one costs you the file that most needed changing.

**Nothing in the new setup is a placeholder, and that is the design rather than a flourish.** `LANE="$(basename "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)")"` makes the container name unique by construction, and `-p 0:5432` asks Docker for any free host port which `docker port` reads back into `DATABASE_URL`. A recipe with `<your-port-here>` in it is one fixed pair again the first time somebody pastes it unedited — which is how the pair being replaced came to be in four places. Measured live: with another lane's `sonny-gw-db-358` already up on 55458, this lane's `docker run … -p 0:5432` was handed **32768**, and `npm run test:db` against it reported **816 passed (816)**, exit 0, with both containers running throughout. That is the collision condition SONNY-355 was filed for, reproduced deliberately and passing.

**The symptom is written into the documentation because it names nothing on its own.** All five places now say it: a suite-wide connection failure — `Test Files 11 failed | 20 passed` with `Connection terminated unexpectedly`, and a fresh `initdb` in `docker logs` inside that run's window — is another lane's container, not a defect in the branch under test. Discard the run and re-run against your own. Two of the five also carry the quieter direction, which is not ruled out and is worse: two lanes on one live database can produce a **pass** that leaned on rows the other lane wrote, and nothing in the output says so either.

**`npm run test:db`'s fallback to `localhost:55433` is deliberately kept**, because a session that sets nothing still has to land somewhere and a named somewhere beats a guessed one. What changed is that it is no longer what the documentation tells you to start — it is described everywhere as right for a lone session and as the collision itself the moment a second lane runs. `server/test/support/database.ts`'s doc comment said "the container `CLAUDE.md` documents", which this branch would have made false, so it says what it now is instead; the constant and the guard around it are untouched.

The changelog's own copy of the command is **not** touched: a merged entry is a dated record of what was true when it was written.

**The documentation half of SONNY-355 gets no selftest arm, and this is that stated plainly rather than left to be inferred.** Nothing it changes lives in `scripts/`. Five prose statements agreeing with each other is not a property a shell harness can assert, and a mechanical check for it — a grep asserting the same five lines appear in five files — would be a check that rots the first time one of them is legitimately reworded, which is the fate `CLAUDE.md` records for SONNY-64's guard. **One incidental fix, since it was in the banner being rewritten:** the box was 81 and 82 code points on different lines and had been since it was written. Every line is 81 now, asserted by measuring the rendered output rather than by counting in the source (`npx tsx -e '…' | uniq widths` → `[81]`).

**SONNY-356 — the tree was never at risk and the evidence always was.** `scripts/mutate`'s lock is per-worktree deliberately, so two lanes running batteries at once is the intended state; their *output* had no such protection. A battery's report had exactly one sink, the caller's stdout, so two lanes redirecting to one path meant the second `>` truncated the first without a word — and a short report cannot be told from a run that printed little. SONNY-350's lane lost one that way and re-ran a seven-mutant battery to get it back. The fix is that the run owns a copy no caller can name: `.build/mutate/<sha>-<stamp>-<pid>/report.log`, both streams, named in the header **before** the first suite starts and again in the summary. A caller's own redirect still works and is still nobody's business; it is simply no longer the only copy. `scripts/warnings` gets the same treatment at `.build/warnings-runs/<sha>-<stamp>-<pid>/report.log` — it runs about 95s and prints a number a changelog entry will quote, which is exactly the shape of tool a session sends to a file.

**The pid in the directory name is not decoration.** The stamp has one-second resolution, so two runs starting inside one second in one checkout would share a directory and the second would append onto the first's report. That is rarer than the cross-lane case and is the same loss. It is asserted against the pid the run itself prints rather than by racing two runs together, because a race is not a check — and the racing version was tried first and passed for the wrong reason, since two stand-in batteries happen to land a second apart.

**The hazard the fix itself introduces, which would have made it a net loss left open.** A tee sits in the script's process group, so a signal aimed at the group reaches it too; kill the tee and the next write to the fifo is a broken pipe, and SIGPIPE's default action kills the process outright — **including a write from inside the EXIT trap, which is where every restore, release and warning in `scripts/mutate` lives**. `trap '' INT TERM` before the tee `exec`s is what prevents it. Measured on this same script with only that trap removed and a stand-in that TERMs the tee mid-mutant: **exit 141 instead of 0**, and a report ending at the last line printed before the kill with no summary under it. **What did *not* go wrong in that measurement is recorded beside it**, because claiming more for a guard than it does is how the next reader stops believing the file: `cleanup()` writes nothing on that path, so the tree was restored and the lock released before `assert_intended_exit`'s own `printf` took the signal. The loss is the evidence and the exit code — a run that ended early with nothing anywhere saying it had. Ctrl-C alone is survivable either way, because bash already ignores SIGINT in a background job of a non-interactive shell, which is precisely why trusting that was not enough.

**Both new guards were proved by removing them, and the arms that hold each one are named rather than counted.** `scripts/mutate selftest` at `85bfd88` → **322 checks passing, 0 failures, exit 0** (`grep -c '    PASS  '` over the run; **307** at `711c92f`, measured by running that revision's own copy from `scripts/` so the stop-hook arm resolves — run from a scratch directory it fails on the hook's path and reports 291, which is the copy's location and not a defect). Three negative controls, each built by one `sed` against the shipped script and nothing else:

- **the tee's `trap '' INT TERM` removed** → `the battery still finishes and exits 0 — expected [0], got [141]` and `and the report is whole rather than ending where the tee died`. The tree check in that arm passes in both versions and says so in its own name; a lock check would too, so there is not one.
- **the report pointed at one fixed path** → `the report is at [/tmp/mutate-nc-shared.log], not under .build/`, `does not carry this run's pid`, `both runs reported […] — one of them has lost its evidence`, and `the first run's report changed underneath it`. That last check is a byte comparison for a measured reason: a shared path is *rewritten* by the second run, so the first report is non-empty and says "Every mutant was killed" too — a check for either of those passes against the defect.
- **the pid dropped from the directory name** → `does not carry this run's pid`, and on that run the two batteries happened to land in one second, so `both runs reported […]` and `the first run's report changed underneath it` fired as well. The pid assertion is the deterministic one; the other two are the real behaviour and depend on the second boundary.

`scripts/warnings selftest` at `85bfd88` → **76 checks, 0 failures**, exit 0 (**67** at `711c92f`). Two negative controls: **one fixed shared report path** → 7 failures including `no report at […]`, `the report is at [/tmp/warnings-nc-shared.log]`, `two runs left two report directories — expected [2], got [1]`; **the pid dropped** → `does not carry this run's pid`. Its two-report arm counts directories rather than naming which sorts first, because which one sorts first depends on whether the runs straddled a second boundary.

**One arm's fixture had to be corrected to exercise the real path.** `scripts/mutate`'s selftest repository carried no `.gitignore`, so `git check-ignore -q ".build/mutate"` answered no and **every battery arm took the temp-directory fallback** — the branch that actually runs in this repository was never the one the selftest exercised, and each arm leaked a `mktemp` directory nothing cleaned. The seed now commits `.gitignore` with `.build/`.

**The selftest arms are what this branch has instead of a mutation battery, and that is a decision rather than a gap.** The changed code is two shell harnesses, which no mutant plan in this repository can reach — `scripts/mutate` cannot mutate itself, by construction and by lock. The three negative controls above are the stronger method in any case: each removes the actual guard and watches the actual arm go red, which is the defect that would happen rather than one a plan chose.

**A live instance of this repository's own zero-that-looks-like-good-news rule, recorded because it happened here.** Verifying the five documentation sites, `git grep -n 'sonny-gw-db' -- CLAUDE.md server/README.md …` answered **nothing at all** — no output, and it reads exactly like "the old name is gone everywhere". It was run from inside `server/`, where those repository-root-relative pathspecs match no file; the same command from the root answers 13 lines. That is the second sighting of this exact shape (the first is in `CLAUDE.md`, from SONNY-134's reviewer), reached the same way: a construct silently answered a question nobody asked, in the reassuring direction.

**PR #168's review round, appended 2026-08-29. Six findings; F1 blocked merge, and all six are taken.** **Every figure in this section is measured at `34af7e8`**, the fix-round head — the docs commit above it changes only this file. The figures earlier in this entry stand for `85bfd88` and are deliberately not restated except where a finding moved one; `git merge-base --is-ancestor` exits 0 for both at this head.

**F1 (blocking, fixed) — the hazard this branch introduced reached further than the guard it shipped with, and the guard was arrived at by the wrong method.** `trap '' INT TERM` on the tee covers TERM and nothing else that matters: bash already sets `SIG_IGN` on SIGINT and SIGQUIT for a background job of a non-interactive shell, so those two held with or without it. **HUP did not** — and a group SIGHUP, which is what a closing terminal or a dropped connection sends, is the likeliest way a forty-minute battery actually ends. Reproduced here 3 of 3 against `main` and 3 of 3 against `85bfd88`, with a stand-in that HUPs the tee and the harness mid-mutant: `main` exits **129**, releases the lock and prints the interruption; `85bfd88` exits **141** with `.git/mutate.lock` **still held**. **This paragraph claimed `cleanup()` is never entered and the mutant left applied, 3 of 3, as the settled account; cycle 2's F2 below re-measured it and that is one of two outcomes, not the one.** Exit 141 and the stranded lock hold in every construction; whether the restore runs depends on the interleaving. The worst case is reachable — it is SONNY-347's own failure mode arriving through the fix for SONNY-356 — and it is not what always happens. The table in F2 is the live figure; this sentence is left as the dated claim it was. **The fix is two layers, because the question the review asked has two answers.** The enumeration now sits above `report_begin` in `scripts/mutate`, one row per route a signal reaches a background process in this group by, each saying whether the EXIT trap survives it: INT and QUIT (bash ignores them for background jobs anyway; trapped here so the property does not depend on a shell behaviour nothing asserts), TERM and HUP (not ignored; trapped), TSTP/TTIN/TTOU (stop rather than terminate, whole group together, nothing lost, deliberately not trapped), **any other catchable terminating signal sent to the group** (kills the tee), and **KILL** (cannot be caught by anyone). The last two rows are why a longer token list is not the answer, and they are the second layer: **this shell now ignores SIGPIPE itself**, from the end of `report_begin`, so a dead tee costs a failed write instead of the process and the EXIT trap always completes. Measured against a SIGKILLed tee — the case no ignore-list reaches — the fixed script releases the lock and leaves the tree clean; with that one line removed it exits 141 with the lock held. Ignoring SIGPIPE must not travel into the suite or this harness would change what it measures, so `run_suite` resets it in a subshell before the exec, checked rather than assumed: `( trap - PIPE; exec perl -e '...' )` reports DEFAULT where the same probe without the reset reports IGNORE. Writes in `cleanup` and `assert_intended_exit` carry `|| true`, because with SIGPIPE ignored a failed `printf` under `set -e` would abandon the release just as surely as the signal did.

**Four negative controls on F1, two per tool, each one `sed` against the shipped script, all re-run at the final tree.** `scripts/mutate` with HUP dropped from the tee's list → exactly the two SIGHUP assertions (`expected [0], got [1]`, and the report missing `Every mutant was killed`), with the SIGTERM half of the same arm still passing, correctly, because TERM is still trapped. `scripts/mutate` with the shell's SIGPIPE ignore removed → `the battery died on a broken pipe when the report writer was killed` and `the lock was left held`. `scripts/warnings` with HUP dropped → `expected [2], got [1]` and its output missing `1 warning(s)`. `scripts/warnings` with the SIGPIPE ignore removed → `the run died on a broken pipe`, exit 141.

**Three things about those arms were got wrong first and are recorded because each is a way an arm can lie.** **(a) A failing signal arm poisoned every arm after it.** It leaves a mutant in the fixture and a lock in `.git/`, so every battery following it in that one throwaway repository fails for *that* reason — 96 failures where 4 were the finding. Both signal arms now restore the fixture after asserting. **(b) An arm passed vacuously.** `scripts/warnings`' SIGKILL arm looked up the tee's pid and killed it; on an empty lookup `kill -9 ""` is a no-op, the run finishes normally, the lock comes off for the ordinary reason and the arm passes having tested nothing — the layer-2 control exited **0**. Both tools' arms now assert they found something to kill first. **(c) The first HUP arms raced two signals and were flaky.** They HUPed the tee *and* the harness and asserted exit 129, which is a bet on which delivery bash processes first; under a concurrent server suite both failed — `expected [129], got [0]` in one tool and `got [2]` in the other — on a tree whose fix was sound. That is this repository's own never-sleep-then-assert-on-a-race rule, broken inside the fix for a different defect. **The arms now signal the tee only**, which loses nothing: the tee's death is the whole discriminator, and the end-to-end group-signal behaviour is the measurement two paragraphs above, where a wall-clock race belongs. Re-run afterwards under deliberate load — six spinning cores plus the server suite — **330 passing, 0 failures**.

**One arm's discriminating power was measured to vary, and it is written down rather than trusted.** `scripts/warnings`' SIGKILL arm asserts both that the run does not die on a broken pipe and that the run lock came off. Only the first is reliable: without layer 2 this shell dies at its next write, which is exit **141** every time, but whether the *lock* is also stranded depends on where that write falls relative to `release_lock`, and `scripts/warnings`' `cleanup()` writes nothing — so it sometimes falls after. The lock assertion failed on one control build and passed on another against the same defect. `scripts/mutate`'s equivalent fails reliably, because its `cleanup()` prints before releasing. The arm keeps both checks and its comment says which one carries it.

Final counts at cycle 1's head: `scripts/mutate selftest` **330 passing, 0 failures, exit 0** (322 at `85bfd88`, 307 at `711c92f`); `scripts/warnings selftest` **83 checks, 0 failures, exit 0** (76 and 67). Cycle 2's counts are at the end of this entry.

**F2 (record corrected, and this is the finding rather than the correction) — two careful measurements disagreed, and the answer was neither of them.** Cycle 1's entry said `cleanup()` is never entered under a group SIGHUP, with `sample.swift` left carrying the mutant, 3 of 3. The reviewer, with the marker as cleanup's *first* statement, got the opposite 6 of 6: marker written, tree clean, mutant gone. **Both are true, and the interleaving picks between them.** Re-measured at 12 runs against the pre-fix script (`85bfd88` and `28b37f5` are byte-identical on `scripts/mutate`), with the instrumentation proved in the invocation shape it runs in — a positive control under SIGTERM, which that script traps, writes the marker and restores every time:

| what the stand-in did | exit | cleanup entered | tree | lock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kill the tee, wait 1s, then HUP the harness | 141, 4/4 | **never** | **DIRTY, mutant applied** | held |
| kill the tee and HUP the harness with no wait | 141, 4/4 | yes | clean | held |
| kill the tee only | 141, 4/4 | yes | clean | held |

**So exit 141 and the stranded lock reproduce in every construction, 12 of 12; whether the restore runs depends on how the tee's death and the HUP interleave.** The worst outcome is reachable and is not what always happens — cycle 1 stated the worst as the settled account, which is a different wrong number in the permanent record and not the safe direction. The same 12 runs against the fixed script: cleanup entered, tree clean, lock released, 12 of 12. What made this findable rather than arguable is that cycle 1's two controls proved the marker *mechanism* worked in a different build; they could not prove it was in the right place in *this* invocation, and that is a different claim.

**F1 (ruled: the arm comes out) — the property is proven, the packaging is not.** Layer 1 does what it says: the same fixture run standalone against a build with HUP removed from the tee's ignore list kills the report writer **5 runs of 5**, and does not under the shipped script. `scripts/mutate --help` has that reproduction under "Demonstrating layer 1", runnable by anyone. What could not be made to work is the same check *inside* the selftest harness, and after several attempts it is out of both files rather than shipped flaky: **a check that fails at random is a check people learn to skip**, which is how SONNY-64's guard stopped existing. **And the dependence IS isolated, by the one measurement taken after the chase was called off — a different question with a yes/no answer: does the PROPERTY hold under `nohup`, as against does the ARM fire there.** It does, and for a stronger reason than layer 1. `nohup` sets SIGHUP to `SIG_IGN`, an ignored disposition survives fork **and** exec, and the tee is not a shell and never resets it — so under `nohup` the tee ignores HUP whatever this script traps. Measured with a real group signal against a battery in a process group of its own (`perl -e 'setpgrp(0,0); exec @ARGV'`, then `kill -HUP -<pgid>` mid-mutant):

| | foreground process group | under `nohup` |
|---|---|---|
| shipped | exit **129**, lock **released**, tree clean, the interruption recorded in the report (3/3) | tee survives, the battery is **not interrupted at all** and completes, exit **2**, 37-line report (2/2) |
| HUP dropped from the tee's list | exit **141**, lock **HELD**, 23-line report, no interruption (2/2) | **indistinguishable from shipped** (2/2) |

**So layer 1 carries the foreground case, and `nohup` covers the same ground for free** — a battery launched the way this project launches long ones is protected either way, which is why an arm can only discriminate where `nohup` is absent, and why three attempts at one failed: it fired foreground **5 of 5** and never under `nohup`, **7 of 7**. Two probes that misled the earlier attempts are now explained rather than merely eliminated: `trap -p HUP` under `nohup` reporting no ignore, and a `python3` SIG_DFL-then-exec probe reporting default, are both true of **bash**, which resets it for itself, and neither says anything about the `tee` bash execs. `ps -ww` was never the cause — the arm fires without it. Cycle 1's blocking finding is closed on this evidence; the arm is **SONNY-367**'s, at high priority, and the reproduction is in `scripts/mutate --help`. Three attempts at determinism were made and each reported as achieved before the next disproved it, which is the stop-and-report trigger reached and passed.

**F3 (fixed, and armed in both tools) — the two layers left a hole that reaches the tee through the caller's own stdout rather than through any signal aimed at the group.** `scripts/mutate <plan> | head -3`: `head` exits, the tee's write raises SIGPIPE, and the file `--help` promises no caller can take away is truncated — measured at a **23-line** report with no summary against **38** unpiped. `PIPE` is in the tee's ignore list now: 38 lines and the summary either way, exit 0. It is a row the first enumeration simply did not have, and it is in there now. Both selftests carry an arm; removing `PIPE` from the list fails exactly those arms in each.

**F4 (closed, and swept rather than patched) — the three tee-signal arms could pass vacuously.** An `awk` that matches nothing makes `kill` a no-op and every downstream check passes having signalled nothing; the same search matching something *else* looks identical from outside. Both shapes had already been found twice on this branch and not carried across. **The search is gone rather than tightened**: `report_begin` exports `MUTATE_REPORT_TEE_PID`, the arms signal that exact pid, and each records the pid it signalled *and* a verdict that names the process — `yes`, `no`, or `not-a-tee:<ps line>` — so a wrong target is reported rather than passing. `scripts/warnings` has no in-process channel to its arm, so it narrows its match to `$3 == "tee"` and asserts what it found before killing it.

Tickets: **SONNY-358** (a revoked provider-side user can never be owed a revocation again, so a reopened-then-closed account leaves live sessions) — the remainder PR #164 closed on one of its return paths and deliberately left open on the other, by founder decision of 2026-08-29. Reviewed by: fresh session per `WORKFLOW.md` step 7, two cycles. **Cycle 1** raised F1 (this branch's headline door-A reproduction ran against the previous invocation's schema), F2 (a changelog claim of a pin that did not exist), F4 (a false sentence about test coverage) as blocking, plus F3 and F5 as non-blocking precision; all five are addressed above and F3's remainder is **SONNY-365**. **Cycle 2** blocked nothing: it reproduced this branch's battery from the committed tree with no wrapper — **11 mutants, 9 killed, 2 survived, 0 unattributed**, same baseline — confirmed every cycle-1 verdict, and found the two killer-list changes to be this branch's own F1 fix visible inside the instrument that exposed it: R1 gains the door-A test it could not name before, and R6 correctly loses it, because R6 touches only the supersession arm and the door-A reproduction never supersedes. It also tested whether the F2 guard pins the *property* or merely the mutant, with three further mutants over the whole `WHEN`: one dies partly on the new guard, so the guard covers more than it was built from, and the survivor was **measured rather than assumed** — it does change the column, but `OWED_PREDICATE` consults the stamp only after `account_closed OR superseded_at`, so no reader in this codebase can observe the difference. The guard pins the only observable direction.

**The ticket asked a design question rather than for a patch, and the answer is what the branch mostly is.** PR #164 gave `sonny.identity_provider_user.provider_session_revoked_at` a single meaning — no revocation is outstanding for this id — and kept it true with migration 0014's trigger, which clears the stamp whenever the identity **observes** the id again. That closes every route on which the user comes back through `resolve()`, and `resolve()` has exactly one production call site, `POST /v1/auth/email/verify`. The ticket's own framing was that `POST /v1/auth/refresh` mints a full session without ever calling it, so a user who returns by refreshing keeps a stale stamp and the second close owes nothing — and that "call the trigger from refresh" is **not** the answer, because leaving refresh alone was only ever safe under an unstated premise: that a recorded revocation implies a dead refresh family. That premise is false, because `ProviderRejected` is recorded as done and the classifier makes any 4xx but 429 `ProviderRejected`.

**Three doors, not one, and the other two were found by this branch rather than given to it.** All three were measured against this tree before anything was written, each ending with `owedRevocationCount` at 0 after a second close and the delete guard letting the account go:

- **A — they come back by refreshing.** The ticket's route, reproduced over real HTTP through the built Fastify app: sign in, close, drain, reopen, `POST /v1/auth/refresh` → 200, close again → owed 0.
- **B — they do not come back at all.** Close, drain, an operator reopens the account, the account is closed again with no sign-in and no refresh in between → owed 0. **No route-level fix could have closed this one**: there is no request to hang one on.
- **C — they come back as somebody else.** Close, drain, reopen, and the next sign-in presents a *different* provider-side user id, so the stamped id is superseded rather than observed → the row reads `superseded: true, revoked: true` and the account owes 0 on a live account, for ever.

**So the decision, stated as the thing a future reader needs and not as a summary of the diff: a recorded revocation is allowed to imply only that the provider was already asked about this id, and that nothing has happened since which would make that answer stale.** It is not allowed to imply that the provider ended the sessions. It cannot be — a mechanism answering 401 or 403 writes the same stamp a real revocation writes — and the moment anything rests on the stronger reading, a lie becomes permanent.

**What follows mechanically is that the stamp is cleared by the events that CREATE an obligation, not by the events that evidence a return.** `OWED_PREDICATE` names exactly two obligations, `i.account_closed` and `pu.superseded_at IS NOT NULL`, so there are exactly two transitions to catch and migration 0015 catches both. Doors A, B and C then stop being three problems: whichever way the user did or did not come back, the **close** that follows owes its own revocation.

**And `POST /v1/auth/refresh` is deliberately untouched.** A refresh serves a live account by construction — `accountForSupabaseUser` refuses a closed or ambiguous one — so it creates no obligation and has nothing to record. Its handler carries that as a comment pointing at the migration, because the next reader of the ticket will look there first. The test that proves the door is closed is still written **on that route**, in `auth.db.test.ts`, rather than moved down to the trigger: a fix one layer down has to be shown closing the door that was open rather than a proxy for it.

Spec sections covered: none directly — this is a defect in the auth gateway's revocation bookkeeping (contract §3.3, §3.6 unchanged).

- **`DELETE /v1/account` still closes, drains its own account, wipes content and answers 204**, and the whole `auth.db.test.ts` and `supersession.db.test.ts` suites pass unchanged apart from the tests this branch added.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **`AFTER UPDATE` with a value-based `WHEN`, never `AFTER UPDATE OF account_closed`.** 0014's F5 gotcha, one table over and in the direction that loses a case rather than gaining one: `UPDATE OF` keys on the *statement's* SET list, and `account_closed` has two writers that disagree about naming it. `sonny.mark_identities_closed` names it; `sonny.derive_identity_closed` is a `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF account_id` trigger that assigns `NEW.account_closed` on a statement that never mentions the column, which is how an identity **moved onto a closed account** changes it. 0005's own header calls that move the third of the three statements that can falsify this flag and the one 0004 forgot. There is a test for exactly it, and mutant R6 — the same line with `OF account_closed` added and nothing else changed — is what proves the test is the reason.
- **Clearing the lease turned out to be load-bearing rather than tidy, and the battery is what said so.** Mutant R5 removes only `revocation_claimed_at = NULL` from the close's clear and is killed by three tests including the refresh reproduction — because the lease the first drain took is minutes old, well inside `sonny.revocation_lease_seconds()` (300), so the re-owed row is invisible to the claim query and the second drain revokes nothing. The expectation going in was that this mutant would survive and need a test written for it; it did not, and the reason is worth keeping: a reopen-and-re-close is fast, so the previous episode's lease is usually still live when the new obligation arrives.
- **Clearing the lease with the stamp costs a bounded duplicate provider call and buys a lease that belongs to its episode.** A drain that claimed a row and died leaves `revocation_claimed_at` set; without clearing it the revocation the second close owes is invisible to the claim query for a whole `sonny.revocation_lease_seconds()`. The cost is the mirror: a drain still inside `signOutAllForUser` when the account closes can have its row re-claimed, and the provider called twice for that user. `drainOwedRevocations`' own docstring already concedes exactly that for any call outliving its lease, and 0014 made the same trade on the come-back arm.
- **The scoping to `superseded_at IS NULL` is the interesting half of the design and is not caution.** A close creates an obligation for the id the identity is *currently* naming — those are the sessions that must stop. An id it already stopped naming had its obligation created once, by the supersession, and a later close says nothing new about it: no session for a superseded id can have been minted through this gateway since, because `accountForSupabaseUser` reads `sonny.identity.supabase_user_id` and refuses one. Drop the clause and a closed account re-owes its whole history on every close. **The first draft of this sentence said every test in the branch still passes and that was false** (PR #167 review, F4) — the reviewer's R4 removes exactly that clause and is killed by 4 tests, one of them this branch's own guard, *does NOT re-owe a superseded id that was already drained when the account later closes*. The test file's comment had it right ("every **other** test in this file") and only this sentence was wrong, in the direction of understating the branch's own coverage.
- **Keeping 0014's observation clear was a decision, not inertia.** With both obligations catching their own transition it is redundant for every route enumerated here. It is kept because it is true on its own terms and because deleting a just-merged fix with no defect behind it is a change nothing asked for. Two writers of one column are a hazard when they can disagree; these cannot — both only ever write NULL, and neither reads the other.
- **A `.db.test.ts` file that does not DROP the schema measures the previous invocation's schema, and this branch's headline reproduction was one of them** (PR #167 review, F1). `up()` applies only *pending* migrations, so on an existing database it is a no-op — and `test/auth.db.test.ts` ran `await up(client)` with no drop. Measured by the reviewer at `d6aab80`, same test, same mutant (0015's `CREATE TRIGGER` deleted), same command: **`1 failed` on a dropped database and `1 passed` on a reused one**, with `pg_trigger` showing the real trigger still installed under the mutant. It is the default workflow rather than a corner case — `npx vitest list --filesOnly` puts that file **first** of the twelve `.db.test.ts` files and all three schema-rebuilders run after it. **What it cost was the reviewer's battery, and the reason this branch's own escaped is the sharper half of the finding.** Their R1 came back `KILLED by 3 test(s)`, all three in `supersession.db.test.ts`, with the door-A test — the one that mutant exists to be caught by — passing. This branch's round-1 R1 reported `KILLED by 4 test(s)` and *did* name the door-A test, because the battery's suite command was a wrapper script kept outside the working tree and that wrapper dropped the schema before invoking vitest. So the implementer had already noticed the gap and routed around it in a file no reviewer could see, instead of fixing it in the file that had it — which is worse than not noticing: the workaround was invisible, uninheritable, and left the defect in the tree for `npm run test:db` and for anybody else's battery. Round 2's wrapper drops nothing, deliberately, so the battery measures whether the fix works rather than whether the harness can compensate for it. The error's direction is a *missed* kill rather than a manufactured one, which is the safe direction; same family as SONNY-305 and SONNY-323 — a correct count above a false evidence line. **Fixed here for this file only; the general form reaches past this branch and is SONNY-366**, filed by the coordinator after this entry first went in without a number. That blank was deliberate: a draft of this bullet cited `SONNY-366` before any such ticket existed, and it was removed — fabricating a ticket id inside a paragraph about false evidence is that paragraph's own failure. The number is cited now because the ticket exists, not because the guess was right. The same shape sits in eight others (`for f in test/*.db.test.ts; do grep -q "DROP SCHEMA" "$f" || echo "$f"; done | wc -l` → 9 before this change, 8 after), it predates this branch, and widening it is a change to eleven files' verification behaviour rather than to this ticket's.
- **The obligation is created correctly and the DISCHARGE has no episode identity, which is a fourth shape this branch does not close** (PR #167 review, F3; **SONNY-365**, high, sequenced with this ticket before SONNY-313). `drainOwedRevocations`' mark-done re-checks whether a row is owed *now* and never whether the provider call it just made covers the obligation that exists *now*, stamping with a `now` captured before its loop began. A drain still inside `signOutAllForUser` when the account is reopened, refreshed and re-closed stamps on the way out and discharges an obligation created after its own call — reproduced by the reviewer against a real database, ending `owed = 0` with the reopen's sessions never revoked. **Not a regression**: 0014 behaves identically, this migration strictly narrows the window, and the lease clear it adds is what makes recovery possible at all, since a second drain inside the window does call the provider again. It qualifies the header's *"whichever way the user did or did not return, the close that follows owes its own revocation"* — true of every route enumerated here and not of that one — and 0014's own generalisation that the conservative direction always happens, which holds only while the account stays open.
- **The whole enumeration rests on an invariant nothing stated: an identity's CURRENT provider-side user id can never be a superseded row.** The reviewer derived it independently and measured 0 violations over 32 rows across 6 databases. It holds by construction of 0014's trigger — the `ON CONFLICT` arm clears `superseded_at` for the id being named — and everything above depends on it: "a refresh succeeds" means "some live identity currently names this id", which under the invariant puts that identity's row on the current side of the close's `superseded_at IS NULL` scoping rather than the skipped side. Break it and the scoping silently starts skipping rows a refresh can still reach. Now stated in the migration header, because an unstated invariant a mechanism rests on is what gets broken by someone who never knew it was load-bearing.
- **`server/test/auth.db.test.ts` flakes under repeated full-suite runs, in two pre-existing ticketed families, and it is not this branch's** — measured rather than asserted, because after F1 the fix round's first full run came back red and the honest question was whether the fix had caused it. **With the F1 fix: 4 full database runs, 2 red, each one test short of 824, both `Error: Test timed out in 5000ms` (SONNY-354's shape) on two DIFFERENT plain `it(...)` tests. Control with only the two `DROP SCHEMA` lines removed and nothing else changed, same machine, same container, same session: 3 full runs, 1 red — a rate-limit assertion, `expected +0 to be 5`, which is SONNY-341's fixed-window shape, with 0 timeouts.** So the file flakes with and without the change, in two different families, and neither failing test touches anything this branch wrote. **A neighbouring lane recorded the same thing independently and it is three entries down in this file**: PR #163's entry reports `npm run test:db` on its own container as *787 passed, 6 failed (793) — every one of the six a `Test timed out in 5000ms` in `auth.db.test.ts`, a file this branch does not modify*, and adds that the pristine tree at `2f36250` fails the same way with a different set. The two remaining green runs on each side both read **824 passed (824)**. `auth.db.test.ts` alone, three consecutive runs with the fix: 40 passed, 40 passed, 40 passed. What this does NOT establish, stated because 4-vs-3 runs cannot: that the change has no effect on the rate. It establishes that the red is not new and not this branch's code, and that the two failing tests are the ones two open tickets already name.
- **A vitest timeout on a plain `it(...)` in `auth.db.test.ts` is counted as a mutation kill, and nothing declares it** — found in this branch's own round-2 battery and reported rather than fixed. R6 came back `KILLED by 2 test(s)`: the real killer, *owes a revocation for an identity MOVED onto a closed account*, and beside it *answers 429 with Retry-After when the per-SOURCE limit is hit* failing with `Error: Test timed out in 5000ms.` — a test whose request path cannot reach migration 0015 at all. That is SONNY-224's manufactured kill, on the server half. `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures` already carries a server-half record (SONNY-335/SONNY-241) whose own reason describes this exact failure, but it declares the wording of `itUnderHangBackstop`'s bound, and the two tests hit here are plain `it(...)` that meet vitest's raw 5000 ms default instead (`grep -n "itUnderHangBackstop" server/test/auth.db.test.ts` → 3 lines: the import and two tests, out of 40). **Deliberately not fixed here**: declaring the bare timeout wording would excuse every vitest timeout including a genuine mutant-induced hang, it needs a measurement of what those tests really cost under load, and it is a change to shared tooling this ticket did not name. R6's verdict stands on its real killer either way.
  - **The route the existing record points at is not closed, and the coordinator's SONNY-354 comment saying it was is corrected on that ticket** (PR #167 cycle 2). This entry never claimed it — the bullet above says the opposite, that nothing declares this shape — and the correction is recorded here so the two documents do not disagree. The record's remedy is migrating a test onto `itUnderHangBackstop`, and **that is a population, not a switch**: `grep -c 'itUnderHangBackstop(' server/test/auth.db.test.ts` → **2** of that file's **40** `it`-sites (`grep -cE '^\s+(it|itUnderHangBackstop)\(' server/test/auth.db.test.ts` → 40); the wider `grep -n` answers 3 lines only because one of them is the import, which is the kind of one-off this repo's counting rule exists for. The reviewer also reports the same timeout in a third file, which this session has not measured and does not restate as its own.
- **The migration round-trip was measured against rows in every state it touches, not an empty database.** Seven `identity_provider_user` rows across five accounts covering live/closed × current/superseded × stamped/unstamped × leased/unleased: `down` leaves the data byte-identical (`diff` of a full column dump, no differences), removes the trigger and function, restores `record_provider_side_user` to 0014's text and the table comment with it, and the behaviour reverts (a close leaves the stamp). `up` again leaves the data byte-identical and the behaviour returns.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **This does not make the stamp trustworthy, and what it does bound is narrower than the first draft said** (PR #167 review, F5). A wrong stamp is re-opened only where a **new obligation** arrives — a reopen and re-close, or a supersession. For the ordinary case, a user who closes their account and never comes back, no transition fires again, `owedRevocationCount` reads 0 and the hard delete goes through exactly as before. "Until the id is next owed, rather than for ever" was true and read as reassurance in the one shape where it delivers nothing; the three copies of it (migration header, `server/README.md`, `revocation.ts`) now say which cases the bound reaches. Narrowing the classifier so that only a response genuinely meaning "the sessions are gone" is recorded as done depends on which mechanism is chosen, and that is **SONNY-313**'s, decided on 2026-08-29 as option 3: leave the mechanism unchosen and report the debt honestly. This ticket closes ahead of it, as sequenced.
- **Access tokens already minted are out of scope and are SONNY-237's** (the denylist), as is JWT secret rotation (SONNY-238).
- **A refresh for a *superseded* id still rotates the family at the provider before this gateway refuses it**, because `deps.provider.refresh()` is called before `accountForSupabaseUser`. That is pre-existing, unchanged here, and sits in SONNY-237's neighbourhood rather than this ticket's; the supersession already makes the id owed, so nothing is lost by it.

The same four lines were misread twice in two days in two opposite directions, and the second misreading — two suites sharing a live database — reached a filed ticket, a changelog entry and `WORKFLOW.md` before anyone opened either file. The detailed incident record is PR #160's entry below (`docs/workflow-carries-the-review-and-verification-rules`, F2 and the grep-count paragraph); this branch adds only the general rule, and the concrete check it states — open one matched file and read what consumes the match — is the one that would have caught both readings.
- **SONNY-360 also gets a `WORKFLOW.md` line, and the decision is stated rather than left open.** A reviewer writing a test and handing it to the implementing lane is a move this process began making routinely during the 2026-08-29 wave and did not make before it, so nothing in step 7 described it. It goes directly under "Reviewers never implement, commit, or push." because it is that bullet's shape rather than an exception to it: the reviewer supplies the scenario and the evidence, the owning session writes the version that lands, and the evidence has to carry the runner's own pass/skip count for the probe. The alternative considered and rejected was leaving it in `CLAUDE.md` alone — but `CLAUDE.md` is where a session learns how to make a claim, and this is a handoff between two sessions, which is step 7's subject.
- **Nothing mechanical is added for skipped tests, and that is a finding rather than a gap.** SONNY-360 asked for the question to be answered either way. A blanket "no skipped tests" check is red on this repository's own documented commands: 12 of the server's test files skip their entire suite when `DATABASE_URL` is absent (`grep -rlE 'describe\.skip|skipIf' server/test | wc -l` → 12 at `711c92f`), which is exactly what `npm test` is documented to do, and the Swift half gates three suites/tests on an environment variable being set (`grep -rnE '@(Test|Suite)\(.*\.(disabled|enabled)\(' Tests | wc -l` → 3 at `711c92f`). A check that fires on the documented command is a check somebody switches off, which is the fate `CLAUDE.md` already records for SONNY-64's guard. The narrower form — assert that a *named* test executed — needs the name from whoever is making the claim, which is precisely the reading the rule asks for, so the guard would cost more than the check it replaces. Nor would a threshold have caught this incident: `1 passed | 1 skipped` is a legitimate reading for any of the twelve files above, and nothing in a count separates that from a probe whose one skip was the entire defect. **The sharpest evidence that skipping is load-bearing is the incident's own test**: it landed at `server/test/supersession.db.test.ts:494`, inside the `describeDb` opened at `:74`, which is `describe.skip` without `DATABASE_URL` — so the test at the centre of this rule is itself skipped by the documented default command, and reads green there.
- **The first draft of this branch committed SONNY-359's own defect, and SONNY-359's own check is what caught it.** The mechanical-guard bullet above originally read "the Swift half carries 12 deliberate `.disabled(` call sites", from `grep -rn '\.disabled(' Tests | wc -l` → 12 at `711c92f`. That count is right and answers a different question: all twelve are SwiftUI's `.disabled()` view modifier appearing as a *string literal* inside source-scanning tests and their doc comments — `#expect(MacAgentSource.count(of: ".disabled(!canSend)", …))` and its neighbours, which grep the product's own source — and not one of them skips a test. Opening one matched file is what showed it, which is exactly the check the new bullet states, and the corrected population is the three environment-gated sites above. It is the whole failure mode in miniature: the number was reproducible, the command sat beside it as the rules require, a reviewer re-running it would have confirmed 12, and the sentence was still false.
- **No guard in the tree reads a skip count today, and one near-miss is worth naming so nobody mistakes it for one.** `scripts/mutate` does read vitest's summary and swift-testing's per-test lines, and it does name `skipped` — six times (`grep -c 'skipped' scripts/mutate` → 6 at `711c92f`), of which five are prose inside comments and the sixth, at `:1317`, is a *boundary verb* in `boundary_re`, the swift-testing line classifier, marking where one event's message ends. None of the six counts anything, and nothing in the script would notice a suite that skipped every test it ran.
- **The new bullets carry one relative reference, and it was verified at this head rather than assumed.** The first says "the write-the-command rule four bullets above", which is `CLAUDE.md:320` counted from `:324` at `711c92f`. It is the same maintenance hazard the section's other relative references carry ("two bullets above", "the rule directly above"); a bullet inserted between them makes it wrong silently. Noted rather than fixed, because renumbering to absolute references would break every existing one and the section is edited in this one place.

Known limitations / deferred scope: none. The mechanical-guard question SONNY-360 raised is answered above as a decision, not deferred.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: none scheduled by this one.

### Branch: fix/identity-reconciles-and-supersession-is-recorded
Status: complete — SONNY-196 and SONNY-230 Done; **SONNY-358 partially fixed here and deliberately left open**, see the stated exception below; written 2026-08-29 before the PR opened, restated after review rounds 1 and 2
Date: 2026-08-29
Tickets: **SONNY-196** (`sonny.identity` never reconciles against Supabase removing unconfirmed identities), **SONNY-230** (a superseded `supabase_user_id` is unrevocable and unrecorded), and — picked up mid-review on the founder's authorisation — **SONNY-358** (a provider-side user id revoked once can never be owed again, which predates this branch), **which this branch closes on one of its two return paths and not the other**. Three tickets, one session, one branch, originally cut from `main` at `2f36250` (PR #158's merge) and **rebased once, onto `7f174e2`** (PRs #161 and #162's merges) as the last branch in the wave. **They are one defect seen from three sides and are fixed as one change to the identity lifecycle**, which is why there is one migration rather than three patches. **Every figure below is measured at `d83e02b`**, the post-rebase head, and **nothing is carried across the rebase.** `server/` moved in the merged range — `git rev-parse 2f36250:server 7f174e2:server` answers `bceb220e…` and `371433b4…`, two different trees, with five files changed under it by PR #163 — so every count this entry cited was taken against a smaller test population, and every one is re-run below rather than translated. The pre-rebase heads it stamped over its life (`cee6676`, `5a4fdb0`, `397e375`, `3fbb53f`, `41370f3`, `b1eed38`) each still resolve in this checkout and each exit 1 under `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD`; they appear below only as dated history and carry no live figure. Touches `server/` only; `Sources/`, `Tests/` and `scripts/` are untouched, so the app half's commands are not in play.

**What was decided, which is most of what SONNY-196 asked for.**

- **The real states of a `supabase_user_id` we hold are three, not two.** *Current* — the last sign-in for this `(provider, subject)` presented it. *Superseded* — a later sign-in for the same `(provider, subject)` presented a different one. *Gone upstream* — the `auth.users` row no longer exists, which is observable only by asking Supabase and which nothing here asks.
- **The reconciliation is the supersession, and it costs nothing.** Supabase removes unconfirmed identities on its own schedule and notifies nobody. What this gateway sees afterwards is the same subject presenting a **different** provider-side user id — which is Supabase reporting the removal, inside the one exchange the sign-in already makes. The gap SONNY-196 describes was never a missing question to ask the provider; it was that there was nowhere to write the answer down, because rule 1's `COALESCE($5, supabase_user_id)` overwrote it.
- **A stale local row is not authoritative and is not trusted for sign-in.** The identity's own `supabase_user_id` is only ever the *current* one; every previous one is kept as history, marked superseded, and owed a revocation from that moment — on a live account, not only on a closed one.
- **A removed provider identity does NOT invalidate our account link**, and this was the genuinely open question the ticket named. The account is keyed on `(provider, subject)`; Supabase pruning an unconfirmed identity is a statement about Supabase's row, not about whether this person still owns that mailbox. Invalidating the link would close someone's account because the provider re-keyed them. What it *does* invalidate is the provider-side **session**: the superseded id is owed a revocation, the new id signs in, the account is the same one.
  - **That reasoning is exact for `google` and `apple` and is weaker for `email`, which this bullet used to elide** (PR #164 review, F7). For the OAuth providers `subject` is an opaque identifier for a *person* and genuinely says nothing about a mailbox. For `email`, `subject` **is** the normalised address (`identity.ts`), so the sentence reduces to "the mailbox says nothing about who owns the mailbox". The case it steps around is the one the founder already ruled on for rule 2 on 2026-08-22 — a mailbox changing hands, after which rule 1 lands the new owner inside the previous owner's account with `created: false` and no flag. **Rule 1 has always had that exposure structurally and this branch does not add to it**, so nothing here is a defect; the decision stands. But a supersession on an `email` identity is a *stronger* signal than the paragraph above credits — it means Supabase minted a fresh `auth.users` row for that address, which is precisely the window a reassignment would sit in — and this branch is the first thing in the system holding the evidence (`superseded_at`, `first_seen_at`, `last_seen_at`, per identity) with nothing reading it for that purpose. `Resolution.linkHint` is the existing "flag, do not guess" channel if anyone ever does. Recorded on SONNY-196 rather than acted on.

**What was deliberately not handled, stated rather than left to be discovered.**

- **No provider probe on the sign-in path.** `GET /admin/users/{id}` would answer "does this user still exist", and calling it per sign-in needs `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` on every gateway that serves sign-in — which reverses the founder decision of 2026-08-27 (SONNY-307, option (c)) that made that key optional precisely so a sign-in gateway need not hold the project's most dangerous credential. It also puts Supabase's latency and availability in front of every sign-in, which is the same objection that keeps `userFromAccessToken` off the request path.
- **No background poller either.** There is no scheduled process to hang one on, and the fact it would discover is one the drain already resolves once SONNY-313 unblocks it: `signOutAllForUser` on a deleted user answers `user_not_found`, which is `ProviderRejected`, which the drain correctly records as done.
- **The upstream-removal case with no successor is therefore unreconciled by design.** If Supabase removes a user and that person never signs in again, this gateway will not learn it. The exposure is bounded and is written down: the row keeps attributing an account that is genuinely theirs, and it keeps working, which is the right answer — the person still owns the mailbox. **Nothing is owed in that state and this sentence used to say otherwise** (PR #164 review, F6): the id is still current on a live account, so both of `OWED_PREDICATE`'s disjuncts are false and `owedRevocationCount` returns 0. "The owed revocation stays owed" described a row that does not exist, which reads as reassurance about something nothing is tracking.
- **Not absorbed, per the kickoff's fence:** SONNY-237 and SONNY-238 (access-token denylist, JWT secret rotation) and SONNY-313 (`signOutAllForUser`, which needs a founder decision). SONNY-313 is made **cheaper but not closed** by this branch — the drain now reaches superseded ids too, so whichever option lands there pays this debt without further work — and that is recorded on SONNY-313 rather than taken here.

**The mechanism.** Migration 0014 adds `sonny.identity_provider_user`: one row per `(identity_id, supabase_user_id)` ever observed, carrying `first_seen_at`, `last_seen_at`, `superseded_at`, and the two revocation columns moved down from `sonny.identity`.

- **It is maintained by a trigger, not by `resolve()`.** `AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF supabase_user_id` stamps `superseded_at` on the id being replaced and upserts the new one. The event is the column changing, so the record is made by whatever changes it — a supersession recorded inside `resolve()` would go unrecorded the first time a backfill, a support script or a future link path wrote that column. This is 0004's shape, where `account_closed` follows the account rather than trusting every closer.
- **Revocation bookkeeping moved wholly**, and `sonny.identity.provider_session_revoked_at` / `revocation_claimed_at` are dropped. A revocation is owed for a *provider-side user*, not for an identity — which the drain already conceded by stamping "every identity naming this provider-side user" rather than the row it claimed. Keeping both would leave two answers to "is this revoked?", which is what 0009 exists to have fixed once already.
- **"Owed" is one fragment, `OWED_PREDICATE`, interpolated into four query sites** — the drain's claim, its mark-done, `owedRevocationCount` and `owedByAccount` — with the delete guard's trigger holding an unavoidable fifth copy, because a trigger body cannot import TypeScript. 0009 exists entirely because the guard and the drain had drifted on one clause; a hand-written copy of a predicate is how that happens again. **This bullet said three for a further round after the fix round made it four**, alongside the same contradiction inside `OWED_PREDICATE`'s own docstring (PR #164 cycle 2, C-F3) — two statements in one document disagreeing about the number the fix was about.
- **`npm run revocations` reports supersessions separately**, per account and in total, because they mean something different to an operator: a closed account's debt is expected and drains away, while a superseded id on a live account is Supabase re-keying a subject underneath this deployment.

Files changed, **10** — nine under `server/`, plus this changelog (`git diff --name-only 7f174e2 d83e02b | wc -l` → 10 at `d83e02b`). **This said "8, all under `server/`", and both of its SHAs sat inside the command rather than beside the figure** — the citation shape a rebase orphans most quietly, because the eye reads them as syntax. It was true at round 1's head and wrong on both counts by the merging head, the README and this file having joined the diff after it:
- `server/src/db/migrations/0014_a_provider_side_user_is_remembered_and_revocable.sql` (new) — the table, the trigger, the delete guard rewritten onto the set the drain reads, the backfill, and the two dropped columns. Its `-- @rollback` restores 0006/0008's columns from the *current* rows and says plainly that a superseded id has no column to go back into.
- `server/src/auth/revocation.ts` — `OWED_PREDICATE`, the claim, the mark-done and `owedRevocationCount` moved onto the child table; new `supersededProviderUserCount`.
- `server/src/revocations.ts` — `owedByAccount` returns `providerUsers` and `superseded` per account; the CLI prints the supersession paragraph and no longer says every line is a closed account.
- `server/src/auth/identity.ts` — no behaviour change. Rule 1's refresh is documented as safe-because-recorded, with why the record is a trigger and why a new id is the reconciliation.
- `server/src/auth/attribution.ts` — no behaviour change. States that this must never read the history table, and why joining it would invert both tickets.
- `server/test/supersession.db.test.ts` (new) — 16 tests.
- `server/test/auth.db.test.ts` — two queries moved onto the child table; no test added or removed.
- `server/test/migrate.db.test.ts` — an explicit 60 s timeout on the 0007 test, argued at the site.

Tests: **round 1's, the fix round's and round 2's figures are all superseded by the post-rebase measurement at the end of this entry** and are not restated here. Each was taken at a head the rebase replaced, against a test population that has since grown by PR #163's five files, so translating any of them forward would attach a number to a tree it was never measured on.

**Mutation battery — the property, not one mutant per changed file.** Eight mutants, each breaking one link in the chain that makes a stopped-naming id both dead and owed: the trigger's supersession stamp, its insert, its come-back clause and its `IS DISTINCT FROM`; `OWED_PREDICATE`; the drain's owed-only mark-done; the delete guard's supersession disjunct; and attribution joining the history table. **Seven killed, one survived; the survivor was fixed and killed** — measured pre-rebase at `cee6676` and `5a4fdb0`, both non-ancestral now. The verdicts **carry** across the rebase, and the four conditions establishing that are at the end of this entry (`scripts/mutate <plan>` and `scripts/mutate <plan> --only R4`, both stamped by the script).

**R4 is the finding worth reading, because the mutant did not find a missing test — it found a wrong sentence.** The migration's comment argued `IS DISTINCT FROM` was needed for "the first id an identity acquires after having been created without one", and a test was written from that reading. That case goes through the trigger's INSERT branch and never reaches the line in question, and the `OLD.supabase_user_id IS NOT NULL` guard above it already settles the old side — so swapping in `<>` changed nothing any test could observe. The case it actually buys is a writer that **clears** the column, where `'x' <> NULL` is NULL rather than true and the cleared id would sit in the history marked current: attributing nothing, because the identity no longer names it, and owed nothing, because nothing marked it superseded. That is SONNY-230's exact state reached through a different door, and `resolve()` cannot produce it because its `COALESCE` never writes a NULL — which is why it needed a test rather than being left to the one caller that happens to be safe. Both the comment and the test are corrected; the battery kills R4 with the new one.

**Two things a reviewer should know about this run's reds, neither of them this branch's.** A `npm run test:db` run during round 1 reported 8 failures and a later one 4, with the set moving between them; the cause was **SONNY-352** — two files in another lane hard-code port 55433 and ignore `DATABASE_URL`, so that lane's suite was writing to this branch's database. Its container is down and the clean re-runs above are what the figures come from. Separately, R6's kill list names two per-address/per-source rate-limit tests that have no connection to a mark-done statement; those are the wall-clock flakes **SONNY-341** is fixing, and R6 has a plausible killer of its own (`does not stamp a live account's CURRENT id while revoking that same id elsewhere`), so the kill stands on that rather than on them.

**Left for others, and made cheaper rather than absorbed.** SONNY-313 (`signOutAllForUser`, which Supabase Auth exposes no endpoint for) now pays a larger debt with the same one decision: the drain reaches superseded ids as well as closed accounts, so whichever of its two options lands revokes both without further work. Recorded on that ticket. SONNY-237 and SONNY-238 are untouched and are the reason the exposure statement above is careful: a superseded id opens nothing at this gateway, because attribution refuses it, and a token minted for it still verifies locally against the project's JWT secret until it expires — which is exactly the gap those two own.

**Review round 1, and the finding that changed the design.** A fresh session reviewed the branch at what was then its head — `397e375`, replaced by the rebase and named here as history; its own ten-mutant battery over the property came back **10 killed, 0 survived**, and almost everything held — the trigger complete on all six write shapes it measured, the migration round-tripping byte-identically over seven seeded states, concurrent re-keying losing nothing, `FOR UPDATE OF pu` avoiding a lock-order inversion, and — the property that matters — a superseded id refused at the gate on the very next request, with both `accountForSupabaseUser` call sites enumerated. **Two findings blocked.**

- **F1 — one root cause, two routes, and the founder authorised fixing the whole thing here rather than half.** `provider_session_revoked_at` was being *written* as "this id has been revoked at least once" and *read* by `OWED_PREDICATE` as "this id has no outstanding revocation". Those are not the same column. Under the first reading a single stamp makes an id **permanently** un-owed, so every close afterwards revokes nothing — reproduced end to end through the real `resolve()` and `drainOwedRevocations()`, ending in an account that hard-deleted cleanly with live sessions never revoked. This branch's route was the `ON CONFLICT … SET superseded_at = NULL` arm, which un-supersedes an id and left the stamp; the comment defending that ("a revocation that happened is a fact about the past") had a true premise and a conclusion that did not follow. **The reviewer then proved a second route needing no supersession at all, which predates this branch**: close → drain → an operator reopens the account → the user signs in again → they close again, measured against `main` at `2f36250` as `owed = 1` then `owed = 0`. Filed as **SONNY-358** and fixed here, because splitting one root cause across two branches is how the second half never gets done.
  - **The column's meaning is now decided and stated where it lives** — on the column, in `OWED_PREDICATE`'s docstring, and in the table comment: *the revocation owed for this id's **current episode** has been performed*. An episode begins when the identity observes the id and ends when a provider call returns. 0014's trigger makes that true by clearing the stamp — and `revocation_claimed_at` with it — whenever the identity observes the id again. That closes the come-back route in full and closes SONNY-358's reopen route **for a user who returns by signing in**, because rule 1's refresh names `supabase_user_id` unconditionally and their next sign-in lands in the same arm. **It does not close the reopen route for a user who returns by refreshing** — `POST /v1/auth/refresh` never calls `resolve()` — which is the stated exception under review round 2 below. This sentence said "on **every** sign-in" until then.
  - **Every writer of the two columns was enumerated against the new meaning**, not just the one the finding named: the drain's claim, its lease release and its mark-done; the backfill; the rollback's copy-back; and now the trigger. That is the whole population (`grep -rn "provider_session_revoked_at\|revocation_claimed_at" server/src`).
  - **Clearing was chosen over the timestamp comparison** the reviewer also offered (`provider_session_revoked_at IS NULL OR provider_session_revoked_at < last_seen_at`). It closes the same two routes, and it decides them by comparing a `timestamptz` written by SQL `now()` against one written from a JavaScript `Date` — two clocks at different resolutions — so ties fall to a `<` / `<=` choice where one direction silently drops a revocation and the other can hand a row back to the drain every lease period forever. Clearing needs no comparison: whichever write commits last is right on its own terms.
  - It also closes F8's stale-lease note, which sat in the same two lines.
- **F2 — `server/README.md` documented the column this branch drops**, plus three more claims this diff made stale: the command table still scoped the debt to closed accounts, the retention constraint named the wrong table, and the service-role-key paragraph pointed at SONNY-196 as the ticket that would call `deleteUser` — a ticket that closes here having decided the opposite. All four corrected, and the page gained the thing the reviewer said it should: that a token naming a superseded provider-side user is refused at the gate immediately, on the same read, with the warning that joining the history table there would invert it.
- **F3** — `owedByAccount` counted rows under the noun "provider-side user(s)" where `main`'s "identity/identities" was accurate; one Supabase user named by two identities is two rows and one drain call. Both owed counts are `count(DISTINCT pu.supabase_user_id)` now, so the total, the per-account figure and `RevocationOutcome.revoked` share a unit as well as a word.
- **F4** — `OWED_PREDICATE`'s docstring claimed the duplication was structurally prevented while `owedByAccount` carried a hand-written byte-identical copy, because the constant had no `export` and could not be imported. Exported; imported; the docstring now counts four TypeScript sites and names the migration's copy as the unavoidable fifth.
- **F5** — the trigger's completeness claim is narrowed from "any writer of that column" to **"any statement that names the column"**, with the reviewer's six measured write shapes, the two that do not fire (a `BEFORE` trigger rewriting `NEW` on an update that does not name the column, and anything under `session_replication_role = replica`), why neither is reachable today, and why `ENABLE ALWAYS TRIGGER` is deliberately not taken — it would also fire the trigger on replicated changes at a subscriber, which is a replication-topology decision a migration has no standing to make.
- **F6 and F7** are corrected in this entry above, at the bullets they belong to. **F8**'s remaining four: the lease release's widened blast radius and the backfill's one unreachable state are written down where they live; the column-ordinal shift across the rollback is harmless (`grep -rn "SELECT \*" server/src/` returns nothing); and the missing `lock_timeout` is recorded in `server/README.md`'s migration-verification runbook as a **SONNY-126** decision, since every migration touching `sonny.identity` has the same property and 0014 is only the first likely to meet traffic.

**Review round 2, and a stated exception under the fix-in-branch rule.** Cycle 2 found nothing blocking the merge: the reopen route is closed end to end over real HTTP with coverage independent of the come-back route, the migration still round-trips across seven seeded states including marked-done, claimed and mid-lease, and the six-writer enumeration was derived independently and matched. Three findings taken, and one deferred by the founder.

- **C-F1 — deferred by the founder's decision of 2026-08-29, and SONNY-358 is the named landing spot.** **This branch does not finish supersession revocation, and a reader must not come away thinking it does.** The whole round rests on the premise that rule 1's refresh names `supabase_user_id` on every sign-in, so the trigger fires and the revocation stamp is cleared. That is true of **every route through `resolve()`** — and `resolve()` has exactly one production call site, `POST /v1/auth/email/verify`. It is **not** true of **`POST /v1/auth/refresh`**, which mints a full session, never calls `resolve()`, and therefore never fires the trigger. The reviewer reproduced SONNY-358's route over real HTTP with the user returning by refresh instead of signing in: **200, the stamp survives the reopen, and the second close owes nothing.**
  - **What is closed and what is not, plainly.** Closed: the come-back route in full, and SONNY-358's reopen route for a user who returns by **signing in**. Not closed: SONNY-358's reopen route for a user who returns by **refreshing**.
  - **Why it is latent rather than live** — the same reason cycle 1's F1 was. `signOutAllForUser` throws unconditionally, so no row reaches a non-NULL stamp in production today. It goes live with **SONNY-313**, and SONNY-358 is sequenced before it at high priority.
  - **The design question the deferral carries**, recorded because it is the part that could be lost: the return-by-refresh path is safe only while **a recorded revocation implies a dead refresh family** — a second premise nobody had written down. That fails wherever `ProviderRejected` records a revocation that did not happen, which is `main`'s deliberate contract ("the provider has no such session … recorded as done") sitting on a classifier where any 4xx but 429 is `ProviderRejected`. A 401 or 403 from SONNY-313's option (b) lands there with every session alive.
  - **The three sentences that stated the premise as "every sign-in" are corrected**, the decision having been made: `identity.ts`'s comment at rule 1's refresh, migration 0014's `ON CONFLICT` comment, and the mechanism bullet above. Each now qualifies the claim to sign-ins that reach `resolve()`, names `POST /v1/auth/refresh` as the route that does not, and cites SONNY-358; the migration's copy also records the unwritten second premise the refresh path's safety rests on. They were left unqualified for one round as a stated choice pending the decision, which is on the PR record. **This is the same shape as this branch's own R4** — a wrong sentence rather than a missing test — and it was sitting in the file the next person reads before touching this code, which is why it is worth a sweep rather than one edit. The population was enumerated rather than sampled (`grep -nE "every sign-in|names .?supabase_user_id|rule 1's refresh"` over the diff's files); two neighbouring sentences that were already scoped to `resolve()` are tightened with the same qualifier, and the test comments describing their own `resolve()` calls are correct as they stand.
- **C-F2 — the over-clearing direction was unpinned, and a surviving mutant is what said so.** The fix round named `does not un-spend a revocation the identity never observed again` as the test stopping the fix being "clear it always". **It cannot**: nothing fires the trigger after the drain stamps in that test, so the state it asserts is never disturbed, and the reviewer's mutant clearing every row of the identity **survived a 60-test run** beside it. The shipped `ON CONFLICT` arm is scoped to the conflicting row by construction, so this was coverage and not a defect. The reviewer's missing test — an ordinary repeat sign-in naming the id the identity **already holds**, after a supersession has been drained — is taken in, and that test's comment now says what it does establish rather than what it was credited with. **The gap was found by a mutant that lived, not by reading the test's name**, and that is worth the sentence: a test whose stated guarantee it cannot deliver reads exactly like one that can.
- **C-F3** — `OWED_PREDICATE`'s docstring headline said "three queries" one line above a body saying four, and the mechanism bullet above said three; both corrected. The episode-meaning paragraph was also spliced between the two bullets of the list it describes, dangling the first bullet's "or" and speaking of "both disjuncts" before the second was stated; moved below the list.
- **C-F4 — no code change, better reasoning.** The refusal of `provider_session_revoked_at < last_seen_at` was recorded as a clock tie-break. Two measured facts are stronger and now replace it: `now() - jsDate` runs **98–103 ms across twelve samples**, a systematic offset rather than a tie that a `<` / `<=` choice could address; and `provider_session_revoked_at` carries the drain's **start** time, captured once before a loop of up to a hundred provider calls, so a comparison against a `last_seen_at` written during that loop would read a completed revocation as still owed. The second is a property of this code rather than of anyone's clock and kills the comparison on its own. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **Restoring correct-by-construction with a *name* does not finish the job, because the assembly goes somewhere and you have to go look.** This is the branch's transferable finding and it cost two rounds to reach. Removing a silent default is right — that is the whole ticket — but a default that was *correct by construction* was also doing work, and a name only gives that work a place to live. When `LocalDataDeletionService.fileURLs` became required, the assembly moved to the shipping factory, where a presence-check guard caught `fileURLs: []` and could not see one store dropped. When `acrossEveryLocalStore` removed the factory's argument, the assembly moved again — into that member's own body, still unheld. **Neither move was visible by reading; both were found by writing a mutant that asked where the assembly went instead of assuming the rename had closed it.** The habit to copy is that last clause: after replacing a default with a name, mutate the new home and see whether anything fails.

- **Three figures on this branch went stale in three different ways, and it is one failure wearing three costumes: a number that was true when written, stopped being true, and left the prose around it standing still.** PR #162's F2 was a battery count measured one commit *below* the fix it described. N4 was a wrong parenthesis written *inside the commit correcting* the previous wrong parenthesis. And a fifth SHA survived a repointing pass by **sitting inside a command** rather than beside a figure — a `git grep … <head> … -- Tests` whose head argument the eye reads as syntax and not as a citation; re-measuring it then showed the command was wrong in a second way nobody had raised, counting comment lines as construction sites. Three instances in one week, on one branch, every one of them found by a reader and none by the writer. What generalises: **the write-the-command rule makes a number checkable and simultaneously creates a place for a citation to hide.** A SHA inside a backtick is not visually a stamp, so a sweep that checks "every SHA this entry cites" has to read the commands too, and a command quoted in prose deserves the same re-run as the figure beside it — CLAUDE.md's own bullet on this now stands at seven defects, two of them this branch's.

Two of those are not fixable by a better pattern: contextual member lookup means `.init()` has no type name to match, and a vendor with no `AgentViewModel` call has no argument label to name. `RoutineStore()` and `.init()` are sugar that omit a name; a required parameter has no name to omit, so the evasions stopped being expressible rather than being caught.

A scan that re-proves what will not build is not a second line of defence — it is a second thing to maintain that can only ever agree with the compiler, and it costs a reader the time to work out which of the two is load-bearing.

The lesson generalises past this branch: **a retired guard is invisible afterwards.** Nothing ever fails to say it is gone, so a retirement has to be argued per symbol, and the suite's header now names all six by symbol for exactly that reason.
- **Removing a default is how you find the call sites that were relying on it, and one of them was a live defect.** `AgentViewModel.makeExecutor` passed five of the executor's six stores and let `clipboardHistoryStore` default, so every fixture that had carefully injected a `ClipboardHistoryMonitor` at a temp root still had the executor *reading* the developer's real `clipboard-history.json`. It takes `clipboardHistoryMonitor.historyStore` now. Nothing but the compiler could have found it.
