Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A step finer than the thing the user can close produces a loop, which is why there are two steps and not three.** The obvious model has one step per beat — sign in, Screen Recording, Accessibility — and it breaks on the first skip: the last two beats are one sheet, so closing it marks only `screenRecording` declined, `accessibility` becomes the next step, and the same sheet re-opens on the same launch. **The unit of skipping has to be the unit of presentation.** What the user walks through is still four beats; `ScreenAccessOnboardingView` already owns three of them and this ticket does not rebuild it.

**A resolver survives a relaunch that a stored position does not.** The tempting design writes down which step the user is on. That value has to be written before the restart and read after it — one more thing to get wrong at exactly the moment the whole ticket is about. Asking live state instead makes the post-relaunch launch take the same path as any other: the same function that answers `.signIn` on a clean Mac answers `.screenAccess` once a session and a grant exist, with nothing recorded about where anyone was. Only what live state genuinely cannot say is persisted — which steps were declined, and whether the sequence is over.

**Deciding first run outside the task that awaits the Keychain read reproduces the exact bug the sequence exists to prevent.** `restore()` is asynchronous and everything after it in `applicationDidFinishLaunching` runs first, so a decision taken beside it rather than inside it sees `isSignedIn == false` on *every* launch — including the one right after the Screen Recording grant, where it hands a sign-in step to a user who signed in ninety seconds ago. That is "grant a permission, come back signed out" wearing a different coat, and it is a two-line mistake that no test of the resolver could catch. `R10` is that mutant, and the scan that kills it reads the ordering inside the launch task rather than the presence of a call.

**A second `ScreenAccessOnboardingModel` is two answers to whether this launch still owes a relaunch.** Settings › Security & Access built its own with `@StateObject`, which was right while it was the only door. First run is a second door, and `screenRecordingRequestedThisLaunch` — the flag that reveals the relaunch guidance — is per instance: a user who pressed Request access in the sequence would find the Settings page showing no guidance for the request it never saw, on the one step where the relaunch is the entire mechanic. Built once in `main.swift` now, threaded down, and the construction-site population is asserted.

**"Nine of the sixty-four" was written as twelve first, and the assertion is what caught it.** The exhaustive property test also counts how often the case it is about actually occurs, because a property nothing can satisfy is a property nothing holds. The count was written from a reading of the conditions rather than from running them — the failure mode `CLAUDE.md`'s counted-number rule names — and it failed on the first run. **The general form worth keeping: an exhaustive property test should assert its own reachability with a number, precisely because that number is the part a session will guess at.**

**Three of this branch's four closing residuals are a wrong sentence beside a correct number, and that is the shape to look for rather than a coincidence.** The changelog said *two* files under `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/` where the command answers 4, in a parenthesis that carried no command to re-run; a test comment said *three in the file* beside an assertion correctly reading `== 2`; a manual row's parenthetical credited a row that never signs in and called a gated step optional. In all three the executable part was right and the prose beside it was not, so nothing red could ever appear — which is precisely why `CLAUDE.md` asks for the command inline, and why the two cases here that had no command are the two that drifted furthest. **The counted-number rule's failure mode is not a wrong count; it is a right count with a wrong sentence next to it.**

**A scan of two lines of source cannot hold a value, and the bug this ticket exists to prevent is a value.** PR #159's review built the R10 mutant and confirmed it dies to exactly one test — and then built two more that keep the statement order and break the freshness: `isSignedIn` read into a local *above* the `await`, and the literal `false`. **Both survived.** All three produce the same user-visible failure, "granted a permission, came back to a sign-in screen", and the scan could only ever see the one that moved a statement. The fix is a behavioural pin: the two lines are extracted into `AppDelegate.decideFirstRunAfterRestoringTheSession()`, and `ProductShellTests.theLaunchDecidesFirstRunOnTheSessionTheKeychainActuallyHeld` seeds an `InMemoryKeychainSecretStore` with a session, asserts the account has *not* read it yet, drives the real method, and requires `.screenAccess` — which is the post-relaunch launch end to end. **The general form: when a defect has several shapes and only one of them changes the code's structure, a structural pin is a pin on the shape you thought of.** The scan is kept beside it and neither replaces the other — the test cannot see a second decision path added elsewhere, and the scan cannot see a stale value.

**The view layer had no coverage at all, and the resolver's coverage read as if it did.** The same review deleted the entire first-run `.sheet` from `CommandCenterView` — the sequence then never reaches any user, on any launch — and 2342 tests stayed green; so did turning the hosted dialog's close control into `set: { _ in }`, which is the *primary* declining mechanism in this entry's own words. Acceptance criterion 1 is "one ordered sequence on first launch", and it was pinned at the resolver, which is a claim about a function rather than about the product. **The lesson is not "add a view test" — this repository has no view-introspection harness, which is why every UI property in it is a source scan — it is that a branch which writes three scans can still leave the one thing that makes the feature visible unscanned**, because the scans went to the parts that felt intricate. `commandCenterPresentsTheSequenceAndBothDecliningControlsReachTheSameCall` covers the presentation, the binding it reads, and both declining routes.

**Two declarations shipped for one round with no production caller, and the shape is worth naming.** `FirstRunCoordinator.deferralLabel` mapped the current step through `FirstRunCopy` — a convenience the deferral bar never used, because it holds the step already and asks `FirstRunCopy` directly. It was reachable, tested, and a second route to one answer, which is exactly the thing that reads as covered while being dead. `FirstRunStep`'s `Identifiable` conformance was the same in miniature: its one purpose is driving a `.sheet(item:)` binding, and that binding was deliberately rejected because an `item:` sheet re-presents when the step changes. **Both arrived from writing the type before the view that uses it**, and neither a compiler nor a mutation battery objects — a mutant of an accessor only tests call has a test to kill it. Both were deleted mid-branch, in a commit the second rebase has since replaced; the test that read the accessor goes through the route the view does, so it asserts what the user sees.

**The sequence does not block the floating widget, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.** It is a sheet on Command Center, so the widget — a separate always-on panel — stays usable throughout, and a user can type a command while the first step is on screen. Blocking it was considered and rejected twice over: requirement 4 says a user who declines gets a Sonny that does less rather than one that is stuck, and making the sequence modal to the whole app is a design decision belonging to SONNY-109's pass, not to the ticket that owns the ordering.

**A test's hermetic fixture is not optional here, and one of the defaults is worse than dirty.** A bare `ScreenAccessOnboardingModel()` in a fixture takes `DefaultAppRelauncher`, whose `relaunch()` ends with `NSApp.terminate(nil)` — a test that reached it would end the test process rather than fail a check. `FirstRunStore` has the ordinary version of the same problem, one domain out: `.standard` is shared by every packaged build on this Mac, and the flag it holds is "first run is over". Neither has a default parameter anywhere on the path from `main.swift` down, which is SONNY-240's rule reaching two things that are not local stores.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The headline acceptance is verified in two halves and only one of them was runnable, exactly as the coordinator's amendment of 2026-08-28 instructed.** "Sign in, grant Screen Recording, relaunch, come back signed in at the next step" needs a live sign-in, which is the identity sitting deferred on **SONNY-280** (its founder-deferral comment of 2026-08-27 and its numbered resume checklist, steps (1)–(5)) — the same gate SONNY-133, SONNY-134 and SONNY-135 declared for their own rows. **The half that is owed is only the signed-in half.** The relaunch-and-resume mechanic itself is a founder row that runs today, because declining the sign-in step reaches the same relaunch on the same sequence; and the resumption is pinned by test either way, with a second coordinator over the same `UserDefaults` suite standing in for the process that comes back. **No agent packaged or launched the app**; `./scripts/package-app.sh` and the Finder run are the founder's, per this repository's standing rule.
- **A second sign-in method is designed for and not built.** SONNY-129 (Google, then Apple near launch) is deferred behind the same sitting. The requirement it leaves here — that adding one must not mean revisiting first-run ordering — is met structurally: the step is satisfied by "a session is held", which is what every method produces, so the buttons land inside `SignInDialogView`'s address step and nothing in `FirstRunSequence.swift` moves. `theSequenceNamesNoSignInMethod` is that claim as a scan, because a file that named a method would be a file the third method has to be added to.
- **Clean-machine testing here is a rehearsal, by the founder's decision of 2026-08-17 not to open the Developer Program account yet.** Nothing in this ticket is blocked by it — the founder can produce a Mac with no Sonny state — but the first genuinely clean first run by someone who is not a founder happens after notarization (row 20, SONNY-108), close to launch. That is why the manual section says how to reset the two keys: without it, every row passes trivially on a Mac that has already been through the sequence.
- **Nothing was left alone that this ticket needed.** The regions SONNY-136 is rewriting — the readiness model and `modelAccessReadiness` in `AgentViewModel`, `PermissionReadinessService`'s account row, the four unreachable-backend sentences, the provider clients' messages — are untouched here by design rather than by luck: this branch changes no file under `Sources/MacAgentCore/` at all, and its one shared file with PR #153 is `Tests/MacAgentTests/ProductShellTests.swift`, where the two diffs sit in different regions (that branch at the stored-property list, a transcription sentence and a doc comment; this one at nine fixture construction sites). A first-run sequence that showed or drove readiness rows would have collided head on, and it does neither.

- **A fixture rule that only a doc comment enforced is now a fixture that cannot be misused.** The F4 fix left two fixtures: one that owns a suite and removes it, and a `makeNonWritingFirstRunCoordinator()` for the nine `ProductShellTests` sites that construct a coordinator and never drive it. Its doc comment carried the rule — *a test that calls `begin`, `refresh` or `skipCurrentStep` must not use this* — and nothing enforced it in either direction that matters: a test could drive one directly, and, less obviously, could hand one to an `AppDelegate` and then await `decideFirstRunAfterRestoringTheSession()`, which calls `begin` from inside the product, which no scan distinguishes from the nine sites that do not. **The second fixture is deleted rather than documented**: every call site now takes a suite it owns and defers its removal, which costs two lines a site and leaves the rule nothing to be broken. `removeAtEndOfTest()` is safe on a suite nothing wrote to, which is what makes the uniform treatment cheap.
- **The test fixtures leaked a `UserDefaults` suite per call for one round, and the litter is on the founder's Mac rather than in the repository.** `makeHermeticFirstRunCoordinator` built `UserDefaults(suiteName: "…\(UUID())")` and never removed the domain, so every suite that was written to left a plist under a name nothing could recognise again — PR #159's reviewer counted **265** of them in `~/Library/Preferences/` from one afternoon, and measured that no other `com.sonny.tests*` domain in this tree leaves any. Fixed here: `FirstRunDefaultsSuite` owns the suite and `removeAtEndOfTest()` is `defer`red at every writing call site, which is the pattern `ProductShellTests` already used at four sites in the file this branch edited. **The files already written are outside the repository and are the founder's to remove** — the closing comment on SONNY-137 carries the one-line command; no agent deleted anything under `~/Library`.

It predates this branch; what this branch changed is *when* it fires, which is now the one point in a stranger's first ten minutes where the app can lose the user outright rather than degrade. **SONNY-349** — `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md:202` defers a curated onboarding example on the reasoning that the surface it assumed may no longer exist; this ticket creates one, so the deferral's stated premise has moved and needs either a fresh reason or a fresh decision, which is SONNY-109's.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **none.**

Next branch: none owed by this one. SONNY-109's UI/UX pass owns how this sequence looks — it ships functional and unpolished by design, which is what row 12's plan §8.2 already recorded for the first-run surface.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The high-water mark had one writer, and it wrote a value that could never refuse anything.** This is F1, and the shape is worth more than the fix. The mark was persisted by `adopt` alone, which stored the claim it had just fetched — whose `issued_at` the gateway sets from the same instant — so the mark was always ≈ the claim's own issue time and `max(serverNow, mark)` could not land past `honouredUntil`. Measured through the production write path: mark minus `issued_at` was **0.0 s**, and a Mac 100 hours past its window answered `entitled` again the moment its owner set the clock back. **Two comments asserted the property and both were true of the arithmetic and false of the wiring**, which is exactly the failure this repository's claims-and-evidence rules exist for — and **the two tests that held it seeded a `(claim, mark)` pair `adopt` cannot produce**, so they were green and silent, in the file whose neighbour warns about precisely that. The manual row could not catch it either: it runs online, where any response re-derives §3.5's offset and the rollback is invisible.

**What replaces it is a time source the user cannot author.** `SonnyBackendClient` now keeps the `Date` header it received paired with a `ContinuousClock` reading, so "that instant plus the real time since" holds however the wall clock is set; the service takes the latest of that, the persisted mark carried forward the same way, and `serverNow()` — and persists only the first two, because a clock pushed a year forward must refuse (it does) and must **not** be written down, or fixing the clock would leave a Mac locked out for a year. `EntitlementJudgement.effectiveNow` is **deleted rather than repaired**: two values cannot have the property its doc claimed, and a function whose doc is stronger than its inputs is how the next reader concludes a gap is deliberate. **The residual is stated rather than implied**: with no observation this process and a mark from the last run, a rollback re-enters the window as far back as the last time the app ran with a correct clock. Closing that needs a time source surviving a reboot that is not the user's, which this Mac does not have.

**Three refusals returned above the refresh that would cure them, and one of them told the user to do something that could not work.** F2. `.noClaim` answered *"Connect once so Sonny can check your plan."* while nothing ever connected — the sentence described an action the code did not take — and the second person to sign in on a Mac met the first one's claim, was refused every gated capability, and was told *"Sign in again"*, which is what they had just done. All three start a refresh now, the foreign claim is **cleared** rather than merely refused, and that state has its own sentence. The security direction was never wrong: a foreign claim is not honoured. What was missing was the way out.

**A justification can be false while the thing it justifies is right, and that is worth separating.** Cycle 3 ruled that seeding `observedServerTime: nil` is acceptable — it is a state a *decoder* produces, and the test asserts the product's behaviour rather than a standard library function's, which is the distinction cycle 1's objection actually turned on — while the reason given for it was false twice over. The comment and this entry both said it was "a legacy state ... a build before this fix wrote it": `EntitlementStore.swift` was added by this branch's own `23fac5b` and has never shipped, so no Mac holds one; and every version of `adopt` computes the mark from a **non-optional** `Date`, so no writer ever produced `nil` either. Corrected in both places to name the decoder, with a **producible** guard added beside it — a stale mark, one response, then the rollback — where `adopt` writes the mark and nothing is seeded at all.

**A property argued in a comment and pinned by no test is a paragraph, and this branch's own rebase is the argument for saying so.** F3. §9's "same transaction as the metering event" is reached here by hook registration order, because the two stores lease their own connections and merging their transactions is the coupling SONNY-300's seam exists to avoid — and `server/src/app.ts` was one of the six files that conflicted on the second rebase. A resolution putting the entitlement registration above the metering one would have inverted the stated property with every test still green. There is a test now, and a mutant that moves the settle before the handler is killed by four.

**The sweep began as a `plpgsql` function in the migration, and a mutation battery proved nothing could test it.** A migration is applied once and recorded in a ledger, so a database that already holds `0013` never re-reads the file — the mutant that restored PR #82's F2 defect therefore ran against the *correct* function still in the database, and the battery recorded it `KILLED` on the strength of an unrelated five-second timeout in a neighbouring test. Two things came out of that. The sweep is now ordinary application SQL beside `reserve` and `settle`, where a mutant reaches it and `reclaims EVERY expired hold across several accounts, not one per period` catches it — and fixing it is a deploy rather than a schema migration, which is the right shape for a bug in a query. And the timeout was a real defect of this branch's own: two connections contending for one row can exceed vitest's five-second default under a battery's load, so that test and the fifty-way race both carry an explicit hang backstop, which is the one wall-clock construct `CLAUDE.md` allows because it cannot be reached except by a genuine failure.

**One metered call is one unit, and that is a consequence of the never-touch list rather than a pricing choice.** A cost-weighted cap needs a credit weight, and credit weights are SONNY-212's. So the cap counts calls, `unitsForMeteredCall` is the single seam a real weight lands in, and what that bounds is stated rather than implied: a leaked token can make at most `SPEND_CAP_UNITS` metered calls in a period, each bounded in turn by §6.1's body limits and §12's deadlines. It does **not** bound the money, because a `/v1/search` and a twelve-iteration screen-control session are the same number of units and nowhere near the same number of dollars. **§9.5's second residual — a settle that absorbs overspend — therefore cannot arise today**, and `settle` takes a boolean rather than an amount to make that structural; it returns the moment the estimate and the actual become different numbers, which is SONNY-212's to weigh.

**`SPEND_CAP_UNITS` has no default and startup refuses without it, which is a deliberate cost.** The alternative reading of "unset" is "uncapped", and SONNY-16 recorded a leaked token billing the founder as an accepted cost — a cap that quietly does not apply is that cost with a mechanism in front of it doing nothing. Three variables join the set a sign-in deployment cannot start without, `deps.ts` names all of them in one message, and `0` is a legitimate value that means this deployment spends nothing.

**The tolerance is applied in both directions on the Mac, which is the inverse of `auth/clock.ts`'s rule, and the reasoning is what inverts.** On the gateway, tolerance is granted to a token that looks *expired* and never to one that looks not-yet-valid, because a token from the future is either the server's own clock being wrong or a forgery. Neither holds on the client: `issued_at` is signed by the gateway, so a forgery cannot choose it, and a claim that looks not-yet-valid means *this Mac's* clock is behind — precisely the error the tolerance exists for. Both edges are asserted at the second.

**The high-water mark is the only defence against a clock set backwards, and `SonnyBackendClient`'s offset alone is not one.** §3.5's mechanism is reused rather than duplicated — server time is the client's own `Date`-header offset — but that offset lives in memory, so a relaunch with no network leaves it at zero and server time collapses onto the local clock. The latest server instant this Mac has ever seen is persisted beside the claim, and the effective now is the later of the two, so an expiry once observed cannot be undone. It is a **floor and never a ceiling**: a clock set *forward* is absorbed by the grace window and past that refuses, which is the fail-closed direction, and there is no upper bound a Mac could know.

**`sub` is the identity that asked, and that is a client obligation rather than a preference.** §5 makes the *account* the billable identity, so the instinct is to bind the claim to it — but the Mac never learns an account id, only `user.id` from §3.2's token response, and without a binding it can check, a claim cached before a sign-out keeps granting capabilities to whoever signs in next for up to its own grace window. So `sub` is the Supabase user id and the claim's *content* is the account's; an account with two linked identities receives a different claim under each, identical in content and distinct in binding.

**The settle is ordered after the metering write rather than sharing its transaction, and PR #147's F6 left exactly this to be weighed here.** The host decision's probe settled inside the metering transaction so "a charge cannot exist without its audit row"; here the two stores lease their own connections by construction, and merging them is the coupling SONNY-300's seam exists to avoid. Ordering buys the same property — the row lands first — and the window between them leaves an audit row and an **unsettled hold**, which `expires_at` and the sweep reclaim. A hold briefly held is strictly better than a charge nothing can explain.

**`test/support/routes.ts`' population scan read a nested route's path wrongly, and this branch's route is what exposed it.** `commonPrefix: false` does not print every route in full: a route whose path is a strict prefix of another's becomes a parent node and the child prints only its own segment, so `GET /v1/account/entitlements` under the existing `DELETE /v1/account` was read as `GET /entitlements` — a path nothing serves. Both callers judge a route by its path, so a nested route would have read as neither-public-nor-listed in the gate's scan and unmetered in metering's: the exact failure both scans exist to prevent, arriving through the scan itself. The parse walks the tree now, and `theScanReadsANestedRoutesWholePath` pins it with a hand-built pair so the fix does not depend on this app still happening to have one.

**`SignInReleaseSwitchScanTests`' token list is split, because two debug-only pointers now share three identifier names.** Its file-set assertion started failing on a file whose `#if DEBUG` guarding was perfectly correct, which would have pushed the next author into renaming a well-chosen identifier to satisfy a test about a different pointer. The guarantee is split where it divides: the two string *literals* are unique to that pointer and must live in one file, and every mention of either list, anywhere, must sit inside an active `#if DEBUG` — which is the property SONNY-106 actually needs.

**A `HEAD` route was the first protected one, and `gate.test.ts` read its empty body as a failure.** Fastify generates a `HEAD` for every `GET`, `isPublicRoute` maps `HEAD` onto the `GET` it mirrors, and `HEAD /v1/health` is public — so until this branch no protected route had a `HEAD` and nothing had ever tried to parse an envelope out of one. The status is the whole of what a `HEAD` can say and is asserted for every route including these.

Known limitations / deferred scope:

- **The client's shipped public-key set is empty, and no gateway has been deployed to have signed anything.** The same shape, and the same statement of fact, as `SonnyBackendHost.productionBaseURL` being `nil`. It refuses every gated capability, which is the direction §5.3.1 requires, and affects no free capability at all. A debug-only override — environment variable or `UserDefaults`, both inside `#if DEBUG` and both held by a scan — is what makes the founder's rows runnable against `./scripts/deploy.sh local`.
- **Rotation without an app release is promised by §5.3 and delivered by nothing.** `GET /v1/meta` is SONNY-204's and is in Backlog; the `kid` selection and the multi-key set are built and waiting for it. Recorded in the contract rather than only here.
- **Nothing is gated.** `CAPABILITY_REQUIRED` is empty and `theGatedRouteSetIsEmptyAndBelongsToRowEighteen` asserts that it is; which capability keys gate which features is row 18's (SONNY-23). The `403` path is driven through an injectable override rather than by gating a real route, and no capability key literal exists under `Sources/` at all.
- **`EntitlementService` has no call site in the shipping app, and that follows from the line above rather than being an oversight.** Row 12 builds the check and row 18 owns the gate, so until SONNY-23 wires one there is nothing to ask it — which also means the background refresh, correct and tested, does not run in the app today because nothing asks a question that would start it. **The obligation row 18 inherits is now written where its session will read it** rather than being left implicit: `decision(for:)` starts a refresh on every state a refresh would cure, so a gate that simply calls it is self-healing, and `discardLocally()` is there for a caller that wants the bytes gone at a moment of its own choosing. Its whole surface is `decision(for:)`, `refreshNow()` and `discardLocally()`, and the ticket that gates a capability is the one that calls the first of them. What is *not* deferred is the wire half: an `entitlement.required` or `entitlement.expired` the gateway raises reaches the user through `SonnyBackendCopy` today, on every one of the five model routes.
- **No live remote round.** Everything was measured against a local Postgres and an in-process app; `./scripts/deploy.sh staging` and `production` still exit 3. The four founder rows are where a real container, a real sign-in and a real cap refusal are met.
- **One bad `Date` header from the gateway permanently disables entitlement on a Mac, and nothing in the product clears it — SONNY-344, high, and it wants a decision before the first real deploy.** Cycle 3's N1. The mark is written from an observation and `recordServerClock` accepts any header later than the last with no bound on how much later, so a gateway whose *container clock* is wrong — a misconfiguration, not an attacker — writes its error into every client that talks to it. Measured on the clean tree: one response with a `Date` a year ahead left the claim refused for a year, the mark creeping forward with elapsed time, and no in-product cure. **It is the mirror of an argument this branch already makes and accepts**: it excluded `serverNow()` from the mark precisely because a wall clock a year forward must not be written down, and the same hazard arrives through the *server's* clock, which is. The likely shape of the fix is named on the ticket and is already in the data — an observation may not move the mark forward by more than the monotonic time elapsed since the previous one, plus a tolerance, which is the relationship `projected` already encodes; refusing to record a jump elapsed time cannot explain costs nothing, because the claim is still judged against the larger candidate for *that* decision. Latent today, because nothing constructs an `EntitlementService`; it lands the moment row 18 wires one, and a first deploy is the likeliest time for a container clock to be wrong.
- **A server test that builds the app and supplies no entitlement store gets a Postgres-backed check against whatever fake connection it has — SONNY-345.** This is what produced the rebase's nineteen `500`s in `content.test.ts`, and it is structural rather than a one-off: sixteen test files call `buildApp`, eight pass an `entitlementStore` and eight do not, and the eight that do not are safe only because of what they happen to reach. Invisible to `swift build` and to a rebase's conflict list alike, so it will recur.
- **`EntitlementService` and `SonnyBackendClient` each take a `monotonicNow` closure and the service's doc says they must be the same one, which nothing enforces — and the disagreement fails permissive.** Handed a monotonic clock that does not advance while the client's does, the service answers `entitled` after a rollback that should refuse. Production cannot reach it: both default to `ContinuousClock.now` and there is no call site. **Recorded rather than taken in this round**, deliberately — cycle 3 classed it a note rather than a finding and the closing round was scoped to the three findings — and the shape that removes the invariant rather than documenting it is to let the client own the projection and delete the service's parameter.
- **`POST /v1/transcriptions` takes a hold and no test asserts that it does.** The population test drives the other four metered routes and asserts `admitted.length === METERED_ROUTES.size - 1`; the exclusion was justified as "exercised by `model.test.ts`", which injects the fake store and never reads its calls. The route is covered by the implementation being population-driven, not by a test, and the comment now says so.
- **Nothing schedules the sweep, and it now sweeps two tables rather than one** (PR #152's review, F4). `npm run entitlements -- sweep` reclaims expired holds *and* deletes rate-limit windows nothing counts against — the second because the per-account limiter changed `sonny.auth_rate_limit`'s load by an order of magnitude, a row per account per minute rather than one per sign-in attempt, and that table's own sweep had no caller outside a test. One command is something an operator can put on a timer; wiring it to one is a deployment decision and belongs wherever the gateway's own scheduling lands. The cut-off is computed from the declared limits, so it can never delete a window something is still counting against.
- **A mutant to a migration file is not reachable by a suite run against an already-migrated database**, which is what moved the sweep out of `0013`. The tables, the indexes and the `CHECK` constraint are still migration-level and still carry that limitation; what holds them is that the suite runs against a database the migrations built, and `keeps the CHECK as a backstop that makes an over-spend structurally impossible` asserts the constraint fires in the database under test.

**A pre-existing scan and a pre-existing suite were both wrong in ways only a new route could show**, and the second is the more instructive: `server/test/content.test.ts` did not conflict on the rebase, was not in the conflict list, and was the only thing that actually broke — nineteen `500`s, because it builds the whole app and every authenticated route in it met a Postgres-backed check against a fake connection. `CLAUDE.md`'s rebase gotcha names exactly this shape, and `swift build` is blind to it twice over.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true):

- **Whether the per-user spend cap is evaluated per iteration or per session**, raised by SONNY-131 and left to this ticket by SONNY-133. **Answered: per request.** A screen-control session is twelve requests and spends twelve units, because the gateway holds no session state and a per-session cap would need one — and because a per-request cap is the one that bounds a leaked token, which is what SONNY-16 recorded. If SONNY-212 wants a per-session price it is a `GROUP BY session_id` over the metering events, which already exist.
- **What the deployment's cap should be**, which is an operator's number today and SONNY-212's allowance tomorrow. Nothing in this repository sets one.

Next branch: `feature/row-12-retention` (SONNY-134) is the remaining half of the pair the row-12 plan marks as parallel-able after SONNY-133, and is server-only.

**Every one of the three was filed as a copy defect, and in each case the ticket's own figure had moved or its premise had.** That is the thread of the branch and it is the reason each entry below leads with what was counted rather than with what was changed. The rule this exercises is `CLAUDE.md`'s *count first, then write the number* — applied to a ticket's own text, which is a stamped measurement like any other and goes stale the same way.

**What a reviewer's step-0 ancestry sweep over this entry finds, said in advance: eleven hex tokens, six ancestors and five deliberately not.** Counted from the entry's own text rather than from this sentence's memory of it: `awk '/^### Branch: fix\/three-surfaces-say-what-they-mean$/,/^### Branch: fix\/three-small-client-defects$/' docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md | grep -ohE '\b[0-9a-f]{7,40}\b' | sort -u | wc -l` → 11 — **this said "→ 9" until SONNY-329 (2026-08-29), and 9 was never this command's answer at any head on `main`**: the bold sentence above it, its own enumeration below it and the command all say eleven, so the figure was a slip beside a correct sentence rather than a measurement of anything; the command also had no `wc -l`, which is why nothing about it looked like a count. Each token is read through `git merge-base --is-ancestor <t> HEAD` with nothing between the command and `$?`. Exit **0**: `be66eeb` (the original cut point), `5a54bbc`, `2664363` and `18c0346` (the three rebase bases, all of them on `main`), and `a55277c` with its full form (the head every figure is measured at). Exit **1**: `d2ed2de`, the head SONNY-233's own description stamps, cited precisely *as* a stamp that still resolves here and is no longer an ancestor — and `d156daa`, `cc86f26`, `0d50bff` and `e6cc390`, the pre-rebase heads, which appear **only in this sentence** and carry no figure anywhere in the entry, because every one was re-measured at `a55277c` rather than repointed.

**This census has now been wrong three times, each time in the same direction, and the third is the most instructive.** It said five tokens while naming two it excluded — the self-refuting form recorded below. Restated after the last rebase it said nine and four, having counted the *final* base and forgotten the two intermediate ones the very same paragraph had just named as rebase bases. Both were caught by running the `awk` command and reading its output, and neither was caught by re-reading the sentence. **A census of a paragraph's own tokens cannot be written and then verified; it can only be read off the command and copied.** That is the whole of the lesson, and it is cheap: the command is two lines above.

**That count was five for one commit, and the sentence that made it wrong was the one naming what it excluded.** It read *five tokens, four ancestors and one deliberately not*, and then said `d156daa` and `cc86f26` "appear nowhere in it now" — which was false the moment it said them, and put them in the population it was counting. A self-referential census is a fixed point only if the stamp is already one of the things counted, which the entry directly below this one recorded going wrong the same way six hours earlier. Caught by running the command rather than by re-reading the sentence.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

The cost is deliberate and is written at the test: a fourteenth store now fails here too, and the sentence a person reads before an irreversible press is worth that stop.

**F4 is the same shape on the Memory page, and its sharpest case is a word the branch itself flagged as doubtful.** `everyMemoryRowsCountNamesTheThingItCounts` compares `countedEntries` against the two properties it reads, so it holds structure — non-empty, lower-case, singular ≠ plural, not "saved" — and cannot see a wrong noun; five of nine were pinned by value and three were not. **F3 replaced a claim with a measurement.** `deletionCopyName`'s doc said it and `LocalStorageLoadFailureSource.label` "say the same thing where the two overlap". Eleven stores are named by both; **seven agree and four differ** — `routines` and `workspaces` (the banner says *saved*), `clipboardHistorySettings` and `outputLocations`. Every difference is correct, which is what made the sentence dangerous rather than merely wrong: it invites a well-meant repair to a failure banner or to a destructive-action disclosure. The doc now names the four and says why a banner and a mid-list phrase want different lengths.

**F5 and F6 are records.** A fifth comment still quoted `0 saved` against a closing comment that said the four live ones were reworded — it is undated design rationale, past tense, naming a string the product can no longer produce, and it is reworded with the correction beside it. And "the twelfth added `func` line" was the seventh; an ordinal into a diff goes stale the moment the diff does, so the sentence names the property instead.

**What the review left as residuals, recorded and not taken.** The adjacency scan matches only line-initial `.help(`, so a tooltip written mid-chain would be invisible to it and to its `== 4` population pin — nothing in the file does that and the textual-scan limits are documented on `MacAgentSource`. `.help` also feeds the accessibility *help* on macOS, so the capsule's label and hint are now the same three words — the clarification cancel has shipped exactly that pattern since SONNY-166, so it is precedent rather than a regression, and no session can observe it. `theCapsuleAndTheMenuBarStillShareThreeWordsForTwoDestinations`'s `count(of: "openCommandCenter") >= 1` is decorative; the `withTitle:` count is the half that actually trips on a rewording. **A red baseline in this fix round was the harness catching the session, not a defect.** A four-mutant re-run of the reviewer's survivors was started and then a test file was edited while it was in flight; `scripts/mutate` reported `BASELINE FAILED` and refused to attribute anything, and the baseline log's reason is `input file … was modified during the build`. The rule the script's own help states — do not touch the tree while a battery holds it — has a second half worth writing down: the tree is checked once, at the start, so a clean check is not a promise that it stays clean. That run is reported nowhere; the battery below is the measurement.

**A row's headline count and a number inside one of that row's entries are different measurements, and the page's own pattern is what makes the second read as a correction of the first.** SONNY-243 was reported as a bug by the person who specified the feature, within a minute of first seeing it, and nothing was wrong: `1 saved` counted the folders Sonny remembers and `2 times` counted one folder's uses. What the page had established everywhere else is that a row's number is the number of things its sheet lists — which is true of Output locations too — so the only available reading of "1" beside "2" was that one of them was broken. **The general form: a surface that has taught a reader to compare two numbers owes them the unit of each.** The repair is words rather than arithmetic, and no number moved.

**Naming the unit on one row would have been the same defect.** The fix was applied to all nine rows, and the argument is not tidiness: a single row reading `1 folder` among neighbours reading `N saved` is words that differ from their neighbours' for a reason the reader cannot see, which is exactly what was reported. **And "saved" was independently wrong for half the page** — the Memory section groups its rows by `LocalStoreKind`, and for the whole `.trace` half nobody saved anything: a task-history row, a copied item, an allowed app and an unfinished run are recorded rather than saved. That was invisible while the word was unitless.

**A ticket's own figures are stamped measurements and go stale exactly like any other, and all three of this branch's had.** `WORKFLOW.md` step 4 says to read the description and every comment and to reconcile the ticket against later conversation. What this branch adds is that the reconciliation has to include **re-deriving the ticket's numbers and re-checking its premises at your own head, before implementing against them** — because a contract written weeks ago reads as current and nothing in it says otherwise.
- **SONNY-233** said "nine of the twelve". At this head it was **ten of the thirteen** — and its figure was already wrong **at the SHA the ticket itself stamps**, in the most instructive way available: `d2ed2de` held **twelve** stores and **twelve** wipe URLs, so "twelve" was right, and the line the ticket names, `CommandCenterView.swift:5129`, named **ten** there (`git show d2ed2de:Sources/MacAgent/CommandCenterView.swift | sed -n '5125,5133p'`). **Nine was the count of a surface the ticket never mentions** — `ContentView.swift`'s confirmation dialog, which named exactly nine at that same commit. The number was correct about the thing the reporter had not found, attached to the thing they had. (`d2ed2de` resolves in this object store and `git merge-base --is-ancestor d2ed2de HEAD` exits 1: a branch head a rebase replaced, which is the convention working rather than a broken citation.)
- **SONNY-251** said "VoiceOver is unaffected throughout — the accessibility labels are separate and solid". That was true of three of its four controls and **false of the one it calls "the collapsed widget's only name"**. Its title's premise — that the file records `.help` as unreliable in the widget — had also been corrected by **SONNY-295** four days after it was filed.

**Enumerate before you subtract, in the direction a ticket points you away from.** SONNY-233 named `CommandCenterView.swift:5129` and one sentence. Sweeping for the *claim* rather than the line number (`git grep -n "clipboard settings\|Shortcut run history\|records of what Sonny did on screen" -- Sources Tests`) found a second surface the ticket did not mention — `ContentView.swift`'s confirmation dialog, naming **nine** of thirteen, one fewer than the page behind it. So the two surfaces describing one irreversible press disagreed with each other as well as with the wipe, and the worse of the two is the one the user reads last. **A ticket's file:line is where the reporter looked, not the population.**

**Removing a drift beats guarding it, when the population is already enumerable.** SONNY-233 asked whether the staleness "deserves a guard". A guard notices drift after it has shipped; an exhaustive `switch` with no `default` makes it impossible to compile. The chain now runs end to end and every link was already there except the first: the sentence is built from `LocalStore.allCases` through `deletionCopyName` (exhaustive), `everyLocalStoreFileIsClassifiedExactlyOnce` pins `allCases` against `LocalDataDeletionService.defaultStoreFileURLs()`, and `theWipesOwnSentenceNamesEveryStoreItDeletes` pins that the sentence names all of `allCases`. A fourteenth store cannot reach the tree unnamed.

**The shorter derivation was rejected, and the reason is worth keeping.** SONNY-233 proposed pointing at the Memory page instead of enumerating, and thought it probably better. Deriving from `MemoryCategory` would have produced **nine** phrases instead of thirteen — four fewer, not three (`awk '/^public enum MemoryCategory/,/^    public var id: String/' Sources/MacAgentCore/MemorySettings.swift | grep -cE '^    case '` → 9; **ten and three** stood here and in `LocalDataDeletionCopy`'s doc comment until PR #155's review recounted them, and the ten came from adding the uncategorised store back, which contradicts the next sentence in this very paragraph) — but the Memory page folds the vision journal, plan details and Shortcut run history under one Task history row, so the sentence would have stopped saying **"records of what Sonny did on screen"**, the most sensitive store in the product. It would also have under-promised by one, since `clipboard-history-settings.json` sits under no Memory row at all by design. **A shorter derivation over a coarser population is a different claim, not the same claim compressed.**

**SONNY-251's durable finding was not the one it was filed for, and the difference is what can be asserted.** It was filed about tooltips. A tooltip is evidence about one hover on one Mac — the founder's 2026-08-26 pass is the only such evidence this project has ever had, and SONNY-295 was careful not to generalise it — and no test in this repository can observe one. Whether a control carries a VoiceOver name is a property of the source, it is the property that was actually broken, and it is the one a scan can hold. So `WidgetControlNamingTests` pins the *pairing*: every `.help` line in `FloatingWidgetView.swift` sits directly beneath an `.accessibilityLabel` line. **Adjacency is deliberate** — it is what a diff shows and what a textual scan can read without parsing Swift, and a control that wants a tooltip and no name has to break the test to get one.

**A count in a doc comment is guidance, and guidance may carry no number — this branch wrote four and removed them in its own last commit.** `CLAUDE.md` records that rule from SONNY-314, and this branch broke it while implementing three tickets *about* stale figures: "today's nine nouns", "nine nouns written by hand", "one of nine", "among eight reading". Each was an honest reading of the tree and each would expire the day a tenth Memory row lands, while continuing to read as current. They are gone, replaced by the population's name and a pointer to the test that asserts it. **The four numerals that stay are dated records of what a literal said before this branch changed it, and their tense was corrected so they stay true** — "named ten of the thirteen stores the wipe *deleted then*", not "deletes".

Behavior added:
- **A generated output filename is validated where it is composed.** Four sites appended a leaf onto an already-validated folder and handed the composed path on unchecked — `PathWhitelist.defaultOutputFile`, `resolveOutputPath`'s directory branch, the zip adapter's default name, and the PDF destinations `FileInventory` composes. A dangling leaf symlink is the shape this closes, because `fileExists` follows it to a target that is not there and reports the path absent, so nothing upstream had resolved it. One leading out of the roots is refused; one staying inside is followed to its target, exactly as each caller's user-named branch already behaved.
- **A nested routine's `ActionPreview` names the file the run will write.** Previously it named `draft-<title>-<stamp>.md` and the run wrote `draft-<title>-<stamp>-2.md`, in both orderings of a draft and a drafting routine, and for two sibling routines. **This bullet said "the approval panel", and so did the code comment, the PR body and the ticket's closing comment — all four were wrong about the surface** (PR #157's review, F2). Nothing in `Sources/MacAgent` reads `ActionPreview` at all (`git grep -c "ActionPreview" -- Sources/MacAgent` exits 1); the approval panel renders `RiskApprovalCopy`, whose file line walks the *outer* plan's steps, where a nested routine's destination can never appear. The contract broken is internal, and it is a real one: `previewChain` seeds each segment's nested preview from `claimed.recordWrite(written)` over exactly these paths, so one wrong answer mis-seeds the next, and any future renderer inherits it. **This branch therefore owes no manual-test row at all**, and the row it shipped with is withdrawn rather than reworded — `docs/sonny-manual-test-checklist.md` records why in place of it (F1).

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
- **A ticket that says a hole is live is a claim to check, and two of this branch's three said so wrongly.** SONNY-264 was filed as a live escape through `/usr/bin/zip`. Measured against a tree carrying the pre-fix composition — this branch with `validateOutputFile` reduced to a bare `appendingPathComponent` — `prepare` **and** `execute` both refuse a plan whose generated zip name is a dangling link pointing outside, and the target is never created: `resolveDefaultOutputs` pins the generated path into the step's `outputPath`, and the next pass through the adapter takes the user-named branch, which has always validated. What was really exposed is the **nested** preview: `previewNestedPlan` handed `preview` an unresolved *stored routine*, and `.createZip` is not on `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations`, so a saved routine carrying a `create_zip` reached the generated branch with nothing resolved — closed by this branch's SONNY-218 half rather than its SONNY-264 half. **This entry, the code and two ticket comments said "the dry run", which names a route nothing calls** (PR #157's review, F3): `preview`'s one caller in `Sources` is `prepare`, which resolves on the line above it, and the product's own dry run goes through `prepare` too. And the same ticket's scope-widening comment names Microsoft Word as a third writer that follows a leaf link, reading `DocumentConverter.swift` as handing Word the destination; it does not — Word saves to a fresh path under `/private/tmp` and the destination is reached by `FileManager.moveItem(at:to:)`. Four writers measured side by side on Darwin 25.5.0 against a dangling leaf link pointing outside a root: `/usr/bin/zip -q <link> a.txt` exits 0 and creates the target out there, `Data.write(to:)` with no options does the same, `Data.write(to:options: .atomic)` replaces the link, and `moveItem` throws `NSCocoaErrorDomain` 516 and touches nothing. **So the fix is not four closed holes.** Three sites were correct only by an ordering nothing states and no test holds, and the fourth only because the two converters shipped today happen not to follow a dangling leaf link. Both are properties of callers; validating where the path is composed is a property of one file.
- **An enumeration of composition sites was short by one, and the missing one was safe by exactly the mechanism this branch describes itself as removing dependence on** (PR #157's review, F4). `AgentActionExecutor.unclaimedOutputPath` composes `<stem>-<n>.<ext>` onto the folder of a destination an adapter validated a moment earlier — the fifth instance of the same shape — and the reviewer measured it safe: the bumped path is written into the step's `outputPath` and re-read through `validateOutputPath` on the next pass, so a dangling link planted at `largest-files-<stamp>-2.zip` is refused by both gates. Leaving it there would have made the fix's own argument untrue of the fix, so it goes through the door too. **Asserting the refusal would have asserted nothing**, since the second pass gives the same answer with or without the change; the discriminating property is the other direction, that a bumped leaf which is a link staying *inside* the roots is now resolved where it is composed, so the path the prepared plan names is the path the bytes reach.
- **The half of the door that is not containment was held by nothing, and a reviewer's battery is what said so** (PR #157's review, F5, mutant V4). Swapping `validateOutputPath` for `validateInsideWhitelist` inside `validateOutputFile` left the whole suite green: containment is killed by six tests, and the parent-exists / parent-is-a-directory half — which SONNY-264's own closing comment records as a deliberate decision — by none. Same shape as this branch's own M4 and R4 survivors. Two tests now hold it, at the door and at the caller the decision was recorded about.
- **A test whose only failure is a `HangBackstop` timeout can never count as a mutation kill, and SONNY-259's first version was exactly that.** Every signature that type emits is declared in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures` — correctly, since a wait that times out may only be reporting the state of the shared main actor — so the mutant deleting `terminate()` from `ProcessBox.cancel` came back `UNATTRIBUTED` at `ba6a3e4`, on a run where the test had failed for exactly the right reason. Understating coverage is the safe direction and it is still a loss: holding that property is the whole of the ticket. The fix is a second issue in undeclared wording, **gated on `HangBackstop`'s own rule rather than a second one invented for it** — a wait that ends without its condition holding ended `.stuck` (past the deadline *and* past `observationFloor`) or `.starved`, `.stuck` is checked first, so reaching the floor is exactly the case that type calls a real failure. And the cascade that would make that dishonest is closed above it: if the *launch* wait's backstop gives up, the test returns before cancelling rather than asserting about a process that never existed. **Anyone writing a new backstop-only assertion inherits this, and the battery will not tell them — it reports `UNATTRIBUTED`, which reads as a harness note rather than as "your test is invisible".**
- **A half-fix repeats itself one layer up unless the whole shape is copied.** SONNY-190 seeded a nested routine's resolve from the run's claims and fixed one ordering; SONNY-220 had to add what the enclosing plan already *names* for the other. SONNY-218's ticket proposes resolving inside `previewNestedPlan` and stops there, which would have been the identical half-fix a third time — `previewChain` had no equivalent of `executeChain`'s `namedByEnclosingPlan.union(PlannedDestinations(namedBy: plan))`, so `[run_routine, create_local_draft]` would still have disagreed. Both halves are here, and the whole preview path now mirrors the execute path parameter for parameter. The battery is what proves each half is load-bearing: the plan-intent half is killed by the reverse ordering, and the claims half is killed **only** by two sibling `run_routine` steps, since such a step carries no `outputPath` and the plan-intent set is structurally empty for it — the same third door PR #96's review found for the execution side.
- **The ticket's own reading of an asymmetry was backwards, and saying so is cheaper than inheriting it.** SONNY-218 calls resolving inside `previewNestedPlan` a change that "makes the two nested closures asymmetric — one resolves, one does not". `executeNestedPlan` re-enters `execute`, whose first act is `resolveDefaultOutputs`, so it already resolved; the preview closure did not. Resolving there is what makes them symmetric. The one asymmetry that *is* deliberate is the opposite of the ticket's: a resolution answering with a **clarification** is not a resolution, so the nested preview falls back to the plan as stored, or `SaveRoutineCapabilityAdapter` would accept a routine it refuses today.
- **`FakeDocumentConverter` diverges from both shipped converters on a dangling leaf symlink, deliberately, and that is now written on it.** It writes with a plain `Data.write(to:)`, which follows such a link, where `moveItem` throws and an atomic write replaces one. That is what lets the docx refusal test prove itself with bytes rather than with an error type; making the double faithful there would make that test assert nothing.

**The durable half of the `HangBackstop` finding is in `CLAUDE.md`, not here, and that placement was the review's judgment call** (PR #157). Three reasons, all of which stand: it is not a defect and will never be fixed away, since it falls out of the declaration mechanism working correctly; the population it applies to is large and growing, so any test written with that helper is a candidate the day it lands; and it fails in the direction that reads as somebody else's problem — a manufactured *kill* prints the line a real one prints, while a manufactured *non*-kill prints `UNATTRIBUTED`, which reads as a note about a busy machine. It sits beside SONNY-315's entry in the `scripts/mutate` section, carrying the remedy rather than the story. This entry keeps the case that found it.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the roadmap and the founders' triage; **SONNY-342** and **SONNY-346** are unattached and untriaged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The Swift half's hang-backstop instrument does not transfer to Node, and that was established by measurement rather than by taste.** `HangBackstop` (SONNY-302) refuses to call a timeout a deadlock until the wait has evaluated its condition 500 times, because in that test process thirty seconds of wall clock buys *two* looks — the count separates "the code never finished" from "this process never got a turn" where the clock cannot. Building the same thing here was the obvious move and it separates nothing. Measured with a throwaway 5 ms interval probe against a Postgres in Docker at four load levels — the machine as found (one-minute load average **42**), 24 shell spinners (**49**), 60-client `pgbench` (**79**), and 40 CPU-bound `node` processes (**155**, rising to **194**) — the probe ticked at **178, 178, 167 and 171 per second** against a nominal 200, with worst single gaps of **12, 12, 14 and 46 ms**. In the run at 171/s the first of the two tests took **2527 ms**, ten times its unloaded cost and half the old 5000 ms budget. So the event loop stays healthy while the work gets ten times slower, and an observation floor set anywhere below the healthy population would have called that run a deadlock — a manufactured kill, which is the outcome the whole mechanism exists to prevent. Node's wait here is IO; it is not a poll queued behind hundreds of `@MainActor` jobs, and the two populations the Swift floor separates are not two populations here. **PR #156's reviewer re-measured the probe four times with the same instrument and widened the result rather than confirming it**: 166.7, 164.7 and 168.1 ticks/s at load averages of 157–164, inside the range above — and a fourth sample at load **99.5**, taken while the Swift suite was running, at **141 ticks/s with a worst gap of 60 ms**, below anything sampled here. That is the point worth keeping, and it strengthens the conclusion rather than qualifying it: a *wider* healthy population is one a floor separates less. It does not reach the 60 s bound either, which would need a 24× slowdown against the 10× measured, and because the wording is declared, reaching it understates coverage rather than manufacturing a kill.

**So what is left is time, and the honest use of it is a bound rather than a threshold.** A genuine hang never finishes; a slow machine finishes late; nothing but waiting longer tells them apart. Sixty seconds is 24× the worst these tests have been measured at under deliberate load and 12× what the reported failures met, and it is the number two other tests in the same file and one in `races.db.test.ts` already carry by hand. It is declared as untrusted all the same, because `mutate-untrusted-failures`' own header says what belongs there is "anything whose failure is a statement about the machine" and a wall clock on work another process owns is exactly that however wide the margin. What that costs is stated at the record: a mutant that genuinely hangs one of those two tests and breaks nothing else comes back UNATTRIBUTED rather than KILLED. What it does not cost is a mutant that makes one of them *wrong* — `underHangBackstop` rethrows the body's error untouched, and `backstop.test.ts` asserts the caught object **is identical** to the thrown one rather than merely equal, so nothing can wrap it and quietly attach the declared wording.

**A periodic timer inside a deadline is the one part of it that runs while the work does, and here it cost coverage.** The first version of the construct kept that 5 ms probe at run time, at 10 ms, and printed its count in the failure message as evidence for a reader — a number already measured as unable to support a verdict. The two tests it guards measure a race between three database transactions, and the probe made one of them a worse detector of the defect it exists for: over the same mutant R1, the plus-tag test caught it in **5 of 9** `--only R1` runs with the probe in place, **8 of 10** with it removed, and **8 of 9** valid runs on `main`'s own copy of the tests grafted onto this branch. Neither difference is decisive at that sample size, which is the point — a diagnostic whose value was already measured as low is the wrong side of an undecidable question to be on. The wait now holds one non-repeating `setTimeout` and nothing else, and `backstop.test.ts` pins that with a source scan rather than a runtime observation, because "nothing repeating is scheduled" is a property of the code and any runtime measurement of it would be a bet on the machine. **`5fd36fb`'s commit message says the probe was kept and is left as written**; this is the correction, the way this repository restamps rather than rewriting a message. (That commit was `60fa6e9` before the rebase; repointing the citation is right here for the reason `CLAUDE.md` gives — a rebase preserves a commit *message* byte for byte, and the message is what is being cited, which `diff <(git log -1 --format=%B 60fa6e9) <(git log -1 --format=%B 5fd36fb)` confirms with an empty output. A figure measured on the old commit's *tree* would have had to be re-measured instead, which is what every one above was.)

**The flake is a cascade, not two independent failures, and its second symptom reads exactly like the defect the tests were written to catch.** SONNY-241 records the pair "failing together" three times and neither prior session could reproduce it. It was reproduced here, inside a battery, on `main`'s copy of `auth.db.test.ts`: the baseline went red with `Error: Test timed out in 5000ms.` on the three-requests-together test and `AssertionError: expected 4 to be 3` on the plus-tag test directly after it. vitest abandons a timed-out test without cancelling its in-flight work and without running its `await app.close()`, so one of those three requests committed its `swarm@example.com` row **after** the next test's `beforeEach` TRUNCATE — and the plus-tag test counts `sonny.sign_in_code_issue` with no `WHERE` clause, so it saw 4 rows where it had made 3. That second failure is the shape of the single-live-code guarantee breaking, and it is debris from a neighbour. It is the exact trap SONNY-241 names: the two candidate diagnoses have opposite fixes and the wrong one hides a real defect. The fix closes it at the source — the first test is no longer abandoned at five seconds — and the cascade remains possible in principle at sixty, because nothing in vitest can cancel work already in flight.

**A scan that matches a call misses every way of reaching the same function without calling it there, and TypeScript has several** (PR #156 review, F2). The guard keeping `HANG_BACKSTOP_MS` and `VITEST_TIMEOUT_MS` from drifting is that `itUnderHangBackstop` is the only door: one call sets both bounds, and a scan over `server/test/**/*.ts` asserts no other file reaches the raw helper. The scan was `/(?<![A-Za-z])underHangBackstop\s*\(/`, and `underHangBackstop` is generic — so `underHangBackstop<void>(…)` is ordinary TypeScript, type-checks, and does not match, because the pattern wants `(` immediately after the name. The reviewer took it end to end rather than stopping at the regex: that shape inside a plain `it`, wrapping a seven-second wait, produced `Test timed out in 5000ms.`, and `classify_failures` returns `T` for that message. **SONNY-335's exact defect, restored, with every guard in the file green** — and the doc comment claiming "`itUnderHangBackstop` is the only door" was stronger than the guard, which watched one door. Three forms missed it (an explicit type argument, an aliased import, a bare reference) and two matched. It matches the **reference** now — `/(?<![A-Za-z])underHangBackstop(?![A-Za-z])/` — so a bare `import { underHangBackstop }` in a non-exempt file is flagged too, which is the loud direction and the right one, since importing it is what precedes calling it. The lesson is the general one this repository keeps paying for: **a scan's own population has to be enumerated, or nobody has watched it fail.** `namesEveryFormThatReachesTheRawHelper` now pins eleven shapes, seven that must match and four that must not, and the fix was verified by rebuilding the reviewer's evading file: the old pattern MISSES it, the new one MATCHES, and with that file present the suite exits 1 naming it.

**A guard against putting a declaration into your own failure has two sides, and closing one reads exactly like closing both** (PR #156 review, F3). `backstop.test.ts` computed a boolean before asserting, rather than `toContain(FRAGMENT)`, and said in a comment why: a failing `toContain` prints its *expected* value, and a guard whose failure carries a declaration is a guard the declaration switches off (PR #112 review, F1). One line later it wrote `expect(message).toContain("work that never finishes")` — whose *received* value is the backstop wording. The reviewer reproduced it by altering `hangBackstopMessage` to drop its description: vitest printed the fragment as the received value and `classify_failures` returned `U` for a real failure. Four sites had it, and the worst was `expect(source).not.toContain("setInterval")`, whose received value is the whole of `backstop.ts`. Every expectation in that file now takes a value that cannot carry the wording — a boolean, a number, a list of paths. **It was never live**, and the entry says so rather than claiming a save: no plan in this repository mutates `server/test/`, so an ordinary battery over `server/src` cannot make one of these tests red. It is erosion of the guard on the declaration's wording, and the direction was the safe one — a kill understated to `UNATTRIBUTED`, never manufactured.

**A test that detects a real defect only most of the time is a different thing from a flake, and a battery cannot tell you which it has.** SONNY-241 describes a silent ±2 on per-mutant counts and attributes it to the flake riding along. Half of that is now gone, and what is left is real: the plus-tag test caught R1 in **8 of 10** runs at `9680033`, and in **8 of 9** valid runs on `main`'s copy, so its miss rate is a property of the test rather than of this branch. The reliable detector is the other one, which named R1's kill in **28 of 28** valid runs across the three arms measured. Read the names, not the count — which is the advice `scripts/mutate --help` already gives, arriving from the other direction.

**The declaration guard was single-half and the way out of its failure was a silent hole.** `UntrustedFailureDeclarationTests` counted a `source` over `TestSourceTree.targets` alone, so the first server-half record would have been counted zero times and failed the suite with a message saying the source appears "under Tests/" and that fewer than declared means a site was reworded or removed — a healthy record, a blind scan, and a message naming three fixes of which the cheapest is to lower the number. Lowering it to zero then passed, because `found == record.sites` is satisfied by a scan that finds nothing when a record declares nothing: the exact defect the count was added for (PR #112 review, F4), reached through the one door it did not watch. Both are closed, and `sites` is refused below 1 on its own terms rather than by comparison, so it is refused whatever the scan found.

**The server tree's comments are stripped by line prefix, not by block span, and that is a decision.** `server/test/` is written in JSDoc throughout, so a `//`-only filter leaves every `/** … */` continuation line in the scanned text and prose about a wording would satisfy a scan meant to find the wording. The obvious fix is `MacAgentSource.strippingBlockComments`, and `CLAUDE.md` records what that costs: a `/*` inside a *line* comment opens a span nothing closes, and every line after it disappears from the scanned text. Dropping the three prefixes `//`, `/*` and `*` cannot do that. It over-drops instead — a real code line opening on `*` goes with them, a site count reads one low, and the suite says so. Over-dropping fails loudly and under-dropping fails silently. **Under-dropping is absent here rather than impossible, and this sentence used to read as the second thing**: a block comment whose continuation lines do not open on `*` is read as code, so prose inside one could satisfy a site count. PR #156's reviewer measured it — a span-tracking scan over `server/test/**/*.ts` at the reviewed head finds **0** lines inside a block comment that the prefix filter keeps — and it is not worth changing the filter for, because a span reader is the trap `CLAUDE.md` records.

**A message nothing asserts is a message a revert does not break, and the first attempt to pin one was itself too weak** (PR #156 review, recorded residual). SONNY-334's description asks by name for the count check's failure message to stop saying "under Tests/" when it means "under the trees this scan knows" — and both callers of `siteCountProblem` asserted only `nil` versus non-`nil`, so the deliverable was exercised only when something *else* failed and reverting the wording broke nothing. Closed here. The first version of the assertion checked the whole returned string for each tree name and **passed against the reverted wording**, because the message's closing sentence names the trees as well; it now checks the *first line* specifically, which is the sentence that reports the count and the one that carried the defect. Proved both ways: green as written, and red on the one-line revert with `the count check's failure message does not name server/test/ in the sentence that reports the count`.

**`server/test` is not an entry in `TestSourceTree.targets`, and could not be.** `LivePermissionCheckerScanTests` pins that list against `Package.swift`'s own test targets, so adding a non-target to it fails the suite — correctly. The other scan suites still walk `targets` only; they are about Swift constructs and have no business reading TypeScript.

**Every guard was proved by reverting exactly one thing.** Deleting the `sites < 1` branch fails `theSiteCountCheckRefusesARecordThatDeclaresNoSites` on `refusedAtZeroFound`. Dropping the server `Tree` from what `testTrees()` returns fails `everyDeclaredSourceStillAppearsAtTheSiteCountItDeclares` with "declares a source that appears 1 time(s) across Tests/. It appears 0." — first against a probe record and then, after SONNY-335 landed, against the real one, which is the failure SONNY-334 predicted arriving from the record it predicted it for. Pointing `serverTestDirectory` at a path that does not exist fails `everyTestTreeThisScanReadsIsReadToSomething`. Zeroing one real record's count fails the new `selftest` arm while the pre-existing "carries the site count" arm beside it still passes, which is the whole point of adding it. Rewording only the new record's `>>> signature` line turns the backstop failure back into a manufactured kill and fails four checks of the new group. The fix round adds three more: rebuilding the reviewer's evading file — `underHangBackstop<void>(…)` inside a plain `it` — the old call pattern MISSES it and the new reference pattern MATCHES, and with that file present the server suite exits 1 naming `zzevade.test.ts`; reverting the count sentence to "under Tests/" and nothing else reds the new wording assertion; and the too-weak first version of that assertion passed against the same revert, which is why it checks one line rather than the whole string.

**The three directions were proved end to end against the real classifier, not by reading it.** `classify_failures` was extracted verbatim out of `scripts/mutate` (15614 bytes) and run over one real vitest log carrying all three failures at `9680033`: the backstop hang → `U`, naming the new signature; a backstopped test whose assertion is simply wrong → `T`; an ordinary test meeting vitest's own `Test timed out in Nms.` → `T`. The third is what makes the record narrow: vitest's own message is shared by every test in this repository, and declaring *it* would excuse every timeout everywhere, genuine kills included.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Only the two tests the tickets name are declared this way.** The two `LONG` tests in the same file already carry 60 s by hand and are untouched; nothing else in the server suite was moved onto the construct, because nothing else has been observed to need it.
- **The cascade is closed at its source and not at its sink.** vitest cannot cancel a timed-out test's in-flight work, so a test abandoned at sixty seconds would still leak a row past the next `beforeEach`. The plus-tag test's whole-table count was deliberately *not* scoped to its own mailbox: the `count(DISTINCT mailbox_key)` assertion beside it is the one that catches the keying defect, and a `WHERE` would hide it.
- **`SONNY-341` is a live flake in the same file and is not fixed here.** `ratelimit.ts` counts against a fixed window, so any test that spends a budget to its ceiling on the real clock fails when its requests straddle :00/:15/:30/:45. Observed once in five runs (the run that started at 13:29:54) and then proved directly by calling `consume` with explicit clocks either side of a boundary. It is not load-dependent, it fires on a schedule rather than rarely, and it reads as a mutation kill the same way — arguably a worse instance of this class than the one fixed here. Filed rather than absorbed because it is a different test and a different mechanism, and its fix changes how a set of tests these tickets do not name control time.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **whether the server half should adopt the construct more widely, and on what evidence.** Two tests carry it because three sightings say they need it. Applying it to every `.db.test.ts` would be a bound applied to tests that have never approached one, which buys nothing and costs a wider declaration; applying it to none but these leaves the next such test to be found the way these were. The measurement that would settle it is a per-test duration distribution over the server suite under battery load, which this branch did not take.

Next branch: unassigned — this is a standalone tooling lane, not a roadmap row.
