Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A population grep is a locator, not a classification, and the block it finds is bigger than the line.** SONNY-205's two commands were re-run and both reproduce, but neither reaches everything the fix had to touch. The 8-app grep needs the literal `quantitative bar`, and §13.7's own gate paragraph is headed *Quantitative pass bar* — the one sentence collision C3 retired, invisible to the sweep written to find it. The two eight-item rosters are list items *under* a matched line, so they never match either. Three blocks were edited that no command in the ticket names, found by reading each match's surroundings rather than the match. The rule that follows is the one SONNY-183 already asks for, one level down: a grep tells you where to look, and what you edit is decided by reading.

**A post-sweep re-run of a supersession sweep's own grep answers *more*, not fewer, and reading it as a result is how a fix reads as a regression.** Every corrected line still contains the word it was found by — a struck "paid-only" is still `paid`, and a note citing §13.7 still cites §13.7 — so `grep -in 'paid' docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | wc -l` goes **25 → 24** (`be66eeb` → `f4cb499`) only because one heading lost a word, and the cap grep — the long `grep -inE` §23's app-list bullet carries — goes **16 → 19** across the same pair, because the annotations name the section they supersede. The checkable figure is the one that subtracts the fix: every touched site carries the string `SONNY-205`, so `grep -in 'paid' docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | grep -vc 'SONNY-205'` → **13** and the cap grep's same form → **2**, both at `f4cb499`, and both remainders are enumerable — the six product-is-paid lines, the four fail-closed-principle lines, §23's own two pricing paragraphs, §13.7's heading, and §24.1's rewritten line, which carries no marker precisely because it was rewritten rather than annotated. Same shape as SONNY-273's rule that a corrected entry must not still match the scan that found it, arriving from the opposite direction: there the fix had to leave the population, here it cannot.

**A figure measured on a working tree and stamped with the tree beneath it is a real reading of a tree that is not the one it names, and this repository has now done it twice.** §23's residual note says `grep -in 'paid'` returns 24; it returns 25 at `be66eeb`. The note is not stale — `git show 87750f0:docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | grep -ic paid` → **24** and `git show 49abb0e:… | grep -ic paid` → **25**, both ancestors, and `49abb0e` is the commit that *wrote the note*, adding the app-list bullet's own residual note — which contains the word "paid" — in the same move. That is WORKFLOW.md §8's 500-against-501 exactly, in a different file, found by re-running a figure rather than trusting it. Left as written, because it was an honest reading of the tree it named, and recorded here so the third instance is recognised rather than re-derived.

**The obvious form of a "nothing cites this" check exits 0, and the clean-zero family has a second direction.** `CLAUDE.md` warns that a search whose engine cannot see the bytes you mean answers a clean zero in the reassuring direction. Renaming §6.5's heading needed the opposite check — that *nothing else* cites it by title — and `git grep -n '6\.5 Paid' -- .` at `be66eeb` exits **0** with exactly one hit, the heading itself. Writing that up as "printed nothing and exited 1" was drafted, and it was false at the tree it named; the true evidence is that it printed *that line and nothing else*. After the rename the same command exits 1 with no output, and `git grep -c '§6\.5' -- . | wc -l` → **5** files on both trees is the positive control that says the search can find things. **The hit count behind that file count is not a standing figure and the spec's copy of this note says so**: 18 at `be66eeb` and 18 again at `7150af5`, and 20 once this entry cited the section twice — which is the self-reference trap arriving inside the paragraph about checking your checks, and was caught by re-running the command at the branch head rather than by re-reading the sentence. **The citation escapes itself**, which is why the count is stable: the pattern written into the file reads `§6\.5`, with a backslash, so it does not match itself — the same mechanism as PR #144's F6, this time working in the writer's favour and worth knowing before someone "fixes" the escape.

**A contract can be stale in a way that makes literal compliance destructive, and the reversible direction is the one to take.** SONNY-276 said to delete two pasted paragraphs from the entry template and keep the copies inside `feature/app-control-consent`'s entry. There are no copies: the phrase occurs exactly once at `58b13a5` (where it entered), once at `efa2a4d` (the tree the ticket was written against) and once at `be66eeb`, and every time inside the fenced block, between the `## Entry Template` and `## Entries` headings. The paste has no original, so deleting alone would have removed the only copy of a reconciliation record. They were **moved** into the entry the ticket says they belong to, verbatim, under a dated note that states the departure. The general rule: when a contract's premise is false, prefer the outcome a founder can reverse in one edit over the one that needs archaeology — and say so in the record rather than in chat, which is what got it ruled on before merge (coordinator, 2026-08-28: it stands) instead of discovered later.

**A scan-defined population regenerates just outside its own scan, and the third generation cannot be closed by a scan at all.** SONNY-273 corrected twenty entries; SONNY-275 is the thirteen its phrase set excluded; **SONNY-339** is three more that neither reaches, one of them `feature/app-control-consent`'s own line, which says "pending at PR-open time" and misses the anchored `PR open` pattern by a hyphen. The other two — PR #146 and PR #151, the newest entry in the file — say the line *will be restated before merge*, and it was not. A looser scan — the same `awk`, matching `pending|not yet|to come|awaiting|still owed|not reviewed` case-insensitively on the `Reviewed by:` line — finds those three among **13** matches at `846424f`, so ten of the thirteen are real review records that merely contain one of those words: **77% false positives**, which is why that ticket says to classify by hand and why the useful outcome is probably a restate-before-merge step in step 7 rather than a fourth sweep. Each generation was filed rather than absorbed, deliberately, so each ticket's number stays checkable against its own re-runnable method.

**A merged-branch list keyed on one GitHub namespace silently drops every merge after the move.** SONNY-273's scan builds its list with `sed -nE 's#^Merge pull request \#[0-9]+ from sauranshbhardwaj/##p'`. The repository moved to the organisation on 2026-08-26, so that form stops matching at PR #123 and every entry after it is simply not in the population — a scan that reports zero because it never looked. Generalised to `[^/]+/` here, which is what makes the list **143** distinct branches (`git log --first-parent --merges --format=%s | sed -nE 's|^Merge pull request \#[0-9]+ from [^/]+/||p' | sort -u | wc -l` → 143 at `be66eeb`; **without `-u` it answers 144**, because `feature/ui-ux-wireframe-fidelity` merged under two pull requests — the scan reads the list as a set, so 143 is the figure, and the pair is worth naming rather than letting the two counts look like a mistake) and what let SONNY-339's two newest instances be seen at all.

**A rule that must be exempted every time its case arrives is describing a case it has no cycles left to serve.** SONNY-170's substance, and it is structural rather than drift: step 7 bounds review at three cycles while `CLAUDE.md` requires a defect found at any point to be fixed before merge, so a cycle-3 finding produces a fix that nothing has read — and step 7 already reserves the full re-check for exactly that kind of fix. Three for three under the 2026-08-17 ruling, always the same trigger. What is written now is a **scoped verification round** rather than a bigger number: standing authorization for the first one, the founder's grant for a second consecutive one (which is what ends the sequence), and a round that verifies named changes and searches for nothing, with anything outside its scope recorded and left whatever its severity. The wrong outcome was a cap of five, which would restore precisely what the cap was set to stop.

**"Three exemptions in one day" is the ruling's day, not the rounds'.** Recorded because the incidents are the evidence for the rule, so their dating is load-bearing: the founder ruled once, on 2026-08-17, in response to the third instance, and all three coordinator grants are dated 2026-08-17 — but by those comments' own timestamps the rounds span **2026-08-17 22:41 to 2026-08-18 18:18** (−04:00). PR #65's ran and merged on the 17th; PR #67's and PR #70's ran on the 18th under a ruling given the day before.

**One figure in this branch's own output was written from memory and corrected on the record.** SONNY-340's description says a grep over `docs/` finds "that one line"; it finds five, of which one names the directive and four use the phrase in passing, so the claim held and the count did not. Corrected by an append-only comment on that ticket rather than a quiet edit. It is recorded here because of where it happened: inside a ticket filed about a rule being unwritten, in the sentence justifying it — which is `CLAUDE.md`'s own note that a parenthesis written while correcting somebody else's record is where attention is lowest.

Known limitations / deferred scope: three tickets filed and left for the founder to triage — **SONNY-337** (a third superseded Power Mode claim, approved-app scope, superseded by row J, with a §26 Non-Negotiable in its population), **SONNY-339** (the three placeholder review lines neither scan matches), **SONNY-340** (the founder's 2026-08-21 right-size-review directive is not in WORKFLOW.md, only in one ticket comment and one changelog line). One line of SONNY-337's population was corrected here on purpose — §24.1's prompt sentence carried all three claims in one clause, and rewriting it for two would have left a session pasting a false statement out of the block the rewrite exists to clean.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **none.** One was open when this entry was written — whether SONNY-276's departure should stand, since its contract said delete and this branch moved instead — and the coordinator ruled on 2026-08-28 that it stands: the contract assumed an original that never existed, deleting would have destroyed the only copy, and the move preserves the record. No revert. Recorded on SONNY-276 as a ruling rather than left as a question, which is the difference between a decision and a deferral.

**What a reviewer's step-0 ancestry sweep over this entry finds, said in advance: 7 hex tokens, six of them ancestors and one deliberately not.** The population is the entry's own text, not the sentence's memory of it — **this said "three" and then listed five more SHAs inside its own paragraph** (PR #151 review, F4), which is the quantified-claim rule failing in the one paragraph written to make a reviewer's job mechanical. Counted rather than recalled: `awk '/^### Branch: fix\/every-stop-reaches-its-catch$/,/^### Branch: fix\/mutate-sees-both-halves$/' docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md | grep -ohE '[0-9a-f]{7,40}' | sort -u | wc -l` → **8**, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <t> HEAD`, read with nothing between the command and `$?`, exits **0** for six of them. They are `d5020b0` (the cut point), `eb24089`, `4384b8d` and `6adbdc0` (the three rebase bases), and `d6f2b43` and `67e71f3` (commits on this branch). **The other two, `b894caf` and `534f317`, exit 1, and that is the correct answer rather than a stale citation**: they are named once each, in the pitfalls section, as the two SHAs one paragraph carried before the second and third rebases renamed it — commits being renamed, not figures being translated.

**The count has no SHA beside it on purpose, and that is this rule's own trap rather than an exemption.** A count of an entry's own tokens is changed by the commit that writes it down: the first attempt said 6 and became 7 the moment the sentence named the commit it was measured at, and the third rebase then took it to 8. Stamping it would need a SHA that does not exist until the stamping commit does. So the command is given, the token list is given in full — a reader checks the list against the file rather than trusting a number — and the count is re-derived at whatever head this entry ships at rather than carried. **Two rebases, and every figure stamped at a pre-rebase head was re-measured at the new tree rather than repointed** — the rule for a rebase, and the opposite of the rule for the 2026-08-24 rewrite.

Tests: the flagged command → **2320 in 161 suites**, exit 0, at `67e71f3`. Baseline **2305 in 160 suites**, exit 0, **re-measured at `6adbdc0`** in a detached worktree — the same figure it answered at `eb24089` and at `4384b8d`, each measured rather than assumed. `swift build` exit 0. `scripts/warnings` **0 warnings**, stamp `67e71f3 (clean)` — the script's own, not inferred. **The known-issue count goes from 2 to 5 and that is deliberate**: three of SONNY-331's four self-tests use `withKnownIssue` to prove a guard fires, which is what `HangBackstopTests`' two existing ones do. A reader comparing runs should not read 5 as a regression.

**Mutation battery through `scripts/mutate`: 9 mutants, 9 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed at `67e71f3`**, over a green baseline of 2320 in 161, and **re-run under PR #150's rewritten harness rather than translated across the rebase** — which is the one figure here where the harness change matters rather than only the tree. SONNY-315's fix in that PR is precisely that a concurrent `withKnownIssue` line landing inside another test's window stopped excusing a real kill, and **this branch is what supplies that ingredient**: it takes the tree from 2 known issues to 5. Same 9/9 under both, so nothing was being excused — but that is now a measurement rather than a hope, and the pre-#150 run it replaces is not cited. The population is one mutant per way each of the five tickets could be present and wrong. **Four results are worth reading rather than counting.**
- **M2 is killed by exactly one test, and it is the region scan.** Reverting the voice catch to `setError` leaves `deliverTranscriptionError` behaving perfectly and simply not called, so the behavioural test passes; only the scan holding the real catch to the seam sees it. That is the whole argument for having both, measured rather than asserted.
- **M4 is also killed by exactly one test** — the one asserting `(error as? URLError)?.code == .cancelled` on the rethrown error. Reminting the stop as a fresh `CancellationError()` still ends the run and still writes nothing, so every other assertion in all three web-research tests passes. Without that one line the choice to rethrow rather than remint would be unheld.
- **M5 is killed by three tests, and two of them are SONNY-320's** — `aStopWhileAPlanIsInFlight…` and `aStopWhileASynthesisIsInFlight…`, on two different routes. That is the one-conformance-two-routes property showing from the other side: `WebResearchSynthesizer` throws `PlannerError.backend` rather than declaring an error of its own, so deleting the planner's conformance breaks synthesis too.
- **M3 had to be rewritten, and the first version is the instructive part.** It was written as the historical `} catch is CancellationError {`, which leaves the arm's own `throw error` with nothing bound: it does not compile. `scripts/mutate` reported it `KILLED (build failure)` and said so in as many words — *"No test evidence: this says the mutant does not build, not that it is covered"* — which is the harness refusing to let a compiler error read as coverage. Restated as a change to the predicate alone, `} catch let error where error is CancellationError {`, it compiles and dies by all three of SONNY-328's tests. **A mutant that does not build is not a kill**, and a battery whose report says "9 killed" over one of those is nine minus one.

Behavior added:
- **A stop during a voice transcription would read as a stop.** Conditional, and the condition is the point: nothing can raise a cancellation on that route today, because `stopVoiceRecordingAndTranscribe` runs it in an unstructured `Task { }` that nothing stores — so no user-visible behaviour changed. What changed is that the route now asks. SONNY-327's first half — whether a transcription should be stoppable at all — is **SONNY-332**, filed with the reasoning rather than dropped.
- **A stop during a web-research source fetch ends the run.** This one is user-visible and is the branch's only manual-test rows. Before it, a stop was recorded as an unreachable source, and the run either completed and wrote a Markdown note listing the sources the user had stopped as *skipped*, or threw `WebResearchError.allSourcesFailed`, which no cancellation predicate recognises, producing a red banner and a `.failed` history row for a deliberate stop.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **Per-source tolerance is intact.** Two of SONNY-328's three tests carry a control arm in the same fixture: an ordinary unreachable source is still swallowed, still named under "Skipped Sources", and the run still succeeds. Every pre-existing `webResearch*` test passes unchanged.
- **A real transcription failure still sets the banner.** SONNY-327's test carries the same kind of control, and M6 — the predicate answering true to everything — dies by it.
- **No call site of `RecordedBackendRequests.only` was rewritten.** The six original files carry the same 7, 3, 8, 4, 1 and 1 lines they carried before.
- **Nothing was wrong at either step-line site.** SONNY-310 closes a coverage gap; the rendered sentence is unchanged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A conformance cannot fix a caller that never asks, and this branch is the three places that did not ask.** SONNY-320's entry stated that as a limitation and filed two of them; this branch closes both, plus a third the same shape. The general form is worth keeping because it will recur: `SonnyBackendError.isCancellation` has tests of its own and they are all about *shapes it can see*. A call site that never consults it is invisible to every one of them, so no amount of coverage on the predicate says anything about the population of its callers. The only thing that catches this class is enumerating the callers — which is what SONNY-320's entry did, and what produced these three tickets.

**A stop that reaches a `URLSession` does not arrive as `CancellationError`, and a `catch is CancellationError` written to guard against a stop therefore guards against nothing.** This is the mechanical core of SONNY-328 and it is worth stating separately from the fix, because the defective code reads *more* careful than correct code would: the loop has an explicit cancellation arm, placed above the swallow, with a comment saying why it is there. Everything about it says "a stop is handled here" except the predicate. The rule that follows is to ask the shared predicate rather than to match a shape — it already knows all four — and to rethrow what arrived rather than mint a fresh error, so the caller reads which layer the stop came from.

**A ticket derived by reading gets its reproducing test before its fix, and here that paid twice.** SONNY-328 said plainly that it had not been reproduced. Writing the three tests first and running them against the unfixed loop confirmed both predicted endings — and also corrected one of them: the first draft of the no-source-loaded test used two sources of which only one stopped, so the loop carried on and *completed*, which is the other ending. The test was restructured to stop every source, which is what a real cancellation does. A test written after the fix would have been written to pass and that error would have shipped inside it.

**Where a per-site assertion is the wrong shape, and SONNY-310 is the case.** Four call sites hand a shared presentation helper the same two fields; two had their arguments pinned and two did not, and the ticket asked explicitly whether the answer was two more asserts or something general. It is both, because the two hold different properties: a population rule reading every call by parenthesis balance catches the *swap*, and per-site pins catch the *receiver*, which the population rule cannot see. What makes the general form possible at all is that the property is textual — `iteration:` must receive an expression ending in `.iteration` — so it can be checked without rendering a view, which nothing in this repository can do.

**And the general form shipped with the same defect it was written to fix, one level up** (PR #151 review, F3). The rule's population was a literal list of two filenames while its own doc comment and this entry both claimed the tree — this paragraph said it caught the swap "at any site including ones that do not exist yet", which was exactly false for a site in a file that does not exist. The reviewer added a third file under `Sources/MacAgent/` carrying the exact swap and all twelve tests passed. It sweeps `MacAgentSource.appSourceFiles()` now, which is recursive over the app target and is what nine existing scans already use, and the probe was rebuilt against the widened version to prove it flags it: the population count went 4 → 5 and the swap failed on its own, two issues, exit 1. **What it now holds, stated at the width it actually has**: every `stepLine` call anywhere in the `MacAgent` target, including files added later. What it does not hold is `MacAgentCore`, which has no such call and no view; and the neighbouring guard against a *hand-written* step line still reads two filenames, which is recorded at that test rather than left to be discovered.

**A guard is shown to flag its defect before its sweep is believed.** SONNY-310's population rule runs the swapped call, a literal argument and a dropped argument through its own predicate inside the test body, before pointing it at the tree. That discipline is `UntrustedContentBoundaryScalarMatchingTests`', after a scan there flagged 0 of 13 historical instances while its doc promised otherwise, and it is cheap enough that it should be the default for any new sweep.

**A helper whose promise nothing checks is a defect even when every caller happens to satisfy it — and tightening it can leave the check itself unheld.** `RecordedBackendRequests.only` passed at any count at or above one. Tightening it failed **no test in the tree**: all 24 call sites really did send exactly one request. That is the finding rather than a relief, and it has a second half that is easy to miss — because no existing test sends two requests and then asks for the only one, the new check was unexercised by the suite it protects, which is the same class of thing it fixes. It ships with its own self-test. The general rule: when a guard is tightened and nothing goes red, the guard now needs a test of its own, because "nothing failed" and "nothing exercises it" are the same observation.

**A `withKnownIssue` test is the way to prove a guard fires, and it moves a number readers watch.** Three of SONNY-331's four self-tests record a known issue by design, taking the suite's count from 2 to 5. Stated in the `Tests:` line above and here because a known-issue count is exactly the kind of figure a later reader compares across runs and reads as a regression.

**A test that asserts a failure *message* must assert the parts, never the sentence.** `HangBackstopTests` states this for its own wordings and the reason is sharper than style: a test's failure text is read by `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`, so a guard quoting a declared signature is a guard that switches itself off. SONNY-331's message test asserts the count and the two paths and was checked by stripping the message back to a bare sentence, which fails it.

**The rebase merged this branch's newest checklist section cleanly and left it stale in the same move.** PR #149 (SONNY-330) folded every backend section's setup into one shared note while this branch was in flight, and added the caveat that rows running a command in the app wait on SONNY-280's resume. Git merged both changes without a conflict — different regions of the same file — and the result was a brand-new section describing a setup of its own that had become a stale copy of its neighbour's, which is the exact drift SONNY-330's note exists to end. **This is the conflict-list gotcha in its documentation form**: nothing conflicted, nothing failed to build, no test could see it, and the only thing that caught it was reading the merged region rather than the conflict list. Fixed in `d6f2b43`. (That commit has been renamed twice — `b894caf`, then `534f317` — by the second and third rebases, and **this is a commit being renamed rather than a figure being translated**: the change is the same one. The ancestry check on the entry's own tokens is what caught it the first time, which is the argument for running that check rather than assuming a citation is still good.)

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **none.**

Tickets: **SONNY-134** (contract §10's content store, its clocks, the delete that reaches everywhere, the incognito run that is never stored, and the snapshots training reads from) and **SONNY-319** (account deletion did not clear the idempotency store's stored responses), folded in by the coordinator's amendment of 2026-08-28. Two discovery tickets came out of it: **SONNY-333** (the app's delete button does not call the endpoint) and **SONNY-335** (two sign-in concurrency tests fail under battery load and read as kills). One session, one branch, cut from `main` at `d5020b0` (PR #147's merge), **two review cycles, and one rebase onto `4384b8d`** (PRs #149 and #150). **Every figure below is measured at `10bcf97`, the last commit on this branch that touches anything a measurement can see** — this entry's own commit sits above it and changes only this file, which `git diff --name-only 10bcf97 HEAD` shows. `d5020b0` and `4384b8d` are bases and carry no figure.

**Three sets of figures have been discarded rather than translated**, which is the rule this entry is most at risk from: the originals at `d04c462`, the cycle-1 fix round's at `0a65151`, and everything the rebase moved. A fix round and a rebase both move the head, and a figure carried across either describes a tree that no longer exists — so each set was re-run rather than repointed. `d04c462`, `0a65151`, `8434232`, `2ae0f8e` and `6507459` are named in this entry's prose as history and carry no live figure; the first two were replaced by the rebase and **do not resolve as ancestors of this head**, which is the convention working rather than a broken citation.

**Server-only, and that was a recorded decision rather than a judgement made while implementing.** The ticket's expected-touched-areas said "`Sources/` only if delete-by-task needs a client call"; the coordinator's amendment and `docs/sonny-row-12-plan.md` §8.2 both say "SONNY-134 is server-only, SONNY-135 spans both", which is WORKFLOW.md step 3's disjointness analysis and is fixed at ticket-creation time. So the conditional resolved to "not needed here" and `git status --porcelain -- Sources Tests Package.swift` prints nothing. **The consequence is named rather than left to be found: `AgentViewModel.deleteTask` does not call the new endpoint**, so "delete means deleted everywhere" is true of the endpoint and not yet of the button. That wiring is filed as its own ticket, and the manual-test row calls the endpoint with `curl` because that is what exists to test.

Behavior added:
- **`sonny.retained_content`** — one row per call holding request text, **voice audio as its own named column**, redacted screenshots, the served response, and provider error bodies, on a **30-day** clock. Written by an app-level hook, never per-route wiring, which is the fourth time this repository has made that choice for the reason `auth/gate.ts` first gave.
- **The clock runs.** A sweeper in the shipping process, advisory-locked so two instances cannot double-sweep, logging every pass and writing a `sonny.content_deletion` row for every pass that took something. `npm run snapshots -- sweep` runs one by hand.
- **`DELETE /v1/tasks/{task_id}`** (§4.6) — removes the live content **and every training-snapshot member copied from it**, records which snapshots lost rows, answers 200 with `requests_deleted: 0` for a task that stored nothing, and reserves 404 for a task belonging to another account.
- **`DELETE /v1/account` reaches content, snapshot membership, and the account's stored idempotency response bodies** — the last of those is SONNY-319, whose function `deleteStoredResponsesForAccount` had existed with no call site since SONNY-300 wrote it.
- **Training snapshots with lineage** (`npm run snapshots -- build|list|trace`), and **the support lookup** (`npm run support -- account|content|accesses|deletions`).
- **Provider error bodies are captured** rather than dropped unread, on all five adapters, with the provider's own request id.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims): metering is untouched in shape and in behaviour — §11's event, its columns, `outcomeFor`, the at-most-once claim and `npm run usage` are unchanged, and the 700-test suite that covers them passes; the four text routes and the vision route serve exactly as before, including the failover chain, the deadlines and the size refusals, with `provider.rejected` and `provider.unavailable` still keyed on the thrown type; the idempotency guarantees are unchanged, including that a released retryable failure re-runs and that its metering claim survives; the auth gate's deny-by-default is unchanged and `gate.test.ts`' population test now enumerates the new route; `DELETE /v1/account` still answers 204 for an already-closed account and still drains owed revocations without aborting partway; and a health-only deployment still serves `/v1/health` with no database, which `./scripts/deploy.sh local` verified.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Content is written after the response; metering is written before it. The difference is deliberate and neither is the default.** `metering/hook.ts` moved its write off `onResponse` and onto `onSend` because a crash between the two drops a billing record for a call already paid for. Two things separate content from that: what is lost differs in kind — a lost content row is a debugging copy of data the user still has on their own Mac, where a lost event is money the gateway cannot bill — and what it costs differs by three orders of magnitude, since a content row can be a 1.2 MB screenshot and `/v1/screen/analyze` runs up to twelve times in one session. Putting that insert ahead of the response bytes would put a multi-megabyte round trip on the critical path of the one feature this row exists to make possible.

**Which forced a seam, and the seam turned out to be a real shutdown fix rather than test machinery.** `app.inject` resolves before an async `onResponse` hook finishes — measured on Node v22 against Fastify 5 and already recorded in `metering/hook.ts` — so every "nothing was stored" assertion would otherwise have been asserting that nothing had been stored *yet*, and would have passed for a storable request and an incognito one alike. That is the worst shape a privacy test can take. `app.contentWritesSettled()` is the signal the writer publishes; `server.ts` awaits it **between closing the server and draining the pool**, because `app.close()` returning means every request has been answered and not that every content row has landed — without it the calls made during a deploy are the ones silently missing. **The entry is added when the draft opens, not when a write starts**, and getting that wrong is the difference between a working signal and one that answers "nothing pending" before the hook has run at all.

**An incognito run is stopped by three things, and only one of them is code anybody has to remember.** The hook refuses before it reads a body, decodes a capture or opens a connection; the table carries a `CHECK` admitting exactly one value of `retention`; and the snapshot builder's `FROM` names that table and nothing else, so **there is no `retention` filter in it to drop**. `content.db.test.ts` runs the builder's own `INSERT … SELECT` with the entire `WHERE` clause deleted, against a **consenting** account that made an incognito call, and asserts the run still cannot reach the snapshot — which is what §10.1's "pin it with a test" was asking for, and what a test of the filtered builder would not have shown.

**A request that declared no `retention` stores nothing either, and that is §2.4.2 rather than a second rule.** An omitted `retention` is a loud `400` on the wire precisely because neither default is safe, and the storage layer takes the same line: content is kept when the caller said `standard` and in no other case. So a body refused before validation contributes nothing, while its metering event is written as usual.

**The multipart route would have silently stored no voice audio, and a test caught it rather than a review.** `/v1/transcriptions` has no `request.body` — §4.4's body is consumed by `request.parts()` inside the handler — so a hook reading `retention` off the body found nothing, `isStorable` correctly read that as "declared nothing", and **the one content type §10.3 singles out as most likely to be overlooked would have been the only one never kept**. That is the warning arriving through a mechanism nobody would have looked at. The field is deposited from the validated `meta` part beside the audio, and `content.test.ts` asserts both the storable and the incognito case on that route.

**A provider's error body had nowhere to go, which is why three adapters each had a comment explaining why they dropped it.** They were right that §7.1's `message` is the wrong home — a body that echoes the request carries the user's own command, and `message` is a field the support lookup reads. What they lacked was a right home. It is now a column on the content clock, and the capture is in `meteredUpstreamCall` — **the one seam every provider call in this gateway passes through** — rather than in `sendUpstreamFailure`, which exists in **two** copies that `model/routing.ts` already carries a warning about keeping in step. A capture present on four routes and absent on the fifth would read like coverage.

**`DELETE /v1/account` cannot answer a failed wipe with a 500, and the fix is a sweep rather than better error handling.** The wipe runs after the close has committed — deliberately, so no content can arrive behind it — and by then `accountForSupabaseUser` no longer attributes the caller, so a 500 meets a 401 on retry and the failure is permanent. That is the exact shape PR #87's third round removed from the revocation path. So the handler logs and answers 204, and `sweepClosedAccountContent` on the same timer takes the content of any closed account that still has some. **That also reaches every account closed before this branch existed** — which SONNY-127's own comment recorded as "retained and unreachable" — with no migration and no backfill, because they are rows the query already matches. A first draft of this handler did throw, and the comment justifying it claimed the retry would work; the claim was false for the reason above and was caught by reading the comment three lines up.

**A snapshot member holds a copy, not a pointer, and `content_id` is deliberately not a foreign key.** The copy is because the live store is on a 30-day clock and a snapshot is not — a pointer would empty a sealed corpus at thirty days and collapse §10.3's two clocks into one. The absent foreign key is because `ON DELETE CASCADE` would let ordinary content expiry silently empty a snapshot and `RESTRICT` would make expiry fail; what `content_id` is instead is a value that keeps naming its source after the source is gone, which is what makes a deletion traceable at all. Same reasoning as 0011's and 0012's `account_id` being a scope rather than a key.

**Consent is enforced twice, and the second is not belt-and-braces.** The builder joins `sonny.account` and requires `training_consent`; a trigger on the member table refuses the row anyway. Training on the content of a user who did not consent is not a defect that can be repaired afterwards, and one predicate in one statement is a thin thing to rest that on. A closed account is refused by both.

**`deploy.sh` not knowing a variable makes it unsettable, and that was found by measuring rather than by reading.** With `CONTENT_EXPIRY_SWEEP_SECONDS=60` exported and neither new name on `PASSTHROUGH_SETTINGS`, the container swept once at startup and never again, and an already-expired row planted in its database was still there **75 seconds** later. Both names are on that list now. Re-run afterwards against the same container and the same database, the sweep took the planted row and logged `contentRows: 1`, and a second row planted without restarting was gone **36 seconds** later on the interval tick — two `expiry` rows in `sonny.content_deletion` exactly 60 seconds apart. Without that list entry, `CONTENT_RETENTION_DAYS` — the founder's confirmed thirty days — would have been a number no deployment could ever be told.

**A comment about a `grep` broke the `grep`.** `content/query.ts`' header explained that §10.2's checkable claim rests on there being no star-select under `server/src`, and spelled the literal form out — so `grep -rniE 'select +\*' server/src` answered with that sentence and the check reported a violation that was a description of the check. It says "star-select" now. Same family as `CLAUDE.md`'s slash-star-inside-a-line-comment gotcha and its warning about a citation that escapes its own parentheses: prose that is also executable text has to be written around the tool that will read it. **Two of §10.2's three checkable figures also moved and are restated rather than left standing** — `training_consent` is in **4** files under `server/src` now, not 1, because this is the first ticket that reads the column for its intended purpose; the figure that binds is the unchanged **0** under `Sources/` and `Tests/`, and the file enumeration behind the third was dropped rather than restated, because a list rewritten by every ticket that adds a query is one that will eventually be wrong quietly.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The app's delete button does not call the endpoint.** Server-only per the recorded disjointness; filed as its own ticket, named on SONNY-134's closing comment and on the manual-test row.
- **A per-task delete cannot reach the idempotency store's stored responses.** `sonny.idempotency_key` is keyed on `(account_scope, idempotency_key)` with no `task_id`, so nothing can name one task's rows. The account-wide wipe does clear them, and adding a column to another lane's table was not this branch's to do. **The bound is one content-expiry sweep past the twenty-four hours**, since the prune runs on that sweep now — this bullet said "bounded by that table's own twenty-four hours" and PR #148's review measured that nothing enforced the bound at all (F2, below). Two things narrow it further and neither is the bound: the payload is a response the user's own Mac already has, and an incognito run stores no body there at all.
- **No snapshot lifecycle number exists.** §10.3 puts snapshots on a separately-consented lifecycle and names none, so `expires_at` is nullable and NULL on every snapshot this builder makes unless a caller asks. `expireSnapshots` skips NULL rather than treating it as "never", so the day a founder sets a number the sweep already enforces it. Founder-owned.
- **`startContentExpirySweeper` itself is not covered by a test**, deliberately and stated in its own doc comment: it is started from `server.ts` and not from `buildApp`, because a suite that builds hundreds of apps must not start hundreds of timers against a database. What the tests drive is `sweepOnce` and `sweepExpiredContent`; what the function adds over them is a `setInterval` and an error boundary, and both were exercised against the real container instead.

**PR #148's review round, 2026-08-28 — five findings, all in-branch, all about the same table.** The reviewer enumerated every content-bearing column rather than reading the three this branch already guarded, and found a **third** content-bearing table: `sonny.idempotency_key.response_body`. All five land there, and the enumeration is why — the branch's three-layer argument was airtight about `sonny.retained_content` and silent about a table it was already reaching into.

**F1 (High) — an incognito run's response body was stored.** `idempotency/hook.ts` keeps the served response for twenty-four hours and had no notion of `retention` at all (`grep -c retention server/src/idempotency/*.ts` → 0, exit 1, at `8789d38`). Measured against a real Postgres driving the real app: `POST /v1/plan` with `retention: "none"` and an `Idempotency-Key` left `retained_content` empty — correctly — and left the model's reply verbatim in the key store, outside the content clock, outside consent, and outside what a per-task delete reaches. **Latent rather than live only because today's client sends the header on one call**, and requirement 6's whole point is that the guarantee must not depend on that. The fix withholds the body for an explicit `"none"` **through the release path that hook already had** for a retryable failure, so the claim, the lease, the fencing token and the fingerprint are written exactly as before: only §9.2's replay row changes, a repeat re-executes, and the second provider call is unbilled because the metering claim survives — the same trade the released-retryable deviation already makes. Recorded as a §14 contract row and in §9.2 and §10.1, not left in a comment. **Keyed on `=== "none"` and not on `!== "standard"`**, so the four auth routes — which have no `retention` field to declare — keep replay; the mutant that widens it is killed by an auth-route test.

**The two hooks read one function now, and that is the part to carry forward.** `retentionOf` is exported from `content/hook.ts` and read by both. Two readings of one field is the worst available shape here: the two stores would disagree about what the user asked for, and the one that got it wrong would be the one nobody was looking at — which is precisely the state F1 found.

**F2 (High) — a bound this branch claimed in three places was enforced nowhere.** `pruneExpiredResponses` had **no production call site**; every reference outside its own definition was a test or a comment, including this branch's sweeper header reasoning about it by name. Measured: a stored response back-dated thirty days past `response_expires_at` survived a full `sweepExpiredContent()`. The twenty-four hours bounded *replayability* — an expired response is already treated as absent at read time — and never bounded retention. The prune runs on the content-expiry sweep now, which is the machinery this branch built and the right home for a second clock rather than a second scheduler. **The policy half stays SONNY-318's**: whether the rows themselves should ever be removed, and what unbounded row growth costs on a real deployment. They cannot simply be deleted — a row carries `metering_claimed_at`, and removing one hands its key a second metering event on day two.

**F3 (Medium) — the middle layer of the three-layer argument could not fire.** `insertRetainedContent`'s column list omitted `retention`, so every production insert took the column's `DEFAULT 'standard'`, and the CHECK could only ever refuse a hand-written statement the gateway cannot emit. Had layer 1 been wrong, the incognito row would have been stored **and labelled `standard`**, and the constraint would have passed it — the exact opposite of the layer's own claim. The declared value is bound now, **deliberately unnarrowed**: a type predicate on `isStorable` would have returned the field to decoration from the other direction, since the compiler would guarantee the literal and a wrong guard would again write `standard` over an incognito call. Carrying `DeclaredRetention` means a wrong guard writes `'none'` and the CHECK refuses it, and an `undefined` binds NULL against NOT NULL and is refused too. **The column's DEFAULT is dropped in the same change**, because a default is what let this go unnoticed and is what would let the next writer omit the column silently.

**F4 (Low) — the closed-account sweep selected only on retained content**, so an account closed with all-incognito usage, or whose content had already expired, and whose in-request wipe threw, was never picked up by any pass. Either residue selects it now.

**Cycle 2 — five records items, and one of them was a real coverage gap.** **G3** is the one that changed code: F3's guarantee is composite — the store must bind the retention it was given **and** the hook must give it the value it checked — and both existing pins drove the store directly, so a later simplification of `retention: declared` to a `"standard"` literal would have kept them green while restoring the defect. With a *correct* guard the two are indistinguishable at run time, so the new test makes the guard wrong on purpose through a hoisted module mock scoped to one flag, drives a real incognito request through the real app against a real Postgres, and asserts the database refused the row and the app logged the refusal naming the constraint. Verified the way the review asks: the simplification turns exactly that one test red and leaves the other forty-eight in its file green. **G1** recounted the tests the fix round added — twelve, not eight. **G2** appended a dated PR note, since the body still carried the false bound verbatim and F1 changed user-visible behaviour the description names. **G4** put the false-zero finding into `CLAUDE.md`'s claims section as a family line beside the exit-code and `\b` rules. **G5** pointed the incognito manual row at both content-bearing tables rather than only the content store, since the finding it hunts lived in the other one.

**F5 (Low) — the missing test.** Every `incognito` assertion in the suite was against one table. **Twelve** tests were added (`git diff 8789d38 0a65151 -- server/test/content.test.ts server/test/content.db.test.ts | grep -cE '^\+ *it\('` → 12, with 0 removed by the same command reading `'^- *it\('`), four of them the pins for the four fixes; **each pin was verified to fail with its own fix reverted and nothing else changed**, before the battery ran. **This bullet said eight**, which was a count from memory and disagreed with the entry's own figures two paragraphs below it — the two content files go 71 → 83, and 71 + 8 is not 83. Recounted three ways that agree: the diff's added `it(` blocks, the per-file totals (`content.test.ts` 31 → 35, `content.db.test.ts` 40 → 48), and the pair's total. **The 83 here and the 84 in the verification paragraph are two different measurements and not a second disagreement**: 83 is the pair at `0a65151`, the end of cycle 1, and 84 is the pair at this head, after cycle 2's G3 added the hook-side pin. Said explicitly because an unexplained pair of near-identical numbers in one entry is precisely what this bullet exists to record going wrong. The rule this broke is the one about writing the command beside the number; the number was written without one, which is exactly when it goes wrong.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Verification, all at `10bcf97` unless stated. **Server-only diff, so the Swift suite and `scripts/warnings` are not owed and could not see it** — `git status --porcelain -- Sources Tests Package.swift` prints nothing, and WORKFLOW.md step 7 states the symmetric case in full. `npm run build` exit 0; `npm run typecheck` exit 0; `npm test` **474 passed, 239 skipped in 28 files**, exit 0 (the database tests skip, announced); `DATABASE_URL=… npx vitest run` **713 passed in 28 files**, exit 0 — of which this branch's two new files are **84** (`npx vitest run test/content.test.ts test/content.db.test.ts` → `Tests 84 passed (84)`); `npm run check:secrets` clean over 491 tracked files, exit 0; `./scripts/check-secrets-selftest.sh` **43 passed, 0 failed**, exit 0. Every exit code read with nothing between the command and `$?`. Migration rehearsed both ways against postgres:17 — `npm run migrate -- down` printed `rolled back: 0013_content_is_kept_on_its_own_clock`, `\dt sonny.*` showed **6** tables where there had been 11, and the second `up` brought all five back with the consent trigger present (`SELECT tgname FROM pg_trigger WHERE tgname = 'training_snapshot_member_consent'` answers it) and the 40-test database file passing on the re-applied schema. `./scripts/deploy.sh local` exit 0, four runs across the two rounds: health-only; with a real `DATABASE_URL`, where the container logged `content expiry sweep` and **actually expired two planted content rows 60 seconds apart**, leaving two `expiry` rows in `sonny.content_deletion`; then, after the fix round, one where the container's first sweep **cleared a back-dated stored response and left one still inside its window** (`storedResponses: 1`, `live-expired` body gone, `live-fresh` body kept); and one against a **stub provider on the host** so a plan call could actually succeed, where `retention: "none"` left `state=released, has_body=f` and `retention: "standard"` left `state=completed, has_body=t`, with the reply present in the second body and absent from the first, and a metering event for both. That last run is F1's fix in the shipping image rather than in a test.

**One measurement in that run was a false zero and is recorded rather than quietly fixed.** `SELECT count(*) … WHERE response_body::text LIKE '%LIVE-MODEL-REPLY%'` answered **0**, which reads as "the reply is nowhere" and is instead what a `bytea` cast to `text` always answers: the hex form, which no plaintext `LIKE` can match. The same predicate answers `f` for the standard row that demonstrably *does* hold the reply. `convert_from(response_body,'UTF8')` is the honest form and answers `t` for that row and `f` for the incognito one.

**Mutation battery — 9 mutants at `10bcf97`, baseline green at 713 passed, all 9 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed.** The plan covers both fix rounds' shapes and the shared reader they rest on: **N1** the incognito guard off (3 tests); **N2** the guard widened to `!== "standard"` (2, including *keeps replay for an auth route*); **N3** the prune dropped from the sweep (1); **N4** the store binding a `"standard"` literal (3); **N5** an undeclared retention silently written as standard (1); **N6** the closed-account sweep narrowed again (1); **N7** the shared reader ignoring the deposited value (1, *keeps voice audio*); **N8** the shared reader ignoring the body (15); **N9** the *hook* binding a literal instead of the value it checked (see below).

**The harness's summary is evidence this time, and was not last time.** The cycle-1 run reported all eight mutants as `KILLED (build failure)` with its own caveat — *"No test evidence: this says the mutant does not build, not that it is covered"* — because `scripts/mutate` could not attribute a vitest kill, so the report was read out of the per-mutant logs by hand. SONNY-323 landed that classifier in PR #150, which this branch rebased onto, and the run above names its killers itself.

**N9's count is one, not the three the summary prints, and the difference is recorded rather than taken.** Its three named failures are the on-point pin plus two sign-in concurrency tests in `auth.db.test.ts` that have no plausible connection to a one-line change in the content write path — which is exactly the shape `CLAUDE.md` says to read the names for. Argued, then measured: an auth route is not a content route, so `request.content` is null and `writeContent` returns before the mutated line, which makes it unreachable for those requests; with the mutant applied and nothing else changed the two tests pass **3 runs out of 3** in isolation while the genuine killer fails, unmutated they pass **5 of 5**, and they did not fire at all in the eight-mutant run over the same tree twenty minutes earlier. They are load-related flakes counted as kills — the gap `CLAUDE.md` names and the classifier cannot close — filed as **SONNY-335**. Nothing here rests on the miscount: N9's real evidence is the single test written for it. **Manual items are the founders'** and are in `docs/sonny-manual-test-checklist.md` under "Retention, deletion, and what support can see"; three of the four queue behind SONNY-280's resume steps (1)–(5) and one is runnable today.

- **The server half's own commands are not owed and were not run**: this branch changes no file under `server/`. vitest was nevertheless exercised throughout, because every shape the new reader knows was copied out of a real run of that suite and the battery below drives it end to end.

**Two real batteries, one per half, because a harness that reads two formats has to be watched reading both.**

- **The server half**, 2 mutants over `server/src/model/limits.ts` with `MUTATE_TEST_CMD='cd server && npx vitest run test/screen.test.ts test/model.test.ts'`: **2 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed, exit 0**. `V1` (the client image ceiling moved by one byte) came back `KILLED by 2 test(s)` naming `test/model.test.ts > the numbers this ticket is held to > carries contract §6.1's body limits` and `test/screen.test.ts > the screen route's numbers > derives §6.1's body limit from the client's image ceiling rather than holding a second literal`; `V2` (the same constant left unparseable) came back `KILLED before any test ran — every test file failed to load`. **The same plan, at the same head, through `main`'s copy of the script** reported both as `KILLED by the compiler — the suite never ran`, above a baseline line reading `PASSED` with no tally at all — which is the whole of what this ticket was about, and both runs stamp `17d6e8e` themselves.
- **The app half**, 1 mutant over `Sources/MacAgent/CommandCenterView.swift` (the greeting's morning boundary widened by an hour), run with the default suite command: **1 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed, exit 0**, `KILLED by 1 test(s)` naming `greetingUsesTheCorrectTimeOfDayPeriod(hour:expectedPeriod:)` — a parameterized test, so the parameterized issue-line path is exercised on real output too. It matters more than its size suggests: every full run of this suite carries `HangBackstopTests`' two known issues, so the classifier meets SONNY-315's ingredient on real output rather than only in a fixture.

**Three "does the guard bite" runs, because an arm nobody has watched fail is not a guard.** The branch adds 34 selftest checks (210 − 176). Each run below reverts exactly one thing and runs the same selftest, and every one of them exits 1:

- `main`'s script (`git show eb24089:scripts/mutate`) with only this branch's four vitest arms spliced in → **185 PASS, 14 FAIL**: 14 of those 23 checks. The other 9 assert things `main` already did right — both battery exit codes, the `not that it is covered` sentence, the `KILLED (build failure)` summary line, and the absences that were already true.
- The shipped script with only `boundary_re`'s verb put back to `recorded an issue` → **204 PASS, 6 FAIL**: 6 of SONNY-315's 11 checks, and they are the load-bearing ones — the exit code, the kill count, the outcome, and both "whose signature is it" assertions.
- The shipped script with only the section gate removed → **208 PASS, 2 FAIL**: the phantom entry is counted as a second killing test and named in the report.

**One more measurement, because "chosen by what the log looks like" is a claim about a population.** Each of the two formats' patterns was run over the other's real logs, all of them produced at this head: the four vitest patterns match **0** lines of the flagged suite's own 5108-line log, and swift-testing's three patterns match **0** lines of the three vitest logs the server battery above wrote (`baseline.log`, `V1.log`, `V2.log` — 22, 73 and 68 lines) or of the 49-line echoed-stdout probe. The selection cannot mistake one for the other on anything this repository actually produces.

Behavior added:

- **A server-half battery names the tests that killed each mutant.** `classify_failures` opens a block on vitest's error-summary entry the same way it opens one on a swift-testing issue line, so everything built on top of that — per-issue classification, `ALWAYS_TRUSTED`, `UNATTRIBUTED` — reaches the server half without a second mechanism.
- **A vitest run that loaded no test file is still reported as a build failure**, in words that name no compiler: `KILLED before any test ran — every test file failed to load`.
- **A vitest baseline prints its own tally** rather than `PASSED` with nothing after it.
- **A known issue closes the block it interrupts**, so its detail is attributed to nothing and the test it interrupted keeps its own message.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):

- **Every swift-testing path the classifier already had**: the per-test summary line, the issue lines SONNY-305 taught it, parameterized issue lines, per-issue classification, `ALWAYS_TRUSTED`, the trapped-process case that names no test, and the baseline's two arms (abort on real red, continue on declared-only red). All 176 pre-existing selftest checks still pass, and the app-half battery above attributes a real kill on a real 2305-test log — including after the rebase put PR #149's changes to `Sources/` and `Tests/` underneath it.
- **Both refusals and the lock machinery**, untouched: dirty tree, untracked file, `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`, `--check`, non-matching and ambiguous mutants, the `scripts/warnings` cross-refusal, stale-lock reclaim, `unlock`, nested-battery refusal, the non-isolated `MUTATE_TEST_CMD` refusal, interrupt and internal-error restore.
- **`mutate-untrusted-failures` is unchanged**, and so is the Swift suite that guards it.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**One classifier reading two formats, not two classifiers.** vitest's error summary has the same structure swift-testing's issue lines do — a line naming the test, then the failure's own message beneath it — so the second format needed a second way to *open a block* and nothing else. That is deliberate rather than economical: SONNY-305 recorded that teaching `failing_tests` a shape `classify_failures` does not know turns a correctly counted kill into a finding, because the caller gates on one reader and attributes with the other. One reader, one answer, and the two cannot drift.

**The shapes vitest is read on were measured, and the ones the ticket proposed were rejected on measurement.** SONNY-323 suggested the progress section's `❯ <file> (N tests | M failed)` and `× <test name>` lines. They cannot do this job: they carry no message, so nothing there can be matched against a declaration and every vitest failure would be evidence by default — the direction that manufactures a kill — and they name the test without its file or its describe block, which is the same merge that costs the swift path a name when two suites share a function name. The error summary carries both the name and the message, both sections list the same failures, and both the default reporter and `--reporter=dot` print it.

**A line a test PRINTED is not a failing test, and this branch shipped that defect for one commit before measuring it.** vitest echoes a failing test's console output above the error summary, under a `stdout | <file> > <test>` header and then the line verbatim at column 0 — exactly where a real entry sits. The first vitest reader here opened an entry on any line of that shape, so a test that logs one mints a failing test that never existed and the mutant is reported killed by it. Found by writing a throwaway test that prints ` FAIL  test/made-up.test.ts > a suite > a test that does not exist` and then fails, and running it: the pre-gate reader classifies that log as two failing tests, the gated one as the single real test. Entries now count only between vitest's own `Failed Tests` / `Failed Suites` heading and the run summary. **The general lesson is the one this repository keeps paying for**: a pattern was written from three real logs and was still wrong about a fourth shape those logs did not contain, and no amount of reading it would have said so.

**`suite_started` needs two tells for vitest and one for swift, and both vitest tells are load-bearing.** Without the banner check, a command that died before vitest ever started — `npm run build && npx vitest run` with the build red — would read as a suite that ran. Without the `Tests  no tests` check, a mutant that leaves a file the transformer cannot parse would be reported killed by a "test" named `test/x.test.ts [ test/x.test.ts ]`, which is a file that failed to load wearing a test's name. Measured both ways on the real suite.

**SONNY-315 is a manufactured NON-kill, and the fix is one word in a regex with a direction argument behind it.** swift-testing records a known issue on a line reading `Test <name> recorded a known issue at File.swift:174:55: Issue recorded`, which carries none of the four verbs that ended an issue block — so its detail lines, one of which is a declared signature, were read as the message of whatever test was mid-issue when it arrived, and that test's kill was excused. The boundary's verb is `recorded` now rather than `recorded an issue`, which closes the block on every kind of record line swift-testing writes rather than on the one wording seen so far. **The anchor was not touched**, because a boundary that fires too eagerly truncates a declared message and manufactures a kill, which is exactly how PR #112's F3 failed. **What no version of this can do**: a message actually *split* by an interleaved record line loses everything after the split. Nothing in a log distinguishes a split message from a foreign event, so the choice is which of the two to be wrong about — and swift-testing emits an event's lines together, re-measured on this head's own 2305-test run: both known-issue events emitted three contiguous detail lines, and the next record line after each is that same test's own `passed after …`, so nothing interleaved inside either.

**The pre-fix classifier reached the right verdict for the wrong reason in the neighbouring case, which is what the second arm holds.** With a genuinely declared failure interrupted the same way, the old reader still said `UNATTRIBUTED` — but naming the *known issue's* signature rather than the failing test's own. The verdict matched, the evidence did not, and only an assertion on which signature is shown separates the fix from the defect.

**The declaration file needs no notion of which suite a signature belongs to; the Swift guard beside it does.** `mutate-untrusted-failures` matches a signature against the text a failure recorded and knows nothing about what produced it — a selftest arm proves a vitest failure carrying a declared signature comes back `UNATTRIBUTED` exactly as a swift one does. But `UntrustedFailureDeclarationTests` counts a record's `source` over the Swift test targets only, so the first server-half declaration will be counted zero times and fail with a message that misdiagnoses itself, and the natural way out of that failure — `sites 0` — passes trivially. Recorded as **SONNY-334** rather than built here: no server-half signature exists today, so there is nothing to observe and nothing to break.

**Two process pitfalls from this session's own hands, both the kind that reads as somebody else's bug.** (1) A first attempt to compare the old and new readers printed `suite_started exit=0` for every log, including logs the old reader could not see — because `$?` was read after a `$(basename "$log")` in the same `echo`. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s exit-code rule exactly, arriving inside the work of a session that had just read it; the corrected probe reads the status into a variable first and answers 1, 1, 1. (2) The first app-half battery aborted at its only mutant with `the tree is dirty after S1`, naming `CLAUDE.md` — this session had edited that file while the battery was running. The guard did its job and cost four minutes; the note for the next session is that a battery owns the whole working tree for its duration, documentation included.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The two seams `CLAUDE.md` records as open stay open**, and neither is this branch's to close: two tests sharing a function name across suites merge, because swift-testing names no suite on either line the classifier reads; and a mutant that *traps* the test process names no test at all, so nothing in the declaration mechanism applies to it.
- **A message split by an interleaved record line loses everything after the split** (the SONNY-315 paragraph above). Not fixable from a log, and safe only because swift-testing emits an event's lines together.
- **Only vitest's error summary is read, so a non-default reporter that omits it yields no name.** The default and `--reporter=dot` both print it; anything else is reported as a run that named no test, which names the log to read and is the safe direction. Not refused, deliberately: a harness that refuses an unrecognised suite command would refuse every future test runner too.
- **The first server-half signature in `mutate-untrusted-failures` will fail `UntrustedFailureDeclarationTests`** and the obvious escape from that failure is a silent hole — **SONNY-334**, Backlog, untriaged. Nothing is broken today; no such signature exists.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: nothing follows from this one. It is delivery tooling, and the roadmap rows are unaffected — what changes is that a row-12 session running a battery over `server/` now gets a report it can read, instead of nineteen lines saying the mutant does not build.

The note says that in its own words rather than implying a run, and names **SONNY-280's founder-deferral comment of 2026-08-27 and its resume steps (1)–(5)** as the gate. **Which rows are runnable before a gate is a claim to verify, not to guess, and it is the half that makes the note worth reading.** Four are named in the note and each was checked against the tree at `d5020b0` rather than reasoned about: SONNY-132's `model routing` row, because `app.log.info(describeRouting(config), "model routing")` sits outside the `if (auth)` below it and every container prints it at startup; SONNY-130's three-minute recording row, because the refusal is thrown before the audio file is read and before any client call; SONNY-130's signed-out row, because a build that has never signed in has an empty token store and `requireSnapshot` throws `notSignedIn` before a request is sent, which is the same state a sign-out leaves; and the rows that already say "Terminal, not the app". **One was deliberately not claimed**: SONNY-131's redaction row looks reachable because the capture-review panel is built before anything leaves the Mac, but a screen-control run plans first and planning is authenticated, so a signed-out app never reaches a capture. The panel is not the first gate on that path, and reading only the panel's call site would have said it was.

**Two migrations landed after SONNY-280's deferral recorded "all ten applied", and the resume's own probe cannot see it** (SONNY-330, filed to that ticket as well as recorded in the checklist). The repository carries twelve (`ls server/src/db/migrations/*.sql | wc -l` → 12 at `92f6693`), and `0011` and `0012` were both authored after that comment (`git log --diff-filter=A --format='%ad' --date=iso -- 'server/src/db/migrations/001[12]*.sql'` → `2026-08-27 22:06:51 -0400` and `2026-08-27 18:11:32 -0400`, against a comment written at `2026-08-27T21:39:52Z` = 17:39 -0400). **Why it hides:** SONNY-280's resume step (4) is the `auth routes are mounted` probe, which sends `{}` and is rejected by the route's own body validation before anything touches the database — so it says "mounted" against a project missing both. **Deleting one of a matched pair is a state a later reader has to re-derive, and the wrappers were the easy half** (SONNY-321). `AgentPlanSchema.responseFormat()` and `WebResearchNoteSchema.responseFormat()` wrapped a bare schema in OpenAI's `json_schema` envelope for `CerebrasPlanner`; SONNY-132 deleted that class and SONNY-130 had already orphaned the second. The eight copies of the fixture count split three-to-five exactly as SONNY-314's session predicted: three past-tense records of what SONNY-240 *found*, which stay verbatim, and five present-tense sentences describing today's tree, which lose the numeral rather than gaining a new one. **One of the five carried two stale numerals, and the ticket's population found one of them.** `SignInView.swift` read *"a **sixteenth** required parameter on an initializer whose **fifteen** fixtures"*. The initializer takes 16 required parameters at `92f6693` — 34 in the signature, 16 undefaulted, 18 defaulted, counted by parsing the signature and splitting on top-level commas — so a new one would be the seventeenth, and the sixteenth required one is `backendClient`, which SONNY-130 added with no default and which is exactly when that word went stale. **A sweep scoped by one token finds only that token**, and this is the ordinary case rather than a near miss: SONNY-314's sweep was for `fifteen`, and a second wrong number sitting in the same sentence was invisible to it. **What stays spelled, and the rule that decides it.** The "thirteen stores" in the same two files is kept, and is now attributed to the two suites that assert it — `LocalDataQuarantineTests.everyLocalStoreIsUnreadableWhenItsFileWasWrittenUnderAnotherKey` and `LocalStorageSecurityTests.everyLocalStoreFileIsClassifiedExactlyOnce`, both `#expect(LocalStore.allCases.count == 13)`. **A count a suite fails on is a different object from a count only prose carries**: the first cannot go stale silently, so it may stay in a sentence; the second can, so it may not. A comment recording that went on SONNY-323.

**PR #147's review, and the six findings not already recorded above.** **F2** is the one a founder would have felt: the last manual row said every command now writes a database row *"after its response"*, written one commit before the write moved to `onSend` and never swept. That is the inversion of this branch's central decision, and it inverts the row's own rationale — the *only* reason a user could feel anything is that the write is now on the critical path, so "after its response" tells the founder there is nothing to look for. The reviewer measured both orders on this branch's own toolchain (Fastify 5.12.1, Node v22.23.1, a 60 ms stand-in for the `INSERT`): on `onSend` the write commits before the client can read the bytes, on `onResponse` the client reads first. **F5**: `outcomeFor`'s doc listed a `409 idempotency.conflict` among the requests classified `refused`, and the hook never asks it about one — both 409 paths leave `request.idempotency` as `null` and the metering hook returns on that before building an event. The function's answer for that input is real and a test drives it; nothing in the gateway consults it, and two files in one directory now say the same thing about the case the entry calls the subtlest rule in the hook. **F7**: `megabytes()`'s doc promised "the exact count kept beside it" and printed only two decimal places — caught on a real report where 192 bytes printed `0.00 MB`. **F8**: the no-price assertion covered `reportSessions` alone while the PR body generalised it to all three; it now drives all three over a corpus touching every route, and **its first draft failed on its own fixture** — a session named `session-price` — which is recorded in the test because a corpus containing a forbidden word defeats that kind of assertion silently.

**F6 is a residual this branch chose not to close, and the reason it is written down is that the branch reversed `onResponse` on exactly the criterion it then stopped applying.** `app.ts` placed metering after the idempotency hook because that is "the order a reader would assume". Traced both ways: **as built**, a process killed between the key's `complete()` and the metering write leaves a `completed` key row with `metering_claimed_at` still NULL, so the client's retry replays, the metering hook returns on `replayed`, and a provider call that was paid for is **never metered, ever**. **Reversed**, a kill between them leaves an event and an `in_flight` key; the lease expires, the retry genuinely re-runs, and its claim is already taken — so the first call is recorded and the re-run is not. Neither order is free and the reversed one loses less, but the window is one database round trip and strictly narrower than the `onResponse` window this branch removed, so it is **recorded rather than changed** — the ticket that should weigh a re-run the gateway pays for and does not record is the one that owns the spend cap. `app.ts` also now states what the single transaction in `writeMeteringEvent` does and does not close, because it is easy to read as covering this: it makes claim-and-insert atomic, and it cannot span two connections that `KeyStore` and `MeteringStore` lease separately by construction.

**The acceptance instrument — a real container, a real Postgres, real rows.** It was run at the pre-rebase head `7da2000`, which is non-ancestral now, so **the SHA is named as history and the figures are the run's own.** What connects that run to the tree that ships is *not* tree identity, and an earlier draft of this sentence claimed it was and was wrong — `git rev-parse 7da2000:server 841c882:server` prints **two different hashes**, because the review's fix round touched four files under `server/src`. The only executable change since the run is `test/metering.db.test.ts`, which no container executes. Nineteen requests were driven at it with the exact wire bodies `SonnyVisionModelClient` and `SonnyBackendClient` build — a twelve-iteration screen-control session, a retry pair under one key, a three-iteration incognito session, one `/v1/plan`, and one request missing `retention`:

- **18 metering events, 18 metering claims, 18 idempotency rows, and zero keys carrying two events.** Nineteen requests and eighteen events is the retry: the repeat replayed the stored response, ran nothing and was recorded nowhere, and both responses carried the same `sonny-request-id`.
- **`npm run usage -- sessions`** answers the per-session question the ticket exists for: the twelve-iteration session as one block with its tokens, image bytes, megapixels and outcomes, and the incognito session beside it as its own block reading `retention none` — **metered identically, which is the case §10.1 says is most likely to be dropped by accident**.
- The request missing `retention` is recorded with `outcome: refused`, `provider` and `model` and `upstream_duration_ms` all null, and its `task_id` still set — read off the unvalidated body, so a refusal is attributable.
