**The second rebase found the trap the first one could not, and the conflict list did not point at it.** PR #136 touched no TypeScript, so nothing could break. **PR #139 landed twenty files under `server/`**, and two of its changes met two of this branch's in a way no conflict marker could show. SONNY-130 added four fields to `Config` and replaced the five hand-written `Config` fixtures with one `testConfig()` in a **new** file, `test/support/config.ts`. This branch had added two other fields to `Config` and **renamed** the constant that file spreads — `TEST_JWT_CONFIG` → `TEST_SUPABASE_CONFIG`, because it had stopped being only about JWTs. Each side touched a different file, so **git merged them clean**, and the result did not compile: `test/support/config.ts(2,10): error TS2305: Module './tokens.js' has no exported member 'TEST_JWT_CONFIG'`.

**`npm run build` exits 0 on that tree**, measured rather than assumed — `tsconfig.json` includes only the sources under `src` and nothing under `test`, so the server's build command is silent about a broken test target in exactly the way `CLAUDE.md` records `swift build` being. **`npm run typecheck` is the command that sees it.** That is why a rebase here runs the typecheck and the full suite rather than reading the conflict list: **seven files conflicted, and the file that broke was not among them.**

**How it was resolved, and the rename got cheaper rather than harder.** The five fixture files took `origin/main`'s version outright — SONNY-130 deleted the fixtures this branch had edited, and its consolidation is strictly better — so this branch's edits to them are gone by intent rather than by accident. `config.ts` and `README.md` were keep-both, both sides' additions being disjoint. The one real reconciliation is a single import: `testConfig()` spreads `TEST_SUPABASE_CONFIG` and carries this branch's two fields. **That rename cost five edits when it was made and costs one now** — the saving `support/config.ts`'s own docstring predicted, collected by the very next ticket to touch it, and recorded there rather than only here.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Supabase's own mailer sends the sign-in code, so this gateway holds no mail credential — and that answers a question two files had been carrying as blocked.** `auth/provider.ts`'s docstring gave "the founder's Resend sending domain is not ready" as the first of two reasons the seam exists, `revocations.ts` and `README.md` repeated it, and SONNY-306's passthrough block recorded mail as pending. It was never the blocker. `POST /otp` with an email is GoTrue's `Otp` handler delegating to `MagicLink`, which composes and sends the message itself and answers `{}` — `message_id` is the SMS branch's, per `openapi.yaml`'s own 200 schema — and `POST /verify` takes the code back. **The code crosses this boundary in neither direction**: the gateway does not mint it, does not receive it, and could not put it in a mail of its own. So `config.ts` grows no `RESEND_*` or `SMTP_*` name, `deploy.sh`'s `PASSTHROUGH` grows none, and the sentence "when mail names land in `config.ts`, they are added here" now describes something not expected to happen. **The sending domain is still owed and still founder-owned**, one layer away and not as code: Supabase's default SMTP is documented as best-effort, non-production, **two messages an hour**, and the fix is a custom SMTP transport configured **in the Supabase project**, after which "your project's Auth server will send messages to all addresses" — still composed and sent by Supabase. That changes deliverability, not this interface. The translation reason is what keeps the seam, and it is untouched.

**The service-role key is deliberately not required, and least privilege is the whole of the argument** (F3; founder decision of 2026-08-27, option (c), taken at the review). The first version required `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` alongside the anon key and made it a fourth trigger for "this deployment intends sign-in". It is the project's **most dangerous** credential — it bypasses every row-level policy and can act as any user — and **exactly one method reaches for it, `deleteUser`, which no code path calls**: account closure revokes sessions and deliberately keeps identities, and the ticket that would call it is SONNY-196's. So the requirement made every gateway serving sign-in hold a key it could not spend, which is a standing risk bought for nothing. It is now absent from the required set, from the intent triggers, and from `deploy.sh`'s passthrough — measured, not asserted: the container's own `printenv` shows six forwarded names and **zero** occurrences of that one. **The cost is paid at the call site**: `deleteUser` throws `ServiceRoleKeyNotConfigured`, which is deliberately *neither* of the seam's two errors, because `ProviderUnavailable` would send an operator hunting a Supabase outage that is not happening and `ProviderRejected` is what `revocation.ts` reads as "already done". **The ticket that lands a caller adds the name back to the required set and the passthrough in the same change**, and that sentence is written in all five places the requirement used to live rather than only here.

**A count in prose is a copy of the count that can go stale on its own, and this branch proved it three times** (N1, N2, N5). F3 changed the number of Supabase names that mean "sign-in" from four to three, and the sweep that followed it changed six sentences in `deps.ts` and missed two — **in the file whose entire subject is that count**. The entry missed two more, one of them three lines below its own corrected sentence, so the entry contradicted itself inside a screen. And `deploy.sh`'s 404 branch told an operator "the three `SUPABASE_` names were not set" directly beneath a line listing four, because `PASSTHROUGH` carries four `SUPABASE_`-prefixed names and only three are the switch — `SUPABASE_JWT_AUDIENCE` is defaulted and therefore no signal of intent. All five are fixed; what is worth carrying is that **the list is the count** — `AUTH_INTENT.length` is what the code reads — and a sentence naming a number is a duplicate of it. The 404 branch now names the three outright rather than making a founder derive them from two adjacent lines.

**A claim about how a mutant dies belongs to the arrangement it is measured in** (N3). `pool.test.ts` said deleting the idle-client `error` listener "takes the test process down with it". Measured, it does not: `FakePool` is a bare `EventEmitter`, the emit is synchronous inside the test body, so the throw lands in vitest's own frame and the `not.toThrow` assertion converts it into an ordinary red test — **2 failed, 237 passed, every file run, no `ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR` and no dead worker.** The process death is real against a live `pg.Pool`, where the emit comes off a socket with no test frame on the stack, and that is the production consequence the listener exists to prevent — but this test does not demonstrate it. Same family as F5: a confident claim about evidence, written inside the thing that produces the evidence, and wrong in a way only running it reveals.

**An interface's error contract is read at the interface** (N4). The seam declares `ProviderRejected` and `ProviderUnavailable`; the Supabase adapter throws a third, `ServiceRoleKeyNotConfigured`, from `deleteUser`. It was documented at the adapter and in the adapter's file header — and the caller it exists for, the ticket that lands the first `deleteUser` call, reads `provider.ts` first and would have found a two-error contract. The exception now sits on `AuthProvider.deleteUser` itself, with why it is deliberately neither of the two and the instruction that whichever ticket lands a caller restores the variable to the required set and the passthrough in the same change.

**A test that builds its own subject is not a test of the wiring, and this one read as one** (F1). The central-invariant test — that the adapter is pointed at `SUPABASE_JWT_ISSUER`, so the project the gateway *calls* and the project whose tokens it *accepts* cannot be configured apart — constructed a **second** `SupabaseAuthProvider` with the URL written into the test and asserted about that, then separately asserted `wiring.deps.provider instanceof SupabaseAuthProvider`. Both assertions passed and neither touched `deps.ts`'s `authUrl`. Proved rather than argued: replacing `authUrl: policy.issuer` with a hardcoded literal leaves the old shape green and fails the new one, **1 failed / 24 passed**, and the failing test is the named one. The fix drives `wiring.deps.provider` itself by stubbing the global `fetch` before `authWiringFrom` runs — the adapter captures `config.fetch ?? globalThis.fetch` at construction — rather than by giving `authWiringFrom` a test-only parameter no production caller passes, which is how the thing under test stops being the thing that ships.

**`pool.ts` had two properties and no test for either, and both are the kind that fail invisibly** (F6). Release-on-throw is the property `db/connection.ts` calls *structural*; without the `finally`, every **failing** request leaks a connection, so a pool of ten drains only under the conditions nobody is watching. The idle-client `error` handler is worse: `pg` emits `error` on the pool with no request in flight — which every managed Postgres causes by closing idle connections, and causes to all of them at once during a database deploy — and an unhandled `error` event on an `EventEmitter` is `ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR` and a dead gateway. Both mutants survived the suite as first written. Both now die, named: removing the `finally` fails `theConnectionIsReleasedWhenTheCallbackThrows` and its release-count sibling, **and** the real-Postgres `theOnlyConnectionComesBackAfterTheCallbackThrows`, where `max: 1` turns a leak into the next lease failing rather than into a slow drift; deleting the handler fails `theIdleClientErrorIsHandled` and its keep-serving sibling. **The fake pool is deliberate for the second property and not for the first**: producing a real idle-client error means terminating a backend from a second connection and then waiting on a timer for an event, which is exactly the sleep-then-assert shape `CLAUDE.md` records as manufacturing mutation kills. The release property is tested both ways, and the real one is the stronger evidence.

**A mutant killed only incidentally has no test that says what it protects** (F7). `subject: session.email ?? email` in the verify route — which would key a Sonny identity on Supabase's view of the user rather than on the address the caller asserted, silently merging two people's sign-ins whenever Supabase's automatic linking had joined them — was already killed, by a **revocation** test that reads identity rows for entirely different reasons. That is a kill and it is not coverage: nothing in the suite named the boundary, so a later change to that revocation test would have removed the protection without anyone seeing it go. Two route-level pins now hold it directly, and under the mutant **3 tests fail** where 1 did. The adapter-side test that claimed to prove the same thing was renamed: it cannot, because nothing in the adapter decides the identity — what it establishes is the *premise*, that the provider's `user.email` really can name a different address from the one just verified.

**Supabase Auth cannot revoke a user's sessions from their id, so `signOutAllForUser` raises rather than approximating.** The operation `revocation.ts` needs is "revoke every session of user X, given X's id and no token of theirs". It is not in GoTrue's API: `openapi.yaml` publishes **43 paths** (`curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/supabase/auth/master/openapi.yaml | grep -cE "^  /"` → 43, read 2026-08-27 — an external file, so the figure is dated rather than pinned to a commit of ours), `/logout` is the only session-revoking one and it is authenticated by the *user's own* bearer token (`UserAuth`), deriving the user from that token rather than from a parameter, and the whole `/admin/*` surface — `generate_link`, `audit`, `users`, `users/{id}`, `users/{id}/factors`, `sso`, `oauth`, `custom-providers` — carries no session route at all. **`ProviderUnavailable` and not `ProviderRejected`, and that difference is the whole design**: `revocation.ts` treats `ProviderRejected` as "the provider says this is already done" and stamps `provider_session_revoked_at`, so rejecting would record a revocation that never happened in the one table that exists to say whether it did. Unavailable leaves the row owed, releases the lease, and lets `npm run revocations` report it — the mechanism working rather than failing. **What the account holder is exposed to meanwhile, enumerated rather than waved at**: nothing at this gateway, because `gate.ts` attributes every authenticated request through `accountForSupabaseUser`, which excludes a closed account, and `/v1/auth/refresh` refuses on the same read. What survives is at Supabase — a refresh token already in someone's hands can still mint Supabase access tokens against the project directly, and those open nothing here. **Two ways to close it and neither is an adapter's to choose**: delete the provider user (`deleteUser`, which takes the sessions with it, and which the account model deliberately does not do because identities are kept for their audit trail), or have the gateway mint a short-lived token for that user with `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` and present it to `/logout?scope=global` — `logout.go` shows that would work even with no `session_id` claim, and it is the gateway forging a user credential. **A founder's decision, recorded on the ticket, not taken here.**

**The seam's contract was read out of Supabase's own sources rather than from memory, and the published spec is wrong in one place that matters.** `POST /verify` for an OTP takes `type: "email"`, which is **not in `openapi.yaml`'s enum** — the spec lags the server. `mailer.go` defines `EmailOTPVerification = "email"` and `verify.go` handles it by checking both the confirmation and recovery token columns and resolving it to `signup` or `magiclink` itself, which is exactly what a code from `/otp` needs, since that endpoint mails a signup for a new address and a magic link for a known one. **Sending `magiclink` instead would refuse every first-ever sign-in** — and would have looked like a Supabase problem.

**GoTrue's error body has two shapes and which one you get depends on a request header, so all three sources are read.** With `X-Supabase-Api-Version: 2024-01-01` the body is `{ code: "<error_code>", message }`; without it the server marshals its legacy `HTTPError`, whose JSON tags are commented *"do not rename the JSON tags!"* in `apierrors.go` and where **`code` is the HTTP status as a number** and `error_code` carries the string. Reading `code` unconditionally would classify every legacy failure as unrecognised; reading it as a code in the legacy shape would classify a `400` as an error named "400". The adapter sends the header, prefers the `x-sb-error-code` **response header** (which `errors.go` stamps on both branches), falls back to `error_code`, then to `code` **only when it is a string**, then to the OAuth-shaped `error`.

**Rejected versus unavailable is decided by an allow-list of caller-fault codes, and the ordering puts 429 above it.** The list is "this is the caller's fault" rather than "this is transient", because the safe direction is asymmetric: an unlisted code treated as unavailable costs a user one retry against a 502, while a transient failure wrongly listed tells a user their code was wrong and, on `email/verify`, burns one of their five attempts. A 429 is unavailable **whatever code it names**, because a rate limit is never a statement about whether the input was correct.

**Supabase's automatic identity linking is reported and never imported, and the mistake it invites is one line long.** Supabase may attach a newly verified address to an existing `auth.users` row, so one `supabaseUserId` can cover several addresses and `user.email` is the row's primary address rather than the one just verified. This product's identity key is `(provider, subject)` and never the email (`docs/sonny-identity-linking-rule.md`). Reading `user.email` back as the subject is exactly how a code sent to `b@example.com` would land on `a@example.com`'s account — so the field is documented at the seam, at the adapter, and pinned by a test that makes the two differ.

**The auth base URL is `SUPABASE_JWT_ISSUER` rather than a variable of its own, and that is a correctness property rather than economy.** GoTrue stamps `iss` with its own API base and `auth/token.ts` compares every token's `iss` against this value exactly, so taking both from one variable makes "the project that mints the tokens is the project that verifies them" structural. Configured apart, a gateway mints at project A and verifies against project B — which presents as every request answering 401 with nothing in the logs to say why. `deps.ts` passes `policy.issuer` rather than `config.supabaseJwtIssuer`, so the adapter cannot be handed a string `requireSupabaseJwtPolicy` would have refused.

**A half-configured sign-in refuses at startup, and choosing the trigger correctly is most of that decision.** Four names mean sign-in and nothing else — `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET`, `SUPABASE_JWT_ISSUER`, `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` — so any of them present is the question, and `DATABASE_URL` and `RATE_LIMIT_SALT` are then requirements the answer carries. **Neither of those two is a trigger**, because a gateway holding a `DATABASE_URL` only to run migrations is a legitimate health-only deployment and treating it as intent would make that shape refuse to start. `SUPABASE_JWT_AUDIENCE` is excluded because it is defaulted, so its presence says nothing. Serving health-only for a partial set was the alternative and is worse than it sounds: it answers `404 resource.not_found` to every sign-in, which is **indistinguishable from the defect this branch fixed** and was measured reading exactly that way on SONNY-306.

**The pool needs an `error` handler or a managed Postgres takes the process down.** `pg` emits `error` on the pool when an *idle* client fails — which every managed Postgres causes, by closing idle connections, and causes to all of them at once during a database deploy. There is no request in flight to attach it to, and an unhandled `error` event on an `EventEmitter` is `ERR_UNHANDLED_ERROR` and a dead gateway, from an event whose correct handling is to log it and let the pool replace the connection. Also: `connectionTimeoutMillis` is set because `pg` otherwise waits **forever** for a free connection, so a database that has gone away turns every request into a hang with no error, no log line and no 500 — sockets accumulating until the process is killed.

**A rejected `app.close()` would have hung the container, and the ordering that makes shutdown correct is what creates that risk.** The pool must be drained *after* Fastify closes, because `close` waits for in-flight requests and those requests hold connections. Written as a promise chain, a rejected `close` skips everything after it: the pool stays open, `process.exit` is never reached, and the container sits there until its orchestrator sends SIGKILL — the shutdown path failing in the one way nobody watches. Each step is attempted and its failure logged rather than propagated. Measured: `docker stop` returns in under a second, exit code 0.

**`npm run check:secrets` scans *tracked* files, so a clean run before `git add` says nothing about the files you just wrote — and this branch was caught by that twice.** First: `authdeps.test.ts` needs an environment fixture, and writing it the obvious way spells `RATE_LIMIT_SALT: "…"` and two siblings — the exact name-anchored shape the scanner refuses, correctly, wherever it appears. The scanner reported **clean over 431 files** while those lines were untracked and **three findings** on the first run after the commit. `config.test.ts` had already solved that and says so in a comment; the fix is the same, binding the values to names. Second, in the fix round: `pool.test.ts` hands `pooledConnections` a connection string its fake pool never dials, and any DSN carrying a password is a finding unless it is the allowlisted local-development shape — **clean over 436 files** before the commit, **one finding** after. Both times the run that mattered was the one after `git add`, and both times the number before it looked exactly like a passing one. **The lesson is about the measurement rather than the fixture**: a scanner whose population is "tracked files" produces a reassuring number for work that is not yet in its population, and that number is indistinguishable from a real one. Run it after staging.

**Two claims in `auth/provider.ts` were stale and one of them was recorded as already fixed.** `userFromAccessToken`'s docstring said "this is the verification SONNY-203's middleware will do for every authenticated route", which is the opposite of what SONNY-203 built — verification is local and symmetric by the founder decision of 2026-08-21 — and **that branch's changelog entry states "the docstring is corrected"** while the correction never reached the file: `git log -- server/src/auth/provider.ts` names only SONNY-127's four commits. Corrected here, in the file the adapter implements, along with the Resend sentence above it. A record that says a correction was made is worth less than the correction, and reads exactly like one that was.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **No Supabase project exists, so no request in this branch has ever reached a real one.** The adapter's tests inject `fetch` and every response in them is one this repository wrote — authoritative about the *translation* (which request goes out, which error class comes back, which fields are read) and silent about whether a live project answers in these shapes. The shapes are not invented: each is cited to `supabase/auth`'s own published sources on the test that uses it. **What is owed is a first real sign-in against a real project**, and it is founder-owned setup rather than work: the project, its JWT secret, issuer, anon key and service-role key, and a Postgres with these migrations applied. Recorded on SONNY-307 with the exact list.
- **`signOutAllForUser` is unimplementable against Supabase's published API**, above. The debt is recorded, reported and bounded; closing it is a founder decision between two named options, now held on **SONNY-313**. `npm run revocations` points an operator at that ticket rather than, as it did until the fix round, at building an adapter that exists in the file beside it (F2).
- **Two auth routes answer 500 where §7.2 says 502**, `refresh` and `signout`, measured at `af3803b` and unchanged since. `email/verify` on the same branch of the same file already answers 502 for the identical condition. It became *reachable* because of this branch — no test fake ever threw `ProviderUnavailable` from those two methods — and `server/src/routes/auth.ts` is in neither this lane's region nor SONNY-130's, so it is filed as **SONNY-311** rather than taken.
- **`SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` is now optional, so `deleteUser` is reachable code with no configured credential in the default deployment.** That is the decision working, not a gap: nothing calls it, and the moment something does, its ticket adds the name back to the required set and the passthrough. What a future session must not do is "fix" the throw by making it a `ProviderUnavailable` — `revocation.ts` and the routes read those two errors as statements about Supabase, and this one is a statement about this deployment.
- **The pool's sizing and its TLS are configuration this branch does not decide.** `max: 10` rests on the gateway never nesting `withConnection` (`gate.ts` releases before the handler runs, and says so); a future route that nests must raise it or, better, not nest. SSL is entirely the connection string's — nothing constructs an `ssl` object and in particular nothing sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, which over the public internet is an encrypted channel to whoever answered.

**A rebase's own tooling has a blind spot on this half of the repository, and it is the same shape as the Swift one.** `CLAUDE.md` records that `swift build` does not build the test targets, so a rebase that breaks them passes it. `npm run build` is exactly that on the server side — `tsconfig.json` includes only the sources under `src` — and this branch measured it: on the tree where SONNY-130's `test/support/config.ts` imported a constant this branch had renamed, **`npm run build` exited 0 and `npm run typecheck` exited 2**. Neither file conflicted. So the rebase rule for `server/` is `npm run typecheck` **and** the full suite, never the build alone and never the conflict list.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **none left open on this branch.** The one this entry opened with — which of the two ways to revoke a closed account's Supabase sessions this product wants — now has its own ticket, **SONNY-313**, with both options written up; it is a founder's to answer and nothing here is blocked on it, since the debt is recorded and reported today. The other decision the review raised, whether the service-role key should be required, was **answered** during the round as option (c) and is recorded above rather than left open.

Next branch: per the roadmap and the user's assignment; this lane holds no further tickets.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The type names still say OpenAI and Tavily, and that is a decision rather than an oversight.** SONNY-130's sixth requirement is that nothing in the client names a provider, and the acceptance criterion asks for a grep. What the grep is actually about is the **model identifier, the vendor endpoint and the provider choice** — the three things that would otherwise need an app release to change — and all three are gone. The names stay for two checkable reasons. `CerebrasPlanner`, on this ticket's never-touch list, calls `OpenAIPlanner.systemPrompt(toolRegistry:)`, so renaming that type is an edit to a forbidden file; and the API contract §4.2, written for this row, cites that same symbol as the post-move prompt builder. The ticket's own never-touch list also *requires* `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `TAVILY_API_KEY` to remain as strings in these four files, so a file-level grep for "OpenAI" could never have been the criterion. What is asserted instead is the property that matters, on the bytes, in three of the four suites — **under two names, not one** (PR #139, F6): `theRequestNamesNoProviderNoModelAndNoVendorEndpoint` in `OpenAIPlannerTests` and `OpenAITranscriberTests`, and `theRequestNamesNoProviderAndNoVendorEndpoint` in `TavilySearchProviderTests`, which drops "NoModel" because no model identifier was ever involved in a search. The entry said one name in three suites; `git grep -c 'func theRequestNamesNoProviderNoModelAndNoVendorEndpoint' -- Tests` answers 2 files.

**The permission-readiness row now reports on a key nothing reads, and that is SONNY-136's to fix** (PR #139, F10). `PermissionReadinessService` still shows an "OpenAI" row saying either "OPENAI_API_KEY is set." or "Export OPENAI_API_KEY before launching Sonny." Both were true before this branch and neither is now: no client reads that key, so a signed-in user with no key sees a readiness row asking them to fix something that does not matter, and a user *with* one sees a green row for a credential that does nothing. It is left rather than fixed because the check and its strings are the environment-variable surface `feature/row-12-degradation` and SONNY-136 own — the same reason `hasAPIKey` and the "export a variable" errors stay — and because what should replace it is a question about readiness copy rather than about this move. A dated comment on SONNY-136 names it.

**One provider name really was still reaching the wire, and it came from a capability description.** The system prompt folds in every capability's description and side effects through `ToolRegistry.plannerDescription`, and two of them named a provider. `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter`'s side-effect list said fetched page content is "sent to OpenAI" — a claim this branch made **false**, and one a user reads in a dry run before approving a network egress, so it is corrected to "to Sonny". `PermissionReadinessCapabilityAdapter`'s "Show readiness for OpenAI key" is **left**, because the readiness check it describes genuinely still reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` and removing that is `feature/row-12-degradation`'s. `theOnlyProviderNameLeftInTheSystemPromptIsTheOneTheDegradationBranchRemoves` pins both halves at exactly one occurrence, so the day that branch lands, the count moving is what says so. **The test found this, not a reading**: the first version of the provider-name assertion covered the whole body and went red.

**The mic would have stayed blocked on exactly the launch this ticket exists to make work.** `voiceConfigurationBlocker` read `hasAPIKey`, and the founder's manual item launches the packaged app **from Finder**, which inherits no shell environment — so `OPENAI_API_KEY` is never set there and the mic would have refused with "No API key is set up. Add one, then relaunch Sonny." while transcription no longer needs a key at all. The live answer is now `nil`; the message, the override seam and `hasAPIKey` itself all stay for `feature/row-12-degradation` and SONNY-136. This is the kind of gate that is invisible from the diff of the thing it blocks.

**`Retention.none` is spelled `notStored`, because a case named `none` silently means `nil`.** `#expect(context?.retention == .none)` compares against `Optional.none` and passes for a context that is absent, which is the opposite of what it reads as — and the first draft of `BackendTaskIdentityTests` was written exactly that way and asserted nothing until the compiler's inference made it visible. The wire value is still `"none"`, because the wire value is the contract's.

**One client per process, and the reason is the refresh guard rather than tidiness.** `SonnyBackendClient` holds the single-flight generation counter that makes ten concurrent `401 auth.token_expired`s cause one rotation; the server reads a second rotation presented past its ten-second overlap as theft and revokes the whole family (§3.3). PR #133 recorded that this was latent because `signOut` was then the only `.bearer` caller — "it goes live the moment SONNY-130 and SONNY-131 add a second concurrent authenticated caller". This branch is that moment, so `main.swift` builds one client and hands it to both `SonnyAccountModel` and `AgentViewModel`, and neither has a default for it.

**`PlannerProvider` has two construction shapes now, and it collapses back to one when the router branch lands.** A planner that runs through the backend needs the run's `task_id` and `retention`; a planner that holds its own provider credential needs neither. `CerebrasPlanner` is the second kind and is never-touch, so a single reshaped closure signature would have been an edit to a forbidden file. The enum documents the transitional state rather than hiding it.

**The audio limit is enforced in different units on each side, and that is the design rather than a compromise.** The Mac caps a *duration* and refuses before sending; the server caps *bytes* at §6.1's 10 MiB. The Mac is the only side that knows a duration honestly — a client-supplied one would be a client-trust decision on the field that decides the bill, which §2.4.1 forbids in general — and at this recorder's bitrate 180 seconds is roughly 2 MB, so the client's cap binds an order of magnitude before the server's, which is the ordering §6.2 requires. The refusal is about **how long the key was held**, not how long the file is: `AVAudioRecorder` stops itself at the ceiling, so a ten-minute hold produces a short file, and a check that read the file's length would have transcribed every over-long recording as an ordinary one.

**A client that meets `401 auth.unauthenticated` signs itself out, and a test driving several routes with one client proves nothing.** §7.2 case 1b, working as specified: the first route's 401 cleared the Keychain entry and every route after it failed with `notSignedIn` before sending. The live suite's first run showed three of four "failing" for that reason alone. A fresh client per route is the fix, and it is written at the test.

**A discovery ticket was filed for something another lane had already filed, and the failure is worth recording.** SONNY-312 duplicated **SONNY-307** — no deployed gateway mounts an authenticated route, because `server/src/server.ts` supplies no `AuthDeps` and no concrete `AuthProvider` exists. SONNY-306's session found it first and filed it 51 minutes earlier; this session reached the same measurement independently while trying to discharge acceptance criterion 1, and filed without reading the board. SONNY-312 is cancelled with that reason on it, and the evidence it carried — that everything *behind* the missing wiring works — is a comment on SONNY-307. **The board is shared state; a session about to file a discovery ticket should read it first.**

**`retention` is validated and deliberately not honoured, and saying so is the point.** §2.4.2's loud `400` is enforced on all four routes. Nothing is stored at all — there is no content store yet — and SONNY-134 builds it together with §10.1's rule that retention is enforced where the storing happens rather than at the call site. Validating now makes the client's half real and testable from the day it ships; claiming the guarantee now would be claiming a promise nothing keeps.

**PR #139's fix round, and the one finding that was a real defect.**

**F1 was the blocker and it was a genuine hole.** A scheduled run's `task_id` was held by nothing: the reviewer measured *both* mutants surviving the whole suite — deleting the mint at the top of `performScheduledRun`, and deleting `id: currentTaskID` from the row it writes. The reason neither showed is worth keeping, because it generalises: `CompletedTaskRecord.id` defaults to a fresh `UUID()` **evaluated per call**, so either break still produces a row with a perfectly valid-looking id, and the scheduled tests that read `record.id` use it only as a lookup key into the plan-detail store — which works whatever the id is. The consequence in production is silent and is exactly what §5.1 exists to prevent: the backend's retained content under one key, the local row under another, and `DELETE /v1/tasks/{task_id}` with nothing to join. `aScheduledRunsRequestAndItsRowAreFiledUnderOneTaskIDOfItsOwn` closes it by asserting the thing the id is *for* rather than that it exists — a real scheduled routine whose one step is a web search, with the `task_id` read off the wire and compared against the row the run wrote, and a foreground run before it so "minted its own" is a claim about two real rows. It answers with **no** search results deliberately, so `web_to_markdown` fails at `noSearchResults` before any page is fetched: `AgentViewModel` passes no `webPageLoader`, so a result that resolved would have been fetched for real.

**Everything else in the round was a claim that was wrong rather than behaviour that was.** Worth naming because they are all the same failure — prose and tests that describe the code rather than being checked against it:

The first draft of the server's assertion went red on `search`, which is what caught it.

``
4289  … aScheduledRunsRequestAndItsRowAreFiledUnderOneTaskIDOfItsOwn() recorded an issue at

Line 4293 is a **declared** untrusted signature, and it belongs to `HangBackstopTests`' own **known** issue on 4291 — deliberate, expected, not red — which a parallel suite printed inside the window the classifier reads for the test named on 4289. The suite line says "with 1 issue", so the killing test recorded exactly one, and it was the expectation. **This is SONNY-224's manufactured kill in reverse**: a mutant that was caught, reported as one nothing caught. Three runs at `29d6f2d` characterise it — full battery → R1 `UNATTRIBUTED`; `--only R1` → `KILLED by 1 test`; full battery again → `12 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed`. **Filed as SONNY-315**, because `CLAUDE.md` already names why this shape survives being looked at: re-running names the test, the reader concludes flake, and the gap stays. The two the reviewer measured surviving are R1 and R2, and each is now killed by exactly one test — `aScheduledRunsRequestAndItsRowAreFiledUnderOneTaskIDOfItsOwn`, on a different assertion each time: the mint deletion fails "the scheduled run's id differs from the foreground run's", the record deletion fails "the wire's `task_id` is the row's id". R3 covers the foreground twin, R4–R6 the deadline and route-mapping shapes, R7–R8 F7's two sentences, R9 F12's scan, and R10–R12 the usage model name, the retention derivation and the audio cap.

**Cycle 2's two findings, both figures, and both about the same habit.**

**G2 — the comment written *while removing a guard* was wrong about the guard that remained.** F11 deleted an unreachable per-part byte check, and the comment put in its place said the ceiling was enforced "twice" and that `bodyLimit` "refuses first by construction". Neither had been measured, and both are false: registering `@fastify/multipart` replaces the body parser for its content type, so the route's `bodyLimit` is **never consulted** for a multipart body. Measured rather than reasoned about — with `bodyLimit` lowered to 1 MiB and `fileSize` left at 10 MiB, a 2 MiB multipart body is **served 200**; with the real config an 11 MiB body raises `FST_REQ_FILE_TOO_LARGE` with `statusCode: 413`, which `errors.ts` maps on its `status === 413` arm rather than on the `FST_ERR_CTP_BODY_TOO_LARGE` name arm. So there is **one** guard, it is `limits.fileSize`, and the `bodyLimit` option stays only because it still bounds a body sent to this route under some *other* content type. **Two comments in one place have now been wrong about this in opposite directions**, the first calling the pair "not redundant" and the second calling it redundant-by-construction, and neither author measured. The comment now says which guard fires and what the test pins — the outcome, not the mechanism — and the two tests' wording no longer attributes the ceiling to `bodyLimit` either.

**G1 — F2's correction reached two of its three sites.** `server/src/model/limits.ts` still said "The 15-second difference between them is §12's", twelve lines above the four literals that disprove it for `search`. Corrected, and a tree-wide sweep for the claim in any phrasing finds no fourth site.

**The habit both name is the one this branch keeps paying for**: a sentence about mechanism, written from a reading rather than from a measurement, in a place where the code is right and only the prose is wrong. F2, F4, F6, F11 and both of these are the same failure, and the count is the point — it is most of the review.

Neither is reachable today — the client does not compress, and nothing any route returns comes near a megabyte — so this is owed work rather than a live defect, and it has no ticket of its own yet. **The sharp edge is on the next branch**: §6.4 says SONNY-131 "flips both in one edit" when the vision client is repointed, and doing that today would send a gzip-encoded body to a gateway with no decoder, which Fastify answers as a malformed body. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A property required to mirror another does not mirror it because two doc comments say so, and the gap can be the one state whose entire purpose is to be seen.** `AgentViewModel.hasVisibleWidgetPanel` and `FloatingWidgetView.state` have each said, in their own doc comments, that they mirror one another and must be changed together. `state` has had a `.controlling` branch since row I. The predicate had **no `visionSessionProgress` term at all** — so a live session with nothing parked on it fell through to the origin-gated `isRunning` branch, was answered `activeTaskOrigin == .widget`, and rendered nothing. The widget resolved to `.controlling` and the panel that draws it was never on screen. Every source scan in the suite agreed, correctly, that each branch was where the file said it was; none of them was looking at whether one property's branch set was the other's.

**The general shape, since this is the second time in a week the same pair has produced a defect** (SONNY-255 was the first — `.permission` ranked below `.controlling`, so an approval raised mid-session was answerable on no widget surface for the whole length of every session). A precedence duplicated across two properties can go wrong in two independent ways: the *order* of the branches can disagree, and the *set* of branches can. SONNY-255 was the first, this was the second, and a test written for either shape does not see the other. What holds it now is positional — `thePanelPredicatePutsTheLiveSessionWhereTheWidgetsOwnPrecedenceDoes` asserts both properties' orderings in one test — and `WidgetComposerStateTests` already holds `composerState` against `state` the same way. Three properties read one precedence; the pins are per-pair, not per-property, and a fourth reader would need its own.

**Unconditional was the right answer for the session term, and the reasoning is the opposite of the one the origin gate below it rests on.** Origin-gating the working panel is deliberate and documented: a Command-Center-origin run already reports itself in `CommandCenterRunningIndicator`, so a widget progress panel would be a second one. The HUD is not that kind of progress — it names the app, carries Pause and Stop, and `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` deliberately has none — so there is no second HUD anywhere for it to duplicate. Writing the term to enumerate the origins that can reach it would have made the origin gate the thing that decides whether a program moving the user's cursor says so.

**The `.scheduled` question is moot and the branch says why rather than leaving it to be re-derived.** Unattended screen control is refused three independent ways — `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations` rejects `.visionSession` at the routine store's write door, `performScheduledRun`'s explicit belt checks the routine's steps, its nested steps and the prepared plan and pauses the schedule, and its fixed `.approved(.tier2)` ceiling cannot satisfy a tier-3 assessment. All three were re-read at `6b72909` rather than copied from the ticket. Were one of them ever to move, rendering the HUD is still the answer this term should give, which is why the reasoning is written as "the question does not arise, and here is what the answer would be" rather than as a guard.

**A pin placed at "exactly one" so that it will one day read zero is worth more than an exemption, and it worked.** SONNY-255's session found the capture review's hand-written step line while writing the scan that forbids either surface hand-writing a session's words. It could have exempted the site. Instead it pinned the population at one and named the ticket in the assertion message, so a *second* hand-written line would fail the scan and the count would fall to zero the moment the type change landed. It did, and the scan no longer names a ticket. **What that pattern does not do** is check the other direction: a count of zero hand-written lines is equally satisfied by a panel that dropped the line altogether, so the scan now also asserts the owner is read at every site that shows one.

**Counting call sites cannot see an argument order, and a scan that only counts reads as coverage.** `stepLine(iteration: preview.maximumIterations, maximumIterations: preview.iteration)` compiles, renders "Step 8 of 2", and satisfies every "the owner is read once here" assertion in the suite. This repository has no way to ask a SwiftUI view what it drew, so the pin has to be the exact call at the exact site — the shape `everySessionControlWearsItsOwnAccessibilityLabel` already uses for accessibility labels. Two of the four step-line sites now carry it and two do not; that is written into the scan's own comment and filed as **SONNY-310** rather than absorbed, since the two unpinned sites are code this branch did not touch.

**A bounded correction has to sweep for the claim, not for the line numbers it was handed.** SONNY-295 named two lines in one file. A third site in a second file — `ResumeOfferPresentation.continueLabel`'s doc comment — carried the same doubt in different words and would have been left asserting the negation of its neighbour. This is the same failure the rules file records against itself in its Approval visibility section, where a bounded edit removed a false premise from the sentence that stated it loudest and left it standing five sentences away. Sweeping by claim found the third site; sweeping by the ticket's `file:line` list would not have.

**What one manual observation establishes is what was observed.** The founder hovered the unfinished-task offer's tick and cross on 2026-08-26 and reported "yes tooltips appeared" — the first direct evidence in this project's record that a `.help` tooltip reaches anything in the floating widget. It is written down as exactly that: one pass, two buttons, one Mac. `micHintPointerEnteredMic`'s claim that `.help()` proved unreliable for the *mic button* is left standing on purpose and the rewrite says why the two do not contradict each other. The two `.help` calls that predate the finding — the compact capsule's and the clarification panel's cancel — are still unhovered by anyone, and now have a checklist row of their own.

**`git grep`'s ERE engine does not honour `\s` either, and it failed silently inside this branch's own work.** `CLAUDE.md` records the `\b` case. Counting the file's `.help` calls with `git grep -nE '^\s*\.help\(' -- Sources/MacAgent/FloatingWidgetView.swift` printed **nothing and exited 1** — byte for byte what a file with no such call looks like — while `git grep -cE '^[[:space:]]*\.help\('` and `git grep -cP '^\s*\.help\('` both answer **4**. Caught only because the answer was obviously wrong; a pattern whose true answer happened to be zero would have been recorded as a measurement. The command is written into the comment beside the number, POSIX class included, with a sentence saying why it is not the obvious spelling.

**Two measurements at once on this machine contaminate each other, and one of the two directions is the reassuring one.** Measured 2026-08-27 at `a85fd08`, before this branch's second rebase: the baseline suite was run in a detached worktree while a battery was running in this one, and came back **red — 2245 tests, 176 issues, exit 1** — every failure a vision-session test, the ones `CLAUDE.md` already records as stalling the process at ten concurrent `VNRecognizeTextRequest`s. Run alone afterwards, the same tree at the same SHA is **2245 in 155, exit 0**. Worktrees isolate the code and the build directory; they do not isolate the machine, the on-device recognizer, or the scheduler. `scripts/mutate --help` states the outward half of this — a battery loads the machine, which is the condition a timing-sensitive test needs to fail — and this is the inward half: **a second suite is what does the loading, and the contaminated run is the one you started, not the one already going.** Neither number was reported until the clean one existed. **What SONNY-302 changes about it, and what it does not:** PR #138's `HangBackstop` now separates a starved wait from a stuck one and both of its wordings are declared in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`, so the *backstop* half of a cascade like this is excluded from a kill count on today's tree. The failures downstream of a run that never finished are ordinary assertions and are not, so the operational rule stands unchanged: run one measurement at a time.

**A battery's *verdict* survives that contention and its *kill count* does not, which is a false reading in the flattering direction.** Measured at `5ad615a` — a head the second rebase has since replaced, so read the figures as true of that branch at that moment. R3 came back `KILLED by 58 test(s)` in 148s on two separate runs, one contended and one that looked quiet. Fifty-eight is not a coverage figure: R1 and R3 are **semantically identical mutants** — both make the predicate answer `activeTaskOrigin == .widget` for a live session — and R1 was killed by 2 in 40s, so the two could not honestly differ. Re-run alone with `--only R3`, R3 is **killed by exactly those same 2 tests in 38s**. The extra fifty-six were cascade: 44 of the recorded issues were `timed out after 30s waiting for: the run to finish` and the rest were assertions downstream of runs that never completed. The classifier of the day excluded the declared backstop signatures, as SONNY-224 built it to, and still counted the downstream assertions, because those are real assertions failing — they are simply not about the mutant. **So the existing rule has a second half worth stating:** a manufactured kill on a mutant nothing caught is the dangerous case `CLAUDE.md` records, and a manufactured *count* on a mutant that really was caught is the quiet one — it reads as broad coverage, it sits beside a correct verdict, and nothing in the report distinguishes it. The cheap check is the one that caught it here: **two mutants that must be equivalent, compared.** At the rebased head, on a quiet machine and against #136's rewritten classifier, R1, R2 and R3 each report `KILLED by 2` and the cascade does not appear at all — which is what a clean reading of these three mutants looks like, and is why the equivalence check is worth keeping rather than trusting a run that happens to look tidy.

**A number written to satisfy the write-the-command-beside-it rule is checked the same way the number is.** `.claude/rules/macagent-ui-conventions.md` carried "13 assertion lines across 5 files at `fef3684`". The stamp was honest and the enumeration complete when taken — `fef3684` is 2026-08-21 and `ResumableTaskRunTests.swift` did not exist there. Today the same command answers 29 across 6. Re-measured here rather than adjusted, and **the file list was re-enumerated with the count**, because a list of names goes stale exactly the way a count does and reads as complete either way.

Net **+13 tests / +1 suite** — unchanged by the rebase, `main` having added no test. `scripts/warnings`: **0 warnings**, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled, three separate runs each stamping `023e29a (clean)`. `scripts/mutate selftest` against the merged script: **all checks passed**, now 176 checks across 37 groups where the pre-merge script had 164 across 35 — #136's two new arms. **Eleven consecutive green full runs at `023e29a`**, eight plain and three each beside a concurrent `scripts/warnings` full recompile, at one-minute load averages of 5.2 to 14.0. The claim that does not depend on load is the mechanism, below.) None of the four was re-run for this entry's own stamping commit, whose diff is this file alone.

Behavior added: none the user can see. No file under `Sources/` is touched.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims): every assertion in `VisionSessionRunTests` is untouched — the 65 call-site lines pass the same conditions and the tests assert exactly what they asserted before. On a machine that is giving the poll loop its turns the deadline is unchanged at thirty seconds and a stuck loop fails there with the same declared wording, because 500 observations arrive in about three seconds and the wall clock is still the binding constraint. `AgentActionExecutorTests.waitForLaunchSignal` is untouched, keeps its own 300 s backstop and keeps its copy of the deadlock wording, which is why that record's `sites` stays at 2. The nine other view-model wait helpers are untouched and their three declaration records are unchanged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A hang backstop's claim is about observations, and the wall clock was standing in for them badly enough to be measuring something else entirely.** The sentence a timeout asserts is "I looked, repeatedly, and it was never true". Thirty seconds was a proxy for "thousands of looks". In this test process it is a proxy for **two**. Both test targets build into one process, `MacAgentTests` is full of `@MainActor` suites, Swift Testing runs suites concurrently, and the main actor's queue under that concurrency is hundreds of jobs deep — so a poll loop gets one turn per lap of that queue and a lap is seconds to tens of seconds. Measured with `6b72909` checked out plus a counting-only probe patch, over five runs (one filtered, four full, two of them red): **537 waits completed and the most observations any of them needed was 62**, p99 25, median 6; **177 waits reached the deadline and 145 of those had made one or two observations**, the longest single blind spell between consecutive looks being **34.0 s**. The two populations are two orders of magnitude apart, which is what makes the count safe to read where the clock was not.

**It is not CPU, and that had to be established rather than assumed, because the ticket's own leading hypothesis was that it was.** A detached probe ticking every 10 ms off the main actor ran at **56–91 ticks/s in every run, red and green alike**, against a nominal 100 — the process was being scheduled normally throughout. The ticket's hypothesis was contention on the on-device Vision recognizer, by analogy with `LocalRedactionLiveVisionTests`' `.serialized` attribute. **That hypothesis is false for this suite and can be retired**: `VisionSessionRunTests` uses `EmptyRecognizer`, `ScriptedRecognizer` and `ThrowingRecognizer`, all of them pure fakes declared in the file, and no test in it constructs a real `VisionImageTextRecognizer`. Serializing the suite would have cost wall clock and fixed nothing.

**The rule that replaces it, and why the number 500.** A timeout may be called a deadlock only once the condition has actually been evaluated `observationFloor` times; until then, reaching the deadline decides nothing and the wait continues, bounded by a ceiling at which it fails as *starvation* in wording of its own. 500 is eight times the worst case ever observed for a wait that finished (62) and 250 times what a starved wait manages. The margin is deliberately coarse — anything between about 200 and a few thousand behaves identically, because the populations are so far apart — and the two ways to get it wrong are named at the constant: small enough for a starved wait to reach, or large enough that a free-running poll loop cannot.

**This is deliberately not a longer timer, which was the founder's whole point in triage.** Thirty seconds survives untouched, and so does the deadlock wording. What changed is what the timeout is entitled to conclude. On an unloaded machine nothing about the behaviour changes at all: 500 looks arrive in about three seconds, so the deadline is what binds, and a stuck loop still fails at thirty seconds.

**Both failure modes still fail, and the ceiling is what keeps starvation from becoming a hang.** `CLAUDE.md` protects exactly one property here — a genuine deadlock fails rather than wedging the run — and it holds in both directions: a healthy process that never satisfies the condition reaches the floor and fails as stuck; a starved one reaches the ceiling and fails as starved. Neither waits forever. The ceiling **overshoots**, and cannot not: it is read inside the poll loop, which only runs when the actor grants a turn, so a wait whose lap is twenty seconds long discovers it is past the ceiling up to a lap late. The measured overshoot on the thirty-second deadline was to about 50 s. The bound is "one lap past the ceiling", which is finite; it is not the tight bound a timing assertion would need, and this is not one.

**The cascade is the reason the old shape cost more than the tests it failed — and the reason the deadlock wording stays declared as untrusted.** A starved wait recorded its issue and *returned*; the test then carried on with a precondition that had never arrived — an approval never raised, a run never started — and every later wait in that test timed out too, at a perfectly healthy six-millisecond cadence. That second wave is indistinguishable from a real deadlock from the outside, and it reaches the 500-observation floor easily. In the fourth instrumented run, **19 of 19** timeouts that had collected a thousand observations or more were preceded, inside the same test, by one that had collected two or fewer; **73 starved waits became 195 issues across 68 test functions**. So load can still reach the deadlock wording, one step removed, and `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures` keeps that record. Understating coverage is the safe direction and the file says so; manufacturing a kill is the failure SONNY-224 exists to prevent. **The open question is whether that record can be dropped once the cascade is gone** — see Open questions.

**The declaration file was coordinated rather than left to drift, and the coordination is the checkable part.** The starvation wording is a sixth record at one site; the deadlock wording is unchanged text, still at two sites — `HangBackstop.wait` and `AgentActionExecutorTests.waitForLaunchSignal` — so its `sites 2` needed no edit, which is the outcome to want: the guard would have failed had the count moved. Both records were then checked end to end against the real classifier rather than by reading it: a throwaway suite drove one starved wait and one stuck wait to a real (not known) issue, and `classify_failures` from `scripts/mutate`, run over that log, returned `U` for both. A third probe recorded a starvation issue **and** an ordinary `#expect` failure in the same test and came back `T`, confirming the per-issue rule PR #112 built still holds for the new wording — which matters, because `HangBackstopTests` failing on an assertion has to stay evidence.

**The pitfall, and it arrived inside this ticket's own work: two of the new tests bet on wall-clock windows and lost, in the exact way the ticket is about.** They were written with `deadline: 0.05` and `ceiling: 0.2` for speed, passed in isolation, and both went red inside a full-suite run **having managed two looks in 10.8 seconds**. `CLAUDE.md` already states the rule they broke — wait on a real signal, and make the state being asserted unable to expire on its own — and it took a red run to notice, because a small deadline reads as an efficiency rather than as a bet. They now assert on **look counts** under wall clocks nothing can approach: the "becomes true" test sets both bounds to an hour so only the condition can end it, and the "never becomes true" test sets the deadline to **zero** and the ceiling to an hour, which isolates the half being tested — the wall-clock half is satisfied from the first instant, the floor is the only thing that can decide, and the wait ends on the exact look that reaches it. Four looks, not four seconds. The one test that must use a clock, the ceiling test, asserts a **lower** bound only, which load can only reinforce.

**Failures now point at the call site.** `sourceLocation` is threaded through `waitUntil` and `waitForIdle` and defaulted with `#_sourceLocation`, so a timeout names the test's own step rather than the helper — with 65 call-site lines among 77 test functions in one file (`grep -cE 'waitUntil[(]'` and `grep -c '^    @Test'` over it; the patterns are bracketed and anchored so prose about them is not counted, which the plainer ones were, and writing them the obvious way moved both numbers by one), that is the difference between a failure that says where and one that says nothing.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The nine other copies of this backstop are untouched.** `ProductShellTests`, `ConsequenceRuleDispatchTests`, `InteractionModeTests`, `WorkspaceDetailSheetTests`, `FollowUpOnTaskTests`, `RunTaskAgainTests`, `ResumableTaskRunTests`, `ClarificationExitTests` and `MemoryCommandCenterTests` still hold wall-clock-only loops in three wordings, and they are exposed to exactly the same starvation. That is **SONNY-261**, which was filed for it, carries a founder-facing policy call this ticket had no mandate to make, and now has a shared home to adopt: a comment on it records that `HangBackstop` exists and that adopting it collapses its three declaration records to one. Not absorbed here, deliberately — SONNY-302 names one suite.
- **`AgentActionExecutorTests.waitForLaunchSignal` keeps its wall clock**, and should: it polls the filesystem for a child process's own launch signal from outside the main actor, its backstop is 300 s, and its comment already argues why scheduling delay cannot reach it.
- **The floor is a constant, not a measurement.** It does not adapt to how busy the process is, and it does not need to while the two populations stay two orders of magnitude apart. If a legitimate wait ever needs hundreds of laps, this becomes a threshold rather than a backstop, and the constant's own comment says which direction each kind of wrongness lies in.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **whether the deadlock wording can stop being declared untrusted.** It is kept only because the cascade can still manufacture it one step removed, and the cascade is now much rarer — a starved wait usually completes instead of aborting. Dropping the record would give a mutation battery back every mutant that genuinely deadlocks the vision loop, which is real coverage in the suite that most needs it. What it needs is evidence, not an argument: instrumented full runs on a loaded machine showing no wait reaching the ceiling over a decent sample. Not attempted here, because "understating coverage is the safe direction" and this branch had no such sample.

Next branch: unassigned — SONNY-302 is a standalone fix lane, not a roadmap row.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**File existence pointed the wrong way for one of the six, and it is the one a session would have been most confident about.** The ticket handed this session five file-existence greps and said in terms that they were a starting point and not the verification. Generic schemas are not: a plan step is still one flat struct with a field per operation and one global key whitelist shared by every operation. Rounding that bullet either way would have been wrong in a way nothing downstream would ever catch, which is why the annotation says two-of-three and gives all three counts with their commands.

It happened again here, in the same lane, to a session that had read it. This branch was cut at `6b72909` and rebased onto `0985e5b` after PRs #134 and #136 landed. `git diff --name-only 6b72909..HEAD | grep -cv '^docs/'` answered **0** before the rebase and answers **4** after it — `CLAUDE.md`, `scripts/mutate`, `server/README.md` and `server/scripts/deploy.sh`, none of them this branch's, all swept in by a range that starts at a base `main` has moved past. At the real base it is `git diff --name-only 0985e5b..HEAD | grep -cv '^docs/'` → **0**, read off stdout. **Reading the old range would have printed a 4 nobody expected**, which is the loud failure; the quiet one is that the *unchanged* answer is what a reader trusts, and every Swift figure in this entry is unchanged. Which is why they were re-run rather than assumed.

**The Swift figures are restamped rather than restated, and that needs the tree-identity proof to be legitimate.** `CLAUDE.md`'s rebase rule says a figure taken before a rebase is re-measured and never translated, because the new base carries `main`'s own changes. Here the new base's changes reach no path any of those figures describes, and that is checked rather than reasoned: `git rev-parse 6b72909:Sources 0985e5b:Sources` prints one hash twice, and so does the same over `:Tests` — the two bases hold **the same tree object** on both paths, and `git diff --name-only 6b72909..0985e5b -- Sources Tests Package.swift Package.resolved` names 0 files. That is `WORKFLOW.md` §8's distinction exactly: a rebase moves content, so a figure is re-measured; a rename over an identical tree is safe. Every command was re-run at `0985e5b` anyway, by the same extract-from-the-Markdown-and-execute pass that wrote them, because a provably identical input is a reason to expect the same number and not a substitute for taking it.

**One conflict, and it was this file's newest-first insertion point — the same one SONNY-289 and SONNY-305 hit.** Resolved keep-both, this entry above SONNY-305's and SONNY-306's, and the resolution was proved rather than eyeballed: all three entries are byte-identical to their sources (45, 55 and 58 lines — this branch's against `37496c3`, the other two against `origin/main`), everything above `## Entries` and everything below the three entries is byte-identical to `origin/main`'s copy, so this branch's contribution to the file is purely additive. The check earned its keep on the first pass: it caught one dropped blank line between this entry's last sentence and SONNY-305's heading — a one-line loss that renders identically in Markdown and would have survived any amount of reading. `docs/sonny-manual-test-checklist.md` merged clean and was checked the same way: delete this branch's 31-line block and the file is byte-identical to `origin/main`'s, so SONNY-306's new rows are untouched.

**An append-first file moves its neighbours' line numbers, and this entry does it to SONNY-289's twice.** That entry restated two citations as `:1415` and `:6576` after PR #129 inserted 49 lines above them. They were at `:1788` and `:6949` when this entry was first written; they are at **`:1901` and `:7062`** at `0985e5b` after #134 and #136 appended two more entries, and at **`:1952` and `:7113`** once this entry lands (`git grep -nE 'sonny-major-release-spec\.md.?:[0-9]+' 0985e5b -- docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` and the same against `HEAD`). Three different pairs for one unmoved sentence, inside a single day. Nothing is wrong with either figure — each was true of the tree it was stamped at, which is what a branch SHA means here (`WORKFLOW.md` §8) — and the dated entry is left verbatim rather than restamped. The transferable part is that **a line number inside `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` has a half-life of about one merge**, because `## Entries` is a single newest-first insertion point every branch writes to. Citations *into* other files are stable; citations into this one are not, and a reader chasing one should expect to re-find it rather than treat a miss as a defect.

**The rebase, and why the conflict list was not the population that could break it.** PR #134 merged SONNY-306's entry in behind this branch. Behavior added:
- **A failing test is found on either line shape swift-testing uses to name one.** The harness read only the per-test summary, `Test <name> failed after …`. A run that records a test's issues and never prints that line named the killing test repeatedly, in `Test <name> recorded an issue …` lines, and the report said `KILLED — the run failed but named no test` with advice to go looking for a crash that had not happened.
- **A mutant whose only red is a declared failure on that path comes back UNATTRIBUTED instead of KILLED** — see the second direction below.
- **The unnamed-kill message says what it searched** — "no test is named on either line shape" — so the remaining case, a trapped process, stops sharing a sentence with the one that was misdiagnosed as it.
- **`ST_OUT` in the selftest is what the report said**, with the echoed stand-in command cut out of it.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **Ordinary battery logs parse identically.** Both readers were run pre- and post-fix over all **147** logs from the twenty recorded battery runs under `.build/mutate/` on the main checkout, and every one produced byte-identical output (`bash scan` over `git show a85fd08:scripts/mutate` against the branch's copy, re-run at `1138384`; the script is in SONNY-305's closing comment). The change is confined to logs of the seam's shape.
- **A trapped test process still reports `KILLED — the run failed but named no test`, correctly**, because a dead process prints no issue lines either. The selftest's trap arm passes unchanged and now pins the message's added sentence.
- **The declaration machinery is untouched.** `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures` has no diff, `ALWAYS_TRUSTED` is unchanged, and a test that *does* get its summary line is classified by exactly the code that classified it before.
- **The ten pre-existing selftest name checks that the `st_run` cut de-vacuumed all still pass**, so they were real assertions that happened to also be satisfiable by the echo — not assertions that were only ever passing because of it.
- **`run_tally` and `suite_started` are unaffected**, enumerated rather than assumed: they read the run-level `Test run with …` line and the `Test run started.` line, both present in the reported case. Those two and the two changed readers are every place the harness reads a suite log.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The seam had two directions and the ticket reported the milder one.** SONNY-305 measured the same mutant at the same tree twice — unattributed inside an eight-mutant battery, named correctly when run alone with `--only`, five identical `recorded an issue` lines both times — and said, correctly, that the kill verdict was right and only the evidence was lost. **The other direction is a wrong count**, found while fixing the first and reproduced against `main`'s copy of the script rather than argued: when a run's only red is a *declared* failure, the classifier saw nothing at all, so it could not reach `UNATTRIBUTED` and the arm above it counted a kill. A declared hang backstop recorded as an issue with no summary line gives `1 killed, 0 survived, 0 unattributed`, exit 0, on a mutant nothing had caught; the fixed script gives `0 killed, 0 survived, 1 unattributed`, exit 2, names the test from its issue line and prints the signature that disqualified it. **That is the manufactured kill SONNY-224 built the whole declaration mechanism to prevent, reached by a road that mechanism never watched** — and it is why this is numbered beside the other three routes to a false measurement in the script's header rather than filed as a misdiagnosis. It was never observed in the wild, which is stated in the selftest arm so nobody reads the stronger claim into it.

**The obvious fix, applied alone, is worse than the defect.** SONNY-305 proposed that `failing_tests` fall back to the issue-line parse. That function is a *gate*: the caller checks it for a name and then attributes with `classify_failures`, which was still reading the summary line only. So the ticket's fix alone gets past the gate and finds nothing to attribute — the same log reports `UNATTRIBUTED — the suite went red, and on nothing that is evidence` above a blank evidence line, exit **2** instead of **0**, turning a correctly counted kill into a finding. That variant was built and run against the new fixture, not reasoned about. **So the fallback delegates to `classify_failures` rather than adding a second regex**, because two engines reading one line shape can disagree — sed is greedy where the classifier's pattern is not — and the disagreement lands exactly in that gap. One reader, one answer. The arm's `st_absent … UNATTRIBUTED` is what notices if someone puts the second regex back.

**A selftest that echoes its own fixture cannot assert that the report named anything.** `scripts/mutate`'s header prints `test cmd   : $TEST_CMD`, and a selftest stand-in is a multi-line shell script, so the whole fixture lands in the captured output before a single mutant runs; every needle a fixture contains then matches itself. Found the way PR #112's F6 was found — a brand-new arm passing a check it had no business passing yet, here "the test is named" going green against a script that had named nothing. Population measured over `scripts/mutate` at `a85fd08`: **10 of 68** `st_contains … "$ST_OUT"` checks inside an `st_run` arm carried a needle their own stand-in contains, and that set is **every** "the test is named" check in the classifier's arms (at `1138384`, with this branch's arms, the same scan answers 13 of 75). Cut once in `st_run` rather than by tightening ten needles, so a future arm gets the safe behavior by default.

**That figure was first written as 11 of 70, and the error is worth keeping.** The first scan ran on a working tree that already carried this branch's own new arm, so it counted that arm's own check among the pre-existing ones — a measurement taken on one tree and stamped with another, which is the failure `CLAUDE.md`'s Claims-and-evidence section already records twice and which arrives here through a session obeying the write-the-command-beside-the-number rule while running the command against the wrong tree. `b9eebdb`'s commit message still says 11 of 70 and is left as written; this repository restamps rather than rewriting a commit message, and the correction lives in `scripts/mutate`'s own `st_run` comment and here. (That commit was `d1648a2` before the rebase. **Renaming that citation is right where re-measuring the two figures above was**, and the difference is what is being cited: a rebase preserves a commit *message* byte for byte — `git log -1 --format=%B` over the two is identical, `diff` exit 0 — while a figure measured on the old commit's *tree* describes a tree the new base has moved.)

**The root cause of the omitted summary line is not established, and nothing here claims one.** SONNY-305's two runs differed in machine load, which is a correlation from two data points. Sweeping the 147 recorded logs found no second occurrence to reason from. What the fix changes is that the omission stops costing anything — which is the only consequence anyone has identified.

Known limitations / deferred scope: **This does not let the harness name a test it was never told about.** A mutant that traps the test process still names none, and tests sharing a function name across suites still merge — the two seams `CLAUDE.md` records as open, both unchanged here. The `st_run` cut removes only the echoed suite command; it is not a general guarantee that a needle cannot match something other than its assertion's target.
