Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Forwarding the credentials does not mount the auth routes, and that is the finding this branch exists to have made.** SONNY-306 was filed on the reasonable reading of SONNY-128's measurement: `deploy.sh local` passed only `SONNY_ENV` and `LOG_LEVEL`, `POST /v1/auth/email/start` answered `404 resource.not_found`, therefore the missing credentials were the cause. They were not the only cause and they were not the binding one. **Measured at `30f36c3` with all five variables confirmed present inside the container, the route still answers `404 resource.not_found`** — the same `code`, `message`, `retryable` and `retry_after_seconds` as with none of them set, the only differing field being `request_id`, which `genReqId` mints fresh per request by construction. Two independent things stand in the way, and both are `server/src/` work this ticket may not do: `server.ts:21` calls `buildApp(config)` with **no `auth` argument**, unconditionally — no flag, no environment variable, no branch — and `buildApp` mounts the auth routes only when one is supplied (`app.ts:156-159`); and **no concrete `AuthProvider` adapter exists**, the only implementations in the tree being three test fakes, which `revocations.ts:66` already says in its own output. Filed as **SONNY-307**. The lesson generalises past this ticket: *a 404 is not evidence about configuration*. Nothing about a missing credential produces `resource.not_found` — a gateway missing one either refuses to start (`exit 78`) or refuses the request with a code of its own. Reading the 404 as a configuration symptom is what made this a deploy-script ticket, and one probe with the variables present would have said otherwise at filing time.

**The passthrough list tracks `server/src/config.ts`, and the script says so in the place a reader would otherwise guess.** That file is the only thing that decides which names the gateway reads: a name in the script it does not read is forwarded to nothing, and a name it reads that the script omits is a credential the one command cannot deliver. The block carries the command that re-derives the schema's whole set (`grep -oE '^  [A-Z_]+:' src/config.ts | tr -d ' :' | sort` → eleven names at `6b72909`) and accounts for all eleven: two set explicitly by the script, three the container's own, one correct empty with no proxy in front, and the five forwarded.

**Mail contributes no variable names at all, and that is a measurement rather than an omission.** The ticket asked for the Supabase *and mail* names; `config.ts` reads none for mail — `grep -cE '(RESEND|SMTP|MAIL)[A-Z_]*' src/config.ts` prints 0 — because the sending side does not exist yet, for the reason `auth/provider.ts`'s own docstring gives: the founder's Resend sending domain was not ready when the seam was built. **`scripts/check-secrets.sh` already carries `RESEND_API_KEY` and `SMTP_PASSWORD` on its name-anchored list**, and that is the trap worth naming: the scanner anticipating a variable is not the config reading one, and a list of secret *names* is exactly what a session guessing a passthrough list would reach for. Read off `config.ts` or not at all.

**`RATE_LIMIT_SALT` is on the list and belongs to neither Supabase nor mail**, which the block states rather than smuggling. `requireRateLimitSalt` refuses to start wherever the auth routes are mounted, so a container carrying the four Supabase names and not that one could not serve a sign-in at all — which is the outcome the single command exists for. Provider credentials are deliberately absent: they belong to the routes SONNY-130 is building, on a branch growing `config.ts` while this one was written.

**A variable set to the empty string is treated as absent, and the alternative is worse than it looks.** All five parse through a non-empty schema, so forwarding an empty one turns a missing credential into a startup refusal — `exit 78`, EX_CONFIG — instead of the health-only degraded mode the script promises, which is the one outcome the ticket rules out. Exercised at `30f36c3` plus this entry's then-uncommitted text, which is why that run's build identifier reads `30f36c3-dirty` — the script's own dirty-tree marking, and repository-wide because `git status` is: with `SUPABASE_JWT_ISSUER` exported empty and two others set, the run reported `forwarding 2 of 5`, named the empty one among the three absent, started, and served health. Exactly `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` and `DATABASE_URL` reached the container.

**The mount statement is probed rather than written down, so it cannot go stale.** A comment saying "auth is not mounted" becomes a lie the day `server.ts` supplies `auth`, and nothing would fail when it did. The script asks the container instead and prints what it answered, so SONNY-307 flips that line with no edit here. **The probe body is `{}` deliberately**: once the route exists, `startBody` rejects it before anything is issued, so the probe can never send a person a code and never needs a database — a deploy script that sends mail as a side effect of deploying would be a worse defect than the one it reports.

**`docker run -e NAME` with no `=` is what makes "never printed" true, and the claim is bounded in the script itself.** The value is read by Docker out of this process's environment, so it never reaches a variable in the script, a command line, `ps`, or any line printed — verified by searching both runs' full output for the value used, → 0. **What that does not mean** is that the value is hidden: the running container holds it in its environment, because that is what forwarding is, so `docker inspect sonny-gateway-local` prints it and so does `printenv` inside it, both measured. That is the same exposure the host's own environment configuration has on staging and production, and it is the exposure a credentialed container is *for*. Stating the narrow version in the file is the point — an unbounded "no value is ever exposed" is the kind of security claim this changelog already records going wrong.

**`bash` here is 3.2, and an empty array is the ordinary case for this list.** `/usr/bin/env bash` on a founder's Mac is GNU bash 3.2.57, where `"${ARR[@]}"` on an empty array under `set -u` is an unbound-variable error rather than zero words. "Nothing was set" is the most common way this script will be run, so the expansion is guarded (`${ARR[@]+"${ARR[@]}"}`) and the arrays are declared at file scope. Without the guard the feature would have failed exactly in the case it degrades to.

- **One shared backend HTTP client**, the first in `Sources/`. Base URL, the §2.2 headers, **an explicit twenty-second timeout on the auth routes** where every existing client runs on Foundation's stock defaults, retry with exponential backoff whose *ceiling comes from the failure's own `code`* rather than one global number, and typed errors for everything.
- **Single-flight refresh, guarded by a generation counter and not by an in-flight flag.** Ten concurrent 401s cause one refresh; a straggler's 401 raised against an already-rotated token retries with what is on hand and asks for no second rotation — which is the case a flag loses, and the case the server reads as theft.
- **The session in the Keychain, as a new account on the existing store**, under its own service so that signing out cannot reach the local-storage encryption key.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A client of our own rather than Supabase's Swift SDK — decided on grounds that are checkable, and deliberately not on a claim about the SDK.** SONNY-128's founder note of 2026-08-17 asked for this to be picked and stated, warning that adopting both leaves the Mac app with two networking stacks, two token stores and two refresh paths, and that the second copy would hold auth tokens. The decision is the client, and the reasoning is not "the SDK cannot do single-flight refresh" — that was never measured here and would be the shape this changelog already records going wrong once, a recommendation argued from an unverified incompatibility. It is two facts from the contract itself. **First, this client has to exist either way.** §4.1 lists **16** endpoints, **6** of them under `/v1/auth/` (`awk '/^### 4.1 The set/,/^\*\*`GET \/v1\/meta`/' docs/sonny-backend-api-contract.md | grep -cE '^\| `(GET|POST|DELETE) '` → 16, the same with `/v1/auth/` appended to the pattern → 6, both at `3904ea0`); nothing in an auth SDK reaches any of the other ten, and seven of those are the routes SONNY-130, SONNY-131, SONNY-134 and SONNY-135 are about to build on — `/v1/plan`, `/v1/research/synthesize`, `/v1/transcriptions`, `/v1/search`, `/v1/screen/analyze`, `/v1/account/entitlements` and `/v1/tasks/{task_id}`. So the SDK would not replace a stack, it would be a second one beside the one SONNY-130 and SONNY-131 are about to build on. **Second, the Mac app never talks to Supabase.** Every auth call in §3.6 goes to the gateway, which is the only side holding Supabase credentials — and the gateway is doing real work in the middle of each one: §3.6's uniform `email/start` response exists so the endpoint is not an account-existence oracle, and the three distinct code failures are *derived from the gateway's own issuance record* because Supabase returns one `otp_expired` for all three. A client that spoke to Supabase directly would lose both.

**Sign-out had to be able to outrank a refresh already in flight, and the fix is the guard rather than a cancel** (PR #133, F1). The reviewer reproduced this against the real client: with a refresh held at the stub, sign-out cleared the Keychain, and releasing the refresh wrote the rotated session straight back — `keychain_holds_session_after_signout=true`, and `restore()` signed the user in again at the next launch. The UI said signed out and a live credential sat on disk. **Two fixes were available and the branch took the airtight one and the useful one.** `performRefresh` reads the generation before its network call and `adopt` refuses a write whose generation has moved; the comparison and the write sit in one method with no `await` between them, so on the actor they are one indivisible step and there is no window for a sign-out to land in the middle. Cancelling the task instead would not have been airtight — a cancel cannot reach a task already past its network call, which is exactly the window that matters — so the handle is *dropped* rather than cancelled, and dropping it does a second, different job: it stops a caller on the *next* session waiting on a refresh belonging to the previous one, which has its own test. Dropping also keeps the copy honest, because the requests riding on that refresh end with `notSignedIn` — true, and the sentence the user needs — rather than the `cancelled` the copy layer renders as an unexplained failure. **Latent rather than live when it was found**: `signOut` was the only `.bearer` caller in the tree, and it goes live the moment SONNY-130 and SONNY-131 add a second concurrent authenticated caller, which is the next branch.

**The refresh request is not retry-safe, against §9.3's own table, and the exception is argued rather than assumed** (PR #133, F2). §9.3 calls refresh safe to retry *with the same key*, and the key is the entire mechanism — the server returns the stored response instead of rotating again. That mechanism does not exist: the gateway reads no `Idempotency-Key` on any route (SONNY-300; `grep -rniE 'idempotency[-_ ]?key' server/ | grep -vE 'node_modules|/dist/'` → **0** at `410f3c5`). So a retry was a second POST of the identical refresh token, and §3.3 makes presenting an already-rotated token past the platform's ten-second overlap the definition of theft, answered by revoking the whole family — the user signed out of every device. Measured before the fix: a `503` carrying `Retry-After: 30` produced two identical refresh POSTs 30 s apart. **Capping the delay below the overlap was the other option and is not enough**, which is why it was not taken: the overlap runs from when the server rotated, and the first attempt's own duration counts against it — this route may sit for its full 20-second timeout before failing, so the window can already be gone before any delay is chosen. The elapsed-time bound that would be correct is more machinery than the alternative deserves, because a failed refresh costs nothing: the next request that needs a token tries again, and until then the access token in hand keeps working.

**A server-named `Retry-After` is bounded by the request's own timeout, and past that the answer is to stop rather than to sleep.** Adjacent to F2 and found with it. `Retry-After` is data from the network with nothing bounding it, and an unbounded sleep sits inside an operation a user is watching: a server bug or a hostile one answering `Retry-After: 86400` would park a sign-in for a day, which is indistinguishable from a hung app and is the client doing it to itself. The bound is the route's own timeout rather than a number picked for the purpose — §12 already says how long the operation may take, so waiting that again between two attempts keeps one operation inside twice its own budget. Past it the request fails with the delay preserved on the typed error, so a surface that wants to say how long still can; it is the sleeping that is refused, not the information.

**The single-flight guard is a generation counter, and an in-flight flag is not enough.** A flag answers "is a refresh running", which loses the straggler: request A refreshes and finishes, then request B's 401 — raised against the token B read *before* that refresh — finds nothing running and starts a second rotation. The server reads a refresh token presented past its ten-second overlap as theft and revokes the whole family (§3.3), so the cost of the miss is the user being signed out. Every caller therefore records the generation of the token it used and asks for "a token newer than this one"; if the cache has already moved past it, no request is made at all. **This is the one place a test had to be rebuilt to be able to fail**: the first version raced instead of ordering, and a mutant replacing the generation check with `false` survived it, because the straggler happened to arrive while the first refresh's task was still parked on the actor. The committed version `await`s the first request to completion before releasing the straggler's reply, so the in-flight task is provably gone.

**Every token write reaches the Keychain before it reaches the client's own cache, and that ordering is the whole ticket.** macOS forces an app relaunch after a Screen Recording grant, so a session held only in memory is lost at exactly the moment a first-run user meets it. Writing the Keychain first also means a failed write cannot leave the process believing it is signed in with something no disk holds — the failure surfaces to whoever asked, and the user is not told they are signed in. The end-to-end test drives the product's own `AppRelaunching` seam rather than simulating beside it: the relauncher reads the Keychain at the instant it is asked to restart, which is the last moment anything in that process can observe, and a fresh model over the same Keychain stands in for the process that comes back.

**The staging pointer has two forms, and the second exists because of this ticket's own headline constraint.** `DefaultAppRelauncher.relaunch()` reopens the bundle with `/usr/bin/open -n`, which starts the new process from launchd's environment and not from the terminal's — so an environment variable set for a debug run is gone the moment the app relaunches, which is exactly when this ticket needs the app to come back working. A `defaults write` value survives that, and survives a launch from Finder, which an environment variable never does. The variable is kept as the more explicit per-launch form and wins when both are set.

**There is no production host, and the code says so rather than guessing one.** `SonnyBackendHost.productionBaseURL` is `nil`. §13 assigns the host to SONNY-125, both remote deploy targets are stubs that exit 3, and the first real remote deploy is owed on SONNY-192. A plausible domain written here would be a confidently stated fact nobody decided, and it would fail as a DNS error rather than as the honest "this build has no backend" the surface can say. The surface handles it: the controls are disabled and the message is its own case. When a host is chosen it is one line, and `noProductionHostIsConfiguredUntilSONNY192ChoosesOne` is the test that fails and names what to update.

**Retry is decided by `code`, and the attempt ceiling is per code rather than one global number.** §7.2 does not ask for one ceiling: `limit.rate` and `provider.timeout` are retried once while `provider.unavailable`, `server.error` and `server.unavailable` are retried with backoff and then given up on. The difference is not cosmetic on a rate limit — the extra attempt spends the user's own budget against a wall that has already answered. The envelope's own `retryable` flag decides nothing, with exactly one exception: `idempotency.conflict` is the one code whose two sub-cases share it (§9.2's in-flight key against §9.3's differing body), and nothing else consults the flag, so a server bug setting it on `provider.rejected` cannot become a retry loop here.

**`Accept-Encoding` is deliberately not set by hand, though §2.2 says every request should include gzip.** URLSession sets it itself and decompresses the reply transparently; setting it here switches that off and hands back compressed bytes. A test asserts this client did not set it, because the mistake looks like compliance.

**Signing out clears this Mac even when the revoke could not happen, and says which of the two occurred.** Order first: clearing before revoking destroys the token the revoke has to present, so revoke comes first. Clearing unconditionally afterwards is the deliberate half — a user who pressed Sign out and is left holding a refresh token because a network call failed has been told something untrue about their own machine, and keeping the credential on disk to preserve a call that may never succeed is the worse of the two failures.

**The two token strings are `internal` to `MacAgentCore`, so the app target cannot name them.** Every view, every view model and the whole executable import the module and get `userID` and `emailAddress` and nothing else. That is the compiler keeping a credential out of a log line rather than a convention somebody has to remember; both string conversions redact as well, for `MacAgentCore` printing one by accident.

**`SonnyLiveGatewayTests` is the one suite that talks to a real gateway, and it is opt-in.** Everything else is fixture-backed, because a suite whose result depends on a network is not evidence. This one covers what a fixture cannot: that the shapes this client builds are the ones a real server parses, and that the server's own envelope and headers map to the typed errors. `SONNY_LIVE_GATEWAY=<url>` enables it and it reports as *skipped* without one. **It is also the shape SONNY-192's staging run takes.**

**`./scripts/deploy.sh local` mounts no auth routes, and the founder's manual pass needs to know that.** The script runs the container with `SONNY_ENV` and `LOG_LEVEL` and nothing else, and `buildApp(config)` with no `auth` argument mounts health only — deliberate, and recorded on `feature/row-12-accounts-email` as "a health-only deployment needs no provider and no salt". Measured rather than read: against the container this branch started, `POST /v1/auth/email/start` answered **`404 resource.not_found`** through the client's own mapper. So the local deployment proves the transport and the error mapping, and a real sign-in needs a local run carrying the gateway's Supabase and mail credentials.

**`link_hint` is decoded and no prompt is built.** The contract names SONNY-128 and SONNY-129 as the owners of surfacing it (§3.6), and this ticket's own description never mentions it; its only reliable trigger is a relay address, which arrives with Sign in with Apple on the next branch. The contract also says a client that ignores the field is correct and gets two accounts. Decoded so SONNY-129 does not re-derive the shape, and filed as **SONNY-301** rather than built.

Known limitations (each one owed to a named place):

- **Acceptance criterion 1's founder half is owed.** "A user can sign in from the app against staging" was split by the coordinator's amendment of 2026-08-26: no staging host exists, so the criterion is discharged against a local deployment and the staging run rides with SONNY-192. What this branch discharged is the mechanical half — the client reaches a real gateway, and its request shapes and error mapping work against one. The sign-in itself is a founder's manual item, because no agent can drive the live app, and it needs a local run carrying credentials per the note above.
- **No production host** — SONNY-192.
- **The Keychain item's protection class was never chosen** (PR #133, F4). `KeychainSecretStore.baseQuery` sets only `kSecClass`, `kSecAttrService` and `kSecAttrAccount`; there is no `kSecAttrAccessible` or `kSecUseDataProtectionKeychain` anywhere in `Sources/` or `Tests/`, and the app is not sandboxed — so the item lands in the file-based login keychain and is not `ThisDeviceOnly`, meaning it travels in a Time Machine backup or a Migration Assistant transfer with the refresh token still valid. Not synchronizable, so no iCloud Keychain sync. **Inherited from the existing store rather than introduced here**, and that store is on this ticket's never-touch list — but the ticket's own words are that it "has never held a credential", and a bearer credential to a remote service is a different asset from a local encryption key. Filed by the reviewer as its own ticket.
- **The gateway implements no `Idempotency-Key` handling at all**, while §9.1 requires the header on every `POST` and §9.2 states guarantees this client's retry design leans on — chiefly that a metering event is written at most once per key, which is what makes a client retry unable to double-bill. The client sends the header; nothing reads it. `grep -rniE 'idempotency[-_ ]?key' server/ | grep -vE 'node_modules|/dist/'` finds **0** lines at `410f3c5`, against **3** for `Idempotency-Key` in the contract. (The word *idempotent* does appear seven times under `server/`, all of it describing other things — a drain, three migrations, three tests — which is why the narrower pattern is the one to run.) `server/` is on this ticket's never-touch list; filed as **SONNY-300**, Backlog and untriaged.
- **One full-suite run out of eight went red in `VisionSessionRunTests`, and it is not this branch's.** Its 30-second deadlock backstop fired on the slowest run measured, 60.9s against 25.4–29.5s for every green one. That suite passes 74/74 in isolation, including under 30× CPU oversubscription, and nothing in this diff touches it. Filed as **SONNY-302** rather than dismissed. (Four further red runs the same evening were this session's own fault and are not evidence of anything: a `kill` of some deliberately-launched CPU load did not resolve in a non-interactive shell and the load ran on through them.)

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): one, for the founder — should `./scripts/deploy.sh local` learn to pass the gateway's Supabase and mail credentials, or does a credentialed container stay a hand-run step for the manual pass? As the script stands it runs the container with `SONNY_ENV` and `LOG_LEVEL` only, so `buildApp` mounts health alone and the four sign-in rows in the checklist cannot be run against it — measured, not inferred: `POST /v1/auth/email/start` against the container this branch started answered `404 resource.not_found`. A deploy-script change, so it is the founder's call rather than this ticket's; raised here, not filed. **The founder-run half of acceptance criterion 1 is deliberately not listed here**: it is owed work with named owners — the checklist's §7 rows and SONNY-192 for the staging run — rather than something undecided, and it is recorded under Known limitations above. Nothing else on this branch is undecided; SONNY-300, SONNY-301 and SONNY-302 are filed and awaiting triage, and F4 is the reviewer's own ticket.

Next branch: **SONNY-129, `feature/row-12-social-signin`** — Sign in with Google and Sign in with Apple — which is what `docs/sonny-row-12-plan.md` §8's dependency order puts next and which this ticket unblocks (§8's table: "Depends on 127, 128"). **SONNY-130, `feature/row-12-gateway-text`, unblocks here too** and depends on the same pair plus SONNY-126, so both become startable at this merge; §8.2 records no disjointness note for that pair, and its own rule is that absence of a note means serial, so they are not marked parallel and which runs first is the coordinator's to assign. Three things a session taking SONNY-129 should read first, each cited where it actually lives rather than where it is easy to assume. **The build order is split and it is on the ticket, not in the plan**: SONNY-128's founder-decision comment of 2026-08-17 puts Google "built early, with the first sign-in work" and Apple "near launch", both still v1 — so SONNY-129 as the plan scopes it may not be one branch's worth of work. §4.3 says only that email code is built first, and does not carry that split. **§4.3 point 3 does carry a prerequisite**: establish which Sign in with Apple flow actually works for a Developer-ID-signed, non-App-Store Mac app before designing against one — which the contract restates in §3.6, leaving the OAuth request bodies as SONNY-129's to fix. And **§8.2's recorded cross-row collision**: SONNY-129 and SONNY-137 both touch Settings and the first-run surface, where SONNY-104's per-app revocation list also lands, and none of the three has been designed.

Behavior added:
- **Command Center's approval panel offers Stop rather than Deny while a session is live** (PR #132's F1), with the session's identity line and step count above the question — the same argument as the widget's, on the surface that had not had it.
- **An approval raised mid-loop during a screen-control session renders in the floating widget.** `.permission` moved above `.controlling` in `FloatingWidgetView.state`.
- **The approval panel carries the session's own statement and its Stop while a session is live** — `WidgetSessionIdentityLine` ("Sonny is controlling <app>") and `WidgetSessionStopButton`, both extracted from the HUD and shared with it, plus the step count.
- **The composer says "Answer above first…" in that state**, where it said "Sonny is working…" over a panel with no question in it.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **An approval with no session live is byte-for-byte the panel it was.** `sessionProgress` is `nil`, so the step rows, the first-run explainer, the escalation line, the Safe-mode egress line, the ✗ and the ✓ are exactly as before; `WidgetApprovalExplainerTests` and §3c's own rows are untouched.
- **The HUD is unchanged in what it says and does.** Its identity line and its Stop are now the shared components rather than inline code, with the same glyph, the same tokens, the same label and the same accessibility string; Pause is untouched. `VisionSessionRunTests`' five HUD tests pass unchanged — the section between its own two `// MARK:` lines (`awk` over `// MARK: - The HUD (SONNY-95)` to `// MARK: - The widget while a mid-loop approval is parked (SONNY-255)`, counting `func … () async throws` → 5).
- **Every other stop path is untouched.** `emergencyStopVisionSession`, `cancelCurrentRun`, the `Ctrl-Opt-Esc` hotkey and the Safe-mode questions' own declines all behave exactly as they did — the panel's Stop calls the first of those, which is what the HUD's Stop already called.
- **The three Safe-mode session questions keep their places** above `.controlling`, in the same order, and `.clarification` keeps its place below it — the branch that was moved is one branch.
- **`AgentViewModel.hasVisibleWidgetPanel` is not touched**, and did not need to be: its `approvalRequest` branch is unconditional and already sits above its origin-gated `isRunning` branch, so the approval reaches the widget whatever started the run.
- **The `panel` switch's case order is unchanged**, which is what keeps `ClarificationExitTests`' region scan — anchored from `case .clarification` to `case .permission` — reading the region it was written to read.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Why the chain moved rather than a composite panel being built.** The ticket left the choice open and named the cost of each: reordering makes the question visible and takes the HUD's Pause and Stop off screen with it; a panel *within* the controlling state keeps both and needs a composite that does not exist. What decided it is that the three neighbours already answer the question. `.captureReview`, `.delegationReview` and `.sessionPaused` are all vision-session states and all already sit above `.controlling`, and what they have in common is not that they are Safe-mode: **each is a continuation the loop is suspended on**. A mid-loop approval is the fourth of exactly that kind — `requestVisionActionApproval` awaits a `CheckedContinuation` — so the rule "a parked continuation outranks a progress report" already described three of four cases and the fourth was the one placed below the line by accident. The HUD is also *inaccurate* in that state, which the composite option would have preserved: `currentAction` is written at the top of the iteration and the approval is raised several steps later, so it names looking at the app rather than the action being asked about.

**§13.4's HUD list includes a Pause button, and Pause-absent-while-parked is a departure from it — recorded here because it was recorded against no section** (PR #132 review, F6). The spec's Live HUD section (`docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md` §13.4) requires the HUD to show: Sonny is controlling app, current app, current step, last action, Pause button, Stop button, **approval required state**, and a link to the action journal. Two things follow. The first is that this branch moves *toward* that list rather than away from it: "approval required state" is precisely what the widget could not show during a session, and now does. The second is the departure — while an approval is parked the panel on screen is the approval's, and it carries the identity line, the current step and Stop but **not Pause**, for the reason in the next paragraph. The other two §13.4 items the widget does not carry are older than this branch and unchanged by it: the action journal link is not built on this surface, and "last action" is the HUD's own `currentAction`, which the approval panel deliberately omits because it is stale at that moment.

**What the reorder had to give back, and the one thing it deliberately did not.** Stop is the emergency control for a program moving the user's cursor, so it travels: `WidgetPermissionPanel` renders the session's identity line, its step count and a labelled red Stop above the question whenever `sessionProgress` is non-nil. **Pause does not travel, and that is a decision rather than an omission** — `pauseVisionSession` sets the attention monitor's flag, which the loop reads at the top of its *next* iteration, so pressed while an approval is parked it freezes nothing (the loop is already frozen on the continuation) and takes effect only after the user answers. A control that appears inert and then acts later is worse than one that is not offered.

**The cross is hidden while a session is live, and this is the part most likely to read as a regression.** It is not one: outside a session the ✗ is the panel's Deny and nothing changes, and *inside* one it calls `cancelCurrentRun`, which ends the whole session rather than declining a step — the same thing the labelled Stop one row above does. Two controls with one effect, on the surface a program driving the user's screen asks from, with the destructive one drawn as an icon-only cross that reads as "skip this step": `cancelCurrentRun`'s own doc comment calls that class of surprise the most expensive this product can produce. So the refusal moves to the row that says what it does. No capability is lost — same call, same single press — and when SONNY-80's standing note lands (a labelled "deny this step" resuming the continuation without cancelling) it returns as a genuinely different control beside that Stop, which is the shape `VisionSessionRunner`'s `nil` arm already anticipates.

**The defect was invisible to every test in the suite, and the reason is worth more than the fix.** `FloatingWidgetView.state`'s ordering is pinned by source scans — `theWidgetsOwnPrecedenceIsWhatMakesTheComposersClassificationTrue` pins it explicitly, and pinned the *wrong* order deliberately, while the sentences naming SONNY-255 as the ticket that owned the defect sat in `Sources/` — `composerState`'s branch comment and `ComposerPresentation.State`'s two cases (`git grep -n SONNY-255 368ab85 -- Tests` exits 1 with no output: no test named it). A scan says where a branch sits in a file. It cannot say what the widget resolves to with a real view model in a real state, and that is the only question that was being got wrong. So `WidgetState`, `state` and `composerState` drop `private`, and **two** tests in `VisionSessionRunTests` run a real session to a real mid-loop approval and read the resolved state off `FloatingWidgetView(viewModel:)` — `theWidgetShowsTheApprovalRatherThanTheHudWhileAMidLoopQuestionIsParked` and `answeringTheApprovalPutsTheHudBackAndTheSessionContinues`. The third behavioural test, `stopFromTheApprovalPanelEndsTheSessionWithoutTakingTheAction`, calls `emergencyStopVisionSession` and asserts on the view model and the journal; it never constructs the widget, and this paragraph said three until PR #132's review, F9. That construction was already in the suite (`git grep -c 'FloatingWidgetView(viewModel:' -- Tests/MacAgentTests/ProductShellTests.swift` → 4), so the widening is two keywords, not a harness.

**The per-app control gate escaped the defect by position, which is why the second wrong doc comment read as true.** `VisionSessionRunner`'s §4.3 gate runs *before* the iteration's first `visionSessionDidProgress`, so on the first capture there is no progress for the precedence to prefer and its approval really did render — and it is the approval a session most often raises, which is how "this renders on the floating widget" survived being read. Every *per-action* approval sits after that progress report and rendered nowhere. Both comments are corrected in place rather than deleted, because the difference between them is an accident of position and reads as nothing.

**Four doc comments asserted the behaviour, not two.** The ticket named `requestVisionActionApproval`'s and `VisionSessionRunner`'s. Sweeping for the claim found two more, both written by PR #107 and both describing the defect as live and unfixed: `ComposerPresentation.State.waitingOnYou`'s "reaches no widget surface at all is a separate, pre-existing defect", and `.working`'s "a live screen-control session lands here **even while something is pending underneath it**" — the second being a doc comment whose accuracy depended on the bug. A fifth statement lived in `docs/sonny-manual-test-checklist.md`, in a SONNY-247 row instructing the founder to confirm the composer says "Sonny is working…" *including* during a mid-session approval, which after this branch is a row that fails when checked as written. It is corrected in place with its history, per that file's own convention.

**A stale enumeration inside the panel being edited, corrected because the edit made it worse.** `WidgetPermissionPanel`'s escalation-line comment claimed `errorGlyph` was used "exclusively by genuine error states" and named two sites by line number. Both numbers had moved, and row I had already added a third site that is no error state at all — the HUD's Stop — so the sentence was false before this branch, and this branch puts that same control in a second panel. Restated as the property that has never been false and is what the sentence was actually protecting: **nothing that asks the user a question is drawn in the failure colour**. Three code sites in the file (`git grep -cE '^[^/]*WidgetTheme\.errorGlyph' -- Sources/MacAgent/FloatingWidgetView.swift` → 3 at `95b1d5f`; the leading-slash exclusion is what keeps the prose out of the count).

The last is the one that stands; the first three are stamped at commits a rebase has since replaced and are kept as the record of when each shape was first held, not as figures about this tree. The set carries R5's three shapes, the four the row extraction moved, and the original six. Those six are described first. Every kill names a test written for that mutant, and none of the killers is a timing-sensitive test (`CLAUDE.md`'s flake-reads-as-a-kill warning). M1, the precedence reverted, is killed by the ordering scan **and** by `theWidgetShowsTheApprovalRatherThanTheHudWhileAMidLoopQuestionIsParked` — which is the evidence that the behavioural test is not a restatement of the scan. M2, the composer's classification reverted, by `everyConditionTheComposerDisablesOnIsClassified` and the same behavioural test. M3 (`sessionProgress: nil` at the call site), M4 (the panel's Stop wired past `emergencyStopVisionSession`) and M6 (the Stop dropped from the panel's session row) by the new panel scans; M5 (the cross kept beside the Stop) by `theCrossIsTheRefusalOutsideASessionAndTheStopIsTheRefusalInsideOne`. M4 is worth naming as the case a runtime test cannot reach: `emergencyStopVisionSession` routes into `cancelCurrentRun`, so swapping them is behaviourally identical here and only a scan can hold the wiring — which is equally true of M8, its Command Center twin. **The five added by the fix round**: R2 (the ordinary approval's `else` arm emptied) by `theOrdinaryApprovalKeepsItsStepRowsAndTheSessionRowReplacesThem`, the test written for it; M7 (Command Center keeps Deny mid-session), M8 (its Stop rewired) and M9 (its session context row dropped) each by `commandCentersApprovalPanelOffersStopRatherThanDenyWhileASessionIsLive`; and M10 — the shared identity sentence reworded, which is the divergence the copy owner exists to prevent — by `bothSurfacesReadTheSessionsWordsFromOneOwnerAndNeitherHandWritesThem`.

**One discovery ticket. SONNY-299** — a screen-control session started anywhere but the widget shows **no HUD at all**: `hasVisibleWidgetPanel` has no `visionSessionProgress` term, so a live session with nothing parked on it falls through to its `isRunning` branch and answers `activeTaskOrigin == .widget`. Measured with a temporary probe rather than reasoned — `state` resolved to `.controlling` while `hasVisibleWidgetPanel` was `false` for a `.commandCenter`-origin run — and reachable through `runTaskAgain`, which dispatches `origin: .commandCenter` and re-plans a screen-control task into a fresh session (`VisionSessionRunTests.runningAgainAScreenControlTaskStartsAFreshSessionAndExtendsNoJournal` is that flow). Filed rather than fixed: it is a different property in a different file, and the unattended case it might otherwise raise is refused three independent ways.

**PR #132 FIX ROUND, appended 2026-08-27. Nine findings, no correctness defect among them — the reviewer's independent hand-trace held the reorder, the gate-ordering claim, Stop's reachability, the hidden cross and the inert Pause, and its harder mutant R1 died to the new behavioural test.** What the round actually found is a set of claims and one un-mirrored surface, which is the class this repository keeps paying for.

**F1, and it is the substantive one: the argument for hiding the widget's cross applied word for word to Command Center, and had not been made there.** `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` still offered a button labelled **"Deny"** wired to `cancelCurrentRun` — which mid-session ends the *whole session* rather than declining a step. The widget's icon-only cross was hidden for exactly that reason; a legible "Deny" is the same claim said out loud, and worse for being legible. Fixed the same way and with no behaviour change on either surface: while `visionSessionProgress` is non-nil the panel shows **Stop** (`emergencyStopVisionSession`, `CommandCenterRowActionStyle(tone: .danger)` — System A's own destructive treatment, not the widget's red) and no "Deny", with the session's identity line and step count above the question. Outside a session it is byte-for-byte what it was.

**The words are now shared and the views deliberately are not.** `ScreenControlSessionPresentation` (`AgentActivityPresentation.swift`) owns the identity line, the step line, the Stop's label and both accessibility names; `WidgetSessionIdentityLine`/`WidgetSessionStopButton` and Command Center's row render them with their own token sets, because `.claude/rules/macagent-ui-conventions.md` forbids either system leaving its surface. **A shared *view* was not an option and a shared *sentence* was the whole risk**: a user reading "Sonny is controlling Safari" on one surface and something else on the other is looking at one session described two ways, 4,000 lines apart, with nothing in either file able to see it. `bothSurfacesReadTheSessionsWordsFromOneOwnerAndNeitherHandWritesThem` holds the population in both directions.

**That scan found a shipped copy defect on its first run, and it is filed rather than fixed. SONNY-303** — `WidgetCaptureReviewPanel` renders `"Step \(preview.iteration) of \(preview.appDisplayName)"`, so Safe mode's pre-send review says **"Step 2 of Safari"**. `VisionCapturePreview` carries no `maximumIterations` (unlike `VisionSessionProgress`), so it is a type change and a product decision — add the field, or drop the "of …" half — rather than a typo, and it is a different panel from the one this branch is about. Tests: **2132 in 146 suites, exit 0 at `1fd80cb`** via the flagged command — the head that merges, and every figure here re-measured there after the rebase and the fix round rather than translated. Baseline **2111 in 145 at `368ab85`**, measured in a detached worktree at that commit rather than assumed. Net **+21 tests / +1 suite**. **The per-ticket counts this entry used to carry are dropped rather than re-pointed** — they were 2124/146 and 2127/146 at heads a rebase has since replaced, and a fix round that touched both tickets' tests has made the split less informative than the head, so restating them would have cost two suite runs to say less. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s rule working in the direction it usually is not: re-measured **or dropped**, never carried forward. **`scripts/warnings`: 0 warnings at `1fd80cb` (clean), 132s**, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled, the script's own stamp. `swift build`: exit 0. Nothing under `server/` is touched, so the server's commands are not owed. **One full-suite run in this branch's history went red across 84 issues and was not the diff** — 37 of them the 30 s deadlock backstop in `VisionSessionRunTests`, fired while another worktree ran a mutation battery and a third built release; the same tree passed with 0 timeouts once the machine was free. That failure mode is declared in `scripts/mutate-untrusted-failures`, which is why the battery below could not read it as a kill.

What changed for the user: nothing visible. Both tickets change prompt text — what the vision model and the web-research synthesizer receive — and every one of those strings goes to a model API and to nothing else. The two manual-test rows this branch adds say exactly that, and exist only to check that a model still behaves the same on the changed prompt, which no test in this repository can assert because no test calls a model.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The fold's shape follows from the position a value lands in, and there are three positions rather than one** (founder, 2026-08-26, recorded on both tickets). An **attribute** — the `id=`/`source=` tokens on a wrapper's opening line — has to stay one *token* as well as one line, so `escapeAttribute` folds every separator to `_`, one character for one. A **field on a line of an otherwise multi-line block** is readable prose that must not begin a line, so line-break runs collapse to the two literal characters `\n`; `_` is wrong here because it destroys every space in a sentence a model is meant to follow, which is the same reason `escapeAttribute` was rejected for the app display name — `Google_Chrome`, for every user, to close a latent hole. The **body of a deliberately multi-line block** is not folded at all. This is written at the shared function because two folds already existed with different markers and a third answer arriving unexplained is how a reader concludes one of them is wrong.

**The fold was hoisted rather than copied, and that was the branch's stated boundary** (SONNY-262). Two private implementations existed — `PriorTaskContext.foldingLineBreaks` and `ClarifiedCommand.foldingLineBreaks` — and this branch needed a third caller. Adding one more private copy, or adding a shared one beside a byte-identical private one, both make the tree worse in the exact way SONNY-262 was filed about. So the fold moved to `UntrustedContentBoundary`, which is where this repository already puts shared text mechanics, and `PriorTaskContext` moved onto it in the same commit — a behaviour-identical change, and `thePriorTaskLineFoldIsNotDefeatedByAMarkBesideTheBreak` still passes unmodified. **`ClarifiedCommand`'s copy is deliberately untouched and SONNY-262 stays open for it**, because the two are not interchangeable as they stand: it drops a *leading* empty piece where the shared one keeps it as a marker, so a question beginning with a line break composes to a different string. That is a behaviour change needing its own decision, not a mechanical swap, and it is recorded at the code as well as on the ticket.

**Folded at the assembly, never per call site.** `VisionSessionRunner` has **thirteen** `history.append` sites (`git grep -c 'history.append' 368ab85 -- Sources/MacAgentCore/VisionSessionRunner.swift` -> `368ab85:Sources/MacAgentCore/VisionSessionRunner.swift:13`; the revision goes *before* the `--`, and the file is untouched by this branch), each interpolating model-authored text — `decision.target`, `decision.rationale`, a delegated run's `instructionText`, a delegated run's `summary`. Folding each of those values at each of those sites is exactly the per-field-by-hand discipline SONNY-198 recorded as the thing that fails: it covers what is there today and not the fourteenth site. `observedBlock` folds the finished entry instead, which covers every value inside it by construction and covers the next site the moment it is written. It is faithful because all thirteen templates are single code-authored lines — the entry has no line structure of its own to lose. The cost, stated: a history entry that deliberately wanted two lines would be flattened, which is the safe direction.

**The web-research half is in scope because a coordinator's amendment on SONNY-226 put it there, and the two later records do not mention it.** The amendment of 2026-08-22 says the scope "must include the web-research observed block, not only the vision one … so this ticket is not scoped to the vision path alone and then closed while the easier-to-reach half stays open". The founder's decision of 2026-08-26 and the kickoff prompt both recite only `windowTitle` and the history entries. Read together, the later record settles *what the fold is* and the earlier one settles *where it applies*; nothing repeals the amendment, and its own sentence anticipates the failure of ignoring it. Resolved in favour of including it, and said here rather than silently. The defect is real and was reproduced at `368ab85` through the real builder, not a lookalike: a title of `Cheap Flights` + break + `Readable text:` + break + a sentence produced a **thirteen**-line block carrying **two** `Readable text:` lines with the forged one first, so a reader taking the first match reads the attacker's sentence as the page.

**`readableText` is the block's body and is deliberately left unfolded, which is a decision and not the half that was forgotten.** Folding it would flatten a whole article to one line — the content the synthesizer exists to read — to close a defect the wrapper already contains, since every forged line stays inside the untrusted pair either way. `theWebReadableTextKeepsItsOwnParagraphs` pins it so a later session does not "finish the job".

**The URLs need no fold, and that is measured rather than assumed.** `escapeObservedURL` takes a `URL` and percent-encodes through `addingPercentEncoding`. Driven three ways at `368ab85` — `URL(string:)` on a string carrying U+000A, on one already carrying `%0A`, and `URLComponents` with the break in `path` — `absoluteString` came back with **zero** line breaks in all three (`https://example.com/a%0AReadable%20text:%20forged`).

**Fold before escape is a convention, not a necessity — and the first version of this entry said the opposite, in company** (PR #130 review, F2). Six records claimed that folding first "puts the token back on one line where `escape` can see it": this entry, the shared fold's own doc comment, `escapedForProse`'s, `escapeObservedField`'s, the MacAgentCore rules paragraph, and the PR body and SONNY-231's closing comment. **It is false.** `escape` does not step over a line break — deliberately, because two lines cannot forge one boundary line — so `UNTRUSTED_OBSERVED_CONTENT_E` + LF + `ND` matches nothing; the fold then substitutes `\` and lowercase `n`, which `escape` does not step over either, so it still matches nothing. The fold swaps one non-match for another. **The branch's own test had been asserting exactly that the whole time**, under a name that promised a neutralisation its assertion disproves — `aLineBreakHiddenInsideADelimiterIsFoldedBeforeTheEscapeLooks`, now `aBreakSplitDelimiterIsANearMissBeforeTheFoldAndStaysOneAfter`. A doc comment and a test can disagree for a whole branch and both stay green, because nothing executable reads the comment — and a test *name* that restates the comment is how the disagreement stays invisible to a reader skimming either one.

**What survives is the half that carries the safety.** The marker's two characters appear in no delimiter, so this fold can never *rebuild* one — unlike `escapeAttribute`, whose fold emits `_`, a delimiter character, and whose fold-escape-fold ordering therefore really is load-bearing. And the two orders agree: over every delimiter split at every interior position by LF and by CRLF, plus hand-written cases — **265 values, 0 disagreements** — `escape(fold(v))` and `fold(escape(v))` are scalar-identical (`foldingBeforeEscapingAndAfterItAgreeOnEveryCorpusValue`). **265 is derived in the test as `5 + Σ(5 + 2·length)` over the four delimiters rather than written as a literal, because the first draft of this sentence said 258** — the size of a scratch probe's differently-built corpus, carried across to the test's own without being re-counted. The suite caught it; prose would not have.

**SONNY-231's second scope item was answered by counting.** "Check whether any other interpolation into `systemRules` or `responseContract` has the same shape" — the whole population of interpolations in `VisionSessionPromptBuilder.swift` is **ten distinct sites**, before this change and after it alike (`git show 368ab85:Sources/MacAgentCore/VisionSessionPromptBuilder.swift | grep -oE '[\\][(][^()]*([(][^()]*[)])?[^()]*[)]' | sort -u | wc -l` -> 10, and the same pipeline over the file at `ca1dd3c` -> 10). `systemRules` interpolates the display name plus `imageWidth`/`imageHeight`; `responseContract` interpolates only those two; both are `Int`, so no other interpolation into either can carry a line break at all. The rest are `decisionPrompt`'s, which composes already-wrapped or already-escaped segments, and `observedBlock`'s two, which fold their own.

**That second stamp said `2efb99e` until PR #130's cycle-2 records round, and it is worth keeping the failure rather than only the fix** — it is this entry's own rule breaking inside the sentence that states it. `2efb99e` is one of the four pre-rebase heads named eight paragraphs above as resolving and being ancestors of nothing; the paragraph that names them ends "every figure below is **re-measured at the new head, never translated across the rebase**", and that phrase is byte-identical to the pre-rebase entry's. So the phrase survived the rebase and this figure did not get the treatment it promises: **the number was carried across, not re-taken**. The number happened to be right — the pipeline answers 10 at `368ab85`, at `1fd80cb` and at `ca1dd3c` alike, re-run at each rather than taken from the reviewer — which is exactly why it survived a fix round, a battery and a cycle-1 review: **a translated figure that is still true reads identically to a re-measured one, and only the stamp gives it away.** The general form, for the next reader: after a rebase, a *claim* to have re-measured is not evidence of it, and the cheapest check is that every SHA the entry stamps passes the ancestry test — one that does not is a figure nobody re-took.

**The regression tests split on line-break scalars, and the reason is that the obvious test passes against the vulnerable tree.** `components(separatedBy: "\n")` cannot see a line a CR forged, so a test written that way reports the right line count about a block that has an extra line — the trap PR #94 found in SONNY-198's own separator test. Every assertion here goes through `scalarLines`, whose set is the same one the fold takes, so a narrowing on either side is visible from the other.

**The suite was shown to flag each defect it names, rather than trusted because it is green.** Four reverts, each run against the new suite alone: backing out `observedBlock`'s folds -> 99 issues; reverting `systemRules` to the bare `escape` -> 85; backing out the web metadata folds -> 119; narrowing the shared fold's character set from `CharacterSet.newlines` to LF alone -> 265, and the pre-existing `thePriorTaskLineFoldIsNotDefeatedByAMarkBesideTheBreak` went red with it, which is the SONNY-262 invariant now being held in one place for three callers.

**Two of the branch's own assertions were wrong and the code was right, which is worth recording because both look like defects at a glance.** A combining mark riding behind a line break is not a break, so it is not folded away and attaches to the marker's `n`: `before` + LF + U+0301 + `after` folds to `before\` + `ń` + `after`. It is one line, which is the property, and the alternative — stripping the mark — would silently edit text this fold has no business editing. And a value of *nothing but* line breaks folds to the **empty string**, not to one marker: the run collapses onto the single empty leading piece with nothing on either side to join. Both are measured and both are now asserted as the behaviour rather than smoothed over.

**A guard that reads like coverage and is not: the web block's escape was held by nothing** (PR #130 review, F1). The reviewer's mutant reduced `escapeObservedField` to the fold alone — no `escape` — and **the whole suite stayed green**. The vision side had `aDelimiterInTheAppDisplayNameIsStillNeutralisedAfterTheFold`; the web side, changed in the same commit, had no twin, and the test that *looked* like one, `everyWebResearchFieldNeutralisesAForgedDelimiter`, was vacuous for that purpose in a way worth writing down: it drove every field with a forged delimiter and then counted lines whose **prefix** is the closing delimiter. A value interpolated into `Title: …` can never begin a line, so that count is 1 whether or not anything was escaped — it was measuring the wrapper's own closing line. It asks occurrence arithmetic per field now (`bare - bracketed == inherent`), and `everyWebFieldIsStillNeutralisedAfterTheFold` is the twin the branch owed. Both kill the mutant. **The general shape: a line-prefix count cannot see a forgery that is not at a line start, which is every forgery an interpolated field can produce.**

**A corpus entry that nothing asserts on is a comment** (PR #130 review, F4). SONNY-226 appended three line-break-carrying entries to `VisionPromptInjectionTests`' standing corpus and its closing comment claimed they exercised the fold. Nothing read them: that suite's tests count delimiters, which those entries contain none of, or read the trusted segment, or drive the decision path. `noCorpusEntryAddsALineToTheObservedBlock` now walks the whole corpus through both interpolated positions and asserts the block's line count, so an entry added later is exercised by being added.

**A test whose name claims more than its assertion can see** (PR #130 review, F6). `thePriorTaskBlockFoldsThroughTheSameSharedImplementation` passes unchanged with the private copy restored — the two implementations were identical, which is the whole reason the move was safe and the whole reason a behavioural test cannot detect it. Renamed to `thePriorTaskBlockStillFoldsEveryLineBreakClass`, which is what it holds, and the structural half moved to `priorTaskContextDeclaresNoFoldOfItsOwn`, a source scan that is itself shown to flag the historical declaration before it is believed.

**A mitigation recorded on another ticket went stale on the day this branch shipped** (PR #130 review, F5). SONNY-219 widened the attribute fold to `.controlCharacters`, accepted that a ZWJ-emoji app name reaches `source=` with its joiners folded, and justified the cost by pointing at the *unfolded* copy of the same name in `systemRules`. SONNY-231 folded that copy. The argument survives only because the two folds take different sets — `.whitespacesAndNewlines ∪ .controlCharacters` there, `CharacterSet.newlines` here, and a ZWJ is not a line break — and **had SONNY-231 taken the obvious one-line swap to `escapeAttribute`, it would have deleted another ticket's recorded mitigation without anyone noticing**. The sentence now says which property it rests on rather than naming a state of the code.

**The `\n` marker collides with something the same prompt says, and "cosmetic" was the wrong word for it** (PR #130 review, F7). `responseContract` tells the model that "a trailing `\n` is delivered as a real Return keypress" — the same two characters this fold injects into attacker-influenced fields of that prompt. What bounds it is not the fold: a `type` action's text is the model's to compose either way, and what it submits is gated by `VisionConsequenceClassifier` and the approval that earns, both of which read the action rather than the prompt. Whether the collision changes what a model does is **not knowable from here**, because it needs a model call and no test in this repository makes one. Recorded at the code as an open edge.

**The rebase auto-merged this entry into the wrong place, silently** (PR #130 review, F3). The changelog is newest-first under `## Entries`; this entry was appended at the bottom of the file, below a hundred others, and the rebase onto `d79e99f` produced **no conflict at all** — nothing in git's machinery is looking at whether a block landed where the file's own convention puts it. It sits under `## Entries` now, above SONNY-288's. The two genuinely mispositioned entries at the file's tail are **not** this branch's to move; SONNY-225 is open for them.

**The battery, at `81e9a05`: 17 mutants, 14 killed, 3 survived, 0 unattributed — and all three survivors are equivalent, with the arguments.** Every mutant's expected killer was written down *before* the report was read, so the results are checked against a prediction rather than rationalised after one. The reviewer's own mutant is R1 — `escapeObservedField` reduced to the fold alone, which left the whole suite green before this round — and it is killed by exactly the two tests F1 asked for, `everyWebFieldIsStillNeutralisedAfterTheFold` and the rebuilt `everyWebResearchFieldNeutralisesAForgedDelimiter`. R7, the SONNY-262 invariant (the fold narrowed to LF alone), is killed by **16** tests across two suites, which is the shared implementation earning its place. R14 and R15 revert **one** web field each — citations, and headings inside the contiguous block — and both die naming that field rather than averaging it away, which is the property the per-field loop claims and would otherwise only have asserted about itself.

**The three survivors are the interesting half.** R13 removes the fold's fast-path guard: without it a break-free value takes the general path, where `components(separatedBy: .newlines)` returns `[value]`, the reduce appends it, and `joined` over a one-element array returns it unchanged — including the empty string, where both paths answer `""`. The guard is running time and nothing else. **R16 and R17 swap the order at the two call sites — escape first, fold second — and both survive, which is F2's correction turned into a measurement.** Under the rationale six records carried before this round, those two mutants should have been killed: if folding first were what lets `escape` see a break-split delimiter, reversing it would change the output. It does not, on any of the 265 corpus values. A battery is where a false rationale becomes visible as a survivor nobody expected, and this one was run *after* the prose was corrected, so it confirms the correction rather than having prompted it.

**Nothing here closes the class, and SONNY-234 is still what does.** Every fix on this branch makes one more forgery unreachable at one more site; the delimiters are still guessable, so a reader should treat this as the interim it is — the same sentence `UntrustedContentBoundary` and `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` already carry.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A "what is still open" table is a claim about the present tense, and nothing makes it decay loudly.** This is the general lesson and it is why the ticket was its own rather than a line in a docs sweep. The document is stamped `4a7d996` at the top, so in principle a reader could treat all of it as a dated snapshot — but §13 is explicitly the live list later work is supposed to consult and tick off, and four of its rows had silently stopped being true. **The fix is not to correct the four; it is to make the column say what kind of statement it is.** The Status column is labelled a board reading rather than a contract term, carries the date and the SHA it was resolved at, and says plainly that "Decided" does not mean "built". A table that dates itself can go stale honestly; one that does not cannot.

**Three of the nine corrections were the document contradicting itself, and a self-contradiction is the cheapest defect to find and the easiest to leave.** §3.1 cited "the 30-second skew tolerance of §3.5" while §3.5 said the value was still SONNY-135's to set. §13 attributed the refresh overlap window to SONNY-127 while §3.3 said — since a correction on 2026-08-21 — that it is the platform's and is 10 seconds. And §3.6 claimed an OAuth sign-in lands on the same account as an email sign-in eleven lines below a table saying such a match "no longer merges on that alone". **Each was reachable by reading two paragraphs of the same document, and each survived a review round that read the diff rather than the file.** A ticket that touches one paragraph reads that paragraph; the contradiction lives in the pair.

**The one that would have cost real work is the OAuth sentence, and it is worth naming what it would have cost.** SONNY-129 builds Sign in with Google and Sign in with Apple. Had it read that sentence and built to it, it would have expected the provider sign-in to resolve onto an existing email account automatically — which is the behaviour the founder removed on 2026-08-22 precisely because a recycled mailbox makes email-matching a takeover path (`docs/sonny-identity-linking-rule.md` §2.1). The rule as built creates a **new** account and returns a `link_hint`, and only rule 4 — a sign-in completed while already authenticated on the target account — joins two existing accounts. A contract that disagrees with the rule doc is worse than one that is silent, because the silent one sends you to the rule doc.

**Deciding which rows were "partial" was the actual judgment, and two of the three would have been wrong either way they were forced.** §13's first row asks for a host *and* two proofs. The host is decided; both proofs were measured and passed — against Supabase Edge Functions, the host the 2026-08-21 decision then moved away from, and §12.2 of the host-decision document says every Edge ceiling stops binding. Marking the row "Decided" would have retired a proof that no longer describes the shipping host; marking it "Open" would have thrown away a settled founder decision. It says both, and points at `server/scripts/deploy.sh` refusing staging and production (`exit 3` at `:113`) as the reason the proofs cannot be re-taken yet. The spend-cap row splits the same way — demonstrated against Postgres 17, and a Postgres property so it survived the host move, but unimplemented. The plans-and-prices row splits a third way: SONNY-17 is Done, but it is a *planning* ticket, so the plan shape is decided while the numbers are deliberately unset and wait on metering that records nothing today.

**A completed ticket is not the same as an answered question, in both directions, and §13 needed both readings.** SONNY-155 is Done and answered nothing itself — it was a triage ticket, and its closure *created* an owner, SONNY-204, which is in Backlog with none of the three things built. SONNY-17 is Done and answered half its row. SONNY-146 is Done and answered its row completely, but in the negative: requests are *not* compressed, the mechanism is built and switched off because the route the client talks to answers a gzip-encoded body with a `500`. Reading a row's status off the ticket's state alone would have got all three wrong.

**The ticket's own line numbers did not match any version of the file, and content is what located them.** The description cites "Line 439 — Until SONNY-115 merges…" and "Line 689 — the refresh-overlap window"; at the branch point line 689 *is* the SONNY-115 sentence and 439 is the `/v1/meta` owner cell, and checking all ten commits that have ever touched the file (`for s in 25f75eb 5727da1 778e441 7445fb0 d0cdfb1 1db893e 8d54bac 5c24df5 a12ef99 f0745f4; do git show $s:docs/sonny-backend-api-contract.md | sed -n '439p;689p'; done`) shows no version where 439 held it. The §13 range 1285–1290 was exactly right. **A line number in a ticket is a citation into a moving file and ages like one** — the same class as the SHA rule, and the reason the descriptions in that ticket were specific enough to survive it.

**Writing the command beside the number caught one of this branch's own defects, in the sentence demonstrating the rule.** The `/v1/health` citation was first written `grep -n 'v1/health' server/src/routes/health.ts` → `29:`. That grep returns **two** lines — the route at 29 and a doc comment at 5 — so the parenthesis was wrong while the number was right. It is now `grep -n 'app.get("/v1/health"' …`. `CLAUDE.md` already says the parenthesis gets the same checking as the number it justifies, and this is a fourth instance of a defect arriving *from obeying that rule*, alongside the three it already records.

**A non-ancestral citation is declared rather than dropped.** `e260575` is SONNY-114's pre-rebase fixture head, cited in §6.1 and §6.4; it resolves and fails `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. It is kept verbatim because a 29–35% compression ratio cannot honestly be restated at a SHA it was not measured at, and the header now names it as the one non-ancestral citation of the four, with the check that separates the two cases. The alternative — silently repointing it at a head where the measurement was never taken — is the mistake `CLAUDE.md`'s rebase rule exists to prevent.

**Two dots compare two trees; three dots compare what you changed — and a base that moves turns the first into a lie.** This entry's `Tests:` field originally read `git diff --name-only origin/main..b5c496f` → one path under `docs/`, which was true when written and false eight hours later. `A..B` in `git diff` compares the *endpoints*, so once `main` gained PR #127's two files the same command printed **three** paths, two of them someone else's work attributed to this branch. The `grep -c` guarding it stayed `0` in both cases, which is the dangerous part: **the count that the claim rested on never moved, so nothing looked wrong.** Had #127 touched `Sources/` instead of `docs/`, that guard would have gone 0 → 1 and this entry would have asserted a docs-only diff over a command that disagreed with it. The fix is `origin/main...HEAD` — three dots, diffing from the merge base — or `git show --name-only <sha>` for a single commit; both are immune to the base moving. **A range command in a durable record must be anchored to a merge base or a commit, never to a branch ref that other people advance.** Same family as the SHA-ancestry rule: a citation that silently changes meaning is worse than one that breaks.

**Rebased a second time, and the conflict was the shared changelog append point — again.** Both rebases were forced by the same thing: `## Entries` is a single newest-first insertion point and every branch writing an entry lands on it, so #129 collided first and #127 second. Resolved keep-both, this entry above SONNY-289's, and the resolution was checked rather than eyeballed: everything from SONNY-289's heading downward — **7028 lines** — is byte-identical to `origin/main`'s copy, and so is everything above `## Entries`, so this branch's contribution to the file is purely additive. That check is worth copying, because a keep-both resolution that silently drops a neighbour's line looks exactly like a correct one in a diff you wrote yourself.

**A dated snapshot is what stops a moving neighbour from looking like rot, and it earned that on first contact.** PR #127 edited `docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md` beneath this branch, adding four lines at 2068 — above both spec-line citations this contract carries. §16.2's endpoint block is cited as "spec lines 2103-2117" and §16.5's migration note as "spec line 2153". **Neither was touched, and touching them would have been the error**, for a reason worth getting exactly right: the citations were read at `4a7d996`, not at any later base, and the drift since is **+15 lines, not +4** — the block is 2118-2132 at `728d1ea` and the note is 2168. PR #127 contributed four of those fifteen; the other eleven accumulated before this branch existed (`git show <sha>:docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | wc -l` → 3093, 3112, 3116 at `4a7d996`, `0df1f49`, `728d1ea`). **The first draft of this paragraph said 2107 and 2157 — the +4 arithmetic — and running the command beside the number is what caught it**, which is the rule in `CLAUDE.md` firing on this entry rather than on the document it describes. The citations are right as dated, verified at their own SHA: `git show 4a7d996:docs/sonny-major-release-spec.md | sed -n '2103p;2117p;2153p'` → `### 16.2 API Surface`, `- \`POST /v1/screen/analyze\`, and the migration note's opening. Re-pointing them at `728d1ea` would attach a reading to a tree it was never taken on, which `CLAUDE.md`'s rebase rule forbids, and would destroy a correct dated citation. **This is the header section this branch added doing the work it was added for**: drift here is ambient and continuous rather than any one neighbour's doing, so without a declared snapshot SHA a reader finds two line numbers that do not resolve and reasonably concludes the document has rotted.

**"Encrypted at rest" is a steady state, not an invariant over every byte, and the note says so.** `LocalStorageEncryption.decode` reads a file with no `SONNYENC1` header as legacy plaintext, hands the value back, and re-writes it encrypted on that same load; a failed re-write is deliberately not a load failure, so the plaintext file survives and the migration retries next time. Writing the flat claim would have been the easier sentence and would have been the same class of overstatement as the one being corrected.

Behavior added:

Thirteen envelope keys are dropped and five added (`comm` over the two sorted key sets: dropped `extra_stats, grouped_by, next_cursor, next_group_offset, next_page_results, prev_cursor, prev_page_results, sub_grouped_by, sub_next_group_offset, sub_total_groups, total_groups, total_pages, total_results`; added `complete, fetched, filter, filter_states, pages`). Nothing in the repository consumes them — `grep -rn 'plane list' --include='*.md' --include='*.sh' .` exits 1 with no output on the tree that became `98cae38`, so there is no call site to break — and keeping a `next_cursor` on the far side of a completed walk would assert the opposite of what happened.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Two bugs in this branch's own first draft came from the same root, and both were caught by the selftest rather than by reading.** `die` ends with `exit 1`, and `resolve_state_filter` was called as `resolved="$(resolve_state_filter "$selector")"` — a command substitution, so the `exit` killed the subshell and the script carried on. Separately, `main` called `list_items "${2:-}" || status=$?`, and a `||` on a function call suppresses `set -e` for the **entire** function body, so nothing downstream aborted either. Together they produced the exact failure this ticket exists to remove: `scripts/plane list nonsense` printed "no workflow state matched", then walked all three pages and exited **0**. The fix is both halves — the call is now `if ! resolved="$(…)"; then return 1; fi`, and `main` calls `list_items` bare so `set -e` stays in force inside it and carries the 2 out as the script's exit code. **The general rule: `die` is safe anywhere except inside a command substitution, and a function invoked under `||` has no `set -e` at all.** Neither is visible in a diff; both are visible in a test that runs the command and reads the exit code.

**Pagination is reconciled, not prevented, and the reconciliation is the whole feature.** Plane's cursor is `per_page:page:offset` — absolute offsets, not a keyset — so a work item created while the walk is in flight shifts every later page by one, and this board is written to constantly by other sessions: its `total_count` read 284 for the coordinator on 2026-08-26, 287 when this session first probed it, and 289 an hour later. There is no ordering that makes offset pagination atomic, so `list` does not pretend to one: it dedupes by `id` so a boundary repeat cannot inflate the count, compares the distinct total against the `total_count` the first page declared, and says plainly when they differ. A benign mid-walk creation therefore reads as `complete: false` and exit 2 with "re-run" rather than as a silent 288-of-287. That is the deliberate trade — a false alarm that costs one re-run, against the failure mode that cost a week of short counts.

**Filtering is on the state id and happens client-side, and both halves were decided rather than defaulted.** Client-side, because the walk has to fetch everything anyway to reconcile against `total_count`, and because a server-side `state=` parameter is not in the v1 API reference this repository works from — depending on an undocumented filter would make the completeness claim rest on behaviour nobody has written down. On the state **id** rather than `state_group`, because this project has two states in the `unstarted` group — `Todo` and `Blocked` — so a `state_group` filter could never select `Blocked` alone, and `Blocked` is the state WORKFLOW.md step 6 requires for a left-open ticket. The selector is resolved before any work-item page is fetched, so a typo costs one request instead of three; the selftest asserts that directly by counting the fake API's request log.

**`env`, not a bare assignment prefix, when a script re-invokes itself with its own configuration overridden.** The selftest runs `scripts/plane` against a local server by setting `PLANE_BASE_URL`, and `VAR=x "$SELF" …` fails with `PLANE_BASE_URL: readonly variable` — bash applies an assignment prefix to its own shell before exec'ing, and this script marks that variable `readonly` at the top. The whole selftest failed 36 of 39 checks on its first run for that reason, with the cause printed on stderr above the failures and nothing else wrong. `env PLANE_BASE_URL=… "$SELF" …` sets it in the child's environment only, and is the form to reach for whenever a `readonly` configuration variable has to be overridden for one invocation.

**A fake API is what makes a "cannot silently truncate" claim checkable at all.** The defect this ticket names is silent by construction: a truncated listing is byte-for-byte the shape of a complete one, so no amount of reading catches a regression and a live run against the real board only ever proves what that board happens to hold today. The selftest serves a synthetic 287-item board over a real HTTP socket through the real `curl` path and asserts on what comes back — including the case that matters, an API that declares 300 and serves 287, where the *only* thing that can notice is the walk's own reconciliation. Two other faults are covered because a real API can produce them and neither is reachable from the live board on demand: a cursor that never advances, and a page advertised with no cursor to reach it. The boundary cases are there for the same reason — a board of exactly `PLANE_PAGE_SIZE` items must be one page and not one page plus a phantom, and an empty board must list as empty rather than as a failure.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **`states`, `modules` and `comments` still take only their first 100 and still say so in the usage text.** They are honestly labelled rather than silently truncating, and their real populations are far below the cap today (`states` → 6, `modules` → 25, live at 2026-08-27T01:1xZ), so none of them is the failure this ticket describes. A ticket's comment thread is the one that could plausibly reach 100 first. Not swept here because the ticket names `list`, and named here rather than left silent.
- **No sentence was added to `WORKFLOW.md`.** Its line 24 already points every reader at `scripts/plane help`, and that text is now accurate and complete — it documents the selector, the exit codes and each output field. Adding a second copy of a CLI contract to a high-traffic process document is how the two drift apart. Recorded as a decision rather than an omission.
- **`PLANE_PAGE_PAUSE_SECONDS` is an environment override with no flag and no mention in the usage text.** It exists so the selftest can run against a local server with no rate limit to respect; a caller who sets it against the real API is defeating the 60-per-minute pacing deliberately, and it is documented where it is defined rather than advertised.
