**Why this class regenerates — stated for the sweep and the next coordinator, not fixed here.** WORKFLOW.md §7 has the changelog entry written before the PR opens, so its `Status:` line is written by a session that cannot know how the merge will go, and its `Reviewed by:` line by one that cannot know whether a re-check will follow. Nothing in the workflow updates either afterwards: the merge is the founder's, at GitHub's control, with no session open on the branch; the entry's figures are re-measured on every fix round and rebase, but the two header lines are the one part of the entry no later commit re-reads — the shape the `Reviewed by:` correction above found, and the shape all three of these have (each was carried through at least one restating docs commit). So every entry's `Status:` line is stale the moment its PR merges unless something touches it, and a re-check posted after the last docs commit leaves an "owed" behind the same way — three entries in two days, after SONNY-273 swept twenty. SONNY-273 swept a snapshot; nothing prevents the next one. Three shapes a mechanism could take, none chosen here: write the line as a dated statement (the "written <date> before the PR opened, and not yet merged then" form — true forever, and silent about the merge, which SONNY-275 calls incomplete rather than false); a post-merge docs commit that stamps the merge commit into the `Status:` line, which is one more small PR per merge, opened by the coordinator or by the next session to touch the file; or accept the drift and re-run the scan above at intervals, which is what SONNY-273 was. Which the repository wants is the coordinator's decision.

**Where PR #118's record lives, and why it is §8 rather than the SONNY-281 entry.** The entry's `Status:` line now says how the branch merged and points at §8; the mechanics — the squash, PR #120, PR #121, the two tree proofs, the two non-merge commits left on the mainline, the email — are in §8, because that is where merge strategy and the rewrite already live, and because the next reader of this shape arrives from `git log --first-parent`, not from a ticket. The one thing §8 now says that it did not on 2026-08-23 is which button: "merge commit, never a squash" was a decision about the result, and GitHub's page offers three controls, two of them wrong in different ways. `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo} --jq '{allow_merge_commit,allow_squash_merge,allow_rebase_merge}'` → each `true` on 2026-08-26, so nothing enforces it; the sentence at the top of §8 and the pointer at §7's merge step are what a person at the control has.

Behavior added:
- **The resume offer's cross declines the task for good, and deletes nothing** (SONNY-282, founder decision 2026-08-25). - **Memory's Unfinished tasks row has a Continue beside Delete.** It runs only what was left of the task through the same `continueResumableTask` the widget's tick uses, under the `.commandCenter` origin, closes the sheet on a real start and stays open on a refusal, is disabled while a task is in flight, and is absent on a row whose remaining work Sonny must not repeat on its own (`mayBeOfferedForResume`, unchanged). It is the one way to pick up a declined task, and it did not exist before this branch — the sheet only ever deleted.
- **Declining one offer moves to the next unfinished task**, rather than going quiet while an offerable record sits on disk.
- **A declined task the user picks up from Memory and that stops again is offered again**: `beginResumableTask` writes its record afresh with no decline, and the session set drops the id on a real start so the disk and the widget agree inside the same launch.
- **Voice answers a clarification** (SONNY-283, founder decision 2026-08-25). The mic button is live and the push-to-talk hotkey records while a question is parked; the transcript is appended to the answer field — fed, not sent — and the user presses Return. The hotkey's summon puts the caret in the answer field.
- **A recording knows what it is for from the moment it starts.** `VoiceRecordingPurpose` is captured beside the origin; an answer whose question has gone by the time the transcript arrives is dropped rather than auto-executed as a command, and a command recorded before a question arrived is refused by `dispatchTranscribedCommand`'s existing guard rather than fed into that question's field.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**SONNY-283's cause was both of the two the ticket named, and the fix needed both halves.** The mic button was `.disabled` because `clarificationQuestion != nil` was a term of `isVoiceTransientlyBusy`, and the hotkey's `canUseVoice` guard refused for the same term, silently — correctly silent for a transient reason, and wrong that this was one. And nothing routed a transcript anywhere but `dispatch`: `dispatchTranscribedCommand` was the only consumer, and it refused during a question by its own guard. Removing the term alone would have re-opened the hazard the term was added for (a transcript dispatched as a command during a pause consumed a card arm and discarded the question — `isVoiceTransientlyBusy`'s old comment records it); adding the routing alone would have left the mic disabled. The term's own comment had already said "voice answering a clarification is a real feature and this does not foreclose it; it is a separate ticket, and the gate has to exist first" — this is that ticket, and the gate moved to the one place that can tell an answer from a command.

**The recording's purpose is decided when it starts, and a delivery that no longer matches is refused in both directions.** A transcription takes seconds; a question can be cancelled or can arrive inside them (a scheduled routine can raise one). Routing on the state found at delivery would run a folder name spoken in reply to a cancelled question as an auto-executing voice command, or drop a command into the answer field of a question the user never saw when they spoke. So `VoiceRecordingPurpose` is captured beside `voiceRecordingOrigin` at `startVoiceRecording`, the live completion passes it to `deliverTranscript` verbatim (a source scan holds that the completion routes and decides nothing), and each mismatch is dropped with a log line, with the matching purpose as the control in the same test. An orphaned answer also clears `preserveUsageForNextStart`, which the transcription had armed for the answer's own `start()`; a refused voice *command* leaves it armed for the next unrelated task, which predates this branch and is not changed by it.

**"Feed the answer field" means fed, not sent.** The decision's words, and its manual item — "confirm it lands in the answer field" — could not be satisfied by a transcript that submitted itself. It is also the safer shape: a voice command auto-executes because a misheard command still meets a planner and a gate, whereas a misheard answer to "which folder?" is one keystroke from running against the wrong folder; the field already has the caret, so sending is Return. Appended rather than replacing, the way dictation lands at the caret in the founder's reference product, with exactly one space however much whitespace either side carried. Whether the founder wants a spoken answer sent on release is left as the open question below; it is a one-line change on top of this, in either direction.

**One `FocusState` for the widget, not one `Bool` per field.** SONNY-247 gave the composer a guarded helper and the clarification panel a private `answerFocused`, which fixed the keyboard and left the hotkey doing nothing: `widgetPresentationRequest` reached only the composer's helper, which correctly declined to focus a disabled field and then had nothing else to focus. `FloatingWidgetView` now owns `FocusState<WidgetInputField?>`, the panel takes a `FocusState.Binding` to it, and every summon runs `focusTheFieldThatTakesInput()`, whose rule — `WidgetInputField.takingInput(clarificationPanelShowing:composer:)` — lives in `AgentActivityPresentation.swift` where a test can hold it off the view. The panel-showing input is read off `state`, the precedence that decides what is drawn, so the caret can never be aimed at a field another panel has outranked; the panel's own two writers (appear, second question) stay, through the shared state. The old test's every count moved to the new shape rather than being dropped.

**A decline is a preference about the widget's offer, not a safety rule — and Memory had no resume door.** `mayBeOfferedForResume` is what Sonny may do *on its own* (PR #105 review F5), and it still gates the offer and every Continue. `isDeclined` is a second filter on the offer alone, so a declined task is exactly as resumable as it was — which raised the question the ticket only half-asked: resumable *from where*? The ticket said "Memory → Unfinished tasks, where it can still be resumed or deleted", and that was not true of the tree: `MemoryEntriesSheet`'s rows had Delete and nothing else. Without a resume door the cross would have been a deletion with the record left visible, which is the shape the founder rejected. So the sheet's unfinished-task rows gained Continue — under the intent-over-enumeration rule, since the decided outcome cannot hold without it — mirroring `runTaskAgain`'s shape (`.commandCenter` origin, close on a real start, stay open on a refusal, disabled in flight) and withheld on the same rule the offer withholds on. Stated on the ticket rather than absorbed silently, because it is Command Center UI that no ticket line named.

**The session set survives the persisted flag, as the write-failure half.** The obvious cleanup was to delete `dismissedResumeOfferIDs` once `declinedAt` existed. It stays, renamed `declinedResumeOfferIDs`, for one case: `save` can fail — a full disk, a store that will not encrypt — and a widget that re-raised the offer while `errorMessage` said the decline could not be saved would loop the user through the same press. So the press is honoured for the session unconditionally, the error (on `errorMessage`, because the user pressed a control — CLAUDE.md's channel rule) says the offer may return after a relaunch, and it does. Held by a test that takes write permission off the store's directory, which is where the product's own atomic write fails. The set is un-declined by `continueResumableTask` on a real start, for the reason its existing comment already argued for the opposite line: a task the user picked up and that stopped again should be offered again, and the disk already says so because `beginResumableTask` writes the record afresh.

**Declining does not touch `updatedAt`, and the test that holds it had to be told about the clock.** A decline is "stop asking me", not activity on the task; bumping the idle clock would buy a declined task a fresh fortnight and move it to the top of the Memory list, when the founder's lifecycle — completes, deleted, or goes idle — is exactly what should still end it. The first version of the test compared `updatedAt` before and after the decline as the run produced them, and could not fail: the store encodes dates at whole-second resolution and both writes landed inside one second, so a mutant that *did* bump the clock passed the test whose name promised it could not. The record is back-dated an hour before the decline now — the same lesson `aTaskInterruptedTwiceStaysOneRecordWithItsOriginalStartTime` learned from PR #105's F7, found here before the battery rather than by it.

**The continuation's origin is a parameter now, and that is what the second door needed.** `continueResumableTask` hardcoded `.widget` because "the offer lives on the widget and nowhere else"; with a Memory door that sentence became false, and a Command Center press claiming `.widget` would move its progress into the widget while Command Center kept its own indicator (`.claude/rules/macagent-ui-conventions.md`'s origin paragraph). So each of the two callers states its own, the body passes it through, and `eachResumeDoorStatesItsOwnOrigin` counts all three sites — because a literal creeping back into the body would silently make one caller a liar. The dispatch-door population scan (`everyDispatchDoorIsClassifiedAndTheClassificationIsChecked`) is unchanged in its counts: the Memory door and the transcript router call existing doors rather than `dispatch(` or `start(`, so seven and seven still hold.

**What the battery cannot see, stated rather than implied.** An answer recording leaving the paused task's plan and step rows alone is the one behaviour here no test reaches: it lives past `AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess`, which a `swift test` process has no bundle identity to survive, and every press in `WidgetVoiceEntryTests` sits behind `try #require(canUseVoice == false)` for that reason. It is the founder's manual row instead — the clarification panel still showing its step rows while the mic is live. Two source scans stand in for the two other things that only run live: that the completion passes the captured purpose, and that the panel's caret binding is the widget's own.

Known limitations / deferred scope: none deferred. Not built, by decision rather than deferral: a spoken answer is not sent on its own (see the open question). Pre-existing and not this branch's: a refused voice *command* leaves `preserveUsageForNextStart` armed for the next task; the `.help` tooltip on the offer's tick and cross may not fire at all (SONNY-244's own finding, unchanged, and still a manual row); an approval raised during a screen-control session reaches no widget surface (SONNY-255).
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): one, for the founder at manual-test time — should a spoken answer be *sent* when the hotkey is released, or land in the field for a Return, as built? The decision's wording ("feed the answer field"; "confirm it lands in the answer field") reads as the latter, and the safer reading was built; the other is `submitClarification()` after the append.

Next branch: whichever the coordinator assigns; nothing here reorders the roadmap.

**2026-08-26, after PR #119's review (four findings fixed, two recorded; the report is on both tickets).** Fix commit `356ce2f`; the docs commit is the one this paragraph lands in, and its SHA is on both tickets and the PR. What changes in the description above, finding by finding:

**F1 (HIGH) — Return on the answer while a spoken answer was still in flight destroyed the pending question.** `submitClarification` cleared the question, the answer, the origin, the binding and the request, armed the restart, and only then called `start()` — which refused on `canSubmit`'s `!isTranscribingVoice` and put nothing back: the pause gone, nothing running, the composed Q&A sitting in the composer where a second Return would dispatch it as a new task, "Clarification needed" showing as a *result*, and the record of the task just abandoned on offer. That window used to need a transcription already in flight when a question arrived; this branch made it the ordinary case (speak, the field holds text, Return lands inside the round trip). Now `canSendClarificationAnswer` — a non-empty answer, a question open, and `!isVoiceInputInFlight` — is the one predicate `submitClarification` refuses on *before it tears anything down*, and both Send controls (the widget's arrow, Command Center's Send) are disabled off it, so the state and the control agree. **All three voice terms, deliberately:** transcribing is the one that destroys state; recording and preparing do not reach `canSubmit`'s refusal, so a Return during them would run the continuation and the words still being spoken would arrive to a question that had gone and be dropped — those words are part of *this* answer, and a recording is a transcription a moment later, so one press must not be answered two ways a second apart. The mic's own control follows the same rule from the other side: it stays pressable while recording so the user can *stop*, which is what makes the answer sendable. The comment above `canSubmit` that claimed answering "proceeds exactly as it did" reasoned about the clarification term alone; it now says which term that is true of and which it is not. `returnWhileVoiceInputIsInFlightKeepsTheQuestionAndTheTranscriptThenLands` drives all three flags in turn on a real question and then the control (the transcript lands, Send returns, Return sends); `theAnswerGateSitsBeforeTheTeardownAndBothSendControlsReadIt` holds the guard's position by offset against every teardown line and the two `.disabled` sites. The manual row is in §3d.

**F2 (MEDIUM) — a declined task's session state and its disk state disagreed after a restart.** `continueResumableTask` was the only site that dropped the id from the session set, while `retryLastCommand` and `runTaskAgain` reached `beginResumableTask` directly, which wrote a fresh record with no `declinedAt` — so cross on the widget, Run again on the Tasks row, fail again: silent this session, offered next launch. The remove now lives in `beginResumableTask`, guarded on `continuing != nil` — the one site every continuation door reaches and the one that writes the record afresh — so all four doors agree, and `aDeclinedTaskRetriedOrRunAgainAndFailingAgainIsOfferedAgainThisSession` drives the two doors that were wrong rather than the one that worked.

**F3 (LOW) — the answer-side guard checked that *a* question was open, not *the* question.** A second question can arrive inside the transcription's round trip, and the answer to the first landed in the second one's field. `VoiceRecordingPurpose.clarificationAnswer` now carries the question's text, captured at recording start, and `answerClarificationWithTranscript(_:answering:)` compares it on delivery — so "refuses both mismatches" is now true of the router as written. `aTranscriptRecordedForOneQuestionIsDroppedWhenADifferentQuestionIsOpen` holds it with the matching-question control.

**F4 (LOW) — the answer arm's comment said the "Clarification needed" summary "ends when the question does", and the stop path contradicted it.** `stopVoiceRecordingAndTranscribe` still cleared `finalSummary`, still logged "Transcribing voice command", and still reset the paused task's usage recorder while the question was open — invisible in the widget, because `.clarification` outranks `.result`, and false as written. For an answer recording the stop path now resets nothing of the paused task's and logs "Transcribing voice answer"; the transcription's cost is added to the pause's own and `preserveUsageForNextStart` carries the whole of it into the answer's `start()`, so the continuation's usage line is the cost of the task the user asked for — the pause, the words and the re-plan. (A *typed* answer's `start()` resets instead, which predates this branch and is left as it is.) Held by region scans inside the completion.

**Recorded, not fixed (below the bar, per the review):** an answer that lands and is then cancelled leaves `preserveUsageForNextStart` armed for the next unrelated task — the same family as the refused-command case already recorded above; and `aDeclineRoundTripsAndAFileWithoutTheFieldReadsAsNeverDeclined`'s "declining does not touch the idle clock" message sits on an assertion nothing in that test declines through — it holds only that `save` preserves `updatedAt`; the behaviour itself is held by `decliningTheOfferKeepsTheRecordAndTheOfferStaysGoneAcrossRelaunches`.

**Owed and not done here: the rebase onto PR #118.** The review's merge order is #118 first, then this branch rebases and reruns the full flagged suite; #118 was still open at `origin/main` `dd4ebae` when this round closed, so there was nothing to rebase onto. Both branches edit `submitClarification` — #118 the composition inside it, this branch the guard at its top — so when it lands the function is read as one thing rather than as a conflict list, per the review.

Behavior added:
- **A sum may end with `=`**, or `=?`, or `?` — `2 + 2 =` is answered `2 + 2 = 4.` by the local calculator like `2 + 2`, from the bare form and from `calc`, `calculate` and `=` alike, and the plan's own summary reads `Calculate 2 + 2.` A conversion may end the same way. At the end only: `2 + 2 = 4` is a statement and stays refused, and `=`, `= =` and `=?` ask what to calculate rather than planning a calculation of `=`, which the prefix path used to do.
- **An answer to a question the instant resolver asked is offered back to the resolver first**, as the rest of the command it was missing: `=` answered `2 + 2` runs `= 2 + 2`; `focus` answered `Focus Writer` runs `focus Focus Writer` and switches to that app; `=` answered `=2+2` runs `=2+2`, the answer taken whole after the join `= =2+2` fails the dry run. The completed command is dispatched as a plain string through the door typed text uses, so the running label, the history row, Run again and Retry all carry it and all get the same answer — and so does Continue after a quit, since the gate reads the question and not the door. **When candidates resolved and none prepared, the first that resolved is dispatched** (re-check R-b): `calc` answered `banana` runs `calc banana` and shows the calculator's own "Could not calculate that expression", the answer typing it gets, rather than a planner refusal. Held by `ClarificationAnswerRoutingTests`.
- **The snippet question asks for the body alone** — "Use the format ;trigger = expansion." — because the answer joins onto the request now; it used to spell out the prefix too, and a user following it to the letter produced a trigger of `snippet save ;sig`.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **A question the planner asked still reaches the planner as request plus exchange**, whole — every test in `ClarificationKeepsTheRequestTests` is unchanged and green, and `typedDirectlyThePlannerGetsTheTextAndAnsweredItGetsTheTextThenTheExchange` asserts the prompt against `ClarifiedCommand.composed` by equality.
- **A planner's question is never completed locally, even when the completion would resolve** — `aPlannerQuestionIsNeverCompletedLocallyEvenWhenTheCompletionWouldResolve`, where "morning" answered "routine" names a saved routine exactly and the exchange still goes to the planner; and a pending question that is not the resolver's own for its request is not completed either (`aQuestionThatIsNotTheResolversForThisRequestIsNotCompleted`).
- **A resolver question whose answer does not complete the command goes to the planner with the exchange, as before** — the Shortcut-not-found question in `aResolverQuestionWhoseAnswerDoesNotCompleteTheCommandStillReachesThePlannerWithTheExchange`.
- The clarification exit's own behaviour: every other test in `ClarificationExitTests` drives `=` and abandons it, and all are untouched and green; the one that answers is re-pinned, not weakened — it now asserts the summary `1 + 1 = 2.` where it asserted only "not the cancelled summary".
- The scheduler's refusal to start under a pending question (`ScheduledRoutineRunTests.aPendingClarificationStopsTheSchedulerFromStartingAnything`) and the voice dispatch's refusal under one (`ProductShellTests`, two tests) drive `=` and never answer it; unchanged, green, swept by `git grep -n 'command = "="' -- Tests` rather than assumed.
- Every run still builds its executor with the live vision environment: `makeExecutor(recordingPolicy:)` is the same call with the same argument, now forwarded through the private overload the dry run uses with `nil`.
- `carriesExchange` and the resolver term in `performStart` are unchanged in code; only their doc comments say more.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The ticket's first question, answered by the capture and not by reading.** Does a clarified command reach the planner in a different shape from the same text typed directly? Yes — request plus exchange versus the text alone — and that is SONNY-248's design and is not the defect: a planner has to read its own question and the answer, and the request is whole at the front of both prompts. What the capture also showed is that `2 + 2` typed directly never reaches a planner at all, so "the same text typed directly" had no planner prompt to compare with; the comparison that mattered was between the doors. **The planner has no calculator.** `CalculatorCapabilityAdapter.metadata.plannerTools` is empty, `OpenAIPlanner.systemPrompt` names no calculate operation, and its last rule is "for any unsupported request, return one unsupported step and explain why" — so "Calculation is unsupported by the registered local tools" is the model complying. Neither refusal sentence appears under `Sources/` or `Tests/` at `dd4ebae` (`git grep -l "registered local tools" dd4ebae` → nothing), because the model wrote them; on this branch the phrase is in three files (`git grep -l "registered local tools"` → `AgentViewModel.swift`, `ResumableTaskRunTests.swift`, this file), every one of them prose quoting the founder's report — this sentence said "anywhere in the repository" for one round and the review caught it (F4). Both of the founder's refusals were therefore one defect, a calculation routed to the planner, reached by two routing rules.

**SONNY-248's resolver term was right for the case it saw and wrong for the questions the resolver raises itself.** Restoring the request to the front of the exchange re-matched the resolver's own prefix, so skipping the resolver for any command carrying an exchange was the correct fix for a *planner's* question — and it silently took every *resolver* question with it. The resolver has seven of its own (`grep -c 'operation: .clarify' Sources/MacAgentCore/InstantCommandResolver.swift` → 7 builders, two of them parameterised — the Shortcut one with three questions and the recent-artifact one with two). **Five are asked on a bare prefix and want the operand that would have followed it** — `=`, `calc`, `calculate` want an expression; `switch to`, `switch`, `focus`, `activate` want an app; `run shortcut`, `invoke shortcut`, `shortcut` want a name; `snippet save` wants the body; `open recent artifact` wants which — **and two are not**: the routine-or-workspace question and the cross-kind question ask which *kind* the user meant, their answers are decisions rather than operands, and they fall to the planner as before, which is correct (this paragraph said all seven for one round; review F3). The planner cannot act on the five: it has no calculator, and every other one arrives as prose about a command whose resolver reading it never saw. **PR #109's own manual checklist, item 4, expected `=` answered `2 + 2` to come back with 4** — the ticket attributes that item to CLAUDE.md, and it is in the PR body — so the item was written expecting a planner to do arithmetic the planner has never been able to do. The test that pinned the routing (`answeringAQuestionTheResolverRaisedGoesToThePlannerRatherThanBackThroughTheResolver`) asserted the planner *was* asked, which is the shape of a test that pins a defect: green, and describing exactly the behaviour the founder reported.

**"The resolver asked this" is read off the question, and the first version read it off the run — which is how the same refusal survived one door over** (review F1). `PreparedPlanSource` is stamped by `AgentRunner.prepare` and cannot be set by any decoded plan, the pause leaves `preparedRun` in place, and `activeTaskPlanSource` already exposed it read-only, so gating on `.instantResolver` looked like using a signal that already existed. The Continue door disproved it at runtime: quit while Sonny is asking what to calculate, relaunch, press Continue, and the paused plan is replayed with `.resumedTask` — so the same question, answered, took the planner path. The gate now resolves the *request* again and completes the answer exactly when that resolution is a `.clarify` carrying the pending question: a property of the request and the question, true through every door that can re-ask one, with nothing for a later door to remember — which matters because PR #119 adds a second Continue under Command Center → Memory that lands on this same path. Pinned end to end by `answeringAfterQuitAndContinueStillCompletesTheCommandForTheResolver`, which builds the relaunch rather than simulating it, and by `aQuestionThatIsNotTheResolversForThisRequestIsNotCompleted` for the identity half, whose second question is set by hand and says so. The doc additions on `activeTaskPlanSource` and `PreparedPlanSource` that named the old reader now record its removal instead.

**The join comes first, the restatement second, and a candidate is workable only when the executor's dry run prepares it** (review F2, the founder's direction). A restatement test is a prefix test and nothing more: `focus` answered `Focus Writer` passes it by coincidence, and read as a restatement Sonny switched to an app called Writer, which nobody named. No word-boundary rule separates that from `calc` answered `calc 2 + 2` — `Focus Writer` begins with `focus ` as surely — so the reviewer's suggested rule was not implemented; it closes the neighbouring shapes and leaves the demonstrated one. Instead `ClarifiedCommand.completions` offers the join first and the answer alone second, and `locallyCompletedCommand` takes the first candidate that resolves to a plan **and** prepares. **Resolution alone is not a check, and the founder's direction only works because of that second half**: the ticket asked whether the resolver validates a named app or Shortcut at resolve time, and the answer is that it depends — a Shortcut, a routine, a workspace and a recent artifact are looked up at resolve time; a running app is checked for *shape* only (`looksLikeRunningAppName`), and a calculator expression is not checked at all (`= =2+2` resolves to a plan to calculate `=2+2`). What checks both is `AgentActionExecutor.prepare`, the dry run every dispatch performs first: `RunningAppSwitchCapabilityAdapter.resolveDefaultOutputs` throws when no running app matches, and `CalculatorCapabilityAdapter.preview` evaluates the sum. So `=` answered `=2+2` joins to `= =2+2`, resolves, fails to prepare, and falls back to `=2+2`, which answers 4 (`anAnswerThatRestatesTheCommandIsTakenWholeWhenTheJoinResolvesButDoesNotPrepare`, which asserts the join resolves as its premise so resolution cannot be what rejected it); `focus` answered `Focus Writer` with both apps running joins to `focus Focus Writer` and activates Focus Writer's bundle (`anAnswerThatOnlyLooksLikeARestatementIsReadAsTheOperandFirst`, whose switcher lists both so the wrong reading would have worked). The dry run is built through a private `makeExecutor` overload with no vision environment, because `makeLiveVisionEnvironment()` assigns `visionUserPauseMonitor` on the way and a routing decision must not do that; a resolver plan never carries a vision step.

**When candidates resolved and none prepared, dispatch the first that resolved — the re-check's R-b, and this ticket's own symptom caught coming back one door over.** The review round's rule composed the exchange for the planner whenever no candidate prepared, and for the calculator that is exactly the refusal this ticket exists to end: `calc` answered `banana` joins to `calc banana`, which resolves, fails to evaluate, and has no restatement to fall back to, so the user got the model's "Calculation is unsupported" where typing `calc banana` gets "Could not calculate that expression: …". The first round had dispatched the join and shown the real error; the dry run made this class one round-trip worse. So `locallyCompletedCommand` keeps the first candidate that resolved and dispatches it when nothing prepared; the exchange goes to the planner only when nothing resolved, which is the replacement-shaped questions. The rule acts only when nothing prepared, so it cannot reorder a candidate that did — F2's Writer test (both apps running, the join prepares and wins) is untouched. Tested as a class, not the reviewer's one example: `calc`/`banana` and `=`/`2 +` (`aCalculationThatResolvesButDoesNotEvaluateIsDispatchedSoTheCalculatorsOwnErrorShows`). **R-c, tightened as asked — and the reason this entry first gave for its mutant surviving was wrong** (round-three re-check). A prepare that comes back with a clarification is not workable (`prepared.clarificationQuestion == nil`). The guard decides anything only when the Shortcuts catalog or a store changes between the resolver's read and the executor's: the two read the same sources with the same keys — the routine and workspace stores through the same `normalized()`, so they cannot deterministically disagree, and the catalog through a process read that `InvokeShortcutCapabilityAdapter.resolveDefaultOutputs` repeats at prepare. The previous round wrote that "under R-b the candidate is dispatched either way", and that holds only when the clarifying candidate is the sole or last one that resolved; with a join whose prepare clarifies and a restatement that prepares, the real code passes over the join and dispatches the restatement while the guardless code dispatches the join. So the mutant was reachable, not equivalent, and until this round no fixture answered consecutive reads differently. `ScriptedShortcutCatalog` now does — first read `["Shortcut X", "X"]`, every read after `["X"]` — and `aCandidateWhosePrepareClarifiesIsPassedOverForOneThatPrepares` asks `shortcut`, answers `Shortcut X`, and asserts the restatement `Shortcut X` is what runs, with the catalog's read count asserted as the premise; the guardless code would run `shortcut Shortcut X` and re-ask. **R-a, recorded by founder decision and not closed:** `focus` answered `Focus Writer` with only Writer running — the join fails prepare, the restatement `Focus Writer` reads as `focus` + `Writer` and prepares, and Sonny switches to Writer, where typing `focus Focus Writer` would say no running app matched. Real, F2's shape narrowed to the not-running case, and not fixed because the consequence is a switched app — visible the instant it happens, reversible, no data touched — while closing it needs per-operation preference machinery (prefer the join's failure over the restatement's success, but only for app-shaped operations). R-b does not reach it, since a candidate prepared; it is pinned as a record (`withOnlyWriterRunningTheRestatementPreparesAndSonnySwitchesToWriterAsRecorded`) so drift is seen. **Its neighbour does change under R-b, and is said rather than left to drift:** with *neither* app running, both readings resolve and neither prepares, so the join is dispatched and fails with "No running app matched Focus Writer." — naming the app the user named — where before the exchange went to the planner (`withNeitherAppRunningTheJoinIsDispatchedAndFailsNamingTheAppTheUserNamed`). **And one sentence the re-review asked to be recorded:** the gate fails honestly when the Shortcuts catalog or a store changes between the question and the answer — the request re-resolves to a different sentence, equality fails, and the exchange goes to the planner, which is the pre-fix path.

**The residual, measured rather than assumed — and the first statement of it was wrong.** Nothing at the string level separates `Focus Writer` from `snippet save ;sig = hello` as an answer to its prefix: both begin with the request. A user who retypes the whole snippet command therefore joins the prefix onto itself, `snippet save snippet save ;sig = hello` is a workable command (the store allows a space in a trigger), and a snippet is **saved** under `snippet save ;sig`. The first version of this paragraph — and of the doc comment and of the test pinning it — said that plan "requires confirmation, so the trigger is shown before anything is saved"; the test, written to assert the approval pause, found none: a new snippet is tier 2, and the consequence rule (`RiskApproval.swift`, tier 0–2 → `.autoRun` unless the plan asks first) auto-runs it. It is recorded as it is: saved silently, visible and deletable on the Memory page. The join wins the trade anyway, because the alternative is the Writer case — a wrong action with nothing to delete. Two things narrow it: the snippet question now asks for the body alone, so the retype is a user overriding the format they were just given (`aSnippetBodyJoinsOntoItsPrefix` holds the intended path), and `retypingTheWholeSnippetCommandJoinsThePrefixOntoItselfAndSavesThatTrigger` pins the residual so it is a record rather than a surprise. A snippet request that already carries part of its body (`snippet save ;sig`, asked for the format) has the same shape and the same outcome.

**The completed command is a plain string, and that is what makes the other doors right for free.** `lastCommand`, the history row, the resumable record and the running label all carry `= 2 + 2`; `request(in:)` of a string with no exchange is itself; Run again resubmits it and gets `4` rather than the question again (SONNY-248's "Run again on a clarified row re-runs the request" still holds for a *planner's* question, where the request is genuinely ambiguous). One consequence: a history row for a clarified calculation reads `= 2 + 2`, not `=`, which is the command the user effectively gave.

**Three things stated as not closed.** The snippet retype above; R-a above, by founder decision; and a calculation phrased as a sentence — `what is 2 + 2`, `convert 5 km to miles` — which matches no resolver rule and reaches the planner, which refuses it for the same reason the founder saw. That is pre-existing, outside this ticket, and filed as SONNY-284.

**A background task's "exit code 0" was the wrapper's `echo`, not the suite's.** The first full run was launched with `…; echo "exit=$?" >> log`, and the harness reported the *command* completing with 0 while the log's last line said `exit=1` — two issues in `ClarificationExitTests`. The log was read before anything was believed, which is the whole of CLAUDE.md's exit-code rule; noted because the notification reads exactly like a pass. The same family, one round later: an edit script whose anchor matched twice refused, the `git commit --amend` after it was not chained on its success, and `894c866` went out as an empty amend — the figure it was meant to carry landed in `d30f2c9` on top, and pushed history was left as it was.

**The review that triggered the round was not on the ticket when the fix round began.** The fix prompt said the full review was on SONNY-281; `scripts/plane comments SONNY-281` listed one comment (this branch's own closing comment, `total_count: 1`) and PR #118 carried no comments or reviews. The round was worked from the prompt's statement of F1–F4, which was complete enough to act on; the reviewer's hand-traced sound findings were not redone, as the prompt asked.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the three shapes above — the snippet retype and R-a are pinned and stated at the code, R-a by founder decision with a later ticket's per-operation preference named as what would close it together with R-b's class; the sentence-shaped calculation is a discovery ticket outside this ticket's outcome.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the roadmap; this is an out-of-band defect fix from the founder's manual pass rather than a roadmap row.

Behavior added:
- **`SecretTextDetector.matches(in:)` folds look-alikes before every class matches.** The whole document, once, through `LatinConfusables.fold(_:)`; every match's range is mapped back into the caller's own string before `coalesceOverlaps`, so `mask(matches:in:)` and `redactCapture`'s line overlap both work on the text the caller passed. The reading SONNY-260 measured at 820 px — `api_key=sk-Abc123Def456Ghi789JklMno012Pqr` with the `a` of `api` as U+0430, the `A` of `Abc` as U+0410, the `o` of `Mno` as U+043E and the final `r` as U+0131 — now masks to the label plus `•••••` and reports one API key at 0.95 (`theLookAlikeReadingSONNY260MeasuredIsMaskedAsAnAPIKey`); a fake-recognizer capture carrying that reading after a Cyrillic prose line paints the key's observation and not the prose (`anObservationTheRecognizerReadWithLookAlikesIsPaintedAndReported`).
- **`LatinConfusables`** — 98 entries (`grep -c '^        0x' Sources/MacAgentCore/LatinConfusables.swift` at `91faa43`) generated from Unicode 17.0.0's `confusables.txt` (dated 2025-07-22) by `scripts/confusables-table`, plus the fifty-two fullwidth Latin letters by arithmetic. The rule is five clauses and the generator is its executable form: not ASCII; mapped by UTS #39 to exactly one scalar; that scalar an ASCII letter; the source itself a letter (general category `L*`); and the source in a block of a script Vision's accurate recognizer can emit — the scripts of its thirty supported recognition languages on macOS 25.5.0 (`VNRecognizeTextRequest().supportedRecognitionLanguages().count` with `.accurate` → 30; Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, Thai, Han, Kana, Hangul; no Greek) — and, since the review round, a sixth: an uppercase source that UTS #39 sends to `l` folds to `I` (F1, below).
- **A one-time-code context word must begin a word** (PR #116 review, F2). `oneTimeCodeMatches(in:)`'s contextual pattern is now preceded by `(?:^|[^\p{L}])` — the start of the text or a non-letter of any script. It was a suffix match before, which the fold turned into a new false positive: an all-caps Cyrillic heading whose look-alikes fold to `…MOTP` (the Russian word for "view"; code points at the code) followed by six digits matched at 0.85, above the threshold. **This changes one pre-existing behaviour**: `Barcode 123456` no longer matches on its `code` suffix. `otp_code=123456` and `verification_code: 483291` still match, which is why the guard is a non-letter and not `\b` — an underscore is a word character and `\b` would have dropped both. Held by `aFoldedCapitalWordEndingInAContextWordIsNotAOneTimeCodeContext`.
- **`HighEntropyFloorMeasurement`** (test target) and the founder-run test `theHighEntropyFloorsCostOnRealCapturesIsMeasuredWithoutChangingIt` — half two's instrument, described under the measurement below. It changes nothing the product does.

The instrument carries its own copy of the rule with the floor as a parameter and `theProbeAgreesWithTheProductAtTheProductFloorInBothDirections` holds that copy to the product; the product never reads the instrument.
- Every pre-existing `LocalRedactionTextTests`, `LocalRedactionImageTests`, `CaptureShellVerdictTests` and `RedactedPayloadStructureTests` case is untouched and green; the mask is still fixed-width, the report shape is unchanged, and `maskedText` still keeps every scalar outside a match — now stated as a property rather than an accident, and held by `ordinaryTextInOtherScriptsIsNotMistakenForASecretAndIsNeverRewritten` (Russian, Ukrainian and Japanese-with-fullwidth screens come back scalar-for-scalar with an empty report) — three hand-written strings, which the review rightly called an assertion rather than a measurement; the measurement is now in the review-round section below: **zero lines newly painted** across 11,385 lines of real text in nine of the fold's scripts and 108 screens of it read by the real recognizer.

- The untrusted-content boundary is untouched: `git diff 25e13a9 91faa43 --stat -- Sources/MacAgentCore/UntrustedContentBoundary.swift` is empty, and its refusal of look-alikes stays deliberate (the rules file now says why beside the fold).

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The fold is the tree's fourth normaliser and is deliberately none of the other three, and the ticket's own worry — that it becomes a second copy of an existing rule — was answered by enumerating them.** `normalized(_:)` in `AutomationStores.swift` and `MacAppCatalog.normalize` fold case and diacritics so names compare — the `.folding(options:)` idiom appears at **13 sites in 12 files** (`git grep -n 'folding(options' -- Sources/MacAgentCore | wc -l` → 13 and `git grep -ln … | wc -l` → 12 at `91faa43`; this entry first said "the three folds" and named `ScreenControlPolicy.normalize` among them, which trims and lowercases and folds nothing — F6) — and none of them turns U+0430 into `a`, because a Cyrillic a is a different letter and not `a` with a mark. `UntrustedContentBoundary.canonicalBase(of:)` matches through canonical equivalence and refuses look-alikes by design — there a look-alike is a forgery to leave alone in text that is never normalised, an unbounded frontier the boundary's own comment declines to chase. Here a look-alike is a misreading to see through on text that goes to a matcher and nowhere else, and the fold's output is used for matching only: **the masked text is never the folded text.** So the fold has one home, `LatinConfusables`, one caller, `SecretTextDetector.matches(in:)`, and a paragraph in `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` saying the boundary must not adopt it. The tests for it compare scalar arrays rather than `==`, for the reason the boundary's tests do: `==` is canonical-equivalence-based and cannot tell a rewritten string from an untouched one.

**UTS #39 is an identifier-spoofing table, not a restoration table, and using it verbatim would have folded digits into letters.** Its prototypes are chosen so that every member of a confusable class maps to one representative: `0` maps to `O`, `1` and `I` map to `l`, Arabic-Indic digit one maps to `l`, Thai zero to `o`, and the fullwidth block is covered for thirty-one letters (`grep -cE '^FF(2[1-9A-F]|3[0-9A]|4[1-9A-F]|5[0-9A]) ;' confusables.txt` → 31; this entry said thirty-two until the review counted) with fullwidth `I` sent to `l`. A fold that took the file as a skeleton would turn a digit into a letter and break the very `hasDigit` check the blob rule rests on. Hence clause 4 (the source must be a letter) and the fullwidth letters by arithmetic (each is its ASCII letter by compatibility decomposition, a definition rather than a resemblance). `digitsSymbolsAndMarksOfOtherScriptsAreNotFolded` and `everyFullwidthLatinLetterFoldsToItsOwnLetterAndNothingElseInTheBlockDoes` hold both. **And the same diagnosis applied to fullwidth `I` was left unapplied to the three capitals in the table that UTS #39 sends to `l`** — U+0196, U+0406 and U+04C0 folded to lowercase until the review's F1 (below); rule 6 is that correction, and `capitalLookAlikesOfIFoldToCapitalIAndTheOthersToL` plus the structural check inside `everyTableEntryIsANonASCIILetterOfAScriptVisionCanEmitFoldingToAnASCIILetter` (no capital folds to `l`) hold it. Rule 4's general category is read from the generating Python's Unicode database, which is 13.0.0 on every Python this Mac has against a 17.0.0 data file (F5): the generator now prints and stamps the version it used, refuses while any in-block candidate is unassigned in it (0 of 107 today), and the Swift test re-checks rule 4 with the platform's own tables, which is the check that actually holds. **The table is generated, and the generator is committed**, because a hand-picked list of "the obvious Cyrillic ones" cannot be checked for completeness by a reviewer and cannot be regenerated when Unicode moves: `scripts/confusables-table <confusables.txt> --check` says whether the block is still what the data produces. The data file itself is not committed (745 KB; the header records version and date).

**Which scripts the fold reaches is a rule about Vision, not about Unicode, and Greek is the case that shows the difference.** Greek alpha, capital alpha and omicron look exactly like `a`, `A` and `o`, UTS #39 says so, and they are not in the table — because the recognizer lists no Greek language and so cannot type them for a Latin glyph. A fold that reached scripts Vision cannot produce would be describing adversarial text, which is the boundary's problem; keeping the population to what the recognizer can emit keeps the rule honest about what the fold is for. `scriptsVisionCannotEmitAreDeliberatelyNotFolded` pins Greek, a mathematical bold A, a Cherokee letter and an Armenian one from the other side, and `everyTableEntryIsANonASCIILetterOfAScriptVisionCanEmitFoldingToAnASCIILetter` walks the generated block against the same block ranges the generator uses.

**Scalar-for-scalar is what makes the range mapping trivial, and byte offsets are the trap it avoids.** Every entry folds one scalar to one scalar, so the folded string has the same scalar count as the original and a range maps back by ordinal — `Folded.originalIndex(of:)` is `unicodeScalars.distance` plus one array lookup, and `nil` mapping on the fast path when nothing folded, which is nearly every string. Three Cyrillic letters ahead of a secret are six UTF-8 bytes before the fold and three after it, so anything carrying a range back by byte offset masks the wrong scalars — **but which byte offset matters.** This entry first credited `lookAlikesAheadOfASecretDoNotShiftWhatIsMasked` and `rangesMapBackToTheOriginalTextThroughWiderScalarsAheadOfThem` with holding that, and they do not (F4): their folded text is pure ASCII, so an ordinal computed from a UTF-8 offset *of the folded text* coincides with the scalar ordinal there, and that mutant (R20 below) survives them. What holds it is unfoldable non-ASCII ahead of the secret — U+0416 and U+4E2D stay two and three bytes wide after the fold — which `unfoldableScalarsAheadOfASecretDoNotShiftWhatIsMasked` now plants, and R20 dies to it by name under a filter — in the full battery R20 still traps on the precondition before any assertion runs and is reported with no test named, as the battery paragraph above records. The mutants that drop or shift the mapping (R3, R4, R7) are held by the original two. Multi-scalar targets (U+0133 to `ij`, U+042B CYRILLIC CAPITAL LETTER YERU to `bl` — the small yeru maps to `ƅi`, and this entry first named the wrong one) are excluded for this reason and stated as excluded. `Folded.originalIndex(of:)` now names a foreign index in a precondition where it can — one past the folded text's end — rather than trapping inside `distance` with `String index is out of bounds`; one that lands inside the folded text's length is not detectable and is why the detector maps only ranges it found in the folded text.

**A single non-ASCII letter at the end of a token defeats `\b`, which is why the vendor and blob patterns needed the fold as much as the label pattern did.** Swift `Regex`'s `\b` is Unicode-aware: U+0131 is a word character, so `sk-…Pq` followed by it has no word boundary before the dotless i, the greedy class cannot find one inside the run either, and the whole vendor match fails — not just the last character. That is why SONNY-260's reading lost all three api-key patterns to four substituted letters rather than one, and why folding is document-wide rather than a label-pattern special case: `everyClassMatchesThroughTheFoldAndMasksTheCallersOwnScalars` puts one look-alike into `Bearer`, `password`, `BEGIN` and `code` and expects each class to match and mask its own scalars.

**Half two, measured: what 28 would paint that 32 does not, and on what.** The founder asked for a false-positive rate on real captures at 32 and at 28. **Real captures of the founder's screen were not available to this session** — `screencapture` from an agent session is refused by the harness before it runs (tried once, blocked; CLAUDE.md now says so) — so the measurement has two parts, and the entry is precise about which is which. **(1) The instrument, committed:** `HighEntropyFloorMeasurement` costs a capture the way `redactCapture` paints it — lines painted, captures touched — by the product detector as shipped (floor 32, every class, the fold included) and then with the tokens the 28 floor would add, printing names, lengths and counts and never a recognized token; `theHighEntropyFloorsCostOnRealCapturesIsMeasuredWithoutChangingIt` runs it over a folder of PNGs through the real recognizer, one command for the founder: `SONNY_CAPTURE_CORPUS=<folder>` in front of the flagged test command with `--filter theHighEntropyFloorsCostOnRealCaptures`. **(2) The corpus, measured here**, through the same instrument from a throwaway probe recorded on the ticket and not committed: real content of seven classes a builder's screen shows — this repository's Swift and TypeScript (312 files), its Markdown (25), its `package-lock.json` and `package.json`, real terminal output from this Mac (`git log`, `ls -la`, `curl -v`, `openssl s_client -showcerts`, `ssh-keyscan`, 14 files), six man pages, three public API responses, and the visible text of fifteen real web pages (GitHub, Wikipedia, MDN, BBC, Vercel, Supabase, Stripe, Docker, Notion, Linear, Hacker News, PyPI, and the two Wikipedia fixtures) — laid out the way each class is shown (hard-wrapped at 80 columns for terminal and man, truncated at 120 for code and JSON, soft-wrapped at 100 for prose and web), **207,587 laid-out lines in 377 files**, measured two ways. *Text level*, every line, in 42-line windows as a reader scrolls: **5,131 screens; painted at 32: 471 lines in 182 screens; at 28: 482 lines in 183 screens** — 11 more lines, one more screen, 29 tokens (28: 7, 29: 8, 30: 7, 31: 7). *Screen level*, 84 screens rendered at 1440×900 in 13 pt Menlo (12 per class), read by the real recognizer and costed by the product detector: **before OCR 34 lines in 13 screens at 32 and 38 lines in 13 at 28; after OCR 34 lines in 18 screens at 32 and 38 in 18 at 28** — four more lines, no new screen, and every one of the extra tokens (5) inside a `package-lock.json` view that already had 19 lines painted at 32 (`grep 'HIGH-ENTROPY-FLOOR-TOTALS'` over the probe's log, re-measured at `91faa43` after the rebase, and at two pre-rebase heads before it, with figures identical to the digit each time, and `disagreements=0` on every line — which, since the review round, means the instrument's blob rule and the product's api-key blobs cover each other in both directions on every capture, not merely that the probe found nothing the product missed). **The corpus is written down file by file** — every class, its command or URL, its layout, and the pages dropped as bot walls — in a comment on SONNY-272 (F7: the review reproduced every figure but had to infer the composition). **What the 29 extra tokens are**, since the founder's cost is "what gets painted": 22 are fragments of `sha512-…` integrity hashes between `+` and `/` in `package-lock.json`; 5 are lines of a PEM certificate dump from `openssl s_client -showcerts`; 2 are Swift test function names with a digit in them — `keepsRecordsWithinTheLast30Days`, `excludesRecordsOlderThan30Days` — the one class the 32 floor never reaches and 28 would: a camelCase identifier of twenty-eight letters or more carrying a digit, twice in 128,138 lines of this repository's code. **Two things about the baseline that matter more than the floor.** OCR itself moved the 32-floor's touched-screen count from 13 to 18 on the same 84 screens — a merged pair of tokens reads as one long blob, a run of digits reads as a spaced pair — so recognizer noise is a larger source of over-painting at 32 than lowering the floor to 28 would be. And 95 of the 105 `one_time_code` matches the baseline made on this repository's Markdown are `NNN-NNN` line-range citations (`CerebrasPlanner.swift:129-131`), painted whole at confidence 0.55 by the spaced-pair shape; that is SONNY-278's discovery, filed rather than fixed. **The floor is unchanged**: the number is on the ticket beside the founder's decision, which is theirs; nothing here argues it either way.

**A whole file measured as one capture lets a fail-closed tail paint thousands of lines, and the measurement had to be restated per screen before it meant anything.** The first text-level run costed each file as one document and reported 13,948 painted lines in this repository's Markdown at 32 — one `-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----` marker quoted in prose with no `END`, whose truncated-block rule paints to the end of the text, exactly as designed for a screen cut off mid-key and exactly wrong for a 23,000-line document. Costing 42-line windows instead gives 132, and the same marker paints the rest of its one screen. Anyone reusing the instrument over text rather than captures: window it.

**Pasting the character is the mistake the rules file warns about, and this branch made it three times before its own sweep caught them — and twice more in the fix round, caught the same way.** Two U+0430s in `LatinConfusables`' doc comment and one in a test comment were typed as the rendered letter — indistinguishable from `a` in a diff — and found by a scan of the changed files for Cyrillic, fullwidth and dotless-i scalars, not by reading; the fix round pasted the Russian word for "view" into two comments and the sweep caught those too. Every scalar in the code, the tests and this entry is an escape or a `U+` code point; the sweep is `python3` over the changed files, and it is cheap enough to run before every commit that touches this area.

**PR #116's review round: seven findings, one of them the blocker this branch's own diagnosis should have caught.** Reviewed at `cbd83dc`, a pre-rebase head (the rebase paragraph above); every fix is in `a5ed02a`; every figure below is re-measured at `91faa43`.

- **F1 (Medium, merge blocker) — three capital-I look-alikes folded to lowercase `l`.** U+0196 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER IOTA, U+0406 CYRILLIC CAPITAL LETTER BYELORUSSIAN-UKRAINIAN I and U+04C0 CYRILLIC LETTER PALOCHKA all carried UTS #39's `l`, because UTS #39 merges `I`, `l` and `1` into one class with the prototype `l` — the very spoofing-table property this entry describes and corrected by arithmetic for fullwidth `I`, and then left standing in the generated block. uk-UA is one of the recognizer's thirty languages, so U+0406 is what Vision types for a Latin `I` exactly as it typed U+0410 for `A` in SONNY-260's reading, and the fold sent `AKIA` to `AKlA`: probed against the detector at the reviewed head `cbd83dc`, `AK` + U+0406 + `A` + U+0406 + `OSFODNN7EXAMPLE` matched nothing, and neither did the palochka form, while fullwidth `I` matched at 0.95. Rule 6 in the generator sends an uppercase source with the prototype `l` to `I` — the only class where the prototype's case disagrees with the glyph's (the two capitals that map to `b`, U+0184 and U+042C, look like a lowercase b and stay) — and **the proof is against the detector, not the table**: `capitalLookAlikesOfIRestoreTheCaseSensitivePatterns` runs all three capitals through `AKIA`, U+0406 through `AIza`, and a 32-character blob whose only uppercase letter is a folded U+0406 through the blob rule, and every one matches at the confidence the clean key would. The lesson is narrow and worth keeping: a diagnosis applied to one instance of a pattern and not enumerated across the population is the subtraction-without-enumeration failure CLAUDE.md already names, in a table of ninety-eight rows read by no one.
- **F2 (Low/Medium) — the fold created a new above-threshold false positive, and the non-Latin cost had been asserted.** The one-time-code context pattern had no leading guard, so a *suffix* was a context word (`Barcode 123456` already matched), and folding turned an all-caps Cyrillic heading into one: the Russian word for "view" folds to `…MOTP`, and with `: 123456` after it matched at 0.85, above the threshold, on a screen that had matched nothing before this branch. The guard is above (a non-letter of any script rather than `\b`, so snake_case labels survive). The measurement the review asked for: **the visible text of 24 real pages in nine of the fold's languages** — Russian (5), Ukrainian (4), Japanese (4), Chinese (2), Arabic (2), Thai (2), Vietnamese (2), Turkish (2), Korean (1); Wikipedia articles and front pages, lenta.ru, ria.ru, pravda.com.ua, nhk.or.jp, yahoo.co.jp, aljazeera.net, thairath.co.th, vnexpress.net, hurriyet.com.tr — **11,385 lines in 284 forty-two-line screens at text level, and 108 of those screens rendered at 1440×900 and read by the real recognizer**, costed by the base commit's detector (copied verbatim from `dcf3304` into the probe) and by the product's, side by side. **Newly painted lines: 0 at text level and 0 through OCR; lines no longer painted: 0 and 0.** The baseline noise is unchanged by the fold: 5 lines in 3 screens at text level and 7 lines in 5 screens after OCR, every one `one_time_code` on digit runs (phone numbers, Korean ID-shaped digits) except one merged blob on a Japanese screen — the same recognizer effects the English corpus shows. Every figure re-measured at `91faa43` (0 lines newly painted at text level and 0 through OCR, the 5 and 7 baseline lines unchanged, identical to the pre-rebase run) from the probe recorded on SONNY-272; the corpus is listed in the same comment as the English one.
- **F3 (Low/Medium) — the instrument's drift guard was never shown to fire, and was one-directional.** Three mutants survived the whole suite: the guard pinned `true`, the disagreement counter deleted, and "a painted line is the line a match starts in". The guard now holds the product's api-key blobs (class *and* confidence 0.5 — an out-of-range SSN shape is also 0.5, and holding it to the probe reported a disagreement on the test file that plants one) to the probe as well as the probe to the product, `cost(ofLines:)` takes the two floors as parameters so `theDriftGuardFiresWhenEitherSideMovesItsFloor` can show it false in both directions and `Totals` counting each, `anotherClassAtTheBlobsConfidenceDoesNotTripTheDriftGuard` pins the SSN case, and `aMatchSpanningLinesCountsEveryLineItTouches` runs a private-key block through the line count. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Founder decision, 2026-08-24 (Sauransh Bhardwaj, recorded on SONNY-266): the set-aside files get a surface, not a cap.** One line and one control in Settings' existing data section, stating how many there are and how much space they hold. No capping and no ageing out — deleting that data is precisely what SONNY-239's design exists to avoid, and a retention number chosen now would be guessed rather than measured. Not a new page, not a per-file list, not a Memory row. The restore path — after a key restore a set-aside file becomes readable while the live one does not, and offering that swap is the real answer — is deferred to SONNY-253 deliberately, because it belongs with the key migration that makes it possible. The property this fixes is narrow and worth stating exactly: the user was told a file was kept and never how many, or how much space, which is disclosure they cannot act on.

**The older question on the same ticket — should the per-row Delete sweep these files once they are visible? — is answered no, and visibility is the reason.** SONNY-266's founder comment of 2026-08-23 moved that question here from PR #110's review, on the argument that it is easier to answer once the files can be seen. It is: the case for sweeping them from a per-row Delete was that leaving them was an undisclosed privacy gap, and the row that now names them, counts them, sizes them and removes them is exactly the disclosure that gap lacked. So `deleteStoreFilesOnly()` is untouched, its doc comment records the re-asking, and disclosed-and-recoverable still beats silent-and-final — more so now that "recoverable" no longer means the whole wipe.

**Three doors, one loop, and a named `Reach` rather than two booleans.** `LocalDataDeletionService` had two doors over one private `delete(sweepingSetAsideFiles:)`; a third that takes set-aside files and nothing else would have been a second boolean, and two booleans a caller can cross. `Reach` is three cases, each doc-commented with the control it serves, and the loop reads `includesSetAsideFiles` before the sibling sweep and `includesStoreFiles` before the store file — so the narrower door is the wipe's loop with one `guard`, the suffix match stays written once, and the attempt-every-file-and-report-what-survived behaviour a privacy delete needs comes for free. `missingFileCount` stays zero for that door: nothing it was asked for was absent.

**One listing, read by the count and walked by the delete.** `setAsideFiles()` is `unique(fileURLs).flatMap(quarantinedSiblings)`, the summary counts and sizes that list, and `deleteSetAsideFilesOnly()` walks the same `quarantinedSiblings(of:)` over the same URLs — so the number on the Data page and the files the press removes cannot come from different populations, which is the property PR #110's fix round had to build for readability the hard way. The view model reads both through the one `LocalDataDeletionService` it was constructed with, which is what makes the fixtures hermetic: `MemoryFixture`'s `wipesRealStoreFiles` now also decides whether the line counts anything, and its doc comment says so.

**The size is the logical size, in Finder's unit.** `URLResourceKey.fileSizeKey`, summed, formatted with `ByteCountFormatter` `.file` — the decimal figure Finder shows first and the unit SONNY-266's own measurement of `clipboard-history.json` (1 011 740 bytes at its cap) is in. Not the allocated size, and not `.memory`, whose binary units disagree from a million bytes up; `theSetAsideCopyAgreesWithItselfOnOneFileAndOnSeveral` pins the style against an independently built formatter, which holds in any locale where a literal "1.5 MB" would not, and checks the two styles differ at that size so the assertion cannot pass vacuously. A file whose attributes cannot be read still counts — it is there and the delete will still attempt it — and contributes nothing to the size rather than failing the summary.

**The control is guarded on a running task, by founder decision on PR #117's review (F3) — and this paragraph said the opposite until that round.** The argument it made still holds: the only writer of a set-aside file is `deleteMemory(in:)` (`git grep -n 'moveAsideAll' 7fead7b -- Sources` → one call site, `AgentViewModel.swift`), which refuses during a run, so the population cannot change under one. What that argument covered was the files, not the error channel. A failure of this control goes to `errorMessage`, which both surfaces suppress while `isRunning` and rank above the task's result once it ends — `performStart`'s `defer` clears `isRunning` and leaves `errorMessage` standing — so a control that could fail mid-run would report a task that ran and succeeded as this delete's failure, and pop the widget for it: the SONNY-201 shape CLAUDE.md documents, arriving through a new door. The wipe and the per-row Delete never face it because their guards keep them out of a run. The guard copied is the wipe's — same page, same row shape, same `isRunning` condition — so the three doors agree; the button is disabled under the same condition, so the guard is the backstop rather than the surface; and `theSetAsideFilesCannotBeDeletedWhileATaskIsRunning` holds both halves, the refusal and the population argument. R8 is the success side of the same seam — `errorMessage = nil` was unpinned because every asserting test started from `nil` — and the success test now starts from a stale one.

**The Memory page's sentence about a kept file follows the files, by pruning a record rather than clearing a list** (PR #117 review, F1). After a per-row Delete keeps files, that page reads "The 2 files Sonny could not read are still on your Mac." beside a Reveal in Finder control that selects them. Settings' narrower control and the whole wipe can each remove *some* of those files and fail on the rest — the Task history row covers four stores, so one press keeps several — and the first version of this branch cleared the whole list and the sentence when *any* named file was gone, retiring the one surface that names a file while that file was still on disk. Three of the reviewer's mutants survived it because every test kept exactly one file. So the bare list is now a record, `LastPerRowDelete` — the row, the deleted count, the kept files and the first failure — read through the old name for the Reveal control, and `MemoryDeletionCopy.perRowDeleteReport` derives the sentence from it in one place: at the press, and again after `pruneLastPerRowDeleteToFilesStillOnDisk()` drops the files that are gone. One of two gone reads "The file Sonny could not read is still on your Mac." beside a control that selects exactly that file; both gone retires both; a failure sentence — about the step that failed, not the files — stays whatever happens to them. The prune runs after either branch of either door, because the wipe's failure branch never reaches the wipe's own clearing, so a partial wipe used to leave the page naming a file it had removed. **Tested at n = 2 at both doors, with one file made immutable** (`FileAttributeKey.immutable`, `chflags uchg` underneath) so a single press removes one and is refused on the other — a partial failure a locked directory cannot produce, since that refuses every unlink in it — and one that needs no privilege gate, because the flag refuses root's unlink too; `everyDirectoryLockingTestCarriesTheGateAndNoOtherTestDoes` keys on `0o500` and is untouched. A first draft of the prune compared the sentence on screen to the record's before rewriting it, a branch nothing could reach: `memoryDeletionStatusMessage` has one writer besides the prune and the wipe's clearing, `deleteMemory(in:)`, which replaces the record in the same breath. The check is gone and `theMemoryPagesSentenceHasOneWriterBesidesThePrune` pins the premise instead.

**Hidden at zero.** A line reading "0 files Sonny could not read" would be new surface for a state most users never reach — the founder's own words for why this is a line rather than a page. The gate is `SetAsideFilesSummary.isEmpty`, a value on the type rather than a comparison in the view body, for the reason `canDelete` and `MemoryRowDestination` already give: a gate written only in a view modifier is a gate no test can read. It reads the count, never the size — a zero-byte file that would not read is set aside like any other, and `theListingCountsEverySetAsideFileAndSumsTheirBytes` pins that.

**The copy is the count and the size, and the product's one name for the files.** "Files Sonny could not read" is what the Reveal label, the confirmation and the delete's outcome already called them, so the row's title is "2 files Sonny could not read", the detail is the size alone, and every sentence — title, confirmation title, confirmation, outcome, failure, the screen reader's label — comes off `MemoryDeletionCopy` through one private `theFilesSonnyCouldNotRead`, which `revealAccessibilityLabel` now reads too. Nothing explains why the files exist or what a later key restore could do with them: that is the standing no-explanatory-copy rule of 2026-08-14, applied as "A precise label is not explanation" says to apply it — narrow the name until no sentence beside it is needed. The confirmation still says what goes and what stays, because every destructive confirmation in the app does. The failure sentence is composed from `LocalDataDeletionError`'s fields — what failed, and how many went first: "Could not delete 1 of the 2 files Sonny could not read: <name>. (<reason>)" — rather than wrapping its `errorDescription`, whose noun is the wipe's "local data files" (PR #117 review, F4). **One sentence is deliberately not "Deleted 0 files"**: when the files went between the page listing them and the press — by hand, or by the wipe in another window — the outcome reads "The files Sonny could not read were already gone.", which does not start with "Deleted" and so renders with the warning glyph, which is right: the state changed under the user.

**The dialog sits on the row: not on the page, not on the button.** The page already carries the wipe's `confirmationDialog`, and two on one node is the shape SwiftUI has dropped one of before; the button sits inside `SettingsAdaptiveControlRow`'s `ViewThatFits`, whose trailing view appears in both layout candidates, and the row is the node rendered exactly once. Everything is System A — the wipe's own row, label, divider and `SonnyButtonStyle(tone: .danger, width: 96)` — with no token added.

**`#expect`'s second argument is a `Comment`, and a `String` does not convert to it.** `#expect(condition, someString)` fails to compile; `#expect(condition, "\(someString)")` is the form. It cost this branch one compile round on two sites and is written here so the next test with a computed message does not pay it again.

**A mutation plan's `from` block is a citation of a tree, and it goes stale the way a SHA stamp does.** Every block in this branch's plan was verified to match exactly once — against the working tree at the moment the plan was written. The confirmation dialog then moved from the button to the row, one indentation level, before the code commit, and chunk 3's pre-flight refused M15 with `0 matches` and ran nothing, which is the harness working. The block was rewritten from `git show 82c92b7:…` and the chunk re-run. So verify a plan against the *committed* tree it will run on, after the last edit, and not against whatever was on disk when the plan was drafted. Same family as the `#expect` trap above: a check that was true when made and silently not true when used.

**`nohup setsid` does not exist on this Mac, and a battery that outlives a tool's ceiling needs to be split, not detached.** The first attempt to run the fifteen in one go tried to detach the chain from the harness's ten-minute limit with `setsid`, which macOS does not ship; `nohup` reported `setsid: No such file or directory` and nothing ran — the harmless failure, and worth recording because the other one is not: a battery killed mid-mutant leaves that mutant applied in the tree and a lock behind it (`scripts/mutate unlock`). `--only` in chunks of six, each about three minutes, is the shape that fits.

**Fix round, 2026-08-24, from PR #117's fresh-session review — seven findings, two Medium, none in the three doors themselves; all seven taken, and every figure below re-measured at `7fead7b`.** The reviewer's own battery verified the doors (R1, R2, R10 caught every crossing, PR #110's F2 shape included) and found five survivors, all on the surface: R3, R4, R5 on the retirement (F1), R8 on the success side of the error channel (F3), R9 on the listing's `unique()` (F5). The substance of F1 and F3 is written into the two paragraphs above, which this round corrected in place — the guard paragraph had said the opposite of what the code now does.

- **F1** — the record and the prune, above. Four tests: a partial removal at the Data page keeps the sentence for the file still on disk, both files gone retires sentence and control together, a partial wipe does the same at the other door, and a failure sentence stands while its control goes. R3, R4 and R5 are in this branch's battery as N1, N2 and N3, each killed by the test written for it.

The row's vertical fallback is not reachable by resizing — `SettingsDialogView` is `.frame(width: 880, height: 620)` — and the list says so rather than inventing a step.

- **F4** — `MemoryDeletionCopy.setAsideFilesFailure` takes the `LocalDataDeletionError` and composes the sentence from its fields — "Could not delete 1 of the 2 files Sonny could not read: <name>. (<reason>)" — instead of wrapping `errorDescription`, whose noun is the wipe's.
