Tests: **1879 in 135 suites, exit 0 at `c85572d`** via the flagged command. Net **+22 tests** (`git diff 94afca1..HEAD -- Tests/ | grep -c '^+    @Test'` = 22 at `c85572d`), one new suite. **`scripts/warnings`: 0 warnings at `c85572d`**, clean tree, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled. Nothing was removed; **three existing tests changed**, each explained in place — `theLoadFailureBannerExplainsItselfOnceAndStillNamesTheAffectedStore` for the banner's new closing sentence, and the two output-location write-failure tests, which is the one behaviour change in this branch a reader should not skip (below).

**Mutation battery at `ff1cf63`: 13 mutants, 13 killed, none survived** (`scripts/mutate`, which stamps its own SHA). The two that matter most for the founder's screenshot: M1 puts the Delete gate back to `count > 0` and is killed by `anUnreadableRowSaysSoInsteadOfZeroSavedAndKeepsItsDeleteLive`; M4 unlinks an unreadable file along with the readable ones and is killed by two, including the one that reads the set-aside bytes back. M5 is M4's mirror — every file moved aside, readable ones included — killed by five, which is what stops a fix for SONNY-239 from quietly breaking the privacy promise every other row's confirmation makes. M6 stops the whole-data wipe sweeping set-aside files and is killed by two. M12 makes that sweep match any name sharing a prefix and is killed by five, three of them pre-existing.

What changed for the user: a memory Sonny cannot read now says so and can be cleared in one press. The Memory row reads "Can't be read" instead of "0 saved", its Delete is live even though the count is zero, the banner that used to return on every launch now ends with where to go, and the confirmation says plainly that Sonny cannot tell them what is in the file and is keeping it rather than deleting it. Pressing Delete renames the file aside and starts that memory over; nothing is destroyed. Separately, the Memory page stops going stale: a task that records a folder, a file, a snippet or an allowed app now updates the row while the user is looking at it, instead of only after they navigate away and back.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Founder decision, 2026-08-23 (Sauransh Bhardwaj, recorded on SONNY-239): Sonny never clears an unreadable file by itself, and when the user clears it the file is moved aside rather than unlinked.** Three options were priced — user-pressed delete, automatic quarantine, and delete-versus-rename. Automatic is out on the consequence rule: deleting data is destructive and Sonny does not do destructive things unasked. The rename half comes from **SONNY-253**, the local-encryption-key architecture decision recorded the same day: a decrypt failure does not prove a file is garbage, it proves the bytes were written under a different key, and under that design a restore or a key migration can hand the key back. `routines.json` and `workspaces.json` hold things a person made by hand. Building any of SONNY-253 is explicitly out of scope here.

**Rename-aside is the *unreadable* case only, and that reading is this session's rather than the decision's literal words.** SONNY-239's decision says "when the user does press Delete, the file is renamed aside", in a ticket entirely about unreadable files. Applying it to readable ones would make every sentence in `MemoryDeletionCopy.message(for:)` false — "This deletes every copied item Sonny has recorded" — for a file the user can see the contents of and has no ambiguity about. Flagged on the ticket so the founder can correct it rather than resolved silently.

**The split is per store, not per row, which is the case a row-level answer gets wrong.** Task history covers four files. Keeping all four because one will not open leaves the user's actual command history on disk after they pressed a control that promises to delete it; deleting all four destroys the one file Sonny cannot prove is garbage. `deleteMemory(in:)` asks `unreadableStores(in:)` — derived from the load failures the view model is actually holding — and unlinks the rest.

**The recovery deliberately goes through no store door, and that is why it can run at all.** Every path into `OutputLocationStore` loads first, `forget(path:)` included, so a store cannot be read, written *or* cleared once its file will not decode. `LocalDataQuarantine` operates on a file URL and knows nothing about what is in it, so all thirteen stores inherit it without a line of store code changing. `LocalDataQuarantineTests` establishes both halves across `LocalStore.allCases` — the gap and the repair — with an exhaustive switch, so a fourteenth store joins that population by failing to compile.

**The failure is reproduced the way the founder's Mac produced it, not with malformed bytes.** Every unreadable fixture in this branch is a valid `SONNYENC1` blob written under one key and read under another. Random bytes exercise the JSON half of `LocalStorageEncryption.decode` and say nothing about the decrypt half, which is the half that actually happened — to SONNY-240's fixtures, and to anyone whose Keychain item is replaced.

**Settings' whole wipe had to learn about the set-aside names, or this fix would have created a privacy hole.** `LocalDataDeletionService` deletes thirteen exact filenames. A file the quarantine renamed still holds the user's folder paths, commands and routines; a wipe that reported "Deleted 13 local data files" while leaving them would be exactly the half-true promise the store list's own comments warn about. `deleteAllLocalData` now sweeps `<name>.unreadable-*` before the file itself, outside the existence check — a store whose own file was already moved aside has nothing at its own path and everything at the suffixed one.

**One behaviour change worth a reader's attention: when a store's file is unreadable, the load banner is now the last word after a run rather than the write failure's own sentence.** A run whose output-location write fails because the file will not decode used to end on "Sonny could not update its list of output locations: …"; the terminal refresh now re-reads that file, records the load failure, and the banner — which names the store *and* the control that clears it — replaces it. Both are true and the more useful one wins; `errorMessage` stays `nil`, which is the property those tests were written for and which has not moved. **This is not a new competition between the two channels**: `refreshSavedItems()` has probed snippets, recent artifacts, clipboard history and allowed apps for readability after every successful run since row J, through `refreshSilentlyReadStoreHealth`, and has always been able to overwrite a write notice the same way. Output locations was simply outside that probe. The two tests now subscribe to `$localStorageNotice` and assert both notices in order, so neither half is lost.

**SONNY-246's description names two rows that never had the defect, and the correction is now a test rather than a note.** It lists Task history and Unfinished tasks among the rows that "all load through the same call". They do not: task history is published by `refreshTaskHistory()`, which `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` already called on every terminal outcome, and unfinished tasks by `refreshResumableTasks()`, called after every write the view model makes to that store. `taskHistoryWasAlreadyFreshWithoutTheMemoryPagesOwnRefresh` is the record, so a change that made either depend on the Memory page's `.onAppear` fails here rather than in another manual pass.

**The refresh hangs off the terminal outcome rather than off each store write, and the cost is measured rather than asserted.** Almost nothing the Memory page shows is written by the view model — output locations and recent artifacts come from `AgentRunner` and the executor, a snippet from a capability adapter, all inside `MacAgentCore`. `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` is the one function every foreground outcome passes through, which is why row 13's resumable-task settle already lives there; the refresh sits beside it, above the same guards, because a suppressed run can still have saved a snippet. **4.7 ms, median of ten reloads with every capped store at its cap** (clipboard history 100 items of 10 000 characters — a 1 011 740-byte file — recent artifacts 100, output locations 50, snippets and allowed apps 100 each; min 4.2, max 5.8; measured at `ff1cf63` with a throwaway harness, deliberately not committed, since a timing assertion in this suite would be a flake). For scale, `refreshTaskHistory()` already runs on this same path at a cost its own doc comment records as 130 ms at the cap.

**The clipboard poll is the one place a naive refresh would have been expensive, and the negative half of that rule is counted rather than inferred.** It ticks once a second; reloading five encrypted files on every tick is 60 decrypts a minute on the main actor for a pasteboard nobody touched. The refresh hangs off `poll()` returning an item. `anIdleClipboardTickPublishesNothingAtAll` counts `objectWillChange` around an idle tick — a reload assigns those `@Published` arrays whether or not their contents changed — with a recording tick beside it as the control, so zero means the guard rather than a subscription that never fired. Asserting the return value alone would have been satisfied by a refresh that ignored it, and mutant M10 proves it: it survives the return-value assertion and dies on this one.

**SONNY-246's second question answered: the entries sheet cannot disagree with the row.** The ticket flagged that a sheet reading on open would be fresh while the row behind it was stale — two numbers disagreeing on one screen. It does not read on open: `MemoryEntriesSheet.entries` computes from `MemoryEntryPresentation.entries(for:viewModel:)`, which reads the same published arrays the row's count reads. One source, so they go stale together and refresh together, which is what `theEntriesSheetAndTheRowCountReadOneSourceSoTheyCannotDisagree` pins.

**The Delete gate is a value on the presentation, not an expression inside `.disabled(...)`, and that is the same lesson PR #98 already paid for twice.** `canDelete` is the control this whole ticket is about; written only in a view modifier it is a gate no test can read, and "greyed out at exactly the wrong moment" is precisely what shipped. Same reason `canChangeRecording` and `MemoryRowDestination` exist.

**Two stores were outside the row-level damaged state, and calling that a residual was the mistake — the fix round below closes it.** The vision session journal and Shortcut run history have no `LocalStorageLoadFailureSource` case, so while the row's damaged state was derived from that dictionary, a corrupt file in either could never mark the Task history row unreadable — which meant `canDelete` collapsed to `count > 0` and an empty task history beside an unreadable `shortcuts-run-history.json` reproduced the founder's original dead end exactly. This entry originally recorded that as acceptable because "Both sit under the Task history row, whose Delete already removes all four of its files", which is true only when that Delete is pressable. It is now, because readability is probed over all thirteen stores rather than read off the eleven sources. The claim that neither store is loaded by `AgentViewModel` was also false and is corrected above. The clipboard switch's own settings file is the third store with no Memory row and remains **not** a residual: `applyClipboardHistoryNoticeChoice` writes without loading first, so flipping the Clipboard history row's switch overwrites a file it could not read.

**`asyncProcessRunnerCancelsRunningProcess` failed during this branch's work and is the known load flake, not a regression.** It took 31.9 s inside a full run and passed in 0.25 s in isolation immediately afterwards. It touches no code this branch changed. **It is SONNY-224, In Progress** — checked rather than copied: `#106`'s entry cites SONNY-250 and SONNY-252 for this test and both are now Cancelled, which `#107`'s entry already records. The rule those entries set is the one this one follows: a kill count in this repository needs this test subtracted before it is quoted. Audited at every head this branch has had. At the final one, `9fe7ace`, it appears in **none** of the four kill lists (`grep -c` over each log → 0, 0, 0, 0). Earlier heads were not so clean and the numbers are kept rather than smoothed: at `b4eb633` it contaminated two — **M12** read "killed by 6" and was really killed by 5, **R10** read "killed by 2" and was really killed by 1, both keeping the test written for them — and at `4750fa2` it was the *sole* reported killer of **U4**, which by this repository's discriminator makes U4 a survivor and is what produced the scan for it. It has also taken out a battery *baseline* three times across this branch, and the harness refused to attribute anything every time, which is it working.

**Fix round, 2026-08-23, from PR #110's fresh-session review (nine findings, all taken).** The review confirmed the enumeration, the founder's three flagged calls, the `errorMessage` property by its own enumeration rather than by trusting the two rewritten tests, and re-measured the 4.7 ms independently. What it found is below, and two of them were data-loss-shaped.

**F1 — a damaged store turned every clipboard copy into a notification.** `recordLocalStorageLoadFailure` reassigned `localStorageNotice` unconditionally. That was harmless while its callers were a page appearing and two deletes the user pressed; SONNY-246 gave it one that fires on every recorded clipboard item, up to once a second. `AppDelegate` sinks that publisher with no `removeDuplicates()`, and `SonnyNotificationService.deliver` uses a fresh `UUID()`, so nothing replaces anything — with the founder's two broken files, two Notification Center banners per copy, and the widget's own notice back the instant after he dismissed it. Before this branch a copy fired none. The fix is the guard `clearLocalStorageLoadFailure` has always had, which is what made the asymmetry a bug rather than a design. **The consequence, stated rather than discovered:** a store failing identically twice now leaves whatever is on the channel in between — a write failure's own sentence, say — standing. That is the intended reading; the condition has not changed, so there is nothing new to tell the user, and the row says "Can't be read" with a live Delete either way.

**F2 — an ordinary Delete destroyed the file the previous press promised to keep.** `deleteMemory` handed its readable stores to `deleteAllLocalData`, which sweeps `quarantinedSiblings(of:)`. So: repair a broken row, use it for weeks, delete it for the ordinary reason, and the bytes SONNY-253 exists to rescue were unlinked — inside a count of files the user cannot see, with a confirmation that said nothing about it, and contradicting `LocalDataQuarantine`'s own doc comment, which is unusually explicit that Settings' whole wipe is the one place the user asks for destruction. The reviewer reproduced it against the real types: `deletedFileCount == 2`, kept file gone. **The tension is real and the resolution is not a compromise:** leaving the sweep out of the per-row Delete means "Delete routines" leaves unreadable routine bytes on disk, which is its own broken promise — but that one is *disclosed* (the user was told the file is kept) and *recoverable* (Settings → Delete Local Data takes it, and that control is already framed as the destructive one), where sweeping destroys promised-kept data undisclosed and with no undo. Disclosed-and-recoverable beats silent-and-final. `LocalDataDeletionService` now has two doors — `deleteAllLocalData()` sweeps, `deleteStoreFilesOnly()` does not — and calling the wrong one is silent in both directions, which is why CLAUDE.md now names both.

**F3 — Settings' whole wipe left one row saying "Can't be read" about a file it had just deleted.** `clearInMemoryLocalDataState`'s four refreshes reach ten of the eleven load-failure sources. The one they never reach is `.taskPlanDetails`, recorded only by `storedPlanDetail(for:)`. The wipe now runs the same evidence-checked sweep over every source, and the evidence check is what keeps it safe: a file the wipe failed to delete keeps its failure.

**F4 — the Task history row said "Can't be read" while twelve readable tasks sat behind it.** `MemoryRowPresentation`'s damaged state was a boolean (`isUnreadable`, renamed to `readability` by this same fix) over a row covering four stores, so one broken plan-detail file replaced the count — and View on that row opens the Tasks page, which listed all twelve. Two surfaces disagreeing on one screen, which is SONNY-246's own symptom reached from the other direction. Worse, the confirmation switched at the same moment from naming everything the press destroys to the vaguer cannot-see-inside sentence, at exactly the press that does the most. `MemoryRowReadability` is now three-way, and the discriminator is what the row can actually show rather than how many of its files are broken — which is why it needs no new published state.

**F5 — a file nothing had tried to load was unlinked, not set aside.** `unreadableStores(in:)` read `localStorageLoadFailures`, which holds what something *happened* to load and fail on. `.taskPlanDetails` is recorded only when the user opens a task's detail; in the ordinary case they have not. Of the four files under the Task history row, exactly one was reliably covered by the rule this ticket exists to enforce. Readability is now probed at delete time through an exhaustive `storeIsReadable` — at most four file reads on a control the user pressed, and it makes "never destroy what you cannot prove is garbage" true of all thirteen stores rather than of the ones something happened to touch. **This retires part of the residual the closing comment recorded** — those files can no longer be destroyed unreadable — **and the fix round below finishes the job**, because "cannot mark a row damaged" turned out to be the founder's original dead end surviving for two stores. On the closing comment's other claim: it said neither store is loaded by this view model, which is false. `deleteScreenRecord` and the task delete both call `visionSessionJournalStore.delete(id:)`, whose first statement is `loadAll()`. The conclusion survives for a reason the false premise hid — both of those loads sit inside a *write the user pressed a control for*, so their failures correctly go to `errorMessage` rather than to a load-failure source.

**F6 — SONNY-246 left two of the nine rows stale, unmentioned in its own classification.** Routines and Workspaces are published by `refreshSavedItems()`, not `refreshMemoryEntries()`, and that call was reached only from the success branches — none on the scheduled path. So a run that created a workspace and then failed, and *every* scheduled run that created one, left the row showing the old count. The new code's own comment used a created workspace as its example while the line it justified did not cover it. Both terminal paths now call `refreshMemoryRowsAfterRun()`, and the redundant success-path call is gone.

**F7 — three new copy decisions sat in view bodies, which is the lesson this branch cites.** `canDelete`'s doc comment states the rule; the confirmation's ternary and the sheet's title and message were left where a swapped branch leaves the whole suite green. All three moved onto `MemoryDeletionCopy`. Mutants R5 and R8 are what that buys — and R8 survived the first attempt at its own test, which read the leaf strings rather than the dispatcher the view calls, which is the same defect one function along.

**F8 — two survivors in the reviewer's battery, both closed.** `endsTheRun`'s `.prepared` arm: a preview-only run writes nothing the Memory rows show, so no behavioural test can tell refreshing after one from not — `everyOutcomeSaysWhetherItEndsTheRun` reads all seven statuses instead. And the evidence check before clearing a load failure, where **the first replacement test did not kill the mutant either**, for a reason worth recording: with output locations, `refreshMemorySurfaces()` at the end of `deleteMemory` re-reads the file, fails again, and records the failure a second time — so a wrongly-cleared banner is restored inside the same call and the mutant hides behind the repair. The test uses `.taskPlanDetails`, which nothing re-probes. That is F3's property seen from the other side: the one source the refreshes cannot reach is the only place the guard is observable.

**F9 and the smaller notes.** The collision counter's stated reason named the one case that cannot happen (four files under one row have four different base names; the real case is one store set aside twice, which is what its test does). `LocalDataQuarantine`'s hand-made-store count said two and omitted `snippets.json`. The clipboard poll's comment said five files where six are read. The 130 ms comparison divided a load by a *write* — `TaskHistoryStore` attributes that figure to `record(_:)` — so the ratio is gone rather than restated. The banner's pronoun now agrees with how many stores are broken, which the founder's own two-file case made singular-for-two. `makeOutputFolder` has its doc comment back.

**Verification of the fix round: 1892 tests in 135 suites, exit 0 at `10b8df0`**; **`scripts/warnings` 0 at `10b8df0`**, clean tree; net **+35 tests, 0 removed** over `94afca1` (`git diff 94afca1..HEAD -- Tests/ | grep -c '^+    @Test'` = 35, `grep -c '^-    @Test'` = 0, at `10b8df0`). **Two mutation batteries at `10b8df0`, 26 mutants, 26 killed, none survived** — the branch's original thirteen re-pointed at the changed code and re-run, plus thirteen new ones covering each finding and both of the reviewer's survivors. The gated directory-locking population goes from nine to eleven.

**One thing deliberately not fixed, and filed instead: SONNY-266.** Nothing prunes, caps or shows the files this feature sets aside. A repair leaves one in Application Support forever, the only thing that removes it is Settings' whole wipe, and in the case the founder's decision was written for — a Keychain item that stays replaced — every repair adds another copy. Every direction is either new user-facing surface, a retention number, or SONNY-253's restore path, which are founder decisions rather than a session's.

**Second fix round, 2026-08-23, from PR #110's fix-round review (nine findings in four groups, all taken; plus a founder decision that landed in the same round).**

**One source of truth for readability, which is three of the nine.** The row's words came from `unreadableMemoryCategories` — derived from the failures something had *happened* to record — while its Delete came from the probe the previous round added. They disagreed in both directions: a confirmation promising to delete a file the press then kept, and the mirror case. The escalated finding is the same root cause at its worst: `LocalStorageLoadFailureSource` has eleven cases against `LocalStore`'s thirteen, so the vision journal and Shortcut run history could never put the Task history row into a damaged state, `canDelete` collapsed to `count > 0`, and **an empty task history beside an unreadable `shortcuts-run-history.json` reproduced the founder's original screenshot exactly** — inside the branch whose outcome is that an unreadable memory is clearable. There is now one published `unreadableStores`, written only by `refreshStoreReadability()`, probed over all thirteen, read by the row, the confirmation and the delete alike, and refreshed at the Memory page's appearance, on every terminal outcome, before a delete acts, and after the whole wipe. The other route — giving those two stores a source — was weighed and not taken: their only loads sit inside writes the user pressed a control for, whose failures correctly go to `errorMessage`, so it would need a new health-probe recording site and a banner sentence naming them that the founder has not seen. **Cost, measured at `2440938`:** `refreshMemoryRowsAfterRun()` is 18.4 ms median on a 1.47 MB tree (6.1 saved items + 4.3 memory lists + 8.9 probe), against 4.7 ms for the lists alone before. The probe re-reads eleven files the loaders just read; that duplication is what buys the single source, and it is stated rather than hidden.

**Guards nothing could see, which is three more.** `if status.endsTheRun` was unpinned — deleting it passed the whole suite — and it is load-bearing well beyond the preview-only exit it was justified by: `performStart` records `.approvalNeeded` the moment it raises the prompt, so without it eighteen milliseconds of encrypted reads run on the main actor, able to raise a storage banner, while an approval panel waits for the user. **The first test written for it did not kill the mutant either**, and the reason is worth as much as the fix: it wrote the snippet *after* the pause had been reached, so the mutant's refresh had already run before there was anything to pick up — the same shape as this branch's earlier R11, where a repair inside the same call hid the mutant. The other two: the banner's "never instruct someone to press a control that is not there" claim, reachable when the only failing source is `.clipboardHistorySettings`, the one with no `memoryCategory`; and the plural kept-file wording. The unproven mutant is covered too — the same source failing with a *different* message must republish, which F1's guard allows because it compares the whole detail string.

**Records that misstated, which is two.** `LocalStorageLoadFailureSource.store`'s doc comment said "Neither is loaded by this view model at all" of the vision journal and Shortcut run history. `deleteTask` and `deleteScreenRecord` both call `visionSessionJournalStore.delete(id:)`, whose first statement is `loadAll()`. The conclusion survived for a reason the false premise hid — both of those loads sit inside a *write the user pressed a control for* — and that reason is what the comment says now. This entry carried the same false sentence and has been corrected above rather than left to be contradicted twenty lines later, and its file list named `MemoryRowPresentation.isUnreadable`, which the first fix round had already renamed to `readability`.

**An empty state that contradicted its own row, which is the ninth.** `MemoryRowDestination.of` routes Routines, Workspaces and Task history to `.page(...)` rather than to the entries sheet, so the previous round's unreadable empty state reached six rows and not those three: with `routines.json` unreadable the Memory row correctly read "Can't be read" and pressing View showed "No routines yet · Ask Sonny to save a repeatable sequence". Routines and workspaces are two of the three stores `LocalDataQuarantine` names as things a person made by hand. All three pages now read their empty states from `MemoryDeletionCopy`, whose unreadable sentence names *where* the control is when the reader is a page away from it — split on `MemoryRowDestination` rather than on a second list. `TaskSearchPresentation.emptyState` gains the same answer, and the unreadable case wins over the search, because a locked store publishes zero rows so every query matches nothing.

**The founder's decision of 2026-08-23: the user is told where the kept file is with a control, not with copy.** The confirmation said the file is still on their Mac and stopped, which is disclosure they cannot act on — and a path in the sentence would not help, since `~/Library` is hidden in Finder by default, besides putting a where-Sonny-stores-its-files sentence in the product the founder's standing rule keeps out. A **Reveal in Finder** control sits beside the delete's result and opens that folder with every kept file selected, through `NSWorkspace.activateFileViewerSelecting`. It goes through an injected opener in the shape `ScreenAccessOnboarding` already uses for `settingsOpener`, which is what makes it testable — and makes the reveal that was already sitting in `runSuggestion(_:)` testable as a side effect, which reaching for a source scan would not have. System A tokens; the plural is covered because the message beside it already branches on how many were kept.

**Second rebase, onto `725be8d` (PR #109: SONNY-248 and SONNY-240).** Four files were expected to conflict and one did — `CLAUDE.md`, where both sides had rewritten the same store-registration bullet. `AgentViewModel.swift` (21 hunks on their side, 39 on this one), `ProductShellTests.swift` and the changelog all auto-merged, which is not the same as being right, so both directions were checked mechanically: every line #109 added is present in the rebased tree (232, 25, 1 and 52 respectively, 0 missing), and this branch's contribution is byte-identical in all eleven files #109 did not touch. The one line of mine that is deliberately gone is the old seventh-step paragraph in `CLAUDE.md`, which SONNY-240 landing made obsolete; the eighth-step sentence this branch added sits after their rewritten version of it.

**The interaction that did not conflict, and could not have.** SONNY-240 removed every local store's default from `AgentViewModel.init`, and this branch had added one new parameter to that same initializer: `finderRevealer`, defaulted to `NSWorkspace.activateFileViewerSelecting`. It is not a store and writes nothing, so the worst it could do is steal focus and open Finder windows in the middle of a suite run — but "a call site that predates the parameter cannot know to pass it" does not care what the parameter is for, which is SONNY-240's whole argument. The default is gone, `atItsRealStoreLocations()` names the live implementation the way it names the thirteen store locations, fourteen fixtures answer with a new `hermeticFinderRevealer` beside the other hermetic seams, and `LocalStoreInjectionScanTests.otherRequiredParameters` gains it so the default cannot come back — that list now being the thing its own count is derived from rather than a literal `2`.

**And that parameter exposed a hole in #109's own signature parser, which is the more useful half.** `splitTopLevel` and `containsTopLevelDefault` both treated the `>` of a `->` as a closing bracket. A closure-typed parameter took the depth to `-1`, so the initializer parsed as **11** parameters instead of 34 — caught loudly by that suite's own `parameters.count > 20` premise check, which is that assertion doing exactly the job it exists for. The quiet half is worse: a *defaulted* closure parameter's own `=` was then never at depth 0, so `hasDefault` came back `false` and the guard would have passed the very thing it refuses. No store has a closure type, so the case had never arisen. Both walkers now skip an arrow's `>` and clamp depth at zero, `splitTopLevel` is internal so it can be run over held samples rather than only against the live signature, and `theParameterSplitterSurvivesAClosureTypedParameter` holds five of them. Mutant **U1** — the default put back — is killed now and would not have been before the fix, which is the demonstration that the hole was real rather than theoretical.

**One line in the shipping app is unreachable from any test, and now has a scan instead.** `atItsRealStoreLocations()` builds the real `~/Library` stores and `noTestSourceAsksForTheRealStoreLocations` forbids calling it, so nothing can exercise the argument that hands the app its live Finder reveal. A mutant replacing it with `{ _ in }` first read as killed by one test — and that test was SONNY-224's flake, so by this repository's own discriminator it survived. `theRealStoreFactoryHandsTheAppTheLiveFinderReveal` reads that one construction's argument list, which is the same instrument `onlyMainAsksForTheRealStoreLocations` reaches for and for the same reason. **The same gap covers the thirteen store constructions beside it and is deliberately not closed here**: `routineStore: RoutineStore()` could become a temp store with the whole suite green. Recorded rather than quietly benefited from; generalising belongs to whoever owns that suite.

**Third rebase, onto `b0c78ea` (PR #111: SONNY-249).** The changelog was the only conflict, and the same mechanical shape as the last one: two entries at one insertion point under `## Entries`, both kept, this branch's newest-first. Nothing else overlapped — #111 changed `PathWhitelist`, `WorkspaceScope`, `SpokenNameNormalization` and the path tests. Verified both directions the same way: all 27 of this branch's files are byte-identical where #111 did not touch them, and every line #111 added is present (310 in `PathWhitelist`, 464 in the new `PathContainmentResolutionTests`, and the rest — 0 missing across all ten files).

**One shape of #111's is reachable from this branch's tests and is not a new user of it.** `PathWhitelist.canonicalURL` keeps its signature and changes behaviour — it resolves the existing prefix now rather than calling `resolvingSymlinksInPath()` on the whole path, which is SONNY-249's fix. `MemoryCommandCenterTests.makeOutputFolder` calls it, and `OutputLocationStore` keys on it. Both are unaffected because the folders in those tests exist before the call, which is the case whose answer did not change; the suite agrees. No line this branch adds names it.

**The enumeration the conflicted-file list does not give you.** PR #111's lesson is that a file which never conflicts can still break, because one branch changed a type's shape and the other added a user of it — and `swift build` cannot say so, since it does not compile the test targets. So after each rebase every symbol whose shape either side changed was enumerated and its users swept across the whole tree: thirteen of this branch's (`TaskSearchPresentation.emptyState`'s new parameter, `MemoryRowReadability`, `deleteStoreFilesOnly`, `endsTheRun`, `unreadableStores`, `finderRevealer` and the rest), nine of #109's (`ClarifiedCommand`, `clarificationSubmittedCommand`, `atItsRealStoreLocations`, the initializer itself, `recordPriorTaskContext`, `submitClarification` and the replaced scan suite) and eight of #111's (`CanonicalPath`, `PathWhitelist.canonical`, `canonicalURL`'s changed behaviour, `WorkspaceScope.contains`' changed parameter type, and the rest). **The finding: no line this branch adds is a new code user of a shape either branch changed.** Two added lines name one — `recordPriorTaskContext` and `atItsRealStoreLocations` — and both are inside comments. The one real interaction was the signature parser above, which no symbol sweep would have found: the compiler and a premise assertion caught it, in that order.

**That finding was first written as a stronger claim, off a sweep that had crashed** — and the post-mortem is worth more than the finding. The sweep ran `git grep -ln -- "$sym" $MYFILES` where `MYFILES` was a **scalar** holding 26 newline-separated paths. This repository's shell is zsh, which does not word-split an unquoted scalar (`SH_WORD_SPLIT` is off, checked), so git received **one** 1289-byte argument, tried to `stat` it, and died: `fatal: failed to stat '<all 26 paths>': File name too long`, **exit 128**, zero output. The command carried `2>/dev/null` and its output was captured in `$(...)` with the exit code never read — so a crash presented as an empty result, and every symbol answered "none", which reads exactly like a clean sweep. That is CLAUDE.md's exit-code rule almost verbatim: a redirect and an unread `$?` between a command and the answer taken from it.

**And the first diagnosis of that failure was itself wrong, which is why it is written down.** It was posted as "`--` before the pattern makes git read it as a pathspec". It does not. Measured at git 2.50.1 against a real array, `git grep -ln -- "$sym" "${FILES[@]}"` and `git grep -ln "$sym" -- "${FILES[@]}"` exit 0 and return the identical 13 matches; the position of `--` was never the problem. A wrong post-mortem in the record is worse than the original claim, because the next reader inherits a rule about `git grep` that is false and would never think to check the shell.

Manual-test items the user still owes: with the packaged `.app`, put an unreadable file where a store lives (or reuse one of the two the manual pass produced) and confirm the Memory row reads "Can't be read" with a live Delete, that the confirmation says Sonny cannot tell you what is in it and is keeping the file, that pressing Delete leaves a `…json.unreadable-…` file beside the original path and the row starts recording again, and that the banner stops returning on relaunch; confirm the banner, before that, ends with "Open Memory in Command Center to clear it."; confirm View on that row shows "Sonny can't read your …" rather than the empty state; confirm Settings → Delete Local Data afterwards leaves no `…unreadable-…` file behind; and, for SONNY-246, leave Command Center on Memory, ask Sonny to write a file into a new folder, and confirm the Output locations and Recent artifacts rows change without navigating away and back. From the fix round: with a store still broken, copy several things while Sonny is in the background and confirm **no** storage notification arrives per copy and a dismissed banner stays dismissed; repair a row, use it, then Delete it for the ordinary reason and confirm the `…unreadable-…` file beside it survives; and confirm Settings → Delete Local Data still takes it. From the second fix round: after a Delete that kept a file, press **Reveal in Finder** beside the result and confirm Finder opens on Sonny's Application Support folder with that file selected — and, with two files kept under one row, that both are selected; make `routines.json` unreadable and confirm the Routines page itself says Sonny cannot read them rather than "No routines yet", and the same for Workspaces and Tasks; and confirm the whole page reflects a store that breaks *while you are looking at it*, without navigating away and back.

**The suite exited 1 and then 0 at the previous head, with no code changed between**, and it is left in this record rather than deleted now that this head is green twice over: `asyncProcessRunnerCancelsRunningProcess` failed one run (16.5s for a test that sleeps 100ms) and passed the next (22.4s). SONNY-224, open, load-sensitive, nothing to do with this boundary — and the reason this entry says exit 0 is not a reproducible property of this tree.

**What is *not* re-measured, and why that is safe.** The reproduction figures are statements about commits that still exist and cannot go stale: seven of nine new tests failing at `94afca1`, and the 34- and 40-link chains escaping at `b705b99`.

Behavior added:
- **Containment resolves the longest prefix of a path that exists and appends the rest as written.** That is one change answering two defects, because both came from `resolvingSymlinksInPath()` resolving nothing at all for a path not on disk — which is nearly every path Sonny is asked to *write*.
- **A symlink is judged by where it leads, at any depth.** `<root>/link/sub/new.md` is refused when the link leaves the whitelist and accepted when it does not, instead of being accepted at depth two and refused at depth one regardless of destination.
- **A folder named in a different case is the folder.** "save it to my desktop as note.md" works, and it worked already without the `as note.md`.
- **A resolution that did not converge is refused, never reported as an answer.** A link that points at itself, or a chain longer than the kernel will follow, is named in the refusal instead of being compared. This is the review round's finding rather than the ticket's, and it is what makes the hop budget a termination bound rather than a security property.
- **A refusal caused by resolution names both paths** — "`~/Desktop/link/sub/new.md` leads to `/elsewhere/sub/new.md`, which is outside…" — and only then, so an ordinary refusal reads exactly as before.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **A path that goes through a `validate...` method is written through the URL that method returned, never the string the plan named** — enumerated across every whitelist call site before the change, and the count is unchanged by it: **13 lines in 10 files** (`git grep -nE "whitelist\.(validate|resolveOutputPath|defaultOutputFile)" -- Sources | grep -v PathWhitelist.swift | wc -l` → 13, and `| grep -v PathWhitelist.swift | cut -d: -f1 | sort -u | wc -l` → 10, both at the head below), plus the static `PathWhitelist.canonicalURL` uses, which sit in three of those same ten files rather than in three further ones — **five before this branch** (at `a03bbe1`) and **four after**, because the fifth is `WorkspaceScope`'s and it now calls `canonical`. `FinderSelectionResolver.selectedDirectoryPath` is the one that returns a raw string, and its caller validates it.
  **The unconditional version of that sentence was false four times, and this entry used to carry it *and* deny it two sections later** (PR #111's review, F1 and F7 — and it is the same shape as the round this entry already records under "Three places said this could not happen"). A leaf appended to an already-validated folder goes through no `validate...` method at all, and four places do that: `PathWhitelist.defaultOutputFile` and `resolveOutputPath`'s directory branch — both in the file whose comment asserted otherwise — plus `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter` and `FileInventory`'s PDF destinations. **SONNY-264 owns all four**, its scope widened and its priority raised on that basis; this branch owns the two comments and this bullet saying what is true. It is a coverage gap rather than a hole because an unvalidated leaf matters only to a writer that follows a leaf symlink, and 18 of the 18 real writes in `Sources` use `.atomic`, which replaces one.
- **`FileInventory.regularFiles` still skips symbolic links when scanning a folder**, so nothing about what gets read or zipped widened with this change.
- **`OutputLocationStore`'s keys are unchanged for every folder it has already recorded.** It records folders that came back from `validateExistingDirectory`, so the stored text was already fully resolved, and re-canonicalising fully-resolved text returns it unchanged — no migration, and `theDeleteDoorFoldsCaseTheSameWayTheRecordDoorDoes`' precondition (that a *deleted* folder's casing is left alone) still holds, which is what keeps that test about `DestinationKey.folded`.
- **Workspace scope still narrows and never widens**, and both its roots and its candidates go through the one arithmetic.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**What this newly refuses, enumerated before it was accepted rather than after.** One class, and it is a real one: a path reached through a symlink that leads out of `~/Desktop`/`~/Documents`. Somebody who keeps `~/Desktop/Dropbox -> ~/Dropbox` or `~/Documents/Code -> ~/dev` and asks Sonny to save there has that working today — the bytes go to `~/dev` — and it stops working, with a refusal that now names `~/dev` so the reason is visible. That is the boundary doing its job: the whitelist is Desktop and Documents, and `~/dev` was never inside it. It is also not a new decision, only a newly enforced one. Three smaller shapes go with it: a symlink loop, at every depth, which used to read as a missing parent and now reads as the link it is; a chain of more than 32 links, which is refused rather than resolved; and, in workspace scope, a not-yet-created file under a link out of the scoped folder, which now escalates instead of running silently.

**And what it newly accepts, which is the half a security review should look at hardest.** A link whose destination is *inside* the whitelist is now followed rather than refused — at depth one it used to be `symbolicLinkRejected`, though it could never have let anything out. A differently-cased spelling of a folder that exists is now that folder. A whitelist root that does not exist yet is resolved the same way its candidates are. **And one this enumeration missed until PR #111's review found it (F5): a path with more symbolic links in it than the kernel will traverse, where enough of them already exist.** Measured at `14c83b3` — 20 existing directory links followed by 20 dangling ones is 40 links, refused by `open` with `ELOOP` and accepted here, because `resolvingSymlinksInPath()` consumes the existing 20 in one call that this resolver's counter never sees. Accepting it is right: what comes back is fully resolved, so the write goes to a known destination inside the boundary instead of walking the chain. It is listed because the section claims to enumerate in advance, and this one was enumerated afterwards by somebody else. None of these widens the region: every one of them is the same physical location the boundary already allowed, named differently.

**The workspace boundary did not move, and one verdict inside it did.** SONNY-249's own warning was that `canonicalURL` is compared through by a workspace's restriction scope as well as by the whitelist, so rewriting path text there could silently move a boundary a user drew. It does not, because both sides of every comparison go through the same function — but one verdict changes and is worth stating plainly: a path spelled `~/Documents/client/x.md` against a scope root of `~/Documents/Client` used to read `.outOfScope` and prompt, and now reads `.inScope` and does not. That is the same folder on this filesystem; the prompt was the boundary failing to recognise its own folder rather than protecting anything. The direction that matters — a link leading *out* of a scoped folder — moves the other way, from `.inScope` to `.outOfScope`.

**Foundation's `resolvingSymlinksInPath()`, not POSIX `realpath`, and the difference is load-bearing.** Measured on Darwin 25.5.0: `realpath` returns `/private/var/folders/…` where Foundation returns `/var/folders/…`, because Foundation strips a leading `/private`. The whitelist's roots are normalised by Foundation, so resolving candidates with `realpath` would have compared two spellings of one path and refused everything under a temporary directory. The visible consequence of using Foundation's is that `/private/tmp/not-allowed.md` now canonicalises to `/tmp/not-allowed.md` — which is what an *existing* `/private/tmp/…` path already did, so this replaces two spellings with one rather than inventing one.

**The one link shape Foundation will not follow, and the writer that will.** A symlink whose own target does not exist is invisible to both halves of the old code: `fileExists` follows the link to a target that is not there and says no, and `resolvingSymlinksInPath()` returns such a path unchanged (measured). So `resolutionPass` reads that link by hand with `destinationOfSymbolicLink` and starts again. This is not a hypothetical shape: `ProcessZipArchiver` hands `outputURL.path` to `/usr/bin/zip`, which opens it and follows the link — and its test writes without `.atomic` for exactly that reason, because Foundation's atomic write happens to *replace* a leaf symlink instead of following it, so an atomic-only test would have reported this hole as closed.

**The review found that the first version of this fix opened a longer hole than the one it closed, and the paragraph that used to sit here asserted it could not.** `resolvingExistingPrefix` followed one link per pass, ran a fixed number of passes, and on running out returned the path it had *reached* — the original minus 33 hops — which `validateInsideWhitelist` then judged. The kernel's own `SYMLOOP_MAX` budget starts again from a shortened path, so it had plenty left to finish the walk. Measured with bytes, at `b705b99`, by the new tests running against that tree: a chain of **34** links and a chain of **40** were accepted as inside and the bytes landed at `<outside>/pwned-34.txt` and `<outside>/pwned-40.txt`; at 63 nothing landed, because the kernel refused the remainder rather than the boundary refusing anything. The reviewer's own harness put the escaping band at 34 through 63 — the exact upper edge depends on how much chain is left after the resolver's hops, so it is theirs as measured and not restated here as mine. **At `94afca1` those same chains were refused with `ELOOP`**, which makes the band a regression the branch introduced rather than a case it merely failed to close.

**Three places said this could not happen, which is the part worth learning from.** The hop budget's own doc comment argued that a chain long enough to exhaust the budget is a chain `open` refuses, "so nothing can be written through a path this resolver gave up on"; the `canonicalURL` doc's two-limits paragraph said an unfollowable link "stays in the returned path" and that `validateOutputPath` and `validateExistingDirectory` refuse those — the write door never looked at the leaf, so it did not; and this entry said the same thing a third time. All three were reasoning about *the same path*, and the returned path is not the same path. A comment that states a cleaner rule than the code follows is how the next reader concludes a gap is deliberate, and three of them agreeing is not corroboration when they were written by one person in one sitting.

**The fix is the property, not a bigger number.** Any finite budget has the same cliff, because the failure is that a non-convergent resolution was reported as a resolution. So non-convergence travels with the path: `canonical` returns a `CanonicalPath` carrying the link it could not follow, `validateInsideWhitelist` refuses such a path before any comparison and names that link, and `contains` takes a `CanonicalPath` rather than a `URL` — the rule is carried by the type, at the one comparison every boundary in the app passes through, instead of by two callers remembering it. `WorkspaceScope` has no error to raise and reads it as `.outOfScope`, which prompts. **The two `isSymbolicLink` checks are gone with it**: once non-convergence is refused outright, every path reaching them is fully resolved and has no link left to find, so they were a second mechanism for a rule that now has one. That also settles the review's F2 — a loop *two* levels up reported "the parent folder does not exist", because the parent was `<root>/loop/sub` and only the link itself was a link — which no longer has a way to happen.

**A constant no test holds is a constant a battery cannot protect, and that is why a green suite and a ten-mutant battery missed this.** The branch's own battery mutated the resolution, the two symlink checks and the refusal wording, all of which were covered, and never mutated the budget. The reviewer's battery did: neutering it to zero and shortening it by one both survived. Both are now killed, by a test that pins the budget from both sides — 32 links resolve and the bytes land at the target, 33 are refused — with both chains ending at the same place inside the root so that length is the only difference between them.

**The residual is check-time-to-write-time, it is pinned as a test, and it is not closable from a path string.** A component created between the resolution and the write is not seen. Its scope is narrower than the first telling of it, and the correction matters because it changes what closing it would cost: 18 of the 18 real writes in `Sources` pass `options: .atomic` (`git grep 'write(to:' -- Sources | wc -l` → 20 and `git grep 'write(to:' -- Sources | grep -c 'options: .atomic'` → 18 at `4ef87fe`; the two that are not are both doc-comment lines, in `DocumentConverter.swift` and in the paragraph #106 added to this file), and an atomic write *replaces* a leaf symlink rather than following it. So the live residual is two narrower things — a leaf planted in front of `/usr/bin/zip`, which the pinned test demonstrates with a non-atomic write, and a directory component planted mid-path, which an atomic write does follow because it puts its temporary file in the destination's parent, and which is not pinned. The threat it leaves is also a different one from the threat this ticket closed: it needs local code execution inside `~/Desktop`/`~/Documents` *and* a race with a run in progress, where the defect fixed here needed neither — a link planted at any time held the door open until somebody noticed.

**Two smaller things the review found, both taken.** `pathAsAskedIfResolutionIsWhatRefusedIt` opened with an `asTyped == resolved` early return that could not fire as its own behaviour — if the two are equal, the test below it is the identical comparison that has just refused the path, so the answer is `nil` either way. A reviewer's mutant deleted it and the suite stayed green; it is deleted, the same way `validatedFileLocationAdditions`' blank-path guard was for the same reason. And `theLowercaseSpellingOfARealFolderResolvesToItForAFileThatDoesNotExistYet` returned silently when its precondition failed, so on a case-sensitive home volume it would have been a vacuous pass that reads exactly like a real one; it now measures the volume and asserts the other branch, the way its sibling in the same file already did.

**The second review round found eight things, none blocking, and the fix itself survived attack** — a 14-mutant battery at `14c83b3` (12 killed, 2 documented equivalent mutants) and a symlink-topology fuzzer over four seeds: **45,832 candidate paths, 25,280 accepted, 0 escapes**, run against a byte-identical copy of the file compiled standalone so `realpath(3)` rather than the code under test decided where bytes landed. Every finding but two was about what the branch *claims*. The two that were not: `CanonicalPath`'s memberwise initialiser was public, so any caller could hand `contains` a hand-built resolved path and get the pre-fix behaviour — the rule back in the callers' memory, which is what the type exists to stop, and it is internal now; and a non-convergent refusal named the link the resolver gave up at rather than one the person could find, so a 33-link chain asked for as `<root>/l1` was refused as `<root>/l33`. It names the first link followed now, which is always a component of the path as asked for, and `aRefusalNamesTheFirstLinkItCouldNotFollowRatherThanWhereItGaveUp` pins it.

**Three claims in this branch were wrong in the same direction, and the direction is the lesson.** The invariant — "the path that was checked and the path the bytes go to are the same path" — was written without its condition and is false at four sites, two of them in the file asserting it; the residual named "the two writers that follow a leaf link" and Word via Apple Events is a third; and the hop budget's comment claimed equivalence with the kernel's own limit, which measurement disproves (20 existing directory links plus 20 dangling ones is 40 links, refused by `open` and accepted here — correctly, because what comes back is fully resolved). Each was a sentence that generalised one true case. **SONNY-264 owns the behaviour behind the first two**, scope widened to all four sites and the Word writer, priority raised; this branch owns the prose, which now says what is true rather than what would be tidy.

**The rebase, and the file that did not conflict.** Onto `a03bbe1`, after #106 (SONNY-242) and #107 (SONNY-244/247). Three files overlapped and **two hunks genuinely conflicted**, both in `PathWhitelist.swift`, both resolved by keeping what each side was actually for rather than by taking a side:

- `errorDescription`'s `.outsideWhitelist` case. #106 replaced "is outside the writable whitelist" with "is not one of the folders Sonny can use"; this branch had split the case into two sentences and given it a third associated value. Resolved as **#106's wording inside both of this branch's sentences**, with #106's comment kept above this branch's — they explain different halves of the same line.
- `canonicalURL`'s doc comment. #106 added a paragraph headed "What it does not resolve", describing both of this branch's defects as measured, **owned by SONNY-249 and not fixed there**. That paragraph existed to point forward at this ticket, and this commit is that ticket landing, so it is superseded rather than dropped — the paragraph that replaced it describes the same two defects as fixed and names the tests.

`EditWorkspaceTests.swift` auto-merged correctly (#106's copy assertion, this branch's three-element pattern), and the changelog conflict was two whole entries at one insertion point, kept both with this one first.

**The third overlapping file did not conflict and broke the build.** `SpokenPathTests.swift` is new in #106 and this branch never touched it, so git merged it silently — and it constructs and matches `PathValidationError.outsideWhitelist` with the two-value shape this branch replaced with three. **`swift build` did not catch it**, because it does not build the test targets; the failure appears only when the suite runs. That is the practical form of "a merge that compiles is not evidence": here it compiled *and* the thing that failed was not what the conflict markers pointed at. Both uses are adapted rather than relaxed, in a commit of their own, and the enumeration that found nothing else is `git grep -n "outsideWhitelist(" -- Sources Tests` and `git grep -n "PathWhitelist.contains(" -- Sources Tests` over the whole tree.

**Proof that the rebase moved no code.** Per-commit, `git show --format= <sha> -- Sources/ Tests/` piped through `shasum`, before and after, with `index` and `@@` lines stripped so a hunk that only moved is not counted as a hunk that changed: **five of the seven commits are byte-identical, and the two that differ are exactly the two conflicts named above.** Without that stripping a third commit also differs, and it is the one that edits the lines the resolutions moved — positional noise, not a change, which is the reason to normalise before comparing rather than after.

**The second and third rebases — onto `86b7ccb` after #108 (SONNY-245), and onto `725be8d` after #109 (SONNY-248/240) — overlapped this file and nothing else.** One conflict each, the same mechanical shape as the first: two entries at one insertion point, both kept whole, this branch's first. The per-commit check afterwards reports **all eleven, then all thirteen, byte-identical**, which is what a rebase with no code overlap should look like and is worth having the check say rather than assume. #109 is the one worth a second look before believing that — it touches nineteen files under `Tests/`, none of them this branch's, and it rewires every `AgentViewModel` fixture; the suite at the rebased head is what settles it rather than the file list.

**Two things about this file are defects on `main` and were deliberately left alone.** #106's own entry sits at the very bottom rather than newest-first under `## Entries` — that is SONNY-225's third recorded occurrence and it is not this branch's to move; and #106's entry cites SONNY-250 and SONNY-252, both since cancelled as duplicates of SONNY-224. A rebase is the wrong moment to tidy another branch's record.

**The one stale prose site outside this branch's bounds was asked about, not assumed, and the founder lifted the instruction for it.** `SpokenNameNormalization.swift`'s doc said "the whitelist's `canonicalURL` is the arithmetic every containment check in the app compares through" — true when SONNY-242 wrote it, and naming the identity overload rather than `canonical` after this branch. A one-word drift whose surrounding reasoning (do not rewrite path text inside the shared arithmetic) is untouched and still right. That file had been put out of bounds at this branch's kickoff, and the reason — an in-review PR #106 to avoid colliding with — had quietly expired when #106 merged. The session recorded the drift and asked rather than deciding for itself that the instruction had lapsed; the founder lifted it for this correction on 2026-08-23, bounded to that one word, and it is fixed. **The instinct is the part worth keeping**: an instruction whose reason has expired is still an instruction, and the cost of asking was one message against the cost of a habit of sessions widening their own scope on judgment calls nobody sees.

**A flake in a kill list reads exactly like evidence.** `asyncProcessRunnerCancelsRunningProcess` reddened the *baseline* of the first battery — the unmutated tree — which aborts the whole run before a mutant is applied, and it took 13.98s for a test that sleeps 100ms because the battery's cold build was saturating the machine. It then appeared as a "killer" of three mutants in the re-run, and of two in the round-2 battery. Every one of those has a real killer beside it, so nothing was lost, but the lesson is to read a kill list rather than count it. **The reviewer's own battery is the sharper instance**: there the flake was the *only* entry on a kill list — mutant M2, one fewer resolution pass, read as "KILLED by 1" and was a coverage hole wearing a green line, which re-running that mutant alone confirmed. It belongs to **SONNY-224**, which already existed and is in progress; this session filed **SONNY-257** for it before finding that, and cancelled it as a duplicate with the evidence moved onto SONNY-224.

Known limitations / deferred scope: the check-time residual above, stated rather than deferred — no ticket, because closing it is a change to how a write site opens a file and that is a decision to take deliberately rather than to leave as an open item. **SONNY-264** carries the review's F3, the one place this branch's own invariant is untrue: `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter` builds its *default* output name by appending to a validated folder and never runs `validateOutputPath` on it, and that URL goes to `/usr/bin/zip`, the one writer in the tree that follows a leaf symlink. Outside every ticket's scope and left for its own, on the reviewer's read and this session's: it predates this branch, it is in a file SONNY-249 does not name, and its impact is an empty file created at a guessed timestamped filename. SONNY-224 carries the flaky test.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: per the roadmap; this is an out-of-band security fix rather than a roadmap row.
