Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The founder chose Supabase Auth with the contract amended, over the gateway owning auth — and the session that recommended otherwise had one of its four stated incompatibilities wrong.** The claim that Supabase could not give §3.3's rotation-with-overlap-and-reuse-detection was false: it rotates, has a **10-second reuse interval** which *is* the overlap window, and on reuse beyond it *"the whole session is regarded as terminated and all refresh tokens belonging to it are marked as revoked"*. §3.3 needed no amendment at all. The amendment is one clause in §3.1 — the access token is a JWT rather than opaque — and **the property that clause protected is preserved rather than dropped**: the client must still not decide anything from it, which is now a contract obligation it keeps rather than one its encoding keeps for it. Recorded because a recommendation argued from an unverified incompatibility is the shape SONNY-126 spent four review cycles removing, and it recurred here on the first architectural question of the next ticket.

**The identity rule is `(provider, subject)`, and the account is deliberately not the Supabase user.** Supabase links on verified email, which is right for the case it covers and cannot express the one that matters: a relay address matches nothing, so the same person becomes a second `auth.users` row. With an account of our own, two Supabase users resolve to one account. **Supabase's behaviour is therefore accepted rather than overridden** — with the account separated it can no longer produce the wrong answer, at worst an extra row our identity table resolves correctly.

**"Does not silently create a second account" is satisfied by the word silently, and that is the honest reading.** The server cannot know that `abc@privaterelay.appleid.com` is the same human as `real@example.com`, and inventing that link is the account-takeover pattern with extra steps. So the second account is created, the relay is **detected and stored** at write time, and a `link_hint` is returned. Guessing would be worse than the thing it prevents.

**Signing up again with a closed account's address made the resolver recurse forever.** Rule 1 excludes identities on a deleted account; the unique constraint on `(provider, subject)` does not. The insert conflicted, the resolver rolled back and retried, and met the identical conflict — a livelock, reachable from delete-account-then-sign-up-again, found by a test rather than by review. The retry is **bounded**, because an unbounded retry on a condition nobody enumerated is a hang waiting for a cause. The other half of the fix went through three shapes before it was right, and the paragraph below is that story; **this paragraph said closing an account "releases its identities" long after it had stopped doing so** (PR #87 second round, F4), which is 0003's design and was replaced by 0004's on this same branch.

**A closed account's identities are MARKED, never deleted — and that decision binds a future ticket, so it lives here and not only in the migration file.** Three attempts, each falsified by the next:

1. **Release them in the DELETE handler.** True only for accounts closed by that one code path. A retention sweep, an operator's `UPDATE`, or the resolver racing a close all left the original stuck state, and after the retry was bounded that state stopped being a livelock and became a permanent `IdentityConflict` — the address unusable by anyone including its owner, which is worse because it no longer even spins where somebody might notice.
2. **Delete them from a trigger** (0003). The invariant does belong to the data, and the trigger made it hold whatever statement closed the account. But `AFTER UPDATE` fires at **statement end**, so the handler's own next statement met an empty table: it read `supabase_user_id` to revoke every provider-side session and revoked **nobody** — reproduced as 0 rows. A sweep also cannot see rows inserted after it fires, so a `resolve()` racing a close still stranded an identity. And it destroyed `link_method`, the audit trail answering "why are these two joined?", along with the ids `provider.deleteUser` and SONNY-196 both need.
3. **Mark them** (0004), which fixes all three at once and buys the guarantee 0003's own header had called impossible. That header said a partial unique index scoped to live accounts "is not expressible" — true only of the form joining to `sonny.account`, which Postgres rejects with *cannot use subquery in index predicate*, and false of the form where the state is denormalised onto `sonny.identity` and the predicate is a plain column. Both forms were tried against a real database before the claim was replaced.

So the schema now carries `sonny.identity.account_closed`, and `identity_live_provider_subject` is `UNIQUE (provider, subject) WHERE NOT account_closed`. **The exclusion the resolver applies and the constraint the database enforces became the same statement**, which is what the whole three-round sequence was chasing: they had disagreed, and every symptom above was a consequence of that one disagreement.

**A denormalised column is a promise to maintain it on every statement that can falsify it, and the second review round found the one that was missed.** 0004 maintained `account_closed` on insert and on close, and not on an identity **moving between accounts** — which is precisely what `linkExplicitly` does. Reproduced against a real database: an identity moved onto a live account kept `account_closed = true`, rule 1 therefore could not see it, and the owner's next sign-in **created them a second account** — the one-person-two-accounts failure this ticket exists to prevent, arrived at from the one path meant to prevent it. It also made 0004's own rollback fail, because that rollback removes rows by joining to `sonny.account.deleted_at` and this row's account is not deleted. 0005 makes the trigger `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF account_id`, makes the close trigger two-way so reopening an account clears the flag, and repairs any row already carrying a flag its account disagrees with.

**The lock order, which is the part that binds someone else.** The close trigger updates `sonny.account` and then `sonny.identity`, in that order, inside one transaction. **Take `sonny.account` before `sonny.identity`, always.** Code taking them the other way — updating an identity and then the account row, which is the shape a training-consent write path has if written naively — deadlocks against a concurrent close. **And the transaction Postgres aborts is the close, not the offending writer**: measured 8 times out of 8 against this schema, because the wrong-order writer takes the identity lock first, so the close is already waiting when the cycle forms, its `deadlock_timeout` expires first, and it is the process that detects the deadlock and rolls itself back. The cost of getting this wrong therefore lands on **account deletion** — the operation with a user waiting on it, and the one nobody would think to look at. That endpoint's owner is **SONNY-203**, not SONNY-128 (see the planning gap below).

**Every counter in this branch is incremented and tested in one statement, and the reason is measured rather than believed.** SONNY-125 showed a read-then-write against a cap overshooting it while reporting success. A rate limit and a single-use code have exactly that shape, and an auth endpoint is where the race is probed deliberately. Both are asserted under concurrency: forty callers land exactly on the ceiling, twelve concurrent verifies of one code produce exactly one session.

**The per-address rate limit refuses silently and the per-source one does not.** A 429 on the address is an account-existence oracle in slow motion — it says *this address has been asked for recently*. A 429 on the source is a fact about the caller, and withholding it leaves them retrying against a wall with no signal. Same mechanism, opposite disclosure, for reasons that do not generalise from one to the other.

**The scanner gained a pattern anchored on variable NAMES, because this branch introduced a secret with no recognisable value.** `RATE_LIMIT_SALT` is `openssl rand -hex 32` — 64 hex characters, no vendor prefix, invisible to all ten patterns that existed. A generic high-entropy rule was rejected for the reason the scanner's own "does not prevent" section already gives: it would flag every lockfile hash and be switched off within a week. **That one pattern was then wrong four separate times, each caught by a different reviewer and each in a way the previous fix had not suggested**: a trailing comma in the bash array appended a literal `,` to the regex so it matched nothing; a `:` separator matched TypeScript's type annotations, making `config.ts` a finding; requiring a bare value after `=` missed every quoted form, six probes' worth; and then allowing a quoted *value* while leaving the *name* bare missed every JSON form — `"RATE_LIMIT_SALT": "…"`, which is how these appear in a Kubernetes secret, a `tfvars` file or a `docker inspect` dump (PR #87 second round, F9). Each is pinned by its own selftest case, and each case was verified to fail against the pattern that preceded it. **A twelfth pattern covers Resend's own key shape**, which nothing did: `RESEND_API_KEY` had a name-anchored rule and no vendor rule, so a key pasted anywhere it did not sit beside its own name had zero coverage. Anchored on `re_` plus the two-segment body an issued key carries, which is narrow enough that the four `re_isolated_test_command` identifiers in this repository are not findings — a single loose run after `re_` catches all four, measured.

**`npm run typecheck` was reported as exit 0 at a SHA where it exits 2, and the mechanism is worth more than the defect.** The command was run, its output was piped through `tail -1`, and the exit code was read from `$?` — which after a pipeline is the exit of `tail`, not of `tsc`. So the terminal printed the *second* line of a TypeScript error and the number `0` next to it, and that pair was read as a pass. The error is `test/auth.db.test.ts(340,9): error TS2322` in the fifth round's own `perAddressOtp()` helper: a two-argument function assigned to a member the fake declared with none. **As a code defect it is small** — test-only, and vitest strips types, so the suite really was green and `npm run build` really was 0, because `tsconfig.json` covers `src/` while `tsconfig.typecheck.json` is the one that reaches `test/`. **As an evidence failure it is not.** `typecheck` is one of six commands `CLAUDE.md` names for the server half and the only one that catches this class, and it was named, run, stamped with a SHA, and reported inverted. The corrected figure: **`npm run typecheck` exited 2 at `ff59800`, `75c2f42` and every SHA between them**, and exits 0 from this round's head onward. **This repository's rule is that a number carries the command that produced it — and here the command was carried and the answer was still wrong, which is the rule's own stated limit arriving in practice**: quoting a command makes a result checkable, it does not make it true, and the checking still has to happen. Third instance on this ticket, after a coordinator's `&&` chain that broke on a `grep -c` returning 0 and printed a fallback that read as a passing check, and the fifth round's `scripts/warnings` stamp inferred from `HEAD` because the header carrying it had been cut off by a `tail`. All three are the same shape: **a shell construct silently answering a question nobody asked.** (PR #87 sixth round, F1.)

**A migration mutant needs a fresh database *and* a statement still standing at the end of the run.** The fifth round found the first half — `up()` skips a migration already in the ledger, so a mutant left in the file never executes and the suite passes for the wrong reason. The sixth round's sweep re-derived every migration-mutant kill this branch ever claimed, on a brand-new database each, and **all of them reproduce**; the concurrency evidence stands. Three mutations survived, and the split is the finding. **Two are inert by construction and correctly unkillable**: 0004 drops 0003's trigger, and 0005 `CREATE OR REPLACE`s 0004's `mark_identities_closed` body, so on any fresh database both are overwritten before a single application statement runs. No test could kill them and none should — but their survival reads *identically* to a real coverage hole, and the fifth round's rule as written would have filed both as gaps. **The third was real**: 0007's plus-tag fold only executes on a deployment that already has issuance rows, so a fresh database can never reach it, and deleting the statement outright left the suite green at 162/162. It had been verified once by hand against deliberately colliding rows — and that verification existed as prose rather than as a command anyone could re-run, which is the same shape as the race battery two rounds earlier. It is now a committed test that rolls back to before 0007, seeds the collisions a real deployment would have, and migrates; both halves of the migration — the fold and the newest-survives dedupe — kill their own mutants.

**Two of the fifth round's new route tests were timing-flaky, and "zero flakes" was measured on the wrong machine.** They issue 35 and 31 sequential `app.inject` calls against vitest's 5000ms default, where the previous worst on this branch was 11. Measured by the sixth-round pass: 0 failures across ~30 idle runs, then 1 of 3 unforced while a cold Swift build happened to be running alongside, and 3 of 8 under deliberate CPU load. So the fifth round's "162 passed, run three consecutive times, zero flakes" was true of an idle machine and false as a property — **and a loaded machine is what CI is**. They carry explicit timeouts now, rather than fewer requests: the request count is derived from `CODE_VERIFY_PER_SOURCE.max` and is the thing being measured. **A flaky security test is a test that gets re-run until it is green**, which is worse than not having it.

**A `/0` prefix in `TRUSTED_PROXIES` reached the exact failure its validator was written to prevent.** `isTrustedProxyEntry` accepted any prefix from 0 upward; `@fastify/proxy-addr` refuses a full-range one, so `0.0.0.0/0` passed validation and then threw `TypeError: invalid range on address` inside the `Fastify(...)` constructor — before `app.ready()`, naming library internals instead of the variable. One character (`bits > 0`). What makes it worth recording rather than just fixing: **`/0` is not a typo, it is how someone writes "trust everything"**, which is what an operator reaches for when they want the old boolean `true` back — so the refusal message now says that there is no such setting and why. And the test added beside it is the property rather than the case: *whatever this validator accepts, `buildApp` must not throw*, iterated over a candidate list that includes the shapes a looser validator would start admitting. That form fails against the relaxed predicate; a list of known-good values would not have.

**`email/verify`'s per-ADDRESS refusal was still an oracle, on the route the round before had just fixed.** Answering `429` to every caller made the attempt *count* readable — 4 tries before the wall at a mailbox someone had verified at, 5 at an untouched one — which is recent activity at an address the prober neither caused nor could observe. `email/start` has made this asymmetry the other way since the first commit, with the comment "a 429 there is the oracle in slow motion", and the fifth round examined this route's error *codes* without looking at its refusal. Gated on the same originator check, so the two cannot drift: the caller who asked for the code still gets `429` and `Retry-After`; everyone else gets the `400` a wrong guess produces. **The residual is stated rather than claimed closed**: body and status now match, timing does not, because the refused path skips the provider call — the same trade `email/start`'s silent refusal already makes.

**0008's delete guard counted a different set than the drain it named as the remedy.** It omitted `account_closed`, which `owedRevocationCount` and `drainOwedRevocations` both require — and never-revoked is the ordinary state of every *live* account, which has never been closed and so has never owed anything. So no live account could be hard-deleted, and the refusal said "Drain them first (`npm run revocations` reports what is outstanding)" — a command that reports nothing for it, because the drain only sees closed accounts. The operator runs the named fix, is told there is no work, and is stuck. 0009 adds the clause. No user-facing breakage, checked rather than assumed: `DELETE /v1/account` soft-deletes and never issues a hard delete, so a user whose provider is unreachable is not blocked from deleting. **A guard whose message names a command that disagrees with it is worse than no guard**, because it costs the reader the time to find that out.

**The disclosure gate is inherited by anyone at the caller's public address, and the record said something narrower.** `sourceHash` is a salted hash of `request.ip`: unforgeable over the wire, and a statement about *where* a request came from rather than *who* sent it. `codes.ts` named only the `TRUSTED_PROXIES`-unset collapse — but measured, with the proxy list set *correctly*, a co-tenant on a victim's NAT gets `auth.code_used` where a caller elsewhere gets `auth.code_invalid`. Household and office are the small version; a carrier's CGNAT egress or a shared VPN exit is the large one. Narrower than the oracle the gate closed, and real. Widened in `codes.ts`, in the API contract's §3.6 and here; the unconditional fix stays a flow token on SONNY-128.

**Four review rounds proved there was no account-existence oracle, and all four proved it about one endpoint.** `POST /v1/auth/email/verify` answers the same question `email/start` refuses to, through an error code. One unauthenticated request per address carrying a code known to be wrong — never calling `email/start` at all — returned `auth.code_used` for a mailbox whose owner had signed in, which the caller did not cause and could not otherwise observe; `auth.code_expired` for one that had asked and never used; `auth.code_invalid` for addresses with nothing. Reproduced end to end. Three things compounded it: `classifyFailure` had **no time bound**, so the signal never decayed — still `auth.code_used` after 400 simulated days; the route consumed only a per-**address** bucket, keyed on the very address being probed, so it never bound — **200 distinct addresses from one source, 0 refused**, while `email/start` refused 192 of 200 in the same run; and nobody had looked, because every round established the property on `email/start`, measured it there down to response timing, and stated it for the system. **That is enumerate-before-you-subtract failing on a security property**: a negative established on one path and asserted about all of them. (PR #87 fifth round, F1.)

**The fix had to resolve a contradiction rather than pick a side, and this is the reasoning.** This ticket's own acceptance criteria require that an expired, a reused and a wrong code each fail with *distinct* errors — and those distinct errors are the oracle. Both cannot hold for an unauthenticated caller probing an arbitrary address. What breaks the tie is asking **who the three codes are for**: the contract wants them because SONNY-128 has to say three different things to a user, and that user is the one who just asked for a code at that address and is typing it. **That person is distinguishable, and the table already stored what distinguishes them** — `source_hash`, written at issuance. So the codes are disclosed when the caller's source matches the issuance's *and* the issuance is recent, and reduced to `auth.code_invalid` otherwise. An attacker who calls `email/start` first to obtain a matching row gains nothing either: their own request becomes the latest row, live and unconsumed, which classifies `auth.code_invalid` whoever the mailbox belongs to. **The client contract is unchanged** — a client in the flow sees exactly what it saw. Recorded as a contract amendment in `docs/sonny-backend-api-contract.md` §3.6 rather than absorbed, the way the rule-2 supersession was.

**What that does not close, because a security claim stated wider than its mechanism is how this finding happened in the first place.** The source match is only as good as `request.ip`: behind a proxy with `TRUSTED_PROXIES` unset every caller collapses to one source and the match is vacuous. That is the same misconfiguration the per-source rate limit degrades under, it is documented in `config.ts`, and the recency bound and the new per-source ceiling still apply there. Closing it unconditionally means `email/start` returning an opaque flow token that `email/verify` echoes — two request/response shapes, landing on SONNY-128. Not built; named as the lever.

**A durable record is only as durable as the row it lives on.** Migration 0006 recorded an owed provider-side revocation as a NULL `provider_session_revoked_at` on an identity — and `sonny.identity.account_id` is `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so one `DELETE FROM sonny.account` took the debt with it. Reproduced: two owed identities, `owedRevocationCount` 2 → **0**, no rows left, and `npm run revocations` printing "no provider-side revocation is owed" and exiting 0 while the sessions were still live. **A report that cannot see the work is worse than no report**, because it is the one an operator acts on. And the triggering statement is not hypothetical: a hard delete of the account row is exactly what `feature/row-12-retention` exists to write, so that ticket would have inherited this on its first day with nothing anywhere naming the dependency. Migration 0008 **refuses the delete** while a revocation is owed. Moving the debt outside the cascade was the alternative and was rejected: it duplicates state `provider_session_revoked_at` already holds, and it would let an account be forgotten while a session it owns is still live — the outcome being prevented, in a smaller size. Refusing states the real ordering, **pay the debt, then delete**, and says so in an error naming the command that clears it. (F2.)

**A claim that is released before the work it claims is not a claim.** `drainOwedRevocations` took `BEGIN; SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; COMMIT` and *then* called the provider, so the row lock covered one `SELECT` and the unguarded window was the entire network call — which that function's own comment described as "of unbounded duration". Reproduced with a 300ms provider: two drains started 100ms apart called `signOutAllForUser` **twice for the same user**; two started *simultaneously* divided correctly, which is exactly why an ad-hoc test finds nothing. It is a **lease** now — one atomic `UPDATE … RETURNING` that writes `revocation_claimed_at` and returns the row it wrote — rather than a longer-held lock, which would pin a connection and a row for however long the provider takes. A lease also **self-heals**: a drain that dies mid-call leaves one that expires. One semantic decision inside it: a *failed* attempt releases the lease immediately, because a lease says "somebody is calling the provider right now" and a failure that has already returned is not that — left set, an operator who fixed the provider and re-ran would be told there was nothing to do. (F3.)

**Three security-critical guards had no test at all, and one of them was this branch's original CRITICAL.** The production refusal of `ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED_ACCOUNT_DELETE`, `linkExplicitly`'s account lock, and the `NOT account_closed` half of its source guard: deleting each left the suite green at 145/145. The gate works — a reviewer drove eleven env-value variants and a real process launch at it — and **that is the shape the founder made this round fix for the race battery two rounds ago**: headline safety evidence living only as a number in a ticket comment with no command left to run. The lock is worse than untested: the third round *deleted* `resolve()`'s `FOR SHARE` on the grounds that `linkExplicitly` still took one, concentrating the guarantee into a single call site — and the test people would assume covers it hand-rolls the SQL on a raw connection and never calls the function. All three are covered now, each proven against its own mutant. (F4, F5, F6.)

**A partial failure needs somewhere to be written down, or it is a permanent one.** `DELETE /v1/account` committed the close and then walked the account's identities revoking each one's provider-side sessions. The walk lived entirely in memory and rethrew anything that was not `ProviderRejected` — so one transient provider error meant every identity ordered *after* it was never attempted, and nothing anywhere recorded that. What made it permanent rather than merely unlucky is the interaction with a check that is itself correct: a closed account can no longer be attributed to its caller, so **the route the user would retry through is the one route they can no longer reach.** Reproduced end to end with a flaky provider — account closed and committed, 500 to the caller, the third identity never revoked, the retry answering 401. A user deletes their account, is told it failed, and a live session survives indefinitely.

Catching and continuing is the obvious half and it is not the fix: it turns several stranded sessions into one, and leaves that one nowhere. The fix is `sonny.identity.provider_session_revoked_at` (migration 0006), NULL until a provider call actually returns, so **what is still owed is a query rather than a lost stack frame** — the deletion route drains its own account on the way through, and `npm run revocations` reports the residual from outside, needing no caller who can still authenticate. Two decisions inside it worth stating: `ProviderRejected` is recorded as done because the provider saying "no such session" *is* the state being asked for, while a timeout is not and marking it done would record an event that did not happen; and the route answers **204 even when a revocation is owed**, because the account really is closed — a 500 would describe an outcome that is not the one on disk and would invite a retry that cannot succeed. (PR #87 third round, F1.)

**A provider's "verified email" flag says who controlled an address when some *other* identity was written — never who controls it now.** Rule 2 linked a new verified, non-relay assertion onto any existing identity with a matching `email_hint`, silently. Reproduced: Human A signs in with Google and account X is created; the mailbox is later reassigned, which is ordinary at a company and ordinary at a free provider; **Human B, a different person who now legitimately owns it, signs in by email code and lands inside account X** with `created: false` and no flag of any kind. Somebody else's tasks, somebody else's subscription. There is no staleness bound that fixes this and cannot be one that means anything: `email_verified` carries no timestamp, and `linked_at` records when we wrote the row rather than when the provider last checked.

**The founder's decision (2026-08-22): rule 2 flags rather than links**, returning `link_hint: "verified_email_matches_existing_account"` exactly as the Apple relay case already does, with the identities staying separate until something explicit joins them. Recency-bounding was rejected because "recently" would be a number with no data behind it that fails *silently* in both directions; accept-and-document was rejected — though several providers do exactly that — because the flagging pattern already existed here for relay addresses, so refusing to guess costs little and reuses a shape the system already speaks. **The cost is stated rather than glossed:** one person with one mailbox signing in by email one day and by Google the next now gets two accounts and a hint where they used to get one account silently, until SONNY-128 surfaces the prompt. **And it supersedes one of this ticket's own acceptance criteria** — "same email by two methods lands on one account" — which the test now asserts the opposite of, with a comment saying so, because a test that quietly inverts a criterion is how a requirement disappears without anyone deciding to drop it.

**A consequence of that decision, and it deleted a guard rather than adding one.** With rule 2 no longer producing an account id, `resolve()` only ever inserts onto an account it created in the same transaction — so the `SELECT … FOR SHARE` that R3 added, and that two review rounds reasoned about, became unreachable. It is removed rather than left in place: a guard that cannot run is not defence in depth, it is a claim about a race nobody is having, and the next reader would reason from it. The same lock for the same reason is still taken by `linkExplicitly`, now the only path that attaches an identity to an account it did not create. What protects the rule-1 path was never that lock anyway but the row count on its refresh, which the existing two-connection race test reaches and always did.

**Two email normalisations, and the table that needed the other one.** `normalizeEmail` keeps plus-tags because it is the *identity* key and merging two addresses merges two accounts; `rateLimitEmailKey` folds them because it is the *mailbox* key and one inbox is one budget. Both correct, and `sign_in_code_issue` keyed every operation — issue, invalidate, consume, classify — on the identity one. So three simultaneous `email/start` calls for `victim@x`, `victim+1@x` and `victim+2@x` shared a single rate-limit bucket (which folds) and each wrote and invalidated only its own row (which did not): **three live, independently guessable codes in one inbox**, a 3× guessing surface against a guarantee this entry states in three places. Migration 0007 renames the column to `mailbox_key` rather than only re-populating it, because `email_norm` sitting beside a function called `normalizeEmail` is what made the mismatch read as correct. **The regression test for that very guarantee could not have caught it**: it raced three requests against one literal address, so it exercised neither half of the mismatch and would have stayed green either way. (PR #87 third round, F4.)

**A misconfiguration whose error came from somebody else's library.** `TRUSTED_PROXIES` was split on commas and handed to Fastify unvalidated, and a typo in one CIDR reached `@fastify/proxy-addr`'s `compile()`, which throws **inside the `Fastify(...)` constructor** — before `app.ready()`, before this server's logger exists. Measured: `TypeError: invalid IP address: not-an-ip`, top frame `parseipNotation` in `node_modules`, no mention of `TRUSTED_PROXIES` anywhere in it. The gateway would not start and the log did not say why, defeating the property `config.ts` exists for. Validated now into a `ConfigError` that names the offending entry — deliberately *with* its value, unlike every other variable this file refuses to echo, because a proxy address is not a secret and there is no fixing a list without knowing which element is bad. (PR #87 third round, F5.)

**The secret scanner's name-anchored pattern was case-sensitive, which was worst exactly where it mattered most.** `RATE_LIMIT_SALT`, `SUPABASE_JWT_SECRET` and `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` have **no vendor-prefix fallback** — a hex salt and a project secret carry no recognisable shape — so the variable name is the only thing that can catch them at all, and the lowercase and snake_case spellings are the natural YAML, Helm, compose and Terraform forms. The patterns are now two arrays: vendor prefixes stay case-sensitive, because an uppercased `sk-ant-` is not a shape any vendor issues and loosening it buys nothing, and name-anchored ones are matched with `-i`. Four selftest cases, each verified to pass — that is, to go uncaught — before the split. (PR #87 third round, F6.)

**A check two documents called "proof" and which compares two arguments to each other.** `linkExplicitly`'s `provenIdentityId !== identityId` consults no session store and no sign-in record: passing a stranger's identity id as *both* arguments satisfies it completely, and the stranger's identity moves onto the caller's account — reproduced against the built output. It is unreachable over HTTP today, because no route calls the function, and **the structural fix deliberately does not land here**: this function has no session store to consult, and inventing one would move the same trust boundary a layer down while looking like it had closed it. The wording in the docstring and in the rule document is corrected to say what the check is, and the constraint is recorded on SONNY-128, SONNY-129 and SONNY-203 — `provenIdentityId` must be derived server-side from a sign-in the process just completed and never accepted as a request field. A deliberate characterization test now pins the unsafe behaviour, so that anyone who makes it a real check has to read why it was not one. (PR #87 third round, F3, wording half.)

**Two fixes from the same review round undercut each other, and only the second round noticed.** The delete handler reads every `supabase_user_id` on the account so it can revoke each provider-side session. Under 0003 it read them *after* the closing `UPDATE` and got nothing, because the trigger had deleted the rows at statement end — so R1 moved the read to before `BEGIN`. Then R1/R3/R19 replaced 0003 with 0004, the rows started surviving the close, and reading first quietly became the wrong half of the trade: an identity joining the account between the read and the close was never revoked, so a session the user had *just added* outlived the account they had *just deleted*. The read is back inside the transaction, after the close, and it is race-free rather than merely luckier: the closing `UPDATE` holds `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` on the account row, and **both paths in this codebase that attach an identity to an existing account take `FOR SHARE` on that same row first** — `resolve()`'s rule 2 and `linkExplicitly` — so a writer either got there before the close and is seen, or is blocked behind it and finds the account closed. A third path, `resolve()`'s rule 1 changing an existing identity's `supabase_user_id`, takes no account lock and is serialised by a different mechanism: the close trigger updates every identity row on the account at statement end, so rule 1's update blocks on that and then matches nothing. **What is not covered, stated rather than papered over: raw SQL from outside these functions** — a retention sweep, an operator's `INSERT` — takes no `FOR SHARE` and no lock this handler holds can reach it. **The lesson is not about this read**: a fix is correct relative to a design, and replacing the design silently re-opens every fix that was reasoning about it. Both rounds' fixes were right when written.

**A destructive route may not break a tie.** `sonny.identity.supabase_user_id` carries no uniqueness constraint and never can — several identities naming one Supabase user is the case the whole separation exists for. What it does not license is two *live accounts* naming one, and both routes that resolve a caller through it were meeting that with `ORDER BY … LIMIT 1`. On refresh that hands out a session for whichever account sorted first; on `DELETE /v1/account` it destroys one of a user's accounts on the strength of a tiebreak and answers `204`, which is the right answer about the wrong account. Both refuse now. The recovery is not lost: signing in again goes through `resolve()`, which keys on `(provider, subject)` and lands on one account without a tiebreak (PR #87 second round, F6).

**Issuing a sign-in code is one step or it is three codes.** `invalidateLive` then `recordIssue` is correct one request at a time and wrong under concurrency: three simultaneous `email/start` calls for one address each invalidated what they could see and each inserted afterwards, and under READ COMMITTED none could see the others' uncommitted inserts — so the address ended with **three** live issuances where the design promises one, and the per-address ceiling is three, which is exactly how many an attacker can arrange. A transaction alone does not fix it, which is the part worth remembering: the writers have to be *serialised*, and there is no existing row to lock for the first code ever issued at an address, so the lock is taken on the address itself with `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. The send stays outside — it is a network call and cannot be rolled back — so racing callers still cause two mails; what they can no longer do is leave our record claiming two codes are live (PR #87 second round, F11).

**The database test files raced each other.** They share one Postgres and `migrate.db.test.ts` rolls migrations back by design, so in parallel it dropped the schema mid-assertion — 22 failures at once, reading `relation "sonny.identity" does not exist`. Vitest now runs files serially. Isolating by giving each file its own schema was the alternative and was rejected: the migration tests would stop exercising the schema names the migrations actually declare, which is most of what they are for.

**A test that names one migration's observable goes stale on the next migration; a fingerprint does not.** `migrate.db.test.ts`'s rollback test asserted only that a ledger row disappeared — vacuous, since the runner writes that row itself whether or not the rollback SQL ran (R17). R17's fix named 0004's trigger, and that broke the moment 0005 became the newest. It now takes a fingerprint of the whole `sonny` schema — every trigger, column, index and function body — and asserts the rollback *changes* it and the re-apply restores it **exactly**. The second half is new: "re-applies cleanly, which is what makes staging a rehearsal" previously checked only that a schema called `sonny` still existed, so a rollback that dropped a trigger and an `up` that forgot to recreate it would both have passed the test whose whole point is that they cannot.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The owed-revocation debt is guarded on the account row only** (PR #87 sixth round, LOW). 0009's trigger fires on `DELETE FROM sonny.account`, and the reviewer enumerated the cascade question rather than reasoning about it: `pg_constraint` shows exactly one foreign key in the schema, `identity → account ON DELETE CASCADE`, nothing cascades *into* `sonny.account`, and there are no rules on it — so no path removes an account row without firing the guard. What is unguarded is a **direct** `DELETE FROM sonny.identity`, a `DROP SCHEMA sonny CASCADE` (which is migration 0002's own rollback), and `TRUNCATE` (row triggers do not fire for it, documented in the function's own `COMMENT`). Not fixed: a guard on identity deletes would refuse the rollback path and the suite's own resets, which is a worse trade than the one it buys.
- **`CODE_VERIFY_PER_SOURCE` is a ceiling per public address, not per person** (PR #87 sixth round). 30 verifies an hour is far above a household and is a hard cap for *every* user sharing a carrier's CGNAT egress or a VPN exit, who cannot see each other to know why. Under the `TRUSTED_PROXIES`-unset misconfiguration it is a second deployment-wide cap that did not exist before, beside `CODE_REQUEST_PER_SOURCE`'s 10. Neither is a reason to drop the limit — without it the route was a working enumeration primitive — and both are reasons to configure the proxy list and to size these against real traffic rather than a guess.
- **One acceptance criterion is superseded rather than met, by the founder's decision of 2026-08-22.** "The linking rule is pinned by tests covering at least: **same email by two methods lands on one account**" — the rule now lands them on *two* accounts and a `link_hint`, and the test asserts that. The criterion's second half (an Apple relay address does not silently create a second account) is met and unchanged. Recorded here rather than quietly satisfied by a reworded test, because the criterion was written before the recycled-mailbox case was known, and inverting a criterion is a decision somebody has to make on purpose.
- **`drainOwedRevocations` cannot actually revoke anything yet, and `npm run revocations` says so in its own output.** It needs an `AuthProvider` to call, and no concrete adapter exists — the same founder-owned Resend/Supabase blocker as the rest of sign-in. The mechanism around it is complete and tested against the fake: the debt is recorded durably, the deletion route drains its own account, and the command reports the residual and exits 1. Wiring that residual to a schedule is one call and belongs to the ticket that lands the adapter.
- **The scanner still cannot see a secret whose name and value are on different lines.** grep is line-based, so pretty-printed JSON or wrapped YAML splits the two halves the name-anchored pattern needs to see together. Filed rather than fixed here (PR #87 third round, F8): closing it means the scanner parsing structure rather than matching lines. It is now named in the script's own "does not prevent" section.
- **Two latent defects found by the fifth round are filed rather than fixed** (PR #87 fifth round, INFO). **SONNY-229**: `email/verify` builds the identity assertion's subject from the *request body's* address rather than from the `VerifiedSession` the provider returned — `VerifiedSession.email` and `.emailVerified` are declared and read nowhere in `src/`. Safe only because the same string is handed to `verifyEmailCode` one line earlier, so the two cannot disagree; it becomes load-bearing the moment a real adapter normalises differently, and the value is the identity key. **SONNY-230**: rule 1's `COALESCE($5, supabase_user_id)` overwrites a superseded provider-side user id, so its sessions are both unrevocable and *unrecorded* — reproduced. Narrow today because Supabase's id for an address is stable, and it interacts with SONNY-196.
- **Two test-integrity items are filed, not fixed** (PR #87 third round, INFO): sign-out-then-refresh is untested even at the fake-provider level, and three concurrency tests share one `pg.Client` rather than a pool — ruled out as currently vacuous by two independent decoys, but a future pg major removing client-side queuing would silently invalidate them.
- **No concrete Supabase Auth adapter is wired.** `AuthProvider` is the seam and every route is tested against a fake, but nothing sends a real code, because the founder's **Resend sending domain (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) does not exist yet** — which the ticket names as founder-owned, blocking, and to be flagged rather than worked around. **Owed:** the adapter, and a real send.
- **Three acceptance criteria are unmet, not two** (PR #87 R12). (1) "Demonstrated end to end against staging" and the founder's three manual-test items need staging plus real email; staging is still stubbed from SONNY-126. (2) **"Training consent defaults to not-consented and can be set through the website's write path. Asserted."** — only the first half is true. The default is asserted and the column is `NOT NULL`, so no user is consented by omission; **there is no write path at all**, because the endpoint the website would call has to sit behind authenticated-request middleware — **SONNY-203's**, since SONNY-128 may not touch `server/` (PR #87 second round, F5). The write itself stays the website's under the same founder decision, so what is owed is the gate, not an in-app toggle. The word *consent* did not appear anywhere in the first version of this entry, which is how a whole unmet criterion went unnoticed. (3) The `AuthProvider` adapter, below.
- **Two criteria said "asserted" and asserted something weaker.** "Refresh rotates the token and the old one stops working" was covered by a test that asserted the response *echoed the token it was given* — the opposite of rotation. R12 made it assert the new token differs, **and left the second half of the criterion still unasserted** (PR #87 second round, F7): nothing replayed the rotated-away token. Half a criterion covered reads exactly like a whole one in a green run. The fake provider now models §3.3's rotation — the most recently issued token is the only one accepted — and the test replays the old one and asserts `401 auth.token_revoked`. "Revocation ends a session server-side" was covered by a test that never reached the provider call, because **there was no successful-delete test at all** — which is how R1 shipped green, with every deletion case asserting a refusal. Both are fixed and both now assert the thing they name.
- **`DELETE /v1/account` is mounted only behind a flag, and that flag has no owner on this branch.** This bullet said the route "takes its subject from a header" (PR #87 second round, F3) — it has not since the first review round's F1, which was a proof of concept that destroyed another account with a made-up bearer token. The route now attributes its caller **from the access token**, through `sonny.identity`, which is exactly what real middleware will do. What keeps it gated is larger and different: **nothing verifies that token at all.** `AuthProvider.userFromAccessToken` is the seam and no adapter implements it, so the route trusts an unimplemented check — it is off by default and `loadConfig` **refuses the flag outright when `SONNY_ENV=production`**.
- **The verification that would lift that gate had no owning ticket, which is the planning gap the second review round found** (PR #87 F5). Token verification, the protected-route middleware and the training-consent write path were all parked on SONNY-128 — the **client** sign-in ticket, whose never-touch list forbids `server/` work — so every one of them was deferred to a ticket that could not have taken it, and this branch's own unmet training-consent criterion had nowhere to land. **SONNY-203** now owns the gateway auth middleware: HS256 with the algorithm pinned, `iss`/`aud`/`exp` checked, `sub` trusted as the user id, and removing `ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED_ACCOUNT_DELETE` once real verification exists. Every reference in `server/`, in the API contract and in this entry was corrected from SONNY-128 to SONNY-203. **Building any of it was explicitly not SONNY-127's**, and none of it is in this branch. One thing for whoever picks SONNY-203 up: its description says "the token check itself is being built into SONNY-127", and that is not what SONNY-127 built — SONNY-127 built the *seam* with no implementation behind it.
- **Supabase's own send ceiling sits above ours.** Custom SMTP raises it from 2/hour to 30/hour project-wide. Our limits are set below it deliberately; if they ever cross, the project limit becomes the real one and returns an error we do not control.
- **Deleting an account does not reach retained content.** Stated on both tickets: this branch closes the row and frees the address while keeping the identity rows; `feature/row-12-retention` sweeps what hangs off `deleted_at`.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): **one** — when the Resend domain exists.

**What "complete" does and does not mean here, corrected after the adversarial review (PR #87 F10).** The first version of this entry called the endpoints complete and proven, which overstated it in a way a reader would act on. Precisely: **no server process mounts these routes.** `buildApp` takes auth as an optional argument and nothing in `server.ts` supplies one, so the running gateway serves `GET /v1/health` and nothing else. The routes are exercised only by tests, through `app.inject`, against a fake provider. **Three security properties land outside this branch:** access-token *verification* (signature and expiry — `clock.ts`'s tolerance is what it will apply, and no route calls it today) and authenticated-request middleware are **SONNY-203's**, and single-flight refresh is SONNY-128's. This sentence assigned all three to SONNY-128 until the second review round found that SONNY-128 may not touch `server/` at all (PR #87 F5). What SONNY-127 does own and has proven is the account model, the linking rule, the code lifecycle, the rate limits, and the token responses.

Next branch: `feature/row-12-social-signin` (Google, then Apple), which this ticket's rule was designed for and must not have to reshape.

### Branch: feature/memory-command-center
Status: complete — SONNY-208 Done; reviewed three times, three fix rounds landed; merged as PR #98, `f01d21a`
Date: 2026-08-21 (fix rounds and rebases 2026-08-22)
Tickets: **SONNY-208** (unified Command Center Memory section over the existing stores, with controls). Row 13's memory half, first of three; the two new stores are SONNY-209 (common output locations) and SONNY-210 (long-running task state), and this page renders them once they exist. Cut from `main` at `7770a48`, rebased onto `e421242` (SONNY-220) on 2026-08-22. Decision frame: SONNY-17's ratification comment of 2026-08-21.
Reviewed by: **three rounds, each fix-then-merge.** (1) Coordinator-run at `5ed794a`, 2026-08-22 — two test findings, nothing structural. (2) Fresh-session at `51e345f`, 2026-08-22 — **two HIGH findings that are one root cause, one reproduced end to end**: the memory switches never reached the scheduled path. (3) Verification pass at `bdf6f06`, 2026-08-22, asking the one question rounds 1–2 had not — **is three all of them?** It enumerated all fourteen writes the scheduled path can perform and found a fourth unguarded one, plus a false premise under round 3's own deviation. All three rounds' findings are fixed below; the page itself was traced control by control to its real write sites in every round and passed on the foreground path throughout. The founder's manual pass cleared the branch to merge on 2026-08-22, all ten checklist items including the scheduled-routine item the rounds converged on. Merged 2026-08-22 as PR #98, `f01d21a`. (The Status line above said the PR had not merged until SONNY-273.)
