Tests: **1704 tests in 126 suites, exit 0 at `b1b2b0f`** via the flagged command, from **1641 in 124** at the rebase base `dac12b9`. Net **+63 tests** (`git diff dac12b9..HEAD -- Tests/ | grep -c '^+    @Test'` = 63 at `b1b2b0f`). **`scripts/warnings`: 0 warnings at `b1b2b0f` (clean)**, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled. **Every figure here is re-measured at the head after each round and each rebase rather than carried**, because `main` has moved under this branch three times and a carried count silently describes a tree that no longer exists; the earlier heads measured 0 warnings too (`86c946e`, `9b11889`, `98e17b4`, `91dd33c`, `75c4ebe`) and the round-3 head measured 1700 in 126, independently reproduced by the round-4 pass. Neither command is re-run for the stamping commit that follows `b1b2b0f`, whose whole diff is this paragraph. Nothing was removed and no existing assertion was inverted; two existing tests gained entries because they are enumeration guards (the sidebar's locked order, and the stored-property-against-the-wipe classification).

**Mutation battery: 8 mutants, 8 killed, none surviving** — 7 killed at `50297aa` and the eighth after the test it exposed was rebuilt, re-run and killed at `17014df` (`scripts/mutate`, which stamps its own SHA). The battery asks whether the switches' guards are load-bearing or whether the suite passes either way: M1 and M2 drop the memory half of the recording conjunction on each side (killed by 5 and 4 tests), M3 stops the enterprise policy overriding the user's own switch (3), M4 makes a per-type switch read only the master one (7), M6 drops `refreshMemoryEntries()` from the wipe (1), M7 hands the executor `.recordEverything` regardless of settings (4), and M8 removes the allowed-apps grant refusal (1). **M5 is the one that mattered**, and it is written up under its own heading below.

What changed for the user: Command Center has a fifth page. It lists the seven kinds of thing Sonny remembers — routines, workspaces, task history, recent artifacts, clipboard history, snippets and allowed apps — each with how many are stored and when the newest arrived, a View that opens the surface that already manages that kind, a Delete for everything of that kind, and a switch that stops Sonny recording more of it. Above them, one switch turns recording off for all seven at once and leaves everything already stored exactly where it is, and a Preferences row opens Settings, which is where the user's own preferences live. Nothing on the page shows what was sent to a model.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The founder's rule was "do not build a parallel memory engine", and the design follows it literally.** §6.10's required memory types were already on disk as Sonny's eleven local stores. `MemoryCategory` names the *rows of the surface*, and `LocalStore.memoryCategory` maps each store onto one of them — exhaustive, no `default`, the same guard `LocalStore.kind` uses and for the same reason: a twelfth store must not be able to arrive on disk, be wiped by Delete Local Data, and be invisible in the one page built to show a person everything Sonny remembers. `MemorySettingsTests.everyLocalStoreIsPlacedUnderExactlyOneMemoryCategoryOrDeliberatelyExcluded` pins the union in the direction the compiler cannot check, because "answers" includes answering `nil`.

**Task history is one row over four files, and the folding is a decision rather than a convenience.** Plan details, the vision-session journal and Shortcut run history all join `.taskHistory`. The first two already hang off a history row — capped with it, suppressed with it, deleted with it by `deleteTask`'s dependents-first ordering — so giving either its own row would offer to delete half of a task. Shortcut run history has no surface of its own and never had one; it is a record of past runs, grouped with the others rather than given an eighth row the founder's enumeration does not name. `clipboardHistorySettings` is the one store excluded outright: that file *is* the clipboard switch, so listing it would offer to delete a preference and re-enable recording the user had turned off.

**The switches are asked at the sites `TaskRecordingPolicy` already guards, and the conjunction is written exactly twice.** `CapabilityExecutionContext.allowsRecording(to:)` and `AgentViewModel.allowsRecording(to:)` are the only two places the two switches are ANDed; every writing site asks through one of them. That is what let four existing guards — the vision journal, recent artifacts, the history row, the plan detail — pick up the new switch without learning about it, and `InvokeShortcutCapabilityAdapter`'s guard changed by one identifier. A boolean checked separately at each of the five layers those sites live in is precisely the shape `TaskRecordingPolicy`'s own doc names as how a switch quietly stops being true.

**Three refusal shapes, not one, and each is the honest answer for its case.** A *trace* store withheld is silent, exactly as "Don't save this task" is silent: nobody asked for a history row, so withholding one is not a failure to report, and the run still succeeds and still shows its result. A *save the user asked for by name* — routine, workspace, snippet — throws `MemoryDisabledError` and names the type, because a silent no-op would report a save that did not happen. **Allowed apps takes a third path and it is the one that could have gone wrong.** `rememberAppControlGrant` returns `false`, which `VisionSessionRunner.resolveAppControl` already treats as fail-closed — the session ends with "Sonny stopped because it could not save that you allowed it to control X", a sentence that is literally what happened. Returning `true` without persisting was considered and rejected: that method's contract to a security gate is "never run on a grant that does not exist", and re-pointing it would have meant editing the vision seam's own promise. The cost is bounded and is the switch's promise rather than a side effect — an app already on the list settles at `.allowed` and returns before that method is reached, so existing grants keep working and only *new* ones are refused.

**Clipboard history keeps the switch it already had.** It is the one type whose per-type control predates this work (`ClipboardHistorySettings.isEnabled`, which `ClipboardHistoryMonitor.poll()` already fails closed on), so the Memory row drives that setting and `MemorySettingsStore` refuses to write a per-category flag for it. Two flags over one behaviour is how a surface ends up reading "on" beside something that is recording nothing. The side effect this carries — answering the clipboard row counts as answering the first-run notice — is correct rather than incidental: choosing here *is* answering it. What the master switch adds is a guard at `startClipboardHistoryMonitoring`, the one place monitoring can begin, so all three of its callers are covered and a fourth cannot forget.

**The switches live in `UserDefaults`, and both reasons are consequences rather than preferences.** A wipe deletes every encrypted store, so a memory switch living in one would be erased by the exact action a privacy-minded user reaches for, and recording would silently resume. And a store that will not decrypt reports a failure and yields nothing, so a switch read that way would fall back to its default, which is *on* — an unreadable file failing a privacy control open. **What that removes is the unexpected fail-open path, not fail-open itself, and the difference is worth keeping straight:** this switch's default really is on, deliberately, so an absent or wrong-typed value reads as recording — what `UserDefaults` removes is the path where that happens for someone who *had* turned it off, because there is no decryption step here to fail. Anywhere this branch's records shortened that to "an unreadable value fails closed", they over-claimed a property the code does not have (PR #98 round-3 review, F6). `UserDefaults` has neither failure mode, holds no user content, and is what `.claude/rules/macagent-ui-conventions.md`'s Preferences rule already sends a non-privacy-sensitive preference to. Booleans are read `object(forKey:) as? Bool ?? true`, never `.bool(forKey:)`.

**The enterprise hook is present and inert, and "inert" is asserted in both directions.** `UnmanagedMemoryPolicyProvider` is the only provider that ships, so `disablesMemory` is false in every shipping path and the page behaves exactly as if the type did not exist — pinned by `theShippedPolicyProviderLeavesEveryTypeRecording`. The composition row 19 will rely on is pinned separately, by a stub provider: a policy that disables memory overrides the user's switch, refuses to store a preference nothing could honour (a stored value the policy overrides on the next read is a control that springs back), locks every control on the row rather than only the toggle, and stops a real dispatch from recording. `isManaged` is a separate field from `disablesMemory` so a managed machine whose policy *allows* memory stays distinguishable from an unmanaged one; that distinction is invisible in behaviour and must not be invisible to whatever later reports why a control is locked.

**A per-type delete reuses `LocalDataDeletionService` with a narrower list, and the URLs come from the injected stores.** Same service as Settings' whole wipe, so a per-type delete inherits attempt-every-file-and-report-what-survived rather than a second routine that stops at the first error. The URLs are resolved through the stores this view model was constructed with, not through `LocalStore.fileURL(fileManager:)`, which answers the *default* location — a fixture pointing its stores at a temporary directory would otherwise have deleted the developer's real files. The mapping switch is exhaustive over `LocalStore`, so a twelfth store cannot be added without someone deciding which injected instance answers for it.

**Two capped stores needed `now` threaded into their new `delete`, and the test that found it would have passed silently.** `RecentArtifactStore.loadAll` and `ClipboardHistoryStore.loadAll` apply an age cap, so a delete that read with `Date()` and wrote back is an eviction pass — and against a fixture pinned to an older instant it read an empty list, matched nothing, and returned without writing, leaving the entry in place. The signature now mirrors `record`'s (`recordedAt`/`copiedAt`), so a caller can pin the instant and tell a delete apart from an eviction. `SnippetStore` and `ApprovedAppStore` are uncapped and take no `now`.

**The wipe had to learn about the four new lists, and that is a defect this branch nearly shipped.** `clearInMemoryLocalDataState` ends with three `refresh…` calls so no surface renders state whose file the wipe just erased. The Memory section publishes four more arrays; without `refreshMemoryEntries()` beside them, wiping local data left the page listing every entry it had just deleted. `ProductShellTests.everyAgentViewModelStoredPropertyIsClassifiedAgainstTheLocalDataWipe` is what caught it — the eight new stored properties failed the suite until each was classified, which is exactly the job that test was written to do, and `memorySettings` is the one that belongs in the *outside-the-wipe* set for the sharpest version of that group's reason.

**A new Command Center page's shared surfaces are now a population scan rather than a convention.** CLAUDE.md's SONNY-180 gotcha says a page that omits `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` / `CommandCenterStorageNotice` / the running indicator shows nothing for a run or approval raised there, and nothing enforced it — a per-page test written today would not have covered the page written tomorrow, which is the whole failure mode. `everyCommandCenterPageRendersTheSharedAttentionAndStorageSurfaces` iterates `CommandCenterDestination.allCases`, asserts the destination set and the scanned set are equal so a sixth page cannot arrive unchecked, and additionally asserts the two self-gating surfaces are **not** inside the `isRunning || isAwaitingApproval` block — nesting a self-gating strip inside that conditional was a real shipped bug on the storage notice, and it is invisible to a check that only counts the token. Tasks is the named exception: it renders `InProgressTaskGroup` in that block, which is the wireframe's own treatment, rather than the compact indicator.

**There is no Memory wireframe, so the baseline was the sibling pages.** `docs/wireframes/` holds one SVG. The page is built from the components the other four already use — `CommandCenterPageHeader`, a bordered collection panel with `CollectionHeader` and hairline-divided 56pt rows, `CommandCenterRowActionStyle` buttons, `SettingsAdaptiveControlRow`/`SettingsControlLabel`/`SonnySettingsToggle` for the two control rows, and the same 28/24/18 page padding — and `CollectionHeader`'s action became optional rather than being duplicated, because a Memory collection has nothing to add: every row is a kind of memory that already exists, and a "+" there would offer to create one.

**Where "edit" lives per type, since the page deliberately builds no editor.** Routines, Workspaces and Task history open the pages that already own their editors; the four types that never had a surface open `MemoryEntriesSheet`, where editing a list of remembered records means removing entries from it. Nothing rewrites a snippet's expansion, because nothing in the product ever has, and inventing that editor here would be exactly the reinvention the ticket forbids. The sheet deletes by *position* into the same published array it enumerated, so a row and the record it removes cannot come apart; an out-of-range index is a no-op, because the array can shrink under a sheet that is still on screen.

**User preferences are surfaced, not stored.** §6.10 lists preferences as a memory type; the founder's answer is the existing Settings under Memory rather than a new store. The page therefore carries a Preferences row that opens the Settings dialog through the binding `CommandCenterView` already owns — no second navigation path, and no restatement of anything Settings says.

**THE UI-FIDELITY ROUND, `9b11889`.** The `sonny-ui-fidelity-reviewer` was run against the built page before the PR, comparing it to the sibling pages rather than to a wireframe (there is none for Memory). Six findings acted on, five of them its own:

- **Every destructive confirmation now says what it takes.** The per-type Delete was title-and-buttons only, which made it the least-explained destructive action in the app despite deleting the most per press — the Settings wipe, the workspace delete and both task deletes all carry a `message:` naming what goes and what stays. `MemoryDeletionCopy` holds one per category, and the two that promise something is *kept* — the files behind recent artifacts, the files tasks created — have that promise pinned by a test rather than left to survive an edit.
- **The entries sheet deleted a row on one click.** Nothing else in Command Center does. It confirms now, like the workspace card and both task rows; a misclick there is unrecoverable, and one of the four types it lists is a revoked app-control grant.
- **The collection was a flat stack of seven rows**, where every sibling that uses this row idiom groups it. It is grouped by `LocalStoreKind` — the classification "Don't save this task" already decides suppression by — so the split is the product's own reading rather than a taxonomy invented for the page, and `MemoryCategory.storeKind` plus a test asserting each row's stores share one kind is what makes that structural. `MemorySection` is a value, like `RoutineCadenceSection`, so the grouping is assertable.
- **Two toggle idioms, forty points apart.** The master row used `SonnySettingsToggle` and the seven rows used `RoutineRow`'s native `.switch`. Both rows use `SonnySettingsToggle` now: `docs/sonny-design-system-reference.md` §2.6 specifies it down to the knob shadow and calls that "the one shadow exception in System A, confined to this one control", which reusing the control honours; a native switch is macOS chrome rather than a Sonny token, so the remaining difference from `RoutineRow` is a difference from the deviation, not from the rule.
- **The empty state named no way out of itself**, unlike `RoutinesView`'s and `WorkspacesView`'s, which pair the condition with the command that ends it. One per type now.
- **The Preferences row listed Settings sections that do not exist** ("Display, theme") and omitted two that do.

**And one the session found in its own read, which the reviewer did not.** A row's switch stayed movable while the master switch was off, so flipping one wrote a preference whose *effective* value could not change and the control snapped back. `MemoryRowPresentation.canChangeRecording` carries the answer now, false for either cause. The same read reversed the other half of that lock: **Delete is deliberately not disabled by the enterprise policy.** Deleting what is already stored is furthered by a disable-memory policy rather than contradicted by it, and locking it would have been the page inventing a restriction the policy never asked for.

**M5 is the finding worth reading, because the test that should have caught it was written and still held nothing.** The mutant deletes the master-switch guard from `startClipboardHistoryMonitoring`, and it survived the whole suite at `50297aa` — including the test written specifically to pin that behaviour. The cause is ordering, not absence: the test switched memory off *after* its own control half had started the timer, and `startClipboardHistoryMonitoring` returns early when a timer already exists, so nothing polled and nothing recorded whether the guard was there or not. Rewritten to switch memory off before monitoring has ever started — where `setMemoryEnabled(false)`'s own `refreshClipboardHistoryNotice()` reaches a nil timer and the guard is the only thing between a live pasteboard and the store — it kills the mutant. The reasoning lives at the test rather than in a battery log, because the next person to edit it would otherwise reintroduce exactly that ordering. **Clipboard history is the only memory type withheld by a timer rather than by a guard consulted at write time, which is why it is the only one whose test could be vacuous this way.**

**THE PR #98 FIX ROUND, 2026-08-22.** The coordinator's review returned fix-then-merge with two findings, both about tests rather than about the page, and one founder decision. Rebased onto `e421242` first; the expected changelog conflict did not occur, which turned out to matter — see the placement note below.

**F1, and it is the one worth reading: a guard whose own doc comment called it load-bearing was held by nothing.** `setMemoryEnabled` and `setMemoryCategoryEnabled` each open with `guard !memorySettings.isDisabledByPolicy else { return }`, refusing to store a preference an administrator's policy could not honour — *"a stored value nothing can honour is a switch that springs back"*. **Removing both guards left the entire suite at exit 0.** The reason it hid is the shape that recurs: the read side folds the policy in independently (`isRecording == isEnabledByUser && !isDisabledByPolicy`), so a broken write guard is masked by a correct read path, and every assertion phrased against that composed value passes for a reason unrelated to what it is named for. The policy test that existed said in its own comment that the switch was "refused rather than written" and checked only the composed read; that comment now says which test owns the write half. The difference is visible in exactly one place — *after the policy lifts* — so `anAdministratorsPolicyStopsTheSwitchesBeingStoredAtAll` reopens a view model over the same `UserDefaults` with an unmanaged provider and asks what was stored, the pattern `theMemorySwitchesSurviveALocalDataWipe` already establishes. It ships with a control, `aSwitchTheUserSetsIsStoredAndOutlivesTheViewModelThatSetIt`, because "nothing was stored" is equally true of setters that never store anything — which is the same failure mode one level down.

**F2: two of the seven types were verified by reading rather than by exercising.** `allowsRecording(to:)` composes `taskRecordingPolicy.allowsWriting(to:) && memorySettings.allowsRecording(to:)`, and `ProductShellTests`' two suppression tests flip only the first term — so recent artifacts and the vision-session journal had their *memory* switch checked by inspecting a conjunction shared with five well-tested paths. Both handovers are now asserted under the per-type switch, under the master switch, and with each per-type switch shown not to withhold the other's store; a companion test keeps the `taskRecordingPolicy` term measured so the conjunction cannot silently lose either side. **Asserted at the seam rather than by dispatching, which is the right instrument and not a shortcut** — `recentArtifactStoreForThisRun`'s own doc records that no command the fixtures can run generates an artifact, so an end-to-end assertion passes either way and a battery once caught exactly that; the vision journal is stronger still, since `makeVisionEnvironment` returns nil without an API key and no test in this repository can execute the live decision at all.

**Second battery: 4 mutants, 4 killed, none surviving** at `b4cc28b` (`scripts/mutate`). Each new test was made to fail before it was kept: F1a and F1b delete the two write guards and are killed by `anAdministratorsPolicyStopsTheSwitchesBeingStoredAtAll`; F2a and F2b rewrite each handover to consult `taskRecordingPolicy` alone — the exact pre-fix reading — and are killed by `theRecentArtifactAndVisionJournalHandoversAreWithheldByTheMemorySwitchesToo`. Combined with the first battery that is **12 mutants across the branch, 12 killed**, both stamped by the tool at their own SHAs.

**The founder's decision on "Allowed apps", recorded here so it is not re-derived** (2026-08-22, on SONNY-208): the fail-closed behaviour **ships as built** — with that switch off a new grant is refused, `rememberAppControlGrant` returns `false`, and the screen-control session ends, while apps already on the list are unaffected. The refusal reuses `VisionSessionRunner.resolveAppControl`'s pre-existing "never run on a grant that does not exist" contract rather than inventing one, and the alternative would have violated it and required editing the risk seam this ticket forbids. **What is deferred is the placement, not the behaviour:** six of the seven switches mean "record less" and this one effectively means "grant nothing new", and it is the only one that can end a task the user is actively running with no in-product explanation possible. Whether it belongs under Memory at all goes to **SONNY-223**, the founders' whole-product pass.

**A placement error the clean rebase exposed, worth stating because the next session will hit it.** Entries in this file run **newest-first directly under `## Entries`**, and this one was appended at the end of the file instead — which is why rebasing over SONNY-220's entry produced no conflict at all, when a conflict is exactly what should have happened. It is moved to the top now. `fix/memory-area-prereqs` (2026-08-21) sits at the end of the file under the same mistake and is **deliberately left where it is**: it is another lane's record, and silently relocating someone else's entry is not this branch's call.

**Two limits of these tests, recorded rather than chased** (the review named both and required neither). `everyLocalStoreIsPlacedUnderExactlyOneMemoryCategoryOrDeliberatelyExcluded` is a value-type union check: it cannot detect whether any writer consults the mapping, and the writers were confirmed to by separate reading. `aRowsSwitchCannotBeMovedWhileTheMasterSwitchOrAPolicyHasMemoryOff` constructs `canChangeRecording` directly rather than reading it off a rendered control, so it cannot catch a view that never wired it. Both are real limits of testing SwiftUI in a repository with no inspection harness, not oversights.

**THE PR #98 ROUND-3 FIX, 2026-08-22.** A fresh-session review at `51e345f` returned fix-then-merge with two HIGH findings that are one root cause, one of them reproduced end to end, plus four surviving mutants and a records correction. Rebased onto `dac12b9` (SONNY-219, SONNY-220's follow-up) — this time the changelog conflict did occur, resolved newest-first.

**The defect, and it is the one this ticket names as worth preventing: the page was correct for a task the user starts and not for a task the scheduler starts.** A user who turns memory off, closes the laptop, and lets a morning routine fire got new rows written into the encrypted store while the switch on screen read off. Reproduced by the reviewer through `checkScheduledRoutines(now:)`: master-off wrote 1 history row and 1 plan detail, task-history-off wrote 1 row, against a foreground control that wrote 0.

**Three writes, one root cause, and the tell that it was a slip.** `recordScheduledTaskHistory` guarded neither the row write nor the plan-detail write, and `performScheduledRun` handed `AgentRunner` the raw `recentArtifactStore` instead of the switched seam. Everything routed through the executor was already correct — including Shortcut run history, which is in the same memory row and is withheld properly, because it is written through a capability adapter and the executor carries `memorySettings`. Only the writes the view model performs itself were wrong. And `makeExecutor` has carried a comment stating the correct rule since this branch started: *the memory switches are the user's standing answer and apply to a scheduled run exactly as they do to a typed one.* The branch stated the rule and then broke it three lines away, in the one place the rule was never re-read.

**Why the fix is not the foreground guard copied verbatim, which is the trap here.** `allowsRecording(to:)` folds in `taskRecordingPolicy`, and the scheduled path must not read that: "Don't save this task" is a **pre-dispatch** toggle — `dontSaveButton` renders only when `!isTaskInFlight` — so the reachable window is the ordinary one, a user flipping it on while composing and not yet pressing Send. `isRunning` is false, `approvalRequest` is nil and `clarificationQuestion` is nil, all three of `checkScheduledRoutines`' guards pass, a routine fires, and reading the policy would strip that routine's traces because of a switch set for a command that has not been sent. That is the same class of defect PR #67's F2 fixed by passing `.record` explicitly, and copying the conjunction would have reintroduced it while fixing this one. **And the term is never one a scheduled run should honour anyway**, which does not depend on any window being reachable: there is no composer in that path, so a user has no way to ask for a routine's suppression, and honouring it could only ever apply a switch set for a different task. `allowsScheduledRecording(to:)` names the asymmetry once, in one place, with the reasoning at the function: **the scheduled path opts out of the composer switch and never out of the standing memory switches.** `aScheduledRoutineStillRecordsWhileAForegroundRunHasSuppressionLeftOn` is the test that would be red had the shortcut been taken, and mutant S3 restores it and dies.

**The tests drive the real scheduler door, not the seam the bug routed around.** Five through `checkScheduledRoutines(now:)`: a control proving the scheduler really writes a row and a plan detail, the master switch and the task-history switch each withholding both, a *different* type's switch not withholding them (so a guard reading only the master switch fails), and the suppressed-foreground-run case above. The recent-artifact handover is asserted at the scheduled seam — for the reason `recentArtifactStoreForThisRun`'s own doc gives, that no command the fixtures can run generates an artifact — paired with a scan proving the scheduled runner reads that seam and that no other store reaches it. **The scan needed care of its own:** `recentArtifactStore: recentArtifactStore` is a *substring* of the correct line, so asserting its absence fails on correct code; the sanctioned handover is removed from the text first and the token asserted absent from what remains.

**The four surviving mutants, and what each one really was.** M1/M2 — `canChangeRecording` was never asserted anywhere in `Tests/`: the test named for the row-switch lock asserted `memorySettings.isRecording` instead, a value-type property already covered by `MemorySettingsTests`, so it passed for a reason unrelated to its name — the identical shape to the previous round's F1, one round later. **And there was no SwiftUI excuse for half of it:** `MemoryRowPresentation` is a plain struct, so the fix was to move its construction into `MemoryRowPresentation.row(for:viewModel:)` where a test can call it. The previous round recorded this as "a real limit of testing SwiftUI"; that was true of the `.disabled()` modifier and false of the value, and the reviewer was right to separate them. M6 — nothing held where "View" goes for any of the seven rows, so Task history could open Insights with the suite green; routing is now `MemoryRowDestination`, with all seven asserted plus the two mappings agreeing about which four open the sheet. M8 — the clipboard delete's poll-timer stop, reachable only in a real one-second window, is scanned rather than run.

**Round-3 battery: 10 mutants, 10 killed, none surviving** at `57bc9d9` (`scripts/mutate`). S1 restores the reproduced defect (killed by 2), S2 reverts the artifact handover (1), S3 takes the copy-the-foreground-guard shortcut (2), M1/M1b hardwire the row lock two ways (1 each), M2/M2b delete the modifier and bypass the factory (1 each), M6/M6b misroute View two ways (1 each), M8 drops the timer stop (1). **One authoring error worth recording rather than hiding:** M6b as first written added `.taskHistory` to a *later* case in the same switch, which an earlier case already matches — an equivalent mutant, and it survived for that reason and not for want of a test. Rewritten to actually move the case, it dies. Across the branch that is **22 mutants, 22 killed**, in three batteries each stamped by the tool at its own SHA.

**F6, a records correction with no code change behind it.** Summaries in this branch's own records shortened the `UserDefaults` argument to "an unreadable value fails closed". It does not: the default is `?? true`, deliberately, so an absent or wrong-typed value reads as *recording*. What `UserDefaults` removes is the *unexpected* fail-open path — a decrypt failure flipping the switch back on for someone who had turned it off — because there is no decryption step to fail. The narrower claim was always the one the code supports; the summary over-reached. Corrected here and at `MemorySettingsStore`'s own doc, with a note not to shorten it again.

**What this round did not touch, because the review checked it and it held:** the population scan (verified twice, including a synthetic sixth destination failing it), delete reaching disk, System A with the §2.6 citation checked verbatim, no explanatory copy, no Data-Sent-To-AI surface, and an empty diff across all six never-touch files. The "Allowed apps" fail-closed behaviour matches `VisionSessionRunner.swift:459` and is the founder's decided position; placement stays SONNY-223's.

**THE PR #98 ROUND-4 VERIFICATION PASS, 2026-08-22.** Round 3 fixed three unguarded writes on the scheduled path; nobody had established that three was the whole population. A fresh session was given exactly that job and enumerated **all fourteen writes to the eleven local stores reachable from `checkScheduledRoutines(now:)`** — seven guarded, six correctly unguarded scheduler machinery (the legacy-plaintext re-encrypt, four `advanceScheduleBaseline` catch-up writes, two `pauseSchedule` refusals), and **one real unguarded write of new memory**. Three was not all of them.

**F1, decided by the founder rather than by the branch: block it.** `routineStore.recordRun`, reached unconditionally from `recordScheduledRunInHistory`, appended a dated entry to `recentRunDates` in `routines.json` — the file the Routines memory row governs — with every switch off. Reproduced through the real door, not inferred. It is the same shape as the three round 3 fixed: a scheduled run putting something new on disk while the switch on screen reads off, on a path the foreground has no equivalent of, and visible to the user as the Routines row's streak badge. **What made it cheap to decide is that nothing in the scheduling path reads `recentRunDates`** — the due-check runs off the routine's schedule and the clock — so the data is display-only and guarding it costs nothing operationally; the badge goes quiet, which is what memory-off means. The counter-argument is recorded at the code rather than dismissed: a routine is something the user deliberately created, so its run log arguably belongs to the routine rather than being something Sonny recorded *about* them. It lost on consistency — the same user, same session, same switch, would otherwise find three kinds of scheduled write silent and a fourth still recording, with nothing to tell them apart. **The deeper question it exposes is SONNY-223's, not this write's:** turning off Routines memory blocks *saving* a routine while still logging runs, which may be exactly backwards, since saving is the deliberate act and logging the passive one.

**F2 — the round-3 deviation is sound and its stated reason was false, in three places.** `allowsScheduledRecording(to:)`'s doc said in the present tense that reading the composer switch is "actively wrong" because `checkScheduledRoutines` "only guards on `isRunning` and `isAwaitingApproval`". It guards on **three** terms: PR #80's F1 added `clarificationQuestion == nil`, closing exactly the window that sentence cited — and the same file documents that third term at length forty lines above the guard. So a sentence asserting a live defect was false about code three hundred lines below it. **The true reason, which is stronger, replaces it everywhere** (`AgentViewModel.swift` twice and this entry once): "Don't save this task" is a **pre-dispatch** toggle — `dontSaveButton` renders only when `!isTaskInFlight` — so the reachable window is the ordinary one, a user flipping it on while composing and not yet pressing Send; all three guards pass, a routine fires, and reading the policy would strip that routine's traces because of a switch set for a command that has not been sent. And the half that depends on no window at all: **there is no composer in the scheduled path, so a user has no way to ask for a routine's suppression** — honouring the term could only ever apply a switch set for a different task, which the toggle's own label rules out. Corrected rather than quietly swapped, because **a correct decision resting on a false premise is one refactor away from being reverted**: a reader who checks the cited mechanism finds it does not exist and reasonably concludes the whole deviation is obsolete.

**F3 — the scheduled twin diverged from its foreground twin in the one way that matters.** The plan-detail guard was inline, so its `return` exited `recordScheduledTaskHistory` entirely and skipped `refreshTaskHistory()`, leaving a row on disk the Tasks list would not show until something else refreshed it — verbatim the defect PR #89's review fixed on this same pair of writes, described in the comment six lines above the guard. The foreground path has been shaped against it ever since: `recordTaskPlanDetail` is a separate function precisely so its early return is local. **Unreachable today and fixed anyway**, because it is unreachable only while plan details and history rows share the `.taskHistory` row — and the guard's own comment says it is kept for the day they do not. A latent defect that arrives with a future refactor is the one shape nobody is watching for. The write moved into `recordScheduledTaskPlanDetail`; a scan pins the shape, since the branch cannot be reached at runtime.

**Round-4 battery: 4 mutants, 4 killed, none surviving** at `9e448ad` (`scripts/mutate`). R1 restores F1's unguarded write (killed by 3), R2 has the run-date guard read the composer switch instead of the standing one (3), R3 widens it so it never withholds (3), R4 puts the plan-detail guard back inline where its return takes the refresh with it (1). Across the branch: **26 mutants, 26 killed**, in four batteries each stamped by the tool at its own SHA.

**The two notes, resolved as records because both were right and undocumented.** `EditWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter` asks no memory switch while its `CreateWorkspace` sibling does: deliberate, because it cannot *create* a workspace — `editWorkspaceSpec` throws `.missingWorkspace` for a name the store does not hold — so every write there edits an entry the user already has, the same category as the view model's own unguarded `markWorkspaceAsTeam`. And `visionSessionJournalStoreForThisRun` is the one seam a scheduled run reaches that still reads the composer switch, a live exception to a rule `allowsScheduledRecording(to:)` states globally; it fails closed and unattended vision cannot execute (three independent refusals), so it stays as it is and is named at both ends.

**What the pass re-measured rather than trusted, recorded because it is the strongest evidence this entry carries:** the flagged suite (1700 in 126 at `bdf6f06`, matching the claim, and confirmed a second time by the battery's own baseline), `scripts/warnings` (0, tool-stamped at `bdf6f06`), and **5 of the branch's then-22 claimed mutation kills re-run by hand — 5 killed, 0 survived**. One figure came back *higher* than claimed (M4 killed by 11 against a claim of 7): not a discrepancy, since the 7 was measured at `50297aa` and stamped at that SHA exactly as the rule requires, and the suite has grown since.

Manual-test items the user still owes: open Command Center → Memory and confirm each of the seven rows shows a count and, where the type carries a timestamp, a newest-entry line; use View on Routines, Workspaces and Task history and confirm each lands on that page; use View on Recent artifacts, Clipboard history, Snippets and Allowed apps and confirm the sheet lists real entries and that deleting one removes it; use Delete on one type and confirm only that type empties; turn one type's switch off, do the thing that would record it (save a routine, copy something, finish a task) and confirm nothing new appears; turn the master switch off and confirm no type records while everything already stored is still listed; turn it back on and confirm recording resumes; press Open settings and confirm the Settings dialog opens; and confirm every Delete raises a confirmation naming what it takes; confirm the seven rows appear under the two group headings ("Saved by you", "Recorded as Sonny works") with counts; confirm the row switches are visibly unavailable while the master switch is off while Delete stays available; **with a routine scheduled and Memory switched off, let it fire and confirm no new task appears in Tasks or Insights and the routine's streak badge does not move — then switch Memory back on, let it fire again, and confirm both do** (the scheduled path is what three of the four review rounds were about, and this is the one item on the checklist no test covers); and confirm no "data sent to AI" surface appears anywhere on the page.

### Branch: fix/escape-attribute-separators
Status: complete
Date: 2026-08-22 (opened 2026-08-21)
Tickets: **SONNY-219** — `UntrustedContentBoundary.escapeAttribute` folded line feed only, and did it in two independently maintained copies. Filed from SONNY-198 via PR #94's fresh-session review (F6). One session, one ticket, cut from `main` at `7770a48` and **rebased onto `e421242`** (`fix/nested-routine-reverse-overwrite`, PR #96) for the polish round — one conflict, the `## Entries` heading, resolved keep-both newest-first. The staleness checks that rebase owed came back clean: that branch touches `PlannedDestinations` and `AgentActionExecutor`, this one touches only the boundary, and the two share no test file. Not a roadmap row: a security-boundary fix, sized to the boundary rather than to the ticket's estimated impact.
Reviewed by: **coordinator-run security review of PR #97, 2026-08-22, at `43cf81a` — four attack lenses briefed to escape the wrapper rather than to validate the fix. This branch's own work verified sound.** The widened fold held against every separator attack aimed at it, *including the one it was most likely to fail*: the fold maps whitespace to `_` and the delimiters are built out of underscores, so a delimiter assembled entirely from foldable separators — all spaces, all tabs, all NBSP, all VT, mixed CR/tab — was driven through both real paths, and every one was contained, because the fold runs before `escape` as well as after. Also defended: all eight line-break characters, all ten horizontal ones, every character outside `.whitespacesAndNewlines` including U+001C–U+001F, U+180E, U+FEFF and ZWNJ/ZWJ, and the nine BIDI controls U+202A–U+202E / U+2066–U+2069 — which the lens declined to inflate into a boundary escape, calling them a distinct visual-spoofing concern. **The negative control reproduced exactly under independent re-execution: 10 fail, 3 pass.** Three small in-file findings, all fixed here in `860bc55`, none of them a live hole: **F2** the C0 information separators sat outside the fold and undiscussed; **F3** the two structural scans walked `Sources/MacAgentCore` while the rule they enforce carries no directory qualifier; **F4** the doc comment credited `_`'s one-for-one-ness when the load-bearing property is the fold–escape–fold ordering, which a maintainer trusting it could collapse. **A CRITICAL was found *beneath* this branch, in a function this diff does not touch — SONNY-222**, deferred by explicit founder decision; see the deferral below.

Spec sections covered: none implemented. §12.4/§12.5's untrusted-content boundary is *hardened*, the same way SONNY-198 hardened the trusted prior-task block one branch earlier — this is the observed-content wrapper's copy of that fix.
Files changed:
- `Sources/MacAgentCore/UntrustedContentBoundary.swift` — `escapeAttribute` folds a new `private static let separators` through a new `private foldingSeparators`, on both sides of `escape` instead of after it. `separators` is `CharacterSet.whitespacesAndNewlines.union(.controlCharacters)`; it was the first set alone until the polish round.
- `Sources/MacAgentCore/WebResearchSynthesizer.swift` — the `private static func escapeAttribute` duplicate deleted; both call sites name `UntrustedContentBoundary.escapeAttribute`.
- `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/UntrustedContentBoundaryTests.swift` — new; **15 tests** (`grep -c "@Test" Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/UntrustedContentBoundaryTests.swift` → 15 at `860bc55`), 13 of them in the first commit and two added with F2.
- `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` — the untrusted-content section now says the attribute fold is part of "the escaping", with the set, the ordering, and what the two scans cover.
- `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` — this entry, plus the dated supersession on `chore/cleanup-sweep`'s SONNY-219 residual bullet.
Tests: the flagged command in `CLAUDE.md` -> **PASS, 1641 tests in 124 suites**, exit 0, at `860bc55`. **Reconciled against the diff rather than against a remembered number**: `git diff --stat origin/main` at `860bc55` → five files, exactly one of them a test file and that one new, carrying 15 `@Test` functions. So this branch adds 15 tests and nothing else, which puts `main` at `e421242` at 1626; that reconciles forward from the 1618 `chore/cleanup-sweep` recorded at `49abb0e` plus the 8 `fix/nested-routine-reverse-overwrite` added — four in `AgentActionExecutorTests`, four in `PlannedDestinationsTests`, per the entry directly below. 1626 + 15 = 1641, and 1641 is what the suite printed. `scripts/warnings` -> **0 warnings, exit 0**, stamped by the script as `860bc55 (clean)`, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` recompiled, 99s. **One mutation battery, 7 mutants, 7 killed** (`scripts/mutate <plan>`, plan kept outside the tree per its own rule) — **at `392c563`, and not re-run.**

**That battery SHA is a stated limit, not an oversight.** `392c563` is this branch's pre-rebase first commit: it measured the same `escapeAttribute` body against the same thirteen tests, and both survived the rebase byte-identical. What it therefore does **not** cover is the polish round — the `.controlCharacters` union, the widened scan, and the two tests added with them. Those carry their own negative controls instead, below, which is the same class of evidence a mutant provides and was cheaper to run than a second battery.

**The negative control is the evidence that matters here, and it was run rather than assumed — three times.**
1. With the two production files restored from `7770a48` and the new test file kept, **10 of the 13 fail** — including `lines.count → 4 == 3` and `closing-delimiter lines → 2 == 1` for the composed attack. PR #97's review re-executed this independently and got 10 and 3, exactly.
2. With `separators` narrowed back to `.whitespacesAndNewlines`, **both** of the polish round's new tests fail: `source=evilsource=forged` for the sweep, and an un-neutralised `source=UNTRUSTED_OBSERVEDCONTENT_END` for the forged-delimiter one.
3. With a probe declaring the fold planted at `Sources/MacAgent/ScanProbe.swift` and removed afterwards, **both structural scans fail naming `MacAgent/ScanProbe.swift`** — which is what proves F3's widening actually reaches the second target rather than merely compiling against it.

**The three that pass in (1) are not "written to pass either way", and this entry said that before the review corrected it.** They are passthrough invariants — the ordinary attribute, the ordinary web id, and observed content keeping its own lines — which this particular regression does not move, but a different one would.

Behavior added:
- An attribute in an observed-content wrapper — the `id=` and `source=` tokens — can no longer begin a line inside the wrapper, whichever of the eight Unicode line separators it carries.
- The same attribute can no longer be split into two tokens by a tab, a non-breaking space, or any other Unicode space.
- Nor by anything that renders as nothing: the C0 information separators, the rest of C0 and C1, DEL, the soft hyphen, ZWNJ/ZWJ, the BOM and the BIDI controls are folded out of attributes too.
- A delimiter *rebuilt by the fold itself* is neutralised, where before the fold ran after `escape` and could assemble one out of a value `escape` had found nothing in.
- The web-research wrapper's `id` attribute is delimiter-escaped for the first time; its own copy folded separators and never escaped.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **An ordinary attribute is byte-identical.** `source=screenshot-of-Google Chrome` still emits `source=screenshot-of-Google_Chrome`, and the benign `id=source-1` the web builder actually passes still emits verbatim — both pinned, and both pass against the unfixed tree, which is what makes them passthrough invariants rather than detectors.
- **Observed content between the delimiters is still not folded**, deliberately: a page body and a window's OCR are multi-line by nature and everything inside the wrapper is untrusted by position. Pinned by `observedContentItselfKeepsItsLines`, so nobody closes it later as a hole.
- **`escape`, `escapeURLValue` and `trustedInstruction` are untouched** — `escape` byte-identically, which is why SONNY-222 is pre-existing rather than introduced — and `WebResearchSynthesizerTests`' three existing wrapper tests pass unchanged.
- **The four delimiter constants and their forwarding aliases are untouched**; this branch removes a helper, not a name any caller uses.
- **The vision prompt's shape is unchanged** for every app whose display name carries no separator, which is every real one — and where it does change, `VisionSessionPromptBuilder.systemRules` still carries the unfolded name in the same prompt.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The duplicate did not predate the rule; the rule and the duplicate shipped the same day, from the same ticket.** The ticket asked which it was, because the answer changes whether this is consolidation or regression, and it is neither in the plain sense. `WebResearchPromptBuilder.escapeAttribute` was written first, at `57d7076` (2026-07-08), when it was the only copy and there was no rule. SONNY-92 then promoted the four delimiter constants out of that type into `UntrustedContentBoundary` (`618350d`, 2026-08-14), wrote a **second** `escapeAttribute` there rather than forwarding the first, and wrote the rule forbidding exactly that (`976e341`, the same day, same ticket). So the duplication was created by the change that outlawed it, and survived a week and one review of the neighbouring boundary. A rule written in the same commit as its counter-example is a rule nobody has yet had to obey.

**The two copies were never identical, and the ticket's evidence said they were.** Both folded `"\n"` and `" "`, but `UntrustedContentBoundary`'s ran `escape(value)` first and `WebResearchPromptBuilder`'s did not. Consolidation was therefore a *widening* of the web path in its own right, not a lift-and-shift — which is why `aDelimiterInTheWebResearchIdIsNeutralisedAndNotJustFolded` exists and why it fails against the unfixed tree.

**Fold-then-escape and escape-then-fold are both wrong, and the fix is both.** The delimiters are `[A-Z_]` only. Escape-then-fold — what shipped — lets the fold *rebuild* one: `UNTRUSTED_OBSERVED CONTENT_END` carries nothing for `escape` to find, and the space fold completes it. Fold-then-escape is no better, because `escape`'s own replacement is `[escaped delimiter: …]`, which contains spaces and so breaks the one-token property the whole function exists for. Folding on both sides is the small correct answer: the first pass makes every rebuild visible to `escape`, the second removes only the whitespace `escape` itself introduced, and it cannot rebuild anything across those brackets because `[`, `]` and `:` are not delimiter characters.

**Widening the fold set widens the rebuild surface, which is the clearest argument for that ordering there is.** `UNTRUSTED_OBSERVED<U+001C>CONTENT_END` now folds into a real delimiter exactly the way `UNTRUSTED_OBSERVED CONTENT_END` did before this ticket — a hardening that manufactures the very forgery it exists to prevent, if the fold runs after `escape`. It does not, so it is contained, and `aDelimiterForgedFromAnInvisibleSeparatorIsNeutralisedAndNotRebuilt` is the pin. **Every character ever added to that set has to be read this way**: a wider fold is only safe while the first fold precedes `escape`.

**"Is the space replacement also under-wide?" — yes, and the honest set is one set, not two.** The ticket asked it as a separate question. It is the same question: the opening line is `DELIMITER id=<attr> source=<attr>`, so the attribute has to stay one *token* as well as one line, and a tab or a non-breaking space ends a token exactly as visibly as a space. `CharacterSet.whitespacesAndNewlines` is both answers at once — Zs, tab, and every line separator — so the fix is one fold rather than a line-break fold beside a widened space fold. Foundation also puts U+200B in `.whitespaces`, which folds for free; not asserted, because a zero-width character splits no token a reader can see.

**Folding `.controlCharacters` on top is defence in depth, and calling it that is the point** (PR #97, F2). `.whitespacesAndNewlines` excludes the C0 information separators U+001C–U+001F while including VT and FF, which sit immediately beside them and are no more line-like; the names — file, group, record, unit separator — are the reason to look twice. The review drove all four through both real paths and found them **inert**: they open no line and defeat no matching. Nothing here closes a live hole. They are folded anyway, because an `id=` or a `source=` has no legitimate use for a control character, and "inert today" is a claim about what the *consumer* renders rather than a property of this boundary. Taking the whole category rather than the four also removes the C1 range, DEL, the soft hyphen, ZWNJ/ZWJ, the BOM and the BIDI controls from attributes — the last of which the review deliberately declined to call a boundary escape, and which are simply no longer this line's problem. **The cost is real and is stated at the code**: an app whose display name carries a ZWJ emoji sequence reaches `source=` with its joiners folded, `Family 👨‍👩‍👧 Sharing` → `Family_👨_👩_👧_Sharing`, while the same prompt still carries the unfolded name in `VisionSessionPromptBuilder.systemRules`.

**`_` stays, runs are not collapsed, and its one-for-one-ness is not what makes any of this safe** (PR #97, F4). The doc comment used to credit it, and that is a failure mode worth naming. One character for one is true, and it is only a *length* argument: it says a folded payload cannot grow the prompt, which is exactly why runs are not collapsed here — deliberately unlike `PriorTaskContext.foldingLineBreaks`, whose two-character `\n` marker really could expand a capped string and whose marker belongs in a field *value* where a reader gains from knowing a break was there. It says nothing about safety. The property that carries the safety is fold → `escape` → fold, and a maintainer trusting the stated rationale could reasonably collapse the two folds into one and silently reopen the hole. The comment now says which property is load-bearing, says that collapsing the folds reopens it, and names the two tests that go red if anyone does. **A comment that credits a real but irrelevant property is more dangerous than one that says nothing**, because it reads as having been thought about.

**Consolidation needed no visibility change, contrary to the ticket's expectation.** Both types live in `MacAgentCore` and `UntrustedContentBoundary.escapeAttribute` is already `internal`, so the private copy could simply be deleted. No forwarding alias was left for it, unlike the four constants, because nothing outside its own file could ever name it.

**Two of the fifteen tests are source scans, and they are here because behaviour cannot express "there is no second copy."** One asserts `func escapeAttribute(` appears in exactly one file; the other asserts no file contains `replacingOccurrences(of: "\n", with: "_")`, which is what a re-narrowed twin under a different name would look like. Both fail against `7770a48`, both naming the two offending files. **They walk both Swift targets and enumerate recursively, which the first version did not** (PR #97, F3): the rule in `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` carries no directory qualifier, so a copy in `Sources/MacAgent` — which imports `MacAgentCore` and hosts the vision-session view model — sat outside the scan and inside the rule. Widened rather than narrowing the prose to match, because the scan is the cheaper half to change and the stronger guarantee to keep. Each target answers for its own file count, so a target that enumerates to nothing cannot make both scans vacuously green; the recursion is `TestSourceTree`'s own lesson applied on the production side, since `Sources/MacAgent` already has subdirectories while `contentsOfDirectory` lists one level. `server/` stays out for a stated reason rather than by omission: it is TypeScript, it cannot declare a Swift function, and it names none of the four delimiters.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **A CRITICAL found beneath this branch, deferred to SONNY-222 by explicit founder decision, 2026-08-22 — which is exactly what the fix-in-branch rule's deferral clause requires.** `escape` neutralises delimiters with `String.replacingOccurrences(of:with:)`, which Swift matches by extended grapheme cluster, so appending a combining mark (U+0301) to the delimiter's final letter changes that letter's `Character` identity, the search misses it, and a near-verbatim closing delimiter reaches the prompt unescaped. Reproduced twice independently by PR #97's review. **Pre-existing, not introduced here**: `git diff 7770a48..43cf81a -- Sources/MacAgentCore/UntrustedContentBoundary.swift` shows only `escapeAttribute` and the new `foldingSeparators` changed, and `escape` is byte-identical to `main`. Reasons for the deferral, recorded so it is not read as convenience — it needs a different technique from this branch's (scalar or byte matching *inside* `escape`, not a wider fold outside it); its tests need an idiom these fifteen do not use, because `hasPrefix`, `==` and `range(of:)` share the same grapheme-cluster blind spot, so a regression test written in this file's style would not detect it; and folding it in here would repeat exactly the scope breach SONNY-198 was right to refuse. **Nothing in the polish round touches it** — combining marks and variation selectors are in neither `.whitespacesAndNewlines` nor `.controlCharacters` — and the comment on `separators` says so in as many words, so the wider fold cannot be misread as having addressed it.
- **PR #97's review has one gap it declined to paper over, and SONNY-222 carries it:** the lens assigned the untouched-paths sweep returned nothing usable, so whether `PriorTaskContext.foldingLineBreaks` — or any other delimited boundary in this repository — shares `escape`'s grapheme-cluster weakness is **not established**. An open question, not a clean bill of health.
- **The `source_url=` and `retrieved_at=` attributes on the web wrapper's opening line do not go through `escapeAttribute`, and do not need to.** Enumerated rather than assumed: `source_url` is `URL.absoluteString`, and `URL` percent-encodes every character in `.whitespacesAndNewlines` — measured for CR, LF, U+2028, NEL, space, NBSP and tab, all of which come back as `%0D`, `%0A`, `%E2%80%A8`, `%C2%85`, `%20`, `%C2%A0`, `%09` — so no separator can reach that line through it; `retrieved_at` is an `ISO8601DateFormatter` string. `escapeObservedURL` is left alone.
- Nothing else deferred, and no discovery ticket filed by this branch: the reconstruction hole and the horizontal-separator half were both inside this ticket's own stated outcome, not adjacent to it.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none of this branch's own. The two the ticket left open — the space set, and consolidate-first versus widen-first — are answered above, both the way the ticket leaned; F2's fold-or-document choice is answered at the code with its cost stated. The one open question in the area belongs to SONNY-222 and is recorded above rather than here, because it is a question about `main` rather than about this branch.

Next branch: not a roadmap row. **SONNY-222** is the loudest thing open in this area, and it is open against `main` rather than against this branch.

- **A routine whose destination nothing else names still writes that exact filename** — the routine as a plan's only step, and the reversed collision plan with the two drafts titled differently, both asserted on the literal filenames rather than on a count.
- **The forward ordering is unchanged**, and `aNestedRoutinesGeneratedDraftDoesNotOverwriteTheOuterPlansOwn` is untouched and passes.
- **`prepare` still resolves against an empty seed**, so within-plan disambiguation is what it was and `aChainWritesOnlyFilesThePreparedPlanAlreadyNamed` passes untouched.
- **PR #96's fix round changed no functional code at all.** Its four commits are one permanent regression test, two corrected comments, one corrected inline command and this entry; the union line and both of its halves are byte-identical to what the review verified.
- **The bump is still blind to the filesystem.** Nothing here consults disk during resolution, which is what leaves the adapters' tier-3 "output already exists" escalation something to say.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
**The two plans get their names at different times, and only one of them can still move — so a fix seeded from execution history can only ever fix one ordering.** This is the durable shape, and it is worth stating separately from either ticket. The outer plan's generated destinations are resolved once, at `prepare`, before anything runs; a step that then arrives at `execute` carrying an `outputPath` is deliberately never regenerated or bumped, because writing somewhere other than where the approved plan said would be a worse failure than a collision. The nested plan's destinations are resolved at execute time. SONNY-190 seeded the nested resolve from `RunClaims` — what earlier units have already *written* — which is exactly right for `[create_local_draft, run_routine]` and structurally incapable of covering `[run_routine, create_local_draft]`, where the routine resolves before anything has executed and the claims are correctly empty. **A seed built from history cannot see the future half of a plan.** The missing half is not history at all: it is the prepared plan's own intent, which exists before the run starts and never moves.

**So the fix is a second value travelling beside the claims, and the reason it is not one merged set is the same reason SONNY-190 gave for not merging them.** `PlannedDestinations` is pre-execution intent; `RunClaims` is post-execution fact. Merging them would make "which is filled in when" a property of one type instead of a parameter, and the parameter is what makes the ordering question answerable. It would also break the invariant `RunClaims` exists to hold: adapters read `hasWritten` to decide real things, and a set containing intentions answers *yes, this run wrote that* for a file nothing has written — whose first consequence is a document the user asked for being skipped because of a PDF that does not exist. The new value is deliberately **not** on `CapabilityExecutionContext` for the same reason, one layer up: a set of intentions an adapter can reach is a set of intentions an adapter can mistake for a claim.

**Which plan moves is a decision, not a coin flip.** The outer plan named its destination at `prepare` and the user approved a panel saying so, so the prepared plan's names are what `aChainWritesOnlyFilesThePreparedPlanAlreadyNamed` holds this executor to. The nested plan resolves later. The later one moves — which is also what the run's own report now shows: in `[run_routine, create_local_draft]` the routine's draft lands on `-2` and the outer plan keeps the name it was approved under.

**Fixing execution alone would have left the only warning a user gets pointing at the wrong file, so the same value is threaded through `assessRisk`.** The tier-3 "output already exists" escalation is a `fileExists` check on the *resolved* path, so assessment has to apply the same bump execution does or it asks about a path the run will not touch while staying silent about the one it will overwrite. Measured with the execute-side fix alone: with the bumped name already on disk, both orderings assessed `tier2` with no escalations, and the run then destroyed that file. **That gap arrived with SONNY-190 and is visible on `main` today in the ordering SONNY-190 fixed** — this ticket did not introduce it, but it creates a second ordering that reaches it, which is what makes closing it part of the fix rather than adjacent to it. The two seeds agree by construction because both are computed from the same resolved plan: `AgentRunner` prepares once and hands that plan to assessment and to execution alike.

**A mutation survivor was read as "this code is dead" when it meant "the suite has a hole", and the hole was a data-loss shape** (corrected by PR #96's review, F1). M2 dropped `claimedEarlierInThisRun.destinations` from the union and the whole suite passed, SONNY-190's own test included. This entry first concluded from that — with an enumeration to back it — that the claims half "covers a population that is empty today", and kept it as defence against a hypothetical future capability. **The conclusion was false and the counter-example is ordinary:** a chain of two sibling `run_routine` steps naming two different saved routines, each holding a `create_local_draft` that generates the same default filename. Nothing blocks that plan — `segmentPlans(in:)`' repeat rule cuts the second `run_routine` into its own unit so the plan classifies `.chain`, and `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations` forbids a `run_routine` *inside* a saved routine rather than two at the outer level — and because a `run_routine` step carries no `outputPath`, the plan-intent half is **empty** there. The claims half is the only thing between the second routine's draft and the first routine's file. Measured both ways: shipped code produces two files with both bodies; under the M2 mutant one file survives holding only the second routine's text, `written.count` still reports 2 and `Set(written).count` collapses to 1 — the silent-overwrite signature SONNY-190 and SONNY-220 both exist to close, reached through a third door. `twoSiblingRoutinesThatEachDraftKeepBothDocuments` is now that shape, and the same mutant is killed by it (`scripts/mutate`, 1 mutant, 1 killed, stamped at `24fa0ba`). **A green suite under a mutant is a statement about the suite, not about the code** — and the failure mode of getting that backwards is not a wasted comment, it is a written invitation to delete the one mechanism guarding a shape nobody tested.

**The enumeration inside that argument was also transposed, in the passage carrying it** (PR #96 review, F2). The split is **three matching, five not**, not five and three — and the member list was right the whole time, which is what makes the error easy to miss and worth recording. Of the eight adapters producing `ActionPreview.writes` (`git grep -l 'writes:' Sources/MacAgentCore | grep CapabilityAdapter` at `24fa0ba`, which prints 8), the **three** that write exactly the `outputPath` their own `resolveDefaultOutputs` pinned are `CreateLocalDraftCapabilityAdapter`, `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter` and `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter`; the **five** that write where no step's `outputPath` names are `DocxConversionCapabilityAdapter` (per-document PDFs inside the output *folder* its step names) and the four store writers, `CreateWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter`, `EditWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter`, `SaveRoutineCapabilityAdapter` and `SnippetSaveCapabilityAdapter`. Their no-collision conclusion still holds — a generated default is `.md`, `.zip` or a Shortcut output and can equal neither a `.pdf` nor a store file — which is why the claims half's reachable contribution turned out to be the nested-routine one above rather than a docx one. CLAUDE.md names this exact failure three times over (SONNY-102, SONNY-145, SONNY-167) and it reappeared inside the paragraph justifying a HIGH data-loss decision, which is the strongest argument yet for the rule it broke: **write the command beside the number.**

**A `/*` inside a `//` comment silently deleted the rest of a file from every source scan that reads it, and only a test caught it** (PR #96 fix round). Satisfying CLAUDE.md's write-the-command-beside-the-number rule meant putting `'Sources/MacAgentCore/*CapabilityAdapter.swift'` into a line comment. `MacAgentSource.read` strips block comments *before* filtering line comments — deliberately, so a `//` line inside a block comment is gone either way — so a `//` line is not protected from the block-comment scanner. Its depth counter opened at that glob's slash-star and never closed, and everything after it in `AgentActionExecutor.swift` vanished from the text the scan reads. Two `RunSummaryProvenanceTests` scans failed deterministically, three runs out of three, reporting **zero** occurrences of a line plainly present in the file. **The scan was doing exactly its job**: the same deletion would have hidden a real rewiring, which is what that suite exists to catch. The rule to carry: *a line comment in a file any scan reads may not contain a `/*` anywhere* — the same shape as `Packaging/MacAgent.entitlements`' ban on a literal double hyphen, and the same cause, a downstream parser enforcing something the language does not. The command was rewritten as a pipe with no slash-star; it prints the same 8, and no number or member changed.

**Two of the type's own guarantees were invisible from every end-to-end test, and needed pinning directly.** The fold and the blank-destination drop cannot be reached through the executor: a generated draft's stem is a lowercased slug, so no real collision can differ only in case, and no adapter resolves a step to a whitespace destination. A mutant deleting either passed the whole suite as it stood before `PlannedDestinationsTests` existed — 1621 tests in 122 suites at `472b32f`, the fix commit. **A construction-time invariant that no reachable input exercises still has to be tested, or it is documentation.**

Known limitations / deferred scope: (deferrals need the user's explicit decision and a named landing-spot ticket)
- **The preview half is unchanged and still belongs to SONNY-218.** `preview` does not resolve — each adapter computes its own default from `context.now()` — so the approval line for a nested routine still names the unbumped path, now in the second ordering as well as the first. Nothing here could have changed that without making `preview` resolve, which is SONNY-218's stated decision to make. The new value is deliberately not threaded into `preview` for the same reason: there is no consumer on that path, and a parameter nothing reads is a false claim that the path is covered.
- **Assessment can still bump less far than execution for a capability whose writes are not its steps' `outputPath`s.** Execution seeds from the claims as well as the names; assessment has nothing to seed from because nothing has run. The residual stands, but **its original justification did not and has been replaced** (PR #96 review): it read "same population as M2 above", and M2's population is not empty. The mechanism check is what carries it instead, and that was verified directly — the five non-matching writers produce docx PDFs and store JSON files, neither of which any generated default can equal, and docx's own skip/rename decision goes through `RunClaims` rather than this seed. Recorded rather than fixed; it is the preview/assessment agreement question, not the data-loss one.
Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):
**Fixing the instance that was reported is not fixing the claim, and three of the four records tickets under-counted their own population.** SONNY-183 named six sites and asked its implementer to sweep by claim rather than by file; doing that found a seventh, `CommandCenterRunningIndicator`'s doc comment — and that one was *load-bearing for a second stale record*, because `docs/sonny-ui-backend-roadmap.md` cited it as the evidence that the gap was still open. SONNY-189 named six and the same method found eleven, two of them in `README.md` and a test suite doc. SONNY-182 named three and the sweep found twelve more, filed as SONNY-205 rather than absorbed, with an inline pointer in both fixed bullets so a reader is told immediately that the bullet is not the whole population. **The generalisable part: a claim has a population, and the ticket that reports one instance is reporting a sample.**

**A stale count can be stale in both directions at once.** SONNY-183 recorded "nine local stores" as the correction to "eight", verified at `f8d6a7a`. Row J landed on 2026-08-21 and there are eleven. Both numbers in one ticket were wrong by the time it was implemented, which is why `RoutineActivationTests`' comment now names the shared pattern instead of a count that has moved twice, and why `docs/sonny-row-c-plan.md`'s subtraction was re-run rather than re-stated.

**The residual SONNY-73 could not reach needed a second field, not a cleverer rule** (SONNY-185). After the first resolve pass, a step that declared the Finder selection and arrived with its own folder is byte-for-byte identical to a genuine declaring step the pin filled in — same `contextSource`, same `inputPath` — so no rule reading those two fields can separate them, and `pinningSelectedDirectoryInput` runs *twice* over one run. The fact only that function knows is whether Finder was read on the pass that filled a step in, so it is written down: `AgentStep.resolvedFromFinderSelection`, resolver-only and decode-excluded on the same terms as `resolvedAppName`. The founder chose the classifier's key over a stricter alternative: **`declared && (pinned || nothing has resolved a path yet)`** rather than `declared && pinned`. The stricter one was exact and was safe today — `classification` is reached from `WorkspaceScopeEvaluator.evaluate` alone, whose only caller is `AgentActionExecutor.scopeFindings`, whose only caller is `assessRisk`, whose first statement resolves — but it would have made this the one place the classifier can go *quiet* about a resource rather than loud, on the strength of an enumeration that can go stale.

**Its commit message under-counted what moved, and the correction lives here because a commit message cannot be edited** (PR #94 review, F7). `8b9d03c` says "three classifier fixtures change and one expectation flips". Four tests changed and **two of them changed an expectation**: `aMixedSelectionDrivenPlanNamesFinderOnceOnTheStepThatDeclaresIt`, which now runs both arms of the plan its own doc comment described as still producing a false Finder finding, *and* `everyAgentOperationIsClassifiedAndTheTableCoversAllThirtyTwoCases`, whose 32-case table drops `.app("Finder")` from all four operations routing through `finderSelectionApp` — its probe carries an `inputPath` and no pin, which is the unpinned arm, the same one the `.visionSession` row beside it already took. The other two genuinely are not expectation changes: one fixture now says in the field what its comment already said in prose, and the resolver-only strip test registers the new field. SONNY-185's closing comment names all four correctly; only the commit title's arithmetic was short.

**A reachability estimate written from the mechanism was wrong by an order of magnitude, in the dangerous direction** (SONNY-190). The ticket priced the nested-routine collision as needing two generated defaults in the same second and said explicitly not to trust that reasoning without a probe. The probe: `Timestamp.fileSafe` is whole-second and two file writes inside one run are milliseconds apart, so on the real clock an outer draft followed by a routine containing one produced **one** file, holding the routine's text, three runs out of three. The user's document was destroyed every time, and the run's own `previews.writes` named the same path twice, which reads as two files. **Measure before pricing; a "narrow window" argued from a timestamp's format is not a measurement.**

**The same discipline then caught this branch over-claiming its own fix, one round later.** PR #94's fix round asked for a correction saying the reverse ordering "was equally broken and equally fixed". The first half is right and the second is not, and one probe settled it: `[create_local_draft, run_routine]` produces two files, and **the same two steps in the other order still produce one**. The asymmetry is a property of *when each plan gets its names*, not of this fix, and that is the part worth carrying. The outer plan's generated paths are resolved once at `prepare`, before anything runs — claims are correctly empty then — and a step that arrives carrying an `outputPath` is never regenerated or bumped afterwards. The nested plan's paths are resolved at execute time, which is the only side SONNY-190's seed can still move. So a nested path can be bumped away from an outer one and an outer path can never be bumped away from a nested one. **SONNY-190 halved a pre-existing bug rather than introducing one** — both orderings destroyed a file before it — and the surviving half is filed as **SONNY-220**, HIGH. Not fixed in that round, which was adjudicated records-and-process with the deep fixes explicitly out of bounds; and worth flagging for whoever takes it that the obvious fix, pre-seeding `RunClaims` with the plan's already-named destinations, would break the post-execution-fact invariant this same entry defends two sentences up.

**A test can name a property and measure something else, and only the killer names show it** (SONNY-198). The battery's LF-only mutant was killed by `aRunOfLineBreaksFoldsToASingleMarker` and *not* by `everyUnicodeLineSeparatorIsFoldedAndNotOnlyLineFeed`, the test written for it — because that test split the emitted block on `"\n"` to count lines, so a CR- or NEL-forged line was not a line as far as its own assertions were concerned. It passed for a reason other than the one its name asserts, against both trees. This is the same hazard SONNY-199 documents from the other side, met in one branch: **read the killer names, not the count.**

**A flake and a kill are the same observation** (SONNY-199). Two mic-hover tests armed the surviving hint's countdown at five seconds and then bet that everything after it would finish inside those five seconds; on a `@MainActor` suite that Swift Testing interleaves with every other `@MainActor` suite, that bet loses under a battery's load. The fix is two constants where there was one — a bounded deadline for a countdown a test cancels and awaits, an unreachable one for a hint an assertion expects to survive — and the hazard is now in `scripts/mutate --help`, because a battery decides a mutant was killed by whether the suite failed and reads a flake as a guard that does not exist.

**An optimization that is unobservable by construction cannot have a non-vacuous test, and saying so is the honest answer** (SONNY-202). Deleting the per-iteration grants cache falls back to a fresh read and behaves identically, so the mutant for it **survives, and is recorded as a survivor rather than papered over**. What can break is the dangerous direction — a cache outliving an iteration — and that is pinned by two existing tests, which the corresponding mutant is killed by.
