Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A test target may depend on another test target, and SONNY-123's contrary claim was wrong.** PR #72's reviewer reported this and the coordinator could not reproduce it, so the ticket required it be rebuilt rather than believed. It was: a `swift-tools-version: 6.0`, `.macOS(.v14)` package whose `.testTarget` names another `.testTarget` in its `dependencies` compiles, resolves the `import`, links, and passes — 3 tests, exit 0, no SwiftPM diagnostic about the edge. The other half of SONNY-123's reason is still true and is why *some* structural change was needed: SwiftPM gives a source file to exactly one target.

**The shared support target is a `.testTarget`, not a plain `.target`, and that is not a style choice.** The ticket's option 2 proposed a plain target under `Sources/`. Probed, it fails: a plain target is in the ordinary build graph, plain `swift build` passes no `-Xswiftc -F .../CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/Frameworks`, and `UnprivilegedProcess.swift` declares a `Testing` `ConditionTrait` so it cannot avoid `import Testing` — the build dies with `no such module 'Testing'` at `Emitting module TestSupport`. Adopting it would have meant adding the framework search path to `swift build` itself and to every caller of it, including `scripts/warnings`, `scripts/mutate` and `package-app.sh`. A `.testTarget` gets `Testing` and `-enable-testing` for free and stays out of `swift build` entirely, which a clean-scratch-path build confirms. `Package.swift` carries this reasoning at the declaration, because the next person to tidy "a test target with no tests" needs it there.

**A hand-written list of targets is a silent-coverage-hole generator, and this one was unheld.** `TestSourceTree.targets` drives every source scan in the repository. Adding `MacAgentTestSupport` to `Package.swift` without adding it to that list would have moved the deterministic stub — the file whose entire job is being the alternative to a live permission checker — outside `LivePermissionCheckerScanTests`' reach, and **nothing would have failed**: the file-count floor stays satisfied, and the per-target sentinel loop simply iterates one target fewer. That is measured, not supposed — it was mutant M2, and it survived the whole suite until `everyTestTargetInTheManifestIsScanned` was written. The list is now required to equal the test targets `Package.swift` declares, parsed out of the manifest rather than restated in a second hand-written list that would fail the same way.

**Three of the five drift-pin tests were obsolete and two were not, and the ticket's acceptance criterion did not distinguish them.** SONNY-172 said to remove the drift pin as obsolete. `TwinnedTestSupportTests` held five tests: `theTwinnedPermissionStubsAreTheSameCode`, `theTwinnedUnprivilegedTraitsAreTheSameCode` and `neitherTwinIsExtendedOutsideItsClassBody` — the last existing only to cover the first's blind spot — genuinely compare a thing to itself once there is one copy. The other two were never about twinning: `theUnprivilegedGatePredicateIsNotInverted` is, by its own doc, the only thing that kills the inverted-`geteuid()` mutant (which once dropped three tests silently while the suite stayed green, 1377 → 1374), and `everyDirectoryLockingTestCarriesTheGateAndNoOtherTestDoes` matches `posixPermissions: 0o500` against the gate across the whole tree. Deleting the file wholesale would have dropped both. The founder confirmed keeping them; the file is renamed `UnprivilegedGateTests` so its name stops claiming to be about twins. **Five older changelog lines still refer to `TwinnedTestSupportTests` by name — those records are true as of their own dates and are not rewritten. `UnprivilegedGateTests.swift`'s header names the old file in so many words, so a grep for it out of one of those records lands on the file that replaced it; PR #92's focused review caught that the header did not, which is why it now does.**

**"Byte-for-byte siblings" was not accurate, and it changed what consolidation meant.** SONNY-172's description said so. The two `UnprivilegedProcess.swift` copies differed on one line each naming the other as its twin; the two `DeterministicPermissions.swift` copies differed substantially — the core one imported `AVFoundation`, used `@testable import MacAgentCore`, and carried `DeterministicMicrophonePermission` and the `deterministic(...)` factory, neither of which the app copy had at all. Only the `DeterministicScreenPermissions` class bodies were identical, which is exactly the surface the drift pin compared — so the pin was accurate about what it checked and the description over-generalised from it. Consolidation was therefore "keep the superset, carry over the one doc line the other had," not a merge.

**`@testable` turned out to be unnecessary for the shared stub.** Everything it touches — `ScreenCapturePermissionChecking`, `MicrophonePermissionChecking`, `PermissionReadinessService` and its initializer — is already `public` in `MacAgentCore`, so the moved file uses a plain `import MacAgentCore`. A support `.testTarget` is still built with `-enable-testing`, so a future helper there can use `@testable` if it genuinely needs internals.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **`Tests/MacAgentTests/MacAgentSourceScan.swift` still holds a core-target concern, and this branch did not move it.** Its own doc (lines 95–101) records that the test for a `MacAgentCore` property — exactly one `AgentRunResult` construction site declaring `.modelAuthored`, row E / SONNY-147 — lives in the app test target only because "the core test target has no source scanner" and a second scanner would have duplicated the comment-stripping discipline. `MacAgentTestSupport` now makes one shared scanner possible, so that distortion is fixable. Out of scope here: SONNY-172 named the two permission helpers, and moving a scanner touches two more suites, one of which carries comment-stripping logic that two separate mutants have already walked through. Filed as **SONNY-206**, Backlog and untriaged, rather than absorbed.
- `TestSourceTree.swift` stays in `MacAgentCoreTests` because both suites using it live there. It is a candidate resident of the support target if a third user ever appears; moving it today would be churn.

Net **+7 tests** (`git diff 66ac0f7..HEAD -- Tests/ | grep -c '^+    @Test'` = 7 at `ffe8f92`). **`scripts/warnings`: 0 warnings at `ffe8f92`**, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled. Nothing was removed. **One existing assertion inverted**, explained in place: `RunTaskAgainTests.runningAgainCarriesTheRecordsWorkspaceWhenItStillExists` asserted an untagged row deliberately, with a comment naming SONNY-195 as the reason, and now asserts `"Research"`.

**Mutation battery at `91e5a28`: 3 mutants, 3 killed, none survived** (`scripts/mutate`, which stamps its own SHA). M1 restores the exact pre-fix tagging — `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` deriving its own name again instead of reading the scope — and is killed by five tests: all four new tagging tests plus the inverted `runningAgainCarriesTheRecordsWorkspaceWhenItStillExists`. M2 drops the tag entirely and is killed by four, the two pre-existing tagging tests among them, which is the guard against a fix that answers `nil` to everything. M3 restores the pre-fix row-write channel and is killed by `aRowWriteFailureLeavesTheTaskLookingSuccessfulAndSaysWhatActuallyFailed` alone — correctly, since the scheduled path was not mutated.

What changed for the user: a task's history row now names the workspace the run **actually ran in**. A task started from a workspace card's "New task here" is filed under that workspace even when the words typed never mention it, and a task whose plan names a workspace that has been deleted — or whose store will not decrypt, or whose name is blank — is filed under nothing rather than under a boundary that never applied, so the workspace card's task count is a number a boundary backs. Separately, a task that ran and produced a result but could not write its history row now says so on the storage notice rather than replacing that result with an error, and a storage notice arriving as a system notification no longer carries a Retry button that would re-run whatever the user last typed.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Founder decision, 2026-08-21 (Sauransh + Bhavya): a history record shows the workspace the run actually ran in, not the one the user intended.** This settles the "record intent vs record what happened" question SONNY-191 raised and left open, and that question governed SONNY-195's answer too. The third option SONNY-191 priced — record the name *plus* a did-not-bind flag, so the row can say so and the count can decide for itself — was not taken: it costs a field on `CompletedTaskRecord` for a distinction nothing in the product currently renders.

**The two tickets were one root cause pointed in opposite directions, and fixing either alone would have been worse than fixing neither carefully.** Both `recordPriorTaskContext` overloads called `WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName` a *second* time, after the run terminated, from a signature that can see neither `explicitWorkspaceBinding` nor whether the store answered. SONNY-195 was the under-tag: an explicit binding the tagger cannot see. SONNY-191 was the over-tag: `directWorkspaceName` reads `AgentStep.workspaceName` straight off the plan with no store access, so a plan-carried name survives the scope failing to bind for any reason. One change closes both, because reading the resolved scope is right in both directions at once — `.unscoped` is exactly the set of runs no boundary applied to, whatever the cause.

**The parameter was removed rather than fixed at both call sites, and the precedent is three lines away.** `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` already derives `trigger` from `activeTaskOrigin` rather than taking it, with a comment saying why: "a second parameter saying the same thing is a second thing to forget to pass." The workspace tag was that second parameter, and it was forgotten in two directions by two different tickets — which is as good a demonstration of the comment as the codebase is likely to produce. `WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName` now has exactly one caller (`git grep -c "WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName(" -- Sources/` returns `AgentViewModel.swift:1` at `ffe8f92`), so the row agrees with the boundary by construction instead of by two derivations happening to match.

**`activeTaskScope`, not `lastAssessedScope`, and the ticket's own suggested fix named the wrong one.** SONNY-191 and the coordinator cross-link both proposed reading `lastAssessedScope`, "the post-terminal record, deliberately never cleared". Deliberately never cleared is exactly what makes it wrong here: a run that throws inside `AgentRunner.prepare` never reaches the line that assigns it, so it still holds the **previous** task's workspace — and that is a live path, the `preparedRun == nil` arm of `performStart`'s catch, which writes a history row. `activeTaskScope` is `.unscoped` again at the top of every `performStart`, is held across an approval or clarification pause (both of which write rows on cancellation), and is cleared in a `defer` that runs after every one of the sixteen `recordPriorTaskContext` call sites. All sixteen were enumerated before the change rather than sampled.

**PR #83's blank-name case closed for free, and it is the one nobody would have written a test for.** F1 added a guard so a blank or whitespace-only workspace name binds nothing without touching the store; the history tag was not covered by it, so a step carrying `workspaceName: ""` produced a guaranteed-unscoped run and a row tagged with an empty string. Reading the scope answers it with the rest. It is reachable with no tampering: the planner schema requires a `workspaceName` slot on every step, `""` is a valid value, `validateStepSafety` checks operations rather than fields so a routine can be *saved* carrying one, and `directWorkspaceName` reads the field off any operation rather than only the workspace ones.

**A unit test of the tagger could never have caught any of this, which is why all five tests drive a real dispatch.** `WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName` behaves identically before and after — it was never the thing that was wrong. What was wrong is *which* answer the row recorded, and that is only observable by dispatching, letting the run terminate, and reading the row back off the file. The four new tagging tests are split across two suites for a fixture reason worth stating: `ProductShellTests` has a real task-history store and holds the bound, deleted and blank cases beside the two tagging tests that already existed there; the unreadable-store case needs a workspace store written under one key and read under another, which is `AgentViewModelLocalStorageTests`' existing shape. Two of them also assert `WorkspaceTaskCount.count(forWorkspaceNamed:in:)`, the workspace card's own figure, because that count is the surface SONNY-191 named and asserting the field alone would leave it unmeasured.

**Scheduled runs were checked and are correct without changing, which is the obvious next question.** `recordScheduledTaskHistory` builds its own `CompletedTaskRecord` and never sets `workspaceName` at all, so every scheduled row is untagged — and under the new rule that is right rather than an omission: `performScheduledRun` executes with `scope: .unscoped` deliberately (a scheduled run has no workspace binding), so the run really did run in no workspace. Recorded so a reader does not file it as SONNY-195's unattended twin.

**SONNY-201: a lost history row is a storage problem, not a task failure — matching the twin rather than inventing a third treatment.** The ticket declined to assume "make it match" and asked the question properly, because a lost row is a heavier loss than a lost plan: the task is absent from the Tasks list, from search, from Insights, and from anything a follow-up could be aimed at, where a lost plan leaves the task fully visible. The founder's answer is still "storage": the run happened, and `errorMessage` means the thing you asked for did not happen. The wording carries the weight instead of the channel doing it. Had the answer gone the other way, both paths would have moved, not one.

**Two documentation lines would have sent the next session straight back to the bug.** `CLAUDE.md`'s write-failure gotcha and `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md`'s local-stores section both said a write failure needs "its own accurate `errorMessage`" — unconditionally, with `applyClipboardHistoryNoticeChoice` cited as the pattern. That was written before `recordLocalStorageWriteFailure` existed and it is what the foreground path kept doing. Both now state what actually separates the two cases: a write the user pressed a control for (`applyClipboardHistoryNoticeChoice`, `deleteLocalData`) really is `errorMessage`, because the thing they asked for did not happen; a write a *task* does as bookkeeping is the notice channel. The scheduled path has followed that rule all along, and the foreground path arrived at it twice by defect — its plan write (PR #89, F4) and now its row write.

**The scheduled row-write test is new too, and that is the point of adding it.** That path was already correct and nothing exercised it, so the property that made it the reference for this fix was itself only a reading of the source. The two new tests are the mirror image of the pair PR #89 added for the plan write — the same directory locked, one level up — and take `TwinnedTestSupportTests`' gated-directory-locking population pin from six to eight.

**SONNY-187 is half closed, deliberately, and the ticket says which half.** The Retry defect is fixed: `localStorageNotice` posted through `postErrorNotification`, which stamps `SONNY_ERROR`, which registers a Retry wired to `retryLastCommand()` — so "your snippets file could not be decrypted" offered to re-dispatch whatever the user last typed, and it is reachable from a bookkeeping write failing during a run that otherwise succeeded, making it an offer to re-run a task that had just worked. Worse on this channel than on the scheduled one SONNY-113 fixed, on the channel's own stated terms: `localStorageNotice` exists precisely so a storage problem is not confused with a task outcome, so posting it in the failure category undid that at the last hop. The fix is SONNY-113's shape exactly — a fourth actionless category and a fourth default-action destination. **The second half stays open**: `localStorageNotice` and `plannerFallbackNotice` both render inside the `else` branch of `if isCompact`, so a notice arriving at an already-collapsed widget sits behind the capsule. Widening the collapse guard for two more channels is a behaviour change nobody asked for, and the two are not symmetrical — a planner fallback is informational and the task ran, a storage problem is ongoing. `FloatingWidgetView.isCollapsible`'s comment already pointed at SONNY-187 and now records which half is done.

**The storage notification opens Command Center, and it gets its own closure rather than sharing the scheduled one.** Command Center because that is where the notice renders as a row on four pages and where Settings' local-data controls are, while the widget shows the same notice with nothing to offer but Dismiss. Its own closure because the two are separate decisions about separate notices that happen to agree today; sharing one would make a later divergence a refactor rather than an edit.

**Why the SONNY-187 test reads the source instead of running it**, which is the same reason SONNY-113's does: `SonnyNotificationService.init?` returns nil without bundle identity, and `UNUserNotificationCenter.current()` aborts the process rather than throwing when there is none — so the subscription being pinned does not exist in a test run at all. The scan asserts the category is registered with an empty action array *and* names the two neighbours that do carry actions, so it fails if the empty array is ever filled in by copying one of them.

Manual-test items the user still owes: with a workspace saved, use its card's "New task here", type a command that does not mention the workspace, and confirm the finished task appears under that workspace in the Tasks list and in the card's count; confirm a task whose workspace was deleted mid-flight shows no workspace chip; and, in the packaged `.app`, confirm a storage-notice banner arriving while Sonny is not the front app carries no Retry button and opens Command Center when clicked.

The survivor is M12 — "declining the per-app question lets the session run anyway" — and it is an **equivalent mutant** rather than a coverage hole: the only Deny in the product routes through `cancelCurrentRun`, which resumes the continuation with `nil` *and* cancels the task, and `requestVisionActionApproval`'s cancellation check throws before that `nil` is ever returned, so the arm is unreachable and removing it changes no reachable behaviour. Behavior added:
- **Which apps Sonny may control without asking now depends on the mode.** Safe starts from nothing, Normal starts from a built-in starter list of 41 apps, Power asks about no app at all. An approval is remembered in one user list, per app, forever.
- **The prompt is an ordinary approval raised at an extraordinary moment**: after the session's first capture has cleared the terminal screen check, so an unlisted terminal is refused before anybody is asked about it, and still on both approval surfaces because it goes through the same call every mid-loop approval does.
- **An eleventh encrypted local store**, `approved-apps.json`, reaching the wipe and classified `.artifact`.
- **A revocation taking effect mid-session.** The standing is re-asked after every capture; a withdrawn grant ends the session rather than re-prompting.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**These two paragraphs were written into this file's v2 entry template rather than into this entry, and are restored here 2026-08-28 by SONNY-276.** They landed in the template block at `58b13a5`, this branch's own cycle-2 records commit, and nothing else in the file ever carried them: at that commit, at `efa2a4d` and at `be66eeb` the phrase occurs exactly once and every time inside the fenced block (`git show <sha>:docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md | grep -n "Rebased onto row E's tenth store"` prints one line number, and it falls between the `## Entry Template` and `## Entries` headings at each). **SONNY-276's contract said to delete them and keep the copies in this entry; there were none to keep**, so deleting alone would have removed the only copy of a reconciliation record the entry does not otherwise carry, and they were moved rather than dropped. They are reproduced verbatim, including what a later branch has since falsified: the wipe test no longer carries a count in its name at all, which is recorded in `feature/memory-output-locations`' entry.

**Rebased onto row E's tenth store, and the reconciliation is the part to check.** This branch was cut from `ef0cf7c` and row E (`feature/task-detail-rehydration`, PR #89) merged while it was in review, adding `task-plan-details.json` as the tenth store. Eleven files conflicted, every one of them a count or a name set, and all were resolved by **combining to eleven — never keep-both**: the wipe's URL list, its filename set, its behavioural fixture and the fixture's three counts, `LocalStore`'s cases and `allCases.count`, the trace/artifact split (six traces, four artifacts, one not-written-by-tasks), `TaskRecordingPolicyTests`' named split, `ProductShellTests`' stored-property enumeration, and the store counts in `CLAUDE.md`, the MacAgentCore rules file and four `README.md` sentences. **Both branches had renamed the same test** — `theWipeReachesExactlyTheNineLocalStores` → `…TheTenLocalStores` on each side — and it is now `…TheElevenLocalStores`. What makes the reconciliation checkable rather than asserted is that those guards are the first things to fail when the arithmetic is wrong, and the whole suite passes.

**"Tenth" is left standing in three dated records, deliberately.** SONNY-140's ticket text, this branch's own commit title, and `docs/sonny-row-j-plan.md` §2.4 all say "the tenth store", which was true when each was written. This repository restamps rather than rewriting commit messages, and `ApprovedAppStore`'s doc comment carries the reconciliation instead: *tenth when this was written, eleventh when it landed*, with a pointer to the assertion rather than a fourth copy of the number.

**The mode has to be an input to the one switch, and the switch has to be ugly.** Row I's changelog warned a future reader against adding a mode axis to `ApprovalContext`. That warning was about *shape*, and this is its case: `safeMode: Bool` is replaced rather than supplemented, because two booleans cannot express three modes and a boolean beside a mode is a derived field that can disagree with its source. The switch scrutinee is the whole tuple `(mode, appControl, effectiveTier)` — 45 written tuples over 5 arms, no `default:`, no wildcard in either authority position. **The verbosity is the mechanism, not an accident of it**, and the second half is the half a reader will be tempted to drop: "no `default:`" alone does *not* make a fourth standing fail to compile, because a wildcard in the standing position swallows it silently. Both were proved rather than argued, in throwaway copies of the tree outside the repository — a fourth `AgentInteractionMode` case and a fourth `AppControlStanding` case each produce `error: switch must be exhaustive` pointing at that switch.

**The founder's correction is one line of the resolver, and it is the line to protect.** It is entirely possible to read the switch's signature and the resolver's signature and still write a resolver that ignores the mode — and built that way the starter list grants standing in Safe too, which silently undoes the one thing switching to Safe is for. The rule: *the starter list contributes standing in Normal and Power, and never in Safe; the user's own approvals contribute in all three.* One test resolves one app three different ways across the three modes, so a mode-blind implementation cannot pass, and a mutant that gives Safe the starter list is killed by it.

**A per-app question is an ordinary approval, and that is what buys the second surface.** The root `CLAUDE.md` claimed the floating widget was the only place a permission state renders. It has been false since branch 10 — `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` reads the same `viewModel.approvalRequest`, renders the same escalation reasons in amber, and wires Deny/Allow to the same entry points, on all four top-level pages (filed as SONNY-112, and corrected there rather than here). The consequence is not a trivium: **reusing the ordinary path put this prompt on both surfaces for free**, where the bespoke widget panel row I used four times would have rendered in the widget only.

**The per-app question is asked after the session's first capture, not at the plan gate — and that resolved a conflict between two founder decisions.** §2.3 says the prompt reuses the ordinary approval path, which is a plan-time path. §4.3 says *"the first capture happens before the control approval"*, so a user is never asked to approve an app whose window is showing a shell. The branch shipped §2.3's reading and PR #88's review caught that it broke §4.3's; the founder chose **capture-first**, 2026-08-21, and the reason is the whole point of the decision: only a capture can reveal a shell in a window whose *app* no name list refuses, so asking first is exactly the accidental-approval trap SONNY-102 names — an unlisted terminal arriving as an ordinary unknown app and somebody allowing one by mistake.

**What §2.3 keeps, and what it costs.** The question is still a `RiskApprovalRequest` from the one requirement function, raised through the same `requestVisionActionApproval` every mid-loop action approval already uses — so it still renders on the floating widget *and* on `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` with neither surface taught anything about it. What it costs is that Safe mode now asks three times before the first click: the session envelope at the plan gate (Safe's standing floor, unchanged), the per-app question after the first capture, and the capture review. Three different questions, in an order the founder chose; recorded here rather than trimmed, because a later session reading only §2.3 will want to fold the first two together and must not.

**The second cost is user-visible and is the one a manual pass meets first** (PR #88 cycle 2, finding 9). Capture-first means Sonny **brings the app to the front and screenshots it before asking whether it may control it** — so somebody who denies has already had the app fronted and captured. That is inherent to the ordering rather than a defect in it: the question §4.3 exists to answer is *what is in that window*, and there is no way to answer it without taking the picture. Two facts bound it, and both are verified rather than asserted. **The capture never leaves the device**: the gate sits above Safe's capture review and above the send, and `thePerAppQuestionArrivesOnlyAfterACaptureThatWasScannedAndNeverSent` asserts the model received no prompt and no payload while the question is open. **The capture is never journalled**: `VisionActionJournalEntry` has no image field at all, and `journal(...)` is called only from `perform`, which the gate precedes — a session refused at the gate writes an envelope (goal, app name, times, reason code) and no screen content whatever. The focus steal itself is not new; `checkIterationStart` has activated the target on iteration one since row I, and what changed is only that a question can now follow it.

**The threading this replaced was removed rather than left dormant.** To word the remembered sentence at plan time, the first implementation forwarded `context.appControl` into `assessRisk` — through `AgentRunner`, `AgentActionExecutor` and a new `CapabilityExecutionContext` field — which meant restating `AgentRunner.approvalRequest`'s "assessRisk takes no context and must never grow one". With the question inside the loop, `VisionSessionContainment.appControlRequirement(context:)` builds the request and the standing reaches no assessment anywhere, so all of it came back out and that comment is a plain invariant again. **A field nothing reads is how the next reader concludes it is load-bearing**, which is why the revert was part of the fix rather than a tidy-up for later.

**Five refusal cases for one gate, because "Sonny stopped because it is no longer allowed to control X" is only true of one of them.** A grant can stop covering a live session five ways and the sentence has to be true of each: the user *withdrew* it; the user *declined* the question; the grant *could not be saved*; the grants file *would not open*; and the gate *could not work out an answer at all*, which is unreachable by construction and fail-closed if it ever is not. **The withdrawal case has four sub-causes of its own**, and that list has been short twice — removed in Settings, erased by a local-data wipe, switched Normal → Safe for an app only the starter list vouched for, and switched *out of Power* for an app nothing else vouched for, since Power's resolver arm consults no list at all and the move to Normal is the one a reader would not expect. **Three of the five shipped carrying a sentence that was not true of them**, which is why there are five cases and not one: the write failure, fixed inside the branch, where a failed write now ends the run with a sentence about the save rather than about permission; the read failure, which PR #88's fix round found reporting a load error as a withdrawal; and the unresolvable arm, which cycle 2 found borrowing *"you did not allow it"* for a path where nobody was asked. The read case is why `visionAppControlState` exists beside `visionApprovalContext`: a *standing* has three values because the one requirement function must answer for all three, and "the file would not open" is not a policy. Both come from one read, so the two cannot drift.

**A plan-level Allow mints no grant, and the guard is structural rather than a condition.** The branch's first implementation wrote a grant on any plan-level Allow whose plan happened to carry a vision target, reading no standing at all — so a mixed plan (a vision step beside a destructive one) minted an app grant that nothing on that panel disclosed, in Normal or Power, for an app only *Sonny's* starter list vouched for. That grant then outranked a later switch to Safe, which is founder decision 4 turned upside down. Moving the question into the session moved the write with it: the only writer is the loop's per-app gate, reached only when the question was asked, so there is no condition left to get wrong.

**Test hermeticity broke and it broke silently.** The first run of the new real-path tests wrote a real `approved-apps.json` into the founder's own `~/Library/Application Support/Sonny/`, because `AgentViewModel`'s default store points at the real path and no fixture was injecting one. The suite was green throughout; nothing about the failure was visible in its output. Every test fixture that builds a view model now injects a store under its own temporary root, the residue was removed, and a rerun confirms the file is not recreated. **The general shape is worth carrying: a new store on `AgentViewModel` is a new hermeticity hole in every fixture that does not inject it, and the store's own tests will not notice.**

**Under test the installed universe is `MacAppCatalog.default`, not the machine.** `InstalledAppResolver.shared` swaps in `FixedAppSource.aliasTableRoster` in a test process. That is why the real-path tests use **VS Code** as their unapproved app: it is in that roster, it is permanently off the starter list (held there by guard (b)), and it is the founder's own worked example — *a developer who wants Sonny inside VS Code approves it by hand, one click, once, ever.* An app chosen merely because it is absent from the starter list today could be added tomorrow and turn those tests green for the wrong reason.

**Three existing guards caught the new store, which is what they were built to do.** The wipe's URL list and its behavioural fixture, `LocalStore`'s classification (row D's SONNY-115, whose comment on SONNY-140 predicted exactly this), and `ProductShellTests`' stored-property enumeration. Each was answered rather than relaxed. The classification call was left to this row rather than made on its behalf, and it is `.artifact`: a grant is not a record *of* what happened, it is the user's own answer to a question Sonny asked, so "Don't save this task" must not discard it.

**Every list-driven guard also passes against an emptied list**, which the SONNY-141 battery demonstrates rather than asserts: the mutant that empties the starter list is killed by the *literal pin* and the evidence-split test, and by neither of the two guards. That is why the literal pins exist, and it is the same reason the exclusion set has one of its own.

**What PR #88's two review cycles found, in one place.** Cycle 1 passed the code and produced the ordering rework above plus seven records fixes. **Cycle 2 also passed the code — no new defect, capture-first holding by construction — and found eight false or stale sentences the previous round's own sweeps had missed**, which is the pattern worth carrying: three of them were sentences a *fix round* had written. "Power is identical to Normal" survived in **nine** places after a three-site fix — eight found by cycle 2 and a ninth by the records round after it, in spec §23's pricing-ladder rationale, where it sat in the *present tense* as the reason a tier had no product reason to exist. The two that mattered most were in `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md`, which `CLAUDE.md` names authoritative and which was contradicting its own consent section two hundred lines below. A paragraph asserting the engine's input "stays row C's boolean seam" survived the very ticket that deleted that seam, because it was **orphaned onto the wrong function** — attached to `markFirstApprovalCompleted`, several functions from the `approvalContext` it describes, which is a failure mode no reader of the right symbol can catch. And the enumerated causes of `appControlWithdrawn` were short for the second time: leaving **Power** mid-session withdraws a standing only Power vouched for, because Power's resolver arm consults no list at all, and the move to *Normal* is the case a reader working from the Normal-to-Safe cause would not expect. The list now states that it has been short twice and that it is derived from the resolver's arms rather than remembered.

**A records round after cycle 2 found six more, and the pattern held: the rebase falsified sentences the reconciliation itself had not looked at.** "The nine stores before it" in `ApprovedAppStore`'s doc and "beside the other nine" in its test were both true at `cbce26c` and wrong the moment the count moved — the third fix-one-miss-its-neighbour here, which is why both files were swept whole and why that test's doc no longer writes the number down at all. This entry carried three wrong counts of its own: "the other nine stores", "four refusal cases" after F7 made it five, and a withdrawal sub-cause list still at three in the very paragraph describing F5's fix that made it four. It also cited a test by a name `7826b2c` had changed — a dangling symbol for the one test the safety argument leans on. **A count restated in prose is a copy, and every copy is a place to go stale**; row E's entry reached the same conclusion independently the day before.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The per-app question's decline arm is unreachable until SONNY-80's control lands.** `VisionContainmentRefusal.appControlDeclined` is fail-closed defense in depth for a labelled "deny this step" control that does not exist yet; today's Deny cancels, and the loop sees a `CancellationError`. Same status as `authorize`'s `approvalDeclined`, which has had it since row I. A battery reports it as a survivor and is right to.
- **The gate re-decrypts the grants file two to four times per iteration**, where one read would serve. Filed as **SONNY-202** (Backlog, untriaged) rather than fixed here: it changes no behaviour and the cost is negligible against a capture, an OCR pass and a model round trip. Its ticket carries the constraint a fix must respect — never cache past one iteration, because re-reading per iteration is what makes a revocation take effect at the next one.
- **Revocation ships on the next branch** (SONNY-144), which is sequencing rather than scope — the founder's nothing-gets-parked directive stands. The mechanism a revocation needs is here: the store, the per-iteration re-resolution, and the refusal that ends a session when a grant goes away. What is missing is the Settings list with a per-row remove and a remove-all.
- **This does not close SONNY-102.** The model narrows the unlisted-terminal gap in Safe and Normal — where an unlisted terminal at least surfaces as an unknown app the user is asked about — and leaves it untouched in Power, which asks about no app. That is a narrowing, not a fix.
- **The starter list is a curated, name-based list somebody maintains.** Its incompleteness fails safe (an unlisted app prompts), which is genuinely better than the deny list's direction and is still not completeness. Stated in its own doc comment so nobody reads a green suite as proof otherwise.
- **Three starter entries were never read from a bundle** — Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Signal, none installed on the founder's Mac. Recorded as their own provenance group and pinned by a test. A wrong entry there fails safe: the app simply prompts.

Per-ticket: 1483/114 at `2988d30` (SONNY-147), 1495/115 at `aa00818` (148), 1506/116 at `0b2d080` (149), 1523/117 at `8b73354` (150), and 1523/117 again at each of the three records commits `b273ca8`, `ae94696` and this entry's own stamping commit — re-run rather than carried, though none of the three touches behaviour and the last two are confined to `docs/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`. Net +64 tests / +4 suites. **`scripts/warnings`: 0 warnings at each of `2988d30`, `aa00818`, `0b2d080`, `8b73354`, `b273ca8` and `ae94696`**, every file in `Sources/` and `Tests/` compiled each time; not re-run for the stamping commit, whose diff is this file alone. Nothing was removed. **Seven existing assertions changed, across five tests in three files, each explained in place**: four in `TaskDeletePresentationTests` (three tests), where row D used `sheetHeight` as a proxy for "a deleted screen record renders like one that never existed" and the tests now assert that on `TaskDetailPresentation.sections` as well as on the height; two in `PriorTaskContextTests` and one in `OpenAIPlannerTests`, the fallback-string pins, the first of which also now asserts the old cause-asserting phrase is absent.

What changed for the user: a finished task now keeps what it produced, and its detail sheet says so — a **Result** block that wraps and can be selected, rendering nothing at all for the tasks that ran before Sonny kept results. The sheet's footer gains **Run again**, which re-asks Sonny with the same words, and **Follow up**, which reopens the task into the widget with an empty box and a chip naming it, so "use ~/Documents/MacAgentDocs instead" does the corrected thing without the command being retyped.

Behavior preserved: an ordinary within-ten-minutes follow-up is unchanged, and so is the ten-minute number; the planners see the same one thing they already saw; `retryLastCommand` and `lastCommand` are untouched; row D's two delete controls keep their position, tone and confirmation copy; the widget's composer is byte-identical whenever no chip is on, including the two circular buttons' position.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**"Run again" re-asks and never replays, and the reason to record is the gate rather than the coordinates** (founder, 2026-08-16). Sonny's gate is pre-execution and whole-plan: `AgentRunner.execute` assesses once, up front, and `executeChain` runs every segment with no re-gating. So re-executing a previously approved plan would carry an approval granted for a world that has since changed — the file that did not exist then exists now, so the destructive escalation that should fire would not. Re-asking through the planner keeps every gate honest by construction rather than by anyone remembering. The two secondary reasons, recorded as secondary: nothing in this codebase replays a stored plan today (both existing repeat mechanisms re-derive from an identifier), and a screen-control replay would click at coordinates that have moved.

**Re-asking re-resolves the workspace binding and re-requests approval, by design** (founder, same date). A task that asked for permission the first time asks again. This will read as a regression to anyone expecting a one-click repeat, which is exactly why it is written down: it is the same property that makes replay unsafe, seen from the user's side. The consequence rule then governs the second run on its own merits — an action that was not destructive in March may be destructive today.

**Running again a screen-control task starts a fresh session and replays nothing.** The stored command is re-planned, may resolve to a vision session again, and is gated as any new vision command is — the terminal deny list, the consequence rule, Safe mode's floor, unattended-never. The journal is **a record of what happened, not a script**, and this is written down because "retry a screen-control task" reads like replaying the clicks and replaying stored clicks blind is precisely the unsafe thing. Pinned end to end: two sessions with different ids, the first byte-for-byte what it was, the new row pointing at the new one.

**The persistence security note — row I's lesson, widened along a new axis.** `PriorTaskContext.plannerContextText` escaped `previousCommand` and `planSummary` and skipped `outcome.plannerText` and `step.plannerText`. Harmless while every run summary was a code-authored adapter string; not harmless once row I shipped a capability whose summary is free text written by a model that had just read the user's screen — and the vision prompt actively asks the model to describe what it saw, so the designed response to an injection attempt was to transcribe it into the one field that reached the trusted block unescaped. **Persistence removes the ten-minute bound that made the original omission survivable.** Two structural answers, not two remembered ones: stored fields reach a planner **only** by being built into a `PriorTaskContext` through its own initialisers, so `escapeForPlanner` is inherited rather than applied; and the stored result carries a provenance-declaring type, because "a structural guarantee is only as wide as the type that carries it" is the row I sentence this row is the test of. **The honest limit, stated so nobody over-reads it:** the type declares provenance and **cannot verify redaction**, because by the time it exists the value is already a plain `String` — `VisionSessionOutcome.Ending.summary` de-redacts at `VisionSessionRunner.swift:34,37` before it ever becomes `AgentRunResult.summary`. Do not make `RedactedPayload` `Codable` to close that: a `Decodable` conformance is a public initialiser in disguise, and its own comment says so. The precedent copied instead is `RedactionReportEntry` — `Codable` by design while the payload it summarises is not.

**Provenance is declared where the text is authored, and two sites forward rather than author.** Enumerated at `ef0cf7c`: 27 `AgentRunResult(` construction sites in `Sources/`, 26 code-authored templates and exactly one — `VisionSessionCapabilityAdapter.swift:278` — carrying free text a model composed. `AgentActionExecutor.executeChain` joins one summary per chain segment and `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` wraps a nested run's summary in a sentence of its own; both carry the provenance forward, because declaring either `.codeAuthored` on the ground that *it* wrote the template would launder the model's text. Of the two only the chain is **reachable today** — a plan may mix ordinary steps with a vision step, which `visionSplitDisclosure` writes a sentence describing, while `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations` refuses `.visionSession` inside a routine outright. The unreachability was established rather than assumed: the first draft of the routine test seeded such a routine and failed with `unsafeRoutineStep("vision_session")`. The forwarding stays anyway, because a hardcoded `.codeAuthored` becomes wrong silently the day a second model-authored capability exists.

**The line the provenance enum draws is who composed the prose, not whether any substring came from a model** — and it has to be stated, because the looser reading makes the enum useless. Nearly every code-authored summary interpolates a value a planner chose ("Zipped 3 files to …/large-files.zip" gets its path from the plan), and so does an error's own description: `VisionDecisionParseError.unknownAction` prints the action name the model asked for inside a sentence this repository wrote. Under a "contains nothing model-derived" reading almost nothing would qualify. Under this one the cases separate the thing that matters: `.modelAuthored` text can be an entire injected paragraph, while a `.codeAuthored` template bounds a model's contribution to the slots it interpolates. Escaping is unconditional either way.

**The heavy half of the record went to a store of its own, and the decision reversed on a measurement** (founder, 2026-08-17, superseding his own of 2026-08-16). The earlier choice — result, plan summary and steps all on `CompletedTaskRecord` — was made on a privacy argument that remains correct: a side store buys little when the backend retains the same content for 30–90 days, and the local copy is the one the user can actually delete. What was missing was a measurement. SONNY-119 then took one at `36cef9e`: the unsplit shape reaches **38.81 MiB** at the 10,000-record cap with `record(_:)` at **307 ms**, against **3.53 MiB** and **130 ms** today — "roughly triples" measured as about **11×**, and these stores are whole-file encrypted, so that is ~39 MB decrypted on every read and re-encrypted on every finished task.

**What the split actually buys is the reads, not the writes, and saying otherwise would invite a later reader to undo it.** A finished task now writes two files instead of one and the summed bytes are similar. The gain is that `TaskHistoryStore.loadAll()` runs several times per task — inside `record(_:)` itself, again in `refreshTaskHistory()`, and again for the Tasks list, search and Insights — while the plan store is read only when someone opens one task's detail or arms a follow-up on it. Moving ~1.7 kB of plan text per record out of the file that is read constantly and into the one that is read almost never is where the time goes. That reasoning lives on `TaskPlanDetailStore`'s own doc comment.

**The split is for size and never for lifetime, and the alignment is built rather than asserted.** The founder's objection to splitting was that "follow-ups on older tasks quietly get weaker with no way to say so" — a silent degradation the product cannot explain under the no-explanatory-copy rule. That objection binds only if the new store outlives its rows by less, so it must not: same cap (read off `TaskHistoryStore.defaultMaxItems` rather than repeated), same oldest-first-by-`completedAt` rule, deleted with the row, suppressed with the row. Same *eviction* needed more than a matching rule, because the two stores stay level only while every row has a plan — and a run that failed before preparing one writes a row with none, so the plan store would fill more slowly, evict later, and keep the plans of tasks the user can no longer see. So `TaskHistoryStore.record(_:)` now returns the ids it evicted and the plan store drops those **in the same write it was making anyway**. Zero extra writes; a demonstrated property rather than a coincidence.

**Two caps, both new, both with their arithmetic.** The result is capped at **1,000 characters**: record size is additive in that field (SONNY-119's own table has "+ result 200 chars, 8 steps" at exactly 374 + 200 + its 1,729 B of steps), so 1,000 bounds a record at ~1.4 kB and the hot file at ~13 MiB at the cap, against the 3.78 MiB SONNY-119 measured today's records at. The plan detail is capped by **one 2,500-character budget** plus a 400-character per-field ceiling — one budget rather than a product of five per-field caps, because a product is a bound nobody can hold in their head: twenty steps at 400 characters of description with sixteen details of 400 each is 136 kB an entry and 1.36 GB at the store's cap — technically bounded, practically not. Steps are kept whole and the remainder dropped, so a truncated plan is a prefix of the real one rather than a mangled version of all of it. Both caps also run on the **decode** path, so a value that reached a file by some other route is bounded when it is read back.

**The one unbounded producer is what motivates the result's cap at all.** Twenty-six of the 27 summary producers are short templates; the vision session's is free text a model wrote. And `TaskHistoryStore.record(_:)` decodes and re-encrypts the entire file on every finished task, so one pathological response would not merely be large once — it would tax every future task for as long as it stayed in the window.

**Why results are stored locally at all, now that the backend retains model traffic.** The founder's decision of 2026-08-16 has the server keeping requests and responses for 30–90 days. That is **not the same thing** as what a task produced and is not a substitute for it, and this is written down so a later reader does not "simplify" task detail into a server read. Three reasons: server traffic is prompts and completions, not the product's own record of a run's outcome; the local copy works offline, and the product is local-first; and the two retention clocks differ, so a task the user can still see could have no server-side record left at all.

**Why no side store was the earlier answer, and why one exists anyway.** The codebase argues for a side store in writing — `TaskHistoryStore.swift:39-41` states the pattern unprompted ("The record holds the link, the side store holds the content"), and `docs/sonny-v1-vision-planner-integration-plan.md:520` posed this exact fork for rows D/E three weeks earlier. The 2026-08-16 decision declined it for three reasons: row J's SONNY-140 already claims the tenth store and already rewrites `theWipeReachesExactlyTheNineLocalStores`, so a row E store would be the eleventh with both rows editing one test; the privacy case is weaker than it looks now that the backend retains command text anyway; and a side store's own cost is follow-ups quietly degrading on older tasks with no way to say why. The 2026-08-17 measurement overturned the first and third: **the store exists, and it neutralises the third by sharing the row's retention exactly.** The first became bookkeeping — row E landed first, so the count is **ten** and row J's SONNY-140 now raises the number rather than setting it, in `theWipeReachesExactlyTheTenLocalStores` and `everyLocalStoreFileIsClassifiedExactlyOnce`.

**The armed follow-up's lifecycle, and the two obvious alternatives that are both wrong.** An armed context keeps the original task's real timestamp and is exempt from the ten-minute expiry, because it was armed by a deliberate user action rather than left behind by the last run. Stamping the original `createdAt` on an unexempted context **silently kills the feature**: `currentContext()` self-clears on read, so a task from yesterday is dropped on the very next read and the follow-up reaches the planner with no context at all, looking from the outside exactly like it worked. Stamping `Date()` instead puts a **false `Captured at:`** inside the trusted block — the one segment the planner's own system prompt describes as authoritative. **Exemption from the timer is not permission to persist:** `consumeArmedContext()` spends it at the moment `performStart` reads it, explicitly rather than leaving it to the `record(...)` that usually overwrites it later, because "usually overwritten later" is a different promise from "spent now" and the gap between them is a follow-up silently attaching itself to the command after this one. Nothing persists an arm across launches.

**The two fallback strings stopped asserting a cause.** `plannerContextText` emitted "- unavailable; prior task failed before preparation completed" and "- none available; prior task failed before preparation completed" for an empty plan summary and empty steps. That names a cause that is only sometimes the reason, and row E made the other case the common one: every task recorded before this row has no stored plan, so a follow-up on a **completed** one would have put those two lines directly above `Previous outcome: completed - …` — a flat contradiction inside the trusted block. They now read "- not recorded" and "- none recorded", true of the live no-plan case and the rehydrated pre-row-E case alike.

**Two chips became three, so the chips got a row of their own** (founder, 2026-08-21). Three chips inline in a 472-point pill leave the text field about **57 points** wide — an estimate from the chips' own text and padding, and the basis the decision was taken on — at the exact moment the user is typing a correction into it. The pill now grows from 40 to 66 whenever any chip is on and is unchanged when none is. The two declined alternatives are recorded because both are tempting: hard-truncating the follow-up chip keeps one row and still leaves the field around 90 points, and a chip that names no task fits easily but reintroduces the invisible state the chip exists to prevent — an invisible trusted block reaching the planner is worse than an invisible workspace binding, which is the case that slot already existed to prevent. Order is the two that were there first, then the new one: compose, do not displace. One consequence had to be handled rather than discovered — the two circular buttons beside the pill were centred against it and would have floated 13 points above the field; they now sit in a 40-point box of their own, bottom-aligned, which is exactly level in both heights and pixel-identical when no chip is on.

**The sheet's height stopped being a branch and became a sum.** With two optional sections the old `record.visionSessionID == nil ? 320 : 560` ternary is a four-case arithmetic, and row D is still adding controls to the same dialog. It is now `base + Σ(present sections)`, and the result section's own share is **derived from its text** rather than fixed, because a fixed allowance either clips a long result or leaves most of a hundred points of white under a short one. The line count is an estimate — nothing outside a live layout pass knows where text wraps — and the block is built so both ways of being wrong are mild: the view gives its scrolling content exactly the height the sheet reserved, so an under-estimate scrolls instead of clipping, and the sheet's existing `Spacer(minLength: 20)` absorbs an over-estimate. Content-sizing the sheet was the sanctioned alternative and was declined for a concrete reason: the screen-record section contains a `ScrollView` whose greediness is currently masked by the fixed height, and **no agent in this repository can look at the result**, so a layout change resting on reasoning alone was the wrong trade.

**A record with nothing to show renders nothing at all.** Row I's rule for the vision section, extended, and it holds harder here: every record written before row E has no stored result, so this is the common path on day one rather than an edge, and an empty state would tell each of those users their task produced nothing when the truth is that Sonny was not keeping results yet — a truth the no-explanatory-copy rule forbids writing down beside it. Two histories collapse into one `nil` in `TaskDetailPresentation.resultText`, so no branch in the body can drift apart.

**The stored plan steps are not rendered to anyone.** They are context for the planner. A list of internal step descriptions on a user-facing receipt is the surface the founder rejected on 2026-07-18 ("logs + summary + activity should just be a flow").

**A tenth store means eleven test fixtures, and the trap is the one this repo has already recorded twice.** Every `AgentViewModel` fixture in `Tests/` injects its own `taskHistoryStore` under a temporary root. A tenth store defaulting to `~/Library/Application Support/Sonny/task-plan-details.json` would have had eleven fixtures writing to the developer's real data — hermetic by accident rather than by construction, which is exactly what the journal's own fixture comments describe. All eleven now inject it.

**The wipe copy is unchanged, and that is a judgment rather than an oversight.** Settings' two enumerations of what a local-data wipe deletes name nine kinds and now cover ten files. The tenth is not a new kind: a task's plan is keyed on that task's row, capped with it, evicted with it, deleted with it and suppressed with it, so "task history" covers it in the user's terms. Row I's screen record earned its own clause because it is genuinely a different thing — a record of the user's screen rather than of Sonny's own bookkeeping. Recorded here so a reviewer can disagree with the judgment rather than find a silent gap; SONNY-109 can overrule it.

**One defect found and filed rather than absorbed — SONNY-195.** A run bound to a workspace whose name its command does not contain writes a task-history row tagged with **no workspace**. `resolveTaskScope` prefers `explicitWorkspaceBinding`; the row's tag comes from `WorkspaceTaskTagging.resolvedWorkspaceName(command:plan:…)`, which reads the plan's workspace steps and the command text and never the binding. Pre-existing, and it reaches every dispatch that binds explicitly — the workspace card's "New task in …" flow included, where the widget chip says "In Research" for the whole run and the row afterwards says nothing. Outside SONNY-149's scope, so it is a discovery ticket; `runningAgainCarriesTheRecordsWorkspaceWhenItStillExists` asserts the `nil` deliberately with a comment pointing at it, so nobody later reads the absence as something run-again broke.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Results are not backfilled onto older records, and never will be.** That information is gone, and inventing it would be worse than its absence. Task detail therefore stays a bare receipt for everything that ran before this row — the common case for a while — and a follow-up on such a record has the command and the outcome but no plan. The product says so by rendering nothing, not by explaining.
- **No wireframe exists for this surface.** `docs/wireframes/` holds one file, `15-SegmentedControl.svg`, unrelated to task detail. Everything here — the Result block, the two footer actions, the chip row — is net-new System A (and System B for the chip) on session judgment, with the widget's chip layout and copy founder-approved on 2026-08-21 and everything else settled by **SONNY-109**'s whole-product pass.
- **A follow-up on a task whose plan store will not read** arms with the command and the outcome, reports the load failure in the usual banner, and is honest about having less to go on. Refusing to arm would trade a degraded feature for no feature, and the founder's objection to a shorter-lived detail store was precisely that follow-ups must not *quietly* get weaker.
- **Deleting a task removes the backend's copy too, and a task marked "Don't save this task" is never retained server-side** — both row 12's, on SONNY-16 and SONNY-134. Row E adds no client seam for either: a stored result and a stored plan are deleted and suppressed by riding a record row D already classifies as a trace.
- The result block's line estimate, and every question about how the two new surfaces actually look, are the founder's manual pass. No agent in this repository can screenshot or drive the live app.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none. SONNY-195 is filed and untriaged, which is a queued item rather than an open question.

Manual checklist for the founder (packaged app):
1. Run a task that produces a file, open its detail: the Result block says what it produced, wraps, and can be selected.
2. Open a task from before this shipped: no Result block at all — no heading, no empty sentence.
3. Open a task with both a result and a screen record: both sections there, nothing clipped, no large gap above the footer. Then a task with a long result: past about six lines the block scrolls rather than the sheet growing.
4. Open a failed task: the failure text is there.
5. Press **Run again**: it runs, and the Tasks page shows it in progress. Run again a task that needed approval — it asks again (intended). Run again one bound to a workspace you have since deleted — it runs unscoped and does not error. Start a task, then open a detail sheet: both footer actions are visibly disabled, and enabled again when it ends.
6. Run again a screen-control task: a new session starts and drives the app live; nothing about it looks like a recording being played back.
7. Press **Follow up** on an old task: the widget comes forward with an empty box and a chip naming the task. Type a correction and submit — it does the corrected thing. Leave one armed fifteen minutes, then submit — it still works. Arm, submit, then submit an unrelated command — the second is unaffected. Arm one and dismiss the chip — the next command is unaffected.
8. With a workspace binding and "Don't save this task" also on, confirm all three chips are readable together and the two circular buttons stay level with the text field. Then confirm the pill is unchanged — 40 tall, no chip row — whenever no chip is on.
9. Run a task, quit, relaunch, open its detail: the result is still there. The encrypted round trip on a real store rather than a fixture.

Next branch: row J (`SONNY-140`'s approved-apps store) now raises the local-store count to eleven rather than setting it to ten. SONNY-109's whole-product UI/UX pass owns the final wording and layout of everything this row put on screen.

**PR #89 CYCLE-1 FIX ROUND, appended 2026-08-21. The review found no shipped defect — the behaviour above is what shipped and the security trace holds — and four guards these tickets required pinned that a mutation battery showed were not. Everything above stands; this block records what the round changed and why the round was possible at all.**

**The shape of the finding, which is the durable half.** Four separate places where a ticket named a property, a test existed with a name that claimed it, and a mutant deleting the property survived the whole suite. Not one of them was a missing test. Each was a test that passed for a reason other than the one its name asserts — the failure mode this repository's evidence rules exist for, arriving in the branch that wrote those rules' latest instalment.

- **`consumeArmedContext` was held by nothing** (M4). SONNY-150 required both halves of the arm's lifecycle pinned; the expiry half was, the spent half was not. `anArmedContextIsSpentByOneRunAndTheNextCommandSeesNoTraceOfIt` passes with the method gutted, because the follow-up's own terminal `recordPriorTaskContext` overwrites the stored context a moment later — which is **precisely** the "usually overwritten later is not the same promise as spent now" gap the method was written to close, quoted in its own doc comment. A test that cannot distinguish the mechanism from the coincidence it was built to replace holds neither.
- **The eviction handoff's plan-less branch was untested in both copies** (M6, M6s). `theHistoryStoreReportsWhatItEvictedAndThePlanStoreDropsThoseInTheSameWrite` writes a plan on every row, so it exercises the branch that already worked. The branch that fires when a run failed before preparing a plan — the exact scenario "same cap, same eviction" exists for, since that run writes a row with none — could be deleted in both the foreground and the scheduled path with the suite still green.
- **The plan store's own eviction backstop was dead to the suite, and its test asserted the opposite of its name** (M8). Three entries against a ten-thousand cap, a local variable named `overCap` holding three, and a closing assertion that nothing had been evicted. It read like coverage from every angle except the one that counts.
- **`AgentEvent.swift` named a test that has never existed** (M9b). `theOnlyModelAuthoredRunSummaryIsTheVisionSessions` was cited as the guard on `summaryProvenance`'s `.codeAuthored` default; `grep` returns one hit, the citation. Worth recording precisely because the first mutant written for it *died*: adding `.modelAuthored` to the calculator adapter is caught, since two fixtures run the calculator and read its provenance back. Moving the same mutant to `RevealInFinderCapabilityAdapter` survived. **Coverage that happens to intersect a property is not a guard on it**, and a battery that stops at the first kill will not tell the two apart.

**What was added.** Three direct store-level tests for `consumeArmedContext`, calling it and asserting on the store rather than through a run that would overwrite it anyway. A foreground and a scheduled eviction test at a cap of two where the evicting row has **no** plan, each asserting both that the displaced row's plan is gone and that the evicting row really stored none — so neither can quietly drift onto the branch that already worked. `TaskPlanDetailStore.maxDetails` became an injectable instance property (the seam `TaskHistoryStore.maxItems` already has, for the reason its doc comment records), and the eviction test now exceeds a real cap, with a sibling pinning that eviction is by `completedAt` and not by write order — a distinction a chronologically-inserted fixture cannot see, and a mutant of its own. `RunSummaryProvenanceTests` enumerates every file in both targets for `.modelAuthored` declarations, in `MacAgentSource`'s comment-stripped scan shape; that scanner gained a core-source accessor rather than a second scanner being built in the other target, because two independently maintained copies of comment-stripping is the failure that file's own doc comment records twice.

**Two guards the seam itself now needs.** An injectable cap is a test seam, and shipping a shorter life through it is the one thing the founder's 2026-08-17 split condition forbids — follow-ups must not quietly get weaker on older tasks. So `noProductionPathPassesACapToThePlanStore` — named `theShippedPlanCapIsTheHistoryCapAndNoProductionPathOverridesIt` until cycle 3 renamed it, since the first half of that claim moved elsewhere and a name that overstates is a claim rather than a label — enumerates the three production construction sites and asserts none passes a cap, and `aPlanStoreBuiltWithZeroFloorsAtOneRatherThanErasingItself` pins the floor. The backstop's own doc comment now states why it is reachable rather than decorative: the handoff carries the evicted ids in the *same* write as the new detail, so a write that throws after the row write already landed loses them for good, and nothing re-derives them.

**One real inconsistency fixed alongside them.** The scheduled path wrapped both its writes in one `do`, so a failure of the *plan* write reported "Sonny could not save this scheduled run to task history" — false, the row was on disk — and skipped `refreshTaskHistory()`, leaving the row that did land absent from the published list until something else refreshed it. Two failures with different consequences and different recoveries now have two catches, two messages and a refresh that happens either way, matching what `recordTaskHistoryIfTerminal` and `recordTaskPlanDetail` already do for a foreground run. They are separate functions rather than one shared helper, so agreeing is something to do rather than something inherited. Pinned by a test that makes the plan store's directory read-only while task history stays writable — the fifth gated directory-locking test in the repository, which moved `TwinnedTestSupportTests`' population pin from four to five.

**And a records repair this branch caused.** SONNY-150 inserted `FollowUpPresentation` into `AgentActivityPresentation.swift` with no blank line after `TaskRecordingPresentation`'s doc block, so that block — the founder's not-Incognito reasoning, and the sentence claiming `TaskRecordingPresentationTests` refuses copy that reads like an explanation — documented the wrong enum, and `TaskRecordingPresentation` had none. Moved back. The same ticket's "compose with it, do not displace it" rule was written about the composer's chips and applies to the file just as well. The store-count sweep also found sites this branch had left at nine: `README.md` in five places, including the now-false "`LocalStorageEncryption` is the encryption/migration mechanism all nine share, not a tenth store" and a line SONNY-181 had itself corrected the day before; `LocalStoreClassification.swift` twice; and `VisionSessionJournalStore.swift`, which still named `theWipeReachesExactlyTheNineLocalStores` after this branch renamed it. Rows D and I's changelog entries correctly say nine and are left: a changelog is history. **This sentence said "two of nine sites" and recorded the sweep as complete, and it was not** (PR #89 cycle 2, F3) — two more sites stayed at nine while everything around them went to ten: `AgentViewModel.visionSessionJournalStoreForThisRun`'s doc comment, which carried *three* stale numbers at once ("the fifth `.trace` store", now the sixth; "the most sensitive of the nine"; and a quotation of the very `LocalStoreClassification` sentence this round had changed to "of the ten"), and `LocalStorageSecurityTests`' own count-assertion comment, which said "nine is now stated in a third place" eight lines above `#expect(fileURLs.count == 10)`. Both fixed. **The lesson is the one this branch keeps relearning about its own sweeps**: a count restated in prose is a copy, every copy is a place to go stale, and a sweep is complete when the pattern returns only history — not when the session stops finding hits. The comment in the security test now deliberately does not spell the number a second time, because a sentence that names it is one more copy to update.

**Two discovery tickets, both about the trusted block and neither fixed here.** **SONNY-197** — `followUpOnTask` drops `record.result?.provenance`, because `PriorTaskOutcome` has no provenance field, so a stored model-authored paragraph enters the planner's trusted block indistinguishable from a template. Not a defect: escaping is unconditional and nothing reads the flag yet, and `PriorTaskContext`'s live path was never-touch for SONNY-150. It is the structural version of this row's own security note, one axis further. **SONNY-198** — `escapeForPlanner` neutralises the two delimiter tokens and nothing else, and the trusted block is line-oriented, so a stored result containing a newline can forge a `Previous command:` line *inside* an intact wrapper. Every trim on the path is `.whitespacesAndNewlines`, which does not touch an interior newline. Pre-existing since row I and out of scope here — but row E is what removed the ten-minute bound on it, and the one model-authored producer writes multi-line prose as its ordinary case, so it is recorded against this row rather than left where nobody would look.

An equivalent mutant surviving is the expected outcome for a drift guard, and recording it as a kill was the error.

**And the class of the error is one this branch files tickets about.** A stamped battery figure that does not reproduce reads exactly like one that does; "six killed" was true of the mutants that ran and false of the mutants the entry described, which is the same shape as a test whose name claims more than its body — cycle 1's four findings, cycle 2's two, and now this. Behavior added:
- **A server that builds, tests and runs**, with `GET /v1/health` returning `{status, version, environment}` — `version` being the build identifier injected at image build time, which is what makes two deployments distinguishable.
