Release, `Sources/` only, cold at `9b8e73f`: `Build complete!`, zero warnings — measured so that the debug-only boundary documented in `--help` is a stated limit rather than a hiding place. **Rebased onto `main` at `407a8d1` (PR #77) after cycle 2 and re-measured there, all three at `edb43c5`: 1410 tests in 111 suites, exit 0; `scripts/warnings` 0 warnings, exit 0, 101s cold; `scripts/warnings selftest` 30 checks, 0 failures, exit 0.** The base for the merged branch is `main`'s own **1410 in 111**, recorded at `03d6a0e` in the entry directly below and unchanged by that merge. The count did not move across the rebase even though PR #77 edited `VisionModelClientTests.swift` — checked rather than assumed: that PR changed existing tests without adding or removing any. **Every SHA above from this branch's own history is pre-rebase and no longer reachable from it**: the rebase rewrote all ten commits, so `c33a5d7` is now `1ff71d1` and the rest likewise. They are kept as written because they name the trees that were actually measured, and re-labelling those measurements with post-rebase SHAs would pair each number with a tree that never produced it — the same error as F5, committed deliberately. Following the convention the entry below sets: the commit that publishes this entry changes only this file, so `git diff edb43c5 <head> -- Sources Tests scripts Package.swift` is empty and the measurement carries forward unchanged; a commit cannot contain its own hash, so the stamp names the commit the runs actually happened at rather than the one that prints them.

Behavior added:
- **`scripts/warnings`** — the whole warning population of the working tree, from a build in which every file was compiled, in about 95 seconds. Exit 0 for none, 2 for some, 1 when no trustworthy measurement was made.
- **A failed build is reported as a failed build**, never as zero warnings, and prints no count at all.
- **A `warning:` line the parser cannot classify suppresses the count** and is printed, rather than being dropped.
- **A second run in the same checkout is refused**, naming the holder; `scripts/warnings unlock` clears a lock a killed run left behind and refuses while its owner is alive.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **No file under `Sources/` is in this diff.** The six fixes are test-local; `routine(named:)`, `visionSplitDisclosure(for:)`, `CompletedTaskRecord.id` and `VisionPointResolver.isInsideImage` are all untouched.
- **No test was added or removed**, and no assertion was weakened. The suite is 1410 in 111 at both ends.
- **Every assertion the six tests made, they still make** — `disclosure?.contains(x) == true` became `disclosure.contains(x)` and `== false` became `!disclosure.contains(x)`, which is the same predicate against a value that can no longer be nil.
- **No incremental rebuild is lost, and no shared build artifact is corrupted.** The script does write inside `.build/` — its own `.build/warnings-scratch/`, and on a failed build `.build/warnings-failed-build.log` — but nothing under `.build/debug/`, which is where `swift build` and the flagged `swift test` keep theirs. So the next ordinary build is as incremental as it would have been, and a build running beside this one shares no artifacts with it: the isolation argument SONNY-176 made for `scripts/mutate`, reused rather than reinvented. **Measured rather than reasoned, at `9edebe8`:** an ordinary `swift build --build-tests` run immediately after a full cold `scripts/warnings` completed in **6.40s**, against the ~90s that same build costs from cold — so the shared incremental state really did survive the run. (PR #78 F2: this line previously claimed the script "never writes" to `.build/`, which is false, and was contradicted by this entry's own note below recording `.build/warnings-scratch` at 800 MB.)
- **`scripts/mutate` is not modified.** The two harnesses share a shape and a `.git/`-scoped lock convention, not code.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The hazard was reproduced on purpose, and the reproduction is the argument.** At `bb4a3de`, with five warnings still live in the tree, one test file was edited and rebuilt: the incremental build recompiled exactly that one file and printed `Build complete!` with **zero** warnings in its output. Five, reported as none, by a build that did nothing wrong. That is why the answer is not a rule telling sessions to check — that rule already existed implicitly and produced five — and why the wipe has no flag to disable it. `scripts/warnings selftest` performs the same demonstration on a throwaway package before showing the harness catch it, so the property is watched firing rather than asserted.

**Counting `warning:` lines gives four different answers on one log, and only one of them is the population.** The same cold build at `bb4a3de` yields 68 lines containing `warning:`, 34 diagnostic headers, and 6 distinct warnings; the compiler repeats each diagnostic across compilation jobs and renders each one again inside a gutter that also says `warning:`. The report prints both the deduplicated count and the raw header count so the gap is visible instead of being a number a reader has to trust. This is `CLAUDE.md`'s quantified-claim rule landing on a build log: count first, with a method that tolerates what it is searching.

**Four of the six were misdiagnosed in the ticket, and the correct diagnosis changes the fix.** The ticket read all four `#require` warnings as redundant calls on non-optional expressions. Only two are: `routine(named:)` returns a non-optional `StoredRoutine` and throws when the routine is absent, so `#require` around it adds nothing. The other two — plus the one the ticket called `try? #require` — sit on expressions that genuinely *are* optional: `String.range(of:options:)`, `visionSplitDisclosure(for:) -> String?`, and `CompletedTaskRecord.id`, which is declared `String?` and documented at length as to why. **What selects the redundant overload is an optional result-type context, and `try?` is only one way to create one.** Swift Testing declares `require<T>(_ optionalValue: T?) -> T` beside a hidden `require<T>(_ optionalValue: T) -> T` — hidden by `@_documentation(visibility: private)`, **not deprecated**, and routed to `NonOptionalRequireMacro`, whose own redundancy warning is the diagnostic (Testing.framework's `arm64-apple-macos.swiftinterface`, lines 565 and 567). Given an argument of type `String?`, the first overload yields `String` and the second yields `String?`; whichever matches the surrounding context exactly is the one chosen. An optional context therefore picks the hidden overload and gets the warning. Measured three ways against `visionSplitDisclosure(for:) -> String?` in one probe file: plain `try` into `let a: String? = ...` **warns**; plain `try` into an inferred non-optional binding does **not**; `try?` **warns**. So the earlier claim here — that `try?` is the mechanism, via a deprecated overload — was wrong twice over, and the surviving true statement is narrower: `try?` warns because it produces an optional context, exactly as an explicit `String?` annotation does. (PR #78 F4.) The fix is therefore `try` plus `throws` on the test — which is what the authors were avoiding by reaching for `try?` — and not the deletion the ticket's reading would have produced. **Re-deriving the list, which the ticket asked for, was not enough; re-deriving the diagnosis was the part that mattered.**

**One of the six sites was hiding a vacuous pass, and the warning was pointing at it.** `PriorTaskContextTests`'s `let closing = try? #require(...)` fed an `if let closing, let injected = ...` that guarded the *only* assertion in the test, so either range coming back nil made the test pass having checked nothing. Both bindings are now required. **The other two `try?` sites were not vacuous, and the first version of this entry said they were** (PR #78 F1, replicated by the reviewer and again by the coordinator by forcing the required value nil in each of the three old forms): `VisionSessionAdapterTests:584`'s `#expect(disclosure?.contains(x) == true)` fails on nil, because `nil == true` is false, and `TaskDeletePresentationTests:88`'s `#expect(record.taskRowIdentity == realID)` fails too, because a non-nil `String` never equals a nil `String?`. Both were rewritten in this branch for clarity once the enclosing test became `throws`, which is worth doing and is not the same thing as closing a hole. The pattern is still worth naming for the one real case, in the terms F4's correction above already establishes — and **"converts a would-be failure into a nil" was itself wrong, the second bad mechanism to appear in this paragraph** (PR #78 N2). There is no would-be failure to convert: in an optional context `#require` resolves to the hidden non-optional overload, which performs **no check at all**, so nothing is tested, nothing fails, and the nil the binding receives was never a caught error — it is the value handed straight back. Measured rather than reasoned: a test whose whole body is `let v = try? #require(alwaysNil())` compiles with the redundancy warning and **passes with zero issues recorded**, which it could not do if anything were unwrapping. What the nil costs then depends entirely on what the code does with it — an `if let` swallows it and loses an assertion, a comparison against it fails loudly — and that is the check both earlier versions of this paragraph skipped.

**Release cannot be covered, and the reason is structural rather than a missing flag.** The test targets use `@testable import`, which requires `-enable-testing`; release does not pass it, so `swift build -c release --build-tests` fails outright with `error: module 'MacAgent' was not compiled for testing`. No single build can cover the test targets and release at once, so the harness is debug — the configuration every session builds and tests in — and says so in `--help` instead of implying coverage it does not have. Release over `Sources/` alone was measured once here and is clean, which makes that a documented boundary rather than an unexamined one.

**The dirty-tree rule is the opposite of `scripts/mutate`'s, deliberately.** A battery rewrites files, so it must run against something a SHA names or its revert step destroys work. This only reads, and checking work that is not committed yet is the entire point — a session that can only measure committed trees learns it introduced a warning after it has already written the closing comment. So the tree is measured as it stands and *described* instead: the report carries the SHA and the uncommitted-file count, so a number still cannot be quoted without the tree it came from.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Nothing runs it for you.** There is no CI in this repository and no hook was added; the founder chose the WORKFLOW.md route (step 5 and step 7) over a `pre-push` hook, which would have cost ~95s on every push, fired on doc-only branches, and been bypassable with `--no-verify`. Stated here because "it is a check, not a gate" is the honest residual, and `--help` says it too.
- Dependency warnings are unreportable by construction — SwiftPM suppresses them for non-root packages, so the compiler never emits them. Warnings from outside this repository's sources are printed under "elsewhere" and not counted.
- One machine, one toolchain (Apple Swift 6.3.3, arm64-apple-macosx26.0). A warning needing a different SDK is not visible here.
- **`.build/warnings-scratch` is a third full build directory** — 800 MB here once warm, measured at `5dd0790`, beside `scripts/mutate`'s 830 MB and the shared `.build/`, which together come to 2.4 GB. Unlike the battery's, its compiled output is emptied on every run and never reused; what persists is only SwiftPM's fetched dependency, so a run needs no network and every run pays the same ~95s cold build. That cost is the mechanism, not an inefficiency in it.
- **One ticket filed: SONNY-184**, from PR #78's cycle-1 review — three hardening residuals in the tool, grouped in one ticket for the founder to split at triage. (a) An unclassifiable `warning:` line stops the run with exit 1 and no count, and the only recovery the message offers is editing `classify_log()`, which blocks a session outside its ticket's scope; the refusal itself is right and must survive whatever replaces it. (b) The selftest does not pin two properties the tool claims about itself — that an ordinary `.build/debug/` survives a run, and that the wipe guard refuses a path that is not its own — and `compute_scratch_path`'s fallback branch is unreachable from it. (c) `scripts/warnings` and `scripts/mutate` hold separate locks and cannot see each other, so a warnings run started mid-battery would compile a mutated tree and attribute the count to a commit that never held that code — the same class SONNY-176 closed one lane over. Backlog, untriaged, unattached. Nothing else deferred.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: unchanged by this branch — it touches no roadmap row.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The symbol sweep cannot tell a live symbol from a filename quoted in a comment, and that is the third correction its method has needed in two branches.** `sweep.sh` asks whether a token appears anywhere under `Sources/` or `Tests/`. `AutomationStores` passes that test — not because a type of that name exists, but because `TaskHistoryStore.swift`'s doc comment says "the twice-documented `AutomationStores.swift` decode rule". So do `ClipboardHistoryService`, `RiskApproval`, `MediaPlaybackService`, `ContentView` and `SonnyWidgetTheme`, each on the strength of one comment somewhere naming its file. A second pass fixes it: for every CamelCase token the sweep calls live, ask instead whether `Sources/` or `Tests/` *declares* it. That pass turned six more names in `README.md`'s architecture bullet from "resolves" into "is a file, not a type", on top of the three the first pass caught outright — `ShortcutsBridgeService`, `WebResearchService` and `WebResearchSynthesizer`, which have zero whole-word hits anywhere under `Sources/` or `Tests/`. **The rule the method has now been given three times, from three directions: a sweep that reports everything resolving is a claim to check, not a result to trust.** PR #76 met it as resolving against the whole tree, then as letting a file resolve its own symbols; this is the same hole a third time, and the only reason it was visible is that the first pass's output was read rather than totalled.

**Re-run the sweep after the fix, because the fix writes new symbols.** The corrected architecture bullet named `ScreenControlEligibility` as the type that refuses a terminal. It is a file; the types are `ScreenControlPolicy`, `ScreenControlVerdict` and `ScreenControlRefusal`. The sweep caught it on the second run, in exactly the bucket it exists for, on a name this branch had introduced sixty seconds earlier. A one-shot sweep would have shipped a fresh instance of the defect it was fixing.

**A closed count needs a population you actually enumerated, and one was withdrawn here before it shipped.** The safety-model rewrite was first written as "five things leave the device and nothing else does". Enumerating the eleven `session.data` call sites under `Sources/` shows five *kinds* of outbound payload but nine files, of which some are fetches of a URL the user named rather than uploads of user data — a boundary that does not survive being written as a closed list. The published sentence names the owners instead and makes no total claim. **The wrong version was the more impressive one**, which is the whole reason CLAUDE.md's rule reads "count first, then write the number".

**Records staleness in this repository clusters around removals, not additions.** Every load-bearing thing wrong in `README.md` was the record of something that had been taken away: the twelve-app launch allowlist (dissolved 2026-08-12 by C12/SONNY-82), dry-run mode (deleted with Command Center's composer, and `.previewOnly` unproducible since the policy dials went on 2026-08-14), Settings as a sidebar destination (a dialog since 2026-07-18), the menu-bar cockpit (replaced by the widget), and `feature/v1-strategy-replan` (merged and gone). An addition tends to get written down because someone is proud of it; a removal leaves a sentence describing a thing that no longer exists, and nothing fails. **The counts are the tell** — a third of the thirty-two corrections were a number or an enumeration that was true once — which is the same shape SONNY-175 and SONNY-180 each found, and the reason both of those swept a whole file rather than patching a bullet.

**A README that advertises a security property the product no longer has is the worst class of stale record.** `README.md` said apps were allowlisted in five places, including the Safety Model's list of what Swift validates every plan against, and including a coverage sentence claiming tests for "app allowlisting". C12 dissolved that gate eight days ago. Nothing in the tree contradicted the sentence loudly — `MacAppCatalog` still holds exactly twelve entries, so a spot-check of the list passes — and the file's own doc comment is the only thing that says those twelve "are not a limit on anything". A reader checking the claim against the catalog would have confirmed it.

**A ticket's own framing of a distinction can be off while its finding is right.** SONNY-181 asks the fix to decide "whether the sentence is counting stores or types — they are different numbers (nine and seven)". Stores and types are the same number: there are nine store types. What numbers seven is *files*, because `AutomationStores.swift` declares `RoutineStore` and `WorkspaceStore` and `ClipboardHistoryService.swift` declares `ClipboardHistoryStore` and `ClipboardHistorySettingsStore`. The README now says nine stores across seven files and names which files hold two. Recorded because the ticket's phrasing is the kind a later session would inherit unexamined, and because it is the same failure the ticket was filed about — a count attached to the wrong population.

**Two claims that read as adjacent were checked separately and only one was wrong.** `README.md`'s Keychain bullet under Permissions — "on an unsigned development build, may prompt for your login password" — is still true — `swift run MacAgent` produces an unsigned binary, and branch 7's entry records exactly that Keychain-prompt loop. What was wrong was the pointer: it sent the reader to "the changelog's branch 7 notes on code-signing", and that entry has no code-signing notes; the real signing story is SONNY-153 and SONNY-156, two entries and a month later. **A cross-reference is a claim and resolves or does not**, and this one had been readable-but-wrong long enough that three sweeps of the file had passed over it.

**SONNY-164's second half was closed by reading rather than writing.** The ticket asks for a correction comment on SONNY-146 covering its closing comment's "could not be confirmed" claim, and says to check whether the existing one is enough before adding another. It is: SONNY-146's comment of 2026-08-17 names both stale sites — this doc comment and its own closing comment — and states that closing comments are append-only, which is why it exists as a comment rather than an edit. Adding a second would have duplicated it and made the ticket's history harder to read, which is the failure mode the instruction was guarding against.

**A stale claim has a population, and a ticket's list of instances is not it.** SONNY-164's contract named two places calling the gzip question unverified: the `compressesRequestBody` doc comment and SONNY-146's closing comment. There were three. The third is `VisionModelClientTests.swift`'s doc comment on `theDefaultEndpointSendsAnUncompressedBodyWithNoContentEncoding` — the test that pins the very behaviour the measurement confirms — and it survived because the ticket was worked as a checklist rather than as a sweep. Caught by PR #77's review, fixed in this round. It is the same finding SONNY-183 records from the other side: the store count and the approval claim were each corrected in the file they were reported in and left standing elsewhere. **Work a records ticket by sweeping for the claim, then check that the ticket's list is a subset of what the sweep found — never the reverse.** The two remaining "unverified" instances live in the `fix/sonny-146-request-compression` entry, in its pitfalls list and its Open questions line, and are deliberately left: they record what that branch believed when it shipped, which is what a changelog is for.

**Line numbers into a file the same branch is editing are measured last, or not written at all.** Three of PR #77's six findings are one mistake in three costumes. §16.5 cited `VisionModelClient.swift:186` — correct at `fa22ef3`, and moved to `:191` by this branch's own SONNY-164 commit two commits later, so it was wrong before the branch was even pushed. This entry's leftovers bullet cited six line numbers in this file, five of which its own 52 lines had already shifted before it was committed — a bullet about stale records, made stale by its own insertion. And SONNY-138's closing comment carries the same `:186` and is append-only, so it needed a correction comment rather than an edit. **CLAUDE.md's rule is that every measurement carries the SHA it was taken at, and a `file:line` is a measurement** — but stamping a SHA that predates your own edits satisfies the letter and not the point. Where the reference points into a file the branch does not touch, stamp it and move on; where it points into a file the branch *is* touching, take the measurement after the last content edit, or give the grep and drop the number. **It then happened a fourth time, inside the round that fixed the first three.** The correction comment written for F4 published four changelog line numbers measured at `b781448` and stamped them at `cc6d40e` — the fix round's own four added lines had already moved all four. It was caught by re-running every published number against the SHA it named before reporting the round done, which is the only step that catches this class at all, and a fourth comment on SONNY-112 corrects it. **The habit that works is not "remember to re-measure" — it is "before you claim a measurement at a SHA, run it at that SHA".**

**The measurement was re-derived rather than carried, and every line number in SONNY-138 had moved.** The ticket's references are stamped at `9cfa090`: `VisionModelClient:117` was `:186` at `fa22ef3` and is `:191` now — moved by **this branch's own SONNY-164 commit**, which grew the doc comment above it by five lines — and `AgentViewModel`'s three URLSession-adjacent lines moved from `:778-779`/`:784` to `:999-1000`/`:1005`. The *finding* survived every move intact — nine files, eleven calls, six credential-bearing, `AgentViewModel` not among them — which is the argument for stamping a SHA rather than for not writing line numbers at all. §16.5 now carries the grep that regenerates them, since row 12 will move all of them again.

Behavior added (all in `scripts/mutate`; SONNY-175 adds no behaviour at all):
- **A second battery in one checkout is refused**, naming the run that holds the lock and the recovery, instead of interleaving with it.
- **The battery builds in a directory of its own** (`.build/mutate-scratch`), so another build in the same checkout cannot corrupt its artifacts, llbuild database or module cache.
- **`scripts/mutate unlock`** clears a lock left by a killed run, and refuses while its owner is alive.
- **A `MUTATE_TEST_CMD` that invokes SwiftPM without a scratch path is refused**, because an escape hatch that can undo a mechanism is part of the mechanism.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The plan format is untouched** — same five directives, same literal-byte matching, same `--only` and `--check`. SONNY-176's first non-goal, and the parse and pre-flight selftest groups that already covered it still pass unchanged.
- **The report is untouched apart from two added header lines.** Nothing was removed or renamed: the SHA line, the per-mutant outcome lines, the survivor block and both exit codes are as they were, and the checks that pin them (`KILLED by 1 test(s)`, `SURVIVORS`, exit 2, the SHA in the summary) still pass.
- **Mutants are applied and reverted exactly as before** — byte-exact backup, `cmp` after restore, `require_clean_tree_after` between mutants. SONNY-176's third non-goal.
- **The dirty-tree guard is unchanged and still fires first among the tree checks**, including its untracked-file half and the `status.showUntrackedFiles=no` hole PR #70 closed, and `--check` still refuses a dirty tree.
- **The interrupt path and the internal-error sentinel are unchanged** — a mid-mutant SIGTERM and a `set -u` death both still restore the file and exit non-zero, and each now also releases the lock.
- **The red-baseline abort, the no-match and ambiguous-match refusals, `--only`'s unknown-id error and the untracked-mutant-file refusal are unchanged.** 58 of the 95 selftest checks are the pre-existing ones, all still passing.
- **The reviewer agent's purpose and depth are unchanged**, SONNY-175's non-goal: five other bug-class bullets, the standing rule, the test command, the hand-trace instruction and the reporting instruction are byte-identical.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The lock is taken before the dirty-tree guard, and that ordering is the design rather than a detail of it.** A battery that is mid-mutant has a dirty tree *by construction*. So a second invocation that reaches `require_clean_tree` first is refused — but for the wrong reason, with a message that prints the mutated file and says "Commit or stash the paths above, then re-run." Followed, that advice commits a mutant. The selftest holds the ordering rather than the outcome: moving `acquire_lock` below `require_clean_tree` still exits 1 on the nested run, and reds precisely the two assertions that say the refusal is not the dirty-tree guard and never tells anyone to commit a mutant. **An exit code is not evidence when two different guards both exit 1 on the same input.**

**The lock lives in `.git/`, and each of the alternatives is wrong for a different reason.** In the working tree it would dirty the tree the very next check insists is clean. In `TMPDIR` it would be scoped to a user's shell environment rather than to a checkout. In `/tmp` it would be machine-wide, when the right scope is per-worktree — WORKFLOW.md already requires one `.build/` per worktree, so two worktrees running batteries share nothing and must not block each other. `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` answers `.git` in the main checkout and `.git/worktrees/<name>` in a linked one, which is exactly that scope, and `git status` never reports anything inside it.

**A refused invocation must never release the lock that refused it.** Knowing where the lock is and owning it are separate facts, so `LOCK_OWNED` is a flag of its own and `release_lock` tests it rather than testing `LOCK_DIR`. It is pinned from inside a live battery: the re-entering stand-in records whether the lock directory still existed after its nested run was refused.

**Isolation was chosen over detection because detection cannot be made complete, and a partial guard that reads as a complete one is the failure this whole script exists to stop.** A poller can watch for other `swift` processes, but a build that starts and finishes between two polls is invisible to it, and no shell script can ask the kernel what compiled into `.build/` while it was not looking. A private scratch directory does not have to notice anything: the other build writes `.build/`, the battery writes its own, and there is nothing to detect. What that leaves uncovered is enumerated in `--help` rather than implied away.

**What a shell script genuinely cannot reach, stated because it happened here rather than because it was imagined.** At 00:23:57 on 2026-08-20 a `git checkout main` and a `git pull` landed in this checkout while a cold build was running — the founder updating `main` after merging PR #75. The build died with `error: input file '.../WidgetVoiceEntryTests.swift' was modified during the build`, and the five files whose mtimes had moved were exactly the five that differ between `661b3df` and `ee9f650`. Neither mechanism in this branch covers that: a process that *writes* the tree, rather than one that builds beside it, is caught only after a mutant finishes, by `require_clean_tree_after`. It is the loud direction — it breaks the build outright rather than quietly changing a result — and it is in `--help`'s residue list for that reason.

**`ps -p <pid> -o command=` is the liveness test, not `kill -0`.** `kill -0` fails with EPERM against another user's process, which would read as "gone" and reclaim a live lock. `ps` answers presence, and the same call answers the pid-reuse question: a pid that exists but whose command line does not say "mutate" is a reused pid, not a battery. The one direction this reads wrong is a pid reused by anything that *does* say "mutate" — another battery, or an editor with the file open — and that error refuses a run rather than allowing two.

**Isolation does not change what is measured, and that was checked rather than argued.** At `ee9f650` the flagged command and the isolated one each reported 1410 tests in 111 suites, and a cold build of each carried the same six warning sites. Without that check the change would have traded one unverifiable claim for another.

**The default suite command is the one line no stand-in can reach, so the selftest reads it as text.** Every other check replaces `MUTATE_TEST_CMD`, which means `DEFAULT_TEST_CMD` — the command every real battery actually runs — is the single thing a selftest never executes, and it is also the line an edit would most plausibly undo by pasting CLAUDE.md's flagged command back over it. Three checks assert its shape against `$SELF`, and pasting the old command back reds all three.

**Each new guard was checked by breaking it, not by watching it pass.** Seven mutations of the harness, run against a copy: `acquire_lock` deleted; `acquire_lock` moved below the tree guard; `release_lock` no-oped; `lock_stale_reason` forced to always report stale and forced to never report stale; the isolation refusal disabled; the old shared-`.build/` command pasted back over the default. Each reds a different, nameable subset — 13, 5, 6, 15, 11, 4 and 3 checks respectively. A guard whose selftest passes either way is not a guard, which is the argument `scripts/mutate` was built on in the first place.

**A symbol checker would have found one of SONNY-175's five findings, and only if it looked in the right place.** Four of the five were live names attached to claims that had gone wrong — a retired workflow named in an agent's selection text, an enum described as having two cases when it has three, and two method signatures that do not compile — and no grep can see any of those. The fifth was two genuinely dead names, and the first version of the sweep *missed them*: it resolved every token against the whole tracked tree, and `docs/sonny-v1-implementation-changelog.md` still names both, because a changelog is a history. Resolving against `Sources/` and `Tests/` instead is what makes the check mean anything. **The durable rule: resolve an instruction about code against the code, never against the record of it** — and a sweep that reports everything resolving is a claim to check before it is a result to trust. Under the tightened method the four files went from 141 identifier tokens (136 live, 2 dead-but-in-the-changelog, 3 external) to 149 (146 live, 0 dead, the same 3 external), across 131 then 139 backticked spans.

**"Plain `swift test` will fail to link" was wrong about how it fails, and it said so in four places.** Sweeping CLAUDE.md turned up a second load-bearing claim, and this one is worse than a dead symbol because it misdirects a debugging session. Measured both ways at `4952a4a`: plain `swift test` fails at *compile*, `error: no such module 'Testing'`, with zero undefined symbols and no `ld:` error — it never reaches a link stage. Add `-Xswiftc -F` alone and it prints `Build complete!`, links cleanly, then dies at *run time* inside `swiftpm-testing-helper` with `Library not loaded: @rpath/Testing.framework`, which is what the two `-rpath` pairs fix. So each half of the flag set answers a different failure at a different stage, and neither of them is linking. The sentence lived in `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, `WORKFLOW.md` and `scripts/mutate`'s own header — one claim, four instances — and all four now say which flag fixes which failure. A fifth instance was deliberately left alone: `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/ShellSurfaceDetectorTests.swift` carries it inside a fixture that simulates a README rendered in a browser, so it is a test's input rather than a claim about this repository, and editing it would change what the test is fed for no reason. **A sweep has to be able to tell a claim from a quotation of one.**

**A sweep that does not exclude the file it is sweeping lets that file resolve its own symbols.** The version used on the agent files excluded a hard-coded `.claude` pathspec, which happened to be right there and is wrong everywhere else: pointed at `CLAUDE.md`, it would have counted every name that appears only in `CLAUDE.md` as resolving, because `CLAUDE.md` is in the tree it searches. It now derives the exclusions from its own argument list. That is the same self-reference hole as resolving against the changelog, met a second time from a different direction, and it is the second time on this branch that the sweep's own method had to be fixed before its result meant anything. **The method is the finding at least as often as the output is.**

**The two dead names are recorded here and deliberately not left in the file that used them.** The house style annotates a correction with what it replaced, and doing that here would have left `CommandCenterTaskActivitySurface` and `viewModel.hasTaskActivity` sitting in an instruction file — where a future sweep would flag them forever, training its reader to ignore the one bucket that matters. History belongs in this entry; the instruction file gets the live rule and a pointer.

**A ticket's description can be wrong about the tree, and the tree wins.** SONNY-175's description states that Command Center has no approval UI of its own, quoting CLAUDE.md's gotcha, and cites `.claude/rules/macagent-ui-conventions.md` as agreeing. It does not agree, and it is right not to: `CommandCenterAttentionPanel` is defined at `CommandCenterView.swift:813`, rendered at four call sites, switches on exactly `.permission` / `.clarification` / `.failure`, and is pinned by `CommandCenterAttentionSurfaceTests`. The bullet was rewritten from the code and the conventions file, per the ticket's own acceptance criterion that each correction says what the live rule is, sourced from where it actually lives. CLAUDE.md's copy of the same wrong claim was filed as **SONNY-180** rather than absorbed, and the founder then folded that ticket into this branch — so it is fixed here after all, from the same conventions section rather than rewritten from scratch, and the identical sentence in `README.md` line 22 went with it.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The default suite command is checked as text and never executed by the selftest.** Nothing in this process runs a real Swift build inside a selftest, so the evidence that the default works is the real battery at `7ee0664`, not the selftest.
- **`.build/mutate-scratch` is a second full build directory** — 830 MB here once warm, measured after the battery at `7ee0664`, against 1.6 GB for the whole of `.build/` — and it persists between runs, which is what makes every battery after the first incremental. The first battery in a checkout pays one cold build, about a minute and a half in this repository.
- **The lock cannot see a battery in another worktree, deliberately**, and a pid reused by anything whose command line says "mutate" reads as a live battery.
- **The sweep's own residue, stated rather than rounded off.** A backticked branch name is a false-positive class for it (`feature/ui-ux-wireframe-fidelity` is one, and its tokens only pass by coincidence). `qlmanage`, `output_dir` and `tspan` resolve to nothing in the repository and are correct as written — a macOS binary at `/usr/bin/qlmanage`, a placeholder in that same example command, and an SVG element name.

The Insights and Workspaces exports it names by way of example are supplied per session by the founder rather than living in the repository. - **The panel's precedence over the hint is unchanged.** `isMicHintSlotFree` has the same definition and the same two readers; what moved is where the rule about it is written, not what it decides.
- **The six-second auto-collapse is untouched.** It is the thing that *causes* the bug's setup — it takes the mic away under a stationary pointer — but nothing about it changed, and the fix works by not keeping a fact that its teardown can falsify.
- **Departure still ends the hint and cancels its countdown**, pinned directly now (`aDepartureClearsTheHintAndLeavesNothingCounting`) rather than only through the model.
- **The tracking area itself is unchanged** — same `rect: .zero`, same `[.mouseEnteredAndExited, .activeAlways, .inVisibleRect]`, same `updateTrackingAreas` re-registration, same one call site in the app. The `.activeAlways` reasoning from tracker #2/#21 stands untouched; this is a different failure with a different cause.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A stored copy of where the pointer is can only be corrected by a boundary crossing, and this one's boundary comes and goes.** SONNY-177 kept `isMicHovered` as "the pointer's truth" and drove the hint off it *changing*. Both events that write such a boolean — `mouseEntered` and `mouseExited` — require the pointer to cross the tracking area's edge **while that area exists**, and this area is created and destroyed with the mic button. The widget's own six-second auto-collapse removes the mic under a stationary pointer: no crossing, nothing writes `false`, and the boolean sits at `true` with the pointer nowhere near the mic. Expanding again and hovering wrote `true` over `true` — not a change — so the hook never ran and that hover showed nothing; leaving finally wrote `false`, the two agreed again, and every later hover worked. **Exactly one hover lost, and always the first**, which is the shape of the founder's report and the reason no time-based or layout-based explanation fits: anything periodic would recur.

**So the fix deletes the copy rather than repairing it.** Repairing it means finding every way the area can appear or disappear under a stationary pointer — the collapse, the panel being ordered out, the view being torn down — and writing the boolean by hand at each, which is a list that has to stay complete forever. An arrival is an event; there is no second answer to "is the pointer here" left to disagree with the pointer. **The general rule, worth carrying past this file: derive from an event when the thing you want is an event, and keep state only for facts that outlive the events that set them.** The hint's own visibility is such a fact, which is why `MicHoverHintModel` is unchanged.

**Two `show`s in a row became reachable, and the suite already said what happens.** `showingAgainReplacesTheCountdownRatherThanAddingASecond` was written under SONNY-177 as a contract for a caller that did not exist, its comment arguing that the edge design made it unreachable. It is reachable now — two arrivals with no departure delivered is exactly the sequence the old boolean swallowed — and the behaviour it pinned is the correct one. A test written for a caller that does not exist yet paid for itself one ticket later; the comment is corrected rather than the test.

**A test that reaches past the entry point the app uses proves the wrong thing, and a battery only catches it if the battery is aimed one layer down.** This branch's own plan asked whether `TrackingNSView` calls its closure on every arrival — it does, and M4 says so. It never asked what the thing on the *other end* of that closure does with a repeat, because the test wired `onEnter` straight to `MicHoverHintModel.show`, while the app wires it to `micHintPointerEnteredMic` and thence to `pointerArrived`. So a mutant adding `guard visibleHint == nil else { return }` inside `pointerArrived` — the shipped bug re-expressed exactly one layer down — survived the whole suite. Found by PR #75's review as F1, reproduced here at `7e68354` before believing it, and fixed by wiring the test the way the app is wired rather than by adding a test beside it. **The general shape: when a fix creates a single entry point, the tests for that fix have to enter through it, or the entry point is untested precisely where it matters most.** It is the same lesson as the slot rule two paragraphs down, arriving one layer up.

**The fix removes an absorber, and that is a real cost rather than a free win.** The old design was level-triggered: a second `mouseEntered` with no departure between wrote `true` over `true` and did nothing. That was the bug — and it also meant a duplicate arrival could never re-show the hint. Every arrival now re-shows it and re-arms the three seconds. `TrackingNSView.updateTrackingAreas` removes and re-adds its tracking area on every geometry change, and the mic's frame does change each time the 40pt row appears and disappears, so *if* AppKit delivers a further `mouseEntered` after such a re-registration with the pointer still inside, the hint would return after timing out — exactly what SONNY-177 was built to stop. **Nothing here establishes whether it does**: no test in this process can, and the branch did not guess at it. Raised as F3 by PR #75's review and answered the only way it can be — a manual item that keeps the pointer moving inside the button for ten seconds, since the item beside it deliberately keeps the pointer still and is the one condition that would not catch it. If that item fails, the first thing to try is *not* re-introducing an absorber (that is the bug): `.inVisibleRect` documents that the area stays synchronized with the visible rect on its own, so the re-registration in `updateTrackingAreas` looks redundant, and adding it once instead of on every geometry change would remove the only mechanism named here by which a duplicate could be manufactured. Recorded as a first move, not as a change made on speculation.

**A rule written as an `if` in a view is a mutant nothing kills.** The first battery run found the slot check unheld: `if isMicHintSlotFree { show } else { dismiss }` could be replaced by an unconditional `show` and the whole suite still passed. It was inherited from SONNY-177's `onChange` hook rather than introduced here, but it sat in code this ticket had just rewritten, so it was closed rather than recorded — `MicHoverHintModel.pointerArrived(slotIsFree:hint:)` now owns the rule and three mutants die on it. What is left in the view is which boolean it hands over, which is genuinely view wiring. **The hint is passed as a closure, not a resolved value**, so "an arrival with the slot taken does not even ask what it would have shown" is observable; a caller that resolved it anyway would make that unfalsifiable.

**An `NSView` is testable in a way a SwiftUI view is not, and that is worth reaching for.** `MicHoverArrivalTests` builds the real `TrackingNSView`, constructs real `NSEvent.enterExitEvent` crossings, and sends them to the real overrides — no seam added for the test's benefit. That covers strictly more than the model tests do: it is the only place that says an arrival repeating itself is still an arrival. What stays out of reach is `makeNSView`/`updateNSView` handing the closures over and what `FloatingWidgetView` puts in them; the manual items are the verification for those, as ever.

**The new sentence was re-measured, not assumed to fit because it is shorter.** At the row's real font (SF Pro Medium 10) against the 444pt the 472pt frame leaves after its 14pt padding: **189.6pt**, against the old sentence's 285.4pt and the configuration message's unchanged 254.1pt. The method was validated by reproducing SONNY-177's two figures exactly before trusting it on the new one. The frame is untouched and the window controller's fitted-size positioning needed no revisiting.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **No session verified any of this visually.** The mechanism is pinned by tests and a battery; that the first hover now works *in the packaged app* is the founder's manual item, and it is the only thing that settles it. The three-second feel and the new sentence are likewise his.
- **F3's re-registration question is open and untested**, above. It is a risk the design takes on knowingly, answered by a manual item rather than by a test, because no test in this process can settle it.
- **Residual A on SONNY-177 is still open** and now reads three seconds: nothing pins that `MicHoverHintModel` counts for the duration it was handed, so a mutant hardcoding the shipping delay inside the sleep survives. Harmless while `micHoverReminderDismissDelay` is the only non-`nil` delay any caller passes; real the moment a second one exists.
- Nothing deferred, no new tickets filed: everything SONNY-179 asked for landed on this branch.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none. The wording is the founder's own, given verbatim on the ticket 2026-08-19; the three seconds is his call from the same pass.

Nothing removed; one test renamed (`theConfigurationMessageIsTheOneTheUserHasAlwaysSeen` → `theConfigurationMessageNamesNoProviderAndStillSaysWhatToDo`) because its old name asserted permanence for a sentence this branch changes. **Mutation battery via `scripts/mutate`: 12/12 killed, 0 survived at `5508b6c`** — twelve mutants covering the four pinned behaviours (the timeout, the re-arm, the no-timeout variant, cancellation on early exit) plus the copy decision and the shipped bug restored verbatim (M9: the reminder given no delay, which is exactly the behaviour the founder asked to change). Behavior added:
- The mic's hover hint clears itself roughly four seconds after it appears, with the pointer still on the mic. Hovering away and back shows it again with a fresh four seconds.
- With voice unconfigured the hint shows the configuration message instead of the shortcut reminder, and that one stays for the whole hover — it reports something broken and what to do about it, so it does not clear itself.
- The configuration message is provider-neutral: "No API key is set up. Add one, then relaunch Sonny." It is one constant, and the hover, the mic press and the push-to-talk hotkey all render it.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The shortcut reminder's wording is unchanged** — moved from a literal in the view to a named constant on the view model, and pinned by exact match so that moving it could not quietly reword it. A mutant that rewords it dies (M11).
- **What pressing the mic does is unchanged apart from the sentence.** The guard, the persistence flag and the refusal path are untouched; SONNY-173's own tests (both surfaces' `errorMessage` and `errorIsPersistent` compared) still pass unmodified.
- **The two class guards still pass unmodified** — no view reads either half of voice readiness, and no `.disabled` predicate gates on the actionable half. The new file was written to keep that true in its *comments* as well as its code (see below).
- **Hover on every other control is untouched**: `AlwaysActiveHoverTracker` has exactly one call site in the app, the mic, and this branch did not change the tracker, its options or where it is attached.
- **The panel's precedence over the hint is unchanged** — `hasVisibleWidgetPanel` was neither read differently nor edited; what is new is that losing the slot now also cancels a countdown.
- **The six-second auto-collapse timer is untouched.** The hint's countdown is a second instance of the same shape, not a change to that one, and the two do not interact.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**"The pointer is here" and "the hint is showing" stopped being one boolean, and that is the whole shape of this change.** While the hint lived exactly as long as the hover, `isMicHovered` could be both facts at once. A hint that times out under a stationary pointer makes them independent: the pointer is still there and the hint is gone. `isMicHovered` therefore stays strictly the pointer's — which is what keeps re-entry detectable, since a second hover is just a `false` → `true` transition of it — and `MicHoverHintModel.visibleHint` is the hint's. Overloading the old one would have made a second hover indistinguishable from a hover already served.

**The unconfigured hint renders the blocker's own text rather than a second string, so "one condition, one voice" is structural.** The obvious build is a new short literal for the hint beside the existing one for the press. That is two strings for one condition, and SONNY-173 is the record of what two strings for one condition do — they drift, and nobody notices until a user sees the two answers. `micHoverHintPresentation` takes the message from the same place the press takes it, so the hover and the press cannot disagree, and SONNY-136 rewrites one constant rather than hunting for the second.

**The delay travels with the message rather than sitting beside it as a constant.** The two variants differ in kind, not in duration: one is a reminder that must leave, the other reports something broken and must not. Modelling that as `autoDismissDelay: Duration?` on the presentation means a third variant cannot be added without someone deciding which of the two it behaves like, and it puts the whole rule — text and lifetime together — at one address on the view model, where the view is already obliged to get its answer.

**The countdown lives on a small view-scoped object because a view cannot be asked what it renders.** This is SONNY-173's lesson applied to a timer instead of a predicate: written inline as `@State` in `FloatingWidgetView` the countdown would be enforced by nothing but a reader noticing, exactly like the existing six-second `autoDismissTask`, which no test can reach. `MicHoverHintModel` exposes its live `Task`, so tests await the real countdown rather than sleeping past it — every test in the new suite finishes in milliseconds and none of them races.

**The guard test scans comments, not just code.** `theCompositeVoiceReadinessIsReadInOneFileOnly` reads each file under `Sources/MacAgent` as raw text, so a doc comment that merely *names* `canUseVoice` or `voiceConfigurationBlocker` fails it as loudly as a real read would. Every new comment in `MicHoverHint.swift` and `FloatingWidgetView.swift` describes the rule without naming the properties — which is why they read the way they do, and is the first thing to know before editing them.

**A hint is gated at show time, not at render time, and the difference is a real bug.** The row only renders when the panel and the compact capsule are both absent, so it is tempting to let the render condition be the whole gate. But a hover that begins while the panel is up would then set the hint's state anyway, and it would appear the instant the panel closed — a flicker attached to nothing the user just did, and for the configuration variant it would wait there indefinitely, having no countdown to expire. So entering only shows the hint when the slot is already free, losing the slot dismisses and cancels, and the slot coming back free deliberately does not re-show: the hint returns on the next real hover.

**What the countdown does under this panel's unusual conditions, stated because a timer here does not live in ordinary circumstances.** The app being inactive changes nothing — this is Swift concurrency, not a run-loop timer, so it is tied to neither key-window status nor an event-tracking run-loop mode, the two ways a naive `Timer` would have stalled precisely when this always-visible, rarely-key panel is most likely to be hovered. Across machine sleep the countdown keeps counting: `Task.sleep(for:)` measures on `ContinuousClock`, which advances while the Mac is asleep, so four seconds spent asleep are spent and the hint is already gone on the first frame after wake — the wanted behaviour for a reminder, and the default rather than something arranged. Occlusion is not a state anything here observes: a countdown started before another window covered the widget still fires on time, and the reverse cannot arise because a covered widget receives no mouse-entered event. **None of those three is exercised by the suite** — sleep and occlusion are not reachable from a test process, and App Nap could in principle stretch four seconds for an app the system considers idle, which would show up as a hint lingering rather than as anything incorrect.

**A measured frame, not an assumed one.** The row is a real layout row participating in `fixedSize()`, and the window controller's positioning reads that fitted size, so new copy is a sizing question rather than a wording one. Both sentences were laid out at the row's real font (SF Pro Medium 10) against the 444pt the 472pt frame leaves after its 14pt padding: the reminder is 285.4pt and the configuration message 254.1pt. Both are comfortable single lines, the frame is unchanged, and the positioning needed no revisiting. Worth keeping for the next copy change — even the old provider-naming sentence measured 419.1pt and would have fitted.

**The ticket's own count of the provider-naming strings was off by one, in a way worth recording.** SONNY-177 states that four user-visible strings name `OPENAI_API_KEY` at `b8534f5`, plus a fifth in a planner message. Recounted here: **four sites carrying five literals** — `AgentViewModel.swift:702` (this branch's), `PermissionReadinessService.swift:78` (two literals, the set and unset halves of one readiness row), `OpenAITranscriber.swift:12` and `OpenAIPlanner.swift:22`. The ticket's "two above" counted the hint's new message, which did not exist at that SHA and does not name the variable now that it does. Everything except `AgentViewModel.swift:702` is SONNY-136's and untouched here. One handoff note for that session: its own list names `AgentViewModel.swift:1377` and `:2090` as duplicates of this sentence, which SONNY-173 has since collapsed into the single `missingAPIKeyVoiceMessage` constant this branch rewrote — one constant to change, not two call sites to find.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Nothing about this is verified visually or interactively by any session.** The countdown's state machine is pinned; the view's three call sites into it — pointer in/out, the slot being taken, the view disappearing — are view wiring that no agent can drive, and the four-second feel is a judgement only the founder can make. The five manual items are the verification, not a formality on top of one.

- Nothing deferred, no new tickets filed: everything SONNY-177 asked for landed on this branch.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**A disabled control is a silent one, so a `.disabled` predicate may only hold reasons that clear on their own.** That is the whole of SONNY-173 stated as a rule. `canUseVoice` folded one *configuration* failure the user could act on together with five *transient* states, and a disabled SwiftUI button never invokes its action — so the guard inside `startVoiceRecording`, which already held the right message, could not be reached from the mic at all. Nothing was missing. The fix names the two halves separately and lets only the transient half reach `.disabled`. **Written to outlive its trigger:** SONNY-136 deletes every provider environment variable and takes `hasAPIKey` with it, which changes what `voiceConfigurationBlocker` reports and nothing else. The tests state their configuration failure through an injected override with a *different* message than the API-key one, precisely so they keep meaning the same thing afterwards.

**The whole predicate moved onto the view model, because a view cannot be asked what it rendered.** An expression written inline in SwiftUI is enforced by a reader noticing, which is how the configuration term got in. As a named property it has one address, one doc comment, and a test that fails when it moves — and the mutation that reverts the *view* line alone (M11) dies against the two source-scan guards, which is the half a view-model test could never cover.

**A `.commandCenter` default with no caller is not evidence of a caller.** The ticket asked for the enumeration rather than an inference from the default, and grep cannot resolve a receiver, so it was taken with a deprecation probe over the compiled package: `toggleVoiceRecording` has **exactly one** call site, `FloatingWidgetView.micButton`, passing `.widget` explicitly; `canUseVoice` had **exactly three** read sites, the two guards and the one `.disabled`. The doc comment claiming a Command Center composer had been stale since that composer was deleted on 2026-07-21. The default is kept, and now says why: the origin reaches `dispatchTranscribedCommand`, where `fromComposer: origin == .widget` decides whether a dispatch may consume a pending workspace-card binding, so a future caller that forgets inherits the answer that consumes nothing.

**The neutral fill was never too transparent — it was too light, and the token was never at fault.** SONNY-174's own diagnosis reads "a white glyph on a 17%-opacity grey fill over translucent glass", which names the right token and the wrong rendering. `WidgetTintedButtonBackground` has two branches, and a non-nil `tint` takes the one that lays `Color.white.opacity(0.94)` down first and composites the tint over it in `.plusDarker`. That recipe is what turns a solid accent into a solid button; run `rgba(153,153,153,.17)` through it and the result is **#EDEDED at alpha 0.95** — a white glyph at **1.16–1.31:1**, which is invisible and reads exactly as the founder put it, "too light for anyone to figure it out." This half held up under review.

**The first fix was wrong, and the reason is the one fact neither the ticket nor the first attempt established: this button has no backdrop of its own.** The composer row is `HStack { composerPill; dontSaveButton; micButton }`, only `composerPill` carries `.widgetGlassPill()`, the enclosing stack has no background, and `FloatingWidgetWindowController` sets the panel fully transparent. So the two circular buttons composite onto **whatever window the user has behind the widget** — never onto the widget's dark glass. Every other untinted-variant button in the app lives inside a `Widget*Panel`, which does sit on glass; `tint: nil` put this one outside that set. **The Deny precedent was true about the code path and did not transfer to the compositing**, which is exactly the kind of claim the enumerate-before-you-subtract rule exists to catch — the code path was enumerated and the surface it draws on was not.

**The consequence, measured over the real backdrop rather than a panel.** `tint: nil` took the fill from 95% opaque to **17%** opaque — the opposite of the ticket's own first lever, "give the fill real presence". It read as darker only because the thing showing through happened to be dark in the case that was checked. Over a white window the two treatments are not merely close, they are **identical**: with a white destination `plusDarker` reduces to the source, so both collapse to `0.932000` and a **1.16:1** glyph. On a white window the first fix was a no-op on screen. Across the sweep the shipped-then-reverted treatment swung 1.16:1 → 17.40:1 purely with the user's desktop. (PR #73 review, F1; the collapse was recomputed independently before the fix round accepted it.)

**The fix that holds: an opaque fill, `tint: WidgetTheme.panelBase`.** An opaque tint resolves through the tinted branch to exactly itself at alpha 1 (`αs = 1` makes the composite the source), which is why `micButton` beside it and this button's own on state were already backdrop-proof and this one was not. **Which token was enumerated over the whole set rather than picked.** System B has ten colour tokens; two are translucent (`neutralButtonFill`, `textMuted`) and the finding disqualifies both. Of the eight opaque ones, five are accents that already mean something — `primaryAction` is this button's own on state, `secondaryCircular` is the mic 12pt away, and `allowAction`/`errorGlyph`/`taskFailureRetry` carry Allow, error and retry — and the remaining two are opaque non-accents disqualified for a different reason: `hairline` draws this same button's rim and `textFull` its glyph, so either as the fill erases the layer it would have to contrast with (each measures 1.00:1 against it). `panelBase` is the one that remains, and the best of them on the numbers. Measured across a backdrop swept 0.0 to 1.0, all constant: white glyph **17.40:1**, hairline rim **3.41:1** against its own fill, **5.38:1** between off and the untouched on state — the widest of any candidate, and a glyph well past the mic's own shipped 2.23:1. An opaque fill matches *some* backdrop at every value (worst case 1.01:1 here, 1.00:1 for both neighbours), which is why the rim, the top highlight and the shadow draw the silhouette — all three backdrop-independent too. On is unchanged at solid `#0091FF`.

**No new token, and the candidate worth adding measures worse.** The ticket permits one only if an existing token genuinely cannot serve. The natural candidate was §3.1's neutral fill pre-composited over `panelBase` and made opaque, `#303030` — the appearance the design actually draws, where a panel exists. It measures **glyph 13.20:1, rim 2.94:1, 4.08:1 from the on state**, worse than `panelBase` on all three. So the rule resolves without needing an exception.

**The shadow rides with the branch, and that is right here rather than merely tolerated.** Only the shadow keys off `tint == nil`; the hairline rim and the white top highlight are unconditional. A non-nil tint carries the heavier `black 0.45 / r12 / y6`, and §3.1 pairs its lighter `0.04 / r8 / y4` with the neutral variant — which is a button *on a panel* that already supplies separation. This button has nothing under it, so the heavier shadow is what separates it from a bright desktop, and it now matches the mic and its own on state, so the row carries one shadow instead of two. Under `tint: nil` the shadow got lighter at exactly the moment the fill stopped drawing the shape, which compounded F1 rather than offsetting it.

**Only the fill lever was used.** The other available lever, a non-white glyph when off, stays unused: a white glyph on an opaque `#1A1A1A` fill is at 17.40:1, and darkening it would hand back contrast the fill just won.

**Those numbers are arithmetic, not eyesight, and the distinction is the point.** They are Porter-Duff source-over with `kCGBlendModePlusDarker` as CoreGraphics defines it (`B(Cb,Cs) = max(0, Cb+Cs−1)`), WCAG relative luminance from linearised sRGB. The backdrop is the **screen**, swept 0.0 to 1.0 and reported at every point including white — which is the correction F2 demanded, because the first round swept the *panel's* colour and the panel is not what this control sits on. **No automated test can judge legibility, and none was written pretending to.** The tests were rebuilt around what is genuinely checkable and is the property that failed: every fill the composer row can render is fully opaque, `neutralButtonFill` is translucent and therefore panel-only, no button passes it as a tint, `FloatingWidgetView`'s own chrome never uses the on-glass treatment, and the control's two states use two different opaque tokens. That is a regression guard, not proof that either state reads correctly. The founder's eye is the verification, and the tests' own doc comments say so.

**The lesson worth keeping is about which surface a claim is measured against.** Every figure in the first round was arithmetically correct and answered the wrong question, because the swept variable was the panel's colour and the control is not on the panel. Enumerating the *code path* — which branch of `WidgetTintedButtonBackground` runs, and that the Deny button takes the same one — is not the same as enumerating the *surface the pixels land on*, and one was done and the other was not. The repo's enumerate-before-you-subtract rule reads naturally as being about call sites; this is the same failure in a dimension that has no call sites at all.

**A test that presses a control must fail closed, not carry on.** The transient-state tests press push-to-talk to prove silence, and a press that gets past the guard reaches `AVCaptureDevice.requestAccess`, which a `swift test` process has no bundle identity to survive. Under mutation that is not hypothetical — several of these mutants make voice *available* in exactly the state the test then presses in. So every press in `WidgetVoiceEntryTests` sits behind `try #require(canUseVoice == false)` rather than `#expect`: a broken gate ends the test on the spot. Without it the battery's own mutants would have driven the machine's microphone.

**The wipe's forcing test earned its keep again.** Adding one stored property to `AgentViewModel` failed `everyAgentViewModelStoredPropertyIsClassifiedAgainstTheLocalDataWipe` immediately, exactly as designed — the fourth time that enumeration would otherwise have been missed. The seam is classified `outsideTheWipe` beside `visionSessionEnvironment`, for the same reason: it is injected infrastructure, not user data.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **`voiceConfigurationBlockerOverride` is production surface that exists for tests.** Accepted deliberately: the repo's own comment on `voiceCannotConsumeAnArmWhileAClarificationIsPending` had already recorded the alternative — "that half is readable, not testable, and its proof is the declaration" — and a ticket whose acceptance criteria demand a mutation-proved test of the no-key press cannot be met by a declaration. It is `nil` in the shipping app, nothing under `Sources/` assigns it, and it follows `visionSessionEnvironment`'s established seam precedent.
- **SONNY-109, the whole-product UI/UX pass, may revisit the "Don't save this task" control wholesale.** This is a legibility fix inside the existing design language and does not pre-empt that; the code comment at the control still records that the control was proposed on session judgment with no wireframe to defer to.
- **Neither fix is verified visually by any session.** No agent can see the live app; both tickets' manual-test items are the real check and are carried into the PR. SONNY-174's light-window item is the one the review predicted would fail against the first attempt, and it is the one that closes this.
- **Residual (a) — closed, in `5276a40`.** The two SONNY-173 class guards left one hole between them: `noDisabledPredicateInTheAppGatesOnAnActionableFailure` scans only inside `.disabled(`, and `theCompositeVoiceReadinessIsReadInOneFileOnly` scanned only for `canUseVoice`, so a view written `if viewModel.voiceConfigurationBlocker == nil { micButton }` would hide the mic exactly when the user has something to fix — SONNY-173's silence rebuilt out of the actionable half alone — and pass both. Nothing did this; it earns the line because it is the obvious wrong fix someone reaches for. The second guard now scans both terms. **Verified in both directions rather than shipped because it looked right:** mutant R1, expressing that hypothetical view, *survived the entire 1399-test suite* at `6932dd7` and is killed at `5276a40` by `theCompositeVoiceReadinessIsReadInOneFileOnly` alone. The assertion still holds unmutated because `AgentViewModel.swift` is the only file under `Sources/MacAgent` containing that term. The test's name is deliberately unchanged — it now under-describes what it scans, but is not false, and renaming would strand the battery records that cite it; its doc comment and failure message name both terms instead.
- **Residual (b) — still open and deliberately unactioned.** `reportVoiceRefusal`'s doc says it "stays silent when the refusal was transient"; it stays silent when the refusal is *only* transient — with no key and a run in flight the hotkey still reports the key message. That behaviour predates the branch and is arguably right; the sentence is what is imprecise.
- **One further residual, outside both tickets and not actioned.** `.claude/agents/sonny-code-reviewer.md:21` still instructs a reviewer agent to look for "a new Command Center page with the command composer that doesn't render `CommandCenterTaskActivitySurface` behind `viewModel.hasTaskActivity`" — present tense, and both symbols are gone from `Sources/` and `Tests/` entirely. So F3's sweep claim above, that every other mention already says the composer is gone, is **one site short**: true of production and docs, not of the agent-instruction files. Corrected here rather than left standing; the file is outside both tickets and untouched. (Found by the cycle-2 verification.)

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: not a roadmap row — two founder-found defects from the 2026-08-19 manual pass. Rows D, E, J and 12 are unaffected, and SONNY-136 remains the ticket that will change what `voiceConfigurationBlocker` reports.

**Mutation battery: 7 mutants, 7 killed at `33c5866`** via `scripts/mutate` (logs `.build/mutate/33c5866-20260819T141642`), and the route there is the more useful record. At `81416e2`, M1–M5 were 5/5 killed: **M1** the microphone seam ignored, reverted to the direct `AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .audio)` call; **M5** `.restricted` no longer sharing `.denied`'s row; **M2** `deterministic(microphoneStatus:)` substituting a live checker; **M3** and **M4** the consolidated stub dropping the grants-on-request flip and the request counting the five absorbed stubs had. **M6** and **M7** — `makeExecutor`'s and `VisionTestContext`'s readiness defaults reverted to a live `PermissionReadinessService()` — **survived** at `81416e2`, and that survival is the finding this branch's last commit answers: they die at `33c5866` against `LivePermissionCheckerScanTests`.

Behavior added:
- `MicrophonePermissionChecking` and `SystemMicrophonePermissionChecker` in `PermissionReadinessService.swift`, with `PermissionReadinessService.init` taking the checker defaulted to the system one. The seam vends `AVAuthorizationStatus` rather than a boolean.
- `LivePermissionCheckerScanTests` — a source scan over both test targets, recursively, forbidding `SystemScreenCapturePermissionChecker(`, `SystemMicrophonePermissionChecker(` and `PermissionReadinessService(`. **The readiness token deliberately carries no closing parenthesis**: matching the argument-free form let partial injection through, since both checkers are defaulted and a call naming only the screen one is still a live authorization read (F3). It also requires every value handed to a `permissionReadinessService:` parameter to be `.deterministic(...)`, because `.init()` is a construction that never spells the type (cycle-2 C1).
- `.requiresUnprivilegedProcess`, a condition trait defined once per test target, on the four tests that force a filesystem failure with directory permission bits.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims): `PermissionReadinessService.currentStatus` returns the same eight items in the same order with the same copy — both its production call sites (`AgentViewModel.refreshPermissions`, `PermissionReadinessCapabilityAdapter`) are untouched and both new init parameters default to the live implementations, so a shipped build reads exactly the TCC and AVFoundation state it read before. `VisionSessionContainment.checkIterationStart`'s guard order is byte-identical; only its doc comment changed. The five hand-rolled stubs' behaviour is preserved where anything reads it, which is narrower than "member for member" and was corrected from that after review: `FixedAccessibilityGrant.hasScreenRecordingPermission()` returned the single `trusted` flag, and its replacement leaves screen recording granted while accessibility is false. Inert, because `VisionSessionContainment` reads `permissionChecker` at exactly one site and asks only `isAccessibilityTrusted()`, and the substitution is documented at the call site. M3 and M4 exist to prove the two behaviours most easily lost in a merge (the accessibility grant flipping on request, the request counts `ScreenAccessOnboardingTests` asserts) are still load-bearing. `ScreenCaptureService`'s two permission gates, `ScreenAccessOnboardingModel`'s relaunch state machine, and the vision session's mid-run revocation stop all keep their existing assertions unchanged.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The microphone seam is detectable in a way the screen seam structurally is not, and that is the reason it vends the platform enum.** `ScreenCapturePermissionChecking` answers preflight booleans, so no test can distinguish an injected `true` from a machine that genuinely has the grant — the SONNY-103 lineage's recorded limit, and why its protection is inheritance rather than detection. The microphone is the one permission macOS reports four-valued. Asking for all four statuses in a single test makes the seam's own correctness machine-independent: no single live status satisfies more than two of the four expectations, because `.denied` and `.restricted` share a row and nothing else does, so at least two assertions fail on any machine. Re-encoding those four cases into a boolean would have thrown away exactly the property that makes the pin work.

**Three of the ticket's four findings had the wrong population, and every line number in it was stale.** The stub count was recorded as four and is six (the shared checker plus two more arrived with `feature/terminal-screen-check`); the root-dependent test count was recorded as two and is four (`aFailedIdBackfillRewriteStillReturnsTheDecodedRecords` and `whenTheRowDeleteFailsTheScreenRecordIsAlreadyGoneAndTheRowSurvives` arrived with `feature/task-history-controls`). Both undercounts came from the same cause: the ticket was measured at a branch head that no longer exists, and the branches that unblocked it were the branches that grew the populations. Fixing half a population leaves section D unsatisfied, so the sweep was re-run rather than trusted — `grep -rn posixPermissions Tests/` for the second, and the protocol's own required method for the first, since a conformance can be declared in ways a type-name grep misses.

**The root-dependency's failure direction is the opposite of what the ticket recorded, and the difference matters.** The finding says the affected tests "would report the opposite of what they pin". Each of the four actually asserts on the *consequence* of the forced failure — a file left unrewritten, a failed path reported by name, a history row that survived — so under root the operation succeeds and the test **fails**. A red suite naming a defect that is not there, not a flattering green. Still machine state deciding a result, and still section D's business, but the SONNY-103 comparison ("failed in the flattering direction") does not transfer.

**A source file belongs to exactly one target here, so one shared stub for both targets needs a `Package.swift` edit.** Both test targets declare an explicit `path:`, which is what makes the file-to-target mapping exclusive. **The first version of this paragraph also said a test target cannot depend on another test target, and that is false** (PR #72 F2) — verified by building it, not by re-reading documentation: a minimal package on this repository's own settings (`swift-tools-version: 6.0`, `platforms: [.macOS(.v14)]`) declaring `.testTarget(name: "BTests", dependencies: ["Lib", "ATests"])` compiles, `import ATests` resolves, and a B test calling an A helper links and passes. The conclusion survives — sharing one file is still a `Package.swift` edit and still the founder's call — but the price was misstated: it may be one line adding `"MacAgentCoreTests"` to the app target's dependencies plus making the stub `public`, rather than a new target. A dedicated test-support target is probably still the better design; the point is that the cheaper option was ruled out on an impossibility that does not exist, and a repository that treats DRY as non-negotiable should get that choice on true premises. One shared stub *per* target is the most consolidation there is short of that, and it is what the ticket's own finding asked for. The build-graph change was not made: it is the founder's call, not a session's, and the ticket did not scope it. The two copies are twinned with a cross-reference in each header. The one thing deliberately not duplicated is the microphone stub, because `currentStatus` is unreachable from the app target's tests.

**A mutation can disprove a comment about a mutation, and did.** This test's first doc comment claimed that substituting a live checker into `deterministic(microphoneStatus:)` would survive, reasoning by analogy from the screen-side pin's recorded inheritance-not-detection limit. It does not survive — that mutant makes all four expectations answer from one live status. Ignoring an argument and defaulting an argument are different mutations, and only running both told them apart. The real survivors were a *fixture's* default reverting to a live service (M6, M7), which is genuinely undetectable by any assertion, because the deterministic default is a state a real Mac can also be in. That is why the answer was a source scan rather than a stronger assertion: the property is about what the source says, so it is pinned where it lives. Same shape as `RedactedPayload`'s construction-site enumeration, and the same comment-filtering care — the scan skips comment-*prefixed* lines rather than every line containing `//`, which is the narrower grep this repo was bitten by during row C.

**The app target's readiness seam is latent, not live, and that was enumerated rather than assumed.** `AgentViewModel.init` also defaults `permissionReadinessService` to a live one, across nine constructions in **nine** files, one each (the count first written here said eight files; corrected after review). None of them makes a live read: `PermissionReadinessService.init` only stores its checkers, and the only two paths to `currentStatus` are `AgentViewModel.refreshPermissions()` — called from `CommandCenterView` and `AppDelegate`, neither exercised by a test — and `PermissionReadinessCapabilityAdapter`, which needs a `.showPermissionReadiness` plan step no test in that target builds. So those nine files were left untouched rather than churned, and the source scan now fails if a future fixture there constructs a live service anyway. Confirmed empirically after the fix round: a whole-suite marker probe on all three live checkers, run single-threaded, reports **zero** reads from either target.
