Re-run twice after the PR #68 records round, same figure: that round changed comment text inside `.swift` files and nothing else, which `git diff` over non-comment lines in `Sources/` confirms is empty. Branch point `64e4d20` measured on this branch: **1289 in 95**, so **+1 test, +0 suites**, which is the one new literal pin.

Behavior added:
- Termius is refused. Sonny will not control `com.termius-dmg.mac` through either door, and the refusal is the same non-negotiable terminal sentence every other entry produces.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The other ten entries, unchanged**, and every list-driven test still drives off the list itself rather than a hand-copy — so the new entry is exercised by `everyListedTerminalIsRefusedThroughTheResolvedAppDoor`, `bothDoorsAgreeOnEveryListedTerminal` and the uppercase spelling assertions without any of them being edited.
- **`normalize` is untouched**, and it is what makes this entry survive the same way `com.apple.terminal` does: Launch Services reports `com.apple.Terminal` with a capital T while the list stores lowercase, and the comparison holds only because `normalize` trims and lowercases with Swift's locale-independent `String.lowercased()` rather than `NSString.lowercased(with:)`, whose Turkish `I` folds to `ı`. Load-bearing, and resting on one small function nobody is likely to think about again.
- **The screen check and its ordering.** `ShellSurfaceDetector` is untouched as behaviour; the deny list still refuses first, at three doors and again per iteration, above it.
- **Nothing was built for the embedded-shell case.** The founder put it out of scope on 2026-08-17. This branch declines to extend that layer rather than removing one.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **The entry is on the rule, not on the word "terminal".** §7.4's test is *arbitrary shell execution with the user's full rights*, which an SSH session meets on the far machine. The list had been built around terminal emulators — a narrower idea than the rule it implements. So this **aligns the list with the rule rather than widening the rule**, and that framing is what makes the next app's decision answerable instead of a fresh argument.
- **`com.termius-dmg.mac` is the whole lesson.** A plausible identifier typed from memory is `com.termius.mac`; the real one carries a `-dmg` packaging artefact nobody would infer. A wrong identifier **fails open** — it matches nothing while sitting in the list looking like coverage — so a guess is worse than an absence. `termiusIsOnTheListUnderTheIdentifierLaunchServicesActuallyHolds` pins the string character for character *and* asserts `com.termius.mac` stays eligible, so a well-meant tidy-up fails a test rather than silently un-banning an SSH client.
- **One method was not enough, and the disagreement is the useful part.** Launch Services' handler registry (`NSWorkspace.urlsForApplications(toOpen:)`) found Termius; scanning every app bundle's `CFBundleURLTypes` found only Terminal and iTerm. Termius is LS's registered default `ssh://` handler while declaring no such scheme in its own bundle — so the more obvious method would have missed the single app the question was about. **Anyone repeating this sweep asks the handler registry.**
- **The evidence record needed a third group, not a bigger second one.** "Established from Launch Services' handler registry on the founder's Mac" is a different claim from "read off a bundle's `Info.plist`", and collapsing them into "verified on a machine" would erase the method finding above. `theEvidenceSplitMatchesTheList` now holds three mutually disjoint groups whose union must equal the list.
- **Count claims were made count-free rather than re-pinned, where no test held them.** **Six** sentences said "ten" in passing — two source doc comments (`ShellSurfaceDetector`, `VisionSessionContainment`), **three** test doc comments (`ScreenControlEligibilityTests`, `ShellSurfaceDetectorTests`, `VisionSessionRunTests`) and one roadmap cell. (Counted off the diff for the PR #68 review, F3; the first tally said four and one test file, written before the wider sweep that found the other two — the file-level list was right and the sentence-level breakdown was not.) None was pinned by anything, all four had already gone stale relative to nobody noticing, and re-pinning them to "eleven" only reschedules the rot. The count now has **one home**: `terminalBundleIdentifiers`' own doc comment, which a test fails on. This is the same shape as the finding filed on the docx branch about a folding rule with two homes.
- **Dated records were left verbatim, deliberately — four of them, named so none is unaccounted for.** Two changelog entries (row I's, and the terminal-screen-check branch's) say "ten" as a statement of what was true when that branch shipped; the founder-decisions doc's 2026-08-16 screen-check section does the same; and **`docs/sonny-row-j-plan.md:349`** still reads "the static ten-name deny list" inside its own **Founder decision, 2026-08-16 (SONNY-102)** paragraph. That last one appeared in neither bucket in the first accounting and is in this one (PR #68 review, F3): it is *left verbatim*, same class and same reason as the other three. Editing any of them would falsify history, so the current truth is carried by a **dated addendum** on the standing ratification instead — the convention that doc already uses for supersessions.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The SSH-client category is not covered, and that is a stated limit rather than an oversight.** Royal TSX, Shuttle, Core Shell, Prompt, Blink, SecureCRT, ZOC, PuTTY and SSH Config Editor are not installed on the founder's Mac, so no identifier for any of them can be established from there — and none was invented. The list grows app by app, with the app in hand.
- **Eight of the eleven entries cannot be corroborated against Launch Services on the founder's Mac; three can.** Re-measured 2026-08-18 by asking LS for each of the eleven: `com.apple.terminal` (`/System/Applications/Utilities/Terminal.app`), `com.googlecode.iterm2` (`~/Applications/iTerm.app`) and `com.termius-dmg.mac` (`/Applications/Termius.app`) resolve; the other eight are not installed. Not evidence the eight are wrong; recorded so nobody reads "checked against Launch Services" as covering the list.
- **The embedded-shell gap is unchanged and out of scope by decision** (founder, 2026-08-17): a shell inside VS Code, a JetBrains console or a notebook cell is controllable. The shipped `ShellSurfaceDetector` still runs as defense in depth; this is an accepted limit on that layer, not a deferred fix, and the primary refusal is intact.
- **The gap is unclosed, and the ticket is closed anyway.** A name-based deny list is never complete; this narrows it by one app. The founder's decision of 2026-08-17 is that a permanent statement of that is a record rather than a ticket, and it now lives in this entry and in the list's own doc comment — which a test fails on.

**PR #68 review — five record errors, all in the file whose accuracy is this branch's deliverable.** The reviewer's verdict was that the code is correct and its guards fire; every finding was prose. That is worth stating rather than softening: this branch's entire deliverable is the accuracy of one doc comment, and five things in it were wrong.

- **F1 (fixed).** The comment said nine of eleven cannot be confirmed from the founder's Mac. Termius is installed there — its identifier was read off Launch Services there, which the same comment records as its provenance three paragraphs above. It is **eight**, and **three** are corroborable. The shape is the tell: eight-of-ten was true, and the update added one to both sides instead of noticing that the new entry belongs on the *confirmed* side. Re-measured rather than reasoned: LS was asked for all eleven on 2026-08-18.
- **F2 (fixed).** "The only entry of the original ten that is installed there" was false, and false before it was written — iTerm is at `~/Applications/iTerm.app` under `com.googlecode.iterm2`, and this same comment said so twenty lines further down. The pre-existing sentence it was rewritten from ("the only entry here that is installed there") was already false; the rewrite restated it in a new form instead of checking it.
- **The root cause of both, now fixed structurally.** The comment ran two different axes together: **provenance** (how an identifier was first obtained) and **corroboration** (whether this Mac agrees now). They are independent — `com.googlecode.iterm2` is published-configuration by provenance *and* corroborated by LS — and the comment now says so explicitly, in two separately headed paragraphs, because conflating them is what produced both false sentences.
- **F3 (fixed).** The sweep accounting said four sentences and one test doc comment; counted off the diff it is **six** and **three**. The tally was written from the first, narrower grep and never re-derived after the wider sweep found two more test files — the exact inversion of this repo's "count first, then write the number" rule, in the same entry that congratulates itself on the wider sweep. `docs/sonny-row-j-plan.md:349` was in neither bucket and is now named as left-verbatim.
- **The two-machines fiction (fixed).** The comment spoke of "the development machine" and "the founder's machine" as though they were two. There is one Mac. It now says so once and uses one name throughout.
- **Two wrap overruns (fixed).** Rewrapping for the count-free edit pushed `ShellSurfaceDetector.swift:147` to 105 columns and `VisionSessionContainment.swift:130` to 111 — the latter briefly the third-longest doc-comment line in `Sources/`. Both paragraphs are rewrapped; measured after, no line this branch adds exceeds 103 columns, and both files are back to the maximum they had before the branch.

Open questions (required): none. The founder settled the one this ticket was blocked on — whether dedicated SSH clients belong on the list — on 2026-08-17, and closed the ticket on 2026-08-18.

Next branch: not a roadmap row. This is an out-of-row entry addition sequenced ahead of the implementation lanes because its decision was already made and its cost is one line plus its records. The locked roadmap is unaffected: rows D, E, J and 12 continue as they stood.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **The two tickets are one surface and the order between them matters.** SONNY-76's fix makes `DestinationKey.folded` decide sameness *across units* as well as within one. Landing it first would have given the new cross-unit path the same under-fold SONNY-79 exists to remove, so the eszett band would have been wrong in the new code too. SONNY-79 went first for that reason, not for size.
- **The fold was chosen by measurement, and the measurement is in the code.** Twelve classes compared against what the volume itself answers — write one name into a temp directory, ask `fileExists` for the other. `folding(options: [.caseInsensitive], locale: nil)` agrees on all twelve; `lowercased()` disagreed on three (eszett, `ﬁ`, `ﬀ`). The table lives on `DestinationKey.folded`.
- **Both tempting strengthenings are wrong; only one of them is pinned, and the record now says so** (PR #65 review, F3). Adding `.diacriticInsensitive` folds `café.pdf` and `cafe.pdf` together where the filesystem does not — that half has a mutation producing a fabricated `cafe-2.pdf` rename and announcing it in the summary. Passing `locale: .current` folds `İstanbul`/`istanbul` together under a Turkish locale, so it would misbehave *only for Turkish users* — and **that half no test can catch on a machine whose locale is not Turkish**, because `.current` and `nil` behave identically there. The original claim that each had a mutation proving it overstated the suite. `theFoldDoesNotUniteTheNamesATurkishLocaleWould` holds what can honestly be held: the trap is real, and the shipped fold avoids it — a genuine regression test on a Turkish machine, documentation everywhere else.
- **This repo's search fold answers a different question, and borrowing it would have been wrong in two directions at once.** `RecentArtifactStore`'s normalisation is `.folding([.caseInsensitive, .diacriticInsensitive], locale: .current).lowercased()`, and every one of those choices is right for search — a user typing "cafe" to find "café" wants diacritic insensitivity, and search is locale-shaped. It is wrong here for exactly the two reasons above. **This is the second time in three branches that reusing a proven definition would have been the wrong instinct** (SONNY-157 declined `WorkspaceBrowserCatalog` on the same grounds), and the shape is worth naming: the risk is not duplicating a definition, it is borrowing one whose *question* does not match. `aDiacriticPairIsTwoFilesAndNeitherRenames` is where that stops being an argument and becomes a red suite.
- **A file this run wrote is not "already exists".** SONNY-76's fix is one clause on the skip test, but finding it needed the observation that the skip branch fires *before* the claimed-destinations check ever runs — seeding the claimed set alone would have changed nothing.
- **Both chain loops accumulate, not only the executing one.** Threading through `executeChain` alone leaves the approval panel naming `report.pdf` while the run writes `report-2.pdf`. `theChainsPreviewNamesTheRenamedDestinationTheRunWillWrite` pins it, and dropping the `previewChain` accumulation fails that test and only that test.
- **The claimed set is accumulated from previews rather than a new return channel**, which is why the adapter needed no new output and why it covers writes from any capability rather than only the docx one.
- **Three doc comments stated the old bound and are updated rather than left to contradict the code.** SONNY-79's own filing warned that absolute claims here were corrected twice on PR #41 and must not come back, so the new statements stay qualified: agreement with the volumes measured, not a reproduction of any folding table, and a volume that folds differently is not ruled out.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The fold is not the filesystem's own table, and the residual is on *this* volume rather than a hypothetical other one** (PR #65 review, F2). The review widened the twelve classes to the whole reachable population against the same APFS volume: 3160 comparisons, the shipped fold under-folding 9 and over-folding none, against 192 under-folds for the fold it replaced. The nine are U+1C80–U+1C88, Cyrillic Extended-C. The empty over-fold column is the load-bearing half, since an over-fold is what fabricates a rename. Their failure mode is unchanged and costs no data: both converters refuse an occupied destination, so such a batch aborts partway rather than losing a file.
- Only the DOCX path claims destinations across units. Other capabilities write through their own paths and are unaffected; nothing else in the plan had this defect to fix.

**PR #65 fix round — F1, and three record corrections.** A fresh reviewing session found one blocking defect and three smaller items; the founder directed a fix in branch.

- **F1 (blocking, fixed).** SONNY-76's rule was "a destination this run claimed is never a skip", which is right when the later unit holds a *different* source and wrong when it holds the *same* one. Two units whose scan scopes overlap — a nested folder pair is enough, since `regularFiles(in:)` recurses — re-found the same document, saw its destination claimed, and renamed: **one source converted twice, a duplicate PDF nobody asked for, and a summary announcing a collision with "another document" that did not exist.** The exact mirror of the defect SONNY-76 fixed, in a narrower input class. Now a document this run has already converted is skipped, checked before the destination rules. It reports as a skip, which restores the true sentence this case had before SONNY-76. **This round keyed that skip on the source alone, reasoning that "already converted" is a fact about the document rather than about where it landed — and that half was wrong; see the re-check's F5 below, which replaced it with a pair.**
- **The shape, and the tradeoff taken.** The review suggested reading source identity out of `ActionPreview.conversions`, which already carries `"<source> -> <destination>"`, at the cost of narrowing the "covers writes from any capability" property. **Declined, and a typed channel added instead** — `ActionPreview.convertedSources`, with the two accumulations combined into one `RunClaims` value. Two reasons. `conversions` is display text rendered as `"Convert: a -> b"`, and taking a correctness decision by splitting it on `" -> "` couples skip-or-convert to a presentation format, on a separator that is legal inside a macOS filename; this repo already has a scar of that exact shape, where a `grep '^designated'` silently dropped the one case its warning existed for because the display form differed. And the "narrowing" is not real: `destinations` still covers any capability, while "which documents has this run converted" has no meaning for a capability that does not convert a source. It is a second property with its own honest scope, not a smaller version of the first.
- **F4(a) (fixed).** `preview`'s `.chain` case dropped `claimedEarlierInThisRun` while `execute`'s threaded it. Unreachable today, since a chain segment is never itself a chain — so no test can distinguish the two versions and none was added rather than one that would pass either way. What it removes is two *public* entry points disagreeing about the same input the first time a chain could nest.
- **F4(b) (not fixed, filed).** `previewNestedPlan`/`executeNestedPlan` pass no claims, so a routine run as a chain unit does not inherit them. Reachable in principle — a routine whose steps convert — and closing it means changing the nested-plan closure signature through `CapabilityExecutionContext` and `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter`, which is wider than a blocking-finding fix round should carry. Filed rather than dropped; see the ticket named in SONNY-76's fix-round comment.
- **F2 and F3 (record corrections).** Both were below the fix bar and both are corrected anyway, because they are claims this branch made that turned out imprecise. F2: the fold's residual is on *this* volume, not a hypothetical other one — the review widened twelve classes to 3160 comparisons and found nine under-folds (U+1C80–U+1C88, Cyrillic Extended-C) and **zero over-folds**, against 192 under-folds for the fold replaced. F3: the claim that both rejected strengthenings had a mutation proving them wrong overstated the suite — the `locale: nil` half cannot be caught on a non-Turkish machine, and `theFoldDoesNotUniteTheNamesATurkishLocaleWould` now holds what honestly can be.
- **Minor (fixed).** `aPDFThatPredatesTheRunIsStillSkipped` asserted `"Skipped 1"`, which the first unit alone satisfies; it now asserts no `-2` file appeared and nothing converted.
- **The fix-round mutation.** Removing the same-source skip fails both new probes and *neither* the discrimination test nor SONNY-76's own — so the fix targets F1 exactly and does not undo what it was fixing.

**PR #65 re-check — F5, and the half of F1's fix that was wrong.** The cycle-3 re-check re-ran F1's probes, confirmed the fix, and found that fixing it had introduced one blocking defect. The founder granted one bounded review round beyond the three-cycle cap, scoped to this fix alone.

- **F5 (blocking, fixed).** F1's same-source skip was keyed on the source path and nothing else, so a later unit asking for the same document in a **different output folder** was skipped — and the user was told a PDF already existed at a destination where none did. Two probes measure it: nested scopes where the inner unit names its own output folder, and one folder converted into two different output folders. In both, the second folder stayed empty and the summary read "Skipped 1 existing PDF outputs." The same defect class SONNY-76 exists to fix, one step over.
- **The contradiction that showed the key was wrong, rather than merely incomplete.** If the *earlier* unit skipped the document — its PDF predated the run — a later unit with a different output folder did convert it, because the claimed set is built from pending records only. So identical user intent got opposite outcomes depending solely on which branch the earlier unit happened to take. The run already treated "a document at a destination" as the thing being asked for; the F1 rationale that "already converted" is a fact about the document alone is the step that does not hold.
- **The key is the pair, and its second half is the destination *folder* rather than the full path.** That is the load-bearing choice and it is not the obvious one. A destination filename is not stable across units: a document renamed to `report-2.pdf` because a sibling took `report.pdf` keeps only its folder. Keyed on the full path, that document's own re-scan computes `report.pdf`, misses its `report-2.pdf` claim, and converts a second time to `report-3.pdf` — **reintroducing F1 for exactly the documents the rename rule touches**, while passing both of the re-check's probes. The folder is also the honest unit of the request: "convert these into that folder" says nothing about the filename, which is this code's to choose.
- **The pair is a type, not a composed string.** `ConversionClaim` folds both halves in its own initializer, so the "both halves are `DestinationKey.folded`" invariant holds by construction instead of at each call site, and no separator can collide with a path. `ActionPreview.convertedSources` became `[ConvertedSource]` for the same reason: the executor needs both halves, and reading them out of `convertedSources` and `writes` positionally would be a correspondence nothing enforces — the same class of implicit contract as parsing the display string, one step quieter.
- **The test gap that let F5 through, closed.** Both of F1's new fixtures built their steps with a helper that sets no `outputPath`, so in every F1 test both units shared one default destination and the differing-destination case had no test at all. Three tests now: the two probes, each asserting the PDF **really lands in the second output folder** rather than only that no skip was announced, and `aRenamedOutputIsNotConvertedAgainWhenALaterUnitRescansTheSameFolder`, which is green before this fix as well as after — it guards the fix rather than probing the defect, and nothing else in the suite reaches a rename that is then re-scanned.
- **Three mutations, at `d05f1fd`.** Collapsing the pair to source-only fails the two differing-destination tests and nothing else. Keying on the full destination path instead of its folder fails only the rename test, with the predicted `["report-2.pdf", "report-3.pdf", "report.pdf"]`. Removing the same-source skip entirely still fails F1's own two probes plus the rename test, so F1's fix is intact and this change did not route around it.
- **F6, F7 and F8 remain open by decision, not oversight.** The re-check's two record gaps (this entry's dropped `Next branch:` line, and a `Files changed` line that predates `RunClaims.swift` and `AgentEvent.swift`) and its low finding about the dead `RunClaims.hasWritten` are all outside the F5 grant, which is explicitly scoped to this fix alone. They are recorded on SONNY-76 for the founder to route.

Open questions (required): none. SONNY-76 offered two directions and the threading one was taken, since the wording-only option leaves the user a document short; SONNY-79 offered three and the fuller fold was taken, measured rather than assumed, with the filesystem-probe option unnecessary once the fold matched on every class tested.

### Branch: fix/sonny-146-request-compression
Status: complete
Date: 2026-08-17
Tickets: SONNY-146 (vision requests sent uncompressed; deflate recovers a quarter to a third of the body losslessly). Spawned nothing.
Reviewed by: **no record establishes a review of this branch, and this line says so rather than supplying one.** SONNY-146 carries two comments — the closing comment and a later live check of the question the ticket left open — neither of them a review; PR #66 has no comments and no GitHub reviews; nothing in this entry narrates a round. The branch merged as `4d83e0f`. Filled in 2026-08-28 by SONNY-275, which found no record to fill it with.

Spec sections covered: none new. Transport for §13's screen-control route, ahead of row 12's gateway.
Files changed: new: `Sources/MacAgentCore/HTTPBodyCompression.swift`; modified: `Sources/MacAgentCore/VisionModelClient.swift`, `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/VisionModelClientTests.swift`.
Tests: CLAUDE.md's exact flagged command -> pass, **1277 tests in 95 suites**, exit 0, at `03b616f`, twice. Branch-point baseline at `317f2e3` was 1272 in 95: **+5 tests, +0 suites**.

Behavior added:
- The vision client can send a gzip-encoded request body. **Off for the default endpoint** — see below.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The default endpoint's request is byte-for-byte what it was**: uncompressed, no `Content-Encoding`. Pinned by a test that constructs the client *without naming the flag*, so what it holds is the production default.
- **`maximumImageBytes` and the 4,200,000-byte contract limit are both unchanged**, and section below says why that is the right answer rather than an omission.
- **`aRequestAtTheCeilingStaysInsideTheHostBodyBudget` is untouched and still passes.** It measures the body as sent, so it would have broken had compression been switched on by default — which is one more reason the default matters.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **`NSData.compressed(using: .zlib)` is raw DEFLATE, not gzip and not zlib.** A body produced by it and labelled `Content-Encoding: gzip` fails to inflate — verified against an independent implementation, which rejected it as "Not a gzipped file". SONNY-146's own 29–35% measurement used that call, which is fine for sizing and wrong for the header. `HTTPBodyCompression` adds the real container: fixed 10-byte header, raw DEFLATE, CRC-32 and length little-endian.
- **The CRC is the part that fails quietly.** A wrong polynomial or table produces a stream that decompresses to the right bytes and is *then* rejected by the receiver's integrity check. Pinned against the published vector `0x414FA339`, and the mutation confirms only that test catches it — the round-trip test passes with a broken CRC.
- **`gzip` rather than `deflate`, on purpose.** RFC 7230 defines `deflate` as the zlib container while much of the deployed world sends raw DEFLATE under that name, so the label's meaning would depend on whichever server is on the far end. `gzip` has one meaning, and `docs/sonny-backend-api-contract.md` §6.4 already obliges Sonny's own backend to accept it.
- **This ticket's `Accept-Encoding` instruction is wrong, and following it would have made the response worse.** URLSession already sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate` on every request with nothing set — measured against a local server. Setting it by hand *replaces* that advertisement with something narrower: the same probe saw `gzip` alone, and `identity`, when each was set. So nothing is set, and the code says why, because an absent header reads like an omission.
- **Compression is a property of the far end, so it travels with `endpoint` rather than being a free-floating switch.** Off for the default endpoint because whether OpenCode's Zen route inflates a gzip body is **unverified** — confirming it needs a live call with a real key, which this session had none of, and it was this ticket's own first requirement. Turning it on unverified risks every screen-control session for about a quarter of the body. SONNY-131 flips the flag and the endpoint together, in one edit, at the one construction site.
- **A mutation caught a test that pinned the wrong default.** The first version of the default-endpoint test went through this suite's `client` helper, which passes the flag explicitly — so flipping the *production* default to `true` left it green. It now constructs the client directly. The whole safety argument rests on that default, and the test that guards it was guarding a helper.
- **Byte-comparing two `JSONSerialization` outputs is unsound.** The body is a `[String: Any]` and key order is not guaranteed, so two serialisations of the same dictionary can differ byte-for-byte at identical length — which the first version of the round-trip test hit. It compares parsed objects now. Flaky rather than wrong, which is worse.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Nothing is compressed in production yet**, and that is the honest state: the capability ships tested and unused until SONNY-131 gives it a far end that is ours. The alternative was enabling it against an unverified third-party route.
- **The measured figure is a floor, not a typical case.** `EGRESS-COMPRESSION-RATIO` prints **0.753** on a 1728×1117 seeded-noise capture — uniform noise is the encoder's worst input and forces the lossy branch, so it compresses least. SONNY-146's 0.650–0.709 on five real captures at `e260575` is the more representative band. The test prints on every run rather than freezing a number into prose, following `theShippingPolicyKeepsEvenItsWorstCaseUnderTheCeiling`.

**The ceiling question, answered rather than quietly moved.** Compression does not change what the ceiling should be, in either place it lives. `maximumImageBytes` bounds the *image*, is checked before the body exists, and exists for legibility and a clear refusal rather than for wire size. The contract's 4,200,000-byte server limit is measured on the **decoded** body by deliberate choice, precisely so a client that compresses cannot smuggle a larger payload past it. What compression does change is the figure SONNY-125 measures against Supabase, which publishes no request-body ceiling at all: the wire body at the ceiling becomes roughly three quarters of ~4.01 MB. If that undocumented limit turns out to apply to the encoded bytes, as a proxy seeing wire bytes would, compression buys real headroom — which is the reason for landing this before that measurement rather than after.

Open questions (required): one, owned and named. **Whether the current OpenCode route accepts a gzip request body is unverified**, and it cannot be answered without a live call. It stops mattering when SONNY-131 repoints the client at Sonny's own gateway, which the contract already obliges to accept gzip — so the answer is "moot on the timeline that matters", not "unknown and blocking".

### Branch: fix/sonny-157-named-browser
Status: complete
Date: 2026-08-17

Tests: CLAUDE.md's exact flagged command -> pass, **1272 tests in 95 suites**, exit 0, at `7977fea`. Branch-point baseline at `8f2207e` was **1265 in 95**, measured on this branch rather than carried forward: **+7 tests, +0 suites** — five on the executor, two on the decoder.

> **Re-stamped after the rebase, and the old figures are not merely stale — their SHAs no longer exist.** This branch first measured 1233 in 92 at `1dc988c` over a branch point of 1226 in 92 at `8b51d6f`. `feature/terminal-screen-check` then merged, adding 39 tests and 3 suites, so the branch point moved to 1265 in 95 and both ends were re-measured rather than one being adjusted arithmetically. The delta is unchanged at +7/+0, which is the invariant worth checking: a rebase that altered this branch's own contribution would show up there. `git range-diff 8b51d6f..f8f2cff 8f2207e..HEAD` reports both commits identical (`1: 1dc988c = 1: 4759dfa`, `2: f8f2cff = 2: 7977fea`), so the work replayed unchanged.

Behavior added:
- `AgentStep.browserName` carries the browser the user named, and a URL-opening step routes there.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **SONNY-152's guarantee, now pinned at the execution layer and not only in the prompt.** A step naming no browser still reaches the system default — `noBrowserNamedStillOpensInTheSystemDefault` asserts the opener receives `nil`.
- **Routine binding.** Still applies when the step names nothing, asserted through the same `preferredBrowser` parameter `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` uses — the real collision, not a simulated one.
- **Workspace binding.** Untouched and does not come through that parameter at all: `OpenWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter` resolves its own browser from the workspace's app list and passes it directly. No file in that path changed.
- **The planner schema's strictness.** `additionalProperties: false` and the every-key-required rule are intact; the new key is in `stepRequiredKeys`, `AgentPlanDecoder.stepKeys` and `baseStepProperties` together.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **Three enumerations re-verified at `8b51d6f`, with one correction to the ticket.** `AgentStep` has **31** stored properties, not the 28 the ticket recorded at `d55c97d` — `resolvedAppName`, `resolvedBundleIdentifier` and `visionGoal` were not in its list. Still none is a browser. The other two hold exactly: one non-nil `preferredBrowser` site (`AgentActionExecutor.swift:1438`), and the adapters hand nil through. **A third consumer the ticket missed:** `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter.swift:320`, the Hacker News open, also reads `context.preferredBrowser`; it is wired the same way here.
- **Planner-visible, not decode-excluded, and the file says why.** `resolvedAppName`'s own comment warns against adding "a second decode-excluded app-identity field", because the exclusion guarantee is per-key and a new key is a new place to get it wrong. This field is the opposite case: the model is the only thing that sees the command text, so it is the only thing that can tell "open example.com in Chrome" from "open example.com". It belongs in both key lists, like `visionGoal`.
- **Precedence decided rather than emergent: the step beats the routine.** A routine's browser is a default inferred from the apps that routine opens; a name on the step is what the user said in this command. The more specific and more recent instruction wins. `aBrowserNamedOnTheStepWinsOverARoutinesBinding` pins it, and inverting the helper fails that test and only that test.
- **Per-operation, not per-plan.** The helper reads the step for the operation being executed rather than the first `browserName` anywhere in the plan, so "open A in Chrome then B in Safari" cannot put both in Chrome. Each adapter asks with its own operation, so each reads the step it is already acting on.
- **Deliberately not gated on `WorkspaceBrowserCatalog`, and this is the judgment most worth reviewing.** The ticket advised reusing it as the definition of browser-capable, and that advice guards against a second definition. But the catalog answers "which of *these* apps is the browser" — the question a workspace's app list poses. When the user names one, that question does not arise. Gating on its five bundle identifiers would refuse a browser the user explicitly asked for, with no visible reason, for browsers like Vivaldi or Orion that Launch Services opens fine. No second definition is created because none is needed.
- **An unresolvable name falls back rather than failing**, matching what `WorkspaceBrowserOpener` already documents for a workspace naming an absent browser: a link opening in the wrong browser beats one that fails mid-open. The opener applies the same rule again, with a log, if the app is installed but refuses to launch.
- **A previous ticket's test assertion was changed, not deleted, and the distinction matters.** SONNY-152's third direction asserted that a named browser "still produce the URL step rather than a clarify or unsupported step" — worded that way precisely so the prompt could not claim routing the system could not do. It now asserts the routing sentence. **The promise got stronger; it was never wrong**, and the test's comment records the arc so a later reader does not read the edit as a correction.
- **Four mutations, all reverted.** Reverting one adapter to `context.preferredBrowser` fails the two routing tests and none of the other three. Inverting precedence fails only the precedence test. Dropping the key from `AgentPlanDecoder.stepKeys` fails the decode test and not the omitted-key one — the schema/decoder drift that would otherwise present as the planner failing wholesale rather than as a missing browser.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **No model has been asked to fill the field.** The suite proves the schema offers it, the decoder accepts it and the executor routes on it; whether a real planner sets `browserName` from "in Chrome" is the founder's attended run and is the manual-test list's first item.
- Only the three URL-opening seams honour it. `play_media` opens on a different seam by an explicit earlier decision (SONNY-51) and is untouched.

Open questions (required): none. The three decisions this ticket flagged as needing one — precedence, not-installed behaviour, and whether to reuse the browser catalog — are each decided above with their reasoning.

The check's own cost is therefore measured directly: **3.9–4.3 ms per call** isolated, printed as `SHELL-CHECK-PER-CALL-MICROSECONDS` on every run. The benchmark behind that figure runs **20 iterations rather than 200**. It was cut while `VisionSessionRunTests` still gated on fixed 2–4 s wall-clock deadlines, where 200 iterations' ~0.8 s of CPU was enough to fail the parallel suite outright — eight full-suite runs went from 0 passing to 6. **`fix/machine-state-tests` has since replaced those deadlines with a 30 s hang backstop, so that is no longer the reason**: at `fea631a` the suite passes 8 of 8 with the benchmark at either count. The lower count stays because spending most of a CPU-second on a diagnostic inside a parallel suite is worth avoiding on its own, and it costs the figure nothing (3,925–4,029 µs at 20 against 3,911–4,261 µs at 200). **Two superseded claims, recorded rather than quietly dropped.** The cycle-2 record said cutting the benchmark was "worse on its own terms" because the figure got noisier — measured on the lighter cycle-2 tree, and it does not reproduce. And the cycle-3 record said this branch tripped the deadline defect where `main` did not, which was true of `f8ad4f3` and is not true of `8b51d6f`. **It has grown across the three rounds — roughly 3.5 ms at cycle 1, 3.9–4.3 ms now — and the reason is that the prompt signal went from three patterns to six** (the bracketed form, the extended arrow, and the minimal-prompt scan), which is what the two review rounds bought. Recorded rather than optimised: it sits beside an OCR pass costing hundreds of milliseconds, inside a loop that already sleeps 800 ms between iterations. Two instrument notes a future reader needs. The 374 ms figure this branch was told to measure against was recorded at `1ce1f66`, before SONNY-114 rewrote the encoder, so the delta is stated against a branch-point number measured here. And the numbers above are *isolated* runs: under the full parallel suite the same figures read far higher (a redaction latency of ~864 ms and a shell-check cost of ~4.8 ms were both observed by the cycle-3 reviewer), because Swift Testing runs suites concurrently. That is a property of the instrument, not of the code, and it is the same caveat as at cycle 2.

Behavior added:
- **Sonny ends a screen-control session when the window it captured is showing a shell.** In all three modes, with the same sentence reaching the panel and the record, and the reason code `screen_shows_shell`. Nothing is sent to the vision provider and no input is synthesized: the refusal sits at the redaction step, above the Safe-mode capture review, the prompt, the send and `perform`.
- **It runs on every capture, not once per session**, at the same cadence as the deny-list re-check — so a shell that appears in the window mid-run ends the session on the next iteration.
- **`ShellSurfaceDetector` reads the joined OCR document already produced for redaction** and reports six independent classes of evidence: a shell prompt, a command run at one (or through a notebook `!` escape), `ls`-style output, a shell's own diagnostic, session chrome, and an interpreter being named as what will run something. **Two distinct classes** are required, as `signalThreshold`.
- **A twenty-six-fixture corpus**, meant to be appended to like `VisionPromptInjectionTests`: twelve that must refuse and fourteen that must not, with the **exact signal set pinned on both halves**. The must-refuse half covers the five the ticket names, an unlisted terminal running oh-my-zsh, an ssh session inside one, a bracketed Linux prompt, and four screens where *nothing has failed* — an idle VS Code panel after `ls`, one with a dev server running, a clean JetBrains run, and a notebook whose commands all worked. The must-not-refuse half covers the three the ticket names plus a README, an email thread with `>` quoted replies, a Dockerfile, Sonny's own Security & Access page, and six pages carrying UI glyphs or address-shaped tokens in prose.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The static deny list still refuses first and is still ten entries.** `ScreenControlPolicy.terminalBundleIdentifiers` is untouched, its three doors are untouched, and `checkIterationStart`'s per-iteration re-read is untouched. `aListedTerminalIsStillRefusedByNameBeforeAnyCaptureIsTaken` pins the ordering as behaviour: a Terminal target is refused with the *terminal* sentence and the scripted recognizer is never called even once, because the adapter answers before a capture is taken.
- **`aTerminalNobodyListedIsControllableAndThatIsTheKnownGap` is intact and unweakened.** It still asserts the gap, and this branch does not let anyone read a green suite as proof of the categorical rule.
- **`RedactedPayload`'s structural non-bypass.** The initializer is still `fileprivate`, the type is still not `Codable`, every field is still `let`, and `onlyTheServiceProducesPayloadsInTheLiveModule` still names exactly one production file. The new field rides inside that boundary rather than around it.
- **Fail-closed redaction, unchanged and now load-bearing for a second thing.** A recognizer that throws, a region outside the image, and an undecodable capture all still produce an error and no payload; `recognizerFailureFailsClosedWithNoPayload` is untouched and still passes.
- **Every existing vision-session flow.** All 51 tests in `VisionSessionRunTests` pass, including the ones this branch did not add: the ordinary Normal-mode run, Safe mode's envelope → capture review → action approval sequence, delegation in all four of its shapes, the emergency stop, the pause/resume machinery, the iteration cap, and the SONNY-114 resampled-coordinate pins.
- **The consequence rule, `RiskApprovalPolicy.requirement(for:context:)` and `ApprovalContext`** are untouched — this branch adds a refusal, not an approval axis.
- **`SecretTextDetector`'s classes and patterns** are untouched. The shell detector is a sibling file, not an extension of them.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **Two independent signs means two independent *classes*, and the first design failed that on its own terms.** A `promptScrollback` signal — fires when three or more lines match the prompt shape — was written, measured against the whole corpus, and then deleted. It worked: every must-refuse fixture passed with a sign to spare. It was wrong anyway, because counting prompt lines once as "a prompt is present" and again as "several prompts are present" is one class of evidence producing a refusal by itself, which is exactly what the founder's condition forbids. Removing it cost the corpus nothing. `repeatingOneClassOfEvidenceNeverReachesTheThresholdByItself` now pins the property so the next signal cannot quietly reintroduce it.
- **No signal subtracts, and that is a security property rather than a simplification.** `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` already says screen-derived signals may add scrutiny and never remove it. A "this looks like source code, never mind" suppressor would be a string an attacker paints on the screen to switch the check off. The one pattern that declines to fire on text it otherwise matches — the shebang exclusion in `shellInterpreterInvocation` — is a statement about what that text *is* (a file's first line, not a command being run) and cancels nothing found elsewhere. The VS Code fixture carries a shebang in its editor half deliberately, and still refuses on the panel below it.
- **The sharpest false positive is a `.sh` file open in an editor, and the fixture is built to be adversarial rather than convenient.** Line 11 of it is `scp "$f" "deploy@$1:$APP_DIR/"` — the closest thing in ordinary shell source to a `user@host:path$` prompt. It lands at **zero** signals, not one, and `aShellScriptOpenInAnEditorIsNotAnInteractiveShell` asserts emptiness rather than merely "does not refuse", so a fixture drifting to one sign fails loudly instead of passing with no margin.
- **A vocabulary is not specificity, and believing it was is the mistake this branch actually made.** The first design read `shellCommandNames` after *any* line-start sigil, and its own comment argued that requiring a real command name is what let quoted email through. The reviewer measured it: of sixteen quoted-reply lines whose first word is in the list, **fifteen fired the signal** — `go`, `make`, `open`, `find`, `top`, `clear`, `exit`, `history`, `man`, `kill`, `head`, `source`, `java`, `touch`, `less`. The only one that did not was `> can you run …`, which is the exact phrasing the committed email fixture used. The vocabulary was doing nothing, because ordinary English is full of command names; what does the work is **position**. The list is now consulted only in the remainder of a real prompt line, or after a notebook `!`. The words stay in it deliberately — after `%` on a prompt they are commands, and removing them would blind the check to `% make release` and `% go test ./...` — and they are now harmless, because a blockquote has no prompt. **The general lesson, since this repo has met it before in another coat: a filter that is specific about its *vocabulary* and vague about its *context* is not specific.**
- **The verdict is non-optional and there is deliberately no "could not tell" state.** An `Optional` or a third enum case would be permission granted by omission — a `nil` a reader treats as "no shell" is precisely the answer an unreadable screen must not produce. Both of `LocalRedactionService`'s producers fill the field from the one detector over the text they actually had, so there is no capture-only special case with an inert value on the other path, and no branch where the field is defaulted.
- **Fail-closed is inherited structurally rather than re-implemented, and the test asserts the session *ends*.** `redactCapture` already threw `detectionUnavailable` when recognition failed, so an unreadable screen already ended the session; the shell verdict simply cannot exist without a successful scan. `anUnreadableScreenEndsTheSessionRatherThanProducingANoShellVerdict` asserts the session outcome, never that a verdict came back clean — the mutation that maps a recognizer failure to an empty observation list is killed by it.
- **Swift `Regex` cost is compilation, not matching, and the two obvious fixes were both rejected.** Measured here: evaluating a regex literal costs roughly 200 µs of compilation against roughly 90 µs of matching, and the pattern's shape barely moves either number — a lazy-bounded prompt pattern and a negated-class rewrite of it came out at 288 µs and 283 µs. Caching the compiled patterns in `nonisolated(unsafe) static let`s was rejected because `Regex` is not `Sendable` for a real reason (it lazily builds a lowered program inside itself) and the suite runs tests in parallel; a documented data race in the file that decides whether Sonny may drive a window is not worth 3 ms. Cheap substring prefilters in front of the expensive patterns were rejected because a prefilter is a second, weaker copy of a pattern's necessary condition, and when the two drift the signal stops firing *silently* — a fail-open bug in a check whose entire job is to fail closed. What was taken is the version with no drift surface at all: signals that are fixed strings use `String.contains`, which is about twelve times cheaper than the simplest regex and is the whole check rather than a filter in front of one. That alone took the per-call cost from 4.07 ms to 3.4 ms.
- **A test that claimed to be exhaustive was not, and this branch is what proved it.** `everyRefusalCarriesADistinctReasonCodeAndANonEmptySentence`'s doc comment promised that "a new ending has to come here and choose a code rather than silently borrowing one". `screenShowsShell` was added to `VisionContainmentRefusal` and the suite stayed green: the list is hand-written, so "exhaustively" described how it had been typed and not anything enforced. Fixed rather than merely appended to — `expectedReasonCode(for:)` is an exhaustive `switch` over the enum, so a new case now fails to compile in the file whose job is to make sure it picked a code. Same family as `identifierProducing(_:)` in `ScreenControlEligibilityTests`. **That fix was itself incomplete and the reviewer caught it** — see the bullet on compiler-forced switches below.
- **The signals were the defect and the threshold was not, and telling those apart is the whole of the cycle-2 fix** (PR #57 F1/F2, coordinator adjudication 2026-08-17). The review found the check refusing documentation pages, GitHub issues, Notion runbooks, slide decks, mail threads and Slack, *and* allowing a VS Code terminal panel whenever the last command happened to succeed. Those read as opposite pressures on `signalThreshold` and are not: they are one defect, in signals that were not specific to what they claimed to detect. The prompt signal accepted `▶` and `»` — a disclosure triangle and a breadcrumb separator — and fired on any line holding an address-shaped token followed anywhere later by `$`, `%` or `#`, so "alice@example.com says the build is 50% faster now" was a prompt. The command signal fired on a bare sigil at line start. Making each specific resolved both at once, with the founder's two-signs rule untouched: a real prompt plus a command typed at it is two classes for an idle panel after `ls`, and a documentation page carrying a lone `$` is now **zero**. All eight of the reviewer's repros land at zero and none of the sixteen quoted replies fires. **Lowering the threshold would have traded one false negative for a worse false positive** — it is precisely what keeps a single `$` from stopping real work — which is why it is now documented on the constant itself as not being the tuning surface.
- **`%%bash` is an interpreter selection, not a command echo, and separating them is what makes a clean notebook refuse.** Both facts were originally read by the same signal, so a notebook where every command succeeded reached one class. Naming an interpreter and running a command are different facts about the world, and a notebook that does both should not have them counted as one — the same reasoning that deleted `promptScrollback`, applied in the other direction.
- **A test the corpus could not fail is not coverage, and the corpus is now built so that it can.** The seven negative fixtures contained no UI glyph, no address-shaped token in prose beside a `%`, and no quoted line whose first word was in the vocabulary; the seven positive ones contained no shell in which nothing had gone wrong. A green corpus was therefore compatible with both defects. It is now twenty-six fixtures, the **exact signal set is asserted on both halves** rather than only the verdict, six of the additions are the reviewer's own repros verbatim, and `theCorpusCoversBothDirections` asserts by name that the F1 and F2 fixtures stay present so a later trim cannot quietly remove what made the corpus able to fail.
- **A structural guarantee needs a structural test, and "I enumerated it" is not one.** The claim that only six fixed strings ever cross the verdict boundary was true and checked by hand — and nothing in the suite would have failed if someone had later added `public let matchedLine: String` to help debug a false positive. That is the leak shape this repository has shipped twice. It is now pinned two ways: `theVerdictHoldsNothingButSignalsAndThatIsCheckedNotAssumed` strips comments from the declaration and asserts the **complete** property list, so any addition fails rather than only the ones a keyword list anticipated; and `twoDifferentScreensWithTheSameSignalsProduceEqualVerdicts` asserts it behaviourally, since a field carrying screen text would make two screens sharing no words compare unequal. The loop it replaced asserted that screen text does not contain the string `interactive_prompt`, which is true whatever the verdict carries.
- **A compiler-forced `switch` in front of a hand-written array forces the author into the file and not into the array.** Round one of the exhaustive-refusal fix added `expectedReasonCode(for:)`, an exhaustive `switch`, and the reviewer pointed out the remaining hole: a new case could take a `switch` arm and never a sample, and then its distinct-code and non-empty-sentence assertions simply never ran while a literal `== 12` kept passing. Closed with a `CaseIterable` tag enum and mappings in **both** directions — the real enum maps to a tag, the tag maps to a sample, the array is built from `allCases`, and the count literal is gone. Neither direction can be satisfied without the other.
- **The battery's one survivor was the round's most useful result.** Fourteen mutations, thirteen killed on the first run; the fourteenth — dropping `(?m)` from the colon-form prompt pattern — changed nothing anywhere in the suite. The reason is subtle and worth carrying: without `(?m)` the `$` in the trailing lookahead means end of *input*, and every colon-form prompt in the corpus happened to be either followed by a space or the document's last line. The uncovered case is the ordinary one — a shell that has printed its prompt and is waiting, with scrollback below it. Fixed with a test rather than a note, and the battery then killed all fourteen.
- **Narrowing a signal to kill false positives can silently take out the feature's own subject, and only a measurement finds that** (PR #57 N2). Cycle 2 made the prompt signal specific, which fixed the false refusals — and removed *any* prompt lacking `user@host`, `bash-N.N`, `➜` or `PS C:\`. Four shapes went from refusing to proceeding and nothing on the branch recorded it; the limitations entry named one glyph ("starship") where the effect was a prompt-style class. That is the more dangerous half: the deny list already covers terminal *applications*, so this check's entire subject is shells inside something else, and those render whatever prompt the user's shell renders — a bare `$ ` being among the commonest. **The lesson is about the record as much as the code**: a limitation written as the theme that prompted it, rather than as the population that was measured, reads as much smaller than it is.
- **The fix for that had to be tightened twice, by documents built to break it.** A minimal `$ `/`% ` prompt is recognised when it repeats and the **last** occurrence is bare. Repetition alone refuses a documentation page with two `$` examples; "some occurrence is bare" alone refuses a LaTeX or config comment block, which uses a bare `%` as a separator — and one of those reached the command signal on the word `source`. Requiring the *last* occurrence to be the bare one is what distinguishes a scrollback, which ends where the cursor sits, from a comment block, which does not. Both halves have a fixture and a mutation.
- **`❯` is a bullet before it is a prompt, and that is a measured trade rather than a preference.** Admitting the chevron to the minimal set under the identical rule refuses an ordinary agenda list ending in an empty bullet — the F1 class this branch already paid for once. So starship, pure and powerlevel10k stay unrecognised, the bullet-list document is kept as a corpus fixture so the trade stays visible, and the bound is stated with the measurement instead of being inherited. `#` is excluded for the neighbouring reason: it is Markdown's heading marker, and a root prompt arrives as `root@host:/#` through the colon form anyway.
- **Two signals can share a failure mode without sharing a class, and that is not independence** (PR #57 N1). `commandRunInAShell`'s prompt half is computed *from* the prompt ranges, so a prompt misfire produced both signals off one line with no second opinion — `priya@acme.io 82% open`, which is what a support-desk or CRM table OCRs to, refused on its own. The derivation is inherent to the case that fixed F2 (a command typed at a prompt is on the prompt's own line), so "require different lines" was not available. What was available was shrinking the shared surface: the sigil may no longer be glued to the character before it unless that character closes a bracket, and the command must be the **first** token after the prompt rather than any of ninety names anywhere in the remainder. **The residual is recorded as an assertion, not as prose** — the invoice line still reads as a prompt shape and now yields one signal instead of two, so the fix removes the refusal and not the misread.
- **A rebase measurement is invalid if the tree was dirty, and the script will not say so.** A paired latency comparison printed the same SHA for both columns because `git checkout --detach origin/main` had failed against an uncommitted changelog edit, so the "branch point" column was actually the branch. Caught by reading the SHA the script printed rather than only the numbers under it. Stamp the SHA on every column, and read it.
- **Safe mode's session-envelope approval comes before the first capture, and that does not contradict the design's "the first capture happens before the control approval".** They are different gates: the envelope approval is the *plan*-level tier-3 gate that already ships, while the sentence in `docs/sonny-row-j-plan.md` §4.3 is about the per-app control consent row J's later branches add. The two are easy to read as contradicting each other. `aWindowShowingAShellEndsTheSessionInEveryMode` answers the envelope approval explicitly in its Safe arm and says why in place.
- **Three of the ticket's own `Sources/` citations had moved before this branch started, and were re-read rather than trusted.** SONNY-114 merged hours earlier: `redactCapture` is `:161-239` not `:146-220`, its fail-closed throw is `:169-172` not `:154-156`, and `RedactedPayload.redactedImagePNGData` is now `redactedImageData` plus a media type and dimensions. Nothing about the design changed, which is the point — the citations were checked because they *could* have changed, not because something looked wrong.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **This does not close SONNY-102 and no record of this work may say it does.** A screen check reads exactly the surface an attacker controls, which is why the deny list stays load-bearing and is not trimmed by one entry; and a shell that is not rendered is not seen. SONNY-102 stays open at high priority.
- **What the check does not reach**, stated as what was measured rather than as a theme:
  - **Structural, and permanent:** a shell in a background tab, a collapsed panel, a scrolled-away region, or any window other than the captured one.
  - **A prompt with nothing typed at it** is one sign and proceeds. So is **a prompt carrying a command `shellCommandNames` does not know** — `% mytool --deploy` is one sign, while `% ./mytool --deploy` is two, because `./` is a shell construct rather than a name that has to be listed. Pinned by `aPromptAloneAndAnUnrecognisedCommandBothStayAtOneSign`.
  - **Prompt styles the prompt signal does not know.** The signal recognises `user@host` (colon and spaced forms), `bash-N.N`, oh-my-zsh's `➜`, PowerShell's `PS C:\…>`, and — since PR #57's N2 — a repeated minimal `$ `/`% ` ending at a waiting prompt. **Anything else is invisible.** The concrete casualty is any prompt whose only glyph is `❯`, which is starship, pure and powerlevel10k in their default configurations — the three most common custom prompts on a developer's Mac. **Said as what it costs a person rather than as a list of prompt themes: a developer running starship inside a VS Code panel is not caught by the screen check.** That is the exact case this feature exists for — the static deny list already refuses terminal *applications*, so an embedded shell is the whole remaining subject — and it is a gap Sonny walks straight past. Measured, not assumed: `❯ ./scripts/deploy.sh` / `zsh: permission denied: …` / `❯` yields `shell_diagnostic` alone and proceeds, asserted by `theMinimalPromptSetExcludesTheMarkdownAndBulletGlyphs`.
  - **Excluding `❯` is a founder decision of 2026-08-17, taken on a measurement, and the cost was named before it was accepted.** It is a bullet glyph before it is a prompt glyph. Admitting it to the minimal set — under the same repetition-plus-waiting-prompt rule that made `$ ` and `% ` safe — was tried and refuses an ordinary agenda list ending in an empty bullet, which is the F1 class this branch already paid for once. **The founder's reasoning, recorded on SONNY-139 so it is not re-litigated: a false stop is worse than a gap**, because a stop is unappealable and the product is not allowed to explain why it happened, while the gap is partly covered by the deny list catching terminal applications outright. Two alternatives were declined: adding the glyph, and spending another round hunting a discriminator that separates a prompt-with-scrollback from a bullet list. The bullet-list document is kept as a corpus fixture (`a bullet list ending in an empty chevron`) so the trade stays visible rather than becoming folklore. `#` is excluded for a neighbouring reason: it is Markdown's heading marker and most config formats' comment marker, and a root prompt arrives through the colon form as `root@host:/#` anyway.
  - **(Corrected 2026-08-17, PR #57 N2.)** This entry previously read only "a starship prompt is also not recognised", which named one theme when the measured effect was a prompt-style *class*: the cycle-3 re-check found four shapes that had gone from refusing to proceeding when the prompt signal was narrowed at cycle 2 — a minimal `$ ` prompt with a failed command, a starship prompt with a failed command, a minimal `$ ` prompt with `ls -l` output, and a bare `% ` prompt with `ls -l` output. **Three of those four are now fixed** by the repeated-minimal-prompt rule and are corpus fixtures marked `(N2)`; the fourth is the `❯` case above, which is the residual. Recording one glyph where the effect was a class is the error being corrected, and it mattered because the deny list already covers terminal *applications* — this check exists for shells inside something else, which show whatever prompt the user's shell shows.
  - **(Corrected 2026-08-17, PR #57 F2.)** This bullet first read "…a window showing a prompt and nothing else, which is one sign and proceeds … bounded in practice by the check running on every capture — the moment anything runs in that shell, a second class of evidence appears and the session ends." **The final clause was false when written**, and the reviewer measured it: `ls`, `cd`, `cd Desktop`, `git status`, `swift build` and `python3 train.py` each produced a full shell session that stayed at one sign and proceeded, because the only things that added a second class were an `ls -l`-shaped listing or something failing. The mitigation the bound leaned on did not exist. It was load-bearing for the disposition "a bare prompt proceeding is acceptable", which is why it is corrected here rather than quietly dropped. All six now refuse — a command typed at a real prompt is itself the second class — and `aSucceedingCommandAtAPromptIsTwoSigns` asserts each of the five the reviewer named. The bound that replaces it is the one stated above, and it is narrower: not "anything runs", but "a *recognised* command, or any `./` execution, runs".
- **The window-scoping guarantee is load-bearing for "end the session" and must be revisited if it ever changes.** `SCContentFilter(desktopIndependentWindow:)` is still the only content filter in the repository, so a terminal behind Chrome cannot end a Chrome session. Any change that widens the capture — multi-window, per-display, a region grab — invalidates the refusal's disposition rather than merely affecting it.
- **An Accessibility-tree signal is deliberately not added.** Recorded during planning as later hardening, not as an omission: it would add a second permission that can be revoked mid-session and a second failure mode, for a second view of a question the OCR pass already answers locally and fail-closed.
- **No new product copy**, per the founder's 2026-08-14 rule. Settings › Security & Access still says only "Sonny will never control Terminal, iTerm, or any other terminal app"; nothing in the app explains that the screen is also read.

Open questions (required): none. Everything the design left open was settled on SONNY-104's answers comment and implemented as recorded. What remains is the founder's five manual items on SONNY-139 — above all whether a real VS Code window with a visible terminal panel refuses while the same window showing a `.sh` file proceeds, which no test on this branch can answer because no test drives the real app.

Next branch: `feature/app-control-consent` (SONNY-140/141/142/143), then `feature/app-control-revocation` (SONNY-144). Row J's three branches are sequential by the founder's own analysis — all three touch the same Settings page and the same vision adapter, so a disjointness check does not pass.

### Branch: fix/machine-state-tests
Status: complete
Date: 2026-08-17
Tickets: SONNY-159 and SONNY-160 (the same flake, filed twice), SONNY-161's second half (raising the deadlines; its first half is row D's), and SONNY-123's first finding plus the DRY half of its third. Spawned nothing.
Reviewed by: **no record establishes a review of this branch, and this line says so rather than supplying one.** None of SONNY-159, SONNY-160, SONNY-161 or SONNY-123 carries a review comment for it, PR #63 has no comments and no GitHub reviews, and nothing in this entry narrates a round. The branch merged as `456df6c`. **One trap for anyone re-checking this:** SONNY-123 does carry a full multi-round review record dated 2026-08-19, and it belongs to **PR #72** on the differently-named branch `fix/sonny-123-machine-state-tests` — not to this one, whose SONNY-123 comment is the implementing session's partially-done report with three findings left blocked. Filled in 2026-08-28 by SONNY-275, which found no record to fill it with.

Spec sections covered: none. Test infrastructure, serving SONNY-106 section D's "No test depends on machine state" v1 condition.
Files changed: new: `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/DeterministicPermissions.swift`; modified: `Tests/MacAgentTests/VisionSessionRunTests.swift`, `ConsequenceRuleDispatchTests.swift`, `InteractionModeTests.swift`, `ProductShellTests.swift`, `WorkspaceDetailSheetTests.swift`, `Tests/MacAgentCoreTests/AgentActionExecutorTests.swift`, `VisionTestContext.swift`. **No file under `Sources/` was touched.**
Tests: CLAUDE.md's exact flagged command -> pass, **1226 tests in 92 suites**, exit 0, at `87ed4f5`. Branch-point baseline at `f8ad4f3` was 1225 in 92: +1 test, the permission-seam pin.

**Why this is worth doing, which is not tidiness.** A suite that fails on the machine rather than on the code teaches sessions to discount red. That already happened, more than once, and the cost was not hypothetical: two sessions spent time reasoning about whether a failing suite was caused by their own branch, and **one made changes on that misdiagnosis before reverting them**. A green run that means less than it appears to is bad; a red run that a session has learned to wave through is worse, because it is indistinguishable from the real regression it will eventually be hiding. SONNY-106 section D states the rule for exactly this reason — a suite whose result changes with the machine running it cannot be evidence.

Behavior added:
- The five hand-rolled wait helpers across `MacAgentTests` now use a 30-second deadlock backstop instead of 2, 3 and 4-second deadlines, and say what a failure at that length means.
- One shared deterministic screen-permission checker for `MacAgentCoreTests`, defaulted into `makeExecutor`, so the suite stops answering readiness questions from whatever this Mac has granted.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **No test's assertions changed, and no polling interval changed.** Raising a backstop cannot make a passing test pass "more": a test that completes still completes at the same moment and asserts exactly what it did before. The only behaviour that changes is what happens when a condition never becomes true.
- **The backstop still catches a real hang** — proved, not assumed: making a wait condition permanently false fails at 30.020 s with the new message.
- **The two readiness tests still assert what they asserted.** They pin the voice-hotkey item's copy, which the injected checker does not touch.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required):
- **Reproduced before fixing, because the tickets said it had not been.** Twelve consecutive full-suite runs on `main` at `f8ad4f3`: eleven passes, one failure — 42 issues, 7.656 s against a 5.2–5.5 s norm. That matches SONNY-159's more careful measurement on a quiet machine (17 of 18 at `d1cea05`; 15 of 16 on `feature/terminal-screen-check` at `315419e`) and SONNY-161's from the other side, where two legitimately heavy task-history tests took the rate from zero in four runs to one in three. After the change: **sixteen consecutive passes, seven of them in the 6.0–7.5 s band that previously correlated with failure** — the contention still happens and no longer fires the deadline. A later confirming run passed at 8.572 s, above the time that previously failed.
- **The deadline was never a timing assertion, and naming it correctly is most of the fix.** Nothing in these suites asserts the vision loop is fast; every test asserts what it did. A deadline exists so a genuine hang fails instead of wedging the run. Read that way, 2–4 seconds was absurd — close enough to real running time that it measured the hardware. Thirty is roughly four times the worst per-test wall clock observed anywhere across the three investigations, chosen to sit outside the range of any real completion rather than tuned to a machine. Tuning to a measured-nothing threshold is what SONNY-161 rejected, correctly, and this is deliberately not that.
- **The mechanism is actor starvation, not slow code.** These targets are `@MainActor` and Swift Testing runs suites concurrently, so every `@MainActor` test interleaves on one actor and any test doing sustained synchronous work pushes its neighbours toward their deadlines. The signature is unmistakable once seen: never a wrong answer, always a timeout, on a test that varies between runs, with labels spread across the whole file.
- **The problem was not confined to the file all three tickets named.** SONNY-159, SONNY-160 and SONNY-161 all describe this as a `VisionSessionRunTests` problem. Sweeping `Tests/MacAgentTests/` for the pattern found **five** hand-rolled deadline helpers, and the other four — in `ConsequenceRuleDispatchTests`, `InteractionModeTests`, `WorkspaceDetailSheetTests` and `ProductShellTests` — were at **2 seconds**, tighter than the ones that were already firing. Fixing only the named file would have left the worst four in place. SONNY-159's own title says `MacAgentTests`, not the one file; the title was right and the bodies were narrower than the problem.
- **SONNY-160 is a duplicate of SONNY-159, filed 17 minutes later, by this session.** SONNY-159 was created 21:53:30Z from SONNY-139's PR; SONNY-160 at 22:10:17Z. SONNY-159 is also the better ticket — it has a measured rate, a traced mechanism, and two ruled-out contributors recorded. The duplicate happened because the filing session checked the neighbour it already knew about (SONNY-123) and did not check for a ticket filed by another lane minutes earlier. Recorded because the fix is cheap and general: before filing, search the board for the symptom, not only for the ticket you remember.
- **A mutation caught an overclaim in this branch's own new test.** Its first doc comment said the test would fail if `makeExecutor`'s deterministic default were reverted to a live service. Reverting it and running the test passes — both halves pass their checker explicitly, so the default is never exercised, and no test can distinguish an injected `true` from a machine that genuinely has both grants. The comment now says the protection is *inheritance* rather than detection. The test does catch a service that ignores its injected checker, which was proved by a second mutation.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Three of SONNY-123's four findings were not taken, because two other lanes are editing those files right now.** Its second finding (two tests depending on the process not being root) is in `LocalStorageSecurityTests.swift`, which `feature/task-history-controls` touches; its fourth (a stale guard-order sentence in `VisionSessionContainment.swift`) is production code `feature/terminal-screen-check` touches; and two of the five permission stubs its third finding wants consolidated live in files that branch touches. Recorded on the ticket with the collision map rather than edited.
- **SONNY-123's first finding is closed only on the screen side.** `microphoneStatus()` calls `AVCaptureDevice.authorizationStatus(for: .audio)` directly with no seam to inject, so the suite still makes one live authorization read. Closing it is a production change to `PermissionReadinessService`, which this test-only work was not scoped to make and which SONNY-136 will rewrite anyway.
- **No artificial load was generated to reproduce.** Two other sessions were building and testing on this machine throughout; deliberately loading it would have risked inducing exactly the false-red in *their* terminals that this branch exists to remove. The natural-load measurement was enough — the flake reproduced on the first run of twelve.

Open questions (required): none of this branch's own. Whether SONNY-160 should be closed as a duplicate of SONNY-159 rather than as fixed is the founder's call and is asked on both tickets.

Next branch: unchanged. Rows D, E, J and 12 are unaffected; this removes a source of false signal in front of all of them.
