Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- A workspace with no browser among its apps opens its URLs exactly as before, through the untargeted default-browser call — pinned by `workspaceWithoutABrowserAppStillOpensURLsInTheSystemDefaultBrowser`, which asserts the browser argument is literally `nil`, not merely that the URL opened.
- The three non-workspace browser callers are untouched and still use the system default: `OpenSafeURLCapabilityAdapter` (a plain "open github.com"), `OpenAppSearchURLCapabilityAdapter`, and `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter`'s Hacker News link. They call the `open(_:)` shorthand, which forwards to `open(_:using: nil)`. **Pinned, not merely asserted** — six `#expect(browserOpener.openedBrowsers == [nil])` assertions at the existing call sites for those three adapters, added 2026-08-03 in response to a PR #21 reviewer finding: this bullet originally made the claim in prose while every one of those tests checked only which URL opened, so a regression targeting a browser there would have kept them all green. Each of the six is mutation-proven live (see below). One of them also covers a routine's `openURL` step, which is the same shorthand reached through nested dispatch.
- Apps still open before URLs, `SafeURL.validateWebURL` still gates every URL, `MacAppCatalog` still gates every app, the workspace-open summary string is unchanged, and the capability stays tier 1 — `workspaceCanBeSavedAndOpened` and the whole `AgentActionExecutorTests`/`AgentRunnerTests`/`QuickDispatchTests` set pass unmodified except for the fake-opener signature update.
- A default-browser open that macOS declines still throws `BrowserOpeningError.failedToOpen` — the fallback is a fallback, not a swallow. Pinned by `aFallbackTheDefaultBrowserAlsoDeclinesStillThrows`, where both the named browser and the default refuse.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered:

**The new signature is the protocol *requirement*, and the old one is the extension — deliberately that way round.** `BrowserOpening` now requires `open(_ url: URL, using browser: MacApp?)`, with `open(_ url: URL)` as a protocol-extension shorthand forwarding `nil`. The tempting inverse — keep `open(_:)` as the requirement and add `open(_:using:)` with a default implementation that ignores the browser — compiles for every existing conformance without edits, which is exactly its problem: a conformance that implements only `open(_:)` would silently drop browser targeting and no one would find out until a workspace opened in the wrong browser again. With the requirement on the two-argument form, that same conformance fails to compile. Six test fakes across three files needed updating; that is the feature working, not friction.

**Browser recognition keys on bundle identifier, not display name.** `MacAppCatalog.resolve` already collapses aliases down to one canonical `MacApp` before recognition ever runs — "Google Chrome" and "Chrome" both land on `com.google.Chrome` — so matching the resolved app's bundle identifier means one source of truth instead of two that can disagree. `WorkspaceBrowserCatalog.browserBundleIdentifiers` also lists Arc, Firefox and Edge, which `MacAppCatalog.default` does not carry yet: adding one of those to the allowlist should make it browser-aware in that same edit, with no second place to remember to update. Both halves are pinned (`recognitionCoversBrowsersTheDefaultCatalogDoesNotCarryYet` asserts the default catalog yields exactly Safari and Chrome *and* that the three absent identifiers are recognized), and a browser-shaped display name with an unknown bundle identifier is asserted *not* to be a browser — the set is the whole rule, nothing infers browser-ness from a name.

**The fallback lives inside `WorkspaceBrowserOpener`, not in the adapter.** The contract that makes the seam readable is "a named browser is a preference, not a requirement" — so the opener owns resolve-or-fall-back, and the adapter just says which browser it prefers. Putting it in the adapter would have meant catching an error there and retrying the other call, which reads as error handling and would have made it easy to swallow a genuine open failure along with an unavailable-browser one.

**Pitfall: a default argument on a `public init` cannot name a `private` static.** The live seams started out `private static func launchServicesOpen` and `private static let logger`, referenced from the initializer's default argument values — which fails with *"is private and cannot be referenced from a default argument value"*, because default arguments on public API are inlined at the call site and so must be at least as visible as the API itself. Both are now `public` with a comment saying that visibility is the only reason. Worth knowing before designing any other injectable-seam type with live defaults.

**The relocation took the whole seam, not just the struct.** `BrowserOpening`, `BrowserOpeningError` and `WorkspaceBrowserOpener` were all sitting in `HackerNewsService.swift`; none of them was ever about Hacker News, and moving only the struct would have left the protocol behind in the same wrong file. All three moved to `WorkspaceBrowserOpener.swift`, `HackerNewsService.swift`'s now-unused `import AppKit` came out with them, and the one existing opener test moved from `ProcessSeamTests` into the new `WorkspaceBrowserOpenerTests` with its own doc comment intact — the one explaining that a discarded `false` from `NSWorkspace.open` made every failed open report success, and that the test injects the refusal instead of using a real unregistered scheme. (An earlier draft of this bullet quoted that comment as *"a unit test must not drive Launch Services"*; that phrase is the heading of the `feature/full-repo-correctness-review` pitfall bullet further up this file, not text that appears in the test. Corrected 2026-08-03 after a PR #21 reviewer finding — the rule it names is the reason the test is written that way, but citing a changelog heading as source-code provenance sends the next reader looking for a comment that does not exist.)

**Verified by mutation, not by a green suite.** Seven reverts in total were applied and the suite rerun on each. Three on the feature itself: the adapter calling `open(url)` again (3 executor tests fail, and the no-browser test correctly still passes); the opener rethrowing instead of falling back (4 fallback tests fail); and `firstBrowser(in:)` returning `apps.first` instead of the first browser (4 ordering tests fail, including the executor-level one). Three more on the *unchanged* paths, added with the reviewer-requested assertions, each forcing one adapter to target a browser it should never target — `OpenSafeURLCapabilityAdapter` (3 red: `openAppAndURLExecutionUseInjectedOpeners`, `routineRunUsesNestedDispatchForMixedChains`, `tierOneVoiceCommandAutoRunsWithoutApprovalDecision`), `OpenAppSearchURLCapabilityAdapter` (2 red), and the Hacker News open (1 red) — six reds across six new assertions, so none is dead recording. And one on the fallback log's punctuation: dropping the trailing-period strip turns `aBrowserThatIsNotInstalledFallsBackToTheDefaultBrowserAndLogsWhy` red while the `.failedToOpen` case correctly stays green, since only one of the two descriptions ends in a period. All seven restored, full suite green afterwards.

**Pitfall the reviewer caught, worth generalizing: prose in this file is not evidence, and the two drift apart silently.** Three PR #21 findings were all the same shape — a confident sentence with nothing behind it. The "three non-workspace callers still use the system default" bullet was pure assertion (fixed above). This entry cited *"a unit test must not drive Launch Services"* as a code comment on the moved test when it is the heading of a pitfall bullet further up this very file, sending a reader looking for text that does not exist. And the fallback log line shipped with a doubled period — `"…com.apple.Safari.. Falling back…"` — because `AppOpeningError.appNotInstalled`'s description already ends in one and the template appended another; four `contains`-style assertions all passed straight through it, which is exactly what substring checks are bad at. The log line is now asserted whole, in both the period-carrying and period-free cases.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **A routine with the same ingredients still does not do this** — "open Safari" then "open github.com" as routine steps opens the URL in the system default browser, because an `openURL` step dispatches to `OpenSafeURLCapabilityAdapter` and its `open(url)` call. Filed as **SONNY-24** (backlog, untriaged) rather than absorbed here: a routine is an *ordered list of steps* where a workspace is a set of apps, so it needs a product decision first (does a browser step bind every URL step, or only later ones?), and fixing it would have meant editing two adapters SONNY-9's expected-touched-areas did not name plus changing the dispatch of a plain standalone "open github.com".
- **Only Safari and Chrome are reachable today**, because `MacAppCatalog.default` carries no other browser and `workspaceRunSpec` rejects any app outside the allowlist. Arc/Firefox/Edge users get the default-browser behavior until the catalog gains their app — a catalog question, not a browser-targeting one.
- **Neither the preview nor the activity log mentions the chosen browser.** Kept deliberately: the ticket's contract is that an unavailable browser is not a user-facing error, and the manual test observes the real outcome directly (the URL opens in Safari). The fallback's only trace is the `com.sonny.macagent`/`browser-opening` `Logger` line. If the silence proves confusing in real use, the act log is the cheap place to surface it.
- No per-workspace browser picker UI, and no `StoredWorkspace` schema change — both explicit non-goals of SONNY-9. Reordering a workspace's apps is currently the only way to change which browser it prefers, and there is no UI for that either.

Open questions for the next chat (required, write "none" if true): none

Next branch: none opened by this session. `feature/sonny-8-widget-composer-focus` (SONNY-8) merged 2026-08-03 ahead of this branch, which then rebased onto it. Roadmap row A's last item is `feature/sonny-10-approval-friction-audit` (SONNY-10, the cheap half of approval-friction work), not yet started — after which row A closes and row B (`feature/workspace-restriction-scope`) is next, still needing its planning phase and the founder decision with the co-founder before any implementation.

Mutation-checked: reverting the fix turns the two apps-only tests red while this one correctly stays green.

Each was audited against its owning adapter's execute path and every one leaves the device on every execution, so none belongs in the conditional branch.

Pinned only at the level it is actually tested: `noExplainerLinesOnceTheFirstApprovalHasBeenResolved` pins the pure function's `isFirstApproval: false` input, **not** the real first-to-second-approval transition — nothing anywhere touches `AgentViewModel.hasCompletedFirstApproval` in tests, a pre-existing gap this branch did not close and should not be read as having closed (recorded by PR #23's fresh-session review, finding F7).
- **`hasCompletedFirstApproval` itself is untouched** — still `private(set)`, still read with `object(forKey:) as? Bool`, and still flipped in exactly two places (`performApproval`'s allow branch, `cancelCurrentRun`'s deny branch). "Two flip sites" is not "two sites that touch a pending approval": `performStart` and `clearInMemoryLocalDataState` also clear `approvalRequest` without flipping the flag, correctly, because neither is the user *resolving* anything. A reader who takes the two flip sites as the complete list of places pending-approval state moves will be surprised.
- **`CommandCenterAttentionPanel` is untouched** — it already rendered all five `RiskApprovalCopy.lines` including `riskReason`, so the two surfaces now agree on the first run instead of diverging. `CommandCenterAttentionSurfaceTests` passes unmodified.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The ticket's own framing — "over-eager tier-3 escalations" — needed recalibrating before the audit could be useful, and this is the single most reusable finding here.** Under `RiskApprovalPolicy.default`, `requiresUserApproval` is true for *both* `.lightweightConfirmation` (tier 2) and `.explicitApproval` (tier 3), and both render the same widget panel. **A tier-2 → tier-3 escalation therefore adds no prompt a user would not already have seen.** Every prompt anyone has ever complained about is something crossing the tier-1 → tier-2 line, not the tier-2 → tier-3 line. Anyone hunting approval friction by grepping for tier-3 escalations is looking in the wrong place.

**Where tier 3 does have teeth is unattended runs, and there it is absolute.** `AgentViewModel` executes a scheduled routine with `approvalDecision: .approved(.tier2)` — the only tier an unattended run can carry — and `AgentRunner` requires `approvedTier >= effectiveTier`. So any tier-3 escalation does not prompt; it *skips the run*, and because most escalation conditions are state-based and sticky, it usually skips every future run too. That is the real cost of a spurious tier 3, and it is invisible in the foreground.

**`dataLeavesDevice` is copy, not gating — worth knowing before touching it.** It feeds one line of `RiskApprovalCopy` and nothing else; no tier anywhere reads it. That is what made the `.openWorkspace` fix safe to make inside an audit ticket: the blast radius is a sentence, not a gate. It also means a wrong answer there is purely a truthfulness defect, which is exactly why it still had to be fixed — a permission prompt that misstates what is about to happen trains users to stop reading it.

**The membership-set-versus-lookup distinction is the reusable rule.** An operation belongs in `dataEgressOperations` only if it leaves the device on *every* execution regardless of its parameters. An operation that merely *names* saved content — a workspace, a routine — cannot be answered by the operation alone and needs a lookup branch. `.openWorkspace` had been filed under the first rule while being the second kind, and `.runRoutine` sitting right beside it with the correct treatment is what made the inconsistency findable. Any future operation that references stored content should be checked against this rule before being added to the set.

**Adversarial verification earned its keep by killing more than it confirmed.** Four fix candidates went in, one came out. Two were rejected on a factual ground the original auditor had missed — `WidgetPermissionPanel` renders `WidgetExistingStepRows` above everything else, so the plan-level `actionDescription` a proposed fix wanted to add is strictly coarser than the per-step titles already on screen. The lesson generalizes: "field X is not rendered" is a grep result, not a finding, until you have read what *is* rendered.

**Wireframe-fidelity exception, stated rather than silent (per CLAUDE.md's rule).** `docs/sonny-design-system-reference.md:155` at `1b67b29` (unstamped and reading 145 until SONNY-290 corrected it on 2026-08-26; 145 is a box-shadow line today) specifies the permission panel as one "Allow access to [resource]" line plus two icon-only buttons — no explanatory lines at all. This branch adds a second `isFirstApproval`-gated line. That is a deliberate, bounded exception, not drift: the first-run moment is the one place `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` explicitly asks for "first-time-specific framing on the panel itself," the existing reassurance sentence is already that same class of accepted deviation, and both disappear permanently once the user resolves one approval, so the panel the wireframe governs is **unchanged in steady state by this branch**.

That narrower claim is the accurate one, and the difference matters. The panel is *not* byte-identical to the wireframe in steady state, and this branch is not what makes it so: `WidgetPermissionPanel` also renders an ungated `escalationReasons` line, so any escalated approval — the hundredth as much as the first — still carries a line the wireframe does not specify. That line predates this branch (it shipped with branch 10's escalation-reason work) and is left exactly as found here, but it is a second, pre-existing deviation from the same wireframe row and is recorded as one now rather than staying implicit — flagged by PR #23's fresh-session review, finding F5.

**Presentation logic that needs a test has to leave the view.** This repo has no SwiftUI view-inspection harness, so a copy change made inline in `WidgetPermissionPanel.body` would have been untestable and would have violated the ticket's "every behavior change has a test that fails with the change reverted". Putting it in `AgentActivityPresentation` as a pure function follows the pattern `TaskGreetingFormatter` and `WorkspaceAvatarInitial` already set. The test that pins *which* `RiskApprovalCopy` field is read gives every field a distinct fixture value, so rendering `undoDescription` by mistake fails loudly instead of shipping a plausible-looking wrong sentence.

Known limitations / deferred scope:

- **Recorded and deliberately not changed — `SaveRoutineCapabilityAdapter` inherits the nested plan's execution-time escalations onto the *save*.** `assessRisk` folds `nested.escalations` and `nested.effectiveTier` into the save's assessment, but `execute` only writes the routine file — it never runs a step. Saving a routine whose `writeMarkdown` step names an explicit `~/Desktop/hn.md` that already exists therefore shows "Markdown output already exists at ~/Desktop/hn.md." on the approval panel for an action that will not touch that file. It is left unchanged because it fails the ticket's clear-misfire bar in both directions at once: the sentence is literally true of the filesystem at assessment time, `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` explicitly requires all three nested closures precisely so nested risk is not silently dropped, and removing the fold would delete the only save-time signal that the routine being saved will later assess tier 3. **This is the primary input to module C's structural work** — the question it needs answered is whether save-time risk means "what this action does" or "what this thing will do when it runs", which is a product decision, not a bug fix.

Behavior added:
- Risk assessment is chain-segmented. `assessRisk` walks `assessmentSegments(in:)`, which splits a `.chain` with the same `segmentPlans(in:)` `previewChain`/`executeChain` already use and hands every other plan to its adapter whole exactly as `previewCapability`/`executeCapability` do. A chain of two `.createLocalDraft` steps now assesses both: the second draft's collision with an existing file raises tier 3 and gates on explicit approval instead of overwriting silently at tier 2. Same for two zip segments and for the Hacker-News-preset-plus-web-research chain.
- Escalations aggregate as a union with exact duplicates collapsed, so two steps colliding with the same file state it once on the approval panel rather than twice in one joined sentence.
- `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter.resolveDefaultOutputs` no longer returns after resolving the first `.writeMarkdown` step, so a `.webToMarkdown` step later in the same plan gets a concrete default path in the prepared plan, its preview, and the approval copy.
- **A chain of Shortcut invocations is assessed at the least-trusted Shortcut's tier, not the first one's** (found by PR #25's review, finding F1). `InvokeShortcutCapabilityAdapter.assessRisk` demotes to tier 1 for a Shortcut with a clean observed success and stays tier 2 otherwise, and it picks its step with `.first(where:)` — so a chain whose *first* Shortcut was trusted assessed the whole plan at tier 1, which under `RiskApprovalPolicy.default` is `.autoRun`. Both Shortcuts then ran with no confirmation at all, including one Sonny had never observed succeed. Now tier 2, lightweight confirmation.
- **A chain running two saved routines assesses both routines' nested plans** (also F1). `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` resolves its routine from the first `.runRoutine` step, so `assessNestedPlan` was never called for the second one: that routine's file collisions — and every other dynamic condition inside it — did not exist as far as the approval gate was concerned, while `executeChain` ran it anyway. A second routine whose nested draft collides with an existing file now raises tier 3 and surfaces the collision reason.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **Every non-chain plan assesses byte-identically.** `assessmentSegments` returns `[plan]` unless `workflow(in:)` says `.chain`, so single-step plans, `[scan, zip]`, `[scanDocx, convertDocxToPDF]`, and the Hacker News preset all take the exact path they took before. `existingZipOutputEscalatesToTierThreeAndLogsRiskEvent`, `existingHackerNewsMarkdownOutputEscalatesToTierThree` and `existingWebResearchMarkdownOutputEscalatesAndMarksDataLeavingDevice` pass unmodified.
- **The approval copy is unchanged for every plan that was already assessed correctly.** `approvalCopy` is still built from the whole resolved plan, and its `metadata` argument is still deduplicated by capability id in step order — segments preserve step order, so iterating segments then steps visits the same steps in the same order as the old whole-plan `capabilityAdapters(in:)` call and produces the same list. `appsOnlyWorkspaceChainedWithALocalSaveDoesNotClaimDataLeavesDevice`, `openingAnAppsOnlyWorkspaceDoesNotClaimDataLeavesDevice` and `runRoutineWrappingOpenURLReportsDataLeavingDevice` pass unmodified.
- **A chain of *different* operations still unions every escalation, in step order** — pinned by `chainOfDifferentOperationsStillUnionsEveryEscalation`, which exists so the dedupe cannot degrade into collapsing genuinely distinct collisions.
- **Chains with nothing to escalate stay at tier 2** — `chainedDraftsWithNoExistingOutputsStayAtTierTwo` guards the opposite failure, a segmented walk inventing escalations.
- **`AgentRunner` is untouched**, as is `RiskApproval.swift`, `UnattendedTrustAdvisory.swift`, and all of `Sources/MacAgent/` (the ticket's never-touch list). The advisory's accuracy improves for free: it reads `effectiveTier` from this same call, so a routine whose second step collides is now correctly reported as needing approval.
- **No adapter's own `assessRisk` needed changing.** Every override picks its step with `.first(where:)` on its own operation, which is correct once it is handed a segment; the only adapter edited was `WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter`, and only where it read *across* the two kinds of output it owns.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The correct segmentation for assessment is "mirror the executor's dispatch", not "always call `segmentPlans`".** `segmentPlans(in:)` splits any plan, but `preview`/`execute` only use it for `.chain`; a non-chain multi-step plan (`[scan, zip]`, the HN preset) is deliberately handed to one adapter whole because the adapter reads across those steps. Calling `segmentPlans` unconditionally would have split `[fetchHNHeadlines, writeMarkdown]` into two segments the executor never runs separately, and assessed a default output path that nothing writes. The invariant worth stating: **assessment must see exactly the units execution sees — no more and no fewer.** That is also why `shouldChainWhenRepeated` did not need to change (SONNY-29's stop-and-report trigger): for the workflows it excludes, execution and assessment both stop at the first occurrence, so nothing is written unassessed.

**`WebResearchMarkdownCapabilityAdapter`'s both-kinds branch is deliberately kept although segmentation makes it unreachable from the executor.** `outputURLsForRiskAssessment` now checks the preset output *and* the research output instead of answering `isHackerNewsPreset` first and returning one of them. Once chains are segmented, no caller hands this adapter a plan carrying both kinds (`.webToMarkdown` maps to a different `Workflow`, so any plan holding both is a chain, and `segmentPlans` never absorbs a `.webToMarkdown` step into the preset's segment). It is kept because a future change to how segments are cut would otherwise quietly restore the under-assessment. **Honest limitation: this branch is therefore not pinned by a test** — mutation-checking it (restoring the either/or) leaves the whole suite green, and only reverting it *together with* segmentation turns `webResearchSegmentOfAHackerNewsChainIsAssessedForItsOwnCollision` red. Pinning it directly needs a `CapabilityExecutionContext` built in a test, which nothing in this suite does today. `resolveDefaultOutputs`'s equivalent fix *is* reachable and *is* pinned, because the executor calls it with the whole unsegmented plan.

**"One URL per kind" is the correct granularity inside that adapter, not "one URL per step".** An earlier draft assessed every `.writeMarkdown` and `.webToMarkdown` step. That over-assesses: `segmentPlans` absorbs consecutive `.writeMarkdown` steps into one preset segment, and `hackerNewsSpec` writes only the first, so a second step's output would gate on a file nothing ever writes. Same reasoning applies to `resolveDefaultOutputs` — resolving a second `.writeMarkdown` step would advertise a destination that is never written.

**Segmenting the walk fixes three distinct classes of under-assessment, not one — and only the first was obvious.** The ticket was written around escalations (a second step's file collision). But the aggregation reads two more things off each segment's assessment, and both were being read off the wrong segment: (1) `defaultTier`, which is *not* a constant per capability — `InvokeShortcutCapabilityAdapter` returns tier 1 or tier 2 depending on the named Shortcut's observed history, so a chain's baseline tier depends on which step you look at; (2) whatever an adapter computes by recursing, which for `.runRoutine` is an entire nested plan reached through `assessNestedPlan`. The second is the worst of the three, because nothing about the outer plan hints that a whole sub-plan went unassessed. **The reusable rule: when an adapter's `assessRisk` derives anything from step-specific state — not just escalations, but its baseline tier or a nested assessment — a first-match walk under-assesses every occurrence after the first.** Both were found by PR #25's review, not by the implementing session, precisely because the ticket's framing pointed at escalations.

**A per-segment walk multiplies an adapter's assessment side effects.** `InvokeShortcutCapabilityAdapter.assessRisk` shells out to `shortcuts list` (it carries a comment about doing this once per execute), so a chain invoking three Shortcuts now runs three enumerations at assessment time instead of one. That is the price of assessing each named Shortcut rather than the first one three times, and it matches what `executeChain` already does — but any adapter whose `assessRisk` is expensive or observable should now assume it is called once per segment.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **Two discovery tickets filed, untriaged, neither implemented here** (WORKFLOW.md step 5 — a session never implements a ticket it created for itself). **SONNY-34**: repeated steps of a non-chaining workflow (`.largestFiles`, `.docx`, `.hackerNews`, `.webResearch`) are silently dropped — "zip the largest files in A and in B" creates one archive and reports success. It is under-*execution*, not under-assessment, so SONNY-29's invariant already holds for it and fixing it is the `shouldChainWhenRepeated` reclassification SONNY-29 named as module C's. **SONNY-35**: `CreateLocalDraftCapabilityAdapter` and `LargestFilesZipCapabilityAdapter` resolve only the first matching step's default output path, so a second draft with no explicit destination stays `nil` in the prepared plan and its timestamped default path is re-derived independently at assess and execute time — the same defect class fixed here for the web-research adapter, in two adapters SONNY-29's scoped requirements did not name.
- **Escalations still carry no structured segment/step attribution.** The ticket asked for escalations "attributed to its segment/step so the approval panel can name which step raised what"; that is satisfied through the reason strings, which already embed the concrete path or name ("Draft output already exists at …/b.md."), and both surfaces render exactly those strings. Adding a field to `CapabilityRiskEscalation` was rejected: it is a public `Codable` type, and rendering it needs `Sources/MacAgent/`, which is on this ticket's never-touch list.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: none opened by this session. SONNY-31 and SONNY-24 are the next two tickets in this session's pre-assigned serial sequence, each on its own branch, serial through merge because all three touch the executor/assessment area.

Behavior added: none. This branch ships decisions and ticket contracts, nothing executable.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The substance lives in two documents, not here, deliberately.** `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md`'s new "Workspace restriction scope (roadmap row B)" section is the durable decision record and the thing to read first; `docs/sonny-branch-b-plan.md` is the full rationale behind the seven ticket contracts, including the per-operation resource-classification table. Restating either here would create a third copy that drifts. What follows is only what a reader of this changelog needs in order to know whether to go read them.

**The scope verdict is four-valued, and that is the whole resolution of SONNY-12's recorded interaction flag.** `.inScope` / `.outOfScope` / `.unconstrained` / `.opaque`. A resource kind a workspace never configured is `.unconstrained` — it produces no new prompts and is *never eligible for branch C's relaxation*. So "users who never configured scope get relaxed tier-3 gating implicitly" becomes structurally impossible rather than something a toggle has to prevent, and no separate per-workspace opt-in is needed. Both two-valued readings fail against state that already exists on disk: "empty means deny all" would escalate every file action in every workspace on day one (no workspace has file locations — the field does not exist yet), and "empty means allow all" would blanket-bless every path, which is exactly the hazard the flag named. `CreateWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter` requires *at least one* of apps or URLs (`guard !apps.isEmpty || !urls.isEmpty` throws only when both are empty), so apps-only and URLs-only workspaces are already normal valid states that a two-valued model would break on the kind they never declared.

**Two hard constraints handed to branch C, recorded in the decisions doc and in row C's roadmap cell.** First, relaxation must be a *requirement* override and must never lower `effectiveTier` — the unattended gate (`approvedTier >= effectiveTier` against a fixed `.approved(.tier2)`), the stale-approval re-check, the `risk.assessed`/`risk.escalated` trace, and `UnattendedTrustAdvisory` all read that field, and lowering it would let in-scope tier-3 work run on a schedule with nobody present. Second, the in-scope tier-2 and tier-3 rules must be one function of `(tier, verdict)`, never two chained rules: branch C decided both that in-scope tier 2 auto-runs and that in-scope tier 3 drops to a lightweight confirmation, so implementing the tier-3 rule as a tier change (3 -> 2) would let the tier-2 rule fire next and make in-scope tier-3 actions silently auto-run. That is the single most likely way this feature ships as a security regression.

**The founder's escalate-and-prompt decision needs no new machinery, which is the largest thing this planning phase de-risked.** `AgentRunner.execute` gates once, entirely up front — the requirement is checked before `executor.execute(plan:)` is ever invoked — and `executeChain` runs every segment with no re-gating, which `.claude/rules/macagentcore-conventions.md` forbids adding. So "this isn't part of X workspace — allow anyway?" lands as a pre-execution, whole-plan prompt identical in shape and timing to every existing risk escalation. No pause/resume/checkpoint infrastructure. The prompt copy is a `CapabilityRiskEscalation.reason`, which both approval surfaces already render as a standalone line — a new escalation *source*, not a new mechanism.

**`.opaque` is the honest name for what a pre-execution gate cannot see, and it is load-bearing rather than a fudge.** A Shortcut's internals (Sonny shells to `shortcuts run <name>`) and a search-driven `web_to_markdown`'s real URLs (returned by the search provider mid-execution) are unknowable when the one gate fires. They never escalate on scope grounds and are never eligible for relaxation, and a plan-level roll-up is `.inScope` only if no step is `.opaque` — so a plan containing a Shortcut can never be relaxed by association with resources that did match. Treating an unseeable resource as in-scope would have the feature grant exactly the permissions it cannot verify.

**Resource classification must be per operation *including implicit resources*, never per field.** Three app/URL touches bypass every existing allowlist with no plan field naming them: `MicrosoftWordDocumentConverter` AppleScript-controls Word from a hardcoded path (`DocumentConverter.swift:71-100`), `NativeMediaOpener` opens `music://`/`spotify:` URIs through its own private prefix check bypassing both `MacAppCatalog` and `SafeURL` (`MediaPlaybackService.swift:985-1035`), and `AppleScriptFinderContextReader` controls Finder. `open_app_search_url` is the mirror-image trap: it carries `appName`, but that field holds a search-target name like "GitHub" and its real resource is the host baked into the template. A field-driven classifier would report all four plans as touching nothing.

**`WorkspaceStore.save` fully replaces the record, unlike `RoutineStore.save`.** Re-creating a workspace by natural language would silently delete its scope configuration — and that path escalates to tier 3 *for replacing the workspace*, so the user consents to replacing contents, not to dropping a security boundary. SONNY-36 carries the merge-preserve fix. This is the same class of bug `RoutineStore.save` already solved for `schedule`/`recentRunDates`, and it was found by comparing the two stores rather than by reading either alone.

**One real spec conflict, resolved rather than papered over.** §10.4 lists "Scope validation" among seven validation layers with "If any layer rejects, the action must not execute" — a hard block that contradicts escalate-and-prompt on a literal reading. Resolution: two different layers, both correct. §10.1/§10.4's scope is the *capability's own* declared operating bounds and stays a hard block; workspace scope is a new *user-declared* layer above it that escalates. A workspace scope can never widen a capability's own bounds or `PathWhitelist` — it only narrows, and it narrows by asking. One consequence worth carrying: a workspace file location outside `~/Desktop`/`~/Documents` is inert, because `PathWhitelist` rejects the path before scope is consulted, so it must be validated and reported at save time.

**A configuration surface is what makes this a feature at all.** Spec §6.9 requires "Edit workspace"; it does not exist, and without it `fileLocations` can never be set, every file resource stays `.unconstrained` forever, and one of the three founder-specified dimensions does nothing. The user chose to ship both halves: SONNY-40 (natural-language editing) and SONNY-41 (a detail sheet that makes the boundary visible). SONNY-41 is net-new UI with no wireframe — `13-MainAppWorkspaces.svg` is a card grid only — built in System A, explicitly *not* inheriting the routine-detail view's System-B-inside-System-A glass treatment, because liquid glass was tried for workspace cards and reverted. Recorded as a stated exception per CLAUDE.md's wireframe rule.

**The persistent active-workspace rejection is not being reversed, and the difference is entirely lifecycle.** "Started from its card" does not exist today — `openWorkspaceWidget` synthesizes the literal `"Open my X workspace"`, so the card starts exactly one kind of task and is not even a distinct signal from the free-text path. SONNY-39 adds a real per-task dispatch: set at dispatch, cleared at terminal state, never inherited by the next command, never a global mode. The wireframes' "Active" badge, Open-vs-Switch branching, and Home's "Personal" scope pill stay unbuilt. SONNY-38 and SONNY-39 are the two tickets a reviewer should check hardest against this.

Known limitations / deferred scope:

- **Nothing implemented.** This is a planning branch; all seven contracts are unstarted. SONNY-36 is unblocked now; SONNY-37 onward is gated on SONNY-29.
- **Hard sequencing dependency on SONNY-29**, recorded on SONNY-37 and in row B's roadmap cell. SONNY-29 rewrites `AgentActionExecutor.assessRisk` into a segment-walking shape and is first in the declared serial SONNY-29 -> SONNY-31 -> SONNY-24 sequence over that surface. This is not only a merge-conflict concern: today `assessRisk` hands each deduplicated adapter the entire unsegmented plan once, so a scope check built on that shape would check the first URL in a two-URL plan and silently ignore the second. SONNY-37 carries an acceptance criterion whose whole job is to prove the rebase happened.
- **`save_routine`'s scoped resources are classified as none** — saving a routine touches one file inside Sonny's own store, and the routine's steps are scoped when it actually runs. This answers, for scope, the same "what it does vs. what it will do when run" question SONNY-10 recorded and SONNY-33 reframes; it is deliberately consistent with SONNY-33's decided direction rather than a separate call.
- **`PathWhitelist`'s case-sensitive prefix comparison on a case-insensitive filesystem** is pre-existing and inherited, not introduced here — but scope matching multiplies its exposure, so SONNY-36 owes it a decision and a test rather than silence.
- **Branch C's non-relaxable floor is explicitly branch C's call**, not decided here. The finding that makes it answerable: no capability in v1 has a default tier of 3, so every tier 3 reachable today comes from an escalation, and all six escalation sites say some form of "X already exists and would be replaced." Branch C's tier-3 clause is entirely about escalated tier 3; the spec's real tier-3 capabilities (send, upload, delete, submit, purchase, share) do not exist yet.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**"Exactly one notification" is an emergent property of pausing, not a counter — and writing it as a counter would have been the bug.** `scheduledRunNotice` is published once per attempt and `AppDelegate` mirrors it to a system notification; a disabled schedule produces no further attempts, so there is nothing left to post. A "have I already notified about this routine?" flag would have been a second source of truth for the same fact, able to drift out of sync with the schedule's actual state — and would have had to be persisted, invalidated on re-enable, and reasoned about on every other path that posts a notice.

**All three `RiskApprovalError` cases pause, not only `.approvalRequired` — because it is the smaller change, not because the other two are reachable.** PR #27's review corrected the original justification here, which claimed leaving them out would keep the bug alive "in two of the three branches that reach it". Neither of the other two is reachable today: nothing in the app ever constructs a `RiskApprovalPolicy` with `tier2Mode == .previewOnly` (`AgentViewModel.swift:467-474` already says exactly this), and no adapter anywhere produces `.tier4` — no capability declares `defaultRiskTier: .tier4`, and every `CapabilityRiskEscalation` in `MacAgentCore` targets `.tier3`. That is the claim carrying the weight; the enumeration first written here ("the only `tier4` references outside the enum declaration are two copy switches in `AgentActionExecutor`") was itself wrong, as PR #27's re-check caught. The complete list is five references, all exhaustive-`switch` arms over the tier enum and none of them a producer: `RiskApproval.swift:92` (the policy `requirement(for:)` mapping, the arm that returns `.refuse`), `:234` (`displayName`), `:249` (`defaultApprovalRule`), and `AgentActionExecutor.swift:721` and `:865` (risk-reason copy). So `.previewOnly` and `.refused` are unreachable, and the honest reason for handling all three is that the `catch` is already unified across them: pausing on one would have meant *splitting* the block and writing a second, divergent outcome for two branches nobody can currently reach. Both are equally permanent for a run with nobody present to approve anything, so if either ever does become reachable, pausing is the behavior that was already correct.

**The pause write must happen inside the store, not from a caller-held copy — and the reason is the suspension point, not a retry loop.** `RoutineStore.pauseSchedule` does its own read-modify-write, exactly like `advanceScheduleBaseline` beside it. The rule it obeys is the one `RoutineStore`'s own type comment states: *never read a routine, `await` anything, then write it back* — a read-modify-write spanning a suspension point can interleave with another main-actor task and silently drop the loser's write, and the scheduler's timer is this codebase's first background writer, so two writers genuinely can want the same record. In `performScheduledRun` the only place to take that copy is before `try await runner.execute`, and the write-back lands after it; `resolveOccurrence`'s advance of `schedule.lastRunAt` is one of the writes that would be reverted, and any concurrent user edit during the await is another.

**PR #27's review corrected this entry's original causal claim, and the correction is worth keeping visible** because a future session reading only the changelog would otherwise inherit a false model of the scheduler. The first version of this paragraph said a reverted `lastRunAt` would put the occurrence back in play and resurrect the forever-retry. That is empirically false, and the refutation is stated here as history rather than as something to re-run, because re-running it now gives the opposite result: at `e766422`, before F3 existed, the reviewer implemented the caller-held write-back and the full suite **passed 461/461** — nothing anywhere observed the reverted baseline, because `RoutineScheduler.decision` returns `.notDue` for any disabled schedule (`RoutineScheduler.swift:46-48`) and every re-enable re-anchors the baseline anyway. A paused schedule cannot retry regardless of what its baseline says. **F3's assertion then closed exactly that hole**: at `d1d71e5` the same mutation reddens `aRoutineThatEscalatesToTierThreeIsRefusedByTheApprovalGate`, so a session that tries it today gets a red suite from the fix, not a green one from the bug. Both facts belong together — the original claim was wrong about *why* the write must happen in the store, and the property is now pinned anyway. The store-boundary rule above is the real, and stronger, justification — it is a documented invariant of the type rather than a downstream symptom.

**H1's comparison has to be against the *trimmed* expansion.** `snippetSpec` trims the step's text and `SnippetStore.save` stores the trimmed value, so comparing raw step text against a stored value would report a change for any saved routine whose snippet step happens to end in a newline — re-opening the identical hole for a subset of routines, in a way no obvious test would catch. `updatedAt` is deliberately excluded from the comparison: it moves on every save by design, so including it would mean nothing is ever identical.

**Never-touch list amended by the user, by exactly one item, for a reason worth generalizing.** `UnattendedTrustAdvisory.swift` was on this ticket's never-touch list — correctly, because its *semantics* are branch 10's structural backstop and nothing here should have touched them. What the list did not anticipate is that the file also holds user-facing **copy describing the very behavior this branch changes**. Manual testing found the advisory still promising the pre-pause behavior, which meant the app was contradicting itself at the moment of highest stakes: the user deciding whether to let a routine run unattended. The user amended the list by that one file, for copy only; everything else on it (`AgentRunner.swift`, the tier definitions and `RiskApprovalPolicy` mapping, `RoutineScheduler.swift`'s date math) stands, and the advisory's gating logic here is byte-identical — same tier-3 threshold, same `try?` assessment, same nil results.

**The generalizable lesson: a never-touch entry protects a file's *behavior*, but copy inside that file can still go stale when the behavior it narrates lives elsewhere.** Three doc comments in the same file were stale for the same reason and are corrected here too, since CLAUDE.md sends future sessions to comments before code. One of them was stale because of *this branch's own H1*: the best-effort paragraph cited "a snippet save that would replace an existing trigger" as an escalation example, which after H1 is only true when the text differs. Nothing else in the repo caught that — a reminder to grep for prose describing a condition whenever the condition itself is narrowed.

**Wireframe-fidelity exception, stated rather than silent (per CLAUDE.md's rule).** `11-MainAppRoutines.svg` specifies the row's right-hand slot as a next-run caption and specifies no paused state at all, because the wireframe predates a schedule that can pause itself. The exception is bounded to the smallest possible shape: the caption occupies a slot that is *already empty* in this state (`RoutineScheduleDisplay.nextRunText` returns nil for any disabled schedule), uses the row's existing warning token rather than a new one, and adds no line to a 56pt row with space for neither. The reason sentence lives in the routine detail view — a surface the ticket names, with room for prose. Pinned by asserting `nextRunText == nil` for the paused routine, so a future change that gives a disabled schedule a next-run caption collides with this test rather than silently stacking two captions in one slot.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The general changed-content collision class remains module C input, unchanged.** H1 fixes the deterministic case — a routine re-saving byte-identical snippet text. A routine whose `.createLocalDraft`/`.createZip`/`.writeMarkdown` step carries an explicit non-timestamped `outputPath` still escalates on every run after the first, correctly (the file really does exist and really would be overwritten), and now pauses instead of skipping forever. That is the intended outcome for this branch, not an oversight: whether a routine should be allowed to overwrite its own prior output unattended is the product question module C owns.
- **The system notification still respects the pre-existing surface-visible gate.** `AppDelegate` posts a notification for `scheduledRunNotice` only when no Sonny surface is on screen. "Exactly one notification" therefore means *at most* one; with Command Center open the user gets the in-app notice instead. That gate predates this branch and is deliberately left as found.
- **Deferred to SONNY-46, ratified by the user 2026-08-05 (PR #27, F6): the `pausedReason != nil` ⇒ `!isEnabled` invariant is documentation-enforced, not type-enforced.** `pause(reason:)` is the only writer and it always disables, `setEnabled(true,)` always clears, and the field's own doc comment states the implication — but nothing stops a future caller assigning `pausedReason` directly on an enabled schedule, which would render a "Paused" caption on a routine that is merrily still running (the row checks `isPaused` before `nextRunText`, so it would also suppress the real caption). Making it structural — a private setter, or folding both fields into one enum so the illegal state is unrepresentable — is a public-API change to a `Codable` type with a persisted, encrypted on-disk representation, so it needs its own migration story and a decision between shapes. That is more than this ticket's scope. **Deferred deliberately rather than silently: the user ratified it and SONNY-46 (Backlog, untriaged) is its named landing spot**, per CLAUDE.md's fix-in-branch rule, which requires both. SONNY-46 also records the one-line presentation-layer hardening that would remove the visible symptom independently of whichever model shape is chosen. **Closed 2026-08-06 by `feature/automation-store-hardening`** — the enum fold, not the private setter; see that entry below.
- **H1's motivating user story is not reachable through the UI today, and that is a separate gap (SONNY-48).** The planner declares no tool for either snippet operation (`plannerTools: []` on both adapters), so it cannot author a routine containing a `save_snippet` step, while `SaveRoutineCapabilityAdapter.validateRoutineSteps` permits exactly that shape — the permissive allowlist is what this ticket's contract was reasonably written against. H1's behavior change is still live and user-facing on the *direct* path (`InstantCommandResolver` resolves "snippet save …" without the planner), and the scheduled composition is pinned by tests at the core layer where it is constructible; what cannot currently be reached is that escalation arriving inside a scheduled routine. H2 is manually verified through the general collision class instead — a `create_local_draft` routine with an explicit output path colliding with its own first run, which is fully authorable and exercises the entire pause path.
- **A paused routine is discoverable only from the Routines list.** There is no aggregate "some routines need attention" indicator anywhere else in the app. Adding one would be a new UI surface, which the ticket explicitly rules out.

Open questions (required, write "none" if true): none.

Next branch: SONNY-24, the last ticket of this session's pre-assigned serial sequence (SONNY-29 → SONNY-31 → SONNY-24), on its own branch after this one merges — all three touch the executor/assessment area, so the sequence is serial through merge.

Nothing regressed — each new pin adds a test that the same revert reddens. A count with no SHA beside it cannot be told apart from a stale one, which is the whole reason F1 was raisable.

Files changed:
- `Sources/MacAgentCore/CapabilityAdapter.swift` (`preferredBrowser` on the execution context, `ExecuteNestedPlan` signature)
- `Sources/MacAgentCore/AgentActionExecutor.swift` (threading)
- `Sources/MacAgentCore/RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter.swift` (browser resolution)

Tests: `env CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH="$PWD/.build/clang-module-cache" swift test --disable-sandbox -Xswiftc -F -Xswiftc /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/Frameworks -Xlinker -rpath -Xlinker /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/Frameworks -Xlinker -rpath -Xlinker /Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/Library/Developer/usr/lib` -> exit 0, **471 tests in 45 suites**, up from the 464 in 45 re-measured on `main` at `af93c5c` (post-SONNY-31 merge). `swift build` -> exit 0.

Behavior added:
- **A routine's URL steps open in the routine's own browser.** `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter` resolves the first browser-capable app among the routine's own `.openApp` steps and passes it into the nested execution; every URL that plan opens *on the injected browser-opener seam* goes there. "Open Safari → open github.com" now lands in Safari rather than the system default.
- **Order-independent, first-wins**, per the founder decision of 2026-08-04 — the first browser-capable app anywhere in the routine binds all of its URL steps regardless of order; order-sensitive binding and a per-routine browser setting were both declined so a routine and a workspace stay one mental model. A URL step sequenced *before* the browser step still binds, and with two browsers the first in step order wins.
- **The binding covers every URL the routine opens *on the injected browser-opener seam*** — `.openURL`, `.openAppSearchURL` and the Hacker News open, since all three read the same context field. **Not `.playMedia`**, which opens through `context.mediaOpener` and reaches `NSWorkspace.shared.open` directly (`MediaPlaybackService.swift:1015`), so a media step carrying an explicit `open.spotify.com`-style URL still lands in the system default browser. The unqualified "every URL the routine opens" was this entry's original claim and was too broad (PR #28, F4); the gap is filed as its own ticket.

Behavior preserved (required, no blanket claims):
- **The ordinary open-URL path is untouched, and this is the branch's central guard.** A plain "open github.com", a standalone app-search URL, and the Hacker News open all still go to the system default. Six pre-existing `openedBrowsers == [nil]` assertions (added by SONNY-9's F1 precisely to make this provable) stay `[nil]`, and each was re-proved live by forcing a browser into its own adapter: `OpenSafeURLCapabilityAdapter` → 2 red, `OpenAppSearchURLCapabilityAdapter` → 2 red, the Hacker News open → 1 red.
- **The workspace path is byte-identical.** `OpenWorkspaceCapabilityAdapter` still resolves and passes its own browser explicitly; it never reads `preferredBrowser`. Its tests pass unmodified.
- **A routine naming no browser is unchanged** — resolves `nil`, system default, pinned by `aRoutineWithNoBrowserStepStillUsesTheSystemDefault`.
- **`WorkspaceBrowserOpener`'s fallback semantics are inherited, not forked.** An unresolvable or uninstalled browser still falls back to the default and logs; nothing in this branch touches that contract or `SafeURL` validation.
- **Scheduled and manual runs behave identically**, pinned through `AgentRunner` at `.approved(.tier2)` — the only tier an unattended run can carry.

Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**The browser is a parameter, never executor state — and the reason generalizes to anything else threaded through `execute`.** The tempting shortcut is a `private var routineBrowser` on `AgentActionExecutor`, set around the nested call and restored in a `defer`. It is wrong for the same reason SONNY-31's caller-held schedule write was: `execute` is `async` and suspends at every step, so executor-held state is readable *and mutable* by any other main-actor task that interleaves — a scheduled routine's browser could leak into a command the user typed meanwhile, and the `defer` would restore a value the other task had already moved on from. Threading it costs 24 mechanical switch-arm edits and buys correctness by construction. **`@MainActor` serializes individual synchronous calls, not the span of an `async` function.**

**Reuse of `WorkspaceBrowserCatalog.firstBrowser(in:)` is the point, not an implementation convenience.** Two definitions of "browser-capable" would drift the moment one gains Arc and the other does not, and the user-visible promise of this ticket is that a routine and a workspace behave the same way. The catalog's own doc comment already anticipated this ("adding one to the catalog makes it browser-aware in the same edit").

**Unresolvable app names are skipped during resolution, deliberately.** `compactMap { try? … }` rather than `try`: a routine step naming an app the catalog no longer knows must fail when *that step* runs, with its own error, not be pre-empted by a different failure raised before any step has executed. Fail-fast here would also have been a behavior change beyond this ticket, since routines dispatch per step today.

**One open question from the discovery note is unhandled rather than impossible, and the difference is a store-boundary asymmetry worth knowing.** It asked whether a nested workspace-open inside a routine should keep winning with its own browser. `SaveRoutineCapabilityAdapter.validateRoutineSteps` rejects `.openWorkspace` (and `.runRoutine`) — but that is the *save capability's* boundary, not the store's. `RoutineStore.save` validates `schedule` and nothing else, so a routine carrying either can be written straight to the store and reach the executor; 52 call-site lines across 48 test functions in 11 files already write routines that way (measured by PR #28's reviewer at `e35ebfd`; this entry's original "nineteen" came from a single narrow grep and was simply wrong), and this branch's own skip-branch test needs that door to exist. This entry originally called the question "structurally moot", which was wrong (PR #28, F5). The asymmetry — `RoutineSchedule.validate()` is enforced at the store's single choke point while step safety is enforced only one layer up — is filed as its own ticket. **Correction appended 2026-08-06 by `feature/automation-store-hardening` (PR #30 review, R2), additive — nothing above is rewritten. Two claims in this paragraph no longer hold.** The "52 call-site lines across 48 test functions in 11 files" figure predates that branch and is itself an undercount: it was measured by grep, which cannot type-resolve a receiver named `store` and misses dotted receivers such as `fixture.routineStore.save(`. The compiler-verified population at `bb63d90` is **74 call-site lines across 57 enclosing functions in 12 files**, reproduced independently by PR #30's reviewer. And "this branch's own skip-branch test needs that door to exist" is no longer true as written now that SONNY-52 validates steps at `RoutineStore.save`: that test's routine is three steps of `.openApp`/`.openURL`/`.openApp`, all legal operations, so what it needs is a *direct-store* door, not an *unchecked-steps* one — the save capability refuses it through `previewNestedPlan` on an unresolvable app name, which no store can evaluate. It still calls plain `save`, and correctly. See this file's `feature/automation-store-hardening` entry for the sweep method and the two sites that did need the sanctioned bypass.

**The SONNY-9 review chain's assertion-flip prediction was exact, and it is the model for how to hand a scope guard forward.** That chain added six `[nil]` assertions *before* this ticket existed, having first proved by mutation that nothing pinned the "before" state. This branch's first test run then flipped exactly one of them — the routine site — with the other five green, which is precisely the signal the chain said would distinguish a correct fix from one leaking into the ordinary open-URL path. A ticket that pins the before-state for its own successor is worth copying.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **No per-routine browser setting** — option (c) at triage, declined. The browser is inferred from the routine's own steps, so a routine that opens no browser cannot be made to prefer one without adding an `.openApp` step.
- **`.switchRunningApp` steps do not contribute a browser.** Only `.openApp` steps are scanned. Switching to an already-running Safari is arguably the same intent, but the ticket's wording is "app-open step" and widening it was not contracted; recorded rather than silently decided.
- **A routine's browser does not reach a nested plan that a *capability* runs on its own** — there is no such path today (routines cannot nest), so this is a note for whoever adds one.
- **`.playMedia` URL steps do not bind (SONNY-51).** They open on the media seam rather than the browser seam, so an explicit `open.spotify.com`-style URL in a routine still uses the system default. Filed rather than fixed: it needs the media seam to accept a browser preference, which is a different seam than this ticket contracted for.
- **`RoutineStore.save` validates schedules but not steps (SONNY-52).** A routine the save capability rejects can still be written directly to the store and executed. Filed rather than fixed: tightening it would change what 52 call-site lines across 48 test functions in 11 files are allowed to write, which is more than a browser-binding ticket should decide. **Closed 2026-08-06 by `feature/automation-store-hardening`** — and the "52 / 48 / 11" figure quoted here and at F5 above was itself an undercount, measured by grep; the compiler-verified population is 74 call-site lines in 57 enclosing functions across 12 files, of which exactly two needed the sanctioned bypass. See that entry below for the method.
- **The routine-browser-binding decision is not yet in `docs/sonny-founder-design-decisions.md` (SONNY-53).** The decision is recorded on SONNY-24 and spelled out in `RunRoutineCapabilityAdapter`'s doc comment, but that document is where founder decisions are meant to live, and it currently has no entry for this one.

**The split between the two files is "does this rule exist outside a ticket's lifecycle?", not "is it important?"** Amendments 4, 5 and 6 govern every claim made in this repo — chat, code comments, ticket comments, changelog prose — and `CLAUDE.md` is the always-loaded file, so they went there. The passing sweep strips `*`/`_`/backticks and collapses whitespace before counting. That is amendment 5's rule catching a defect in the verification of amendment 7, on its first run — the under-counted phrase was the reviewer-worktree rule's.

**Dates in this repo are local, and Plane's are UTC.** SONNY-57's own description dates the review cap 2026-08-06 because Plane stamped the triage session at `2026-08-06T02:28:47Z` — 22:28 on 2026-08-05 in the machine's zone. Every date in the changelog and the founder-decisions doc is local, so the UTC date would have read as a future one against everything around it. The amendment is written 2026-08-05, with the deviation from the contract's literal wording recorded on the ticket rather than made silently. Architectural decisions / pitfalls discovered (required, write "none" if true):

**Count call sites with the compiler, not with grep — this branch's headline measurement correction.** The discovery note said nineteen direct `RoutineStore.save` sites; PR #28's re-check said 52 lines across 48 functions in 11 files. Both are wrong, and both were produced by grep, which cannot resolve a receiver named `store` to a type and silently misses dotted receivers (`fixture.routineStore.save(`) and multi-line calls. The reliable method is to make the compiler enumerate: annotate the method `@available(*, deprecated, message: "PROBE")`, build with `--build-tests`, and collect the warning locations. **The real population at `bb63d90` is 74 call-site lines across 57 enclosing functions in 12 files** — 1 in `Sources/`, 73 across 11 test files — and one further entry that is the synthetic `macro expansion #expect` buffer rather than a source line, which is exactly the kind of double-count a naive grep of compiler output would also get wrong. The same technique proves the negative afterwards: compiling a probe file that tries all four routes to the illegal `RoutineSchedule` state returns four errors ("extra argument 'pausedReason'", two "get-only property", "'activation' setter is inaccessible"), and it does so through `@testable`, which widens `internal` but *not* `private(set)`.

**Determine which call sites must migrate empirically, not by prediction.** The store check was added first and the suite run; the failures *are* the population that needed the bypass. Exactly two of 74, both writing `.openWorkspace` routines. Predicting would have been wrong in a load-bearing way: this branch's own contract, the discovery ticket, and the test's own doc comment all assumed SONNY-24's skip-branch test needed the bypass, and **it does not**. That routine is built entirely from legal operations; what the save capability refuses about it is `previewNestedPlan` failing on an unresolvable app name — something no store can evaluate, because it needs a capability execution context. So the store's check is deliberately a *subset* of the capability's, and plain `save` is still the correct door there.

**Keeping the bypass `internal` cost one import and was worth it.** `ProductShellTests` lives in `MacAgentTests`, which imported `MacAgentCore` plainly, so the choice was `public` on the bypass or `@testable` on that one import. `public` would have put a "write a routine the store would refuse" method on the app target's API surface, which is the exact property the ticket exists to remove. A test target reaching in through `@testable` is not the same thing as the app being able to.

**An enum with a payload is the only shape that makes the invariant structural, and hand-writing its `Codable` is part of the cost.** A private setter leaves `Decodable` open; validating in `RoutineStore.save` turns a decoded legacy file into a save failure rather than a repair. The enum closes both — but it changes the persisted shape, so it needs a decoder that reads the old one. Two decisions inside that decoder are worth carrying forward: (1) **the flat `{"state": "…", "reason": "…"}` payload rather than Swift's synthesized `{"pausedBySonny": {"reason": "…"}}`**, because `routines.json` is a file a person occasionally reads while debugging a schedule and because it survives a Swift-side case rename; (2) **the illegal legacy state repairs rather than throws.** Enabled is the fact the scheduler acts on, the reason is the stale half, so the reason is dropped — the same answer `setEnabled(true, now:)` has always given, applied at the last door it can be. A display glitch must never cost a user their routines file. A schedule carrying *neither* shape still throws, exactly as the synthesized decoder did, so the tolerant branch cannot quietly become "default to disabled" for a genuinely damaged file.

**A test that iterates the list it is testing is self-fulfilling, and needs a literal pin beside it.** `savingRejectsEveryForbiddenStepOperationWithTheOperationNamed` loops `StoredRoutine.forbiddenStepOperations`, so deleting an entry from the list would not fail it — it would silently stop testing that entry. Mutation M2 (drop `.openWorkspace`) proves the point: it reddens only `theForbiddenStepListIsExactlyTheSixOperationsRoutinesMayNotContain`, the test that asserts the literal set. Both tests are needed; either alone is a hole.

**The `previewNestedPlan` asymmetry is deliberate and should stay named.** SONNY-24's entry recorded the store/capability split as a defect. Half of it was — the forbidden-operation list, now closed. The other half is structural: the capability can preview a nested plan and the store cannot, so a routine refused for an unresolvable app name will always be writable at the store level. Neither end should read as the complete guarantee, and both now say so in their own doc comments.

Known limitations / deferred scope:
- **The load side is unchanged, per SONNY-52's contract, and it is a recorded non-goal rather than a silent one.** A `routines.json` that already holds a forbidden step still decodes, loads, and executes exactly as before; `loadAll` does not validate, and the legacy-plaintext migration re-writes whatever it decoded. Only the write door is hardened.
- **`setSchedule`, `advanceScheduleBaseline`, `pauseSchedule` and `recordRun` can re-persist such a routine but can never introduce one.** Verified by enumeration, not assumption: across `RoutineStore`'s eleven methods, `steps` is assigned nowhere — the only path by which step content enters is whole-`StoredRoutine` replacement inside `persist(merging:)`, reachable only from `save` and the sanctioned bypass. That is a consequence of the load-side gap above, not a second write door.
- **A `routines.json` written by this build will not load on a build older than this branch.** New encodes write `activation` and neither legacy key, so an older binary's synthesized decoder throws `keyNotFound` on `isEnabled` and the whole file fails to load (surfaced, per the store convention, not silently emptied). Forward migration was contracted; downgrade compatibility was not, and dual-writing both shapes would put two drifting sources of truth on disk. Recorded because it makes rolling *back* past this branch a data-visible event rather than a quiet one.
- **An empty-string legacy `pausedReason` on a disabled schedule still decodes as paused**, with an empty reason, exactly as it rendered before. No writer can produce it; only a hand-edited file can. Left literal rather than special-cased, because mapping it to `disabledByUser` would be an invented behavior change under cover of a migration.
